papers.title: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing: The operational value of continual machine learning
papers.abstract: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

papers.intro:
Maintaining production machines is crucial for ensuring process quality (Ollila and Malmipuro 1999), particularly given that maintenance can account for up to 70 %70\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of total production costs (Madu 2000). In the U.S. alone, machine maintenance is estimated to cost $50 billion annually (Thomas 2018). To reduce these costs, manufacturers increasingly rely on predictive maintenance, where machine learning models predict maintenance needs before failures occur and thereby support proactive maintenance interventions (Thomas 2018, Scaife 2024). Predictive maintenance is now widely used across industries such as transportation (Rokhforoz and Fink 2021), consumer goods (Mazhar et al. 2007), and manufacturing (Menanno and Salsano 2023).

Predictive maintenance models are regularly updated as new data becomes available to adapt to the new production environment. However, in practice, this task is more difficult than it may initially appear. New data are often generated by newly introduced product configurations that arise from changing customer requirements, new materials, or modifications to production processes. These changes alter machine operating conditions and often lead to different patterns of machine wear and maintenance needs (Senoner et al. 2023, Chen et al. 2026). At the same time, previously produced configurations may remain in operation or reappear due to recurring orders, seasonal demand, or production planning decisions; see Figure 1 for a conceptual schematic. Consequently, predictive maintenance models must not only learn from newly introduced configurations but also maintain predictive performance on configurations encountered previously. This setting corresponds to a domain-incremental learning problem, where new product configurations enter the prediction task while previous configurations remain operationally relevant.

Addressing this problem is challenging for two reasons. First, modern manufacturing systems generate massive volumes of sensor data. For example, a single jet engine can produce more than 1 TB of data per day (Jordan and Lin 2018), and similar volumes are common in industrial manufacturing environments. Retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining predictive maintenance models from scratch is therefore often infeasible. Second, naïvely updating a machine learning model with data from newly introduced product configurations can overwrite knowledge acquired from earlier configurations. As a consequence, predictive performance on previously encountered configurations may deteriorate when these configurations reappear in production. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as forgetting or, in machine learning literature, as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989, Zenke et al. 2017).

Second, naïvely updating a machine learning model with data from newly introduced product configurations can overwrite knowledge acquired from earlier configurations. As a consequence, predictive performance on previously encountered configurations may deteriorate when these configurations reappear in production. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as forgetting or, in machine learning literature, as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989, Zenke et al. 2017).

Several machine learning approaches have been proposed for learning from evolving data, yet none directly addresses the requirements of our setting. A common strategy is periodic retraining, where models are re-estimated using both historical and newly collected data (Cui et al. 2018). However, retraining requires access to historical manufacturing data and is therefore often impractical in high-volume manufacturing environments, where such data cannot be stored. Fine-tuning updates a predictive model using only newly observed data, but it is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting because model parameters adapt exclusively to the most recent observations (Zenke et al. 2017) and will thus have a low performance on older configurations. Similarly, online learning methods are designed to adapt models to incoming observations and evolving distributions (Gama et al. 2014, Losing et al. 2018). However, these approaches typically prioritize performance on the current distribution and do not explicitly seek to preserve performance on previously observed domains once they are no longer present in the data stream. Finally, manufacturers may maintain separate models for individual product configurations (Chen et al. 2026). While operationally feasible in some settings, such approaches scale poorly as product portfolios expand and do not allow knowledge sharing across configurations.

Motivated by these challenges, we study the operational value of continual machine learning for predictive maintenance in manufacturing. Continual machine learning provides a general strategy for updating machine learning models sequentially while mitigating catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017, Zenke et al. 2017). We empirically analyze the operational value of continual machine learning using real-world maintenance data from Bosch, a leading manufacturing company, covering 25 product configurations over a period of five years. The data are characterized by a domain-incremental learning problem and represent a realistic high-volume manufacturing environment in which historical sensor data cannot be retained for practical reasons and where new product configurations are introduced sequentially over time while old product configurations reappear. For our empirical analysis, we integrate different model-update strategies into a common decision-analytic framework that combines continual machine learning with robust optimization to explicitly account for both domain-incremental learning and predictive uncertainty. We further compare continual machine learning approaches against a broad set of alternatives, including fine-tuning, online learning, and configuration-specific models. Across an extensive series of numerical experiments, we find that continual machine learning consistently outperforms these baselines in both predictive performance and maintenance cost and can offer considerable cost savings.

papers.title: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.

papers.intro:
ICU records are sparse because measurements are taken at different frequencies and often in response to a patient’s evolving condition. The absence and timing of a measurement can therefore carry information about both physiology and care processes (Tan et al., 2023). This makes ICU time series a relevant test bed for SSL. Unlabeled measurements are abundant, but the measurement process complicates the choice of learning signal.

Prior clinical SSL studies use reconstruction, forecasting, contrastive learning, or combined pretext tasks (Tipirneni and Reddy, 2022; Labach et al., 2023; Yèche et al., 2021; Oufattole et al., 2024). Their differences are hard to attribute when cohorts, representations, encoders, augmentations, and evaluation also vary. A systematic review of structured-EHR foundation models found similar heterogeneity in features, temporal representation, SSL objectives, and adaptation, with compute often underreported (Guo et al., 2026). Frozen probes test whether task information is linearly accessible. Fine-tuning tests whether a pretrained initialization remains useful after label-driven adaptation. Either alone can hide a protocol-dependent ranking.

papers.title: Advancing the Calibration-Compute Frontier of LLM Classifiers via Asymmetric Duos
papers.abstract: The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable predictive performance across a wide range of tasks and domains (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023; Touvron et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Minaee et al., 2024). These capabilities can be further increased for downstream tasks through fine-tuning methods (Hu et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024; Lialin et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). Despite the strong predictive performance of LLMs, these models often remain poorly calibrated and exhibit overconfidence (Guo et al., 2017; Xiong et al., 2024; Leng et al., 2025; Shorinwa et al., 2024), and fine-tuning procedures can further amplify this behavior (Jiang et al., 2021). LLMs being overconfident in their predictions can yield serious problems for critical decision-making domains (Kumar et al., 2023), and being overconfident can also undermine the reliability and restrict the use cases of LLMs in those domains (Li et al., 2025). Therefore, in real-world applications, these neural networks should also be able to indicate when they can be incorrect (Guo et al., 2017). This capability is known as uncertainty quantification or confidence calibration.

papers.title: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
papers.abstract: We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

papers.title: Angular dependence of the low-temperature skyrmion state in Cu$_2$OSeO$_3$
papers.abstract: In the cubic chiral magnet Cu$_2$OSeO$_3$, a low-temperature skyrmion state (LTS) and a metastable tilted conical state emerge for magnetic field along $\langle 100\rangle$, both stabilized by magnetocrystalline anisotropies. We report how these states evolve when the magnetic field is rotated from $\langle 100\rangle$ via $\langle 111\rangle$ to $\langle 110\rangle$. Measurements of the magnetization and the AC susceptibility are combined with broadband microwave spectroscopy on the same cuboid sample at 5\,K. In the microwave spectra, the characteristic gigahertz excitations, notably the counterclockwise gyration mode of the skyrmions, provide a direct indicator of the character of the magnetic states and a qualitative measure of their volume fractions. Both techniques consistently show that signatures of the LTS decrease in strength under rotation and are observed only for field directions within ${\sim}20^{\circ}$ of $\langle 100\rangle$. In this range, the field values at which the skyrmions unwind remain essentially unchanged. In contrast, signatures of the tilted conical state persist up to ${\sim}40^{\circ}$, beyond which the conventional sequence of helical, conical, and field-polarized states is recovered. Thus, the tilted conical state, while being a prerequisite for the nucleation of the LTS under field sweeps, is not sufficient for its formation.

For the stabilization of this high-temperature skyrmion lattice, thermal fluctuations are key [1, 8], and the field orientation only subtly influences the orientation of the skyrmion lattice, owing to weak magnetocrystalline anisotropies [6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].

In Cu2OSeO3, additionally a skyrmion state emerges at low temperatures close to the transition between the conical and the field-polarized state, accompanied by a tilted conical state in which the propagation directions of conical domains tilt away from the field direction [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. This low-temperature skyrmion state (LTS) and the tilted conical state are observed for field along the easy ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle axes, but not along ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle or ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle [21, 22], indicating that magnetocrystalline anisotropies are crucial, possibly assisted by exchange anisotropies [23, 24, 25, 26]. Although the LTS represents the ground state in a finite field range, its nucleation at low temperatures is kinetically limited, resulting in a pronounced dependence on the temperature and field history [14, 27]. The tilted conical state always forms before the LTS and is considered an intermediate state for its nucleation, potentially connected with the presence of domain boundaries [16, 28, 19]. Accordingly, cycling the field within the tilted conical state increases the volume fraction of the LTS [14, 27, 29].

Given the decisive role of the anisotropies, the dependence of the tilted conical state and the LTS on the field direction is an obvious question. So far, however, the magnetic phase diagram has been determined only for the high-symmetry directions, and the LTS has not been studied for oblique fields. In small-angle neutron scattering on Zn-substituted Cu2OSeO3, rotating the field at 5 K from ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle via ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle to ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle revealed increasing deviations of the conical propagation direction from the field direction close to ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle, attributed to the tilted conical state, while the LTS was not addressed [24]. Further, an LTS nucleated for field along ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle was found to persist when the crystal was subsequently rotated by up to 40∘40^{\circ} [14]. The range of field directions in which the tilted conical state and the LTS form, however, has not been determined.

In small-angle neutron scattering on Zn-substituted Cu2OSeO3, rotating the field at 5 K from ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle via ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle to ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle revealed increasing deviations of the conical propagation direction from the field direction close to ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle, attributed to the tilted conical state, while the LTS was not addressed [24]. Further, an LTS nucleated for field along ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle was found to persist when the crystal was subsequently rotated by up to 40∘40^{\circ} [14]. The range of field directions in which the tilted conical state and the LTS form, however, has not been determined.

Here, we address this question at 5 K for field directions from ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle via ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle to ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle, combining magnetometry and broadband microwave spectroscopy on the same sample. The microwave spectra complement the phase boundaries inferred from magnetometry by a direct fingerprint of the magnetic states in terms of their characteristic gigahertz excitations [30, 31, 32]. In particular, the counterclockwise gyration mode of the skyrmions signals the presence of the LTS and provides a qualitative measure of its volume fraction [27, 29]. Both techniques consistently show that signatures of the LTS are confined to field directions within ∼20∘{\sim}20^{\circ} of ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle, whereas the tilted conical state persists up to ∼40∘{\sim}40^{\circ}.

papers.title: Training-Free Anonymization of Driving Data with Promptable Segmentation and 3D Human Mesh Recovery
papers.abstract: Camera recordings for autonomous driving contain faces and license plates that should be anonymized before labeling, sharing, or training. Dedicated detectors can miss small plates and faces behind vehicle glass. We present FM-Anonymize, a training-free anonymization pipeline that combines promptable segmentation, 3D human mesh recovery, and generative replacement. SAM 3 locates people, faces, and vehicles and searches zoomed vehicle crops for plates, occupants, and windows. SAM 3D Body assesses face visibility from head orientation and projects head regions for blurring. Optional diffusion inpainting replaces eligible blurred heads with synthetic faces, guided by estimated pose and keypoints. On PP4AV, the blur pipeline protects 97.8% of faces and 95.5% of plates, the highest privacy recall of all compared methods at their default settings. On our recordings, where the localization thresholds were set, it protects 97.1% of faces and 93.4% of plates, compared with 93.7%/73.0% for UrbanAnonymizer, 42.7%/40.7% for EgoBlur, and 96.6% of faces for deface. Synthetic replacement raises full-body keypoint average precision over blurring from 54.1% to 79.6% on our recordings and from 39.9% to 68.3% on PP4AV. Code and configurations are available on https://github.com/max-a-ai/FM-Anonymize

papers.intro:
Autonomous driving (AD) relies on recorded sensor data that often captures identifiable people: pedestrians and cyclists, drivers behind windshields, and individuals linked to vehicles through license plates. Such recordings raise data-protection concerns under the GDPR [1, 2], while the EU AI Act places data-governance requirements on high-risk AI systems [3]. We therefore target anonymization before recordings enter annotation, sharing, or training workflows, reducing exposure of personal data from the outset. Protecting privacy, however, must be balanced with preserving the information that makes these recordings useful. Blurring faces can obscure head orientation and facial keypoints needed by labelers and perception models [4]. The challenge is thus to suppress identifying information while retaining the visual cues needed to interpret road users and their behavior.

The challenge is thus to suppress identifying information while retaining the visual cues needed to interpret road users and their behavior.

Existing anonymization pipelines differ in how they locate and modify sensitive regions. Public driving datasets use dedicated processing pipelines: nuScenes filters face and plate detections using projected 3D boxes [5], A2D2 uses a segmentation network to blur plates and pedestrian heads [6], and Argoverse 2 blurs faces and plates [7]. Open-source tools such as deface [8], EgoBlur [9], and UrbanAnonymizer [10] rely on dedicated detectors. These approaches can miss small or partly occluded targets, while enlarging the anonymized regions can remove useful scene content [4]. Generative methods instead replace sensitive regions with synthetic content to retain a more natural appearance [11, 12, 13, 14], but still depend on reliable localization. This leaves two connected challenges: finding regions that require protection and modifying them while preserving information useful for perception.

papers.title: Markov-Equivalent Conditional Independence Graphs on Path Spaces
papers.abstract: Causal discovery for continuous-time stochastic processes with latent confounding typically faces a trade-off between (i) approaches that are highly informative about the causal structure but are difficult to test statistically, and (ii) approaches that admit practical tests from data but yield more coarse-grained conclusions, potentially not leveraging the direction of time. We introduce W-separation, an asymmetric graphical criterion for directed mixed graphs defined as a quaternary relation that allows distinct conditioning on past and future components. This added flexibility yields a highly informative graphical independence model while preserving testability. W-separation satisfies a global Markov property for a broad class of stochastic differential equations with latent confounding, linking it to conditional independence relations among coordinate processes that are testable from data. A central result of this work is the full characterization of W-Markov equivalence classes: we show that every equivalence class admits a unique greatest element that serves as a canonical representative and a principled target for learning algorithms. In addition, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which directed or bidirected edges can be added without altering the induced independence model.

papers.title: Breaking feature collapse in self-supervised time series encoders
papers.abstract: General-purpose time series encoders promise a single backbone that generalises across tasks and domains; however, they currently do not scale. We trace this down to a critical point of failure: under the predominant masked data modelling supervision, the encoder's output tokens partially collapse. This is the natural consequence of supervising encoders only in the input space, which leaves no constraint against redundant token dimensions in the feature space. We introduce OTISv2, which suppresses the collapse by complementing the reconstruction objective in input space with two objectives in the feature space: a self-distillation loss against an exponential-moving-average teacher, and a KoLeo regulariser. Under matched training, the resulting encoder reduces the cosine similarity and lifts the effective rank of its output tokens relative to its predecessor, and it scales monotonically from 7.1 M to 116 M parameters where its predecessor declines. It matches or surpasses existing general-purpose time series encoders across 143 uni- and multi-variate datasets. To foster further research, we release our code and pre-trained weights.

papers.intro:
In recent years, general-purpose backbones have transformed natural language processing (NLP) and computer vision (CV). In CV, for instance, the DINO family (Caron et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2024; Siméoni et al., 2026) provides dense features that transfer, without retraining, to classification, segmentation, depth estimation, and retrieval across natural, satellite, and medical imaging. Time series analysis is now undergoing the same transition: general-purpose encoders like UniTS (Gao et al., 2024), MOMENT (Goswami et al., 2024), and OTIS (Turgut et al., 2026) have been proposed as backbones that can serve various tasks across domains as diverse as electrocardiography (ECG), electroencephalography (EEG), audio, and weather. These backbones are pre-trained via masked data modelling: patches of their input are hidden, they learn to reconstruct them, and dense features that transfer are assumed to follow. The most effective family on this frontier is currently OTIS, which matches much larger families using only 7.17.1\,M parameters by explicitly tailoring tokenisation, masking, and the reconstruction objective to time series properties.

Observation. On closer inspection, however, general-purpose time series encoders currently do not scale. At the frontier, OTIS-7.1M comes within 0.60.6 percentage points (pp) of MOMENT-308M in downstream performance across 143143 datasets, despite being 43×43\times smaller; a tiny encoder rivalling a much larger one, the opposite of the scaling trend observed in NLP and CV. A universal backbone should improve noticeably with capacity; current general-purpose time series encoders do not.

papers.title: Laser Processing for Energy Applications
papers.abstract: Laser processing has emerged as a transformative technology in the energy sector, enabling precise, efficient, and scalable solutions for energy generation, storage, and sustainability. This chapter explores the diverse applications of laser technology in energy applications. It begins with an overview of laser-driven inertial confinement fusion for energy production, highlighting key experimental facilities and crucial laser parameters. The role of lasers in solar energy harvesting is examined, including photovoltaic cell optimization, concentrated solar power, and laser-assisted recycling of solar modules. The chapter further reviews recent developments into laser-based techniques for enhancing electrochemical performance through surface texturing at various scales. Advancements in lithium-ion battery technology are also discussed, focusing on next-generation materials, battery manufacturing processes, and the impact of laser techniques on performance, safety, and scalability. The chapter concludes with insights into future prospects for laser applications in sustainable energy solutions.

papers.title: Bias Conditioning and Long-Range Electrostatics for Consistent Machine-Learning Potentials of Electrified Interfaces
papers.abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) of electrified interfaces need the bias as input, but it is unclear whether a scalar electrode charge suffices and whether short-range models capture the non-local response. We add charge and field conditioning to short- and long-range MLIPs. State-of-the-art field-conditioned short-range models overpolarize thick water films nearly twofold and miss work-function shifts at stepped Pt. Our long-range model captures both, needs only the electrode charge at metals as input, and reproduces ab initio simulations of the Pt(111)--water interface.

papers.title: Localization transition in a spin chain with an exact Fock-space tree
papers.abstract: Many-body localization is often pictured as Anderson localization on the graph of many-body configurations. Strongly correlated disorder and a dense net of loops, however, make this graph hard to analyze. We introduce a local disordered spin-1 chain in which a single domain wall explores an exact binary tree of configurations. Random fields create strongly correlated disorder on this tree, as in generic interacting systems, while the absence of loops keeps the problem tractable. We rigorously bound the spreading of the domain wall at strong disorder, and efficient numerics on exponentially large trees indicate a localization transition at finite disorder strength.

papers.title: Predictive Test Optimization Without Historical Failure Data
papers.abstract: As software systems grow in size and complexity, their test suites become increasingly expensive to execute, delaying feedback and wasting resources. State-of-the-art predictive test optimization methods use machine learning to select tests relevant to a change, typically trained on historical failures. This depends on failure histories and is susceptible to label noise from flaky tests. We introduce the novel method of co-evolution labeling for predictive test optimization, deriving test relevance from tests and code changing together in the version history. These data are widely available and less noisy. We train and evaluate models with failure and co-evolution labels on three large projects---from industry and open source; each with thousands of tests and more than 1M LOC. Co-evolution labeling nearly matches the failure detection capabilities of failure-based models, with an overall Average Percentage of Faults Detected of 0.88, while being more resistant to label noise and requiring no test result history. Co-evolution labeling offers a practical, immediately deployable path to faster pipelines and reliable predictive test optimization.

papers.title: Measuring and Optimizing Energy Efficiency in ICT: A Multi-vocal Literature Review on Data Centers, Cloud Computing, and LLM-Driven Code Optimization
papers.abstract: Rapid growth in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) increases electricity use and environmental impact. Addressing this challenge requires a systematic, software-centric view of how energy and related sustainability attributes are measured, reported, and improved. We present a comprehensive Multi-vocal Literature Review (MLR) integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature to map current practice in measuring and optimizing energy use in ICT software, with emphasis on data centers and cloud computing environments (DCCCEs). First, we synthesize how sustainability is measured across ICT by proposing a taxonomy organized along metric domains (power/energy, energy efficiency, environmental impact) and component granularity (from applications, to containers/VMs, and system-of-systems levels). We summarize measurement approaches and the tooling landscape that implements them. Second, we review optimization strategies at the software and system levels, covering dynamic power and resource management, VM/container consolidation, energy-aware software and system design, and cross-layer, system-wide methods relevant to DCCCEs. Third, we examine how large language models (LLMs) are applied to code generation and transformation for resource-efficient software, noting that most studies target code generation (predominantly in Python) and evaluate runtime and memory, with fewer works directly reporting energy. Hardware- and network-level telemetry are treated as data sources for software-level analysis. We identify gaps in vendor-neutral telemetry, consistent measurement and reporting practices, network-level metrics, and unified, cross-layer optimization frameworks, and outline directions for improving reproducibility and comparability. We screened 635 records (2010-2025) and included 181 sources (122 peer-reviewed, 59 gray).

papers.title: Endogenous Preferences as Vulnerability Signals: Discovering Universal Adversarial Triggers for LLM Utility Degradation
papers.abstract: Deployed large language models must remain useful when untrusted text enters their prompt context. Adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods typically define the failures they seek through task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. We ask whether a frozen model's clean behavior can reveal a reusable context vulnerability when its task-level form is unknown, and downstream task feedback is withheld. To study this question, EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design that compares the same frozen victim on clean and span-modified versions of each unlabeled instruction. Without a task-level target, the clean pass supplies the victim's preferred response-onset token as an instruction-conditioned reference; Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how insertion weakens that preference. An auxiliary generator supplies bounded-span proposals; EPD guides its update and ranks the pool without access to downstream information. The highest-scoring victim-specific span is fixed before evaluation and reused unchanged across all held-out inputs. Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater average degradation than every evaluated baseline under the reported protocols. Matched protocol ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection followed by fixed reuse than for null-context fixed reuse or per-input generation. Transfer recurs across proposers with proposal-dependent strength; output-level analyses identify victim-specific associations between trigger families and downstream failure patterns. Thus, clean behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs yet manifest through structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation. The code and data will be released upon acceptance.
papers.intro:
Prompt context becomes an attack surface whenever untrusted text is processed alongside a benign request. The resulting failure need not involve prohibited content: an inserted span may instead disrupt reasoning, answer format, or instruction following and reduce benign utility. If the same span produces such losses across unrelated requests, it exposes a reusable context vulnerability. Can the clean behavior of a frozen victim model reveal such a span when discovery neither specifies the downstream form of failure nor receives feedback from downstream tasks?

Prompt context becomes an attack surface whenever untrusted text is processed alongside a benign request. The resulting failure need not involve prohibited content: an inserted span may instead disrupt reasoning, answer format, or instruction following and reduce benign utility. If the same span produces such losses across unrelated requests, it exposes a reusable context vulnerability. Can the clean behavior of a frozen victim model reveal such a span when discovery neither specifies the downstream form of failure nor receives feedback from downstream tasks?

Adversarial search and robustness evaluation typically begin by specifying either the behavior to induce or the task-level criterion to degrade. Universal-trigger methods use objectives defined by labels, target classes or tokens, or task losses (36), while automated jailbreaks reward harmful compliance, refusal bypass, target matching, or judge success (52; 21; 4; 26; 44; 30). Prompt-robustness work examines predefined changes in wording, spelling, punctuation, formatting, or semantics (51; 3; 32; 49). Availability-oriented attacks target instruction redirection, guardrail activation, resource exhaustion, or system-channel poisoning (11; 47; 8; 17). These methods make specified failures tractable, but leave open whether the model’s clean behavior can guide discovery when no task-level manifestation is specified during search. Withholding downstream feedback prevents the search objective from defining in advance what counts as task-level failure; utility change on held-out tasks therefore measures transfer rather than direct optimization.

papers.title: ScopeBench: Evaluating Cultural Norm Scope Awareness in LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety evaluation in large language models treats harm as culturally invariant, yet a model cannot correctly apply a safety norm without knowing whose norms bind. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark that treats cultural scope as a first-class safety dimension. It comprises 3,323 norms spanning 49 countries across nine cultural clusters, each annotated as Universal or Specific. We define three scope error types identically across four evaluation tasks: Scope Inflation, Scope Deflation, and Scope Displacement. Evaluating 21 frontier LLMs across seven model families, we surface three structural failures. First, the dominant error type inverts with prompt format: Scope Deflation reaches 70% in single-answer classification, while Scope Inflation reaches 33% when each candidate culture is judged independently. Second, scope-classification accuracy is empirically decoupled from behavioral safety: the six classifiers achieving at least 97% Task 1 accuracy still produce harmful responses to 40-42% of scope-violating statements. Third, no model is safe in interaction, with harmful-response rates ranging from 29% to 51% across the cohort, excluding one model that systematically refuses the task. We release all data, code, and model outputs to establish cultural scope as a distinct alignment axis.

papers.intro:
Consider three scenarios that any globally deployed language model must handle: a user in Saudi Arabia asks whether it is appropriate to decline alcohol at a business dinner; a user in Japan asks about bowing protocols when greeting a senior colleague; a user in Indonesia describes a premarital cohabitation arrangement and asks for advice. Each query poses the same underlying question: is the relevant norm one that binds every user universally, or one that applies only within a specific cultural community? Getting this wrong in either direction carries consequences. A model may impose a culture-specific obligation on users outside its scope, or relativize a universal protection that should apply to everyone. Existing safety evaluation frameworks provide no way to measure either failure.

Recent work on LLM safety and cultural evaluation has developed along two largely separate tracks, each of which leaves this question unaddressed. Safety benchmarks measure whether models refuse harmful content (Mazeika et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Han et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2025), but apply a single global harm judgment regardless of the user’s cultural context: they ask whether a behavior is harmful, not whether its harmfulness is universal or culturally contingent. Cultural evaluation benchmarks measure what models know about specific cultures (Chiu et al., 2025; Myung et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024) or whether they adapt their responses to cultural context (Rao et al., 2025; Durmus et al., 2024), but treat the scope of a norm as a given rather than as the object of evaluation (Hershcovich et al., 2022). Neither line asks the question that conditions both: does this model know whom a norm is meant to bind?

The dataset contains 3,323 norms spanning 49 countries across nine cultural clusters, each labeled Universal or Specific through a dual-anchored protocol: culture-specific norms are validated by in-country researchers with native-level familiarity, while universal norms are anchored in international human-rights frameworks (United Nations General Assembly, 1948) and cross-cultural safety datasets (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Forbes et al., 2020). papers.title: Searching for Anisotropic Cosmic Birefringence with SPT-3G
papers.abstract: We search for anisotropic cosmic birefringence using two years of data from the SPT-3G instrument on the South Pole Telescope. Anisotropic cosmic birefringence refers to a theorized dependence of the refractive index of the vacuum on the polarization of light that varies across the Universe in a statistically isotropic manner. Such an effect would manifest as a direction-dependent mixing of the $E$ and $B$ polarization modes of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), caused by rotation of the polarization angle as photons travel from the CMB last scattering surface to us. We present a measurement of the power spectrum of the rotation angle $\alpha$ in six bins across the angular multipole range $20 < L < 2048$, finding no evidence for cosmic birefringence with the spectrum consistent with zero. At 95% confidence, we set a new best upper limit on the amplitude of a scale-invariant birefringence power spectrum of $A_{\rm CB}<0.027$. Additionally, we place upper limits on a scale-dependent white noise model. We translate the scale-invariant upper limit to constraints on the axion coupling constant and primordial magnetic field strength, finding 95% confidence limits of $g_{\alpha\gamma} < 1.7\times 10^{-2}/H_I$ and $B_{\rm 1\,Mpc} < 9.6\,{\rm nG}$ respectively. We expect these limits to improve several-fold with the complete SPT-3G survey.

Modern cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments, such as SPT-3G [61], Simons Observatory [28] and BICEP Array [37], are producing ever-more precise measurements of the polarization anisotropies of the CMB in the quest to better understand conditions in the very early Universe. These polarization measurements also facilitate tests for more exotic physics, such as cosmic birefringence [43], which would rotate the polarization plane of photons as they travel through the cosmos. Such a birefringence signal could indicate the presence of axion-like particles (ALPs) or primordial magnetic fields (PMFs), which we expand upon in §II. Axion-like particles could create an achromatic isotropic [27, 19], anisotropic [49, 15], or time-varying birefringence signal [24], while primordial magnetic fields could create a chromatic, static or nearly static isotropic or anisotropic birefringence signal [44, 34].

papers.title: The Human Side of ML Engineering: Analyzing the Collaboration and Communication Skills in ML Job Postings
papers.abstract: Studies of Machine Learning (ML) practice highlight the importance of combining technical expertise with interpersonal capabilities, particularly collaboration and communication. However, evidence on how ML job postings express these skills is scarce, and prior work largely relies on keyword-based analyses that overlook implicit expression. We analyze demand for these skills in ML job postings across regions, industries, and seniority levels, and compare it with software engineering (SE) roles. We collected 1,000 postings (500 ML, 500 SE) from five continents via a semi-automated pipeline. For annotation, we synthesized a taxonomy of collaboration and communication sub-categories from prior work and used an LLM as a third annotator alongside two humans, enabling detection of context-dependent and implicit skill references. Collaboration appeared in 88.6% of ML postings and communication in 72.2%, far above prior keyword-based estimates for AI roles. Roughly one in five collaboration and one in four communication requirements were expressed only implicitly. Decomposing these requirements into the taxonomy's sub-categories reveals what aggregate figures conceal. Collaboration is demanded predominantly as integration across role boundaries rather than team membership. Communication is mostly required in generic terms, with fewer than half of the postings requiring it naming whom the candidate must communicate with. ML and SE postings demand interpersonal competence at statistically indistinguishable levels but orient it differently, SE toward team practices and ML toward presentation and audience-facing interaction. Within ML, the advertised role separates interpersonal profiles more sharply than any other dimension, including the contrast with SE.

papers.intro:
Digital transformation is reshaping the competencies that define employability across industries (Cascio and Montealegre, 2016; van Laar et al., 2017). In technical domains such as software engineering (SE) and machine learning (ML), a growing body of research shows that professional success depends not on technical proficiency alone but also on the interpersonal capabilities required to operate within complex, interdisciplinary teams. Studies of ML practice in particular identify collaboration and communication as persistent challenges. Building production ML systems requires sustained coordination between data scientists, engineers, and domain experts, and breakdowns at these interfaces are a recurring source of project friction (Nahar et al., 2022; Mailach and Siegmund, 2023; Azamnouri, 2025; Azamnouri et al., 2026a). Translating technical artifacts into organizational value thus depends as much on communication and coordination as on algorithmic skill. While the importance of digital and technical hard skills is widely acknowledged, there is growing consensus that human agency, reasoning, and interpersonal abilities remain irreplaceable by automation (Poláková et al., 2023). Within information technology (IT), the rapid emergence of complex socio-technical systems has amplified the demand for professionals who combine technical competence with sophisticated non-technical abilities (Ternikov, 2022). Whether and how this documented importance is reflected in the requirements employers actually articulate when hiring for ML roles, however, remains largely unexamined.

Building production ML systems requires sustained coordination between data scientists, engineers, and domain experts, and breakdowns at these interfaces are a recurring source of project friction (Nahar et al., 2022; Mailach and Siegmund, 2023; Azamnouri, 2025; Azamnouri et al., 2026a). Translating technical artifacts into organizational value thus depends as much on communication and coordination as on algorithmic skill. While the importance of digital and technical hard skills is widely acknowledged, there is growing consensus that human agency, reasoning, and interpersonal abilities remain irreplaceable by automation (Poláková et al., 2023). Within information technology (IT), the rapid emergence of complex socio-technical systems has amplified the demand for professionals who combine technical competence with sophisticated non-technical abilities (Ternikov, 2022). Whether and how this documented importance is reflected in the requirements employers actually articulate when hiring for ML roles, however, remains largely unexamined.

The term soft skills encompasses the interpersonal, communicative, and self-regulatory abilities that allow individuals to coordinate effectively in a workplace setting (Sayfullina et al., 2018). Whereas technical or domain knowledge concerns what is being done, soft skills concern how work is carried out through behavior and interaction (Tamburri et al., 2020). Major occupational classification systems acknowledge this distinction by labeling such competencies “transversal skills” (ESCO11 1 European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations classification, maintained by the European Commission: https://esco.ec.europa.eu/) or “cross-functional skills” (O*NET22 2 Occupational Information Network, sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor: https://www.onetonline.org/), in recognition of their applicability across heterogeneous tasks involving interaction, coordination, and complex decision-making.

ML, a subset of artificial intelligence (AI) concerned with algorithms that learn from data and improve performance over time, has evolved from an academic niche into a foundational element of global industrial strategy (Poláková et al., 2023). ML systems are no longer confined to specialized technological functions but are deeply embedded in healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and the public sector. As these systems are integrated into mainstream operations, collaboration between ML engineers, data scientists, and non-technical stakeholders has become an essential feature of professional practice. Recent evidence indicates that adaptability, critical thinking, teamwork, and communication appear in nearly twenty percent of AI-related job postings (Vu and Oppenlaender, 2026), reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of ML work. Engineers and data scientists must regularly translate complex analytical findings into actionable insights for decision-makers without a technical background. As ML systems exert greater influence on societal outcomes, empathy, ethical awareness, and collaborative problem-solving have likewise shifted from supplementary attributes to core professional requirements for the responsible development and deployment of these systems.

As ML systems exert greater influence on societal outcomes, empathy, ethical awareness, and collaborative problem-solving have likewise shifted from supplementary attributes to core professional requirements for the responsible development and deployment of these systems.

Despite the apparent significance of these competencies, scientific literature provides little focused evidence on the concrete demands for collaboration and communication skills in ML roles specifically (Piorkowski et al., 2021; Mailach and Siegmund, 2023). Existing job-posting analyses have largely concentrated on generic IT positions or traditional SE roles (Galster et al., 2022; Poláková et al., 2023), and consequently do not account for regional differences or the unique socio-technical demands of the ML lifecycle. A second limitation is methodological. Prior work has relied predominantly on keyword-based extraction, which fails to capture the indirect ways in which recruiters express the need for soft skills. A job posting may not contain the word communication, yet may nonetheless require “the ability to explain solutions to non-technical partners”. Similarly, collaboration may surface only as a request for “a team player in an agile environment”. Detecting such implicit expressions at scale demands more sophisticated extraction techniques. Conversely, exhaustive manual annotation is costly, slow, and prone to inconsistency when applied to large multilingual corpora. To navigate this trade-off, the present study employs large language models (LLMs), specifically the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm (Zheng et al., 2023; Gu et al., 2026) integrated with a human-in-the-loop annotation process, to analyze multilingual job-market data with a level of contextual sensitivity that keyword pipelines cannot achieve. Our findings suggest that this hybrid approach can substantially reduce the human labor required for large-scale text evaluation, though LLMs at present complement rather than replace human judgment.

papers.title: Quantifying the Dominance and Emergence of Brightest Cluster Galaxies in SPT and Planck Clusters: A Novel Application of the Gini Index
papers.abstract: We introduce the Gini index (G) as a metric for studying the emergence of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) by quantifying the disparity in the light distribution of galaxy cluster cores. The Gini index collapses the skewness of the bright-end luminosity function to a single statistic, and provides a measure for the light dominance of the BCG over other cluster members that is more robust than the magnitude gap. We argue that the Gini index is far less sensitive to short-term changes in the cluster dynamical state than the magnitude gap and solves its known degeneracies by taking the entire cluster membership into account, making G a more sensitive metric to long-term BCG assembly. We apply the magnitude gap and Gini index to a progenitor-selected sample of 92 South Pole Telescope- and Planck-selected cluster cores at 0 < z < 1 with corresponding Hubble Space Telescope F110W and F200LP and Sloan Digital Sky Survey g and r photometry. Based on both parametric and empirical tests, we find no statistical evidence for evolution in G or $\rm M_{1,2}$ over 0 < z < 1, and find that BCGs have not grown significantly (2${\times}$) faster than the cluster population for z < 1 at 3${\sigma}$ confidence. This implies that BCGs achieve dominance and establish defining properties early (z > 1) in massive clusters. In general, we find that the Gini index is a valuable and relatively straightforward measurement, with well-controlled systematics, that could be applied to much larger samples to study BCG dominance and emergence.

papers.intro:
Galaxy clusters contain a rich array of co-evolving components, including hundreds to thousands of (mostly) red galaxies, a hot intracluster medium (ICM), diffuse intracluster light (ICL), and a massive dark matter halo. The processes driving the coevolution of these components are complicated, but many are connected to the evolution and growth of the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG). BCGs are a special population of galaxies with nearly uniform properties [128, 84, 35, 133, 81, 40, 117, 120]. They are the most massive galaxies in the Universe (M∗≳1012​M⊙\rm M_{*}\gtrsim 10^{12}~M_{\odot}), with ancient stellar populations of mean ages >10​Gyr\rm>10~Gyr [35, 127]. They are found in the centers of massive (M500>1014​M⊙\rm M_{500}>10^{14}M_{\odot}) galaxy clusters, and often host radio-bright AGN [133, 12]. One defining property of BCGs is their luminosity dominance over the other cluster members, with magnitudes typically ∼\sim1–2 mags brighter than the next brightest member [42, 135], and little intrinsic scatter in luminosity across the population [112, 114, 66, 105]. This is a testament to the extreme hierarchical growth experienced by BCGs throughout their histories.

papers.title: Geometrically Disentangling Concept Learning from the Language Modeling Loss
papers.abstract: Language models acquire a vast array of concepts and abilities from next-token prediction alone. We introduce an interpretability framework that exposes how this single loss relates to the development of different concepts at different points during pretraining. We propose Concept Energy, a measure of the concept-specific alignment between a concept subspace and the average gradient outer product (AGOP) of the next-token-prediction loss. The concept subspace captures where the concept currently lives in the model's representation; AGOP captures the directions to which the loss is most sensitive. Across 19 checkpoints of Pythia-410M and -1B and 12 lexical, syntactic, and semantic concepts, we find that the first peak in Concept Energy generally occurs at or before the steepest increase in probe decodability. Furthermore, whereas probe performance usually increases monotonically throughout training, Concept Energy is not confined to a single peak; some concepts exhibit sustained or repeated engagement across pretraining, suggesting that concept learning may require continual reinforcement or occur at multiple points. Our results indicate that the loss contributes to concept learning in a myriad of ways that simple probe performance alone cannot reveal.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) acquire different concepts and capabilities throughout pretraining, but the aggregated training loss cannot reveal when and how particular behaviors, circuits, and features appear, stabilize, or reorganize over the course of training. A growing body of work examining behavioral learning curves, e.g., evaluating on downstream tasks, has found that LLMs seem to abruptly acquire some abilities. Emergence is often defined as the abrupt appearance of abilities as models scale [47]; grokking is the training-time counterpart, in which test accuracy jumps long after the training set has been memorized [36]. However, behavioral measures can make model development appear more abrupt than measures of internal changes. In several controlled settings, such transitions are preceded by gradual internal reorganization that is invisible to standard evaluation metrics: hidden progress in sparse-parity learning [4], circuit formation before the grokking transition in modular arithmetic [32, 26], and early residual-stream restructuring before in-context learning improves [34, 22]. These results motivate a geometric-precedence hypothesis: concept-specific signals in the loss geometry precede the largest improvements in concept decodability or model behavior. Uncovering these hidden dynamics requires studying full training trajectories rather than isolated final-checkpoint snapshots, a paradigm known as developmental interpretability [41].

Concept-centric analyses start from a concept of interest, define a proxy (e.g., a probe or a downstream evaluation) or representation, and track the changes of the performance of the proxy or the representation directly across training checkpoints [14, 25, 38, 31, 3].

In this work, we bridge the concept-centric and optimization-centric views. We begin with a set of predefined concepts of interest (e.g., part-of-speech tag, named entity type), operationalized as low-rank linear subspaces induced by probes. We then ask, when during pretraining does the loss geometry actively concentrate on a concept subspace? To address this, we examine the loss geometry within concept subspaces. Specifically, we define a metric called Concept Energy to measure how much of next-token loss sensitivity is concentrated on a particular concept at a certain point during pretraining. Concept Energy is based on the projection of the average gradient outer product (AGOP; 37, 10), which identifies the directions in representation space to which the next-token loss is most sensitive, onto the concept subspace. A probe tells us whether a concept can be linearly decoded from the representations; Concept Energy tells us whether the next-token loss gradients actively concentrate along the directions that encode it.

We find evidence for geometric precedence in both Pythia-410M and -1B [8]. The earliest clear Concept Energy event precedes the steepest rise in decodability in 11 and 9 of the 12 probing tasks, respectively. Concept Energy provides a distinct perspective on top of probe performance alone; several concepts whose probe performance rises steadily and consolidates at a plateau nevertheless exhibit Concept Energy curves that rise, form a peak and then go down, and even have multiple distinct peaks across pretraining (see examples in Figure 1). This suggests that the next-token loss can exert pressure on a given concept subspace in a multi-phase pattern. We further investigate the ordering between Concept Energy and behavior by comparing a subject–verb agreement probe with the model’s grammaticality performance on the minimal-pair benchmark BLiMP [46], and the divergence between models’ output distribution and reference n-gram distribution. In both cases, the energy event precedes the behavioral event. Together, these results suggest that geometric precedence is a common pattern across tasks, and that the loss geometry within a concept subspace, concept decodability, and model behavior can follow distinct trajectories.

papers.title: Early Spectroscopy of the Type II SN 2024phv Suggests Short-Lived Circumstellar Interaction
papers.abstract: We present the high-cadence light curve and rapid spectroscopy of the Type II SN 2024phv, discovered just 16.8 hours after the estimated explosion time. The early light curve exhibits a rapid 2 mag rise over the first day of observation, and spectra at 1.7 and 2.6 days reveal weak, narrow emission lines, suggesting moderate interaction with circumstellar material during the first few days after explosion. Models of shock-cooling emission provide a reasonable fit to the light curve after day 2, implying minimal interaction at later epochs, and yield a best-fit progenitor radius of $R=390\pm90\,R_{\odot}$. We also compare our earliest spectra with radiation hydrodynamical models of exploding red supergiants to measure circumstellar densities of ${\sim}10^{-12}$ g cm$^{-3}$ within a few stellar radii of the progenitor, followed by a sharp dropoff in the density profile. This rapidly decreasing profile leads us to conclude that the progenitor of SN 2024phv had an extended atmosphere and/or closely confined circumstellar material, likely from rapidly increasing or eruptive mass loss prior to explosion. In the context of other supernovae discovered at similarly early phases, SN 2024phv points to a diversity in the mass-loss rates of red supergiant stars in their final years.

papers.intro:
Type II supernovae (SNe II) result from the collapsing cores of hydrogen-rich red supergiant (RSG) progenitors, the final evolutionary phase of stars with zero-age main sequence (ZAMS) masses of 8−30​M⊙8-30M_{\odot}. Multiple lines of evidence have revealed various levels of circumstellar material (CSM) around exploding RSGs. In particular, “flash” spectra taken within a few days of explosion show narrow emission lines from the CSM, ionized through interaction with the hot, expanding ejecta [28, 93]. The fact that these are seen in a significant fraction of SNe II [49, 12, 13] implies that significant mass loss during the final ∼\sim1–10 years of the RSG lifespan is common (though see Kochanek 51 and van Loon 91 for interpretations that do not require enhanced mass loss). Hydrodynamical modeling has also required extended, lower-density material outside of the photosphere to match the fast-rising early light curves of SNe II, especially in the bluer bands [61, 62]. Capturing these short-lived phenomena requires a concerted observational campaign (see Sand et al. 71 for a review).

Programs that specialize in early discovery and rapid follow-up of SNe have greatly increased the sample of SNe II with early spectroscopy over the past decade [39, 40, 1, 3, 4, 80, 12, 13, 36, 83, 45, 47, 85, 8, 9, 66, 79, 76, 77, 58, 95, 54, 22, 30, 70]. However, within this sample, there is a wide diversity of strengths of emission features in the early spectra, even controlling for phase, ranging from the sharp Lorentzian profiles in SN 2023ixf [79, e.g.,] to the weak, broad, flat-topped “ledge” feature around 4500–4900 Å of SN 2021yja [40]. The ledge feature is alternatively treated as broad, blueshifted He II [14, 1, e.g.,], a blend of He, C, and N features [80, 12, e.g.,], or a signature of an extended RSG atmosphere [20, i.e., not related to CSM;]. Exploring this diversity is critical to constraining the range of mass-loss rates in the population of RSGs.

In the absence of CSM, the early light curve is powered by shock-cooling emission, the radiation of energy deposited in the ejecta by the initial SN shock. Models of this emission developed and revised by [69], [72], and [60, 59] can be used to constrain properties of the progenitor, especially the pre-SN radius, which in turn are important for understanding possible mass-loss mechanisms. However, in many (or even most) cases where the rising light curve was sampled densely enough to constrain these models, they are not able to reproduce the rapid rise, presumably contributed by circumstellar interaction [39, 40, 41, 1, 21, 83, 66, 44, 47, 77, 30, e.g.,]. Investigating when or if these models apply, and how to interpret the results, is thus an important piece of the mass-loss puzzle.

papers.title: Classification of critical points of heat kernels on flat tori and Riemann theta functions
papers.abstract: For any two-dimensional flat torus $E_\tau:=\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb Z+\mathbb Z\tau)$ and any $t>0$, we prove that the heat kernel $p_{\tau}(z,t)$ has either four or six critical points on $z\in E_{\tau}$ (i.e., including four trivial critical points and at most one pair of nontrivial critical points). This is interestingly consistent with Lin-Wang's remarkable result (Ann. Math. 2010) for the Green function. The key idea is to show that any nontrivial critical point (if it exists) is a nondegenerate global minimum point. Furthermore, we classify the types of all critical points, as well as the splitting phenomena that occur when the number of critical points changes. Applications to Riemann theta functions are also given.

papers.title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated growing capabilities in specialized domains (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2026e), highlighting the importance of effectively transferring these capabilities across models. On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an important paradigm for this purpose, transferring knowledge from teacher models to student models (Agarwal et al., 2024). However, our findings reveal that OPD can transfer not only beneficial capabilities but also latent security risks embedded in teacher models.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated growing capabilities in specialized domains (Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026d; Zhang et al., 2026e), highlighting the importance of effectively transferring these capabilities across models. On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an important paradigm for this purpose, transferring knowledge from teacher models to student models (Agarwal et al., 2024). However, our findings reveal that OPD can transfer not only beneficial capabilities but also latent security risks embedded in teacher models.

A key advantage of OPD is its ability to provide teacher supervision dynamically according to the current behavior of the student model. It samples online trajectories from the student’s current policy and continuously optimizes the student using teacher supervision. However, we find that OPD can also implicitly transfer conditional backdoors from the teacher model to the student model. Without directly injecting backdoor labels into the student model, the corresponding triggered behavior can be inherited solely through distillation supervision from the teacher model. This differs from conventional backdoor attacks, which typically require explicitly associating a specific trigger condition with a predefined behavior during target-model training (Zhao et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2023). We show that OPD can efficiently propagate an existing backdoor in the teacher model through online teacher supervision with only a very small amount of trigger exposure. Such sparse trigger exposure also increases attack stealthiness, making potential triggers difficult to detect in advance through inspection of the training data alone.

During OPD, the teacher supervision is then transferred to the student model through only a small number of triggered inputs. At inference time, simply inserting the trigger into an arbitrary prompt is sufficient to bypass the safety mechanisms of the student model, while the model continues to exhibit safe behavior in the absence of the trigger. This conditional behavior makes the backdoor difficult to detect.

papers.title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
papers.abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning

papers.intro:
Crop yield forecasts are crucial in agricultural science. For example, when drought threatens maize production in East Africa or heat waves reduce wheat yields in South Asia, the speed and accuracy of yield predictions influence whether humanitarian organizations pre-position food aid, governments initiate emergency imports, and commodity markets accurately price risk (Mirón et al., 2023). However, despite decades of research, crop yield forecasts remain subject to substantial uncertainty arising from systems complexity, data limitations and modeling approaches, limiting their usefulness for agricultural decision-making, especially under a changing climate (van der Velde and Nisini, 2019). The crop yield forecasting community lacks a systematic understanding of which modeling paradigms perform most reliably across diverse geographic regions, environmental conditions, crop types, and stages of the growing season (Sweet et al., 2025; Kallenberg et al., 2026). Furthermore, a wide range of modeling approaches exists for crop yield forecasting, including statistical models, process-based crop models, machine learning, deep learning, and foundation models, as well as hybrid approaches (Basso and Liu, 2019; Schauberger et al., 2020; Gavasso-Rita et al., 2023; Han et al., 2025). While several studies report improvements, few works offer results across several crops and countries (Paudel et al., 2021; Paudel et al., 2022; Paudel et al., 2023). Typically, comparisons are restricted to a single country, crop, or modeling paradigm, limiting conclusions about generalizability across diverse agricultural systems (Sweet et al., 2025; Kallenberg et al., 2026; Miranda et al., 2026; Davis et al., 2025).

Moreover, crop yield prediction poses a broader challenge for machine learning, as models must generalize across both spatial and temporal dimensions. Yield variability is largely determined by persistent spatial differences in productivity between administrative regions, whereas year-to-year variability within regions is smaller and primarily influenced by weather anomalies and extreme events (Frieler et al., 2017). Consequently, while a model may demonstrate strong overall predictive performance by replicating long-term spatial yield patterns, it may still fail to capture the inter-annual variability. For example, a model may correctly predict that one region consistently out-yields another because of more favorable soils or management, yet may still fail to predict severe yield losses during a drought year. While such a model achieves high overall accuracy, it provides limited value for early-warning applications that depend on anticipating inter-annual anomalies, demonstrating the importance of sufficient spatial and temporal evaluation schemes.

papers.title: Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control
papers.abstract: Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.

papers.intro:
In predictive control, multiple input sequences may achieve the same objective while exhibiting different behaviours. For example, different initializations of a nonlinear model predictive control solver may yield distinct locally optimal solutions (Huang et al., 2025; Julbe et al., 2025), while human demonstrations may follow different routes around an obstacle. Such variations can give rise to multimodal distributions over control sequences or joint state-input trajectories. Diffusion models provide a way to learn these distributions from data obtained through numerical optimization, simulation, or human demonstrations (Janner et al., 2022; Urain et al., 2024). Once trained, the model generates finite-horizon sequences through a reverse denoising process, allowing different modes of the learned distribution to be sampled. In what follows, we refer to the trained diffusion model together with its reverse denoising procedure as the pretrained diffusion sampler.

In predictive control, multiple input sequences may achieve the same objective while exhibiting different behaviours. For example, different initializations of a nonlinear model predictive control solver may yield distinct locally optimal solutions (Huang et al., 2025; Julbe et al., 2025), while human demonstrations may follow different routes around an obstacle. Such variations can give rise to multimodal distributions over control sequences or joint state-input trajectories. Diffusion models provide a way to learn these distributions from data obtained through numerical optimization, simulation, or human demonstrations (Janner et al., 2022; Urain et al., 2024). Once trained, the model generates finite-horizon sequences through a reverse denoising process, allowing different modes of the learned distribution to be sampled. In what follows, we refer to the trained diffusion model together with its reverse denoising procedure as the pretrained diffusion sampler.

The distribution induced by the pretrained sampler reflects the behaviours and constraints represented in the training data. At deployment, additional safety requirements may arise, for example when a new obstacle occupies a previously traversable region. Sequences that remain likely under the pretrained sampler may then violate the deployment constraints. Retraining the diffusion model whenever these requirements change is costly. We therefore seek to adapt the pretrained sampler to the deployment constraints while keeping the trained model parameters fixed.
