While these energy fluxes are relatively well quantified, establishing a robust quantitative relationship between water vapor phase transitions and atmospheric kinetic energy generation remains a challenge.

Currently, the magnitude of atmospheric mechanical power remains uncertain. Among more recent estimates, Pauluis and Dias (2012) stated that the total power associated with atmospheric motions is not known precisely but is likely on the order of 5​W​m−25~\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}. Pauluis (2015) cited the results of Laliberté et al. (2015) as supporting this magnitude. In contrast, Bohren and Albrecht (2023) reported a broader range of 22–5​W​m−25~\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}, whereas Kleidon (2021) argued, on theoretical grounds, that the rate should not exceed 2​W​m−22~\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}. Finally, observational estimates of Lorenz available potential energy generation yielded only about 1.2​W​m−21.2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} (Romanski and Rossow, 2013). Part of this discrepancy concerns the distinction between kinetic energy generation by atmospheric winds, WKW_{K}, and total atmospheric power, W=WK+WPW=W_{K}+W_{P}, which also includes the gravitational power required to lift precipitating water, WPW_{P}, of approximately 1​W​m−21~\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} (Pauluis and Dias, 2012). Yet a robust observational assessment of both contributions using independent diagnostics remains lacking, thereby preventing a reliable validation of theoretical approaches against observations.

Theoretical predictions of atmospheric power generation are also subject to considerable uncertainty. In moist heat-engine formulations, mechanical work is commonly evaluated using entropy budgets that depend on irreversible processes associated with water vapor diffusion and cloud microphysics (Pauluis and Held, 2002; Singh and O’Neill, 2022). These processes are difficult to constrain independently, complicating the observational validation of theoretical power estimates (Jansen et al., 2026). This highlights the need for transparent, quantitative predictions that can be tested against independent observations.

An important finding of moist atmospheric heat-engine theory is that moisture-related irreversible processes can substantially reduce thermodynamic efficiency below the Carnot limit (Pauluis and Held, 2002; Pauluis, 2011). However, a lower efficiency does not necessarily imply lower mechanical power. The maximum Carnot efficiency corresponds to the reversible limit of an infinitely slow cycle, while the power generated by an actual circulation depends on both its efficiency and the rate of energy transfer. Furthermore, latent and sensible heat fluxes are not independent of atmospheric circulation. They depend on winds and atmospheric temperature and humidity distributions, and could be substantially different in the absence of the water cycle. Thus, understanding the role of water vapor phase transitions in atmospheric power generation requires us to consider not only how moisture affects the efficiency of a given thermodynamic cycle, but also what circulations become possible when the water cycle is present.

Hertz estimated the mean temperature difference between evaporation and condensation to be approximately 15​K15~\mathrm{K}. At a temperature of about 300​K300~\mathrm{K}, this corresponds to a Carnot efficiency of approximately 5%5\%. papers.title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
papers.abstract: Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. Based on the foundation models DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn interpretable concepts related to distinct organoid morphologies. We annotate concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background) and compute their dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks. The spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets. Filtering concepts by spatial label in the DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC for three of the five tasks. Qualitative analysis of the most relevant concepts further reveals a confounding factor introduced by our preprocessing in one task. Through such insights, interpretable concepts could help improve the reliability of classifiers and guide the future development of organoid representation models. The trained SAEs will be made available upon publication.

Deep learning is increasingly used to process brightfield microscopy images of organoids [8, 15, 14, 10, 2, 18]. Deep learning models show superior performance compared to interpretable handcrafted morphometrics, such as shape, intensity, or texture-based features for organoid analysis and in other biomedical fields [8, 3]. However, training datasets in brightfield microscopy can exhibit batch effects or other confounding features.

papers.title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
papers.abstract: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.

papers.intro:
Transitioning to a sustainable energy system built around renewables is essential to international strategies for climate change mitigation [1]. Concentrating solar power (CSP) is a promising complement to photovoltaics for achieving this goal because, unlike photovoltaics, it can store thermal energy at relatively low cost [2, 3]. Solar tower power plants are a particularly scalable form of CSP [4]. A field of several thousand mirrors, known as heliostats, tracks the sun and reflects sunlight onto a receiver located on a central tower. The receiver heats a working medium, and the resulting thermal energy is either converted into carbon-neutral electricity or used in industrial processes [3].

Despite this potential, broad deployment is hindered by high investment and operating costs as well as demanding control requirements [5, 3]. A key difficulty is that small imperfections in heliostats across the field accumulate and significantly affect the plant’s optical performance. Heliostat surface deformations caused by weathering and aging, together with kinematic misalignments arising from manufacturing, installation, and calibration errors, distort the flux density distribution on the receiver [6, 7]. This distortion is not negligible: a 1 mrad1\text{\,}\mathrm{mrad} tracking error offsets the reflected beam by approximately one meter at a one‑kilometer distance, and accumulated optical errors can reduce energy yield by ten to twenty percent [3, 8]. The many heliostats in a field make it impractical to measure each component manually and monitor how their deviations evolve over time. Because these deviations cannot be estimated precisely, solar tower power plants rely on conservative safety margins and human oversight, limiting achievable operating temperatures and the degree of automation. The large number of heliostats and their unknown component-level deviations turn efficient operation into a challenging, high-dimensional control problem, where each heliostat must be assigned an aim point such that the resulting flux density distribution on the receiver is optimal subject to thermal safety limits [9, 10].

Digital twins of CSP plants constitute a powerful tool for meeting these operational requirements and enabling autonomous, cost-effective operation [11, 5]. At the core of such a digital twin is a Monte Carlo ray tracer: representative light rays propagate through a three-dimensional scene, reflect off heliostats, and concentrate on the receiver, where their energy is accumulated to obtain a flux density distribution. Established CSP ray tracers [12, 13, 14, 15] accurately predict the flux density distribution from a given plant model. From a machine-learning perspective, they are limited to forward simulation: they map plant parameters to the resulting flux density distribution. Conversely, inverse rendering seeks to recover underlying plant parameters, such as heliostat surface geometry and kinematics, from measured flux images. Because conventional ray tracers are not differentiable, they do not provide the gradients required for scalable inverse rendering or efficient gradient-based optimization of operational variables such as heliostat aim points. This limits their applicability for plant operation because acquiring the physical parameters required for accurate prediction is too costly and time-consuming at plant scale.

papers.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

Agentic AI assistants are increasingly transforming software engineering, enabling autonomous repository exploration, code modification, testing, and complex development workflows [1, 2]. Unlike conventional question–answer interactions, these systems operate through sequences of model invocations, tool executions, and delegated subtasks. As their adoption grows, understanding the computational resources required to sustain these workflows becomes increasingly important for assessing the environmental footprint of AI-assisted software engineering [3].

As their adoption grows, understanding the computational resources required to sustain these workflows becomes increasingly important for assessing the environmental footprint of AI-assisted software engineering [3].

Measuring the resource demands of agentic AI presents challenges that extend beyond conventional LLM inference. Each model invocation may reuse accumulated conversation history, retrieved code, and tool outputs, causing the processed context to grow throughout a development session. Although prompt caching avoids redundant prefill computation [4, 5], cached context can still contribute to attention computation and memory-access costs during inference [6]. Moreover, agentic workflows may delegate tasks to subagents whose internal model invocations are not fully visible in parent-level execution records. These characteristics complicate the relationship between reported token counts, actual inference operations, and estimated energy consumption.

papers.title: Searching for Autoregressive Neural Architectures from Fundamental Operations
papers.abstract: Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.

papers.intro:
Neural Architecture Search (NAS) aims to automate the process of finding a purpose-built neural architecture for a given task (Elsken et al., 2019), which can be useful to find novel architectures or to substitute expensive human expertise. A NAS algorithm generally has three main parts: the search space containing candidate architectures, the search algorithm navigating through the space to choose a suitable architecture, and a performance estimation function that scores candidate architectures. A search space is considered to be expressive if it entails a broad range of neural architectures. The downside of expressivity is that it increases search complexity, making it more computationally expensive to search. That is why many search spaces restrict expressivity by constraining the space of possible architectures (Liu et al., 2018; Zoph & Le, 2016; Cai et al., 2018). Arguably, such inexpressive search spaces are the reason why NAS did not discover architectural breakthroughs, like Self-Attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), before humans did (Wan et al., 2022). The DARTS search space (Liu et al., 2018) for example, searches among architectures that resemble repeating cells of convolutions. Consequently, running NAS using DARTS can find good convolutional architectures, but could never make the leap to vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020).

papers.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

papers.intro:
Understanding how opinions evolve across multiple issues is an important problem in opinion dynamics. Individuals hold opinions on a range of interconnected issues, and a change in their views on one issue may influence their positions on others. In multidimensional opinion models, the interdependencies are commonly represented by logic matrices, so that the evolution of each individual’s opinion depends on both interpersonal influence on the social network and the logical correlation between issues [15, 9]. The multi-layer structure of opinions can also be extended to study other coupled social processes, for instance the coevolution of opinions and decisions [23, 6], and the interplay between epidemic spreading and opinion evolution [18, 16].

Individuals hold opinions on a range of interconnected issues, and a change in their views on one issue may influence their positions on others. In multidimensional opinion models, the interdependencies are commonly represented by logic matrices, so that the evolution of each individual’s opinion depends on both interpersonal influence on the social network and the logical correlation between issues [15, 9]. The multi-layer structure of opinions can also be extended to study other coupled social processes, for instance the coevolution of opinions and decisions [23, 6], and the interplay between epidemic spreading and opinion evolution [18, 16].

A complementary line of research, which motivates this paper, considers sequential discussions with opinion evolution occurring on two time scales: opinions evolve within each discussion, while model parameters are updated between discussions. In [11], a self-appraisal mechanism is introduced into issue-dependent DeGroot models [7]. Within each issue, agents update their opinions as weighted averages of their neighbours’ opinions, while their self-weights are updated between issues according to their influence on the consensus value reached for the preceding issue. The self-appraisal mechanism has been further studied for the Friedkin–Johnsen (FJ) model [12], which considers agents’ attachment to their initial opinions, i.e., stubbornness. Sequential opinion dynamics can also describe repeated negotiations where path-dependence occurs, i.e., the outcome of one discussion shapes the starting point of the next. This is modeled by the concatenated FJ dynamics [20, 21], where each discussion is described by an FJ model, and the final opinions every preceding model serve as the initial conditions of the next. As a concrete application, the concatenated FJ model framework has been applied to study consensus formation in the United Nations climate change negotiations culminating in the 2015 Paris Agreement [2].

In complex negotiations, voting is a common mechanism to conclude a discussion round, and its outcome can influence participants’ willingness to compromise in subsequent rounds. However, feedback from voting outcomes to opinion dynamics has received relatively limited attention, though introduced in previous work [14]. This paper studies a concatenated FJ model with such voting feedback. Once opinions converge within an FJ event, a vote takes place, with its outcome represented by the median of the final opinions. Each agent’s stubbornness in the next event depends on the distance between its own opinion and the voting outcome. An agent becomes intransigent (i.e., fully stubborn), if this distance exceeds a common acceptance threshold; otherwise, it compromises by becoming partially stubborn. Unlike [14], where agents’ stubbornness changes monotonically across events, our model allows switching in both directions between full and partial stubbornness. This captures the idea that an agent’s willingness to negotiate depends on how closely the collective outcome aligns with its own position.

This captures the idea that an agent’s willingness to negotiate depends on how closely the collective outcome aligns with its own position.

Our theoretical analysis characterizes the asymptotic behavior of this model. The main analytical challenge is that the voting outcome depends on the entire opinion profile, inducing a nonlinear coupling between opinions and stubbornness. Moreover, the presence of fully stubborn agents means that the dynamics need not be contractive. Nevertheless, we establish convergence of the opinion vector over any fixed strongly connected network, for every nonnegative acceptance threshold (Theorem 1). We further show that consensus is guaranteed when the acceptance threshold is at least half the difference between the largest and smallest initial opinions (Theorem 2). Finally, for complete graphs with uniform influence weights, we prove that, under the same threshold condition and a suitable bound on the heterogeneity of agents’ partial stubbornness levels, the set of compromising agents is nondecreasing across discussion events (Theorem 3). Thus, once an agent compromises, it continues to do so in all subsequent events.

papers.title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
papers.abstract: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

Diffusion and flow-based generative models learn a time-dependent vector field that transports samples from a simple base distribution to the data distribution by integrating an ODE (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023). Flow Matching (FM) trains a parametric field by regressing to the conditional velocity of a chosen probability path, enabling simulation-free training. Sampling, however, still requires integrating the ODE over many steps, and reducing this cost remains an active area of research.

Diffusion and flow-based generative models learn a time-dependent vector field that transports samples from a simple base distribution to the data distribution by integrating an ODE (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023). Flow Matching (FM) trains a parametric field by regressing to the conditional velocity of a chosen probability path, enabling simulation-free training. Sampling, however, still requires integrating the ODE over many steps, and reducing this cost remains an active area of research.

One line of work learns a direct map between different points along the generative trajectory, enabling large jumps in time with a single model evaluation, either by distilling a pretrained model or by training from scratch (Salimans and Ho, 2022; Song et al., 2023; Albergo et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025). While distillation requires a pretrained teacher, direct training from scratch can be optimisation-sensitive and therefore requires substantial stabilisation and tuning. An alternative approach keeps the FM objective but changes the coupling between noise and data on which it trains. The regression target depends on how the endpoints are paired, and the choice of couplings can yield straighter trajectories that can be integrated in fewer steps. Several approaches construct such couplings using optimal transport (Pooladian et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024; Mousavi-Hosseini et al., 2026). These couplings require no pretrained model, but the improvement they yield is limited. The most prominent approach, rectified flows (Liu et al., 2023), instead obtains couplings from a pretrained teacher. In this case, each noise sample is integrated through the teacher’s probability-flow ODE to generate a datapoint, and a student is trained with FM on the resulting pairs. Recent improvements have shown that a single rectification step can be enough for state-of-the-art few-step generation (Lee et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025). However, this procedure remains expensive, as it requires pretraining the teacher.

The empirical probability-flow ODE maps entire regions of prior space to the same data point, so it determines which region corresponds to a data point, but not a unique endpoint within that region (Figure 4). Surprisingly, the pretrained and closed-form constructions largely associate the same data points with the same regions of prior space, but select very different endpoints within those regions. We explain this failure theoretically, identify the two quantities that control it, the dataset size NN and the dimension dd, and show empirically that by moving the whole construction into lower-dimensional spaces, the closed-form couplings become better teachers.

papers.title: Mapping the obscured Galactic disk: ERIS J-band low-resolution spectroscopy of 27 Classical Cepheids
papers.abstract: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are standard candles and key tracers of young stellar populations. However, their use in the most obscured regions is hampered by the high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy offers major advantages by greatly reducing absorption corrections and enabling access to regions of the Milky Way that are still poorly sampled. In this work, we determine the atmospheric parameters and abundances of Fe, Mg and Si for a sample of 27 CCs based on observations with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode ($R \sim 4000$). Combining PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and non local thermal equilibrium grids, we simultaneous optimise the atmospheric parameters through spectral fitting. This method is validated with a direct comparison with high-resolution optical investigations and re-analysis of archive optical spectra for the targets in common. The results show good consistency in both metallicity and chemical abundances. We obtain mean abundance ratios of $\mathrm{\langle[Mg/Fe]\rangle=0.01\pm0.12~dex}$ and $\mathrm{\langle[Si/Fe]\rangle=0.10\pm0.09~dex}$, in agreement with reference samples. Moreover, we provide for the first time the Mg and Si abundances of 12 CCs. Finally, we have found distinct kinematic properties for two of the most distant Galactic CCs, located at Galactocentric distances of $\mathrm{\approx 28-29~kpc}$ and with extreme values of vertical height, $\mathrm{\approx +4.8~kpc}$ and $\mathrm{\approx -5.3~kpc}$; more data are required to constrain their nature. Our results confirm that J-band spectroscopy at low-resolution can be used as a good diagnostic for the chemical investigation in highly obscured Galactic regions, otherwise inaccessible at optical wavelengths.

papers.intro:
Classical Cepheids (CCs) are cornerstone distance indicators and powerful tracers of the structure and recent chemical evolution of the Milky Way (MW) and nearby galaxies. These radially pulsating variables are intermediate-mass stars (approximately 4 to 11 M⊙M_{\odot}) in the central helium-burning phase, known as the "blue loop" (see Bhardwaj 2020 and Bono et al. 2024 for recent reviews). CCs provide a unique high-resolution map of the chemical enrichment history of the Galactic thin disk due to their youth (age < 300 Myr), their wide spatial distribution (from ∼\sim 4 up to ∼\sim 30 kpc, da Silva et al. 2023; Nunnari et al. 2026; Trentin et al. 2026), and their well-known distances thanks to the period-luminosity relation (Freedman and Madore 2024) and Gaia parallaxes (Ripepi et al. 2022; Ripepi et al. 2026; Gaia Collaboration 2023).

Although most chemical studies of Cepheids have been conducted in the optical range (see e.g. Genovali et al. 2015; Luck 2018; Kovtyukh et al. 2022; da Silva et al. 2023; Trentin et al. 2024a; Trentin et al. 2026; Nunnari et al. 2026), near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy offers decisive advantages for probing the structure of the Galaxy. The main benefit is the drastic reduction in interstellar extinction at longer wavelengths, allowing for observation of Cepheids in highly obscured regions, such as the inner Galactic disk (Galactocentric radius, RGC\mathrm{R_{GC}} < 5 kpc) or the far side of the Galactic plane (RGC\mathrm{R_{GC}} > 20 kpc), which are hard to reach with optical instruments (Ryde et al. 2007; Matsunaga et al. 2023; Catanzaro et al. 2026). As a result, the radial chemical gradients constrained by the CCs suffer from limited sampling in the innermost and outermost regions of the disk. Furthermore, NIR period-luminosity relations are intrinsically more accurate than optical ones because they are less sensitive to the temperature width of the instability strip and to variations in bolometric corrections (Bono et al. 2024).

However, spectroscopic abundance analysis in NIR bands presents significant technical challenges. Compared to the optical coverage, the number of available atomic lines is considerably limited (Proxauf et al. 2018; Aleyna Şentürk et al. 2026). In particular, in the J-band the overall scarcity of spectral features makes it difficult to simultaneously and accurately constrain the main atmospheric parameters (Bergemann et al. 2012; Gazak et al. 2014; Lardo et al. 2015; Davies et al. 2017), i.e., effective temperature (Teff\mathrm{T_{eff}}), surface gravity (log⁡g\mathrm{\log g}), metallicity ([M/H]\mathrm{[M/H]}) and micro-turbulence (vmic\mathrm{v_{mic}}). However, this spectral domain offers well-isolated iron and α\alpha elements (Mg, Si, Ca, Ti) lines. Many published NIR line lists, including the J-band lines, suffer from uncertainties in oscillator strengths (log​g​f\mathrm{log}\,gf) and lack laboratory validation as extensive as that available for optical transitions (Andreasen et al. 2016; Kondo et al. 2019; Ryde et al. 2019; Elgueta et al. 2024; Aleyna Şentürk et al. 2026). This issue is particularly evident in low-resolution spectra, where the blending of the few available features further complicates the identification of discrete spectral lines (Davies et al. 2010; Gazak et al. 2014). Nevertheless, different studies highlighted the potential of low-resolution J-band spectroscopy (e.g. Bergemann et al. 2012; Bergemann et al. 2013; Bergemann et al. 2015; Gazak et al. 2014; Gazak et al. 2015; Patrick et al. 2015; Patrick et al. 2016; Patrick et al. 2017), especially for estimating the atmospheric parameters in red supergiants.

In recent years, several studies have begun to explore the potential of NIR spectroscopy for Cepheids. The calibration of these methods for Cepheids is made even more complex by their intrinsic variability. During a single pulsation cycle, a Cepheid can experience temperature variations of up to 1000 K and changes in surface gravity of nearly 1.0 dex (Proxauf et al. 2018; da Silva et al. 2022). Inno et al. (2019) provided the first metallicity measurements for obscured Cepheids in the inner disk using medium-resolution spectra (R ∼\sim 3100) obtained with ISAAC@VLT. Minniti et al. (2020) used NIR spectra of 30 CCs from X-SHOOTER@VLT (R ∼\sim 8000) to derive the radial metallicity gradient at the far side of the disk; a work carried out in Minniti et al. (2021) where the authors traced the spiral structure. Matsunaga et al. (2023) extended the analysis to 16 CCs in the inner disk (RGC\mathrm{R_{GC}} = 3–5.6 kpc) using high-resolution spectra (R ∼\sim 28000) in the Y-J bands obtained with WINERED@Magellan-Clay, thereby determining the metallicity gradient in this critical region for the first time. Elgueta et al. (2024) provided an astrophysical calibration of the log⁡g​f\mathrm{\log}\,gf values for spectral lines in Y-J band based on the optical abundances reported by Luck (2018), laying the groundwork for a consistent metallicity scale between optical and infrared spectroscopy. This work has been extended in Elgueta et al. (2026), where the authors provided a robust infrared line list for abundance determination, based on Gaia FGK benchmark stars. Recently, Catanzaro et al. (2026) validated a list of NIR lines for abundance analysis in H-K bands, although their atmospheric parameters were derived in part through photometric approaches or empirical calibrations. They used spectra of 23 CCs from IGRINS@Gemini with R ∼\sim 45000. Finally, Urbaneja et al. (2026) validated Cepheid metallicities against the optical reference scale using low-resolution SpeX/IRTF (Y-J band, R ∼\sim 2000) spectra. The spectra were analysed with a Bayesian full-spectrum method based on MARCS model atmospheres (Gustafsson et al. 2008), TURBOSPECTRUM spectral synthesis (Alvarez and Plez 1998; Plez 2012), and the MAUI framework (Urbaneja 2026).

papers.title: DRaGAN: Dynamic Graph Attention Network for Multi-Radar Point Cloud Encoding in Automotive Radar Perception
papers.abstract: Radar represents a key modality for weather-robust perception. Unlike optical sensors such as camera and LiDAR, radar can penetrate fog, rain and snow due to its longer wavelength, and recent hardware advances have steadily improved its spatial resolution, thus making it increasingly relevant for autonomous systems. While processing raw radar data requires substantial memory computation, most existing work has focused on preprocessed point-cloud data similar to LiDAR. However, the sparse radar points and sensor-relative anisotropy make LiDAR-oriented encoders suboptimal. To address this problem, we present DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network for multi-radar point clouds. DRaGAN introduces a sensor-relative Fourier encoding of angle and range to capture fixed-aperture radar characteristics, gated short- and long-range hub nodes along each sensor's line of sight for efficient local-global message passing, and attention-guided dynamic rewiring that prunes weak edges and adds a bounded number of latent connections restricted to two-hop neighborhoods. This reduces the number of processed edges in deeper layers while preserving representation quality. On TruckScenes, DRaGAN improves test NDS by 10.10 points over the evaluated RadarGNN baseline and reduces the reported model FLOP count by 63.7%. This trade-off includes an increase in model latency from 40 to 53.16 ms and in trainable parameters from 1.2M to 1.7M on the evaluated implementations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/chr-is-tof/DRaGAN.

papers.intro:
Radar provides a complementary sensing modality for autonomous vehicles and robots, particularly in adverse weather. Due to its longer operating wavelength, radar is generally less affected by atmospheric scattering than camera or LiDAR, whose visibility, range, and measurement quality heavily degrade in fog, rain, and snow [1]. Radar sensors are low-cost and can be mounted behind RF-transparent body panels, offering protection from direct contamination. Radar point clouds are considerably sparser than LiDAR, thereby reducing downstream data volume and enabling faster processing with lightweight models. Although radar lacks high-resolution geometric detail, it directly measures radial (line-of-sight) Doppler velocity, a strong cue for identifying and characterizing dynamic objects [2].

Due to its longer operating wavelength, radar is generally less affected by atmospheric scattering than camera or LiDAR, whose visibility, range, and measurement quality heavily degrade in fog, rain, and snow [1]. Radar point clouds are considerably sparser than LiDAR, thereby reducing downstream data volume and enabling faster processing with lightweight models. Although radar lacks high-resolution geometric detail, it directly measures radial (line-of-sight) Doppler velocity, a strong cue for identifying and characterizing dynamic objects [2].

Recent approaches have demonstrated the capability of radar-only perception by relying on raw FFT processed recordings [3, 4, 5], but large data and model sizes limit real-time system integration [2]. Thus, a sparser data representation in the form of point-clouds is preferred. Notably, point-cloud processing techniques adapted from the LiDAR domain [6] introduce significant discretization errors and computational overhead when applied to sparse points distributed over a large area. Therefore, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown strong potential for modeling non-Euclidean radar data with high accuracy [7]. Several methods have constructed graphs directly on radar points and applied GNN-based feature extraction for downstream tasks like object detection and segmentation [8, 9, 10]. However, existing work tends to treat radar points similar to LiDAR recordings and does not consider unique recording properties of fixed-aperture radar from multiple sensors. Additionally, computationally expensive graph edge connections are currently generated statically and persist between irrelevant node pairs, which increases arithmetic load in deeper network layers. We address this research gap.

Specifically, we introduce DRaGAN, a dynamic graph attention network tailored to point clouds acquired by multiple fixed-aperture radars distributed around a vehicle. DRaGAN targets to reduce the arithmetic work of graph message passing while preserving local and cross-sensor information exchange. Unlike rotating LiDAR, fixed-aperture radar measurements exhibit viewing-angle-dependent variations in return intensity, noise, localization uncertainty, and Doppler characteristics relative to the sensor boresight [11]. To represent these spatially varying measurement properties, we employ a sensor-relative Fourier encoding of each point’s range and off-boresight angle, complemented by learned sensor-specific embeddings. Local message passing is performed on a graph constructed from spatial and Doppler proximity. Furthermore, attention-guided graph refinement reduces the number of node-node edges processed in deeper layers by pruning weak connections and introducing a bounded number of latent-space connections. We evaluate both operation count and realized latency because reduced arithmetic complexity does not necessarily imply faster execution for irregular sparse workloads. To enhance global context aggregation, we introduce sensor-specific short-range and long-range hub nodes that facilitate region-aware information exchange across the graph. We evaluate DRaGAN on the large-scale TruckScenes dataset [12], which contains dense radar measurements from six vehicle-mounted sensors with sensing ranges of up to 200 m. The main contributions of this work are: • A sensor-relative Fourier encoding that represents the range- and viewing-angle-dependent characteristics of distributed fixed-aperture radars. • Gated short- and long-range sensor hubs that enable controlled local-to-global and cross-sensor information exchange. • An attention-guided rewiring strategy with bounded two-hop candidate generation that reduces node-node edge processing in deeper layers. • A joint evaluation of detection performance, operation count, graph size, and realized GPU latency, exposing the trade-off between arithmetic complexity and sparse-operator efficiency.

papers.title: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence
papers.abstract: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020; Cohen et al., 2023). Nevertheless, they frequently generate plausible but factually incorrect statements (Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). One contributing factor is that common training and evaluation protocols reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, encouraging models to answer even when their knowledge is insufficient (Kalai et al., 2025). Such guesses are often highly specific: models may provide an unsupported day or city even when their predictions reliably support only a year or country (Yona et al., 2024b; Boggust et al., 2025).

Large language models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters (Petroni et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2020; Cohen et al., 2023). Nevertheless, they frequently generate plausible but factually incorrect statements (Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). One contributing factor is that common training and evaluation protocols reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, encouraging models to answer even when their knowledge is insufficient (Kalai et al., 2025). Such guesses are often highly specific: models may provide an unsupported day or city even when their predictions reliably support only a year or country (Yona et al., 2024b; Boggust et al., 2025).

Abstention provides one response to this problem (Brahman et al., 2024) but discards any partial knowledge the model possesses. Another is to communicate uncertainty through linguistic markers such as probably or I think (Yona et al., 2024a), though these leave the factual claim itself unchanged. A complementary strategy is to adapt answer granularity. Human speakers choose levels of abstraction according to available information and conversational demands (Hobbs, 1985; Mulkar-Mehta et al., 2011a). When the exact answer is uncertain, a coarser answer can remain both correct and informative. Figure 1 illustrates this idea: Sampled birth dates disagree on finer details but converge on 1879. Selecting one response would overcommit to an uncertain date, while abstaining would discard the shared information. Answering with the common year preserves useful information without asserting unsupported detail.

Whether models can internalize this behavior and directly produce answers at an appropriate granularity remains less explored. Motivated by evidence that fine-tuning is better suited to using existing knowledge than acquiring new facts (Gekhman et al., 2024), we construct model-specific fine-tuning targets using agreement across sampled responses and recognition of supplied answers at different granularity levels. These signals identify the finest supported answer, with abstention targets when sampled responses lack sufficient agreement. Fine-tuning teaches the model to produce these answers directly.

papers.title: All-sky spectroscopic survey of bright {\delta} Scuti stars from TESS Projected rotational velocities and pulsation characteristics
papers.abstract:
Context. The second most numerous class of pulsating stars -- $\delta$ Scuti ($\delta$ Sct) -- lack a homogeneous, large-scale spectroscopic sample in the Kepler and TESS era, limiting our understanding of how rotation shapes stellar pulsations. Aims. We analyse projected rotational velocities ($v \sin i$) from high-resolution spectroscopy alongside 2-minute TESS photometry to establish empirical links between stellar rotation and pulsation parameters. Methods. Combining observations from three high-resolution 'echelle spectrographs with two spectral libraries, we assemble an all-sky sample of 262 $\delta$ Sct stars ($R = 25\,000$ to $115\,000$). We derive $v \sin i$ via three independent methods and extract pulsation frequencies and amplitudes from TESS light curves. Results. The $v \sin i$ distribution is unimodal, with a mean of $120.3	ext{ km s}^{-1}$ and peak probability at $113.8	ext{ km s}^{-1}$. Minimum ($
u_{m min}$), dominant ($
u_{m dom}$), amplitude-weighted ($
u_{m AW}$), and power-weighted ($
u_{m PW}$) frequencies decrease with $v \sin i / v_{m crit}$, whereas maximum frequency ($
u_{m max}$) does not. Fast rotators show a narrower range of photometric and pulsation amplitudes than slow rotators, and their lower mean stellar density ($ ar{ho}$) cannot fully explain the frequency decrease. Calibrating Gaia's $v_{m broad}$ against our measurements removes its systematic offset, enabling use across larger $\delta$ Sct samples. Multi-spectrum comparisons reveal method discrepancies mainly for fast rotators ($v \sin i > 200	ext{ km s}^{-1}$) and inter-spectrograph offsets up to $20	ext{ km s}^{-1}$. Conclusions. We present the largest homogeneous high-resolution $v \sin i$ sample for bright $\delta$ Sct stars in the TESS era, showing that $v \sin i$ measurements in pulsating stars require careful treatment across instruments and velocity regimes.

papers.intro:
The pulsating stars of δ\delta Scuti (δ\delta Sct) are situated where the classical cepheid instability strip crosses the main sequence; their cores are therefore in the stage of burning hydrogen. This population of pulsating stars of early A- to late F-type has masses in a range of 1.5 ℳ⊙1.5\text{\,}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} to 2.3 ℳ⊙2.3\text{\,}\mathcal{M}_{\odot} (Murphy and Gautam, 2026), temperatures in a range of 6000 K6000\text{\,}\mathrm{K} to 9000 K9000\text{\,}\mathrm{K} (Uytterhoeven et al., 2011; Kurtz, 2022), luminosities of 2 to 50 ℒ⊙50\text{\,}\mathcal{L}_{\odot}, and frequencies between 4 d4\text{\,}\mathrm{d} (Breger, 2000; Aerts et al., 2010) and 70 d70\text{\,}\mathrm{d} (Bedding et al., 2020). The frequency of 4 d−14\text{\,}{\mathrm{d}}^{-1} is commonly used as a distinction between δ\delta Sct (>4 d−1>$4\text{\,}{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}$) and γ\gamma Doradus (γ\gamma Dor) stars (<4 d−1<$4\text{\,}{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}$), although many authors adopt 5 d−15\text{\,}{\mathrm{d}}^{-1} as a dividing threshold (Handler and Shobbrook, 2002; Grigahcène et al., 2010; Balona et al., 2011; Uytterhoeven et al., 2011; Skarka et al., 2022; Skarka and Henzl, 2024).

Generally, both radial and non-radial pressure (p) mode pulsations exist among δ\delta Sct stars. Some of these stars can have hundreds of frequencies that require p, gravity (g), and Rossby (r) modes (Saio et al., 2018; Henriksen et al., 2023), rotational splitting, nonlinear combinations of frequencies, as well as additional complexities such as variable amplitudes on longer timescales (Kurtz, 2022). Alternatively, they can have ridge-like frequency clusters, as studied by Antoci et al. (2026). The complexity of their pulsation spectra makes the identification and interpretation of individual modes challenging, particularly in hybrid pulsators (Grigahcène et al., 2010; Kurtz et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021). A large fraction of δ\delta Sct stars have frequencies also in the γ\gamma Dor range (Uytterhoeven et al., 2011; Balona, 2014; Balona et al., 2015; Skarka et al., 2022). Pulsation modes are primarily excited by the classical κ\kappa mechanism operating in He ii ionisation zones (Cox, 1963; Chevalier, 1971; Aerts et al., 2010). Antoci et al. (2014) showed that the opacity mechanism alone cannot explain oscillations, and turbulent pressure in the hydrogen ionisation zone also contributes to the excitation of pulsations, mainly moderate radial p modes.

The last two decades have seen enormous developments in asteroseismology, thanks to the launch of space missions CoRoT (Auvergne et al., 2009), the Kepler space telescope (Borucki et al., 2010), and most recently, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS, Ricker et al. 2015). Space photometry provides precision about 100 times better than ground-based photometry, with nearly continuous, evenly sampled data (Kurtz, 2022). This precision and the sheer number of objects observed have increased the number of known pulsating stars and allowed us to probe their interiors. Building on the Kepler era, TESS brought the possibility of ensemble studies of δ\delta Sct stars across the whole sky, see e. g. Antoci et al. (2019); Cunha et al. (2019); Bedding et al. (2020); Barac et al. (2022); Gootkin et al. (2024). Another advantage of TESS is its long-term observational coverage, with observations spanning multiple sectors and, for some targets, several years. Two-minute cadence data are also available for many stars. Additionally, TESS all-sky coverage includes many early-type hotter stars not observed by Kepler, along with bright stars that can be observed by smaller telescopes.

In light of these recent discoveries and the huge amount of precise photometric data, we decided to carry out a comprehensive study of bright, manually vetted δ\delta Sct stars with high-resolution spectroscopy. We aim to understand the influence of projected rotation v​sin⁡iv\sin i on stellar oscillations and excited pulsation modes. We also revisit the results of previous studies in the context of high precision photometry from short cadence 2-minute TESS data and search for scaling relations. We observed 262 bright (VV mag < 7) stars and gathered 307 high-resolution échelle spectra.

papers.title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development
papers.abstract: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.

papers.intro:
For a PDE problem with given geometry and boundary conditions, it is not surprising that AI agents are capable of developing an accurate numerical solver. The AI-developed solvers for a fixed PDE problem can be evaluated through PDEAgent-Bench (Hang et al., 2026) or CFDLLMBench (Somasekharan et al., 2026). However, for an industrial-level Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver, solving a fixed PDE is not enough. The solver must be able to handle different geometries, boundary conditions, and material properties. The inputs of held-out cases should not be provided during development. Therefore, for a single task, the AI agent is required to develop a CAE solver that can generalize across cases with varying inputs. In this paper, we introduce CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate the ability of AI agents to develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize across inputs.

Therefore, for a single task, the AI agent is required to develop a CAE solver that can generalize across cases with varying inputs. In this paper, we introduce CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate the ability of AI agents to develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize across inputs.

We consider an extreme example. The task is to develop a solver for the governing equations of a 2-dimensional incompressible flow of a Newtonian fluid. The solver predicts velocity and pressure fields for given inputs. If the AI agent is only required to solve the task for fixed inputs, and the inputs are provided to the agent during development, then the agent can compute and store the answer during development, then return it during evaluation. This does not demonstrate that the agent can develop a reusable solver, since the resulting solver only works for these fixed inputs.

To evaluate the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers, we evaluate solvers on the same task with different cases, each case containing inputs and the reference used for scoring. All cases are distinguished into Public cases and Held-out cases. Public cases provide public inputs and example outputs during development. The example outputs have the required format, but their values are random. Held-out cases contain inputs that vary in geometry, material response, initial states, or boundary-condition types. These held-out cases are not provided to the agent during development. In summary, the public cases are used in both development and evaluation, while the held-out cases are only used in evaluation.

Using the RC7 release, we evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings. At medium effort, some AI-developed solvers receive full score on all public cases of a task. However, all AI-developed solvers got 00 score on at least 1 held-out case of the same task. Also, most 0-score cases reach numerical scoring, which means the solver runs successfully and the output format is correct. However, the output fails the accuracy requirements. These results show that the current best models are not capable of developing an industrial-level reusable CAE solver without human involvement.

Several works have explored the ability of AI agents to develop numerical solvers. CodePDE (Li et al., 2025) uses debugging and iterative refinement to improve AI-developed PDE solvers. PDEAgent-Bench (Hang et al., 2026) evaluates whether AI agents can develop accurate enough PDE solvers using libraries such as DOLFINx, Firedrake, and deal.II. CFDLLMBench (Somasekharan et al., 2026) evaluates AI agents on CFD-related tasks, including code generation and OpenFOAM workflows. PDEBench (Takamoto et al., 2022) evaluates machine learning models by providing simulation datasets covering different initial conditions, boundary conditions, and PDE parameters. The reference solution is also provided to compare the machine learning based methods with traditional methods. These works mainly focus on developing solvers or completing simulations for given problems. For an industrial-level CAE solver, such complete information is impossible to gain during development.

papers.title: RevealLO: Global-Scale FWI Including Long-Period Major-Arc Surface Wave and Multi-Orbit Body Wave Data
papers.abstract: Global full-waveform inversion (FWI) has matured significantly in recent years, but resolution in the southern hemisphere often remains limited due to sparse receiver coverage. To address this problem, we constructed RevealLO, a global-scale FWI model that updates its predecessor REVEAL by expanding the inversion time window from 1 hour to 3.5 hours. The extended time window incorporates both minor-arc ($R_1, G_1$) and major-arc ($R_2, G_2$) surface wave arrivals, as well as late-arriving multi-orbit body waves, thereby increasing azimuthal coverage beneath ocean basins and the southern hemisphere. We simulate 3-D viscoelastic wavefields using the spectral-element solver Salvus on global fourth-order cubed-sphere meshes, and update velocity structure by successively broadening the period band from 100 - 200 s to 60 - 200 s. Measurements and adjoint sources are based on time-frequency phase misfits, which are suitable for both large-amplitude surface and low-amplitude multiply-reflected body waves. For iterative optimization, we employ a mini-batch stochastic trust-region L-BFGS algorithm, followed by mesh reprojection onto the $33~s$ REVEAL baseline mesh and lowermost-mantle regularization. RevealLO preserves short-period whole-Earth body wave fits while improving azimuthal sampling and mitigating trade-offs between unmodeled azimuthal anisotropy and isotropic structure in the upper and mid mantle.

papers.intro:
Over the past decade, full-waveform inversion (FWI) has developed into a high-resolution method for imaging the Earth’s interior. By exploiting complete waveform segments rather than isolated travel-time picks ([1]; [2]), FWI accounts for complex wavefield phenomena such as multipathing, wavefront healing ([3]; [4]), and finite-frequency sensitivity ([5], [6], [7]). Although current global tomographic models exhibit agreement at long wavelengths, structural discrepancies persist at shorter scales [8]. These differences are primarily driven by data selection choices, phase windowing, parameterization, and inversion strategies employed by different research groups. REVEAL was recently developed as a global-scale FWI model utilizing a multi-scale FWI strategy [9]. To mitigate non-linearity, improve convexivity, and avoid cycle-skipping, the iterative construction of REVEAL progressed from long to short periods, ending at a minimum period of 33 s. The maximum length of the seismograms was set to 1 hour, mostly due to cost constraints. While this approach includes direct body waves and minor-arc surface waves, it omits potentially valuable information contained in later arrivals. Specifically, truncating seismograms at 1 hour excludes surface waves traveling along major-arc paths, thus limiting upper-mantle sensitivity in the southern hemisphere and beneath ocean basins, where seismic station density is lower than in the northern hemisphere. To illuminate these regions, it is necessary to take advantage surface and body waves that sample the Earth at epicentral distances that exceed 180∘180^{\circ}. To close this gap, we performed a long-period/long-duration update of REVEAL, leading to RevealLO. The primary modification in the construction of RevealLO is the incorporation of 3.5 hour seismograms, which include major-arc (R2,G2R_{2},G_{2}) surface waves, multi-orbit body waves, and few multi-orbit surface waves (e.g., G3G_{3}). Further multi-orbit arrivals are drowned in the noise of the considered period bandpass, thus we truncate to 3.5 hours for one full orbit of the wavefield. The main effect is to increase the coverage of the southern hemisphere upper mantle and transition zone. Starting from a regularized version of REVEAL model, we revise the long-period structure by successively broadening the period band from 100 - 200 s to 60 - 200 s. For this, we simulate 3-D viscoelastic wavefields on global fourth-order cubed-sphere-like meshes using the spectral-element solver Salvus [10] and reduce waveform fit iteratively using a mini-batch stochastic trust-region L-BFGS method [11]. We quantify waveform misfits and compute adjoint sources using the time-frequency phase misfit [12]. This allows us to eliminate the effect of unknown earthquake magnitude, and to incorporate both high-amplitude surface and low-amplitude body waves. In the following, we provide a detailed report on the construction of RevealLO, including data selection parameters and azimuthal coverage metrics (Section 2), forward solver implementation, regularization, and mesh reprojection (Section 3), and the resulting structural updates, comparisons with REVEAL, and waveform misfit validations (Section 4).

papers.title: On the blow-up of the one-particle Lieb-Thirring constant in dimension two
papers.abstract: We establish three-term asymptotics for the one-particle Lieb-Thirring constant in dimension two as $\gamma\to 0$ and identify, up to rescaling and symmetries, the profile of the asymptotically worst potential. The proof uses the well-known relation between the one-particle constant and an integral moment of optimizers of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality. Through the optimizers' characterization as positive, vanishing solutions of the nonlinear elliptic equation $-\Delta Q + Q = Q^{s}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, the essence of the proof lies in the asymptotic analysis of solutions $Q$ as $s\to\infty$.

papers.title: Accessing Electrode Edges: Upright Mounting for Site-Specific Cryogenic Atom Probe Tomography of Lithium-Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: Cryogenic atom probe tomography (cryo-APT) is increasingly being used to map the three-dimensional distribution of highly reactive species in heterogeneous materials, including those found in battery systems. However, site-specific preparation of localised features and liquid-solid interfaces remains challenging, particularly when regions of interest (ROIs) are concentrated along electrode edges that are difficult to access using conventional mounting geometries. Here, we present a cryo-APT workflow incorporating an upright-mounting procedure that enables targeted specimen preparation of localised regions using plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) microscopy and milling under cryogenic conditions. We first demonstrate the approach using an electrolyte-wetted graphite electrode, successfully preparing and analysing a specimen containing both an edge-localised electrolyte deposit and the underlying graphite and Cu current collector. We then apply the workflow to a cycled graphite electrode, targeting Li dendrites concentrated around the electrode perimeter and successfully preparing and analysing the targeted Li-rich region. Beyond battery systems, this approach offers potential for site-specific cryo-APT of edge-localised features across a broader range of material systems, where conventional specimen preparation geometries may limit access to ROIs.

papers.title: Exploring the link between predictive uncertainty and the sim-to-real gap in deep learning models utilizing synthetic data
papers.abstract: Today, state-of-the-art methods for quality control (QC) are based on Machine Vision, combining deep learning (DL) models with camera-based inspection. Yet, the integration of such solutions in industrial applications is often impeded by data sparsity and trust in model reliability. While synthetic data offers a promising approach to generate the necessary data with perfect annotations, it poses risks related to performance degradation due to the possible occurrence of the sim-to-real gap. This study conducts experiments using the ensemble method to estimate the predictive uncertainty of DL models trained on synthetic data. The results show that predictive uncertainty increases under the sim-to-real domain shift. However, the observed performance drop is dominated by a systematic sim-to-real bias rather than by ensemble disagreement.These findings contribute to the effective utilization of synthetic data in industrial settings while highlighting the importance of risk assessment for the deployment of DL solutions for QC tasks.
papers.intro:
In recent years, the utilization of deep learning (DL) in various industrial sectors has gained significant momentum. Especially for quality control (QC) applications, Machine Vision (MV) solutions, combining camera-based inspection and DL evaluation, are considered state-of-the-art methods Kim et al. (2025). However, the integration of such MV approaches is often impeded by data sparsity, a lack of expertise, and a lack of trust in the reliability of DL Ahangar et al. (2025). In assembly environments, trust in the behavior of employed approaches is particularly crucial, as a failing QC system may allow incorrectly or incompletely assembled products to proceed downstream, potentially resulting in costly rework, product recalls, or safety hazards for end users Baltag and Morariu (2022). One way to establish trust in DL models is through a thorough risk assessment, including, especially, an uncertainty estimation of the model’s behavior. Yet, acquiring such assessments for DL models remains a challenging and labor-intensive endeavor and is therefore often omitted both in the literature and praxis Gawlikowski et al. (2022).

The disadvantage of synthetic data as a training basis is the risk of performance degradation when applied to real-world data due to a potential sim-to-real gap between the real-world and the simulation. papers.title: EP241206a: A Sub-kilosecond X-Ray Flare Possibly from an Active Galactic Nucleus with a Flux Increase over 3 Orders of Magnitude
papers.abstract: EP241206a is a fast X-ray transient detected with the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) on board the Einstein Probe. The event exhibited a single-peaked soft X-ray flare with a duration of $\sim 500$ s and a peak flux of $1.0 \times 10^{-9}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in 0.5--4 keV, spatially coincident with a spectroscopically confirmed active galactic nucleus (AGN) at $z = 0.62$. Follow-up and archival observations revealed persistent X-ray emission at a level of $\sim 5 \times 10^{-13}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$, corresponding to $L_{2-10 \mathrm{keV}} \simeq 2.3 \times 10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ if associated with the AGN; the WXT flare reached an estimated peak isotropic-equivalent rest-frame 2--10 keV luminosity of $\sim 1.4 \times 10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$, implying a peak-to-persistent luminosity contrast of over 3 orders of magnitude. Optical spectroscopy detected broad Mg II and H$\beta$ emission lines, suggesting a black hole mass of $\sim 3.8 \times 10^{7} M_{\odot}$ and Eddington ratios of 0.8 at the persistent state versus an apparent peak ratio of $\sim 4.6 \times 10^{3}$ during the flare. The extremely short duration and high apparent peak luminosity favor a jet origin, likely due to magnetic reconnection in the inner regions of a relativistic jet. Alternative scenarios include a jet-in-the-jet or a gamma-ray burst occurring within the AGN disk. However, the physical association between the transient and the AGN is not firmly established; for the radio-loud and X-ray-detected AGN counterpart class, the trial-corrected chance probability is $4.9 \times 10^{-3}$. EP241206a may represent an example of a broader population of unidentified fast X-ray transients detected with WXT.

papers.title: Data-Driven Predictive Control for Autonomous Vehicle Racing under Varying Friction
papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DPC) predicts future outputs by combining recorded input-output trajectory data such that the combined trajectory approximately matches a measured initial trajectory and tracks a provided reference. This paper investigates to what extent and under which conditions DPC using data pooled across operating conditions retains the prediction accuracy of DPC using data from the current operating condition. In autonomous vehicle racing, the tire-road friction varies between racetrack sections and tire sets. If the initial trajectory and the recorded data originate from different frictions, prediction accuracy of DPC degrades. Ensuring the frictions match requires knowing the friction during recording and estimating the current friction explicitly. Instead, we pool data recorded at different frictions. We compare the prediction accuracy of DPC using data recorded under the current friction (matched), a different friction (mismatched) and data pooled from both frictions. We evaluate in simulation and small-scale vehicle experiments in the Cyber-Physical Mobility Lab (CPM Lab). Our results show that pooled data keep the multi-step root-mean-square prediction error within 1.5 times that of matched data, whereas mismatched data increase it by a factor of 2.2 to 3.4. To assess how this prediction accuracy carries over to control, we evaluate the tracking error from the raceline in closed loop. In simulation, DPC with pooled data tracks comparably to nonlinear model predictive control (13.7 cm versus 13.3 cm) and close to DPC with matched data in the CPM Lab, differing by 0.1 cm on the low-friction tires (1.6 cm versus 1.5 cm) and by 0.2 cm on the high-friction tires (0.9 cm versus 1.1 cm). DPC thus provides partial adaptation to varying friction, without a dedicated adaptation method.

papers.intro:
Data-driven predictive control (DPC) predicts future outputs by combining recorded input–output trajectory data such that the combined trajectory approximately matches a measured initial trajectory and tracks a provided reference [1, 2]. For linear systems, a linear combination of recorded trajectories is itself a valid trajectory of the system. For nonlinear systems, a linear combination of recorded trajectories only approximates the system dynamics. Moreover, recorded trajectories capture the system dynamics only at the operating conditions at which they were collected. Data recorded at an operating condition different from the current one may degrade the prediction accuracy of DPC. Ensuring that the recorded data match the current operating condition requires knowing the operating condition during recording and estimating the current one.

The tire parameters of the vehicle model are influenced by friction, so the accuracy of a vehicle model identified at one friction level degrades at other friction levels [5]. Such online adaptation requires structural model knowledge and a dedicated adaptation method [6, 7].

Closest to our approach, Spielberg et al. train a neural network on data from dry and snow-covered roads, to predict the vehicle motion from a history of past states and inputs [13, 14]. In this paper, we neither select, adapt, nor train a vehicle model; instead, we apply DPC with data pooled from trajectories recorded at different friction levels.

papers.title: OGHReS: Discovery of a giant hub-filament system at the edge of the Galactic molecular disc
papers.abstract: We present the discovery and characterisation of G195.65$-$0.10 (also known as the $\lambda$-complex), a giant hub-filament system identified by the Outer Galaxy High Resolution Survey (OGHReS). The complex contains 61 spatially and kinematically coherent HiGAL clumps with a mean velocity of $V_{\rm LSR}=32.85$ km/s and a velocity dispersion between clumps of 1.97 km/s. A $Gaia$ parallax measurement of the central emission-line star MWC 137 associated with an embedded cluster gives a heliocentric distance of 5.2$^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$ kpc, placing the complex at a Galactocentric radius of 13.2 kpc. The molecular structure spans approximately $35\times63$ pc and contains $\sim 1.6\times10^{5}$ M$_\odot$ of molecular gas, including $\sim 5 \times 10^{4}$ M$_\odot$ in dense clumps. The molecular emission is organised into three prominent velocity-coherent filaments that converge on a dense central hub. Of the associated clumps, 16 are protostellar and 45 are gravitationally bound but currently starless. The protostellar clumps are significantly more concentrated towards the hub than the starless population, with median projected offsets of 6.65 and 15.83 pc, respectively. Moreover, the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the protostellar clumps decreases significantly with increasing distance from the hub, indicating that the most evolutionarily advanced sources are preferentially located in the central region. These results reveal a systematic concentration of dense gas and increasingly evolved star formation towards the hub, with organised large-scale gas motions throughout the filamentary network. The $\lambda$-complex therefore provides an unprecedented laboratory to understand hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc.

papers.intro:
Filamentary molecular clouds are now recognised as a fundamental component of the Galactic interstellar medium and play a central role in the star formation process. They are observed over a wide range of spatial scales, from giant molecular filaments (GMFs; Li et al. 2013, Ragan et al. 2014, Ragan et al. 2015, Abreu-Vicente et al. 2016, Colombo et al. 2021, Mookerjea et al. 2026) extending for hundreds of parsecs and tracing spiral structure, to the dense filamentary networks embedded within giant molecular clouds (André et al. 2014, Inutsuka et al. 2015, Li et al. 2016, Mattern et al. 2018, Schisano et al. 2020). Some of the largest filamentary structures are associated with major segments of spiral arms and have become known as the so-called “bones” of the Milky Way (Goodman et al. 2014, Zucker et al. 2018), emphasising the importance of filaments in defining Galactic structure (see Hacar et al. 2023 for a recent review).

Dense filaments are also intimately linked with star formation. Young stellar objects are preferentially found within filamentary structures (e.g. Lada et al. 2012), while high-mass star formation is frequently concentrated towards dense hubs formed where multiple filaments intersect (Myers 2009, Motte et al. 2018). These hub-filament systems (HFSs) exhibit enhanced concentrations of dense gas, embedded clusters, and massive protostars, and observations increasingly suggest that material is funnelled along the filaments towards the central hub, potentially regulating the formation of stellar clusters and high-mass stars (e.g. Schneider et al. 2012, Mallick et al. 2013, Peretto et al. 2013, Peretto et al. 2014, Motte et al. 2018, Williams et al. 2018, Zhou et al. 2022).

Large catalogues of HFSs have recently become available through systematic surveys of the Galactic plane via H​e​r​s​c​h​e​lHerschel data. Kumar et al. (2020) identified many thousands of candidate hub-filament systems in the Hi-GAL survey (Elia et al. 2017), demonstrating that approximately 10 per cent of dense Galactic clumps reside within these structures. However, despite their abundance, almost all currently known HFSs are located within the inner Galaxy. Indeed, approximately 98.5 per cent of the Kumar et al. sample lies at Galactocentric radii smaller than the Solar circle (Rgc=R_{\rm gc}=8.15 kpc; Reid et al. 2019, GRAVITY Collaboration et al. 2019). Only 52 candidates are found in the outer Galaxy and these are all located on the far side of the Galactic disc at heliocentric distances exceeding 20 kpc, making detailed studies of their internal structure extremely difficult. Moreover, these distances are kinematic in nature and therefore likely to be quite uncertain, further complicating the analysis and interpretation of their properties.

Moreover, these distances are kinematic in nature and therefore likely to be quite uncertain, further complicating the analysis and interpretation of their properties.

The scarcity of well-resolved outer-Galaxy hub-filament systems represents an important limitation for understanding clustered star formation under environmental conditions that differ substantially from those in the inner Milky Way. One of the main reasons for this scarcity is that there has yet to be a systematic search for these systems in the outer Galaxy; Kumar et al. 2020 focused their efforts towards the inner Galaxy Hi-GAL catalogue (Elia et al. 2017) that was available at the time. The outer Galaxy has lower gas surface densities (Heyer et al. 1998), lower metallicities (Lépine et al. 2011, Esteban et al. 2017), weaker spiral perturbations and reduced stellar densities, all of which may influence the formation, evolution and star-forming properties of filamentary molecular clouds. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the hub-filament paradigm established from studies of nearby and inner-Galaxy regions also applies in these more extreme environments.

Located at a Galactocentric radius of 13.2 kpc (heliocentric distance of 5.15 kpc), the complex is consistent with being associated with the Outer-Norma arm and is one of the most distant well-resolved hub-filament systems currently known.
