papers.title: Conditions for mass-loading: Investigating jet-disk material exchange in strongly magnetised accretion flows
papers.abstract: Relativistic jets are produced by accreting black holes across a wide range of masses, from stellar-mass X-ray binaries to supermassive active galactic nuclei (AGN). In low-luminosity AGN, these jets are believed to be powered by strongly magnetised accretion flows, a picture supported by Event Horizon Telescope and VLBI observations of M87. The jets often exhibit high-energy flaring emission which, if partly hadronic, implies that baryons must be loaded into the jet and accelerated despite strong magnetic barriers. However, the mechanism behind this remains unclear. We present high-resolution, three-dimensional General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of a high-spin Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD), a strongly magnetised accretion regime. Using passive Eulerian tracers, we track the exchange of material between the jet and disk to quantify mixing. We find that magnetic flux eruptions, a hallmark of MAD accretion, expel magnetic flux tubes initially filled with jet material (expected to be pair-dominated in real systems). Through magnetic reconnection during these eruptions, this material is mixed into the disk. Crucially, the same flux tubes reconnect the disk back to the jet, allowing disk material, expected to be primarily hadronic, to infiltrate the jet sheath and boundary. This disk-to-jet injection offers a natural mass-loading mechanism that does not require the jet to be globally baryon-dominated. The resulting ejection-injection cycle may instead drive episodic hadronic acceleration, providing a viable pathway for high-energy emission in relativistic jets.

papers.intro:
Relativistic jets represent one of the most ubiquitous phenomena across astrophysical objects and scales, first unwittingly discovered in the nearby galaxy M87 over a century ago (Curtis, 1918) and later found to be polarised (observed at optical wavelengths; Baade 1956), a key step towards establishing them as structures originating due to ordered magnetic fields. The recognition of quasars as distant, luminous galaxies (Schmidt, 1963, e.g.,) and the theoretical framework for accretion-powered systems (Lynden-Bell, 1971, e.g.,) established jets as fundamental components of black hole physics. Much later, Very Large Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations confirmed relativistic bulk motion through proper superluminal motions (Reid et al., 1989; Biretta et al., 1989; Biretta et al., 1999, e.g.,). Over subsequent decades, jets have been identified across a remarkable range of systems harboring or forming black holes: including stellar-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs) where the jets exhibit superluminal motion (Mirabel and Rodríguez, 1994; Fender, 2003, e.g.,) to the most luminous active galactic nuclei (Bridle and Perley, 1984; Begelman et al., 1984, AGN; e.g.,), and more recently in neutron star mergers (Mooley et al., 2018, e.g.,) and tidal disruption events (Bloom et al., 2011; Cendes et al., 2024, e.g.).

Within this larger topic, there is a long-standing question regarding the origin of high-energy accelerated, hadronic particles called cosmic rays, that requires a better understanding of jet composition and potential sites for acceleration. Current instruments cannot directly measure the jet composition, and broadband Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) modeling alone remains highly degenerate between leptonic and hadronic scenarios (Böttcher et al., 2013; Cerruti et al., 2015; Madejski and Sikora, 2016; Romero et al., 2017; Blandford et al., 2019, e.g.). To make progress on this question, it is important to better constrain how and where hadronic material manages to enter the jets, and is the loading continuous, or does it occur in episodic events? Some progress has been made on measuring composition via source-specific observations where a few black hole jets show direct signatures of baryonic material. For example, the black hole XRB 4U 1630-47 displays Fe XXVI lines at 0.66​c0.66c (Trigo et al., 2013; Trueba et al., 2019); another black hole XRB SS 433 also displays Doppler-shifted Balmer, HeI, Fe XXV/XXVI consistent with baryonic jets moving at ≈0.26​c\approx 0.26c (Margon et al., 1979; Abell and Margon, 1979; Marshall et al., 2002), where cc is the speed of light. However linking these results to acceleration sites and mechanisms remains challenging.

Historically, the prime candidate site proposed for extreme particle acceleration in AGN jets is a putative recollimation shock that occurs around the Bondi radius (RBondi=2​G​M/cs2R_{\rm Bondi}=2GM/c_{s}^{2}; where csc_{s} is the speed of sound, and, MM is the mass of the black hole). The Bondi radius (hereafter RBR_{\rm B}) is the gravitational capture radius of the black hole’s ambient medium, where the inflow transitions from quasi-spherical to disk-dominated, depending on its residual angular momentum (Homan et al., 2015; Zech and Lemoine, 2021; Nalewajko et al., 2014b, e.g.). In the nearby low-luminosity AGN M87, the prominent HST-1 knot at ∼60\sim 60 pc (∼105​rg∼RB\sim 10^{5}r_{g}\sim R_{B}) has long been considered to be associated with a reconfinement shock (Stawarz et al., 2006). HST-1 is observed to be a site of particle re-acceleration, with a major multiwavelength outburst peaking in 2005 and exhibiting correlated variability from radio through X-rays (Harris et al., 2009; Stawarz et al., 2006). If protons are entrained into these acceleration zones and sufficiently accelerated, they can potentially be a source of neutrinos. The association of AGN jets with high-energy neutrinos is supported by candidate neutrino events from sources such as TXS 0506+056 (IceCube Collaboration et al., 2018), while recent work has identified other radio galaxies, including 3C 403, as candidate neutrino-emitting sources (Bruni et al., 2026). More broadly, AGN contributions to the extragalactic γ\gamma-ray background (Ackermann et al., 2016) and the diffuse neutrino flux (Aartsen et al., 2017) depend sensitively on the fraction of jets that carry sufficient baryons for hadronic acceleration (Stecker and Venters, 2013; Sahakyan, 2018), and where that acceleration occurs.

papers.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
papers.abstract: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org

Formal program specifications define the correct behavior of a program over all valid inputs, providing the reference against which implementations can be proved correct or tested. Yet writing such specifications in an interactive theorem prover requires substantial expertise and effort, making specification a fundamental barrier to scaling formal code verification and generation. As AI models make rapid progress in generating code and proving its correctness, this barrier becomes increasingly important: realizing the promise of formally correct code requires automating specification itself. Autoformalization from natural-language programming problems offers a path forward, but immediately raises a central question: when does a generated formal specification faithfully capture the intended problem?

Formal program specifications define the correct behavior of a program over all valid inputs, providing the reference against which implementations can be proved correct or tested. Yet writing such specifications in an interactive theorem prover requires substantial expertise and effort, making specification a fundamental barrier to scaling formal code verification and generation. As AI models make rapid progress in generating code and proving its correctness, this barrier becomes increasingly important: realizing the promise of formally correct code requires automating specification itself. Autoformalization from natural-language programming problems offers a path forward, but immediately raises a central question: when does a generated formal specification faithfully capture the intended problem?

This question is particularly important in modern code-generation pipelines. Large language models (LLMs) can generate solutions to programming problems (e.g., LeetCode) from natural-language descriptions. These solutions can be evaluated using input-output test cases, which provide scalable reward signals for reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025; Ruan et al., 2026). However, passing test cases does not guarantee correctness, as a solution may still fail on untested inputs (Shi et al., 2026). Formal verification offers a stronger guarantee. Given a specification, which consists of a precondition defining valid inputs and a postcondition characterizing correct outputs (Endres et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026), a theorem prover like Lean can formally prove that an implementation satisfies its specification for every valid input. This guarantee depends on the specification correctly capturing the natural-language problem, yet producing such specifications at scale remains difficult. Manually curating specifications requires substantial expert effort: Clever and Verina contain only 161 and 189 problems, respectively (Thakur et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026a). Automated methods can scale further, but may produce incorrect specifications (Dougherty & Mehta, 2025; Bursuc et al., 2026; Dougherty et al., 2026). Scaling specification therefore requires more than generating formal statements. It also requires efficient and scalable feedback on whether generated specifications match the source problem, analogous to the test-case feedback used to train code-generation models.

Training specification generators has been explored in auto-active verification languages, where a verifier, like an SMT solver, provides the reward by checking candidate specifications on test cases (Yan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Baksys et al., 2025). In Lean, prior work checks generated specifications by turning each test case into a theorem to be proved, a method known as symbolic specification testing (Lahiri, 2024; Ye et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026). These theorems can require nontrivial proofs, especially when the specification involves unbounded quantifiers. If a proof cannot be found, the test case may be left unresolved or evaluated by an LLM judge. Thus, unlike in code generation (Wang et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), test cases do not directly provide cheap rewards for training specification generators in Lean (Table 1).

papers.title: Gaia as a 0.1 arcsec point-source survey across the sky: dynamical scene reconstruction from one-dimensional scans
papers.abstract: Gaia has observed every detected source on the sky 50 to 100 times, each time through a window of about 1 by 2 arcseconds at a different scan angle. The resulting one-dimensional flux profiles to be released in Gaia DR4 encode the two-dimensional arrangement of nearby point sources at ~0.1 arcsecond resolution. Repeated observations also constrain their relative motion. We present a method to model the scene with a mixture of moving point sources. Complementing Gaia DPAC's source-environment reconstruction, our approach focuses on close, blended companions and models their relative motion. We first fit each window with a few point sources and obtain their along-scan positions. We then triangulate these positions from different scan angles to identify candidate sources on the sky. A joint forward model of all windows measures positions, fluxes, relative proper motions, and parallax differences, even for blended components. In simulations, we recover companions at separations smaller than the instrumental profile width. For a moving companion at ~75 mas separation with a flux ratio of ~0.2, we obtain a separation precision of ~0.1 mas and a relative proper-motion precision of ~0.1 mas/yr per component, even in a scene contaminated by a third source. These precisions assume a known instrumental profile and independent Gaussian noise. We also recover differential parallax for a chance-aligned source. Modeling nearby contaminants prevents significant biases. With a Gaia-like instrumental profile, sampling and scan law, we show a sensitivity of ~5 mag in contrast at separations of 50-150 mas, and we discuss its dependence on the color term of Gaia's line-spread function. Wide-field ground-based optical surveys generally operate near the atmospheric seeing limit. The Pan-STARRS1 survey covers roughly 30,00030{,}000 square degrees with typical image quality of about 1.21.2 arcseconds (Chambers et al., 2016), while the Rubin Observatory is designed to survey 18,000 square degrees with a median delivered image quality near 0.7 arcseconds (Ivezić et al., 2019). Space telescopes are unaffected by seeing conditions. Euclid reaches about 0.18 arcseconds over 14,000 square degrees, although its wide survey largely avoids the Galactic plane (Euclid Collaboration et al., 2025). Close stellar companions are common and span a wide range of separations, but most are unresolved in low-resolution images. Detecting them requires techniques whose sensitivity depends on separation and contrast (Moe & Di Stefano, 2017). Repeated high-resolution observations can both identify companions and measure their relative motion (Vrijmoet et al., 2026). These measurements provide dynamical information even when the observing baseline covers only a small fraction of an orbit (Pearce et al., 2015). A survey with a known selection function would constrain companion occurrence as a function of separation and flux ratio, in the field as in clusters and associations.

Gaia offers repeated observations of every source on the sky at high angular resolution along each scan, over a brightness range from G≈3G\approx 3 to G≈20.7G\approx 20.7 (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016). Its rectangular aperture produces an anisotropic diffraction pattern, narrowest in the along-scan direction. The corresponding line-spread function (LSF) has a characteristic FWHM of ∼ 100{\sim}\,100 mas (Rowell et al., 2021) and is sampled at 5959 mas per pixel (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016). Its shape depends on source color, position in the focal plane, and time (Rowell et al., 2021). For sources fainter than G≃13G\simeq 13, the astrometric windows are normally binned over 1212 across-scan pixels and transmitted as one-dimensional profiles (Rowell et al., 2021). Each profile constrains source positions along one direction. Observations at different scan angles together deliver information about their two-dimensional arrangement.

Reconstructing source environments from scanning astrometry has precedents in Hipparcos (Quist & Lindegren, 1999) and Gaia (Harrison, 2011; Harrison et al., 2023). Within Gaia DPAC, the Source Environment Analysis Pipeline (Harrison et al., 2023, SEAPipe;) relies on a weighted stack of the window samples in the primary source’s co-moving frame. The weighting prefers low flux levels, so samples contaminated by the primary’s flux are down-weighted and the stacked image keeps the sky level around the primary (Harrison, 2011). Sources identified in the image are fitted to the window samples. In the image-subtraction version of the pipeline, they are then removed and the search is repeated. Here we use Gaia’s one-dimensional windows to identify close, blended companions and measure their relative motion. SEAPipe and our approach differ in how they find candidates. The SEAPipe stack needs no model of the instrumental profile, so it is robust to its variations, and it essentially aggregates flux. The instrument model and the motions enter only when the sources identified in the stack are fitted to the window samples. We instead model the LSF already in the reduction of every window and accept the costs of that model, discussed in Section 6, to achieve improved localization and to monitor the scene in time. Beyond the candidate search, this paper recovers companions at separations below the FWHM of the LSF, and calibrates the detection limits and the color bias for a Gaia-like LSF.

For a scene of a few moving point sources, we fit each window separately and obtain along-scan detections. Each detection defines a line of possible positions on the sky. Accumulating these lines across scan angles identifies candidate sources at their intersections. We refer to this mapping from detections to sky lines as backprojection. This geometry is closely related to the Radon transform used in tomography (Radon, 1917; Kak & Slaney, 2001), but here we accumulate fitted source detections to identify candidate point sources. We account for relative motion by propagating detections to a common reference epoch using a fitted motion model. A joint forward model of the original windows then measures the components’ positions, fluxes and motions.

papers.title: Thermal emission spectroscopy of the ultra-hot Jupiter HAT-P-70b: NIRPS constraints on its refractory and volatile content
papers.abstract: Context. The chemical makeup of exoplanets provides insight into their origins and internal structures. High dayside temperatures on ultra-hot Jupiters vaporise refractory species and dissociate volatile molecules such as water. Cooler nightsides enable condensation (e.g. Fe) and cold-trapping (e.g. Ti), as compounds transition out of the gas phase. These contrasting conditions make dayside emission spectra a probe of both elemental inventories and atmospheric chemistry in the gas. Aim. We characterise the dayside atmosphere of the ultra-hot Jupiter HAT-P-70b via thermal emission spectroscopy, constraining its refractory and volatile budget and assessing thermal dissociation and cold-trapping. We focus on the abundances of rock-forming elements (Fe, Si, and Mg) and the depletion or survival of Ti and H2O. Methods. We analyse secondary-eclipse observations of HAT-P-70b acquired with NIRPS. From the emission spectrum, we infer the planet's atmospheric thermal structure and composition using a well-mixed retrieval framework. Results. We detect emission signatures from Fe, Mg, V, Si, and OH, but no significant H2O signal. The presence of OH and absence of water indicate strong thermal dissociation, with water likely depleted by more than 90% in the probed layers. The retrieved temperature profile shows a pronounced thermal inversion. Elemental abundance ratios (Fe/Si, Mg/Si, V/Si) are broadly consistent with solar-like composition, while titanium appears sub-solar, possibly due to partial condensation and nightside cold-trapping. Conclusions. HAT-P-70b's dayside atmosphere is dominated by refractory species and strong thermal processes. The detection of OH and absence of H2O indicate efficient water dissociation, while sub-solar titanium suggests nightside cold-trapping. Refractory element ratios are consistent with solar values, supporting a link between planetary and stellar compositions.

papers.intro:
The chemistry of gas giant exoplanet atmospheres is governed by a fundamental division between refractory and volatile species. Refractory elements–metals and silicates (also commonly referred to as rocky elements)–are characterised by a superior heat resistance and elevated condensation temperatures (Lodders, 2003). In cold environments, only volatile species with a low condensation temperature (such as water–H2O) can exist in gas phase, while refractory compounds require higher temperatures to vaporise and thus are commonly found in liquid and solid form. This condition is typical of planetesimals being accreted in planetary bodies, where the most abundant refractory species like iron (Fe), silicon (Si) and magnesium (Mg) are sequestered in solids. In hot environments, such as those of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters, the temperatures can exceed 2000 K, causing the refractory metals to evaporate and exist in their atomic (or even ionised) gas phase, substantially contributing to the overall gaseous budget of the planet. At equilibrium temperatures above 2000 K, the atmosphere of ultra-hot Jupiters is thus assumed to be close to chemical equilibrium, cloud-free (as condensation can be “ruled out”), and populated by atoms and ions (Kitzmann et al., 2018). However, condensation can still occur on the colder nightside of the planet and in the terminator regions which are observed mostly in transit. Refractory elements with high condensation temperatures (e.g. titanium–Ti, scandium–Sc, and aluminum–Al) can rain-out on the nightside of the planet becoming cold-trapped at high pressures (deep atmospheric layers). The cold-trapping inhibits these species to mix and circulate back to upper (lower pressures) atmospheric layers (Hoeijmakers et al., 2024; Pelletier et al., 2023, as in WASP-121b and WASP-76b;), leading to apparent depletion relative to chemical equilibrium expectations. Indeed, Ti-bearing species (e.g. Ti, titanium oxide–TiO, and ionised titanium–Ti+) are often not detected in the atmospheres of the colder ultra-hot planets using the cross-correlation method (with a few notable exceptions that showcase the hottest temperatures, such as WASP-33b, KELT-9b, TOI-2109b, TOI-1518b, WASP-189b, and MASCARA-1b; Cont et al. 2022; Hoeijmakers et al.2018; Simonnin et al.2025; Pelletier et al.2026b; Guo et al.2024). Atmospheric characterisation likewise tends to constrain ultra-hot gas giant atmospheres as being deficient in gaseous titanium (Hoeijmakers et al., 2020; Merritt et al., 2020; Kesseli et al., 2020; Tabernero et al., 2021; Maguire et al., 2023; Gandhi et al., 2023; Pelletier et al., 2023; Hoeijmakers et al., 2024; Pelletier et al., 2025; Pelletier et al., 2026a, e.g. WASP-121b and WASP-76b;). However, for planets with very high estimated nightside temperature (Tnightside≳2000T_{\mathrm{nightside}}\gtrsim 2000 K), titanium signatures are more readily detected (e.g. in KELT-9b), suggesting that cold-trapping becomes less and less efficient as the temperature increases.

In contrast to Ti, chemically similar but less naturally abundant vanadium (V) is more ubiquitously detected in the atmospheres of ultra-hot Jupiters (Prinoth et al., 2023; Pelletier et al., 2023; Vaulato et al., 2025a). However, their oxides (i.e. TiO and VO) are strong optical absorbers and thought to drive thermal inversions observed in hot Jupiters atmospheres (Fortney et al., 2008). The temperature increase boosts the ionisation of metals such as Fe, sodium (Na), and potassium (K), which release free electrons in the atmosphere which, in turn, pair with atomic hydrogen (as the extremely hot atmospheres of gas giants transitions from H2- to H-dominated) to form the hydride ion (H-) which has bound-free interactions in the optical and near-infrared, and free-free transitions at longer wavelength (Parmentier et al., 2018; Arcangeli et al., 2018; Vaulato et al., 2025b). With H2O being a major opacity source in the near-infrared (Gandhi et al., 2020), its dissociation can strongly affect observed spectra. Equilibrium chemistry predicts that water molecules break down when temperatures exceed 2000 K (Kitzmann et al., 2024), releasing hydrogen and oxygen which recombine to form molecular hydroxyl (OH). Consequently, these gas giants provide ideal laboratories for testing planet interior models and for assessing the assumption that planetary bulk compositions reflect those of their host stars.

papers.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: The impact of a large JWST/NIRCam PSF library on exoplanet imaging detection sensitivity
papers.abstract: The excellent infrared sensitivity of JWST allows direct imaging of young low-mass (below $\sim1$ M$_{\text{Jup}}$) giant planets for the first time, with several JWST programs being carried out for this purpose. However, the detection sensitivity of these observations crucially depends on subtracting the residual light of the host star to reveal faint astrophysical signals. This requires high quality observations of reference stars to build an empirical starlight model. Here we present a homogeneously processed reference star library of targets observed with programs GO 4050, GO 5835 and SURVEY 6005, which enable PSF subtraction via reference star differential imaging. These observations were taken with the MASK335R coronagraph mask and in dual-filter F444W/F200W mode. Our library consists of 247 observations (counting both filters separately) of 100 different stars of spectral types mostly F to M, with a total of 1110 individual integrations. We explore the PSF subtraction hyper-parameters with the KLIP algorithm (Soummer et al. 2012) that maximize sensitivity, and we show the performance of our library compared to and in addition to contemporaneous reference observations. We show that our library improves sensitivity at close separations in most tested cases, with improvement factors from $\sim1.3$ to $\sim2$ at some separations. As practical recommendations, we find that our library is best used as a complement to contemporaneous reference observations to further improve sensitivity, since in all our experiments contemporaneous references are needed for best sensitivity. We make the PSF library publicly available for the high-contrast imaging community.

papers.intro:
With its exceptional IR sensitivity, JWST is capable of directly imaging much lower mass and much colder giant planets than any other current observatory. This opens previously unexplored regions of exoplanet parameter space. On exoplanet demographics, constraints on the occurrence rate of wide-separation sub-Jupiters become possible for the first time [12, 13]. On atmospheric studies, imaging of planets at record-low masses and temperatures can yield insights into planet formation and composition (e.g., Bardalez Gagliuffi et al. 6, Matthews et al. 47, Lagrange et al. 33, Sanghi et al. 59).

Diffracted starlight in the stellar point spread function (PSF) has a complex morphology, often with patterns that look identical to planet signals [53, 26, 46]. Especially at close angular separations from the star (e.g. within ∼3\sim 3 arcseconds for JWST/NIRCam in the F444W filter), it is our ability to subtract starlight without over-subtracting exoplanet light that sets the imaging sensitivity floor [50]. This is particularly important for JWST, since it has lower angular resolution than 8-10 meter ground-based telescopes11 1 For reference, the pixel scale of the long wavelength channel of JWST/NIRCam is ∼63\sim 63 mas [30], compared to ∼14\sim 14 mas for the Gemini Planet Imager [41] and ∼12\sim 12 mas for SPHERE/IRDIS [42]. Instead, PSF subtraction is typically done via reference star differential imaging (RDI). In RDI, a bright reference star is observed right before or after a science sequence. Algorithms like KLIP can then be used to construct a PSF model from the reference observations and subtract it from the science image. This is for several reasons: both stars can have different spectral energy distributions, aberrations in the telescope are constantly evolving, and imperfect pointing accuracy. For this reason, several JWST programs have opted for a “self-referencing” strategy, where a handful of science targets are observed back-to-back in sequence. In this way, the science targets themselves can be used as reference star PSFs for other science targets. A clear way to enhance the sensitivity of high-contrast observations with JWST is a large reference PSF library. A large set of observed PSFs is likely to have enough diversity to capture most details in most PSFs, enabling effective PSF removal. Here we present a compilation of a large PSF library using data from various JWST programs collectively referred to as the JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: GO 4050, GO 5835 and SURVEY 6005. All of these programs share the same observing setup and thus can serve as suitable reference PSFs for each other. These are also common observing setups for exoplanet imaging in general, so this library can be used to improve sensitivity (particularly at close angular separations of the star) in a large number of datasets. This paper is organized as follows: in Section II we describe the surveys our library was constructed from; Section III outlines the data reduction and the PSF library construction; Section IV describes a suite of tests performed to identify PSF subtraction parameters that maximize sensitivity with our library; Section V describes the best sensitivities achieved in the background-limited regime and the speckle-limited regime; in Section VI we investigate the sensitivity improvements of using a large PSF library. Finally, we discuss some of our findings in Section VII, including practical recommendations for JWST post-processing, and conclude in Section VIII.

papers.title: Complex Interplay between Outer Disk Dynamics and Inner Water Reservoir
papers.abstract: We present a homogeneous characterization of outer disk dust and gas properties for 51 protoplanetary disks from the JWST/MIRI Cycle 1 programs, combining new ALMA observations with archival data. Visibility fitting with frank recovers more and higher-contrast substructures in the mm continuum than image-plane analysis, placing the innermost features of several disks at 4-5 au and leaving only three disks featureless at the current resolution. CO gas disk sizes span $\sim$60-1000 au and correlate strongly with mm continuum sizes, with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$ ranging from 1.4 to 9.7 (median 2.95). We then connect these outer disk properties to JWST/MIRI inner disk water diagnostics. We find no global correlation between the cold-to-hot water flux ratio ($F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$), a proposed proxy of cold water enrichment by pebble transport, and any single outer disk parameter, including $R_{\rm mm}$, $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$, and innermost substructure location. Three compact ($R_{\rm mm}<30$ au), structureless disks with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}>4$ show both elevated $F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$ and cold water emission near the snowline temperature, consistent with unimpeded inward drift of icy pebbles. For structured disks, the water properties instead vary widely at fixed gap location, reflecting the sensitivity of the inner disk water content to multiple factors, including gap leakiness, grain size, and thermal history. Linking outer disk dust evolution to inner disk water content thus requires carefully selected samples with detailed constraints on these additional parameters.

papers.intro:
The composition of planets is set, in part, by the volatile budget available in the protoplanetary disk during the epoch of planet formation. Within the inner few AU of the protoplanetary disk, gas-phase molecules including H2O, CO2, HCN, and C2H2 trace the local chemical environment, where rocky planets assemble. Water is of particular interest, both as one of the most abundant volatile species and as a tracer of the delivery of oxygen-rich icy material to the inner disk [122]. Understanding how this inner disk water reservoir is built up and replenished over time is therefore central to the broader question of how planets acquire their volatile inventories.

Water is of particular interest, both as one of the most abundant volatile species and as a tracer of the delivery of oxygen-rich icy material to the inner disk [122]. Understanding how this inner disk water reservoir is built up and replenished over time is therefore central to the broader question of how planets acquire their volatile inventories.

Infrared spectroscopy provides the main window into this reservoir. Spitzer/IRS observations first established that water vapor and simple organics are common in the inner region of T Tauri disks [22, 99, 91]. Water has a dense forest of rotational transitions across mid-infrared wavelengths, with upper-level energies (EupE_{\rm up}) from a few hundred to several thousand Kelvin, that together probe different regions of the disk, from the hot innermost AU to the cooler gas near the water snowline. Retrieving this radial information is essential as it ties the observed emission to the physical processes acting at each location [14]. Spitzer/IRS could not access it, however, because its resolving power (R∼600R\sim 600–700) left transitions blended and slab-model fits carry large uncertainties in derived gas properties [97]. The Medium Resolution Spectrometer [127, MRS; R∼1800R\sim 1800–4000,] on JWST/MIRI [93] now separates many individual lines, and curated lists of unblended transitions allow water excitation conditions to be characterized across the disk population [15, 39]. These advances make it possible to robustly test what physically regulates the inner disk water reservoir.

One leading hypothesis is that radial pebble drift from the outer disk plays a central role. Beyond the water snowline (∼\sim1–3 AU in the midplane for young Sun-like stars), water vapor condenses onto dust grains, forming icy pebbles that populate the cold outer disk. Aerodynamic drag drives these pebbles inward [126], and once they cross the snowline, sublimation of their ice mantles can enhance the local gas-phase water abundance [25]. High-resolution ALMA imaging has shown that gaps and rings are common in the millimeter (mm) dust distribution of disks [4, 71], which may act as pressure bumps that trap dust pebbles and regulate this process. Disk models that track pebble drift together with ice sublimation and vapor transport predict that the strength and duration of the resulting water enrichment depend sensitively on whether and where such bumps intercept the drifting pebbles [20, 61, 60, 75]. Dust opacity, grain settling, and the broader thermal and chemical disk evolution may also modulate the observed water content [102, 47, 21, e.g.,].

The first observational evidence that outer disk structure shapes the inner water reservoir came from Banzatti et al. [12], who used Spitzer spectra to show that compact mm disks tend to have brighter water emission than their more extended and often structured counterparts. This built on earlier work linking the inner disk HCN-to-water emission ratio to outer disk dust mass [83]. JWST/MIRI has since enabled more direct tests. Banzatti et al. [13] reported excess cool water emission near the water ice sublimation front (∼\sim200 K) in two compact, mostly featureless disks relative to two large, gap-bearing ones, consistent with pebble drift proceeding largely unimpeded in the former (see also Arulanantham et al. 10, Romero-Mirza et al. 95). Larger samples have complicated this picture. Focusing on compact disks (mm disk size << 40 au) alone, Temmink et al. [112] found cold water emission ranging from enhanced to depleted, indicating that outer disk size does not by itself set the inner disk water content. Similarly, Gasman et al. [39] found that resolved mm gaps do not always suppress cold water emission across disks spanning a range of substructures. Banzatti et al. [15] then pointed out a number of factors (including binarity, inner cavity, and cloud contamination) that may affect inner water emission properties beyond pebble drift. The observational link between outer disk dust dynamics and inner disk water content thus remains unsettled.

papers.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

papers.intro:
Threat hunters face large volumes of unknown binaries and must decide quickly and safely which ones deserve scarce human attention (Bailey et al., 2007; Bayer et al., 2009). Dynamic analysis is the de facto standard (Egele et al., 2012), but it is costly (Botacin, 2024), requires a secure environment in which it can execute the sample (Graziano et al., 2015), and can still be evaded by environment-aware (Kirat et al., 2014; Miramirkhani et al., 2017) or stalling malware (Kolbitsch et al., 2011; K"uchler et al., 2021). On the other hand, static analysis avoids execution and can in principle inspect the entire program, but may be impeded by packing and obfuscation (Moser et al., 2007). It also carries a scaling cost: a single binary can decompile into hundreds or thousands of functions (Marcelli et al., 2022), far more than an analyst or a fixed LLM context window can read. These constraints motivate a bounded first pass that clears likely benign samples, flags samples with malicious evidence, and escalates cases that cannot be resolved from available static evidence.

Dynamic analysis is the de facto standard (Egele et al., 2012), but it is costly (Botacin, 2024), requires a secure environment in which it can execute the sample (Graziano et al., 2015), and can still be evaded by environment-aware (Kirat et al., 2014; Miramirkhani et al., 2017) or stalling malware (Kolbitsch et al., 2011; K"uchler et al., 2021). On the other hand, static analysis avoids execution and can in principle inspect the entire program, but may be impeded by packing and obfuscation (Moser et al., 2007). It also carries a scaling cost: a single binary can decompile into hundreds or thousands of functions (Marcelli et al., 2022), far more than an analyst or a fixed LLM context window can read. These constraints motivate a bounded first pass that clears likely benign samples, flags samples with malicious evidence, and escalates cases that cannot be resolved from available static evidence.

The consequences of these decisions are asymmetric. Within an intake workflow, clearing malware as benign is difficult to recover from because the sample leaves the analysis queue. Escalating a benign sample does consume downstream analysis resources, but the error can still be corrected. A triage procedure should therefore expose uncertainty rather than forcing every sample into a committed benign or malicious verdict. We represent this uncertainty through a third verdict, suspicious, which routes the sample to deeper analysis.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are a plausible tool for this setting because they can interpret decompiled code and use external tools to acquire additional context (Yang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2023). Code property graphs (CPGs) provide a corresponding navigation substrate by combining call relationships with control- and data-flow information in a queryable program representation (Yamaguchi et al., 2014; Weiss and Banse, 2022). However, these capabilities do not remove the underlying scale constraint. Whole binaries remain too large or costly to inspect exhaustively (Wang et al., 2026), many recovered functions contain boilerplate or library code, and unbounded agent exploration is expensive and difficult to compare reproducibly (Mohammadi et al., 2025). This raises the empirical question we study: how do current LLMs behave when they must triage a binary from a small, graph-selected subset of its functions, and how does model choice affect the balance between clearance, malware detection, and escalation?

To investigate this question, we introduce TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed, graph-guided pipeline for static triage of Windows PE binaries. The system receives a CPG obtained from a decompiled binary together with its PE metadata and operates in three stages. First, an LLM-free heuristic ranks the recovered functions and analyzes the highest-ranked ones to initialize an evidence dossier. Second, an agent expands this dossier by following call-graph leads under a fixed exploration budget. Finally, a reporting agent reviews the frozen dossier and returns a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. TRIAGE-CPG therefore provides a common evidence interface through which different models can be compared under the same constraints.

papers.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Observed Sensitivities to the Wide-Separation, Cold, Sub-Jupiter Exoplanet Population
papers.abstract: We present a sensitivity analysis of three recent JWST direct imaging programs (GO-4050, GO-5835, and SURVEY-6005) designed to build a demographic study of sub-Jupiter mass ($0.1 - 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$) exoplanets in nearby young associations and moving groups. We find that these programs are sensitive to sub-Saturn to Jupiter mass exoplanets with effective temperature (T$_\mathrm{eff}$) as low as $\lesssim 250$ K, already at $\sim 2$ arcsec. A comparison with the SHINE survey confirms that the improvements in mass sensitivity provided by JWST high-contrast imaging surveys outpace current ground observation for masses $\lesssim 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$ and separations between $\sim20-500$ au, opening up a novel parameter space to explore. Overall, this analysis provides a robust framework for interpreting future exoplanet detections. By correlating photometrically derived properties (e.g. mass, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and separation) with theoretical model predictions, we show how the access to potentially low detectable masses (sub-Saturn to Jupiter) strongly depends on the expected atmospheric chemistry of the exoplanet population.

papers.title: Two new Li-rich dwarf stars in M 4: abundance patterns and possible origins
papers.abstract: Context. Li-rich stars are rare, and only 16 are known in globular clusters (GCs), spanning evolutionary stages from the main sequence turnoff to the red giant branch. Their origin is still debated, but GCs provide a unique environment to discriminate among proposed mechanisms for Li enrichment. Aims. We aim to characterise two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars, 44606 and 58195, in the GC M 4 (NGC 6121) and investigate their origin among the formation channels proposed in the literature. The previously known Li-rich star in the cluster, namely 37934, was re-analyzed for comparison. Methods. We performed a standard abundance analysis based on 1D model atmospheres in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) on high-resolution Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES). We measured the projected rotational velocity and searched for chromospheric activity. Results. We derive A(Li)= 2.58, 2.51 dex for stars 44606 and 58195, respectively, significantly different from the A(Li) distribution of normal dwarfs in M 4. For the known Li-rich star 37934, we obtain A(Li)= 3.01 dex, consistent with previous work. We estimate detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Nd) in the three stars. None of our targets show detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity. Conclusions. The Li-rich stars analysed here are unevolved, ruling out in-situ Li production. Planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs, and we detect no present-day rotation or activity. By exclusion, the most plausible remaining scenarios involve different types of interaction with a companion, including dynamical interactions, mass transfer, and mergers. Currently, we have not detected a companion.

papers.intro:
Lithium (Li) is one of the few species produced during Big Bang nucleosynthesis, which predicts a cosmological abundance of A(Li) ≃\simeq 2.7 dex (Fields, 2011; Fields et al., 2020). However, the typical Li abundance encountered even in the least processed stellar environments, i.e., metal-poor dwarf stars in the halo, is significantly lower, A(Li) ≃\simeq 2.2 dex (Spite and Spite, 1982). One possible explanation is atomic diffusion, where gravitational settling transports Li from the surface layers into the stellar interior, leading to a lower observed surface abundance (Korn et al., 2006). After the main sequence, the surface Li of low-mass stars is further diluted by two mixing episodes: the first dredge-up at the base of the red giant branch (RGB) and the RGB bump (Gratton et al., 2000; Lind et al., 2009; Mucciarelli et al., 2012).

After the main sequence, the surface Li of low-mass stars is further diluted by two mixing episodes: the first dredge-up at the base of the red giant branch (RGB) and the RGB bump (Gratton et al., 2000; Lind et al., 2009; Mucciarelli et al., 2012).

Within this framework, we need to better understand the mechanisms that alter surface Li abundance in stars. In this respect, Li-rich stars, i.e., stars significantly richer in Li than similar stars, offer a unique perspective. The frequency of Li-rich stars is ≲\lesssim 1% of the disk stars in the Galactic field population and in open clusters (Deepak et al., 2020) and most of them are in the red clump evolutionary phase, i.e., they are burning helium in the core. Different explanations have been proposed for the existence of Li-rich stars, including: Li production through the Cameron-Fowler or other related mechanisms (de La Reza et al., 1996; Charbonnel and Lagarde, 2010; Denissenkov, 2010); mass transfer from a companion able to produce Li, or Li enhancement caused by dynamical interaction with binary companions (Casey et al., 2019); engulfment of a planet or other sub-stellar companion (Siess and Livio, 1999); or production by novae (Romano et al., 2021; Matsuno et al., 2025). Another possibility is that Li, mostly 6Li, is produced in flares in the atmosphere of stars (Ramaty et al., 2000; Tatischeff and Thibaud, 2007; Mott et al., 2017), although it is difficult to explain the entirety of the Li observed in Li-rich stars this way. No firm conclusion has been reached on whether a single mechanism explains all cases, or whether different mechanisms operate at different evolutionary stages or simultaneously.

Globular clusters (GCs) represent a peculiar environment, a crowded ensemble of old, metal-poor, and low-mass stars that has been extensively explored spectroscopically, yielding so far only 16 Li-rich metal-poor stars (one in M 5 Carney et al. 1998; two in NGC 362 Smith et al. 1999; D’Orazi et al. 2015b; one in M 3 Kraft et al. 1999; one in M 68 Ruchti et al. 2011; one in NGC 6397 Koch et al. 2011; one in M 4 Monaco et al. 2012; two in M 68, one in NGC 5053, one in NGC 5897, two in M 30 Kirby et al. 2016; two in ω\omegaCen Mucciarelli et al. 2019, one in NGC 1261 Sanna et al. 2020). Despite their much lower frequency than Li-rich stars in the field and in open clusters (0.2% for the RGB, 1.6% for the AGB, and 0.3% for all giants; Kirby et al. 2016), these Li-rich stars do not cluster around a single evolutionary stage. They span the full magnitude range, from the tip of the RGB to the main-sequence turnoff. Some additional considerations can be made in the case of GCs. First, planet engulfment seems unlikely as an explanation, since only one planet has been found so far in GCs (Cai et al., 2019), out of a present sample of about 4000 known exoplanets. Second, the contribution from novae through galactic chemical evolution can be excluded, since it starts to become important only above [Fe/H] ≃\simeq –1 dex (Romano et al., 2021), although we cannot exclude the pollution by a companion in a nova-like binary system (Matsuno et al., 2025). Third, the lack of concentration around a specific evolutionary stage makes direct Li production in the stars themselves less viable. This leaves binary interactions as the most likely explanation, either through mass transfer from a companion that can produce Li or through dynamical interactions with a companion star that can enhance surface Li abundance. This, of course, does not exclude the possibility that a few giants among the 16 known Li-rich stars actually produced Li themselves, but this should be rare and limited to red giants.

papers.title: Multimodal Fusion with Pre-trained Models for Psychotherapy Outcome Prediction from Emotional Dynamics
papers.abstract: In-session emotional dynamics are associated with psychotherapy outcomes but difficult to measure at scale. Pretrained multimodal models provide automated access to facial, vocal, and textual signals, yet clinical datasets remain small. Our research question is how pretrained multimodal representations can best support psychotherapy outcome prediction under data scarcity. Three studies use 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine session-level outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS). Study 1 asks whether deep learning outperforms classical machine learning: a two-stage deep pipeline, first predicting window-level valence/arousal and then session outcomes, transferred poorly (best single configuration, $r=.078$). Study 2 asks which representation and preprocessing choices work best: statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models achieved average $r=.406$ across nine scales under per-scale configuration selection, up to $r=.490$ for symptom distress, with complementary modalities and no significant benefit from manual affect annotations or therapist features. Study 3 asks whether deep learning remains inferior under these choices: classical models outperformed an optimized single-stage deep model at the single-configuration level ($r=.281$ vs. $.222$) and on all nine scales under matched per-scale selection ($.406$ vs. $.252$). The results suggest that under clinical data scarcity, pretrained representations with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned aggregation.

papers.intro:
Emotions are a central component of psychotherapy, serving as both targets of therapeutic change and indicators of underlying clinical processes. A meta-analysis of 42 studies found a medium-to-large association between patients’ emotional expressions during sessions and treatment outcome [1], and in-session affective experience, characterized by negative valence and high arousal, has been shown to predict subsequent symptom reduction [2]. Yet despite the established clinical relevance of emotional dynamics, their systematic assessment remains a major methodological bottleneck. Traditional approaches rely on post-session self-report questionnaires, which compress rich temporal processes into single retrospective judgments subject to recall bias [3], or on manual observer ratings, which are time-intensive and difficult to scale beyond small research samples [4].

Traditional approaches rely on post-session self-report questionnaires, which compress rich temporal processes into single retrospective judgments subject to recall bias [3], or on manual observer ratings, which are time-intensive and difficult to scale beyond small research samples [4].

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have begun to address this measurement gap. Video-based emotion recognition [5], sentiment analysis of therapy transcripts [6], and vocal affect detection [7] have each shown promise for capturing continuous emotional signals in naturalistic therapeutic settings. Prior automated work in psychotherapy has examined modalities largely in isolation and has often represented non-verbal channels by scalar affect outputs aggregated to coarse session-level summaries, leaving open whether the non-verbal channels lack outcome-relevant signal or whether the signal is lost in how their representations are extracted and aggregated. However, most automated emotion recognition systems are developed and validated on non-clinical datasets: acted performances, crowd-sourced recordings, or laboratory interactions. Such data differ substantially from psychotherapy in their affective characteristics. Therapy sessions involve subtle, often suppressed emotional expressions from patients with clinical disorders who may exhibit flattened affect, emotional incongruence across modalities, or patterns that deviate systematically from normative emotional displays [8, 9]. This domain shift poses a fundamental challenge for transferring pretrained models to clinical applications.

A critical open question, however, concerns how best to extract clinically relevant signal from these pretrained representations. The dominant paradigm in multimodal affective computing favors increasingly complex architectures: hierarchical temporal encoders, cross-modal attention mechanisms, end-to-end differentiable pipelines. They learn to fuse information across modalities and time [14]. While such approaches have achieved strong performance on benchmark datasets with tens of thousands of labeled samples, their suitability for clinical research settings is unclear. Psychotherapy datasets are inherently small due to privacy constraints, informed consent requirements, and the high cost of clinical data collection and annotation. Under these conditions, architectural complexity may become a liability rather than an asset, as models with many parameters are prone to overfitting when training data is limited.

These multimodal features are extracted from 106 annotated psychotherapy sessions from 88 patients and used to predict standardized clinical questionnaires assessing symptom severity, emotional well-being, and in-session affect. Our design directly addresses this open question by testing whether richer representations, denser statistical pooling, and finer temporal granularity capture non-verbal signals that off-the-shelf affect summaries overlook; Figure 1 summarizes the three-study roadmap.

papers.title: Many faces of integer semidefinite programming
papers.abstract: We first establish several properties of integer positive semidefinite matrices, extending known results for binary and ternary positive semidefinite matrices. We then show how to reformulate an integer quadratic program (IQP) as an equivalent integer semidefinite program (ISDP). We distinguish three cases, namely IQPs with two, three, or more than three distinct integer values, and provide several ISDPs for each case. Each reformulation yields either a binary ISDP, a ternary ISDP, or a rescaled version of one of these. The results show that ternary SDP formulations for problems with three distinct integer values provide SDP relaxations with fewer constraints and, in the case of equally spaced integers, also smaller matrix variables than binary-based SDP relaxations. For quadratic problems whose variables can take more than three distinct integer values, one can choose among three formulations based on the size of their matrix variables, the number of constraints, and the strength of the resulting SDP relaxations. We also show how to reformulate a mixed-integer QP as a mixed-integer SDP.

papers.intro:
Integer semidefinite programming can be viewed as a generalization of integer linear programming in which the vector of variables is replaced by a positive semidefinite (PSD) matrix variable whose entries are constrained to be integer. It has recently been shown that integer semidefinite programs (ISDPs) admit significantly different formulations for several classes of problems compared to traditional modeling approaches, and also enable the development of new algorithmic techniques, see e.g., [9, 10]. It is also well known that optimization problems in which variables take values in the set {−1,1}\{-1,1\}, such as the max-cut and max-kk-sat problems, can be formulated as ISDPs [13]. There exist binary SDP formulations for binary quadratically constrained quadratic programs and binary quadratic matrix programs [9]. Recently, it was shown how to model ternary quadratic problems as ternary semidefinite programs (TSDPs) [8].

We do not refer to these two types of matrices as general integer matrices. In this paper, we exploit existing and new results on integer PSD matrices to reformulate IQPs as binary or ternary SDPs, or their rescaled versions.

papers.title: Tunable topological droplets on supercoiled DNA under tension
papers.abstract: DNA--protein co-condensation is an important regulatory mechanism for gene expression and repair. For straight DNA under constant stretching forces, co-condensation is ``all-or-nothing'': above a critical force, condensates are prevented from nucleating, while below it the entire molecule collapses into a droplet. Here we show by coarse-grained simulations and analytic theory that DNA supercoiling mechanically differentiates the condensation substrate: DNA plectonemes constitute force-insulated pockets on which condensates can nucleate even above the critical force. The size of the resulting droplets is tunable through the applied force and linking number. Surface tension drives the coarsening of multiple plectoneme-associated condensates into a single topological droplet. Magnetic tweezers experiments with spermine reproduce both the force-dependent collapse and the supercoiling-dependent condensation.

papers.title: Growing length scales while approaching the glass transition
papers.abstract: Even after decades of research, the nature of the glass transition is controversially debated: Kinetic freezing phenomena, purely local strain-mediated effects, or collective phenomena including a hidden phase transition are usually discussed. In this work, we check reports on clusters of correlated particles in supercooled liquids which grow upon approaching the glass-transition. We specifically focus on dielectric studies providing approximate access to the four-point correlation function, which allows insight into the evolution of so-called amorphous order. Existing temperature-dependent data derived from the three-point correlation function or higher-order dielectric susceptibilities are modeled using the random first-order transition theory combined with the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann law. This ansatz enables detailed predictions concerning normalized correlation lengths or the number of correlated particles as function of temperature and fragility. It provides a good fit to the experimental data for all materials investigated, including network and molecular glass formers and polymers. We conclude that length scales and corresponding particle numbers determined by the different methods used are at least similar and closely related to those considered by the theory. Moreover, the model predictions on the fragility dependence of the number of correlated molecules are at least approximately fulfilled. Existing criticism concerning an apparent lack of criticality in the temperature dependence of experimental correlation lengths is discussed in terms of this fragility dependence: All available data are well consistent with a hidden phase transition which is best revealed for the most fragile liquids.

papers.title: Giant Raman Optical Activity in Chiral and Polar Ni$_3$TeO$_6$
papers.abstract: Raman optical activity (ROA) measures the difference in Raman scattering intensity for right- and left-circularly polarized light and reflects the chirality of excitations. In solids, ROA is commonly very weak. For the phonons of chiral and polar Ni$_3$TeO$_6$, we find a giant ROA with magnitude 100 times higher than commonly reported for molecules. The systematic analysis based on phonon selection rules allows the chiral and achiral scattering channels to be separated. First-principles calculations of the Raman tensor at finite phonon momentum relate the effect to the phonon modulation of the band-geometric and band-dispersion contributions to optical gyrotropy. This establishes Raman optical activity as a probe of electron--phonon modulation of the band geometry in an insulator.

papers.intro:
Chirality, the breaking of all inversion symmetries of static objects or dynamic motions, is one of the fundamental concepts in nature. Its relevance encompasses all fields of science, from the handedness of electroweak interaction to the function of biomolecules in life science. Similarly, it also plays a remarkable role in a plethora of phenomena in condensed matter physics, from the basic, long-known concept of optical activity to more recent discoveries like Klein tunneling of chiral fermions in graphene [27] and orbital momentum monopoles in chiral systems for use in orbitronics [67]. Chiral bosons, or specifically chiral phonons, are a much more recent discovery [73]. The term implies a unidirectional circular motion of atoms. They are expected to have a strong impact on the physical properties of materials [72, 13, 53, 14], specifically applications such as controllable phononic heat transport [38, 12, 52]. They are also promising as robust information carriers for solid state quantum information applications [11], specifically because they can be selectively manipulated by coupling with circularly polarized light [12, 50]. Raman scattering has recently been rediscovered [12, 26, 25, 63] as a detection method for chiral systems by utilizing the phenomenon of linear wave-vector shifts that lead to energy splitting of degenerate phonon modes close to the Γ\Gamma point [56, 57, 55, 17, 22, 8]. However, the small momentum transfer from visible light to the material causes the effect to be extremely weak. Using higher energy photons is one way to circumvent this problem [65]. Another way to detect chirality of vibrations that has been long established in spectroscopy of chiral molecules [5, 4, 3, 6] could be Raman optical activity (ROA), which instead of an energy splitting measures the difference in scattering intensity for incident left- or right-circularly polarized light (L/R). This effect, first described by Barron and Buckingham in 1971 [5], originates from the finite influence of magnetic dipole- and electric quadrupole transition moments in chiral systems. Besides the conventionally considered interaction in Raman scattering, which assumes electric dipole transitions for both the absorption and emission part of the scattering process, this creates additional, chiral scattering terms in the Raman intensity: IRaman∝Ip​p+Ip​m+Ip​Θ+higher​orders.\centering I_{\mathrm{Raman}}\propto I_{pp}+I_{pm}+I_{p\Theta}+\mathrm{higher\ orders}.\@add@centering (1) Here, Ip​pI_{pp} is the usual achiral contribution due to purely electric dipole processes, while Ip​mI_{pm} and Ip​ΘI_{p\Theta} are the chiral electric dipole - magnetic dipole and electric dipole - electric quadrupole contributions. Although ROA has been established first and foremost as a technique for identifying chiral molecules, the principle can be applied just as well to crystals. Nevertheless, only few results for ROA on crystalline materials have been reported, and those mostly show weak effects [39], or acquire chirality only through external influences like magnetic field [60] or chiral charge-density waves [36]. More recently, a ROA-like signature in Raman spectra of NiCo2TeO6 was attributed to ferroaxial phonons [44]. Ni3TeO6 crystallizes in the chiral and pyroelectric space group R​3R3 [48, 7, 66, 74], with planes of edge-sharing NiO6 and TeO6 octahedra that are stacked in a spiral pattern along the c axis. Below TN=52T_{N}=52 K [74, 49], collinear antiferromagnetic order emerges and is accompanied by a spin-induced electric polarization change [49, 28]; related first-principles work on the spin-flop transition in the isostructural Ni2InSbO6 is reported in Ref. [51]. Here, we show that in this material, some phonons display a ROA that is orders of magnitude higher than what has been reported for naturally chiral solid state systems. Additionally, selection rules for the chiral and achiral scattering contributions allow for complete separation of the two components in the Raman spectrum for one phonon type by controlling the polarization of incident and scattered light. From the modeling perspective, although tools to compute ROA for molecules exist [9, 59, 46, 40], the situation is fundamentally different for a periodic solid: Optical responses are intimately connected to the quantum geometry and topology of the band structure. Transition dipole moments are directly related to the components of the quantum geometric tensor, while the magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments are directly related to the interband Berry curvature. Berry-geometric effects are most commonly discussed in connection with electronic transport, where avoided crossings close to the Fermi level often dominate intrinsic responses such as the anomalous Hall effect. In an insulating optical response, however, there is no Fermi surface: the relevant geometric information is carried by virtual transitions between occupied and empty bands over a finite energy window. The present results demonstrate that phonons can strongly modulate these interband geometric matrix elements and the accompanying band-dispersion terms, making Raman optical activity a sensitive probe of electronic band geometry in an insulator. The splitting of chiral EE phonons along the chiral cc axis contributes to the ROA of the EE modes.

papers.title: Robust Optimal Network Reduction for Distribution Systems
papers.abstract: Network reduction replaces large networks with smaller equivalents to speed up power flow and optimization studies. Optimal Kron-based Reduction of Networks (Opti-KRON) finds the optimal set of nodes to faithfully represent a large-scale radial network for representative loading scenarios. Under unseen nodal injections, however, its accuracy can drop. This paper extends Opti-KRON to uncertain nodal injections using robust uncertainty sets and a Wasserstein ambiguity set, with voltage magnitude error guarantees. To improve scalability, we develop a presolve screening step to eliminate redundant constraints and variables while preserving the feasible set. We also adopt adversarial constraint generation to reduce memory requirements by iteratively adding worst-case nodal injections. On a real 8,387-node feeder at a threshold of 0.001~p.u., the reduction removes 49.9% of the nodes. For one uncertainty set, adversarial constraint generation cuts the required memory by a factor of more than 18.

papers.intro:
The computational burden of power flow and optimization problems in distribution systems increases with network size. Network reduction lowers this burden by replacing a large feeder with a smaller equivalent network. However, reducing network size introduces modeling errors.

The computational burden of power flow and optimization problems in distribution systems increases with network size. Network reduction lowers this burden by replacing a large feeder with a smaller equivalent network. However, reducing network size introduces modeling errors.

Various network reduction methods have been developed to reduce distribution networks while preserving the accuracy of nodal voltages [1, 2]. Optimal Kron-based Reduction of Networks (Opti-KRON) formulates network reduction as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) that selects the nodes to keep. It minimizes the number of kept nodes while keeping the voltage magnitude errors within a threshold for a set of representative loading scenarios [3, 4, 5]. Kron reduction eliminates the other nodes from the nodal admittance equations and gives an equivalent network on the kept nodes [1].

Optimal Kron-based Reduction of Networks (Opti-KRON) formulates network reduction as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) that selects the nodes to keep. It minimizes the number of kept nodes while keeping the voltage magnitude errors within a threshold for a set of representative loading scenarios [3, 4, 5]. Kron reduction eliminates the other nodes from the nodal admittance equations and gives an equivalent network on the kept nodes [1].

The accuracy of Opti-KRON depends on the loading scenarios considered during the reduction process. As nodal injections vary due to changes in demand and generation, operating conditions outside these scenarios may result in voltage magnitude errors above the threshold. Robust optimization accounts for such variations by considering a set of possible realizations of uncertain nodal injections [6]. However, the resulting robust optimization problems can be computationally prohibitive for large feeders. To address these challenges, this paper makes the following contributions: • Robust optimal network reduction: We extend Opti-KRON to uncertain nodal injections through robust uncertainty sets and a Wasserstein ambiguity set. Under LinDistFlow, the voltage magnitude error is linear in the injections for a given reduction, which allows exact reformulations of the error constraints. • Scalable solution methods: We develop screening rules based on voltage differences within candidate clusters and bounds on error coefficients to eliminate infeasible node assignments and redundant error constraints. We also adopt adversarial constraint generation to avoid constructing large robust counterparts by iteratively adding worst-case nodal injections. • Validation on realistic networks: We validate and compare methods on large-scale distribution feeders.

papers.title: What's the Difference? Voice Design and Confirmation Bias in AI-Assisted Self-Diagnosis: Anthropomorphic vs. Machine-Like Voice Output
papers.abstract: As symptom checkers based on artificial intelligence (AI) are becoming common entry points for health information, their influence on lay users' diagnostic decisions raises questions about trust and bias. Of particular concern is confirmation bias, the tendency to favour information that supports one's existing belief while discounting information that contradicts it. One of the central design choices for such systems is the style of voice: whether they should present themselves with a human-like (anthropomorphic) or a clearly machine-like (xenomorphic) voice. This study investigates whether the voice design of an AI symptom checker modulates confirmation bias in self-diagnosis. In a within-subjects online experiment (N = 81 participants, 648 trials), participants selected a diagnosis and rated their confidence, then heard an AI-generated recommendation that either confirmed or contradicted their initial choice, delivered by an anthropomorphic or a machine-like voice, before deciding again. We observed a strong, direction-dependent influence of the AI: participants revised their diagnosis in 45.7% of trials when the AI contradicted them versus 1.2% when it confirmed them (generalised linear mixed model, GLMM, p < .001); confidence rose under confirmation but barely moved under contradiction (robust linear mixed model, p < .001); and decisions took longer after contradiction (Gamma GLMM, p < .001). This effect did not differ between the two voices (no voice or interaction term was significant, smallest p = .282), even though a manipulation check confirmed the voices were perceived as markedly different. The findings suggest that the direction of an AI recommendation, rather than the anthropomorphism of its voice, drives confirmation-related bias in AI-assisted self-diagnosis.

Symptom checkers based on artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly used as accessible tools for preliminary health assessment. By allowing users to enter symptoms and receive possible diagnoses or triage advice, these systems may support early orientation before professional consultation. However, prior research has raised concerns about their diagnostic reliability, safety, and suitability for laymen (Wallace et al., 2022; Mentzou et al., 2025).

By allowing users to enter symptoms and receive possible diagnoses or triage advice, these systems may support early orientation before professional consultation. However, prior research has raised concerns about their diagnostic reliability, safety, and suitability for laymen (Wallace et al., 2022; Mentzou et al., 2025).

In medical decision contexts, the interaction between human judgement and AI recommendation is particularly sensitive. Users may not only benefit from AI support but also become vulnerable to automation bias, relying too strongly on automated recommendations even when they are wrong (Kücking et al., 2024; Qazi et al., 2026; Rosbach et al., 2025).

In medical decision contexts, the interaction between human judgement and AI recommendation is particularly sensitive. Users may not only benefit from AI support but also become vulnerable to automation bias, relying too strongly on automated recommendations even when they are wrong (Kücking et al., 2024; Qazi et al., 2026; Rosbach et al., 2025).

Such reliance is further shaped by cognitive biases, that is, systematic deviations from rational judgement that arise from the way people process information. One of the most studied biases is confirmation bias, the tendency to seek out, weigh more heavily (i.e., perceive as higher in quality), and more readily accept information that is consistent with one’s prior beliefs while discounting information that contradicts them (Nickerson, 1998). In self-diagnosis contexts this bias is particularly relevant: users typically form an initial assumption about their symptoms, and they may therefore be more likely to accept AI feedback that supports that assumption than feedback that challenges it. This carries a concrete risk: when both the user and the AI are wrong, an agreeing recommendation can produce a false confirmation (Rosbach et al., 2025). A layperson may, for instance, be falsely reassured that their symptoms do not require immediate medical attention and therefore fail to seek help in time.

Voice-based AI assistants add another layer to this interaction: spoken recommendations are not perceived as neutral information, since vocal characteristics shape perceived credibility, social presence, and trust (Seaborn et al., 2021), and trust in healthcare voice assistants has been shown to depend on perceived usefulness, content credibility, service quality, and risk-related factors (Zhan et al., 2024). This raises a central design question: whether patient-facing AI should imitate human interaction or present itself as clearly non-human. Anthropomorphic design is often pursued precisely to make a system feel familiar and to engender trust; a machine-like (xenomorphic) design instead emphasises the system’s artificial nature and may reduce patient confusion by clearly distinguishing AI from human physicians (Milford et al., 2025).

While previous work has examined the accuracy of symptom checkers and trust in healthcare voice assistants, less is known about how the voice design of an AI symptom checker influences users’ diagnostic decisions after confirming or contradicting advice. This study addresses that gap, testing whether users exhibit a general confirmation bias toward the AI - across diagnostic choice, confidence, and response time - and, as its primary question, whether the strength of that bias is moderated by the AI’s voice design (anthropomorphic vs. machine-like). This paper makes three contributions: (i) a controlled within-subjects design that isolates the direction of an AI recommendation from its vocal presentation in a self-diagnosis task; (ii) mixed-effects evidence for a strong, direction-dependent confirmation bias across choice, confidence, and response time; and (iii) the finding that this bias is unaffected by whether the AI speaks with an anthropomorphic or a machine-like voice, despite a successful perceptual manipulation.

papers.title: Characterizing nonlocal Sobolev spaces as generalized Bessel potential spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study nonlocal Sobolev spaces $H^{\rho,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $p \in (1,\infty)$, defined via a general class of nonlocal gradients $D^\rho$ associated with a kernel function $\rho$. As our main contribution, we establish three new equivalent characterizations of these spaces. First, we describe $H^{\rho,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ in terms of Fourier multipliers involving the symbol of the nonlocal potential associated with $D^\rho$. Second, we give a thorough functional analytic treatment of the nonlocal $\rho$-Laplacian $\Delta^\rho$, which allows us to represent general nonlocal Sobolev spaces through its square root $(-\Delta^\rho)^{1/2}$. Third, we show that $H^{\rho,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ coincides with the image $g_\rho * L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for a suitable convolution kernel $g_\rho \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$, which confirms that these spaces are genuine potential spaces. These results generalize the well-known fact that, in the special case of the Riesz kernel, the resulting fractional Sobolev spaces coincide with the classical Bessel potential spaces. In this spirit, the present work can also be viewed as introducing a natural notion of generalized Bessel potential spaces.
