The Riesz fractional gradient was probably first studied in its own right in [20] by Horváth and then very prominently in the more recent works [33] and [34] by Shieh and Spector (see their papers also for further historical comments and mentions of earlier appearances of the same object in the literature), even though it is closely related and owes its name to the Riesz potentials introduced by Riesz already in [29] (see also [30]). As established in [33], the function spaces associated to the Riesz fractional gradient coincide with the fractional Sobolev spaces known as Bessel potential spaces, going back to the work [2] by Aronszajn and Smith. These spaces have been the object of intensive study since the 1960s and play a key role in the modern fields of potential theory, harmonic analysis and interpolation theory (see, e.g., the classical references [2, 38, 9, 39, 1], as well as the recent works [6, 3]), not mentioning many others. However, Riesz fractional gradients are only a model example of a wider class of nonlocal gradients, where the common local gradient is replaced by an integral over the first order difference quotient weighted with a general kernel ([25, 7, 13, 8]). Nonlocal gradients have gained popularity in applied mathematics over the course of the last decades as an alternative approach to models involving conventional differential operators, and important applications comprise peridynamics and nonlocal hyperelasticity (see, e.g., [37, 24, 4]). Mathematically speaking, nonlocal gradients provide a means to enforce relaxed regularity requirements, in contrast with classical Sobolev spaces, upon the functions in question, while a lot of elements in the standard functional analytic toolbox, as a generalized fundamental theorem of calculus, Poincaré-type inequalities, compactness properties, and embedding relations, are usually still available in this broader setting ([12, 13, 8]).

papers.title: Inferring accretion bursts in intermediate-mass protostars from asteroseismic imprints
papers.abstract: During star formation, objects may gain the majority of their final mass through regular and intense bursts of mass accretion. For bursts of the FU Orionis-type (FUor), accretion rates can climb to $10^{-3} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$ during short windows of time, amounting to just a few percent of the main accretion phase. To study the occurrence of such events observationally, signatures of the current accretion bursts and tracers of recent bursts are crucial. We investigate the potential to identify accretion bursts in protostars and pre-main sequence stars of intermediate mass using asteroseismology. We use the stellar structure and evolution code MESA to evolve stellar models from the protostellar seed phase of $0.01 \ \text{M}_\odot$ and $1.5 \ \text{R}_\odot$ up to $4.0 \ \text{M}_\odot$ with a constant accretion rate of $10^{-6} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$. A single accretion burst is initialized during the accretion phase. The stellar oscillation code GYRE is employed to compute the resulting asteroseismic properties of the models. Accretion bursts of up to $10^{-3} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$ are sufficient to cause the convective cores of the models to recede, leaving behind a chemical trace which manifests itself in the form of quasi-periodic dips in the g-mode period spacing. This effect is strongest during the outburst, but also lingers for up to 475 years before the convective core is re-established and the dips are gone. Our experiment shows that a single accretion burst leaves an imprint in the deep interiors of protostars and pre-MS stars of intermediate mass, and that this imprint can be captured with asteroseismology. Our results are most conclusive for burst magnitudes greater than $1\times10^{-4} \ \text{M}_\odot \text{yr}^{-1}$, corresponding to FUor-type bursts.

Stars form during the gravitational collapse of dense molecular cloud cores. However, most of their final mass comes not directly from the cloud but rather from a protostellar disk that forms shortly after the protostar due to non-zero angular momentum in the cloud. The character of this so-called disk-mediated protostellar accretion depends not only on the physical mechanisms that drive mass and angular momentum transport in the disk, but also on the immediate circumdisk environment, and may be unique to each object (Hartmann, 2009).

Stars form during the gravitational collapse of dense molecular cloud cores. However, most of their final mass comes not directly from the cloud but rather from a protostellar disk that forms shortly after the protostar due to non-zero angular momentum in the cloud. The character of this so-called disk-mediated protostellar accretion depends not only on the physical mechanisms that drive mass and angular momentum transport in the disk, but also on the immediate circumdisk environment, and may be unique to each object (Hartmann, 2009).

One plausible formation scenario is variable accretion with episodic bursts (Hartmann and Kenyon, 1996; Vorobyov and Basu, 2015). Here, the protostar acquires a substantial portion of its final mass (Dunham and Vorobyov, 2012; Meyer et al., 2021, up to 50%;) via short but intense episodes of mass accretion, often exceeding 10−4​M⊙​yr−110^{-4}\ \text{M}_{\odot}\ \text{yr}^{-1} at the peak, while having low-rate quiescent accretion in between the bursts. Such bursts are known as FU Orionis-type eruptions (Ambartsumian, 1971, FUors, after) and several dozens of such objects have been identified to date (Audard et al., 2014; Connelley and Reipurth, 2018; Fischer et al., 2023).

The exact mechanism of the burst in FUors has not been determined so far and many possibilities have been proposed in the literature (see a review in Audard et al., 2014 and more recent mechanisms in Dullemond et al., 2019; Borchert et al., 2022; Demidova and Grinin, 2023; Nayakshin et al., 2023; Skliarevskii and Vorobyov, 2023; Cecil and Flock, 2024). Regardless of the triggering mechanism, the bursts affect the evolution of both the star and protostellar disk via energy release at the stellar surface during the burst phase, and are an important ingredient of star and planet formation. For instance, bursts can evaporate volatile species and alter the chemical composition (Rab et al., 2017; Molyarova et al., 2018; Guadarrama et al., 2024), shift the snowlines (Cieza et al., 2016; Tobin et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024), and affect dynamics, dust growth, and refractory species in protoplanetary disks (Hubbard, 2017; Vorobyov et al., 2020a; Vorobyov et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Colmenares et al., 2024). Furthermore, bursts can affect the pre-main sequence (pre-MS) evolution of stars, contributing to a luminosity spread in stellar populations and triggering peculiar excursions on the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram in single star evolution (Baraffe et al., 2012; Kunitomo et al., 2017; Jensen and Haugbølle, 2018; Elbakyan et al., 2019; Meyer et al., 2019). Bursts can also leave imprints on the stellar pulsation modes in δ\delta-Scuti and low-mass protostars (Steindl et al., 2021; Steindl et al., 2022b; Jørgensen et al., 2025).

To assess the impact of outbursts on star- and planet formation, it is important to have a census of FUors that is as complete as possible. The FUor-type outbursts in low-mass protostars (0.5<M⁡[M⊙]<1.50.5<M\ [\text{M}_{\odot}]<1.5) are short-lived events, lasting from tens to perhaps a few hundreds of years (Audard et al., 2014). Only about half of known burst sources were observed in the pre-burst quiescent phase (Vorobyov et al., 2021), making their identification as FUors firmly established. The other so-called FUor-like objects were not observed before outburst and were mainly classified as FUors based on their peculiar spectral characteristics (Connelley and Reipurth, 2018).

Identifying current and past FUor-type bursts in the young intermediate-mass protostars (1.5<M⁡[M⊙]<7.01.5<M\ [\text{M}_{\odot}]<7.0; YIMS) may be even more challenging than in their low-mass counterparts. Recent numerical simulations suggest that outbursts in YIMS can be long-lived phenomena, up to several kyr (Das et al., 2025a). This makes it difficult to identify the outburst objects as FUors because the onset of the burst likely occurred before photometric observations began. For example, a long-lived outburst in RNO 54 (Hillenbrand et al., 2023) was not classified as a FUor for more than half of its estimated 130+ yr outburst duration. Therefore, having a definitive identifier of a source that is undergoing a FUor outburst, particularly in the rarer YIMSs, will help improve the completeness of the known sample of FUors.

papers.title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction
papers.abstract: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

papers.intro:
Predicting near-term hospital discharge from electronic health records (EHRs) is a clinically valuable yet methodologically challenging task. In particular, models trained on clinical notes may become susceptible to implicit temporal leakage, where discharge-related phrases appear in notes written close to or after the decision point, potentially inflating predictive performance. While recent clinical NLP studies report strong performance using large language models or fine-tuned transformers, such gains often obscure whether models rely on clinically valid signals or spurious lexical shortcuts [1, 2].

In particular, models trained on clinical notes may become susceptible to implicit temporal leakage, where discharge-related phrases appear in notes written close to or after the decision point, potentially inflating predictive performance. While recent clinical NLP studies report strong performance using large language models or fine-tuned transformers, such gains often obscure whether models rely on clinically valid signals or spurious lexical shortcuts [1, 2].

Existing approaches [3, 4] typically treat interpretability as a post-hoc explanatory tool, rather than as a mechanism to enforce input validity. As a result, explanation methods such as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are often used to rationalize predictions after training, without preventing models from learning leakage-prone cues in the first place. This raises broader concerns about robustness, generalizability, and deployability in real clinical settings. For example, progress notes authored on the operative day frequently contain phrases such as “anticipate discharge tomorrow,” “likely home POD1,” or abbreviated tokens such as “dc” or “DC.” Although such notes precede the formal discharge event, they encode downstream clinical decisions and act as direct proxies for the target label. Models trained on these notes can therefore achieve inflated performance without learning clinically meaningful predictors of readiness for discharge.

We evaluate this approach using retrospective EHR data from 1,956 elective spine surgery encounters at a large academic medical center.

papers.title: Observables and Symmetries in Causal Fermion System
papers.abstract: We investigate the interplay of observables and symmetries in the framework of causal fermion systems (CFS). We show that position observables transform covariantly under unitary symmetries and for static CFS we derive their Heisenberg-type evolution. To give these results a geometric interpretation, we establish conditions under which spacetime isometries induce symmetries of CFS constructed from solutions of the Dirac equation. The crucial link is provided by the Dirac equation itself, which relates the infinitesimal generators of the geometric and CFS symmetries. In static spacetimes, this allows us to identify the generator of the induced unitary symmetry with the spatial Dirac Hamiltonian.

papers.intro:
The framework of causal fermion systems provides a unified description of spacetime and quantum matter in terms of a measure on a space of linear operators [1, 2, 3]. The operators encode the local correlations of quantum states, and spacetime is identified with the support of the measure. The dynamics are governed by the causal action principle. In the continuum limit, the equations of general relativity and the gauge field interactions of the Standard Model emerge from its Euler–Lagrange equations [4, 5]. Recently, the continuum limit analysis has been extended to general globally hyperbolic spacetimes [6]. Moreover, quantum field theory has been recovered in a suitable limiting regime [7, 8]. The framework has also given rise to novel phenomenological proposals, including a mechanism for baryogenesis and effective collapse models [9, 10, 11]. Taken together, these developments establish causal fermion systems as a leading candidate for a unified theory of fundamental physics.

Symmetries play a fundamental role in modern theoretical physics. In [12], it was shown that, for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, continuous maps preserving the causal action principle are induced by unitary or antiunitary transformations of the underlying Hilbert space. Correspondingly, symmetries of a given causal fermion systems are realized by such transformations that leave its measure invariant [13, 14, 15]. Symmetries have also been investigated in the context of causal variational principles, where Noether-like theorems give rise to conservation laws expressed through surface layer integrals [14, 16, 17]. This development also opens connections to relational observables and quantum reference frames [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24].

While position observables in causal fermion systems can be associated with arbitrary spacetime regions, there is no a priori prescription for relating observables at different times. To make dynamical predictions, we therefore need to identify how these observables evolve. A one-parameter group of symmetries provides precisely such a relation through its action on spacetime. We show that the invariance of the measure under unitary conjugation implies the covariance of position observables. For a strongly continuous one-parameter group of symmetries, this covariance leads to a Heisenberg–type evolution equation generated by the corresponding self-adjoint operator. In static causal fermion systems, where the symmetry acts by time translations, this gives the familiar form of temporal evolution for position observables. Effective collapse models provide an interesting contrast, as stochastic perturbations can break the symmetry in individual realizations, even when it is retained at the ensemble level [10, 11]. Motivated by the role of commutation relations in these models, we also investigate sufficient conditions under which position observables commute with the symmetry generator.

To investigate symmetries in causal fermion systems constructed from Lorentzian spacetimes, we draw on the extensive mathematical literature on the Dirac equation. Its theory on curved Lorentzian spacetimes is well developed, including the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem on globally hyperbolic spacetimes, finite speed of propagation of solutions [1, Theorem 4.5.2], and the construction of propagators [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. The spectral theory of Dirac operators and their Hamiltonian formulations, particularly on stationary and static spacetimes, have likewise been investigated extensively [30, 31, 32]. The action of spacetime isometries on spinor fields and the associated spinorial Lie derivatives are also well understood [33, 34, 35]. These constructions rely on established functional-analytic tools, including strongly continuous unitary groups, self-adjoint generators, and invariant-core arguments [36, 37, 38, 39]. Particularly important for our purposes is the conserved Dirac current, which gives rise to a positive-definite scalar product on solutions that is independent of the choice of Cauchy hypersurface [25, 40, 29],[1, Section 4]. Together with the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem, this provides canonical unitary identifications between the Hilbert space of Dirac solutions and the Hilbert spaces of initial data on different Cauchy hypersurfaces. In this work, we carefully distinguish these Hilbert spaces and systematically identify the different maps between them, including Cauchy evolution, geometric transport under spacetime isometries, and the induced unitary transformations. The induced unitary action of spacetime symmetries on Dirac solutions has already been investigated in the causal fermion systems context by Finster and Reintjes [41], who studied its implications for the fermionic signature operator and its spectral subspaces.

papers.title: Representability of Galois extensions
papers.abstract: We study faithful Galois extensions in a presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category $\mathscr{C}$ by a dualizable $\mathbb{E}_1$-group $G$. We prove that these extensions correspond to colimit-preserving symmetric monoidal functors from $\mathrm{An}^{\mathrm{B}G}$ to $\mathscr{C}$. Under suitable assumptions, we use this correspondence to construct a Galois pro-anima that classifies Galois extensions in $\mathscr{C}$. This generalizes the \'etale fundamental groupoid of commutative rings and Mathew's weak Galois groupoid.

papers.title: Optimal Quadrature and the Curse of Dimensionality for a Veronese Class
papers.abstract: We study integration on a $3^d$-dimensional trigonometric space whose unit ball has all coordinate mixed partial derivatives bounded by one. With evaluations anywhere in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we determine the exact minimal worst-case error among all deterministic algorithms using at most $n$ function values. An optimal quadrature formula is obtained by truncating an exact product quadrature formula on $\{1/2, 1/2+\pi\}^d$. All weights are positive. For each error tolerance $0<\varepsilon<1$, the information complexity grows exponentially in $d$ with the common base $\Lambda\approx 1.10546546$. The correction of order $\sqrt{d}$ to the logarithm of the information complexity and the corresponding error limit are determined by the standard normal distribution function. For $b\ge 1$ and $n=\lceil b^d\rceil$, the error tends to one, one half, or zero according as $b<\Lambda$, $b=\Lambda$, or $b>\Lambda$.

papers.title: Lipschitz bounds and gradient continuity for the Trudinger equation
papers.abstract: We establish local spatial Lipschitz and gradient H\"older estimates for general nonnegative weak solutions to Trudinger's equation $\partial_t u^{p-1}=\Delta_pu$, $p>1$. The estimates are uniform across the zero set. The proofs combine Bernstein-type estimates for power transformations, smooth approximation, and comparison with exponential barriers near the zero set.

papers.abstract: For a positive integer $n\ge 2$, we look at the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation $$ n(x_1+\cdots+x_n)=x_1\cdots x_n. $$ Denoting by $f(n)$ this number we show that $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \log f(n)/\log n=0$.

papers.title: Towards Informed Autonomy Design: Understanding the Interplay of Function Characteristics and Autonomy Preferences in Automotive Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive, autonomous interactions receive high interest in the field of intelligent assistants, including the automotive domain. A central challenge, however, is identifying appropriate levels of autonomy for different functions while maintaining user acceptance and trust. This work examines how function characteristics relate to suitable autonomy levels and whether these relationships generalize across functions. We conducted an expert workshop to define autonomy levels and identify relevant function characteristics. We then collected data from 126 participants, who rated 14 in-vehicle functions regarding autonomy preferences and function characteristics, from which we trained machine learning models to predict appropriate autonomy levels. Building on our findings, we developed our prototypical Autonomy Design Assistant that supports designers in making autonomy-related decisions, which we evaluated qualitatively with nine experts. Our results suggest that function characteristics can rank functions by their suitable level of autonomy and thereby guide more informed autonomy design decisions, whereas predictions for individual users remain uncertain.

papers.intro:
Intelligent assistants enable new functionalities and enhance user experiences, thus becoming key differentiators in the automotive industry (Lee and Jeon, 2022). Numerous car manufacturers developed on-board assistants, such as Mercedes’ MBUX Virtual Assistant (AG, 2022) and Renault’s digital avatar Reno (Renault, 2025). These assistants, commonly known as conversational agents, are typically activated by user requests (Meurisch et al., 2020), to which they promptly respond (Xi et al., 2023). These agents primarily perform simple, reactive tasks (Meck et al., 2023; Meck and Precht, 2021; Du et al., 2024a). Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly in Large Language Models, have significantly enhanced the reasoning and anticipation capabilities of AI models (Zhang et al., 2024). This progress allows creating assistive systems that can initiate interactions and actions proactively, thereby improving efficiency and effectiveness. Current commercial applications in automotive (AG, 2022) as well as in smart home applications (Panay, 2025) still mainly focus on proactive suggestions, while AI agents’ function-calling capabilities can enable autonomous action execution based on context (e.g., user states (Stampf et al., 2022)) through task-specific functions or API calls, allowing AI systems to anticipate user goals and act on behalf of the user (Bérubé et al., 2024).

Further, users desire proactivity in intelligent in-vehicle systems (Schmidt and Braunger, 2018). Consequently, proactive systems are extensively studied in the automotive domain (Semmens et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021; Mathis et al., 2023a; Schmidt and Braunger, 2018). However, significant concerns exist regarding appropriateness in specific contexts, loss of control, privacy (Reicherts et al., 2021; Meurisch et al., 2020), and interference in multi-party settings (Zargham et al., 2022). As one aspect of appropriateness, several works addressed the question of when to interrupt the user proactively (Semmens et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2021; Mathis et al., 2023a). Further, Meck et al. (2023) investigated how to communicate when being proactive to meet user preferences. Another aspect is the question, which functions should be proactive. Typically, research on proactivity in the automotive domain leverages exemplary use cases as a basis for investigation. However, existing work suggests that user preferences regarding proactivity highly depend on the use case (Schmidt et al., 2019; Mathis et al., 2023b). Accordingly, the generalizability of use-case-specific findings remains unclear, limiting their scalability to other use cases. Further, the question of how much autonomy users prefer for considered use cases remains open.

papers.title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
papers.abstract: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.
papers.intro:
Density-functional calculations [1, 2] are now routinely carried out in automated workflows, which produce materials databases and the training data of machine-learned models [3, 4, 5, 6]. The results of different codes agree at the level of meV [7] in comparisons with matched settings, but whether an individual calculation has reached an acceptable solution is rarely tested. A calculation is declared converged when successive energies agree and the residual of the density or potential is small. Neither criterion is sufficient: a stalled or oscillating iteration can fulfill both, and so can an unstable self-consistent solution or the self-consistent solution of a Hamiltonian that is not the derivative of the reported energy. The common practical safeguard, agreement between different algorithms, fails as well when the algorithms share the same Hamiltonian. For high-throughput data the consequence is not only an energy error: a falsely converged state can carry the wrong magnetic moment or the wrong band gap, and even the wrong sign of the gap, into every quantity and every model derived from it.

Three properties are at stake and must be distinguished. A state is self-consistent if its density and Hamiltonian satisfy the fixed-point condition of the Kohn-Sham equations. It is variationally stable if no descent of the implemented free energy is accessible from it within the tested variational space. A self-consistent state can be a saddle point. The Hamiltonian is consistent with the energy if it is the derivative of the implemented energy functional. Conventional stopping criteria can wrongly suggest any of the three. We use false self-consistency as an umbrella term for a calculation that is reported as converged but fails at least one of them, not only for states that violate the fixed-point equations.

papers.title: Energy spectrum of trions in semiconductors
papers.abstract: Energy levels of trions in a bulk semiconductor crystal are calculated by two different numerical methods. On the one hand, we construct the finite-element solution of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation in the total angular momentum representation. On the other hand, we use the Gaussian expansion method (GEM), applied to each of the three Faddeev components of the wave function. The results for the total angular momenta $J=0$ and $J=1$ of the trion were obtained for a wide range of the hole-to-electron mass ratios covering most existing semiconductor compounds. The dependencies of the energies on the mass ratio for trions in a bulk crystal qualitatively agree with the results for a simplified model of a trion in a 1D quantum wire, for which the three-body energies can be calculated with arbitrary precision as well as easily approximated using Born-Oppenheimer potential-energy curves. A comparison of our results with data from other publicly available three-body codes as well as with the energies of well-known atomic counterparts, in particular, with vibrational energy levels of the molecular hydrogen ion, shows a good agreement and confirms the accuracy of the numerical data. We found that GEM significantly improves the precision of the obtained trion energies compared to previous calculations. Our calculations demonstrate that, for most semiconductor compounds, only one trion state with zero total angular momentum exists.

Electron-hole bound states such as excitons and more complex three- and four-body states such as trions and biexcitons are a key focus of semiconductor spectroscopy [51, 61, 54, 93, 75, 94, 90]. These few-body systems in confined geometries — particularly in heterostructures and transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) monolayers [122, 29] — have attracted significant attention due to their potential use in room-temperature excitonic devices [36, 3, 16] and sensors [85, 20]. This is equally promising for the bulk structures that exhibit excitons with large binding energies [35, 106, 42, 41, 52, 79], that are higher than the characteristic energy of lattice thermal vibrations.

These few-body systems in confined geometries — particularly in heterostructures and transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMDC) monolayers [122, 29] — have attracted significant attention due to their potential use in room-temperature excitonic devices [36, 3, 16] and sensors [85, 20]. Although in conventional bulk semiconductors such as GaAs and CdTe, excitons have relatively small binding energies, their ground-state and excited-state peaks can be rather well observed experimentally [51, 71, 49]. Even smaller binding energies of trions and biexcitons make them more difficult to measure, as their diffuse peaks overlap with much sharper excitonic lines. This is why, despite their long-standing theoretical prediction [69], the first observation of trions (also known as charged excitons) was only possible after the development of growth techniques for heterostructures containing quantum wells (QWls) [58]. Reducing the dimensionality increases the binding energy of electron-hole complexes [22, 11, 57], thus enabling the corresponding peaks in the spectra to be resolved experimentally [113, 60]. The large binding energies of electron-hole complexes in bulk Cu2O and ZnO crystals make these structures promising candidates for observing trions as well. However, achieving uncompensated electrons and holes in these structures remains challenging [115].

Trions in bulk semiconductors are the simplest solid-state three-body systems. For bulk materials, many-body effects, giving rise to trions, can be successfully explained in terms of quasiparticles (or dressed particles) [62]. Therefore, a convenient framework of effective few-body Hamiltonians, allowing for an application of variational methods, is widely used [57]. However, for example, in TMDC monolayers trions appear at much higher densities of charge carriers. For such systems, the properties of trions can only be described from a proper many-body point of view, in particular within the Fermi polaron approach [25, 79, 112]. In this context, it is somewhat surprising that the spectra of trions, at least for the simplest bulk model of two bands with parabolic dispersions, have not been calculated so far. The main reason is probably that the three-body problem with the Coulomb interaction allows only a numerical solution [32]. An analytical solution for the ground state of a three-body system is only known for contact (zero-range) interactions in one dimension [81]. Short-range and long-range interactions between the particles, as well as additional spatial degrees of freedom make the problem analytically intractable. In QWls, the situation is even more complicated: one-dimensional confinement breaks the translational invariance and introduces quantization of the center-of-mass motion. Even studying excitons in QWls requires a computationally complex numerical solution to the three-dimensional Schrödinger equation [60, 9, 11, 12]. Furthermore, due to strong spin-orbit coupling, an accurate theoretical description of exciton spectra in bulk crystals requires one to go beyond the simple parabolic band approximation, i.e. to take into account the complex valence band structure [118, 104, 108, 107, 95, 43, 41]. A simplification can be found for very narrow QWls or quantum wires, for which the center-of-mass quantization is so strong that the relative motion of the charge carriers can be completely separated. Therefore, even within the simplest two-band model, the trion in a QWl is a multidimensional problem that can only be solved by calculating the ground state characteristics using the variational approach with predefined wave functions [114, 116, 121, 124].

In the present article, we study the energy spectra of X+X^{+} trions, consisting of an electron and two holes. The simplest two-band model with parabolic dispersions of the conduction and valence bands is assumed. We obtain spectra of trions in both the bulk crystal and the one-dimensional geometry (cylindrical quantum wire) and map out their unified dependencies on the effective mass ratio. Our study also covers the mass range of the X−X^{-} trion model, which is mathematically identical to the X+X^{+} model by a formal interchange of electrons and holes. Both X+X^{+} and X−X^{-} trion ground states in bulk materials were extensively studied theoretically [121, 21, 78], whereas the existence of excited states is still debated.

Similar one-dimensional three-body models have already been studied before, see Refs. [82, 83, 38, 39]. These works, however, disregarded the interaction between heavy particles, considered only zero-range interactions with the light particle, and mainly presented ground-state energies. In our article, we consider the long-range interactions in all three two-body subsystems and calculate not only the ground state but many energy levels of excited states. Thus, in contrast to Refs. [110, 111], we accurately reconstruct the energy spectrum of the one-dimensional three-body system and observe how it depends on the mass ratio. The exact energy levels are compared with the Born-Oppenheimer [15] approximation as well.

papers.title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

papers.intro:
Seismic interpretation is fundamental to characterizing subsurface structure, stratigraphic architecture, and geologic bodies from reflection seismic data. It provides essential information for geological understanding and for decisions throughout seismic exploration and subsurface development (Geng and Wang, 2020; Yu and Ma, 2021; Mousavi and Beroza, 2022; Khosro Anjom et al., 2024). Deep learning has substantially advanced the automation of seismic interpretation, with specialized models developed for fault detection (Xiong et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019a; Gao et al., 2022; Dou et al., 2024), seismic facies classification (Liu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Kaur et al., 2023), geobody delineation (Gao et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2025), and horizon interpretation (Geng et al., 2020; Roncoroni et al., 2022). These advances still depend heavily on scarce field interpretations or large-scale synthetic training data (Wu et al., 2023). High-quality field labels are costly and time-consuming to obtain, while models trained mainly on synthetic data may suffer from distribution shifts when applied to field surveys. These limitations become particularly severe when only a few annotated sections are available for a new interpretation problem.

High-quality field labels are costly and time-consuming to obtain, while models trained mainly on synthetic data may suffer from distribution shifts when applied to field surveys. These limitations become particularly severe when only a few annotated sections are available for a new interpretation problem.

Despite their different targets, many seismic interpretation tasks rely on common patterns in reflection data. Seismic facies are characterized by recurring variations in reflection amplitude, texture, and geometry that reflect different depositional and stratigraphic settings (Alaudah et al., 2019; Di et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021). Faults appear as local disruptions or offsets of otherwise continuous reflection events (Xiong et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019a). Geobodies such as salt structures and channels produce distinct changes in reflection amplitude, morphology, and continuity because their properties differ from those of the surrounding formations (Gao et al., 2021). Although their prediction targets differ, these tasks all draw on recurring reflection patterns at different spatial scales (Harsuko and Alkhalifah, 2022; Wu et al., 2019b). Most task-specific deep-learning workflows learn representations separately for individual targets and datasets. As a result, the same structural information is relearned for each task from limited annotations. This redundancy motivates a shared seismic representation that can be reused across interpretation tasks.

Foundation models offer a route toward reusable seismic representations. Pretrained vision models can transfer useful features to geophysical data (Guo et al., 2025), while recent seismic foundation models have demonstrated the feasibility of learning from large collections of unlabeled seismic data (Sheng et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026; Ordonez et al., 2026; Archibong et al., 2025). Their downstream applications commonly rely on full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient encoder adaptation (Chai et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021). Masked and reconstruction-based objectives (He et al., 2022; Bao et al., 2021), adopted by several seismic foundation models, learn contextual dependencies by recovering missing content but do not explicitly encourage geological patterns to be separable or patch relations to remain spatially stable. Both properties are especially important in extreme few-shot settings, where downstream supervision is insufficient to substantially reorganize the pretrained feature space (Zhou et al., 2023).

Both properties are especially important in extreme few-shot settings, where downstream supervision is insufficient to substantially reorganize the pretrained feature space (Zhou et al., 2023).

This raises a central question for seismic foundation models: can large-scale unlabeled seismic data be organized during pretraining into a dense representation that is discriminative, spatially coherent, and directly reusable across interpretation tasks? We hypothesize that reusable dense representations require both feature discrimination and spatial coherence. Discriminative self-supervised learning can promote separation in feature space (Caron et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2023), while constraining feature relations keeps the spatial associations among geologically related features stable (Bardes et al., 2022; Wen et al., 2025; Siméoni et al., 2025). We therefore investigate whether discriminative seismic pretraining combined with explicit preservation of dense feature relations can produce representations that remain directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

Here we test this hypothesis with SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model pretrained on 5.34 million unlabeled 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. The overall framework is illustrated in Figure 1. SeisDFE adopts a progressive three-stage pretraining strategy. Stage I performs large-scale discriminative self-supervised learning on unlabeled seismic data. During Stage I, feature-similarity analysis reveals that prolonged optimization can coincide with a loss of local spatial coherence. Stage III further introduces multi-resolution adaptation to improve the consistency of the learned representation across input scales. The resulting encoder serves as a shared dense feature extractor that can be coupled with lightweight task-specific heads or decoders for different seismic interpretation problems.

These results support a role for seismic foundation models beyond task-specific initialization, as a shared feature basis for data-efficient seismic interpretation.

papers.title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

papers.intro:
On-policy distillation (OPD) (Li et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2024b; Lu and Lab, 2025; Yang et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026c; Song and Zheng, 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2024) transfers the capabilities of a strong teacher to a student through token-level supervision on trajectories generated by the student. This distinguishes OPD from conventional knowledge distillation and supervised fine-tuning (Gou et al., 2021; Hinton et al., 2015; Ye et al., 2025), which typically rely on fixed, teacher-generated responses. Accordingly, OPD has recently attracted growing attention, with applications ranging from reasoning (Li et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026a; Hou et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026) to relatively simple agentic tasks such as web search (Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2026b) 11 1 In industry, OPD is viewed as an effective capability-merging method (Team, 2026; Team, 2025; Xiaomi, 2026; Ma et al., 2026; GLM, 2026), enabling the integration of specialized capabilities from multiple teachers (usually derived from reinforcement learning) into a single student of the same size.. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of OPD in long-horizon tasks that require interaction with an environment, such as software engineering (SWE), remains underexplored.

However, dense supervision alone does not guarantee that OPD will improve SWE agents. An erroneous action can modify repository contents or alter the observations that inform subsequent decisions, requiring the teacher to score histories that differ from those generated under its own policy. Moreover, long interaction histories make teacher scoring costly. Practical approximations, such as restricting scored candidates or training on fixed trajectories, change how supervision is used or where it is applied. These considerations make SWE a demanding setting for examining both the effectiveness and the limitations of on-policy teacher supervision. Recent analyses of OPD also highlight the importance of reliable supervision over long trajectories (Li et al., 2026).

We further examine whether effective distillation requires continually refreshed student trajectories. Following the offline approach explored in Lightning OPD (Wu et al., 2026), Offline SWE-OPD collects trajectories from the initial student and precomputes teacher supervision before optimization. This decouples rollout collection, teacher scoring, and student training, allowing the stages to share a GPU pool. The fixed offline trajectory distribution may diverge from the distribution induced by the evolving student policy. Hence, it is necessary to evaluate the offline variant through both downstream resolve rates and end-to-end resource use.

Across three teacher-student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, our experiments demonstrate that vanilla OPD can improve instruction-tuned coding agents. For example, distillation on ScaleSWE with Qwen3.6-27B as the teacher increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. In our internal-data experiments, offline SWE-OPD reduces end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4% for Qwen and 72.6% for GLM while also bringing improvement. The offline pipeline also accepts a teacher with a different tokenizer: merging generated tokens whose spans differ between the two tokenizations following the simplest method GOLD (Patiño et al., 2025a), GLM-4.5-Air distilled from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 improves on all three benchmarks. These results indicate a favorable trade-off between task performance and computational cost under the evaluated training budgets. Our experiments also reveal a limitation of evaluating distillation solely through its training objective. Although the top-K loss improves the Qwen student, the GLM student develops severe repetition even as its training loss decreases. In contrast, sampled-token training remains stable in the evaluated configuration. An analysis of the implemented top-K loss identifies a support-mass gradient that can shift probability outside the scored candidates, even at teacher-student agreement. This provides a potential failure mechanism for the top-K loss. Together, these findings motivate evaluating SWE distillation through task success, training behavior, and resource cost, and distinguishing supervision coverage from the reliability of the resulting updates. Using cached teacher supervision on fixed trajectories collected from the initial student halves GPU-hours while maintaining satisfactory performance relative to online training. • Reliability beyond loss reduction. This work is designed as a controlled study of vanilla OPD for SWE. We intentionally avoid combining OPD with reinforcement learning, data filtering, or specialized optimization techniques, allowing us to examine whether on-policy teacher supervision alone can transfer agentic coding capabilities across model scales. Therefore we believe that there remains room for further improving student performance, and we release our code to facilitate future exploration.

papers.title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark
papers.abstract: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at $\rho = 0.92$ over 32 models.

papers.intro:
Many established legal benchmarks use classification, multiple-choice, or short-answer formats [8, 29, 23]. This permits standardized automatic scoring, but does not represent how case-based tasks in German legal education and the First State Examination assess legal reasoning. A typical case task requires a complete legal opinion (Gutachten): identify the issues and governing norms, state the requirements of each norm, apply them to the facts, and reach a conclusion. The same structure recurs over the issues and sub-issues of the case. A correct final conclusion can therefore conceal missing or incorrect intermediate analysis, which label-based benchmarks do not measure directly [8, 29, 23]. Evaluating the full reasoning document is necessary for this examination setting [46].

Several recent benchmarks include open-ended legal tasks. GreekBarBench asks questions from five areas of the Greek bar examination, supplies chapter-level statutory context, and requires citations to both articles and case facts [10]. LEXam contains 2,841 open-ended questions from law examinations and accompanies them with guidance on the expected reasoning approach [22]. For German law, BenGER evaluates complete exam-style case solutions alongside short doctrinal tasks, but disables retrieval and tool-use endpoints for the evaluated systems [46]. Retrieval-focused benchmarks address a different stage: LegalBench-RAG measures whether a system locates the relevant spans, not whether those spans improve a complete legal opinion [51]. These benchmarks therefore emphasize different stages of legal problem solving. Their complementary designs motivate evaluating statutory recall, retrieval, and downstream use within the same document-level task.

We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), a benchmark that scores statute retrieval and long-form legal writing on the same 81 state-exam-style public-law cases, drawn from the University of Passau’s State Examination Preparation Course in Public Law. Each case pairs a fact pattern (Sachverhalt) with an extensively reasoned reference solution. The task is document-level: a model receives the case and writes a complete German legal opinion (Gutachten), including a table of contents and an assessment of every question raised. The reference solutions average 7,080 words, compared with 924 for the case facts, and contain substantially more statutory references. This asymmetry is part of the task: the model must determine much of the governing law rather than extract it from the question. The cases are also broad and rarely repeat: the topics their authors label are mostly unique to a single case, and one case raises a median of eight of them across a median of twelve law books. Keeping the cases and reference solutions non-public also reduces the risk that they enter model-training corpora and contaminate the evaluation [59]. A direct text-overlap analysis finds no evidence of exact-solution memorisation of the reference solutions (Section 3.2).

papers.title: Large deviations and the asymptotic geometry of Lorentz balls
papers.abstract: We study the uniform distribution on finite-dimensional Lorentz balls $B_{q,p}^n$ in the range $1<p<q<\infty$. We prove a Sanov-type large deviation principle for the empirical measures of the absolute coordinates of a random vector uniformly distributed on $n^{1/q}B_{q,p}^n$. The rate function is given by an entropy deficit under a weighted quantile constraint. We show that the entropy maximizer is unique and characterize its distribution function as the unique increasing solution of a nonlinear boundary-value problem. The limiting distribution has compact support, for which we obtain an explicit bound. These results establish the conjectured empirical limit of Kabluchko, Prochno and Sonnleitner [Journal of Functional Analysis, 288(1):110682, 2025] in the range $1<p<q<\infty$. As consequences, we determine the exponential volume asymptotics of Lorentz balls and obtain asymptotic independence of any fixed number of coordinates. We also prove a law of large numbers for Lorentz norms with finite parameters and use it, together with the volume asymptotics, to obtain a Schechtman--Schmuckenschl\"ager type theorem for intersections of volume-normalized Lorentz balls. We further derive a variational formula for the logarithmic intersection asymptotics. The proof combines an exponential change of measure with quantile interpolation and a variational argument that does not assume regularity of the maximizing quantile in advance.

papers.title: Share your Screen and Talk to Gemini: How Young Learners Interact with Multimodal GenAI While Solving Scratch Tasks
papers.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.

papers.intro:
In Scratch, children can learn to program by assembling visual blocks and creating animations, games, and stories (Resnick et al., 2009). When a program behaves unexpectedly, learners need to connect that behavior to the block(s) that produced it. In the classroom, providing individual debugging support is difficult when many learners need help at the same time. Teachers in lower secondary school describe this situation as the “hands-up problem” (Gale and Sentance, 2026). GenAI can offer on-demand assistance for programming (Prather et al., 2025), but research in higher education also identifies risks involving incorrect information and over-reliance (Prather et al., 2023; Prather et al., 2025; Bernstein et al., 2025). At the same time, scoping reviews of GenAI in computing education report a research gap at the secondary level (Stone, 2024; Philbin and Sentance, 2025; Barendsen et al., 2025), and an overly positive narrative (Kohn et al., 2026).

Research on young Scratch learners (aged 6-12) has explored hints (Greifenstein et al., 2023a) and GenAI-based guidance (Chen et al., 2024; Druga and Ko, 2025). However, text-based conversations with GenAI require learners to read explanations and type questions, while working with task instructions and block labels. This sometimes leads to children not reading hints precisely or not at all (Greifenstein et al., 2023b). These findings lead us to consider alternatives to text-heavy assistance. Verbal interactions may be an alternative to reduce literacy barriers (Chen et al., 2024) (i.e., reduce reading and writing demands so pre- and early readers can succeed (Dietz et al., 2023)). Multimodal generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models can combine verbal and visual context from screen sharing or cameras and respond with text or audio with low latency (Google, 2025). These models could support learning across subjects and digital or physical settings without requiring integration into a specific learning application.

Our goal is to investigate the quality and use of a GenAI tutor with screen sharing during Scratch lessons in grades 5 and 6. We use the term GenAI tutor to refer to Gemini 2.5 Flash Native Audio Preview in Google AI Studio, instructed through a system prompt to support children with Scratch tasks without revealing the solution. Children interact with the tutor by voice while sharing their Scratch browser tab. Our exploratory study combines an expert pilot with an analysis of classroom recordings and questionnaire responses from 23 children. We address the following research questions: RQ1 How can the GenAI tutor’s verbal responses be characterized while supporting a child with a Scratch task? RQ2 How do fifth- and sixth-graders interact with the GenAI tutor while working on Scratch tasks? RQ3 How do children perceive the GenAI tutor as a dialogue partner in terms of instructional support, trust in its responses, and verbal communication? The present study contributes (1) an evaluation scheme adapted to verbal interactions with screen-sharing data as context, (2) a classroom analysis of tutor responses and children’s interactions, and (3) insights into children’s experiences and perspectives.

papers.title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
papers.abstract: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. papers.title: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
papers.abstract: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

papers.intro:
Emotional appeals (EAs) refer to attempts to evoke emotions in an audience to support a claim, and belong to the pathos dimension of argumentation, alongside ethos (speaker’s credibility) and logos (logic) (Kennedy and others, 2006). EAs have often been discussed as fallacies, but argumentation theory does not consider them fallacious by default (Brinton, 1988; Walton, 2010; Manolescu, 2006). Prior work argues that EAs can be reasonable when they are supported by the context and used appropriately (Brinton, 1988; Manolescu, 2006; Macagno and Walton, 2010).

In natural language processing (NLP), however, whether an EA is justified has received little attention. Prior work mainly studies the relation between emotions and argument convincingness (Habernal and Gurevych, 2016; Wachsmuth et al., 2017; Chen and Eger, 2025). EAs are also frequently modeled as fallacies or propaganda techniques (Da San Martino et al., 2019; Helwe et al., 2024). Such formulations do not distinguish between EAs that are warranted by the context and those that are not. For example, an appeal to fear may be reasonable when there is sufficient evidence of serious danger, but fallacious or manipulative when such evidence is absent. papers.title: On the Power-Law Duality in Wigner-Yang Quantum Mechanics
papers.abstract: In this work we first revisit the Hooke-Newton duality and its generalisation to arbitrary power laws in classical and quantum mechanics. We then consider Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics on the real line, which is a deformation of standard Heisenberg-Schr\"odinger quantum mechanics closely related to Dunkl's differential-difference operator formalism. We consider the corresponding eigenvalue problem for the harmonic potential and a Coulomb-like potential. We observe that the Hooke-Newton duality is also applicable to these deformed quantum systems allowing us to solve the eigenvalue problem of one by mapping it onto the other system. This approach is then generalised to arbitrary power-law potentials in Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics. Whereas in standard quantum mechanics the classical re-scaling of angular momenta has to be applied to Langer-modified quantum angular momenta, Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics requires a rescaling of deformation parameters similar to the Langer-type modification but involving the reflection operator. The energy coupling-constant exchange, however, remains the same in all three cases, classical mechanics, quantum mechanics and Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics.

papers.intro:
The Hooke-Newton duality is probably the oldest known duality of physics. This duality describes the mapping of orbits for a test particle following Hooke’s law of elastic springs [1] into orbits of Newton’s law of gravity [2]. According to Chandrasekhar’s reading of Newton’s principia [3] this duality was already know to both, Hooke and Newton. In fact, Newton’s principia contains several examples of such duality between different power laws of forces beyond those of the linear force law of Hooke and the inverse-square force law of Newton.

This duality was then revisited independently by Kasner [4] and Arnol’d [5]. See also more recent articles like [6, 7, 8]. The same problem in arbitrary dimensions has also been discussed from the supersymmetric interest [11]. The duality of radial equations with multi-terms of power potentials was studied in connection with the quark confinement [12].

Purpose of this presentation is to investigate a possible power-law duality within the frame work of Wigner-Yang quantum mechanics (WYQM). WYQM is a deformed version of standard Heisenberg-Schrödinger quantum mechanics (HSQM) involving a nonlocal deformation via the reflection operator. In contrast to the radial HSQM with configuration space being the positive half-line, WYQM is defined on the full real line but exhibiting a singular nonlocal potential term of the form ν⁡(ν−R)/|x|2\nu(\nu-R)/|x|^{2}, where ν\nu is the deformation parameter and RR stands for operator representing refection with respect to the origin x=0x=0. Naturally this potential term may play the role of a centrifugal term with the angular momentum being replace by the deformation parameter. Hence, it is natural to expect a duality relation in WYQM similar to what is known in HSQM.

The duality relation implies an exchange between energy and coupling constants accompanied by a rescaling of the classical angular momenta in both systems. Section 3 then reviews this duality relation for the corresponding radial problem in non-relativistic HSQM. Again the same exchange between energy and coupling constants occurs, but the rescaling of angular momenta is now to be applies to the Langer-modifed quantum angular momentum. A brief outlook to further possible investigations is also provided.

papers.title: Federated versus Centralized PV Capacity-Factor Forecasting: A Non-Inferiority Study Across Seven Stations in North Macedonia
papers.abstract:
Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables collaborative model training through model updates when local operators cannot pool raw operational data. This study evaluated whether federated training was non-inferior to centralized training for PV capacity-factor prediction across seven stations in North Macedonia. A common multilayer perceptron was used in an offline forecasting comparison with a 24-hour timestamp lag. Exploratory validation compared local, centralized, Federated Averaging, and Federated Proximal (FedProx) training. FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) was selected for a confirmatory comparison under a protocol fixed before test evaluation. The comparison used past-only offline inputs, five paired training seeds, macro-averaged mean absolute error (MAE), a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.005, and a paired day bootstrap with 10,000 repetitions over 49 test dates.
  Results: FedProx achieved a macro-MAE of 0.128397, compared with 0.133405 for centralized training. The paired difference (FedProx minus centralized) was -0.005008 (95% confidence interval: [-0.009926, -0.000537]). The upper confidence bound was below the prespecified margin, satisfying the non-inferiority criterion. All five seed-specific differences favored FedProx, and its mean MAE was lower at six of the seven stations. Post hoc calendar sensitivity analyses did not change the conclusion.
  Conclusions: These findings support further evaluation of federated forecasting for collaboration under data-pooling constraints. The study demonstrates predictive non-inferiority within the evaluated setting. Benefits for energy commitments and battery scheduling remain potential applications requiring operational evaluation.

papers.intro:
PV has emerged as one of the most promising renewable energy technologies worldwide. Annual PV installations are growing exponentially, reaching nearly 700 GW in 2025 and nearing 1 TW in annual capacity [11]. Solar intermittency still challenges technology penetration and reliability by inducing weather-driven fluctuations, grid instability, reserve requirements, etc. Additionally, incoming solar radiation is expected to be altered in future climates due to greenhouse gases, aerosols, and cloud cover, which complicates long-term planning [55, 7]. This underscores the need for PV power forecasts in complex meteorological conditions. Forecasting relies on either direct power predictions or indirect methods that first model solar irradiance before converting it to power [5]. In radiometric terms, solar irradiance is the instantaneous radiant power incident per unit area (W/m2), whereas solar irradiation is the radiant energy per unit area integrated over a specified time interval (J/m2 or Wh/m2). Accurate prediction of this parameter is important for grid integration and energy markets, but it remained highly immature in the last decade compared to other energy forecasting [15]. PV operators and aggregators in day-ahead electricity markets use generation forecasts to decide how much energy to commit for each trading interval. Forecast errors expose them to imbalance-settlement costs [6]. Operators of PV plants coupled with battery energy storage systems (BESS) use forecasts to plan when and how much to charge or discharge, subject to battery energy and power limits. Forecast-informed scheduling has been investigated in hybrid PV–wind plants with storage, linking generation predictions to operating decisions [53]. These applications motivate reliable forecasting, although operational value depends on the decision strategy and operating conditions as well as prediction accuracy.

Solar-forecasting methods relied on physical and statistical approaches earlier. Physical methods used solar geometry, clear-sky radiation models, atmospheric radiative-transfer models, and numerical weather prediction (NWP) to describe the influence of meteorological conditions on incoming radiation. Statistical approaches extracted temporal relationships from historical irradiance or PV-power measurements using persistence models, autoregressive models, regression methods, and exponential smoothing techniques [20, 52]. Although these methods provided considerable accuracy, their reliability is often limited under rapidly changing cloud conditions and nonlinear relationships between climate parameters and PV output. Further, machine-learning-based models were subsequently adopted to model the nonlinear relationship between solar radiation, meteorological variables, and PV output. Approaches based on artificial neural networks, support-vector regression, fuzzy systems, decision trees, and ensemble learning demonstrated improved reliability compared with conventional statistical models, particularly for short-term forecasting [5, 48, 2]. The development of deep learning further expanded this research direction by enabling the automatic extraction of temporal and spatial features from large and heterogeneous datasets. Recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and hybrid CNN–LSTM architectures have been increasingly reported for solar forecasting, using historical time series, NWP data, satellite observations, and total-sky images as inputs [49, 40]. More recent studies have focused on hybrid and ensemble frameworks that combine physical knowledge with data-driven models, as well as on probabilistic forecasting approaches that quantify the uncertainty associated with future PV generation [47, 2]. This evolution reflects a gradual transition from single-site deterministic prediction toward spatially distributed, uncertainty-aware, and operationally oriented forecasting systems [52].

Recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and hybrid CNN–LSTM architectures have been increasingly reported for solar forecasting, using historical time series, NWP data, satellite observations, and total-sky images as inputs [49, 40]. More recent studies have focused on hybrid and ensemble frameworks that combine physical knowledge with data-driven models, as well as on probabilistic forecasting approaches that quantify the uncertainty associated with future PV generation [47, 2]. This evolution reflects a gradual transition from single-site deterministic prediction toward spatially distributed, uncertainty-aware, and operationally oriented forecasting systems [52].

Existing studies have focused on improving model architecture and input features, but less attention has been paid to integrating data configuration for solar forecasting. Recent studies have addressed signal non-stationarity through decomposition, pairing Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN) or variational mode decomposition with LSTM ensembles [38, 17], while others incorporated sky-camera or webcam imagery alongside meteorological covariates for short-horizon irradiance forecasting [4, 42]. Some studies explored LSTM and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) variants tailored to specific settings, including dynamic sunrise-sunset windowing with online learning [46], net-load forecasting in mixed solar-wind microgrids [43], and hybrids combining GRU with gradient boosting, swarm optimization, or model-predictive control for real-time dispatch [22, 21, 44]. CNN-LSTM architectures were further extended with dimensionality reduction, physics-informed constraints, and attention-based encoder-decoder designs to better capture spatial-temporal dependencies and incorporate domain knowledge such as clearness index and shortwave radiation [34, 54, 13]. More recently, Transformer-based architectures and Reformer variants have reported better stability and applicability over recurrent baselines for both short-term and ultra-short-term forecasting [23, 45, 25], and generative approaches based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diffusion models have been proposed to produce probabilistic forecasts under complex weather conditions [14, 26]. A few studies have reported PV prediction as a reinforcement learning problem, using actor-critic or policy-gradient formulations with auxiliary outlier detection and interpretability analysis [51, 56]. Luo et al. proposed a physics-constrained LSTM for improved robustness under sparse data [27], while Akhter et al. proposed a Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA)-optimized RNN–LSTM and compared it with genetic algorithm (GA)- and particle swarm optimization (PSO)-based variants across three PV technologies [3]. Huang et al. combined CEEMDAN decomposition with an ensemble of deep temporal convolutional networks [19], Abdel et al. introduced a convolutional-gated recurrent architecture with bidirectional residual blocks [1], and Cortez et al. developed a correction-based pipeline refining LSTM/GRU/MLP forecasts with an LSTM autoencoder [9]. Hu et al. addressed spatial heterogeneity using a graph attention network (GAT) to select representative stations before ensemble forecasting at the regional level [18]. Finally, Kumar et al. proposed an asymmetric actor-critic reinforcement learning framework for irradiance forecasting across climatically diverse sites [24], and Wang et al. used an LSTM-based TimeGAN to generate weather-correlated PV, load, and scenario data for system planning [50]. While these studies collectively demonstrate progress in architecture design and cross-site model selection, none address data locality or privacy-preserving training constraints.

papers.title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
papers.abstract:
Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially.
  Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality.
  Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.

Spatial domain approaches such as Least Significant Bit [20] were computationally inexpensive but vulnerable to compression, noise, and image transformations. Frequency-domain methods based on the Discrete Cosine Transform [21] and wavelet transforms [22] offered improved robustness. Hence, interest grew in the use of Machine Learning to develop robust watermarking schemes.

These limitations motivated the adoption of deep-learning-based watermarking, beginning with convolutional approaches such as Hiding Images in Plain Sight [23]. This was an early convolutional neural network (CNN) based approach to embed one image (watermark) inside another image (original). However, the embeddings was vulnerable to removal with JPEG compression. Authors of [24] built on the idea of HIPS to introduce HiDDeN, an end-to-end trainable model that embedded a message within any image while preserving perceptual similarity to original image. It consists of an encoder that embeds the message, a noise layer during training that simulated real-world distortions like cropping, blurring and compression, and a decoder that recovers the message. Additionally, an adversarial discriminator was used to encourage encoder to produced images that looked visually similar with embedded watermarks.
