papers.title: An abstract observability criterion via translation hulls, with applications to transport systems
papers.abstract: We establish an observability criterion for translation-covariant families of operators on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$. Under continuity of the observed cell energies, a common summable localization bound, and reconstruction up to a locally collectively compact error, observability is equivalent to the absence of nonzero uniformly local invisible states on every configuration in the full translation hull. For one-dimensional transport systems satisfying the Kalman rank condition, this yields localized observability in the intrinsic Kalman--Jordan energy space for arbitrary real Jordan structure and nonzero speeds. For unions of observed intervals with a uniform positive lower length bound, the sharp condition is that the slowest characteristic travels farther than the gap supremum. Observability fails at equality even when this supremum is not attained. Duality gives exact controllability in the dual energy space. We also obtain sharp criteria for translating observation regions and scalar transport with an integrable convolution kernel. The reconstruction hypothesis is also necessary for observability. An anisotropic heat-flux example shows that it applies beyond coercive multiplication-plus-compact Gramian decompositions.

Uniqueness and observability are closely related, but they are not equivalent. The absence of nonzero invisible solutions does not prevent sequences of unit-energy states from becoming arbitrarily weakly observed. On bounded domains, such sequences can often be ruled out by a compactness–uniqueness argument. Once an estimate has controlled high-frequency losses, compactness produces an invisible limit of nonzero energy, and unique continuation forces that limit to vanish [2].

papers.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

papers.intro:
Visual feedback helps scientific agents select actions and assess their results [1, 2, 3]. Recent advances in multimodal agents span visual information retrieval and understanding, coding with visual feedback, and computer use [4, 5, 6, 7]. papers.title: Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification
papers.abstract: Medical image classifiers require not only high accuracy but also reliable predictions under small input perturbations. Certified robustness provides mathematical guarantees of prediction stability, but preserving these guarantees when adapting pretrained models to new tasks remains challenging. We propose a fine-tuning approach based on quantum-inspired orthogonal butterfly layers that preserves the Lipschitz bounds of pretrained certified networks. Inspired by quantum circuits of reconfigurable beam splitters, these layers preserve orthogonality by construction using only $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ trainable parameters. Their structured design enables efficient classical implementation and offers a path toward future quantum implementations with logarithmic circuit depth under suitable connectivity assumptions. Controlled experiments on MNIST and MedMNIST demonstrate improved certified robustness compared with conventional alternatives and, in the DermaMNIST transfer, greater resistance to the tested attacks than low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We then apply it to trichoscopic image classification for alopecia diagnosis and alopecia areata activity assessment. By adapting a certified ImageNet-pretrained network, butterfly fine-tuning achieves approximately twice the certified accuracy of conventional fine-tuning and LoRA, with comparable classification accuracy on the same backbone and data split and similar empirical resistance to the tested adversarial attacks. Larger robustness guarantees, including certificates covering certain image-processing transformations, can be obtained at the cost of reduced accuracy. These results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired butterfly layers for parameter-efficient adaptation of medical image classifiers while preserving the mathematical guarantees underlying certified robustness.

papers.intro:
Deep learning has achieved remarkable performance in medical image analysis in many different fields, including dermatology. For hair-loss disorders, deep neural networks have been used to measure the extent of hair loss [51, 28] and hair density [44], and to analyse scalp images [43]. They have also been applied to trichoscopic images to classify androgenetic alopecia [24], diagnose hair-loss disorders, and assess alopecia areata activity [8]. Their adoption in clinical practice, however, raises an important question: are their predictions robust to small image perturbations? A model may achieve high test accuracy while remaining sensitive to small, even imperceptible, changes that alter its predicted diagnosis [23]. Indeed, stress tests of dermatology classifiers have shown that even simple changes, such as rotating an image or photographing the same area again, can affect their predictions [90, 61]. This sensitivity raises concerns about their safety in clinical use [41], and regulators now explicitly require or recommend robustness [22, 84]. Test accuracy alone cannot establish whether a particular prediction will remain stable when the input changes.

Certified robustness addresses this concern by providing a mathematical guarantee: for each image, any input perturbation within a certified radius, measured under a chosen norm, leaves the model’s prediction unchanged [85, 14, 53]. One way to obtain such a certificate is to bound the Lipschitz constant of the network, which, combined with the classification margin, allows the certified radius to be computed for each prediction using a single forward pass [83, 3]. While this does not guarantee that the predicted diagnosis is medically correct, it establishes that the prediction is stable. In practice, obtaining useful Lipschitz bounds often requires architectures specifically designed to control them. For image classification, networks such as BRONet [46] have demonstrated meaningful certified robustness on ImageNet. However, applying these networks to specialized medical domains presents an additional challenge. Medical datasets are often too small to train such models from scratch, making it necessary to adapt pretrained networks through fine-tuning. Conventional fine-tuning, however, can alter their Lipschitz bounds and compromise the original robustness guarantees.

Because they preserve Euclidean norms, multiplying a pretrained layer’s weight matrix by an orthogonal matrix leaves its Lipschitz bound unchanged [13, 3, 54, 70]. In particular, circuits built from Reconfigurable Beam Splitter (RBS) gates combine simple rotations between pairs of coordinates while preserving orthogonality for any choice of parameters [42, 47]. This substantially reduces the number of trainable parameters compared with a general orthogonal matrix. These transformations can be computed efficiently on classical hardware, as in all our experiments [47]. Their direct correspondence to quantum circuits also opens the possibility of future quantum implementations, although any practical advantage would depend on data encoding, hardware connectivity, and measurement requirements [42, 47].

papers.title: Powering the Space Elevator
papers.abstract: Powering the Space Elevator is a report on the work of an International Space Elevator Consortium study group tasked with determining the technology options for delivering power to the climbers on the space elevator at any altitude above Earth. The book covers options such as laser power beaming, microwave beaming, a solar-powered climber, and delivering power through the electrical conductivity of the tether. This report starts with the reference conceptual design of a climber from the 2023 study report, "The Climber/Tether Interface of the Space Elevator," and adds features to the climber that allow it to ascend or descend the elevator tether. The strengths and limitations of current technologies are identified, along with areas for future research.

papers.title: When the Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks on LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become used more commonly across a variety of fields, a growing body of research has highlighted particular concerns surrounding model security. Notably, prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into prompts, are particularly simple to implement yet capable of inducing devastating effects on the fidelity of model outputs. While there is substantial research surrounding attack models and their effects on chat-based models, browser add-ons, and coding agents, the impact of these same attacks on industrial LLM-generated artifacts has been left largely unexplored. As LLM-enabled agents are increasingly used to skim and generate industrial documents such as Safety Data Sheets (SDS), Quality Control (QC) documents, and Digital Product Passports (DPP), it remains unclear how adversaries may influence these systems to manipulate generated compliance artifacts. This work aims to address this core inquiry by examining how a variety of prompt injection attacks can compromise LLMs with industrial document generation tasks. The study finds that injection attack success varies significantly across different models. Active falsification injections are most successful under all scenarios, while models tend to be most robust against passively injected override requests.

papers.intro:
The generation of industrial artifacts with Large Language Models (LLMs) is gaining increasing attention due to the complex nature of information retrieval and transformation. However, many other LLM generation application fields, such as code generation[1], embedded browser models[1], and agentic applications[2], have noted that prompt injection attacks pose a real threat to model output fidelity and the viability of fully automated LLM generation systems. While prompt-injection risks have been extensively studied in conversational agents, coding assistants, and retrieval-augmented systems, little work has examined how such attacks affect the generation of structured industrial compliance artifacts whose outputs may subsequently drive operational, regulatory, or safety-critical decisions. This work seeks to bridge this gap by carrying out several attack scenarios on simulated industrial artifact generation using a variety of LLMs to measure the viability of these attacks on the emerging field.

papers.title: Network sampling: a comparative review
papers.abstract: Network sampling is essential for the study of real world systems, since access to the topological structure and dynamical characteristics of a complex system is usually infeasible, and can also prove computationally intractable for large and dense networks. However, the field still lacks systematic methodologies that allow a procedural analysis of sampling plans for connected data. Hence, this study aims to compare network sampling methods through the usage of multivariate statistical analysis and machine learning techniques that are anchored in network metrics' estimation of synthetic and real-world networks. It was demonstrated that no single sampling strategy dominates both cases, although Forest fire and Frontier sampling have presented the most consistent performance across all topologies investigated. The impact of each structural property of these networks for principal component analysis and classification results were also discussed, with consistent pattern groups seen for both data types. Transfer learning aimed at real-world network identification has also demonstrated that realistic structural connections can be correlated to well-known network models through the usage of sampled subgraphs' properties for model training, providing an avenue to real-world network characterization through sampling methodologies.

papers.intro:
Complex network theory defines networks as a representation of systems through graphs, which can be a way to approximate and describe interactions in real-world structures [25]. Given its interdisciplinary nature, system such as neuronal networks, underground metropolitan transport lines, epidemiological contagion maps on social networks, rumor propagation via digital media, protein interaction maps, the topological structure of the internet, among several others, can benefit from a representation of its topological structure as sets of vertices and edges, allowing their study within the context of pairwise complex networks [18, 4].

Due to an increase in interest on the usage of such representations to real-world systems by the scientific community in the past two decades, network data has also been made more accessible through online repositories of such datasets. However, there is still no well-structured and clearly defined set of procedures for analyzing network data from an analytical perspective. Studies such as those by Kolaczyk [10] that compile knowledge about statistical procedures in networks remain scarce and pioneering.

Among the topics covered in network statistics, sampling stands out as a necessary stage for inferential procedures. It can be also applied in the characterization of a population in which data is scarce or expensive to process computationally. Classical sampling theory has extensively described various methods that are widely used in demographic, electoral, medical, and industrial studies, among others. However, in the context of network sampling, this body of knowledge proves to be limited in applicability due to the fact that the properties of a network depend not only on its constituent components, but also on how connections are drawn from them. Pioneering works such as those by Ove Frank and collaborators [7, 8], in which network sampling is addressed in a probabilistic manner, remain scarce because, due to the nature of this type of data, sampling methods that can represent the diverse topological characteristics of an entire network within a reduced subset of that network are difficult to obtain. The problem becomes even more complex if the goal is to generalize and structure its properties using mathematical approaches from probability theory and inference.

papers.title: Radar Panoptic Transformer: Semantic-Guided Mask Queries for Dynamic Scene Understanding
papers.abstract: Automotive radar provides long-range sensing and direct Doppler velocity measurements, but its sparse and non-uniformly sampled point clouds pose significant challenges for panoptic segmentation. Dynamic objects often yield only a few detections amid a dominant static background, providing limiting the geometric cues for separating object instances. We propose \emph{Radar Panoptic Transformer (RPT)}, an end-to-end point-based network that incorporates radar-adaptive feature extraction with semantic-guided mask prediction. Its backbone aggregates pose-aligned temporal context through grouped vector attention and learns per-point neighborhood radii conditioned on range, azimuth, and radar cross section (RCS). Point-wise semantic predictions initialize queries at likely foreground detections and guide masked cross-attention through query-point class agreement, producing instance masks without geometric clustering. An auxiliary RCS-consistency loss matches instance-level statistics between predicted and annotated instances. RPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on RadarScenes with $71.6\%$ mIoU and $82.2\%$ PQ. We further evaluate RPT on MAN TruckScenes, where it outperforms the evaluated baselines in a long-range, full-surround radar setting with sensing ranges up to $230\,\mathrm{m}$. RPT achieves real-time end-to-end inference at $31$\,Hz on RadarScenes, exceeding the sensor frame rate.

papers.intro:
Reliable autonomous driving requires a holistic understanding of dynamic scenes, including the semantic structure of the environment and the identification of individual traffic participants. Panoptic segmentation provides this representation by assigning each sensor measurement a semantic class and, for thing classes, an instance identifier [1]. Although extensively studied for cameras [2] and LiDAR point clouds [3, 4], panoptic segmentation from automotive radar remains less explored. Radar provides distinct sensing capabilities, including direct radial Doppler velocity measurements, long-range operation, and robustness to adverse illumination and weather [5, 6]. In particular, Doppler information provides an additional motion cue for distinguishing individual traffic participants, motivating radar-based panoptic segmentation for dynamic scene understanding.

Radar perception has predominantly focused on object detection and tracking [5, 6, 7], which yield object-level outputs rather than semantic labels and instance identities for individual radar detections. Achieving such point-level panoptic prediction is challenging as radar measurements are sparse and non-uniformly sampled, with sampling density varying across range, viewing angle, and target reflectivity [8, 9]. Distant objects may also be represented by only a few detections, while static returns dominate the scene [10]. Fixed-radius neighborhoods are poorly suited to spatially varying sampling density, while the severe foreground-background imbalance hinders reliable identification of sparsely represented dynamic instances. Radar panoptic segmentation remains a recent research direction [11]. Existing approaches use refinement pipelines that rely on class-agnostic upstream instance estimates [12, 11], use fixed-radius neighborhoods, and have largely been evaluated at shorter operating ranges.

We perform extensive evaluations on RadarScenes [10] and the long-range MAN TruckScenes benchmark [15], where our proposed RPT consistently outperforms existing methods.

papers.title: T2T Technical Report: Synthesizing GUI Agent Trajectories at Scale from Video Tutorials
papers.abstract: Training generalist GUI agents requires large volumes of interaction trajectories comprising screenshot sequences paired with grounded UI actions, yet collecting such data through human demonstration is expensive and difficult to scale. Although public software tutorial videos contain rich operational demonstrations, their continuous pixel streams lack discrete action boundaries, semantic intents, and precise spatial coordinates, making them difficult to use directly for model training. To address this, we present T2T (Tutorial-to-Trajectory), a fully automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI agent trajectories at scale. T2T spans desktop, web, and mobile platforms to convert unannotated video tutorials into structured, executable interaction trajectories. To guarantee trajectory quality, T2T combines active segment filtering, keyframe identification via localized UI change, shortcut-free observation frame selection, presence-aware grounding, and two-stage action-space normalization. These refined trajectories are then converted into multi-task training views spanning navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B on a subset of the more than one million human-annotation-free training samples generated by this pipeline. Evaluations show that the model achieves consistent gains across multiple benchmarks covering desktop, web, and mobile environments, including OSWorld-G, ScreenSpot-Pro, AndroidControl, and AgentNetBench, indicating improved core capabilities in grounding, step-level instruction execution, and trajectory-level decision-making. Notably, all gains are achieved without any in-distribution training data from target domains. Learning exclusively from trajectories extracted from public videos via the T2T pipeline, the model exhibits cross-application and cross-task generalization capabilities.

Large language models and vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding natural language, generating code, and reasoning over visual content (OpenAI, 2024; Qwen Team, 2025a; Chen et al., 2024), increasingly serving as general-purpose foundations for a wide range of intelligent applications. A natural next step is to translate these capabilities into concrete task execution in the digital world. Unlike web APIs or command-line interfaces that expose structured endpoints, the vast majority of software, from productivity suites and creative tools to enterprise systems and mobile applications, is designed primarily for human interaction through graphical user interfaces. This makes GUI the de facto universal interface to the digital world, but also one that demands perceptual and motor skills traditionally reserved for human users: recognizing UI elements from pixels, understanding spatial layouts, tracking state changes across screens, and executing precise sequences of clicks, keystrokes, and gestures (Cheng et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026a). GUI agents, autonomous systems built on top of LLMs and VLMs that perceive screen content and perform such actions on behalf of users, bridge this gap by operating directly at the interface level, automating tasks across arbitrary applications without requiring dedicated APIs or developer-side instrumentation. Feeding unsegmented raw videos into vision-language models (VLMs) is computationally prohibitive and practically infeasible due to strict API limits and context windows. Pruning the vast majority of frames that contain non-interactive content (e.g., introductions, static slides, or idle pauses) and identifying informative frames are essential for efficient and effective video processing. (2) Visual Target Leakage and Shortcut Learning. Naively sampled screenshots often suffer from severe visual shortcuts. High-production tutorials frequently overlay colored boxes or arrows, training models to locate annotations rather than comprehend UI pixels. Similarly, taking screenshots at the exact action timestamp leaves the cursor directly hovering over the target, encouraging models to learn a trivial “read-the-cursor” shortcut. (3) Coordinate Hallucination under Target Absence. Standard grounding models may instead rely on layout priors (e.g., close buttons in corners) and hallucinate coordinates even when the intended target element is temporarily absent or occluded, injecting noisy coordinates into the training distribution. (4) Action Space Heterogeneity and Misalignment. Speech narration and screen activity are temporally asynchronous. Furthermore, raw video extraction produces a heterogeneous vocabulary of non-standardized action names, which must be mapped into unified, platform-conditioned tool-call schemas.

In this report, we present T2T (Tutorial-to-Trajectory), a fully automated pipeline designed to overcome these challenges. Starting from raw public videos, the pipeline proceeds through three stages: (1) Video Filtering and Preprocessing. We prune non-interactive video segments using cursor-based sparse probing as a user activity proxy, and enforce strict visual annotation filtering to eliminate superimposed highlights, arrows, and bounding boxes that cause label leakage. (2) Trajectory Extraction and Action Spatial Grounding. Instead of relying on noisy global frame differences or asynchronous audio transcripts, we pinpoint discrete action timestamps by scoring localized UI changes (explicitly discounting full-screen turnovers) and extracting settled before/after frame pairs. A vision-language model then derives task context, sub-step plans, and target referring expressions. To prevent the model from simply memorizing pointer positions, we perform a backward search for pre-action screenshots where the cursor is away from the target element. A three-tier presence-aware grounding cascade then localizes target elements, explicitly discarding unverified coordinates to prevent label noise while repurposing rejected steps as negative abstention samples. (3) Action Normalization and Multi-task Conversion. We normalize heterogeneous extractor action vocabularies through a two-stage normalization scheme into unified, platform-conditioned tool-call schemas (computer use, browser use, and mobile use). Finally, trajectories are rendered into complementary multi-task training views (navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding) to maximize data efficiency.

papers.title: Optical response of quantum metals
papers.abstract: Strongly interacting quantum systems display puzzling electrical transport properties whose interpretation remains controversial. Many theoretical and phenomenological analyses assume that the complex behaviour observed in such `quantum materials' originates either from quasi-particles dressed with an anomalous electron self-energy or from collective excitations associated with hydrodynamic flow. Despite their distinctly different starting points, the underlying assumption is that dissipation of electrical current arises from the relaxation of the total momentum of charge carriers. This classical description breaks down in the absence of long-lived charge carriers. In such strange metals dissipation seems to be governed by the rate at which equilibrium is thermally restored, and it has been suggested that this constitutes an upper bound, known as the `Planckian limit'. Here we show that in this quantum regime a description of the conductivity in terms of relaxation rates no longer suffices: strange metal transport is carried instead by fast-decaying current fluctuations, which together with quantum detailed balance give rise to the widely observed Planckian dissipation. The distinction between classical and quantum metals becomes transparent when experimental data is analysed in terms of the current-current correlation function instead of the optical conductivity. When applied to the cuprate superconductors, such analysis uncovers that the strange metal response is present at all doping levels, and that a second, classical component develops above optimal doping. This simple, but powerful, approach further highlights essential features associated with superconductivity, (pseudo-)gaps, provides fresh insight in the properties of metals, and identifies key areas where progress in our theoretical understanding is needed.

papers.title: Power Line Detection in Point Clouds with Point-SAM and RANSAC
papers.abstract: This article deals with the problem of detecting the position of power lines in airborne laser scanning point clouds. We address both the problem of segmenting power lines from background like ground and vegetation and of identifying individual lines. For segmentation we compare a rule-based approach with one based on transfer learning (Point-SAM). For individual line detection, we derive the mathematical formulas for RANSAC applied to 3D catenaries and compare it with a non-parametric method (TriplClust). All methods are evaluated on a newly created dataset "PowLiDFR", which we make publicly available. The samples have been taken from the French project LiDAR HD and cover a variety of terrain layouts and point cloud resolutions. On this dataset, an unsupervised transfer learning outperformed a mere rule-based segmentation, and for individual power line detection, RANSAC was better in following the shape of catenaries than the non-parametric algorithm.

papers.title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
papers.abstract: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

papers.title: Horrocks-Mumford sheaves on toric varieties
papers.abstract: Previous work of the authors introduced the class of Horrocks-Mumford sheaves over normal algebraic k-varieties, the most prominent example being the classical Horrocks-Mumford bundle on projective four-space. For a smooth semiprojective toric variety, we derive an explicit description of these sheaves in terms of finitely generated graded modules over the Cox ring which we use for an algorithmic treatment. In particular, we discuss some explicit examples, their indecomposability and local freeness.

papers.title: Energy and Radius Estimates for Molecules
papers.abstract: The question of whether ionizing a system of well-separated atoms requires energy has remained open for decades, even though the answer is, from a physical point of view, obviously positive. The analog question for a system of molecules is even more challenging, partly because the molecular geometry is not known a priori and may change when electrons are added or removed. In this work, we investigate and analytically solve the first problem in the special case of a mixture of hydrogen and helium atoms. As a consequence, the van der Waals law for a system of hydrogen and helium atoms, which was proven in [6] assuming our result, now follows as a corollary without assumptions. Moreover, we prove a new lower bound for the `size' of a stable molecule with several nuclei, which improves upon the lower bounds from [1] with even less assumptions. Using among others this lower bound, we prove that it costs energy to ionize a system consisting of an $H_2$ molecule and a perfectly conducting half-infinite plate, provided that they are well-separated. The long-range asymptotics of their interaction energy was analyzed in [3] assuming our result.

papers.title: Excitonic magnetism and competing valence bond solid instabilities in $d^4$ ruthenium compounds
papers.abstract: Spin-orbit entangled $d^4$ Mott insulators serve as a rich playground for unconventional magnetism and competing quantum electronic ground states. Intra-ionic spin-orbit coupling $\lambda_{\rm{SOC}}$ generates a non-magnetic $J_{\rm{eff}} = 0$ singlet ground state separated from an excited $J_{\rm{eff}} = 1$ triplet. The effective intra-atomic gap ${\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$ between the ground state and lowest excited state is determined by $\lambda_{\rm{SOC}}$ and non-cubic crystal field ${\Delta}_{\rm{cf}}$. The intersite magnetic exchange $J_{\rm{ex}}$ induces dispersion of the excited $J_{\rm{eff}} = 1$ triplet. When the triplet bandwidth $W_{\rm{t}}$ overcomes ${\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$, the system undergoes long-range magnetic ordering which is viewed as a condensation of spin-orbit excitons and called excitonic magnetism. In this review, we systematically survey representative $d^4$ ruthenium compounds across four distinct structural connectivities of Ru-ligand octahedra, from K$_2$RuCl$_6$ with isolated octahedra, corner-sharing perovskite Ca$_2$RuO$_4$, edge-sharing honeycombs, to corner-sharing pyrochlores, and map them onto a conceptual parameter axis of $W_{\rm{t}} / {\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$. We demonstrate that $d^4$ ruthenium compounds not only represent evolution from a $J_{\rm{eff}} = 0$ Mott state to excitonic magnetism but encompass a broader competition of diverse electronic phases arising from spin-orbit coupling, exchange interactions, electron hopping, crystal field and bond covalency inhabiting similar energy scales. Near excitonic quantum critical point, where $W_{\rm{t}} \sim {\Delta}_{\rm{eff}}$, lattice geometry and chemical bonds of constituent atoms play a decisive role in selecting the electronic ground state, frequently driving valence bond solid formation that pre-empts excitonic quantum criticality.

papers.title: Multi-Rate Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
papers.abstract: Flow-matching point-cloud upsamplers refine sparse inputs into dense point clouds by integrating a learned velocity field with a fixed temporal discretization. However, local reconstruction requirements vary substantially across a shape, while a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. We propose Multi-Rate Flow Matching (MRFM), a patch-adaptive framework that selects an integration budget for each local patch at inference time while keeping the learned velocity field frozen. MRFM relaxes the discrete budget into a continuous variable, optimizes it online through differentiable soft rollouts using an input-derived geometric fidelity objective, and projects the result back to a discrete budget for the final solver rollout. Experiments on PU1K and PUGAN show strong reconstruction quality, while matched-budget permutation and multi-factor analyses demonstrate that the benefit depends on patch-specific allocation rather than on the step distribution alone. MRFM is accuracy-oriented and intentionally uses additional test-time optimization to obtain more suitable local temporal resolutions.

papers.intro:
Point-cloud upsampling aims to recover dense, uniform, and geometrically faithful point sets from sparse observations. Sparse, noisy, and non-uniform point clouds are the default output of most 3D sensors, yet downstream tasks assume denser, more regular geometry: robotic mapping and SLAM need locally complete surfaces for reliable registration, LiDAR-based 3D detection for autonomous driving degrades on sparse or occluded returns, and AR/VR rendering needs smooth, hole-free surfaces [5], [14], [9]. The same sparse-to-dense problem also arises beyond 3D vision, for instance in sparse-view medical surface reconstruction or physical-field reconstruction from a limited sensor array. The problem is therefore not only to add points, but to infer plausible local geometry while preserving the structure the sparse observation already supports, particularly around boundaries, thin parts, and unevenly sampled regions where small local errors noticeably affect the reconstructed surface.

Sparse, noisy, and non-uniform point clouds are the default output of most 3D sensors, yet downstream tasks assume denser, more regular geometry: robotic mapping and SLAM need locally complete surfaces for reliable registration, LiDAR-based 3D detection for autonomous driving degrades on sparse or occluded returns, and AR/VR rendering needs smooth, hole-free surfaces [5], [14], [9]. The same sparse-to-dense problem also arises beyond 3D vision, for instance in sparse-view medical surface reconstruction or physical-field reconstruction from a limited sensor array. The problem is therefore not only to add points, but to infer plausible local geometry while preserving the structure the sparse observation already supports, particularly around boundaries, thin parts, and unevenly sampled regions where small local errors noticeably affect the reconstructed surface.

Early learned upsamplers such as PU-Net and its successors [19] expand sparse points in a learned feature space and substantially improve point distribution and geometric fidelity, but do so through one-shot or staged expansion rather than an explicit refinement trajectory. More recent methods instead treat upsampling as iterative or generative refinement – optimizing point coordinates, denoising, or transporting a learned flow – with PUFM [9] and PUFM++ [10] representing the current state of the art for flow-matching-based upsampling. These flow-based methods make the temporal discretization of the learned trajectory an explicit design choice, which motivates asking whether the same discretization is equally appropriate for every local region.

These flow-based methods make the temporal discretization of the learned trajectory an explicit design choice, which motivates asking whether the same discretization is equally appropriate for every local region.

Local reconstruction difficulty, however, varies substantially within a single shape – smooth, well-observed regions may need only a coarse trajectory, while boundaries, thin structures, and sparsely sampled neighborhoods require finer refinement – yet a shared solver budget applies the same temporal resolution everywhere. The closest adaptive mechanisms address a different axis of this problem: PUFM++ redistributes a shared global time grid [10], Grad-PU applies gradients to point coordinates rather than the solver budget [4], PatchScaler groups image patches by diffusion difficulty [8], and TG-MSFM gates multi-scale velocity components over time [16], but none of them selects a patch-specific flow-matching budget from the response of a frozen point-cloud upsampler. Even a spatially varying budget is not simply recoverable from the input geometry alone: curvature or density are informative descriptors, but they do not measure how the learned flow actually behaves on a particular patch, or whether that patch would benefit from additional refinement.

papers.title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

papers.title: A Neural Density Functional for Spatial Structure and Orientational Ordering in Two-Dimensional Lattice Hard Rods
papers.abstract: We study spatial structure and orientational ordering of horizontal and vertical hard rods on a two-dimensional square lattice using neural classical density functional theory. We construct two convolutional architectures that exploit the symmetry relating the rod orientations: a direct-$c^{(1)}$ network (learning the map between the first functional derivative of the excess free energy and the inhomogeneous density, $c^{(1)} \leftrightarrow \rho$) and a $\Phi$-network (learning directly the map between free energy and density, $F_\text{ex} \leftrightarrow \rho$). Both networks use exactly the same inhomogeneous grand-canonical Monte Carlo density profiles and one-body direct correlation targets. Both neural representations substantially improve the predicted density profiles relative to the Lafuente--Cuesta lattice functional. The resulting free energy landscapes, however, differ between the two representations. Furthermore for the direct-$c^{(1)}$ network the integration along different density paths produces different free energies. As a result, the transition to nematic ordering for rods with aspect ratio 8 is strongly first order for the direct-$c^{(1)}$ network while only weakly discontinuous for the $\Phi$-network. The latter is a reasonable approximation to the continuous transition found in simulations, demonstrating that subtle entropic free energy differences are accessible in neural cDFT.

papers.title: The rise and fall of 1A 1118-61: First evidence for frequency hysteresis of quasi-periodic oscillations in an X-ray pulsar
papers.abstract:
Context. Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) are commonly observed in accreting X-ray pulsars (XRPs), but the physical mechanisms governing their frequency evolution remain poorly understood.
  Aims. We investigate the evolution of the QPO during the 2026 outburst of the Be/X-ray pulsar 1A 1118-61, focusing on its frequency-luminosity relation during the rising and declining phases of the outburst.
  Methods. We analyzed X-ray timing and spectral observations obtained with SRG/ART-XC, NuSTAR, and Insight-HXMT. We measured QPO centroid frequencies and amplitudes, compared their evolution during the rising and declining phases of the outburst, and examined the associated changes in the X-ray spectral shape.
  Results. We detected a prominent QPO with a centroid frequency ranging from approximately 37 to 114 mHz. Its frequency-luminosity relation follows two distinct branches, with QPO frequencies approximately 35% higher during the rise than during the decline at the same luminosity. The frequency evolution along both branches is consistent with Keplerian motion near the inner disk edge. The X-ray spectral shape also follows different evolutionary tracks during the rising and declining phases.
  Conclusions. We report the first evidence for QPO frequency hysteresis in an XRP. The observed separation between the rising and declining branches suggests that the characteristic timescale of the QPO depends not only on the instantaneous luminosity but also on the accretion history. We discuss possible implications for the disk-magnetosphere interaction.

In strongly magnetized XRPs, QPO frequencies span a broad range, from below 1 mHz to the Hz regime, potentially reflecting different physical mechanisms operating in the accretion flow.

At the lowest frequencies, QPOs have been detected in the ultraluminous XRPs M51 ULX-7 (0.5–0.6 mHz; Imbrogno et al. 2024) and M82 X-2 (3–4 mHz; Feng et al. 2010), as well as in the near-Eddington Be/X-ray pulsar (BeXRP) SXP31.0 (0.8 mHz; Salganik et al. 2026a). One possible explanation for such low-frequency oscillations is magnetically driven warping and precession of the inner accretion disk (Shirakawa and Lai, 2002). This mechanism has been explored in the context of ultraluminous XRPs accreting at super-Eddington rates (Veresvarska et al., 2025) and has also been considered for the 0.8 mHz QPO in SXP31.0 (Salganik et al., 2026a).

Two commonly invoked interpretations of QPOs in accreting XRPs are the Keplerian frequency model (KFM), which associates oscillations with orbital motion of inhomogeneities near the inner edge of the accretion disk (van der Klis et al., 1987), and the magnetospheric beat frequency model (BFM), in which the observed frequency corresponds to the difference between the local Keplerian frequency and the neutron-star (NS) spin frequency (Alpar and Shaham, 1985). In both models, the QPO frequency is related to the disk truncation radius, which depends on the mass accretion rate and the NS magnetic field. For a dipolar magnetic field and a constant disk–magnetosphere coupling factor, the KFM predicts νQPO∝L3/7\nu_{\rm QPO}\propto L^{3/7}, with approximately the same scaling expected in the BFM when the spin-frequency correction is negligible.

However, the observed frequency–luminosity behavior is not always consistent with these simple predictions. Multiple QPOs at distinct frequencies, occasionally occurring simultaneously, have been detected in 4U 0115+63, with no clear correlation between their frequencies and X-ray flux (Dugair et al., 2013). A similar lack of correlation has been reported in Cen X-3 (Raichur and Paul, 2008). By contrast, recent spectral–timing observations of 1A 0535+262 revealed a QPO frequency–luminosity relation, νQPO∝L0.62±0.01\nu_{\rm QPO}\propto L^{0.62\pm 0.01}, steeper than predicted by the standard Keplerian frequency model, along with QPO-phase-dependent variations in the cyclotron line (Kong et al., 2026). The QPO frequency decreased from approximately 0.09 to 0.07 Hz as the outburst declined, suggesting a connection between the oscillations and the evolving accretion conditions (Devasia et al., 2011). papers.title: Weights & Caches: LLMs Can Program Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Neural networks are typically programmed through optimization, rather than by explicitly specifying their computations. Recent work on weight-space programming suggests that large language models (LLMs) can instead reason about and manipulate neural-network weights directly. In this work, we show that LLMs can directly program statistical computations in tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose parameters enable inference across different datasets. We investigate three complementary settings using GPT-6 Astra, without gradient-based optimization. First, Astra directly programs nanoTabPFN from zero-initialized weights, achieving a mean ROC AUC of 0.849 across 20 TabArena datasets, compared to 0.876 for a pretrained baseline. Second, Astra diagnoses and repairs a signed-product regression failure in pretrained TabPFN-3.5, restoring near-perfect predictions on held-out synthetic datasets while preserving performance on TabArena-Lite, with only a 0.08% average relative increase in error. Third, it writes KV-cache-editing programs that steer TabPFN-3.5's predictions on unseen synthetic datasets, demonstrating transformations such as reversing linear trends and converting sine waves into approximate square waves, without modifying model weights. Together, our findings suggest that LLM-driven programming could complement gradient-based optimization across TFMs' development and usage, while offering a new way to investigate and intervene in their internal computations.

Neural networks are typically programmed indirectly: rather than specifying the computations they should perform, we optimize their parameters on data and rely on the resulting weights to implement useful algorithms. This paradigm was recently challenged by weight-space programming (WSP), which shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason about neural-network weights and directly construct or modify them [Takehi et al., 2026].

These costs motivate investigating whether statistical computation can be programmed directly into TFM architectures, rather than learned. But programming a TFM need not start from scratch. Furthermore, we can edit the KV-cache of TFMs that store forward-pass activations, representing the TFM’s fitted prediction model. Editing the KV-cache can steer predictions while leaving the weights untouched.

papers.title: Linear Algebra over Bands
papers.abstract: We introduce Eckmann-Hilton operators on bands, which allow for a suite of matroidal constructions, in particular, matroid unions and matroid stable intersections. This enables the construction of general linear monoids over bands. Geometrically, we show that matroid stable intersection extends the transverse intersection of linear spaces over fields and the stable intersection of tropical linear spaces, lending new insight into intersection theory on bands.

papers.intro:
Methods from linear algebra are universally useful in all areas of mathematics. Bands, introduced by Baker-Jin-Lorscheid [3], are a generalization of rings that can be used to describe many settings in algebraic combinatorics, in particular, oriented matroids and tropical linear spaces as in [4]. Their work builds on earlier studies of matroids with coefficients, developed by Baker-Bowler in [2] and originating in work of Dress-Wenzel [5]. Beyond matroid theory, bands provide a unified framework to study algebraic geometry in these settings. For this, methods in linear algebra are useful to define and study universal notions of tangent spaces and vector bundles, as well as many more.

papers.title: TRACK: Tool-Augmented Reasoning over Time Series for Fault Diagnosis in Power Management System
papers.abstract: Fault diagnosis in power management systems running multiple loads relies on experts manually inspecting current and voltage waveforms, which fails to scale across deployed units. We present TRACK, which pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to produce structured, physics-grounded diagnostic reports, calling tools for exact, verifiable calculations. It operates on-device, keeping proprietary sensor data local and avoiding expensive API calls. We introduce a rubric-based framework that evaluates these reports by scoring structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability through per-criterion verdicts. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, TRACK achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, whereas the best encoder-probing baseline reaches only 58% accuracy.

papers.intro:
Modern power management systems supply and protect multiple independent loads (components that consume electrical energy and convert it into work) through central or zonal power management units that continuously senses voltage and current across each channel. From electric vehicles to industrial robotics and grid infrastructure, nearly every electromechanical system depends on power management, and a single undiagnosed fault can halt the entire system. When faults occur, such as an LED failure, connector degradation, or fan stall, diagnostic signatures emerge in the sensed waveforms. Interpreting these signatures requires applying circuit-level physics (e.g., Ohm’s law, power dissipation) and reasoning across multiple channels to isolate the root cause. In practice, this diagnosis is often performed manually by domain experts, a time-intensive and costly process that fails to scale across large deployments.

Electromechanical systems generate proprietary data with limited bandwidth yet carry onboard compute, motivating fault diagnosis at the edge rather in the cloud. Thus, we ask: can a multimodal Small Language Model (SLM) track diagnostic signatures in sensed load voltages and currents, producing reasoning traces, like chain-of-thought explanations Wei et al. (2022), that are both physically grounded and actionable?

The challenge is fourfold. First, the model must combine multivariate time series data with varying baseline values (reference measurements under normal operation) and run on-device under memory and compute constraints, so a SLM is required. Second, the generated reasoning must contain a series of correct numerical calculations (e.g., current and voltage analysis), a traditionally difficult task for SLMs because of their fragile numerical representations Bhattacharya et al. (2025). Third, the model must reason over deviation patterns and explain them, especially for out-of-distribution (OOD) faults. Finally, evaluating the quality of physics reasoning requires domain-specific criteria that standard Natural Language Processing (NLP) metrics, which rely on text overlap, fail to capture.

papers.title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

papers.intro:
In many applications of computational statistics and machine learning, it is important to develop models that achieve both high predictive accuracy and a high degree of interpretability. In fields like medicine and insurance, for instance, it is desirable or even necessary to analyze how predictions are generated in order to ensure that the model behaves in a desired way. This stands at odds with the nature of state-of-the-art machine learning methods like random forests [5], XGBoost [7] or artificial neural networks (ANN), which achieve high predictive performance by optimizing complex black-box architectures at the cost of interpretability. Driven by the need to align the increasing use of modern black-box models with the demand for model interpretability, the field of interpretable machine learning (IML) has gained significant popularity and importance [9, 18].

Suppose we are analyzing the popular Boston housing dataset [10, 21] and fit a model to predict median housing prices based on socioeconomic information like the average room number per dwelling, pupil/teacher ratio, or distance to the nearest employment center. The dataset consists of 506 observations (referring to districts) and 13 features. In this simple example, it is easy to achieve near perfect prediction accuracy with a black-box method like XGBoost, see the near-zero training error in Figure 1A. However, if such a model should be used to inform policy makers about how features like the pupil teacher ratio or the distance to employment centers influence house pricing, the model does not offer an interpretation of the relationships between single features and the generated predictions. IML methods aim to provide such insights into the underlying behavior and decision-making processes of machine learning models.

In recent years, several software packages with IML functionalities have contributed to improvements in this field [3, 17, 18, 20]. Of particular interest for machine learning models are model-agnostic interpretability methods, which are largely model-independent and can be applied to a wide range of learners (including tree-based ensemble methods and ANN) but also to more traditional models like linear regression or generalized additive models. Model-agnostic interpretability is usually achieved post-hoc, meaning that the model of interest is post-processed after it has been fitted. Examples of such methods include permutation feature importance, partial dependence plots (PDPs), accumulated local effects (ALEs), local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) and Shapley-value-based feature attribution (see, e.g., Molnar [19] for a comprehensive overview).

The focus of this paper is on functional decomposition [22], which is a core concept of model-agnostic IML [18]. The basic idea of this approach is to replace the original black-box model by a surrogate model yielding exactly the same predictions as the original model. In contrast to the predictions of the black-box model, however, the surrogate prediction function is constrained to be a sum of subfunctions depending on subsets of the features only. More specifically, the subfunctions are defined by sets of main effects (depending on one feature each), two-way interaction effects (depending on pairs of features each), and higher-order interaction effects. These effects can be visualized using e.g. line plots or heatmaps, thereby allowing to understand the influence of individual features on the prediction function. papers.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

To study this question, we make three empirical contributions. Second, we study a Parcae-style architecture (Prairie et al., 2026), which confines recurrence to a dedicated latent workspace between Transformer encoder and decoder stages, and assess whether its stabilising adapter transfers to the looped-hybrid architecture. The first two contributions reduce inference memory through architectural changes. The third one leaves the architecture unchanged but reduces the number of persistent KV groups through training.

papers.title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
papers.abstract: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

Clinical voice agents are now deployed to autonomously conduct routine follow-up calls (Adams et al., 2025), making automated triage increasingly necessary. Patient frustration is one state such systems should detect: frustrated patients may disengage, answer tersely, or hang up before clinically important information is said (Klein et al., 2002; Hernandez Caralt et al., 2025). How a patient sounds should change what happens next. A clinician who heard strain in an otherwise fine answer would probe further, and the agent should too. Whether these systems can tell that has happened is largely unknown. We study a per-turn decision: whether each patient utterance is frustrated or not.

papers.title: Controllability of Acoustic Waves by Point Sources: Reachable States and Stable Reconstruction
papers.abstract:
We study the terminal controllability of the three-dimensional acoustic wave equation driven by finitely many fixed point sources, with zero initial data and time-dependent amplitudes supported in a finite interval. Although finitely many fixed sources cannot control the whole energy space, we establish the following results:
  (i) For source amplitudes in the first-order Sobolev space in time, the terminal state has finite energy if and only if all amplitudes vanish at both endpoints of the control interval.
  (ii) We derive an exact frequency-domain identity for the terminal energy involving a Gram matrix whose diagonal entries are one and whose off-diagonal entries are given by the sinc function, depending on frequency and source separation.
  (iii) For every positive control time, the terminal control operator is bounded below and is an isomorphism onto its closed reachable range, which has infinite codimension even among states satisfying the finite-propagation support condition.
  (iv) We establish a necessary and sufficient radiation-field criterion for reachability, provide stable reconstruction of the unique controls, and characterize the best approximation of non-reachable targets.
  The optimal coercivity constant equals one before the shortest source travel time. At long times, it decays as the inverse square of the control time for two sources and as the inverse fourth power for three equally spaced collinear sources. We also obtain upper bounds for general configurations and illustrate the theoretical results through reproducible Galerkin computations.

This description leads naturally to two levels of control. At the ideal level, the source amplitudes qjq_{j} are prescribed independently, and the question is to characterize and reconstruct the terminal states generated through the propagation map STS_{T}. At the physical level, the amplitudes are constrained by the effective bubble dynamics and must be generated by admissible incident waves. The present paper is devoted to the ideal level. The tracking study by Mukherjee and Sini [31] constructs ideal amplitudes for finite-dimensional projected pressure trajectories and studies their realization by resonant microstructures; its whole-space projection retains the boundary contribution of the observation region. The optimal-control study by Mukherjee and Sini [30] considers finite-band wave–actuator systems and the cost of the input driving the internal amplitudes. Our current terminal-state problem uses the complete outgoing field, without a finite spectral projection. In particular, uniqueness of the full-state source history is consistent with nonuniqueness after a finite-dimensional observation. Passing from ideal to physical control is an important further step: it requires characterizing the amplitudes that can be produced by incident fields, estimating the associated control costs, and relating the resulting terminal states to waves scattered by finite-size bubbles. This second level is not addressed here and will be the subject of forthcoming work.

In these applications one chooses source histories to cancel an unwanted field or to synthesize a prescribed acoustic field in an observation region; see Nelson and Elliott [32] for active sound control and Onofrei and Platt [34] for acoustic source synthesis with controlled near fields. papers.title: GENMETA-Lite: A Fast and Flexible Approach to Federated Learning with Disparate Covariate Information Across Studies
papers.abstract: Meta-analysis is foundational to federated learning, where one learns parameters by combining information across studies without sharing individual-level data. Handling missing and disparate covariates across studies is a major issue due to potential introduction of bias and decreased efficiency. We previously proposed a generalized meta-analysis estimator (GENMETA) to build a unified regression model using information on parameter estimates from sub-models and a reference population to estimate the joint covariate distribution. Building on that work, we present a linear estimator (GENMETA-Lite) as a practical, non-iterative method for multivariate meta-analysis, extended to handle heterogeneity in covariate distributions across studies, coarsened covariates, and model selection. Simulations demonstrate that our estimator has robust performance compared to estimates from na\"ive inverse-variance weighted meta-analysis or multiple imputation with individual-level data (approximately 4 to 100-fold reduction in mean squared error), even when underlying assumptions of linearity and homogeneous distributions are violated. We apply the method to fit a breast cancer risk prediction model with data from five studies (N = 313,851). Our study shows GENMETA-Lite is a robust federated learning approach for building regression models by combining information across disparate studies. An R package implementing these methods is made publicly available.

papers.intro:
Meta-analysis is widely used to combine parameter estimates across multiple studies when reanalysis of pooled individual-level data is infeasible due to privacy concerns, data access challenges, or computational limitations (Fleiss, 1993). Because meta-analysis only requires a single transfer of summary statistics (e.g. coefficient and variance estimates) rather than individual-level data, it preserves privacy and can be implemented in a federated learning setting (McMahan et al., 2017; Kairouz et al., 2021). Additionally, meta-analysis has been shown to be asymptotically as efficient as using pooled individual-level data in many common scenarios (Olkin and Sampson, 1998; Mathew and Nordström, 1999; Lin and Zeng, 2010).

Fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes that the regression models from each study were adjusted using the same set of covariates (Anderson, 2021; Becker and Wu, 2007; Nieminen, 2022). However, covariates missingness at the study-level may occur by design due to different study aims or administrative limitations, or at the model-fitting stage due to inconsistent covariate adjustment (Debray et al., 2019). If correlated covariates are differentially missing across study models, this will result in biased parameter estimates, and a standard fixed-effect multivariate meta-analysis would be inappropriate.

Several methods have been proposed to combine regression estimates across models fit with disparate covariates (i.e. “reduced” models) into a final model that contains all desired covariates (i.e. “full” model). One framing, known as synthesis analysis, aims to combine univariate model coefficients into a full multivariate model, for which a series of methods have been proposed (reviewed in Noon et al. (2026)). To combine estimates from more complex reduced models, bias correction terms have been proposed, but these require either access to individual-level data with outcome information (Ray et al., 2022; Yoneoka et al., 2015) or, when only summary statistics are required, the proposed method becomes intractable for models with more than three covariates (Yoneoka and Henmi, 2017). Another method, GENMETA (Kundu et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2023), based on generalized method of moments (Hansen, 1982; Imbens, 2002), has been proposed for complex, non-linear settings. GENMETA requires only summary statistics from each study as well as a joint distribution of all risk factors estimated in a reference population. An iteratively reweighted least-squares algorithm is used to optimize a complex function that links the full and reduced model parameters. While this estimator is efficient and enjoys consistency and asymptotic normality properties, because it is optimizing over a non-convex function it often struggles to converge as the number of studies or covariates grow.

Thus, motivated by the data example discussed below, we propose a more practical estimator called “GENMETA-Lite.” This closed-form linear estimator approximates the GENMETA procedure while eliminating convergence issues. We show that it has only moderate bias even when the linearity assumption is violated. Furthermore, we have implemented additional functionalities to handle covariate shifts between the studies and the reference population, coarsened variables (i.e. measurement error), and model selection. Since GENMETA-Lite requires only model summary statistics and covariate covariance matrices estimated in the studies and/or a reference population, this estimator can be applied in a privacy-preserving, federated learning context. We also make available a user-friendly R package implementing the different functionalities of GENMENTA-Lite.

Our article is organized as follows. In section 2 we describe the motivation for the new method, driven by the formation of a large, diverse cohort consortium aimed at developing a universal breast cancer risk prediction tool. In section 3, we introduce our new method, GENMETA-Lite. Section 4 details the extensive simulation experiments used to investigate its performance relative to other off-the-shelf methods in the face of common data challenges. Section 5 provides results from a real-world data example using a subset of cohorts from the cohort consortium. Section 6 summarizes our method, its performance and practicality, and proposed future work.

papers.title: Stabilization of LaH$_{10}$ with Thorium: Superconductivity in (La,Th)H$_{10}$ up to 232 K near 1 Mbar
papers.abstract: Ternary lanthanum-based hydrides are among the best high-temperature superconductors. Here we show that substituting La with thorium stabilizes La(Th)H$_{10}$ clathrate structure at $\sim$1 Mbar while only minimally suppressing superconductivity. The resulting cubic (La,Th)H$_{10}$ phase, synthesized from relatively air-stable La$_2$Th, La$_3$Th and La$_5$Th alloys, reaches an onset $\textit{T$_c$}$ = 232 K at 134 GPa, as confirmed by contact resistance measurements. Superconductivity was verified by two independent methods: electrical resistance and contactless radio-frequency measurements under applied magnetic fields at various pressures. Using a record-high pulsed current of 380 mA, we investigated critical phenomena in P6$_3$/mmc-(La,Th)H$_9$ at 173 GPa, which allowed for the experimental determination of a single superconducting gap within the s-wave model: $\Delta(0) = 37 \pm 4.5$ meV and $2\Delta(0)/kT_c = 4.9 \pm 0.6$. The La-Th-H system is chemically rich: in addition to the decahydride and nonahydride mentioned above, we also identified nanocrystalline I4/mmm-(La,Th)H$_4$ (5-6 nm grain size), (La,Th)H$_6$, as well as $hP13$, $cF80$ and $A15$ phases with compositions of (La,Th)H$_{5.75-6.25}$ and $\textit{T$_c$}$ $\approx$ 83 K at 70-80 GPa, and a possible (La,Th)H$_{16}$ polyhydride.

papers.title: Torsional Hall Viscosity of Massive Chern Insulators: Finite Temperature and Chemical Potential
papers.abstract: We study the torsional Hall viscosity $\zeta_{\rm H}$ of Chern insulators at finite temperature and chemical potential. Our analysis considers the massive Dirac fermion and two deformations: a constant out-of-plane magnetic field and a momentum-dependent mass described by the single-block Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (BHZ) Hamiltonian. For the massive Dirac theory, we show that temperature and chemical potential lead to UV-finite corrections and that a chemical potential outside the bulk gap modifies $\zeta_{\rm H}$ even at zero temperature. In a constant magnetic field, the response of massive Dirac fermions is dictated by the relativistic Landau-level spectrum, leading to a plateau structure at zero temperature that is smoothed at finite temperature. The jumps are proportional to the Dirac mass and inversely proportional to the squared magnetic length and the newly occupied Landau-level energy. Finally, we present a detailed study of the correction to $\zeta_{\rm H}$ in the single-block BHZ continuum model due to temperature and chemical potential. For parameters relevant to (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells, the magnitude of the jump across a mass domain wall retains its vacuum enhancement due to the BHZ deformation as long as the chemical potential lies sufficiently deep inside the gap compared with the thermal energy. Our results extend the theory of torsional Hall viscosity to experimentally relevant conditions and may facilitate its future detection.

papers.intro:
Hall viscosity is a nondissipative transport coefficient characterizing the transverse response of momentum to geometric deformations in systems with broken parity or time-reversal symmetry [1, 10]. In two-dimensional gapped systems, particularly quantum Hall states, it provides a geometric probe with connections to orbital spin and electromagnetic response [26, 25, 9, 4, 5]. For relativistic fermions, geometric deformations can be described by coupling the theory to a background geometry with torsion, and the corresponding parity-odd response defines the torsional Hall viscosity ζH\zeta_{\rm H} [14, 15, 24]. This description is particularly natural in crystalline systems, where torsion is associated with lattice dislocations [16, 7]. Torsional geometry has been further developed as a framework for studying topological phases, quantum anomalies, and the thermal Hall response [6, 30, 8, 12, 11, 13].

This description is particularly natural in crystalline systems, where torsion is associated with lattice dislocations [16, 7]. Torsional geometry has been further developed as a framework for studying topological phases, quantum anomalies, and the thermal Hall response [6, 30, 8, 12, 11, 13].

The massive Dirac fermion provides the simplest continuum model in which the torsional Hall viscosity can be studied analytically. Its absolute bulk value contains an ultraviolet-sensitive contribution, whereas differences between distinct gapped phases, in particular the jump across a mass domain wall, are well defined once a common renormalization prescription is chosen [14, 15, 24]. However, the relativistic Dirac model provides only a simplified description of the electronic structure of realistic topological materials. A natural extension is provided by the Bernevig–Hughes–Zhang (BHZ) Hamiltonian, originally introduced to describe HgTe quantum wells [2]. The full BHZ Hamiltonian consists of two blocks related by time reversal and describes the quantum spin Hall phase, which was subsequently observed experimentally in HgTe/(Hg,Cd)Te quantum wells [18]. Closely related BHZ-type effective Hamiltonians also describe inverted InAs/GaSb quantum wells [20, 17] and arise in ultrathin films of three-dimensional topological insulators such as Bi2Se3, where the low-energy theory contains massive Dirac fermions with quadratic momentum-dependent mass terms [32, 21]. These systems provide experimentally accessible settings in which the simple Dirac description is replaced by a momentum-dependent band structure.

For the Hall-type response considered here, time-reversal symmetry must be broken. It is therefore natural to focus on a single block of the BHZ Hamiltonian, which by itself describes a massive Chern insulator. A physical motivation for this reduction is provided by magnetically doped HgTe quantum wells. In (Hg,Mn)Te systems, exchange coupling to polarized Mn moments breaks time-reversal symmetry and modifies the two BHZ sectors differently, leading to quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) physics, with a weak magnetic field applied to induce the Mn polarization [23, 19, 27]. Such quantum wells and related topological insulators have been realized experimentally, and their topological transport properties have been studied in detail [27, 28, 31]. The single-block BHZ Hamiltonian therefore provides a simple effective description of the parity-odd sector relevant for the torsional response of a topological quantum well with broken time-reversal symmetry.

Measurements are necessarily performed at finite temperature, while the chemical potential in semiconductor quantum wells and thin films can be varied through doping or electrostatic gating. The occupation of the states contributing to the response therefore changes with both TT and μ\mu, especially when the chemical potential approaches a bulk band edge or crosses a Landau level. Extending the calculation to finite temperature and chemical potential is thus an important step toward determining whether the vacuum torsional Hall viscosity, and in particular the enhanced response found for the single-block BHZ model, can persist under experimentally accessible conditions.
