papers.title: STORMGUIDE-FL: Stochastic Remote Guidance for Efficient Mining of Federated Streaming Data
papers.abstract: Federated Learning enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices ("clients") while preserving data privacy. However, real-world deployments involve clients that observe continuous data streams from evolving environments while operating under strict resource limitations. Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.

papers.intro:
The rapid evolution of digital technologies and the exponential growth of data, in conjunction with the increasing demand for data protection by society (Parliament & Union, 2016; U.S. Congress, 2022), have underscored the significant importance of Federated Learning (FL) (McMahan et al., 2017) in the modern era of artificial intelligence. This innovative methodology embodies the shift towards decentralized data processing that enables collaborative learning without direct data exchange: advanced FL systems harness multiple nodes, diversified access points, and distributed collection mechanisms, organized into a server-client meta framework instead of relying on centralized repositories. Although the acquisition process of data points employed to train the global FL model allows a high degree of flexibility, this also introduces various challenges due to the non-stationarity of the data observations and the independence of the FL clients in real-world scenarios.

Client edge devices deployed in production environments such as trail cameras (Jagannathan et al., 2025), medical sensors (Feng et al., 2024), financial monitoring systems (Ardakani et al., 2023) and industrial equipment (Ahn et al., 2023), continuously observe non identically and independently distributed (non-IID) data streams. In this setup, processing, storing, and communicating becomes prohibitively expensive, particularly for clients with limited resource availability. Unlike traditional static datasets, these continuous streams of sensed observations arrive sequentially, typically without labels, and are subject to various forms of concept drift (Hinder et al., 2024) over time. Statistical properties of target variables can shift abruptly, such as when new regulations alter financial reporting requirements overnight, or gradually, as patient demographics change in a hospital over months or years (Chibwe et al., 2024). Such changes give rise to concept drift in the local scope, where each FL client must continually adapt to evolving local data distributions in order to remain accurate and relevant. This phenomenon refers to persistent divergence in client updates due to asynchronous or skewed observation histories, which leads to poor convergence and degraded global model performance (Karimireddy et al., 2020).

papers.title: Hands-On Beyond Classrooms: Elevating Control Engineering Education with Take-Home Labs
papers.abstract: This study shows how take-home laboratories can be integrated into control engineering education to strengthen hands-on learning in both introductory and advanced courses. The work provides evidence that a compact experimental platform can support conceptual understanding, student engagement, and course performance in a broadly applicable way. Control engineering courses often rely heavily on theory and simulation, which may limit students' ability to connect abstract concepts with practical implementation. Low-cost take-home laboratories offer a scalable alternative that can help bridge this gap across different educational settings. The curricular change, consisting of the introduction of take-home laboratory kits into the semester projects, was intended to improve students' motivation, deepen their understanding of core control principles, and enhance their performance in coursework and final assessment. Students used the kits for modeling, identification, and control design tasks, while learning outcomes were evaluated through questionnaires, midterm test scores, and final exam grades. Student feedback indicated strong acceptance of the new format and improved understanding of the subject matter. Statistical analysis showed a significant difference between cohorts before and after the curricular change, with modest but measurable effect sizes. The results suggest that take-home laboratories can support both motivation and academic performance, while also improving students' appreciation of the practical relevance of control engineering.

papers.title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
papers.abstract: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.

papers.intro:
Autonomous manipulation on moving conveyor belts is a pivotal challenge in industrial automation because unmodeled belt and robot dynamics, sensor delays, and kinematic uncertainties hinder precise tracking. Classical model-based controllers guarantee stability yet degrade under model bias or localization noise [1]. Pure reinforcement learning (RL) approaches are adaptive but data-intensive and impractical to train exclusively on hardware [2]. Hybrid methods alleviate these limitations by combining model-based and data-driven control. Residual learning enables an RL agent to augment the nominal controller, leveraging model knowledge for stability and sample efficiency while locally compensating for modeling and sensing errors [3]. Learning-based model predictive control has likewise achieved high-precision trajectory tracking on compliant robotic arms by integrating a Gaussian process–based model correction and an online disturbance estimator [4]. Similarly, data-driven trajectory optimization has been shown to improve motion accuracy in precision systems without modifying the underlying low-level controllers [5]. Researchers have also addressed the simulation–to-reality gap by, for example, pairing simulated pretraining with domain randomization across varied parameters [6] or constraining policy updates near nominal trajectories to improve transferability and convergence [7]. Alternative iterative approaches address model mismatch through repetitive control and run-to-run optimization [8], while data-efficient optimization with digital twins accelerates controller tuning by substituting costly real experiments with simulated trials [9]. Learning-based iterative controllers achieve high-precision tracking through compensation across repeated executions [10, 11], and adaptive Bayesian optimization uses Gaussian process models to improve performance over multiple runs [12]. In dynamic grasping and conveyor picking, deterministic planners predict object motion for interception [13], adaptive controllers reconfigure trajectories in real-time [14], and multi-agent RL with replay optimization enables interception on moving platforms [15].

We propose a control framework that augments a nominal inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a data-driven residual Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) policy to address autonomous manipulation on moving conveyor belts. The proposed framework contributes three elements: (i) a principled architecture that integrates model-based control and reinforcement learning for real-time refinement of the control signal through zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, (ii) a varying delay-compensated Kalman filter for vision-based state estimation under sensing latency, and (iii) a power-spectral tracking error lower bound derived from the closed-loop sensitivity. The SAC agent is trained entirely in simulation without any real-system data and compensates for modeling and sensing uncertainties, including kinematic bias, unmodeled dynamics, belt flexibility, measurement latency, and noise, by refining the commands generated by the nominal controller. We validate the proposed controller on a real robot using a vision-based robot cell with a dead–time–compensated Kalman filter and digital twin simulations, achieving sub-millimeter tracking accuracy that surpasses the performance limit on a class of model-based baseline controllers across varying conveyor speeds.

papers.title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
papers.abstract: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $\epsilon$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

A neural network can reach nearly perfect training accuracy while test accuracy remains near zero for many epochs before improving abruptly. This delayed generalization is called grokking (Power et al., 2022). One can distinguish two aspects of a grokked solution: the computational procedure used to compute the function, which is called its algorithm, and how that procedure is implemented across neurons, which is called its circuit. Modular addition is a well-understood example of grokking and a central task in mechanistic interpretability of small networks. Its algorithm and circuit can both be analyzed at the neuron level: the network represents each operand as an angle on a circle at a few frequencies and adds the angles, a periodic computation carried by the neurons tuned to those frequencies (Nanda et al., 2023; Gromov, 2023; Chughtai et al., 2023). When we say that two networks learn the same algorithm, we mean that they share this Fourier-based computation (Appendix B.3).

Our central hypothesis is that circuit concentration depends on how the learning rule distributes credit across neurons, where credit denotes the learning signal assigned to a neuron. Backpropagation with Adam assigns unequal credit, and the neurons that receive little of it end with small outgoing weights (Figure 1b). To isolate this effect, we modify backpropagation so that every neuron receives the same credit magnitude while its gradient direction is preserved, and we compare runs that share the data, initialization, loss, optimizer and hyperparameters. Equalizing credit increases the effective neuron count, computed from the outgoing weight norms, from approximately 154154 to 254254 of 256256 neurons in the first hidden layer while retaining the periodic computation. Training loss remains the same within a few percent, and test accuracy is about two percentage points lower. Applied after grokking, the same intervention redistributes the outgoing weights of an already learned circuit at unchanged test accuracy. papers.title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control
papers.abstract: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.

Building climate control with an electric heat pump is defined by the minimization of the electrical energy of the heat pump, subject to comfort bounds on the zone temperature [1, 2]. The bounds, however, admit two formulations that define different controllers.

In a hard-constrained formulation, the controller minimizes the energy subject to no violation of the bounds. This controller is determined by the bounds, but the problem can become infeasible, and its behavior in that case has to be defined separately [3]. In a soft-constrained formulation, the controller minimizes the energy plus a weighted penalty on the violation [4]. This problem is always feasible, but each weight gives a different operating point on the energy–comfort trade-off [5, 6].

How difficult the bounds are to hold depends on disturbances outside the controller’s influence, the weather and the internal gains, and on the occupancy, which sets when the tighter bounds apply. MPC solves an optimization problem over a model of the building and treats the comfort bounds as a constraint with a slack variable, whose weight determines whether the formulation is soft or hard. Even under the hard formulation, the comfort bounds hold on the building only as far as the model and the forecasts of the disturbances are accurate. Stochastic MPC replaces the bounds with chance constraints, at the cost of a model of the disturbance distribution [1]. A Lagrangian reinforcement learner enforces the bounds on average over the disturbances [7, 8], and its Lagrange multiplier acts as a weight that is adapted during training. Comparisons of the two methods, including on the common benchmark BOPTEST [9], fix one formulation per method [10, 5], which leaves open how much of the difference between the methods is due to the formulation.

We quantify the cost of each formulation in energy and in comfort, and we examine whether the trade-off between the two changes predictably with the weight of the soft formulation, so that the weight can be used to select an operating point on the frontier.

papers.title: Quantitative approximation for Fourier neural operators in controlled ordinary differential equations
papers.abstract: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) avoid the curse of parametric complexity when approximating the solution operator of certain partial differential equations (PDEs). While recent studies primarily focus on PDEs, in this article we derive upper error bounds for approximating the solution operator of controlled ordinary differential equations (CODEs) $\dot{y}=f(y,u)$ using a FNO. Under a Carath\'eodory setting and suitable regularity assumptions, including a smallness condition, we prove that the size of the FNO grows at most algebraically in $1/\varepsilon$, namely like $\varepsilon^{-(1+d/(2(s-1)))}$ up to logarithmic factors for GELU networks, and is thus sub-quadratic for sufficiently smooth $f$, where $d=1+n_y+n_u$ and $s$ denotes the Sobolev regularity of $f$. Our proof is based on emulating the Picard iteration through the layers of the FNO while exploiting the differentiation formula of the discrete Fourier transform. This result contributes to the quantitative approximation theory of FNOs for physically motivated problems and provides a theoretical foundation for leveraging a FNO as efficient forward surrogate for the solution operator of CODEs, especially in inverse parameter estimation where repeated evaluations of the forward operator are needed.

papers.intro:
Neural operators, acting between infinite-dimensional function spaces, constitute a natural extension of classical finite neural networks. In recent years, they have attracted considerable attention in the field of machine learning due to their ability to enabling surrogate modeling of high-dimensional and complex physical systems. Such systems can be modeled by partial differential equations (PDEs) or controlled ordinary differential equations (CODEs), whose numerical solving may become time consuming, particularly when repeated evaluations are required. Using neural operators to replace the solution operator of a PDE or CODE, where the latter also acts as an operator between function spaces due to the presence of control functions, may work out this issue. Once a neural operator is learned, it allows for a faster computational interference time while also maintaining an architecture that enables the processing of batched data. This also makes them an encouraging tool in solving (Bayesian) inverse problems via the Ensemble Kalman Inversion, especially in cases where a large data set of multiple experiments is present.

Various different architectures to realize a neural operator were introduced over the last years. One of the most promising ones is the so-called Fourier neural operator (FNO) which employs the (inverse) Fourier transform inside the network’s layered structure. While Universal Approximation Theorems of the FNO are well studied and suggest that any continuous operator can be approximated, quantitative approximation studies show that FNO faces exponential growth in model complexity, the so-called curse of parametric complexity [33], even when approximating CrC^{r}- or Lipschitz-regular operators. The curse of parametric complexity is an infinite-dimensional analogue to the well-known curse of dimensionality common in high-dimensional approximation problems.

This article starts with introducing a system of CODEs under a Carathéodory setting, that is that the controls uu do not need to be continuous, to determine appropriate mathematical assumptions to show the well-posedness of such a system while also deriving a continuous solution operator. This results in reformulating the CODE as a fixed point integral formula and thus, we follow the idea of emulating the Picard iteration by relying on the differentiation formula of the (discrete) Fourier transform to realize the integration of the controlled ordinary differential equation. Our article is organized as follows: • In Section 2 we introduce the controlled ordinary differential equation y˙=f⁡(t,y,u)\dot{y}=f(t,y,u) under suitable assumptions, such that we obtain the existence of a continuous control-to-solution operator. As we are interested in deriving error bounds for approximating this solution operator with a Fourier neural operator, we start to sharpening the assumptions on the CODE such that we can apply tools from Fourier analysis. • The Fourier neural operator is being formally introduced and defined in Section 3. Since deriving error bounds requires to quantify the network’s size, we define the Ψ\Psi-FNO which relates to the numerical implementable version of a FNO. Afterwards, we state known quantitative approximation results regarding finite neural networks, as we need to approximate ff by such networks. At the end of Section 3, we propose a Picard type fixed-point iteration scheme which produces an approximate output to the true solution of the CODE while also allowing to be emulated through the layers of Ψ\Psi-FNO. • In Section 4 we establish the main result. Due to the nature of the given example, it is the case that a large data set of multiple physical experiments is present. We therefore propose to utilize the learned FNO in an Ensemble Kalman Inversion which is extended to a Kaczmarz-like structure.

papers.title: Causal Regularization for Robust Prediction
papers.abstract: Prediction is an important use of a statistical model. However, predictive systems typically struggle when the environment, in which they were trained, changes. Robust prediction that can deal with distributional shifts has become an active research area. Existing approaches tend to make strong assumptions in order to achieve prediction guarantees. In this paper, we only require finite second moments in the training data to obtain sharp prediction guarantees. We generalize causal regularization to a framework that uses two environments and measures the differences between them through a generalized risk difference induced by changes in second-order moments of the covariates and response. By defining a sieve of out-of-sample distributions, we derive a worst-risk decomposition over increasing classes of environments and obtain a closed-form estimator that interpolates between OLS and the regularization limit solution. Causal interpretation is recovered under the inner-product invariance condition and when the conditional mean of the target given its causal parents remains invariant across environments. Our results show that the proposed estimator can achieve prediction stability over a broad class of perturbed environments, even when trained on a limited set. The framework separates two goals: robustness as a stable prediction under weak assumptions and causality as a stronger property obtained with additional invariance structure.

papers.intro:
Prediction models are commonly trained under a limited set of conditions and subsequently applied in environments that may differ from those observed during training. Changes in populations, experimental conditions, or external interventions can alter the joint distribution of the predictors and the response. Consequently, associations that provide accurate predictions in the training data may become unstable in new environments, leading to a substantial deterioration in predictive performance. This is an instance of a wider problem of out–of–distribution generalization that studies how models predict outcomes when the characteristics of the training data differ from the testing ones (Liu et al., 2023). When data from multiple environments are available, their heterogeneity can provide information about the stability of a predictive relation. Differences across environments can help distinguish associations that depend on the observed data from relationships that remain stable when the data-generating system changes. This motivates the construction of predictors that retain good performance across environments rather than optimizing predictive accuracy in a single training distribution. This is the objective of this paper and what is referred to as robust prediction.

Prediction models are commonly trained under a limited set of conditions and subsequently applied in environments that may differ from those observed during training. Changes in populations, experimental conditions, or external interventions can alter the joint distribution of the predictors and the response. Consequently, associations that provide accurate predictions in the training data may become unstable in new environments, leading to a substantial deterioration in predictive performance. This is an instance of a wider problem of out–of–distribution generalization that studies how models predict outcomes when the characteristics of the training data differ from the testing ones (Liu et al., 2023). When data from multiple environments are available, their heterogeneity can provide information about the stability of a predictive relation. Differences across environments can help distinguish associations that depend on the observed data from relationships that remain stable when the data-generating system changes. This motivates the construction of predictors that retain good performance across environments rather than optimizing predictive accuracy in a single training distribution. This is the objective of this paper and what is referred to as robust prediction.

There is a connection between stability across environments and causality. Indeed, causal mechanisms are identified as processes that do not change unless we directly intervene on the outcome. Consequently, it is possible for causal relations to provide stable predictive information when the data distributions change. In that case, the patterns that stay invariant across different distributions are used to identify the underlying causal structure under suitable assumptions. This connection between invariance, causality and robustness provides a common perspective on causal inference and prediction under heterogeneous or perturbed data (Bühlmann, 2020). However, the resulting methods differ as their guarantees still depend on structural assumptions about the data-generating process and the interventions. Invariant causal prediction (ICP) (Peters et al., 2016) is an identification procedure: it attempts to find those predictors whose conditional relationship with the response remains invariant across different environments. Causal Dantzig (Rothenhäusler et al., 2019), similar to ICP, uses invariance via moment conditions, but relies on linear structural models and assumes that the interventions are sufficiently informative. These two methods have the same type of conditional identifiability issues when the observed environments do not provide enough variation or when their invariance assumptions are violated. Anchor regression (Rothenhäusler et al., 2021) and causal regularization (Kania and Wit, 2025) represent an alternative approach to the two introduced above. Indeed, both methods take a more predictive and optimization-based perspective. However, anchor regression requires observing the anchor variables and is formulated within a linear model with additive shifts. Causal regularization requires an observational reference environment as well as a linear data-generating process. Both constraints will likely become restrictive when all observed environments are perturbed, when both predictors and the response are affected by interventions, or when the relationship among predictors and the response variable are non-linear.

There is a connection between stability across environments and causality. Indeed, causal mechanisms are identified as processes that do not change unless we directly intervene on the outcome. Consequently, it is possible for causal relations to provide stable predictive information when the data distributions change. In that case, the patterns that stay invariant across different distributions are used to identify the underlying causal structure under suitable assumptions. This connection between invariance, causality and robustness provides a common perspective on causal inference and prediction under heterogeneous or perturbed data (Bühlmann, 2020). Although the proposed predictor is linear in its parameters, the joint data-generating mechanism of the predictors and the response need not be linear. The proposed criterion combines predictive accuracy in the two training environments with robustness to distributional changes. We show that it admits a worst-case risk interpretation over classes of unseen environments whose second-order moments are controlled by those observed during training. The resulting framework is predictive in its general form, while a causal interpretation is recovered under additional invariance conditions. We study separately the conditions under which the limiting parameter admits a causal interpretation. papers.title: Unveiling the Multi-Phase Outflow in NGC 4151 with JWST Observations - I. Integrated Properties of the Outflow
papers.abstract: The biconical outflow of the nearby Seyfert 1.5 AGN NGC 4151 has been studied across the electromagnetic spectrum, yet mapping its multiphase structure with a single facility has remained challenging. Leveraging the broad wavelength coverage of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), we present new near- and mid-infrared observations tracing the ionization stratification of these outflows with a unified dataset. We analyze emission lines originating from molecular gas to highly ionized plasma and analyze the ionized gas using a 5-component Cloudy photoionization model covering three primary phases. Applying the footprint line method to characterize the X-ray emitting gas, we find that it holds the largest share of the total mass, suggesting that it is a primary candidate for driving AGN feedback in this system.

papers.intro:
Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are responsible for some of the most energetic phenomena in the Universe, with the central engine capable of outshining the rest of the host galaxy. The release of vast amounts of energy from the accretion disk around the supermassive black hole (SMBH) results in interaction between the AGN and the interstellar medium of the host. This is commonly referred to as feedback, and often takes the form of winds of ionized gas, which are widespread among the AGN population (e.g. 47, 75, 67). Importantly, AGN feedback has been highlighted as one of the necessary phenomena to explain galaxy properties and evolution (e.g. 48, 14) emphasizing the importance of studying these processes in detail. AGN outflows and their role in shaping galaxies have been heavily discussed topics, especially since the 1990s (28, and references within). This time-frame also corresponds to a noticeable increase in investigations into the outflows of NGC 4151.

NGC 4151 is a nearby (z = 0.0033, 15; d = 15.8 Mpc, 76) Seyfert 1.5 galaxy that has been extensively observed and studied across the full range of the electromagnetic spectrum. The bolometric luminosity of this target has been measured to be Lbol = 1.4 ×\times 1044 erg s-1, which corresponds to an Eddington ratio of 0.03 [36], however, the continuum is highly variable (e.g. 61) which could lead to significant uncertainties in Lbol. NGC 4151 is also variable in its intrinsic absorption, which has been detected across the X-ray, UV and optical energy ranges (e.g. 27, 38). Additionally, the nuclear region is notably devoid of star formation (SF) based on the absence of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon (PAH) features [65].

This was further supported by the available HST spectroscopic data, which demonstrated that the emission lines towards the southwest of the central engine are blueshifted, while those on the northeast side are redshifted [31, 34]. Spectroscopic investigations into the X-ray emitting regions of NGC 4151 found that the gas is dominated by photoionization [50, 1]. As demonstrated by the wide range of wavelength regimes through which the outflow in NGC 4151 has been studied, previous research suggests the presence of multi-phase structure in the outflow (spanning a range of density and ionization). Feedback from the lower-ionization components, such as those traced by [O iii] 5007 Å ([O iii] thereafter), have been accurately measured using spatially resolved kinematic data [9, 44]. However, the absence of X-ray Integral Field Units (IFUs) currently limits our ability to obtain similarly constrained measurements of the X-ray-emitting phase.

These lines typically have ionization potentials greater than that of O vii (IP = 138 eV) with some exceptions [23]. As demonstrated in both [22] and [23], the outflow in NGC 7469 does not appear to induce significant globalized feedback into the surrounding ISM, most evident by the presence of a nuclear starburst ring at approximately 500 pc from the AGN. The primary hypothesis is that the bicone is primarily oriented out of the plane of the host galaxy, representing a weak coupling scenario [29]. In contrast, the well-defined orientation of the bicone in NGC 4151 in the plane of the host allows us to assume a strong coupling scenario for this target [12, 13].

papers.title: Seeing Isn't Resolving: Visual and Linguistic Disambiguation with Conversational Grounding
papers.abstract: Visual grounding benchmarks usually do not consider the contextual uncertainty of real-world scenarios. In this study, we construct a novel benchmark, the Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D) dataset. It consists of human-robot conversational multimodal interactions covering different types of ambiguity, arising from visual and linguistic categories. We evaluate the capabilities of different state-of-the-art Visual Language Models (VLMs) for ambiguity recognition and resolution. We compare dialogue context grounding performance for visual and linguistic ambiguity resolution. Our experiments show that VLMs can substantially improve the resolution of linguistic ambiguity, especially Japanese zero anaphora, by using dialogue context. We further conduct a comparative analysis to understand whether grounding improvements arise from the semantic content of the dialogue or from its conversational structure.

Visual grounding is the task of localizing visual regions described by referring expressions in natural language, and has achieved substantial progress on standard benchmarks (Plummer et al., 2017; Rohrbach et al., 2016). However, these benchmarks evaluate models under idealized conditions where referring expressions are unambiguous, single-target, and context-independent (Xiao et al., 2026), even if such assumptions are not valid for real-world settings. This limitation motivates the need to address ambiguity in referring expressions in realistic scenarios such as human-robot interaction.

Ambiguity resolution in language has been widely studied, particularly at the lexical and sentential levels (Gonzalo et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2023; Schouten et al., 2023; Karamolegkou et al., 2025). Multimodal ambiguity resolution is equally important, and tasks such as visual question answering have attracted particular attention (Stengel-Eskin et al., 2023; Nam et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). However, such tasks capture only part of the referential communication required in human-robot interaction. To achieve appropriate interaction grounded to the world, computational systems must be able to properly interpret references that depend more heavily on the situational context. In real-world scenarios, user utterances contain diverse forms of instructions and omissions, and resolving them requires the use of various types of information, such as dialogue history DeVault and Stone (2009), pointing Constantin et al. To clarify the extent to which multimodal systems can address these problems, and where their limitations lie, we introduce Japanese evaluation for Ambiguous visual Grounding with Dialogue (JAG-D). JAG-D contains 480 carefully curated instances, each combining an image, an instruction, and a dialogue history. We prioritize annotation quality over benchmark scale, limiting the dataset size so that human experts, with more than eight years of experience in discourse structure annotation, can thoroughly verify each instance. The utterances in JAG-D contain diverse ambiguities arising from both visual and linguistic factors, and the dataset consists of situations in which these ambiguities are expected to be resolved by referring to the dialogue history.

We also find that using additional dialogue context substantially resolves linguistic ambiguity, especially ambiguity caused by zero anaphora, whereas its contribution to resolving visual ambiguity is limited. papers.title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems
papers.abstract:
Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions.
  We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions.
  Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated.
  The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.

Constraints can improve consistency and transparency, yet a meaningful rule need not be appropriate in every decision context [4]. papers.title: Objectify, Don't Delete: Complaint-Derived Evaluation of Ambient Clinical Notes
papers.abstract: Evaluating the quality of AI-generated clinical notes is hard: standard metrics like ROUGE measure lexical similarity to reference notes, while expert checklists encode what committees believe matters. Neither captures what clinicians actually complain about. Recent work has shown that evaluation criteria can be mined from user feedback and filtered to criteria that LLM judges can reliably enforce. We argue that this is where much of the value is lost. The criteria that fail enforceability are disproportionately the ones clinicians raise most often, because high-frequency complaints are stated as several questions glued together. No yes/no judgment can grade such composites as posed. We introduce an objectification step that rewrites such criteria into sets of scoped, determinate decisions. We demonstrate the approach through an evaluation pipeline that mines criteria from complaints, objectifies them, and deploys LLM judges against both planted defects and production notes. Across eleven defects planted into ACI-bench reference notes, objectified judges localize violations with median recall of 0.95, while reference metrics change by at most 0.037. Given the complaint as one broad question, the same judges still find every planted defect, but they also flag 70% of the unperturbed reference notes; one section-pair question per call raises Youden's J from 0.30 to 0.72 (by 0.19 to 0.26 with prompt effort matched). We release ACI-Defect, a perturbation benchmark; clinician-reviewed instance-level labels showing quality gaps in the ACI-bench gold standard (32 of 40 notes contain hallucinations; 40 of 40 omit discussed facts); and grounding-judge verdicts. On 1,446 production notes, mean instance-rate burden falls at every clinician-rating step (rho=-0.15), a small association. Defect counts have to be kept per span rather than collapsed into one pass/fail bit per note.

papers.intro:
AI-powered ambient clinical documentation systems transcribe a patient-clinician encounter and draft a structured clinical note. They are now deployed at scale. As with any AI-generated content, it is essential that the quality and clinical safety of the generated notes be rigorously monitored. Manual review of these notes does not scale, has high inter-rater variance, and cannot be run on every production note within a short span of time. Hence, focus has shifted to automated methods of measuring quality, one of which is by comparing a note to a gold note (Yim et al., 2023), termed reference-based measurement. This form of measurement fails due to the subjectivity in constructing a gold note. There is not just one perfect gold note. Two clinicians documenting the same encounter produce materially different, equally acceptable write-ups. Lexical and embedding similarity to a single reference is the protocol followed generally in practice (as demonstrated in ACI-bench (Yim et al., 2023) which reports ROUGE (Lin, 2004), BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2020), BLEURT (Sellam et al., 2020), and MedCon (Van Veen et al., 2024)). However, while it penalizes legitimate stylistic variations, it remains insensitive to clinically harmful errors that barely change nn-gram overlap, such as a fabricated normal exam finding or an Assessment sentence leaking into the History of Present Illness.

papers.title: How Elasticity and Chiral Damping Shape Domain-Wall Creep
papers.abstract: Asymmetric domain-wall expansion in the creep regime provides an experimentally accessible probe of the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (iDMI) and, in principle, chiral damping. However, severe discrepancies with complementary measurement techniques and the lack of a model describing the full experimental phenomenology of the creep of chiral domain walls, limits the application of these measurements. Here, using a symmetry decomposition of the velocity curve, we derive an analytical model describing the coupled influence of domain-wall stiffness and chiral damping in the creep regime. Their interplay generates the antisymmetric distortion that shifts the velocity minimum away from the DMI field. Applied to Co-based magnetic multilayers, the model yields iDMI values consistent with BLS and flow-regime benchmarks and identifies the reasons for the longstanding discrepancy. The model provides insights for possible strategies to measure chiral damping via creep dynamics of domain walls.

papers.title: Model-free stiffness measurement of microscale soft contacts by far-field traction force microscopy
papers.abstract: The microscale stiffness of soft materials governs their contact mechanics, adhesion and friction, yet it is surprisingly difficult to measure. Micro or nanoindentation is typically used, but extracting stiffness from these measurements requires using contact mechanics models (e.g. JKR), whose assumptions often break down for soft adhesive contacts. Here, we introduce far-field traction force microscopy (FF-TFM) to extract stiffness without using any contact model. We drag a colloidal probe mounted on an atomic-force microscope across a soft surface, measuring the friction force while imaging the displacements of fluorescent tracers on the substrate. Far from the contact, in the elastic limit, these lateral displacements depend solely on the friction force and the substrate stiffness, and fitting them with the point-force solution thus gives the substrate's Young's modulus directly. We successfully match bulk rheology moduli with FF-TFM for six different silicone elastomers, where JKR fits to indentation data underestimate moduli by as much as 40\% of their bulk values. Our approach also enables tracking how the probe slips across the surface. We find that soft contacts can "pre-slip" with no detectable signature in the force signal, unlike stiffer contacts. FF-TFM thus offers a contact-model-free route to measuring microscale stiffness and slip behavior in soft materials.

papers.intro:
Stiffness is a key material property. It controls how much a material deforms under an applied force and its knowledge is thus essential to design any structural or mechanical component, in particular whenever contacts between two (or more) bodies are present. While the mechanistic origin of contact stiffness has been exhaustively investigated for hard surfaces, i.e. between two metals, the advent of a broad emerging class of new soft materials, such as functional elastomers or hydrogels, requires new methodologies and new understanding. Measuring stiffness of soft materials at the macroscale is now a routine task. It is carried out either by tensile testing to obtain a material’s Young’s modulus (EE) or via shear rheology to measure its shear modulus (GG), whereby EE can be obtained through knowledge of the material’s Poisson’s ratio ν\nu.

However, it is extremely challenging to transfer these tests onto microscopic samples, and this limitation presents far-reaching implications. Microscale contacts in fact govern the performance of many soft materials of high relevance, where surface deformation controls not only the contact area, but also adhesion and friction [1, 2, 3, 4]. In particular, living systems are highly sensitive to microscale contact stiffness, where cells sense the stiffness of their immediate surroundings and change their behaviour in response [5, 6]. For example, macrophages sense the stiffness of an implant surface, and the response determines how much inflammation and scarring will follow [7]. Matching the contact stiffness of an implant with its host tissue has thus become a key goal in bioelectronics design [8]. Contact stiffness also matters for most soft devices. For example, the sensitivity of soft tactile sensors is set by the stiffness of structures only a few hundred micrometres in size [9]. Soft robotic grippers also often rely on micropatterned sensors and small scale contacts under conditions of varying friction and adhesion, e.g. wet versus dry contacts [10, 11, 12]. In all of these cases, it is vital to characterize and engineer microscale contact stiffness.

papers.title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
papers.abstract: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.

Many robots, vehicles, and wearable devices see the same environment more than once. A delivery robot drives the same warehouse floor every day. A person wearing an AR headset walks through the same building on many occasions. We call each such pass a session. Each session is tracked by the device’s own visual or visual-inertial odometry. The classical way to detect overlap is to build and maintain a 3D map of visual landmarks and match new observations against it, as in ORB-SLAM3 Atlas [1], Maplab [2, 3], and COVINS [4]. A map gives strong geometric evidence for a match, but is expensive to store and keep optimized; bundle adjustment grows linearly in landmarks and cubically in poses, so this cost grows with every session and with the size of the environment. A well-built map is also rarely what downstream modules want, since planning and navigation seldom consume a landmark cloud directly.

papers.title: D\'ej\`a-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating
papers.abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present D\'ej\`a-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from D\'ej\`a View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, D\'ej\`a-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

Robots that move fast or operate in poor lighting need the 3D geometry of their surroundings, and their own motion through it, with little delay, yet these are exactly the conditions in which frame cameras blur, saturate or under-expose [1, 2]. Event cameras avoid much of this: each pixel asynchronously reports brightness changes as they happen, giving microsecond temporal resolution and a much higher dynamic range than conventional cameras [3, 4]. These make events an attractive modality for 3D reconstruction in such scenes [5].

We therefore distil geometry from an RGB model instead: a frozen RGB teacher sees RGB frames, and an event student learns to reproduce what the teacher computes from events paired with those frames alone, transferring the teacher’s priors to events [1, 5]. Because the student inherits those priors but not the sensor, it can keep predicting structure where the teacher’s frames saturate (Fig. 1).

papers.title: OmniTag-LLM: Multilingual Multitask Speech Tagging
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs promise to replace the traditional cascade of specialist speech models with a single system that, from one audio clip, jointly transcribes and labels emotion, gender, language, and named entities. Yet most benchmarks still score these tasks in isolation, and largely in English. We introduce OmniTag-Bench, a five-language benchmark (en/de/es/fr/it) and training recipe for joint understanding: one audio clip in, one JSON object out (transcript, emotion, gender, LID, token-level NER). We evaluate ten open multimodal LLMs and a LoRA fine-tuned Qwen3-Omni on a unified prompt and scorer. Beyond aggregate scores, OmniTag-Bench reveals a systematic failure mode: several strong models often transcribe or translate non-English speech into English, inflating multilingual WER. Fine-tuning improves the base model on NER, emotion, and WER while nearly doubling accuracy on independent human-labeled emotion corpora, suggesting transferable gains beyond pseudo-label imitation. The fine-tuned model also generalizes to unseen but related languages, transferring to held-out Dutch. We release prompts, the scorer, and the labeling pipeline.

papers.intro:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are emerging as general-purpose interfaces for audio understanding, where a single model, given one audio clip and one prompt, can emit labels for several complementary tasks that a traditional pipeline distributes across dedicated expert systems [6, 5, 12, 20, 47, 15, 17, 39, 14] (Fig. 1). This consolidation is appealing, yet these generalists still trail purpose-built specialists on each individual task. A rapidly expanding ecosystem of open-weight omni and speech LLMs, spanning four to thirty billion parameters [47, 46, 29, 25, 30, 49, 45, 35, 11], is narrowing this gap, making it timely to measure how closely one model can approach specialist-level performance across the full annotation stack.

A rapidly expanding ecosystem of open-weight omni and speech LLMs, spanning four to thirty billion parameters [47, 46, 29, 25, 30, 49, 45, 35, 11], is narrowing this gap, making it timely to measure how closely one model can approach specialist-level performance across the full annotation stack.

Yet evaluation has not kept pace. Instruction-following audio suites such as AIR-Bench [50], Dynamic-SUPERB [24], and AudioBench [43] broadened testing beyond single tasks; ISA-Bench [26] probed instruction sensitivity, and MMAU [34] extended coverage to speech, sound, and music reasoning. These suites nonetheless largely (i) grade one question per query rather than all tasks jointly; (ii) target English, confining multilingual evaluation mainly to ASR and language identification (ML-SUPERB [36] scales to 100+100+ languages but scores encoder representations, not MLLM generation); and (iii) accept free-form answers that are hard to grade reliably at scale. One competency thus remains unmeasured, namely whether a single model can deliver joint, structured, multilingual output from one prompt for multilingual input. OmniTag-Bench fixes the instruction but demands all five tasks (ASR, emotion, gender, language identification (LID), and named-entity recognition (NER)) at once across five languages (English, German, Spanish, French, Italian) as a single JSON object, stressing format compliance and cross-lingual consistency rather than instruction variety.

We close this gap with a benchmark, a model, and a broad empirical study. High-quality manual labels for emotion, gender, and NER are costly to obtain at scale, so, following common practice, we distill them offline from specialist teachers, a Whisper-based classifier [33] for emotion, a lightweight audio classifier [2] for gender, and GLiNER2 [51] for NER. These distilled labels both supervise the joint model and backfill those missing from individual corpora, whereas transcripts and language remain native throughout. The pipeline itself is dataset-agnostic, so given any audio collection it can produce training-ready labels for all five tasks, falling back to a dedicated specialist wherever native annotations are unavailable. For transcription it uses Qwen3-ASR-1.7B [37] and for LID a w2v-BERT language-identification model [18], completing the five-specialist set of Fig. 1. We then evaluate the resulting model against ten open baselines under one joint, multilingual protocol. Specifically, we contribute: 1. OmniTag-LLM. A multilingual multitask speech-labeling model built on Qwen3-Omni. Fine-tuning improves the base model on every task (Table III), with the most diagnostic gains on held-out, human-labeled emotion corpora independent of the distillation teachers, evidence of transferable rather than merely imitative competence. The gains also carry over to Dutch, a language outside the five training languages (Section V-E). 2. OmniTag-Bench and curated label sets. Five language splits with closed-vocabulary JSON targets for ASR, emotion, gender, LID, and NER (NER from MSNER [28]; all labels native except teacher-pseudo-labeled emotion), evaluated under an identical prompt and scorer for all systems. 3. A broad model survey. Ten open-weight MLLMs spanning 44B–3030B parameters and four serving back-ends, under one joint decoding protocol. 4. A cross-lingual failure analysis. Identification, quantification, and partial mitigation of a pervasive “transcribe-into-English” failure mode, with practical implications for multilingual MLLM reporting.

papers.title: Optimal Coordination of Multiple Ancillary Service Provisions in Active Distribution Networks
papers.abstract: We propose a multi-rate model predictive control (MPC) framework for coordinating primary frequency control (PFC), automatic generation control (AGC), and voltage control (VC) in active distribution networks. The framework allocates distributed energy resource (DER) flexibility among these three ancillary services while retaining their different update rates. To account for the intertemporal flexibility of electric vehicle aggregations and aggregations of buildings with thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs), we incorporate time-varying power-energy envelopes into our multi-rate MPC formulation. These constraints couple the combined PFC and AGC response to the demand-side flexibility available later in the prediction horizon. Furthermore, the input-multirate structure enables coordinated ancillary service provision by DERs with different response dynamics. The controller optimizes the three services together, allowing fast regulation to be coordinated with the developing slow response within the available DER flexibility. We demonstrate the coordinated provision of the three ancillary services through closed-loop simulations on a modified IEEE 33-bus system using a nonlinear differential-algebraic model.
papers.intro:
The transition toward renewable-dominated power systems presents new challenges for frequency regulation and voltage support. As converter-interfaced renewable generation continues to replace conventional synchronous units, the availability of conventional resources providing these ancillary services decreases [1]. This motivates ancillary service provision by alternative resources. Meanwhile, the growing deployment of distributed energy resources (DERs), including dispatchable generators, battery energy storage systems (BESSs), electric vehicles (EVs), and thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs), offers controllable flexibility in distribution networks (DNs). Their controllability is transforming traditionally passive DNs into active networks with significant operational flexibility [2, 3, 4]. Although individual DERs generally have limited capacities, their coordinated aggregations can enable active DNs to provide voltage support and frequency regulation to the upstream grid [5].

As converter-interfaced renewable generation continues to replace conventional synchronous units, the availability of conventional resources providing these ancillary services decreases [1]. This motivates ancillary service provision by alternative resources. Meanwhile, the growing deployment of distributed energy resources (DERs), including dispatchable generators, battery energy storage systems (BESSs), electric vehicles (EVs), and thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs), offers controllable flexibility in distribution networks (DNs). Their controllability is transforming traditionally passive DNs into active networks with significant operational flexibility [2, 3, 4]. Although individual DERs generally have limited capacities, their coordinated aggregations can enable active DNs to provide voltage support and frequency regulation to the upstream grid [5].

Existing studies have investigated PFC and AGC using controllable loads and other flexible resources [6, 7, 8, 9], and voltage support using distributed active power sources and flexible loads [10, 11, 12, 13]. Although these studies highlight the capabilities of DERs in active DNs for frequency and voltage regulation, they mainly focus on single ancillary services or one control layer at a time. In the case that the same DER portfolio participates in multiple services, the feasible allocation depends on their joint use of device and network capability [14, 15]. For example, hierarchical architectures separate slow scheduling from fast regulation [16, 17], with fast control actions determined under the allocation set by the supervisory layer. By contrast, centralized MPC can jointly optimize DER setpoints within a common constrained problem, coordinating their use of the available flexibility [18]. In fact, jointly coordinating multiple services within a common optimization also requires reconciling their inherently different control time scales.

In fact, jointly coordinating multiple services within a common optimization also requires reconciling their inherently different control time scales.

PFC and VC require fast adjustments, whereas AGC provides a relatively slower response over a longer interval [19]. Despite these different time scales, the corresponding services rely on the same underlying DER and network capabilities, including active and reactive power availability, voltage limits, and branch current capacity [20, 21]. As a result, service schedules that are feasible when determined independently may become incompatible when implemented simultaneously. A further challenge is how to accommodate these different services within a single optimal control framework. Updating services at the fast rate introduces AGC decisions at each fast control interval, which increases the number of optimization variables. In contrast, adopting a common slow update rate reduces the computational burden but restricts PFC and VC to less frequent updates. This will limit their ability to respond promptly to fast system variations. This trade-off motivates a multi-rate control framework that retains the respective update rates of different services while optimally coordinating DER flexibility for the joint provision of multiple ancillary services.

Multi-rate model predictive control (MPC) accommodates different measurement or control update rates within a finite horizon formulation [22]. Subsequent studies have extended multi-rate MPC to applications in which measurements or actuators operate at different rates. In networked control, a distributed MPC formulation incorporates state measurements available at different sampling rates and adjusts controller coordination according to the available measurements [23]. More recently, a unified multi-rate MPC formulation has been developed for a humanoid robot to coordinate joint and jet engine actuation with different update rates [24]. These applications illustrate how a multi-rate structure accommodates different measurement and actuation requirements within predictive control. The same principle is relevant to ancillary service provision in power systems, where PFC, AGC, and VC have different time scales and response requirements but share the available DER flexibility. Coordinating these services therefore requires both suitable update rates and an allocation that accounts for their combined use of the participating resources.

The framework jointly allocates available DER flexibility among the three services, accommodating their different update rates and the intertemporal flexibility of demand-side resources. The resulting finite horizon problem admits an equivalent convex reformulation as a quadratic problem for receding horizon implementation.

The framework jointly allocates available DER flexibility among the three services, accommodating their different update rates and the intertemporal flexibility of demand-side resources. The resulting finite horizon problem admits an equivalent convex reformulation as a quadratic problem for receding horizon implementation.

The main contributions are summarized as follows. 1) Multi-Rate Coordination: We first formulate a continuous-time multi-rate optimal control problem and then parameterize the control inputs and discretize the DER dynamics to obtain a finite-horizon MPC formulation. The resulting centralized multi-rate MPC jointly optimizes the PFC, AGC, and VC setpoints on a common time grid, with each service updated at its prescribed rate. DER response models capture how the physical outputs develop following setpoint adjustments, accounting for different device dynamics. The distribution system model then maps these outputs to bus voltages, branch currents, and service delivery. Together with DER capability limits, network operating constraints, and demand-side power–energy constraints, these models define the admissible service allocation over the prediction horizon. Hence, the three services operate at their different update rates while their use of available DER flexibility is coordinated within a single finite-horizon problem. 2) Demand-Side Flexibility: Demand-side flexibility is characterized not only by available power capacity but also by the duration over which the response can be maintained [25]. Based on aggregate flexibility models [26, 27, 28], we therefore introduce time-varying power–energy envelopes for EV aggregations and aggregations of buildings with TCLs. These envelopes bound aggregate power and cumulative energy deviation from baseline consumption, capturing how current power use affects the flexibility available later in the prediction horizon. 3) Comparative Assessment: Compared with approaches focused on individual ancillary services [6, 12], the framework accounts for the interaction among PFC, AGC, and VC through shared resources. Previously proposed hierarchical architectures separate slow scheduling from fast regulation across different control layers [16, 17]. In contrast, C-MPC combines centralized service allocation with an input-multirate structure, allowing fast regulation and sustained support to be coordinated according to the different service requirements and DER response dynamics. This coordination allows the PFC allocation to account for the developing AGC response and their shared use of available DER flexibility.

papers.title: Inequality-Constrained Optimization via Sliding Mode Control
papers.abstract: We present COSMIC (Constrained Optimization via Sliding Mode for Inequality Constraints), a continuous-time solver for inequality-constrained optimization. COSMIC couples primal gradient-flow dynamics with multiplier dynamics derived from sliding mode control laws on a manifold defined by the smoothed Fischer-Burmeister function. We prove that COSMIC's trajectories reach this manifold in finite time from any primal initial point, after which the dynamics reduces to the gradient flow of a logarithmic barrier function. This yields a control-theoretic interpretation of barrier methods while allowing infeasible initialization. For strongly convex problems, we further establish exponential convergence to the minimizer. To address the numerical stiffness that arises in discretization, we develop a modified discrete-time algorithm. We validate COSMIC across various machine learning applications, demonstrating its ability to solve optimization problems accurately while scaling effectively to high-dimensional settings.

Inequality-constrained optimization problems, which subsume equality constraints, are prominent in various control, robotics, and machine learning applications, where the inequality constraints typically encode safety requirements or system and resource limitations. Classical approaches to solving (1) include projection-based methods, primal-dual algorithms, and penalty methods. The system-theoretic view of algorithms offers an alternative framework for analyzing and designing optimization algorithms through the lens of control theory (Dörfler et al., 2024). This perspective has recently provided a control-theoretic interpretation of saddle-point flows, where the primal variables act as the plant of a dynamical system, and the Lagrange multipliers act as PID controllers that enforce constraint satisfaction (Cerone et al., 2025; Centorrino et al., 2026a). While PID controllers offer asymptotic convergence in these methods, sliding mode control (SMC) offers finite-time convergence and robustness to bounded uncertainty (Khalil, 2002). Recent work applies SMC for equality-constrained problems (Diana et al., 2026) with finite-time convergence. However, to date there is no first-order SMC-based solver for inequality-constrained problems, with convergence guarantees.

papers.title: Controlling Mode-Locking in Liquid Light
papers.abstract: Mode-locking is the process by which the phases of many cavity modes organize collectively into a stationary state. In lasers, mode-locking originates from the interplay of gain, loss, dispersion and nonlinearities, most commonly resulting in the emission of short pulses. However, pulse formation is prevented when the gain recovery is fast enough to suppress amplitude fluctuations. Mode-locking then produces an extended state of nearly constant intensity, whose dynamics is governed by the phase. Yet, a general framework for designing the phase of such extended photonic states remains lacking. Here we introduce a hydrodynamic approach to designing extended photonic states, in which the phase dynamics are understood and controlled as a flow of liquid-like light. The intensity, clamped by fast gain, plays the role of a constant density, the instantaneous frequency that of a flow velocity, and the programmable radio-frequency modulation applied to the laser acts as a potential landscape that controls the flow. We derive analytical solutions connecting the applied modulation to the instantaneous frequency and hence to the spectrum emitted by the laser. We further provide experimental evidence for the liquid light shaping framework by measuring the frequency comb spectra emitted by a fast-gain semiconductor laser around \SI{1.6}{\micro\m} under the control of a programmed modulation, and comparing them to the ones predicted by the analytical solution. The hydrodynamic picture of mode-locking provides a predictive design principle for frequency combs, pointing toward a programmable synthesizer of light, and establishes fast-gain lasers as an accessible, electrically driven platform for nonequilibrium fluids of light.

The locking of many oscillatory degrees of freedom into a common phase relationship is ubiquitous across physics, from synchronized pendulum clocks to injection-locked oscillators and arrays of Josephson junctions[42, 1]. In photonics, this process is known as mode-locking. It requires a mechanism that couples cavity modes and then selects a steady state by constraining their amplitudes and phases. In active mode-locking, both mechanisms are effectively linear: a modulator transfers energy between neighboring modes, while dissipation selects the lowest-loss state, a pulse[19, 29]. However, both roles can be taken over by an optical nonlinearity, as in passively mode-locked lasers with saturable absorbers, Kerr lensing or additive-pulse mode locking[36, 10, 26, 48, 34]. Similarly, in coherently driven passive resonators, the Kerr nonlinearity couples the modes and maintains cavity and temporal solitons[32, 5, 23, 28]. The dynamics is then governed by master equations of the complex Ginzburg–Landau type, which balance gain, loss, dispersion and nonlinearity[20, 18, 4, 17]. In all these cases, the selected state is localized in a pulse.

Mode-locked lasers with fast gain recovery, however, behave in a considerably different way. Gain that recovers faster than any mean-field timescale of the system cannot sustain strongly amplitude-modulated patterns[27, 47]: gain suppresses intensity fluctuations and sets the intensity at a constant value. A finite recovery time, T1T_{1}, limits the response bandwidth, rendering gain saturation less effective for intensity variations faster than 1/T11/T_{1}[7]. The resulting state extends over the entire round-trip, while the dynamics is carried by the phase. When the modes are locked, the time-derivative of the phase, the instantaneous frequency, sweeps periodically. Mode-locking then requires the selection and stabilization of a phase profile under the constraint of nearly uniform intensity. Such frequency-modulated states are now established in quantum cascade[25, 21, 40], interband cascade[49], quantum well[9, 50], quantum-dash[43] and quantum-dot lasers[14], as well as in optical parametric oscillators[15, 51]. Because the intensity does not drop to zero, the phase and the instantaneous frequency are defined at every point of the round trip, and the state is described by their local profiles along the cavity. Therefore, features related to local variations on the extended background can be studied, such as Nozaki–Bekki solitons[38], phase turbulence[39], and laminar–turbulent transitions[52]. As these local properties also govern the robustness of the mode-locked states, they have been studied in the context of laser noise[45], comb instabilities[44], or preservation of collective oscillations[12].

This description of extended laser states through their local properties connects naturally to the physics of quantum fluids of light[8]. In these systems, intensity variations and phase gradients play the roles of fluid density and velocity, while dispersion and nonlinear interactions govern their collective dynamics, providing a framework for phenomena such as sound waves[53, 16], superfluid flow[3], quantized vortices[30], dark solitons[2] and shock waves[54]. Lasers can be classified as incoherently pumped fluids of light, sustained by gain and loss, whose phase is selected by nonlinear dynamics rather than imposed by an external coherent drive[55, 56]. This connection suggests that the local properties of extended mode-locked states can also be understood as properties of a flowing fluid[12, 41]. For actively modulated fast-gain lasers, the challenge is to turn this interpretation into a predictive tool for stationary states of the flow, making the fluid description into a design algorithm for the laser field and its emitted spectrum.

Here, we establish a mapping between actively modulated fast-gain ring lasers (Fig. 1A) and fluids of light, and exploit it to design their emitted spectra. Through a Madelung transformation[33], the intensity of the field becomes the density of a fluid and its instantaneous frequency the flow velocity (Fig. 1B–C). Since the fast gain enforces a constant intensity, the density is fixed and the light behaves as a one-dimensional liquid whose dynamics lies in the flow. Then, programmable radio-frequency modulation, which maps to a variable potential landscape, sets the velocity of this liquid (Fig. 1 D). We find these velocities analytically and use the solution to design instantaneous frequency profiles, and their corresponding output spectra (Fig. 1 E). Unlike a mass-conserving one-dimensional fluid, whose flow must be uniform at constant density, an active photonic fluid can sustain a nonuniform flow at nearly constant density through gain and loss: it branches away from splitting points located at the potential maxima and meets with opposite velocities at interfaces where a discontinuity appears. We design peaked and flat-top comb spectra and provide experimental evidence for the analytical solution. Electrically programmable combs of this kind could find use in applications that require specific wavelengths with fast tunability, such as spectroscopy, where power can be concentrated on the absorption features, or optical communications, where power can be redistributed among channels.
