papers.title: ThinkWise: Learning When to Think in Large Multimodal Reasoning Models via Visual and Difficulty Perception
papers.abstract: Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) extend large language models to heterogeneous modalities, demonstrating strong potential across a wide range of open-ended tasks. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been widely adopted to improve reasoning performance in LMRMs; however, existing approaches overlook the critical role of visual perception uncertainty in guiding reasoning processes. We term this limitation Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where the misalignment between visual perception uncertainty and reasoning depth leads to over-allocation of deep reasoning under uncertain visual grounding, resulting in unnecessarily long reasoning trajectories and degraded performance. To address this issue, we propose ThinkWise, a perception-aware RLVR framework that jointly models task difficulty and visual perception state to regulate reasoning depth. Specifically, we introduce an instance-adaptive visual perception modeling mechanism that enables context-aware calibration of perception uncertainty, leading to more accurate perception estimation. We further design a structured reward formulation that jointly considers perception, correctness, and task difficulty. In particular, an answer reward provides supervision for correctness, a perception- and difficulty-conditioned length reward adaptively regulates reasoning depth, and a perception reward encourages trajectories with stronger visual grounding. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkWise consistently improves the trade-off between accuracy and reasoning efficiency across both 3B and 7B models. These results highlight the importance of perception-aware reasoning and establish a principled framework for advancing LMRMs.

papers.intro:
Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) extend the generative capabilities of large language models to heterogeneous modalities, enabling unified understanding and reasoning over text, images, and other signals, and thus holding great promise for a wide range of open-ended tasks (Yao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2025a; Meng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b). At the core of these capabilities lies multimodal reasoning, which can be naturally decomposed into two fundamental components: multimodal perception and logical reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025). Prior studies (Chu et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Jian et al., 2025) have shown that accurate visual perception is often the primary bottleneck, as it provides the essential visual basis upon which effective downstream reasoning critically depends.

Recent advances in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) have demonstrated strong effectiveness in enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), and have emerged as a dominant paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning capabilities of MLRMs by training them solely with rewards derived from the correctness of final answers (Chen et al., 2025b; Shen et al., 2025a; Shen et al., 2025a; Peng et al., 2025). Given the critical role of visual perception, namely extracting task-relevant information from the image, more recent approaches have introduced dedicated mechanisms to strengthen this capability. One line of work (Xia et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025) enforces structured visual outputs to anchor perceptual grounding during reasoning. Another line (Chu et al., 2025; Jian et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2025) promotes visual re-attention to mitigate attention drift over long reasoning trajectories. The third line (Xiao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a) uses external visual perception rewards to alleviate reward sparsity and mitigate hallucinations.

The third line (Xiao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a) uses external visual perception rewards to alleviate reward sparsity and mitigate hallucinations.

Despite extensive efforts showing that improving visual perception enhances reasoning performance, optimizing perception in isolation remains insufficient for effective multimodal reasoning. A critical limitation lies in the failure to effective alignment visual perception quality and reasoning depth, which we term Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where reasoning depth is allocated without considering whether a confident perceptual foundation has been established for the given task. In conventional LLM settings, models tend to allocate longer reasoning trajectories to more challenging problems, implicitly trading increased reasoning depth for improved accuracy. However, this situation becomes more complex in multimodal scenarios, where uncertainty in visual perception can introduce additional complexity. When reasoning depth is governed solely by task difficulty, models may over-allocate deep reasoning to cases with uncertain visual perception, leading to unnecessarily long trajectories and degraded performance. Although prior work (Xiao and Gan, 2025) extends task difficulty to incorporate externally defined measures of both problem complexity and visual perception difficulty, the absence of intrinsic perceptual assessment limits its effectiveness, and thereby highlighting the need for a more principled, perception-aware reasoning paradigm.

Building upon the above observations, a central challenge in multimodal reasoning is how to jointly model visual perception uncertainty and task difficulty to guide reasoning depth allocation. Addressing this requires moving beyond difficulty-driven strategies and explicitly incorporating perceptual uncertainty into the reasoning process. Our key insight is simple yet fundamental: deeper reasoning should be encouraged only when additional computation is both necessary and supported by sufficient visual involvement, namely when the task is difficult and the current trajectory remains strongly grounded in visual perception. Concretely, we design multiple perception–correctness constraints to regulate reasoning behavior. When visual perception is strong, incorrect trajectories, especially on difficult problems, are encouraged to continue reasoning to refine their responses, while correct trajectories are encouraged to remain concise to avoid unnecessary computation. In contrast, when visual perception is weak, deeper reasoning is discouraged regardless of correctness, as extended reasoning under insufficient visual support tends to amplify unreliable perceptual premises or reinforce shortcut-like solutions that are not grounded in the image. This perception-aware reasoning paradigm improves reasoning effectiveness by mitigating ineffective deep reasoning and reducing deductions caused by weakly visual perception, while also enhancing efficiency by avoiding redundant computation when deeper reasoning is unlikely to be beneficial.

papers.title: Neural Latent Gaussian Process for 3D reconstruction of Mouse Brain Lipids
papers.abstract:
We address the problem of reconstructing continuous three-dimensional lipid profiles of the mouse brain from lipid measurements acquired only on a sparse set of two-dimensional tissue sections. Using MALDI-MSI measurements from coronal sections of two densely sampled and six sparsely sampled mouse brains, registered to the Allen Mouse Brain Common Coordinate Framework (CCF), we seek to interpolate the measured hundreds of lipid profiles across the unobserved voxels of the reference brain. We introduce a Neural Latent-Space Gaussian Process (LGP) architecture for this task and critically evaluate its ability to reconstruct spatial lipid distributions, using held-out mouse brain sections to assess generalization.
  We propose a Gaussian Process prior for the distribution of low-dimensional lipid profiles across the mouse brain (with Mat\'ern or a Riemann manifold kernel). This allows us to encode 3D coordinates in a small number of latent 3D volumes that are then mapped to particular lipids using a multilayer perceptron (MLP). We performed an exhaustive analysis over a range of algorithms from simple linear regression, XGBoost, MLP to state of the art models such as Neural Transcriptomic Field, graph-based SPA3D for spatial omics reconstruction and DEEPSPATIAL. We additionally evaluate GPLFR as an alternative Gaussian-process-based approach.
  Across 173 measured lipids, LGP outperforms all evaluated baselines, including recent spatial-omics models and GPLFR, achieving a mean correlation of 0.613 and demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach for sparse 3D lipid interpolation.

papers.title: Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks: Constrained Deep Learning for Sex-Specific Multi-Population Longevity Forecasting
papers.abstract:
We introduce Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained deep learning framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that embeds actuarial knowledge into LSTM training through differentiable penalty terms. Applied to a high-longevity 6-country cluster (Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, West Germany, Netherlands, Japan; 1956-2020), the framework is a challenger to the Li-Lee benchmark and unconstrained neural approaches.
  Our central finding is that monotonicity constraint intensity lambda functions as a continuous governance dial with a quantifiable accuracy-stability trade-off. At lambda = 0.01, 30-year forecast confidence intervals narrow by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost. At lambda = 0.1, they narrow by 25% at only +0.84% RMSE cost. This trade-off is invisible to standard hyperparameter optimizers, which select lambda by minimizing one-step RMSE, the wrong metric for structural constraints in recursive forecasting.
  The framework adds three contributions: (i) residual-calibrated process noise that eliminates double-counting in the dual uncertainty framework, reducing confidence intervals by 53-60%; (ii) a 5-seed model ensemble with a coefficient of variation of 1.06%; and (iii) a time-varying credibility weight Z(t) = exp(-alpha t) connecting to Buhlmann credibility theory for blending neural and actuarial predictions. A 10-year out-of-sample backtest (trained on 1956-2010, validated against observed HMD life expectancy for 2011-2020) yields a mean absolute error of 0.38 years, with 11 of 12 country x sex combinations within the 90% confidence interval. The model produces regulatory-grade outputs including Solvency Capital Requirements under the Swiss Solvency Test (ES 99.0%: +1.91 years, CHE Male) and Solvency II, reverse stress testing, and model-based stability verification (amplification ratio 1.02x).

papers.intro:
The systemic increase in human life expectancy is one of the most significant financial risks facing the modern insurance and reinsurance industry. For institutional players such as Swiss Re and Munich Re, the accurate quantification of longevity risk is not merely a pricing exercise but a fundamental requirement for capital adequacy under the Swiss Solvency Test (SST) and Solvency II frameworks [1]. An underestimation of future life expectancy improvements translates directly into under-reserving of annuity and pension liabilities — a risk that compounds over decades and can threaten solvency.

An underestimation of future life expectancy improvements translates directly into under-reserving of annuity and pension liabilities — a risk that compounds over decades and can threaten solvency.

Traditional stochastic mortality models, primarily the Lee-Carter framework [2] and its multi-population extension by Li and Lee [3], have served as the industry benchmark for over three decades. These models rely on the assumption that mortality dynamics can be captured by a linear drift in a latent time index, and that coherent populations share a common trend from which individual deviations are stationary and mean-reverting. While mathematically elegant and computationally tractable, these assumptions are increasingly strained by demographic reality. The mortality improvement deceleration observed across high-income countries since approximately 2011 represents a structural shift that linear models cannot capture without ad-hoc modifications.

papers.title: 3D Radiative Transfer Simulations for Characterization of the Optically Thick DART Ejecta Plume
papers.abstract: The Hyperion package is a three-dimensional Monte-Carlo radiative transfer approach to modeling dust ejecta. Because it has proven to be a powerful tool for simulating optically thick environments with complicated structure, we are applying the routines to observations of the DART impact on asteroid Dimorphos. Our analysis focuses on the LICIACube LUKE red-filter image acquired 175 s after impact, when the near-surface plume remained dense and not strongly structured. The model incorporates the updated Dimorphos shape model, spacecraft and solar geometry derived, and size-dependent scattering properties of realistic dust particles. We adopt an axisymmetric conical ejecta geometry and iteratively adjust the particle size distribution (PSD) and vertical number density profile to reproduce observed brightness profiles extracted from the LUKE image. We find that a power-law PSD with slope k = 3.0 and a number density peak located at approximately 120 m above the surface best reproduces the brightness contrast between the illuminated surface, the bright ejecta plume, and the adjacent dark band produced by shadowing within the optically thick material. The resulting best-fit model implies a total ejecta mass of 1.25 x 10^6 kg within 500 m of the impact site.

papers.intro:
The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was NASA’s first planetary defense mission designed to test the kinetic impactor technique by striking Dimorphos, the secondary of the Didymos binary asteroid system, and measuring the resulting orbital deflection Rivkin and Cheng (2023); Daly et al. (2023). One of the main mission objectives was to quantify the momentum transfer efficiency of the impact, including the additional recoil imparted by escaping ejecta, commonly expressed through the momentum enhancement factor, β\beta. Prior to impact, Dimorphos orbited Didymos with a period of approximately 11 h 55 min; following the collision, its orbital period decreased by about 33 minutes, demonstrating a substantial deflection and confirming the importance of ejecta-driven momentum enhancement Thomas et al. (2023); Naidu et al. (2024); Scheirich et al. (2024).

(2023); Naidu et al. (2024); Scheirich et al. (2024).

The properties and evolution of the ejecta plume are therefore directly linked to the impact physics and momentum transfer efficiency. Imaging obtained immediately after impact revealed a highly structured and rapidly evolving ejecta cloud. In addition to the pre-impact DRACO images from the DART spacecraft, the Italian LICIACube CubeSat, contributed by the Italian Space Agency (ASI), performed a close flyby and acquired high-resolution images of the ejecta plume from distinct viewing geometries Dotto et al. (2024); Farnham et al. (2025). These data show a complex, optically thick plume containing bright ejecta regions and pronounced shadowed structures, including a dark band adjacent to Dimorphos. Interpreting such features requires a quantitative framework that accounts for multiple scattering, attenuation, and three-dimensional geometry.

Radiative transfer provides a framework for describing how radiation propagates through complex media such as dusty environments. As photons pass through these media, they undergo absorption, scattering, and thermal emission processes that are governed by the radiative transfer equation (RTE). Because the RTE is an integro-differential equation without a general analytic solution for realistic three-dimensional geometries, numerical approaches are required Steinacker et al. (2003); Steinacker et al. (2006); Dullemond and Turolla (2000); Dullemond (2002). In optically thick and spatially structured environments, simplified one-dimensional or optically thin approximations can lead to systematic biases because the radiation field depends sensitively on geometry, multiple scattering, and shadowing effects. A widely adopted numerical approach is the Monte Carlo method, in which the radiation field is represented by discrete photon packets that are tracked as they move through a spatial grid with prescribed density distributions. The interactions of each packet with the medium are determined by random sampling of probability distribution functions for absorption and scattering events. Advances in computational capability now permit fully three-dimensional simulations for complex geometries Wolf et al. (1999); Harries (2000); Gordon et al. (2001); Misselt et al. (2001); Wood et al. (2001); Wood et al. (2002a); Wood et al. (2002b); Whitney et al. (2003); Whitney et al. (2004); Dullemond and Dominik (2004); Jonsson (2006); Pinte et al. (2006); Min et al. (2009). Open-source tools such as Hyperion Robitaille (2011) provide flexible frameworks for multidimensional radiative transfer modeling.

While three-dimensional radiative transfer has been applied in planetary atmospheres and astrophysical systems, particularly in cases involving strong horizontal inhomogeneity, its use in small-body environments has been more limited. In many cometary or dust-tail applications, the material is assumed to be optically thin and geometrically simple Marschall et al. (2020); Bockelée-Morvan et al. (2004); Debout et al. (2016). The DART ejecta plume, however, represents a rare case in which the low-altitude environment is both optically thick and geometrically structured, making it particularly well suited for three-dimensional radiative transfer analysis. In this study, we apply the three-dimensional radiative transfer code Hyperion to model the ejecta plume as captured by the LUKE images acquired 175 s after impact. By comparing synthetic images with the actual observations, we constrain the particle size distribution, vertical number density structure, and total ejecta mass of the near-surface plume. This approach enables a physically consistent interpretation of the observed brightness morphology and provides quantitative insight into the early-time ejecta properties following the DART impact.

papers.title: AI climate trajectories shaped by growth, power choices and decarbonization
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a major source of electricity demand, yet its operational greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions remain difficult to resolve geographically. We develop a facility-level global inventory of AI-oriented data centers and extend it to 2030 using documented expansion plans and grid-policy scenarios. Under Current Policies, emissions increase from 20.4 MtCO$_2$e in 2024 to 68.7 MtCO$_2$e in 2030, with parameter-side Monte Carlo 5th--95th percentile ranges of 19.3--21.0 and 60.8--73.9 MtCO$_2$e, respectively. Only six geographies, representing less than 3% of projected capacity, avoid rising emissions. Grid decarbonization consistent with net zero by 2050 lowers projected 2030 emissions to 48.3 MtCO$_2$e, but fossil-based behind-the-meter generation erodes this benefit. Under that scenario, the U.S. behind-the-meter emissions penalty exceeds the combined AI-data-center emissions outside the United States. These findings support coordinated capacity planning, faster access to low-carbon electricity and limits on routine fossil-based behind-the-meter supply.

papers.title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
papers.abstract: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

Recent corpora synchronize motion capture with force-plate measurements (Werling et al., 2024), extending beyond steady gait to tasks like cutting, lunging and jumping (Scherpereel et al., 2023). Learning-based methods use such data to map kinematics to ground reaction forces (GRF), either through direct regression (Mourot et al., 2022) or generative modeling (Tan et al., 2026). Their predictions can violate physics, for example by loading the ground during flight or placing the center of pressure (CoP) outside the foot, since a loss term at best encourages physical consistency. The learned mapping is also opaque, going from motion to force directly without modeling the actuation and body dynamics that produce it, and therefore cannot drive a simulated body or robot.

Alternative actuation models, including learned gains (Yuan et al., 2021), muscle models (Li et al., 2026) and direct torque control (Cotton, 2025), have not been systematically evaluated against measured forces.

papers.title: Teralizer: A Tool for Generalizing JUnit Tests into Property-Based jqwik Tests
papers.abstract: Background: Property-based testing validates properties across many generated inputs and can thereby detect regressions that conventional unit tests miss. However, writing property-based tests is challenging for practitioners, which limits their adoption. Tool: Teralizer automatically generalizes JUnit tests into property-based jqwik tests for regression detection. Through single-path symbolic analysis, it extracts from each test execution a path condition, which characterizes the inputs that follow the same execution path, and a symbolic output expression, which computes the expected output for these inputs. The generalized tests generate inputs that satisfy the path condition and use the symbolic output expression as the oracle. Results: In our evaluation, generalization increased the mutation scores of EvoSuite-generated test suites by 0.8 to 3.9 percentage points. On the EqBench benchmark, generalizing the test suites that EvoSuite generated with 1 s per class reached the mutation score of EvoSuite's 60 s test suites with 31.9% less total runtime. Availability: Teralizer is available as open source at https://github.com/glockyco/Teralizer.

papers.intro:
Unit tests are widely used to detect regressions, i.e., unintended changes in program behavior. Since a conventional unit test validates the method under test (MUT) only for specific input-output pairs, regressions that affect other inputs remain undetected. Fig. shows an example. The method approvedAmount approves loans of up to FULL for applicants with a credit score of at least 80, and the unit test fullApproval validates this behavior for a score of 90 and a requested amount of 20. A refactoring that merges the two calls of Math.min unintentionally changes the condition score >= 80 to score > 80. Applicants with a score of 80 are thereby approved for at most PARTIAL instead of FULL, but the unit test fullApproval still passes.

papers.title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
papers.abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.
papers.intro:
Market makers supply liquidity. Each maker posts a price at which it will buy and a price at which it will sell, on either side of a fluctuating market price, and competes with other makers for the traders who take these quotes. A maker earns the distance between its quote and the market price on every unit it trades and loses when the price subsequently moves against the resulting position. Order flow that tends to arrive just before such a move is called toxic, and it is the main reason why quotes cannot be arbitrarily tight.

Each maker posts a price at which it will buy and a price at which it will sell, on either side of a fluctuating market price, and competes with other makers for the traders who take these quotes. A maker earns the distance between its quote and the market price on every unit it trades and loses when the price subsequently moves against the resulting position. Order flow that tends to arrive just before such a move is called toxic, and it is the main reason why quotes cannot be arbitrarily tight.

When one maker becomes better informed about the direction of the next price move, two effects act on the spreads of its competitors. We call the first the protective force. The better-informed maker trades more of the harmless flow and less of the toxic flow, so the flow left to the other makers is worse on average. The adverse-selection logic of models with informed takers (Glosten and Milgrom, 1985; Kyle, 1985) then implies that the others should widen their quotes to break even. We call the second the competitive force. The better-informed maker quotes more tightly and wins more fills, which pushes the others to tighten in order to keep their share of the flow. Which effect dominates is an open question. Informed-taker theory does not carry over directly, because an informed competitor, unlike an informed customer, never trades against the other makers’ quotes. Private signals, inventories and the public history of quotes all enter each maker’s strategy, and the resulting repeated stochastic game has no closed-form solution.

papers.title: When Does Label-Free Deconfounding of Document Embeddings Work?
papers.abstract: Document embeddings encode spurious attributes that can distort semantic comparisons; yet supervised erasure requires metadata that is often unavailable. We systematically investigate label-free deconfounding across corpora and embedding models. Our results show that label-free methods improve semantic utility over unprocessed embeddings, while simple geometric approaches recover much of the supervised benefit, sometimes matching metadata-supervised erasure in linear confounder recoverability and semantic utility. We identify two distinct causes of ineffective erasure: poor proxy-confounder alignment and insufficient intervention coverage. Crucially, confounder recoverability and semantic utility are distinct dimensions of deconfounding success: utility can improve despite residual confounder information, while stronger suppression does not necessarily improve utility. Moreover, reduced linear recoverability can coexist with substantial nonlinear recoverability. Together, these findings distinguish confounder discovery from intervention effectiveness and highlight the importance of evaluating nuisance suppression alongside semantic preservation.

papers.intro:
Text embeddings underpin semantic search, document retrieval, classification, and clustering (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). These applications rely on a simple assumption: documents with similar meanings should be close in the embedding space. Yet embeddings also encode attributes such as language, source, genre, publication venue, writing style, and author identity. In heterogeneous corpora, such attributes can distort embedding comparisons. They may bring unrelated documents closer together or separate documents that describe the same events, arguments, or topics (Yang et al., 2021; Fan et al., 2025). Consequently, retrieval and clustering may reflect how a corpus was assembled rather than the semantic relationships it aims to recover.

Consequently, retrieval and clustering may reflect how a corpus was assembled rather than the semantic relationships it aims to recover.

Concept erasure offers a way to reduce these distortions. When confounder labels are available, supervised erasure can improve semantic comparisons (Fan et al., 2025). In practice, however, the relevant metadata may be unavailable, incomplete, or unreliable. For example, source provenance can be lost as text datasets are compiled and repackaged (Longpre et al., 2024). This motivates label-free erasure: identifying and suppressing nuisance structure using only pooled embeddings. We study this setting without confounder annotations, textual descriptions, population priors, or a predefined number of confounder classes.

Distinguishing these challenges is essential for understanding why erasure succeeds or fails.

Our results show that label-free deconfounding can recover substantial semantic utility benefits without confounder labels. In our primary evaluation, all three methods improve the mean semantic utility over unprocessed embeddings, while simple geometric approaches sometimes match metadata-supervised erasure despite incomplete confounder removal. However, both the effectiveness of confounder suppression and the relative performance of different methods depend on the geometry of the corpus and the embedding model. Together, these findings highlight the importance of distinguishing confounder discovery from intervention effectiveness and evaluating semantic utility alongside both linear and nonlinear confounder recoverability.

papers.title: Galerkin methods for unconventional superconductors with long-range interactions on 3D lattices
papers.abstract: We develop an analysis and a B-spline Galerkin method for the matrix-valued Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) gap equation of unconventional superconductors with general long-range interaction kernels on arbitrary Bravais lattices. We define the BCS free energy functional on lattices, show that it is bounded from below, and characterise solutions of the gap equation as its stationary points. For non-repulsive kernels, we prove that fixed-point iteration never increases the free energy and drives the residual to zero. The algebraically decaying tails of the interaction are described by Epstein zeta functions, so the method applies to any power-law exponent $\nu>0$, including exponents at or below the lattice dimension such as dipolar interactions in three-dimensional lattices. In the B-spline Galerkin basis, the singular convolutions correspond to block-circulant matrices whose eigenvalues are lattice sums, applied without quadrature at FFT cost. Each iteration takes log-linear work and linear memory, and Broyden updates accelerate convergence. By engineering a suitable dispersion for a prescribed gap, we obtain non-trivial analytic singlet and triplet solutions of the gap equation with power-law interactions on the integer lattice at zero temperature, to our knowledge the first ones. Benchmarks against these solutions and against highly resolved numerical data show convergence rates determined by the B-spline degree and the regularity of the solution. Finally, we compute a nodal superconductor with long-range interactions on the three-dimensional fcc lattice: a chiral state with a line node and two topologically non-trivial Weyl point nodes. On 16 cores, the method reaches a residual of $1.5\times10^{-13}$ for 6.3 million complex unknowns in less than two minutes.

papers.intro:
Superconductivity is the quantum phenomenon where a material exhibits vanishing electric resistance when cooled below a critical temperature TcT_{c}. Although discovered already in mercury by Onnes in 1911, the first breakthrough in its microscopic understanding occurred only in 1957 in the work of Bardeen, Cooper, and Schrieffer [4] that explained superconductivity as the result of the formation of a coherent state of bosonic electron pairs, so called Cooper pairs bound together by an effectively attractive interaction mediated by lattice vibrations, called phonons. The pairing between electrons is quantified by the superconducting gap Δ⁡(𝒙)∈ℂ2×2\Delta(\bm{x})\in\mathds{C}^{2\times 2}, where 𝒙\bm{x} is the electron separation or its Fourier transform Δ^​(𝒑)\hat{\Delta}(\bm{p}), where 𝒑\bm{p} is wave vector, in general a matrix valued quantity, that describes the binding energy of the Cooper pair, the spatial or momentum structure, as well as the spin structure of the superconducting state. A non-zero gap signals the presence of superconductivity. To date, we are aware that the structure of the gap in wave vector and spin degrees of freedom can become very complicated and determining the gap numerically is therefore a challenging task, especially if the gap is slowly decaying in real space, and if the interaction between electrons is long-ranged [16, 31].

In this work, we present an efficient and general numerical method for efficiently solving the nonlinear BCS gap equation for electrons on arbitrary dd-dimensional Bravais lattices, based on B-spline Galerkin discretisation combined with a pseudo-differential operator treatment, including both singlet and triplet channels, finite temperature, as well as attractive electron-electron interactions that may include general power-law kernels accompanied by a compactly supported near-field term. The method offers log-linear scaling in both, work and memory, and permits realistic simulations of unconventional and topological superconductivity, in one-, two-, and three-dimensional lattices. In particular, it opens the door to realistic simulations of three-dimensional nodal states.

We begin by providing a brief account of the most relevant experimental discoveries and theoretical advances in unconventional superconductors and proceed with discussing the relevance of long-ranged interactions in current superconductivity research. We then provide an overview of previous mathematical and numerical works in the field.

Until the mid-1970s, the superconducting gap was assumed to have a simple structure, smooth and with vanishing relative orbital angular momentum with opposite spins of the participating electrons. This is referred to as ss-wave pairing, following the naming of atomic orbital symmetries, and the resulting materials are called conventional superconductors. The first discovery of unconventional Cooper pairing, exhibiting a more complicated structure of the gap function, was made by Osheroff in 1971 [50] in superfluid 3\,{}^{3}He, whose A- and B- phases are examples for odd momentum and spin-triplet pairing [40], where also the diagonal elements of the gap matrix can be non-zero. In solids, unconventional superconductivity was discovered in heavy Fermion compounds in 1979 in CeCu2Si2 [60], followed by the discovery of unconventional pairing in organic conductors [36]. In those cases, electron-phonon coupling cannot explain the appearance of superconductivity, as it is dominated by the Coulomb repulsion. Here, other forms of effective interactions play a role in creating the superconducting state, many of which are closely related to the presence of magnetic ordering in the vicinity of the superconducting transition. Unconventional pairing received broad attention with the discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprate compounds in 1986 [6], where the pairing interaction arises not from phonon but from electronic correlations [54]. Other examples for unconventional pairing include iron-based superconductors [38], where the three-dimensional structure is particularly important, see [61] for a review. For general reviews on the phenomenology of unconventional superconductivity and an analysis of the arising symmetries, see [59, 62, 49]. An odd gap function in the wave vector argument, referred to as odd-parity pairing, implies the existence of topologically protected boundary modes [19, 37, 39, 53, 56], topological surface states exist even in the presence of nodes (points in momentum where the gap matrix vanishes) [55], and resulting topological Majorana zero modes are currently sought for as building blocks of error-resistant qubits for quantum computing purposes [1, 46]. A current candidate for odd-parity superconductivity is the material UTe2 [51, 43].

Long-ranged electron-electron interactions are a potential route to achieving such exotic states of matter. Their realisation ranges from dipolar and Rydberg-dressed gases [3, 20] to cavity-mediated interactions [29]. Furthermore, effectively long-ranged electron-electron are created when approaching a quantum critical point. Here, fluctuations of the order parameter mediate an effective interaction whose range diverges at the critical point [45]. In previous works, we have shown that interactions decaying as a power-law of the distance can yield mixed-parity and topologically non-trivial superconducting states [16], where the interaction kernel is described in terms of Epstein zeta functions [25, 26, 13]. We have further shown that topological Majorana edge modes that arise from long-range interactions in a pp-wave superconducting string inherit the long-range interactions even if their wave functions do not overlap [31].

papers.title: Sada-ASR: A Production Multidialectal Arabic Speech Recognition System
papers.abstract: Callers to Arabic customer-service lines speak their own dialect, while speech recognizers are built and evaluated mainly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). A recognizer that mishears the dialect breaks the call before anything else can help. We present Sada-ASR, the speech recognizer of EchoNova's production Arabic voice agent. On a 120-hour test set of MSA and eight dialects, it has the lowest word and character error rates of twelve systems, against eleven from Microsoft, ElevenLabs, Google, OpenAI, Speechmatics, IFM, Cohere, NVIDIA and Audar: 11.69% word error rate against 13.51% for the strongest, Microsoft's MAI-Transcribe-2 (a lead of 0.74 points on clips unaffected by that system's fixed number and script conventions), and 15.52% against 16.96% averaged over varieties. Its largest margins are on Omani (4.30 points), Egyptian (3.78) and Saudi (2.19) speech; it is level on Syrian and loses on Lebanese (24.96% against 23.05%), mostly because it writes Lebanese words in MSA forms and is less verbatim. On six public test sets its average word error rate under the leaderboard's current scoring is 17.17%, below every published figure we found, among them Falcon-ASR (20.92%), Jais-ASR (22.85%) and Audar-ASR-V1-Turbo (23.17%), though none of these states that it used that scoring, so the comparison is indicative. We describe the data pipeline and methodology behind Sada-ASR and release a 20-hour subset of the test set with our scoring code.
papers.intro:
Arabic is diglossic [1]: Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) is the language of writing, news and official documents, while everyday speech happens in regional dialects that differ from MSA and from each other in vocabulary, pronunciation and morphology. A caller to an Arabic customer-service line speaks their dialect, not MSA. Dialects have no standard orthography [2], and speakers mix in English words [3]. Speech technology built and evaluated mainly on MSA meets this speech at its weakest point.

papers.title: The Deepest Pairs of Points Are Not as Deep as Conjectured
papers.abstract: Given any finite set of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, Neumann-Lara and Urrutia \cite{NLUr88} proved in 1988 that there is always a pair such that every circle through the two points encloses a positive fraction of all points. While Edelsbrunner et al.\ \cite{EHSS89} showed that the fraction is at least $\sfrac{1}{2} - \sfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}} = 0.211\ldots$, Urrutia \cite{Urr02} conjectured that the constant $\sfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$ in the upper bound proved by Hayward, Rappaport and Wenger \cite{HRW89} is best possible. We disprove this conjecture by lowering the constant to $\sfrac{3}{14} = 0.214\ldots$. The new bound also disproves a related conjecture by Ramos and Via\~{n}a \cite{RaVi09} on finite sets in convex position in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Finally, we generalize the latter extremal question to finite sets in possibly non-convex position, for which we prove the first linear lower bound, with constant $\sfrac{(2-\sqrt{2})}{6} = 0.097\ldots$.

papers.title: Optimal Pattern-Avoidance Bounds for Binary Search Trees
papers.abstract:
Self-adjusting binary search trees (BSTs) perform better than balanced BSTs if the access sequence has additional structure. For example, splay trees serve a sequential access sequence in linear time. Pattern avoidance captures regularity in an access sequence and unifies several classic examples of efficient BST access, such as deque and traversal sequences. A central question is how well a BST algorithm can exploit a pattern-avoiding access sequence.
  We present an online BST algorithm that serves an access sequence avoiding a permutation pattern $\pi$ in linear time, matching the information-theoretic lower bound. The algorithm does not need to know that pattern $\pi$ a priori. Our results answer an open problem asked by [Kozma 2016, Problem 44, strong variant]. Previously, the best known offline bound was optimal only for constant-size patterns [Berendsohn, Kozma, and Opler, STOC'24], and the best known online bound was superlinear [Chalermsook, Pettie, Yingchareonthawornchai, SODA'24] even for a constant-size pattern. As a corollary, our BST algorithm yields an optimal sorting algorithm for a pattern-avoiding sequence that supports online insertions. Previously, an optimal sorting algorithm was achieved using a mergesort-like approach [Opler, FOCS'24] in a batch setting.
  A key technique is to apply recursive split decomposition [Chalermsook, Chuzhoy, Saranurak, ToC'23] jointly in time and space, along with the Marcus-Tardos proof of the Stanley-Wilf conjecture. We show that the framework can be implemented online using $k$-finger BSTs, which is of independent interest. Finally, this framework also yields a constant-factor-approximation FPT algorithm in the offline setting.

papers.intro:
A self-adjusting binary search tree (BST) is an online algorithm that must handle the input request and readjust its structure without knowing future access requests. It can outperform balanced BSTs such as AVL and red-black trees [AVL62, Bay72] when the input sequence exhibits structure, patterns, or regularity. Pattern avoidance is a classical notion in enumerative and extremal combinatorics, with algorithmic roots in Knuth’s analysis of stack sorting [Knu68]. In the BST setting, the study of structured access sequences dates back to the introduction of splay trees, with classic examples including sequential access and preorder traversals [ST85, Tar85]. These examples have been generalized to a common framework based on permutation pattern avoidance [CGK+15b]. For a permutation pattern π\pi, a sequence over [n][n] is π\pi-avoiding if no subsequence has the same relative order as π\pi. For example, the sequence (1,2,…,n)(1,2,\ldots,n) avoids (2,1)(2,1). The central question is how well an online BST can exploit this “easy” structure hidden in the sequence.

papers.title: Spatial phase coherence and its applications to masking and adaptive neighborhood sizing in multitemporal InSAR
papers.abstract: We examine spatial phase coherence (SPC), a measure of the correlation between the wrapped phase time series of two pixels in a stack of single-look synthetic aperture radar acquisitions. A pixel and its adjacent neighbors share speckle through the point spread function, so that decorrelation alone does not lower their SPC below a floor. We find that masking pixels whose mean SPC to their eight neighbors is well below that floor, as in parts of layover and shadow areas, is an inexpensive complement to geometry-derived layover and shadow masks. For distributed scatterer pixels, averaging SPC over a fixed set of neighbors that share no speckle yields a proxy for the local coherence, the phase coherence indicator (PCI), that is available before the selection of statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs). In phase estimation, averaging more pixels reduces noise but may also increase the bias in heterogeneous areas. To relax this trade-off, we propose to enhance SHP selection algorithms by scaling the search window size according to the PCI and truncating the set of selected pixels where a smaller nested set agrees clearly better with the phases at the center. In simulations of a TerraSAR-X and a Sentinel-1 stack with 44 and 79 acquisitions, we apply this adaptive neighborhood sizing (ANS) to established amplitude- and covariance-based SHP selection algorithms with thresholds that adapt to the PCI. Without ANS, the largest tested search window size has 13 to 29 % more phase linking error than the best of the tested sizes. With ANS, the largest window has the lowest error of the tested sizes, 11 % lower than that of the same selection at its best tested size without ANS. On a real TerraSAR-X stack, the mask based on SPC flags pixels in building shadows that a terrain model misses. On real Sentinel-1 stacks, ANS preserves dense fringes on a slowly deforming slope and in part on a fast landslide.

papers.intro:
In multitemporal interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR), phase estimation and phase linking over distributed scatterers rely on averaging observations from selected neighboring pixels (Ho Tong Minh and Tebaldini, 2023). This raises three questions for each pixel to be estimated, namely whether an average over its neighbors can represent it at all, which neighbors are statistically homogeneous with it, and how large the set of averaged pixels should be. We call the pixel to be estimated the center pixel, or center, and the set of averaged pixels the ensemble.

This raises three questions for each pixel to be estimated, namely whether an average over its neighbors can represent it at all, which neighbors are statistically homogeneous with it, and how large the set of averaged pixels should be. We call the pixel to be estimated the center pixel, or center, and the set of averaged pixels the ensemble.

The first question arises in particular for pixels in layover and shadow areas, which are typically masked. In layover, scatterers at several heights are projected onto the same pixel in the synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image, so that subtracting a topographic phase may introduce systematic phase inconsistencies. In shadow, the phase is often dominated by noise that is less correlated between neighboring pixels than speckle. Geometric layover and shadow maps derived from the acquisition geometry and a digital elevation model (DEM) (Kropatsch and Strobl, 1990) can identify these areas, but they depend on the accuracy of the DEM. Layover and shadow caused by objects that are not included in the model, such as buildings and trees, are another limitation. Layover has also been detected from the data itself. Tupin et al. (1996) use the amplitude, Zhu et al. (2017) the local fringe frequency of an interferogram over high-rise buildings, and Rossi and Eineder (2015) the number of times each SAR pixel occurs in the geocoding of an elevation model generated from the interferometric data, without external data. Tupin et al. (1996) also detect areas without topographic phase from the filtered coherence and the confidence of the local fringe frequency estimates of an interferogram. These areas include shadow, decorrelated areas and surfaces without backscatter.

Established processing frameworks such as SqueeSAR (Ferretti et al., 2011) identify statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs) by tests on the temporal amplitude distributions (Even and Schulz, 2018; Parizzi and Brcic, 2011). Later tests also use the interferometric phases (Dong et al., 2018; Song et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2022). Other approaches collect pixels of similar intensity by region growing (Vasile et al., 2006) or weight pixels by the similarity of their surrounding patches (Deledalle et al., 2011; Deledalle et al., 2015). SHP tests that compare the temporal mean amplitudes or intensities of two pixels lose their significance level when the speckle is temporally correlated. On a coherent target the speckle changes little between acquisitions, so that the means of two pixels of the same surface keep the difference of their speckle. A threshold set for independent samples or for one assumed coherence therefore holds only at that coherence.

Averaging reduces noise, but its extent determines how much spatial detail is retained. Strongly decorrelated targets need larger ensembles to reach a given precision (cf. Rocca, 2007, Eqs. (5.22) to (5.25)). Where the phase varies rapidly in space, as in areas with strong spatial gradients of line-of-sight deformation, a smaller ensemble may suffice if the coherence is high enough, whereas a large one blurs fringes and lowers the estimated coherence (Zebker and Chen, 2005). The averaging neighborhood has been adapted to this in shape and size. For single interferograms, directional windows follow the local fringe orientation (Lee et al., 1998), and the intersection of confidence intervals (ICI) rule chooses, for each pixel, the largest window whose local polynomial estimate stays consistent with those of smaller windows (Katkovnik et al., 2002; Katkovnik et al., 2008). For stacks, Pepe et al. (2021) adapt a fixed multilook window to the phase by removing the pixels whose phases deviate from the multilooked phases of that window and comparing the deviations of the remaining pixels with those of the pixel that deviates least. In other SHP-based processing, however, the coherence matrix is usually estimated from all pixels that the SHP selection accepts (Jiang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2022, e.g.,), also where the phase varies within the search window. Chi et al. (2022, Section 3.2 and Eq. (13)) instead shrink the search window of an SHP selection at each pixel until a coefficient of variation of the phase of the time-averaged differential interferogram falls below a threshold, which requires unwrapped interferograms.

papers.title: The Maxwell Bethe-Sommerfeld problem I: Thin-layer induction and results for planar TE modes
papers.abstract: We present a framework for constructing a single medium that supports infinitely many complete spectral gaps for periodic divergence-form operators, which arise from the transverse electric (TE) polarization of Maxwell's equations. The construction proceeds by inductively inserting a seed medium with a prescribed spectral gap into a thin layer of the unit cell. As a result, we obtain densely many counterexamples to the Bethe-Sommerfeld Conjecture (BSC) for divergence-form operators. Moreover, we prove that the thin-layer construction controls the gap topology: by carefully selecting the seed medium, one can realize a single operator with any prescribed configuration of gap Chern numbers. This is the first of two papers that contains all the fundamental ingredients for the thin-layer induction. In the second paper, we will apply this framework to disprove the BSC for the full three-dimensional Maxwell operator.

papers.title: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
papers.abstract: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

To infer the interior from the surface temperature, we need two ingredients: a heat conduction model and the shape of the object. For an object without an existing shape representation such as a mesh or CAD model, we need to reconstruct the shape from the images.

For the heat conduction model, we use the following: in a thermal steady state, the interior temperature of a homogeneous isotropic solid object without internal heat sources satisfies the Laplace equation (Carslaw and Jaeger, 1959), subject to appropriate boundary conditions on the object’s surface: surface with known temperatures modeled as Dirichlet boundaries, insulated or convecting faces can be modeled as Neumann or Robin boundaries. The finite element method (FEM) solves this boundary value problem on a volume mesh of the object. Boundary element methods (BEM) and, more recently, grid-free Monte Carlo solvers (Sawhney and Crane, 2020; Sawhney et al., 2023; Sugimoto et al., 2023) can solve such boundary value problems efficiently and without volumetric meshing. However, all of these methods require the object’s surface geometry to be given in advance, as a mesh or an implicit surface. Obtaining a simulation-ready mesh from images, though, takes a chain of separate tools: an image-based mesh reconstruction tool, a repair pass that removes stray pieces and closes holes, and, for a finite-element solver, volumetric meshing where the run time grows steeply as its elements shrink (Section 6.4). Radiance field methods, neural or Gaussian, instead take the images as they come and reconstruct thermally consistent scenes directly from the captured views (Ye et al., 2024; Hassan et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), but they treat temperature as a learned appearance attribute and do not connect the representation to the heat equation, so they cannot predict the temperature inside the object.

We present a method that bridges this gap: a Gaussian radiance field (Zhang et al., 2026) reconstructs the object from visible-spectrum images, and the surface it renders is sampled into the point cloud on which a boundary integral equation (BIE) is discretized. Thermal images set the temperature at the surface locations they observe, while a physical prior, such as insulation or convective cooling, applies in the remaining areas. A single solve of the direct BIE then yields the temperature at any interior point. We do not implement meshing at any stage, surface points require no connectivity, and the interior is never discretized. For accuracy, we sample points from the rendered surface, with a depth-slope filter that rejects pixels that straddle two surfaces, and a density subtraction keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. Our method is also differentiable, so the gradient of a loss on the predicted temperature reaches the boundary conditions and the geometry, and the same solve recovers what the camera cannot see.

papers.title: A singular minimizer of a uniformly convex Hessian-dependent functional
papers.abstract: We construct a smooth, uniformly convex Hessian-dependent energy functional, which admits a singular $C^{1,1}$ minimizer on $\mathbb{R}^5$ that is a two-homogeneous normalization of Cartan's five-dimensional cubic. Our construction relies on constructing a quadratic null Lagrangian for the Hessian that is suitably non-degenerate on the image of the Hessian for the candidate minimizer. This complements a partial regularity result previously obtained by the authors in this setting, and demonstrates that one cannot hope for a fourth-order version of classical second-order elliptic regularity theory \`{a} la De Giorgi-Nash-Moser.

papers.title: Quantitative surface approximations for Maxwell scattering in nonlocal plasmonics
papers.abstract: We establish quantitative surface approximations for Maxwell scattering by a fixed collection of smooth, separated metallic particles described by the hard-wall generalized nonlocal optical response (GNOR) model. As the ratio $\eta$ of the reference screening length to the particle size tends to zero, regularized first-order and second-order transmission conditions approximate the electric far-field operator with errors $O(\eta^2)$ and $O(\eta^3)$, respectively. The estimates retain retardation and are uniform on compact subplasma frequency intervals with fixed positive damping and for a bounded dimensionless diffusion-to-pressure ratio. The proof combines exact elimination of the longitudinal field, a uniform weak bound for its boundary density, and smoothing by exterior observations. The same error orders hold for fields observed at a fixed positive distance from the particles. We also justify thin-coating representations on bounded tangential wave-number ranges for a planar interface and on fixed finite spherical angular subspaces. For each fixed quasistatic spherical multipole with a simple local pole, the first- and second-order models approximate the pole and its residue with errors $O(\eta^2)$ and $O(\eta^3)$, respectively.

papers.intro:
Plasmonic resonances arise from collective oscillations of conduction electrons in metallic particles and produce strong electromagnetic field enhancement. For particles described by local permittivity, their mathematical analysis is well developed. Layer potential techniques relate the resonances to the spectrum of the Neumann–Poincaré operator and therefore to the geometry of the particles [2, 5, 6, 3]. Many of the most striking effects are multiscale. In nearly touching particles, for instance, the field concentrates in the gap, on a length much smaller than the particle size [36, 37]. When the scales are separated, asymptotic reductions and effective models become central to the analysis of resonant structures [1].

Plasmonic resonances arise from collective oscillations of conduction electrons in metallic particles and produce strong electromagnetic field enhancement. For particles described by local permittivity, their mathematical analysis is well developed. Layer potential techniques relate the resonances to the spectrum of the Neumann–Poincaré operator and therefore to the geometry of the particles [2, 5, 6, 3]. Many of the most striking effects are multiscale. In nearly touching particles, for instance, the field concentrates in the gap, on a length much smaller than the particle size [36, 37]. When the scales are separated, asymptotic reductions and effective models become central to the analysis of resonant structures [1].

Electronic screening introduces a further small scale, internal to each particle. Nonlocal effects appear when the electric field varies on this scale, as it does near small particles, sharp curvature, or narrow gaps. A local permittivity is then no longer sufficient and the constitutive law must account for spatial dispersion. A convenient semiclassical description is the generalized nonlocal optical response (GNOR) model [22]. It treats the conduction electrons as charged fluids whose current responds to the electric field, a pressure gradient, and the diffusion of an induced charge. The pressure confines the induced charge to a screening layer at the metal surface. Diffusion damps this charge and accounts for size-dependent broadening [30, 31]. A dimensionless parameter ζ≥0\zeta\geq 0 measures the diffusion relative to pressure, and ζ=0\zeta=0 gives the widely used hydrodynamic Drude model [27, 21]. The hard-wall form of the model forbids electrons to leave the metal. Rigorous effective interface laws are available in other electromagnetic settings. For a periodic layer of plasmonic nanoparticles above a conducting plane, Ammari, Li, and Zou [4] use homogenization to obtain a Leontovich impedance condition that captures the collective resonances. Here, the eliminated scale is the screening length inside fixed particles, and local Maxwell fields are retained on both sides of each interface. This also avoids resolving the screening layer, which volumetric discretizations of the coupled system must do [20, 11].

papers.title: Towards Inter-satellite Laser Metrology for Formation Flying Interferometry
papers.abstract: Context. The direct detection and atmospheric characterization of terrestrial exoplanets has been highlighted as a key science focus by the US ASTRO2020 Decadal survey and the ESA Voyage 2050 plan. This will require a new generation of telescope which is able to meet the contrast requirements necessary to image a planet many orders of magnitude fainter than its host star - a technological feat which currently limits our observation capabilities. In the mid-infrared, the most viable solution has been shown to be a formation-flying nulling space interferometer. Aims. In this work, we present the initial prototype for an inter-spacecraft metrology system. This system is a sub-system of the Pyxis/SEIRIOS interferometer, a formation-flying interferometer which serves as a technology demonstrator for the LIFE mission. Methods. We have designed a multi-stage metrology system using three interferometric measurement techniques, covering varying distance resolution ranges. Digital Interferometric (DI) ranging provides the coarsest measurement, while a differential phase read-out provides sub-nm precision. Multi-wavelength interferometry is employed to overcome the phase ambiguity associated with the differential phase readout. Results. A single-wavelength electronic noise floor below 20 pm RMS over 10 s was measured by applying a common photodetector signal to both readout channels, a factor of 28 below the 560 pm requirement. For the multi-wavelength readout, the obtained electronic noise RMS was 556 nm at 10 second integration, decreasing to 200 nm below 3 second integration. The full optical measurement in laboratory air is currently limited by environmental path fluctuations. Conclusions. We demonstrate an initial prototype system for precision ranging between satellites for formation-flying nulling interferometers.

papers.intro:
Since the first confirmed detection of an exoplanet in 1992 (Wolszczan and Frail, 1992), exoplanet research has become a major subfield of astrophysics, with over 7000 exoplanet detections made to date. In 2021, the ASTRO2020 Decadal Survey from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine recognized the field and identified the investigation of Earth-like exoplanets as a key science theme for the next decade (Monnier and others, 2019). ESA made a similar statement in the ESA Voyage 2050 plan (Snellen et al., 2019). To fulfill the science themes identified in ASTRO2020, we must focus on obtaining spectra from the atmospheres of terrestrial exoplanets in order to learn about its constituents, its formation, and whether life could be present. However, detection and characterization of these planets is an ongoing challenge with current instrumentation, which has biased the population of detected planets on the basis of what is actually feasible to observe (Ortiz, 2025). This means that smaller Earth-like exoplanets orbiting Sun-like stars tend to go undetected, compared to larger high-SNR exoplanets orbiting dimmer stars (Scalo et al., 2007). Furthermore, transmission spectroscopy and direct detection are the only methods of exoplanet detection that can actually retrieve atmospheric spectra (Piaulet-Ghorayeb et al., 2024) – the former being geometrically limited (Wright and Gaudi, 2012) and the latter being viable only to young large stars on the outer edges of their host solar system (Zurlo, 2024).

For direct imaging, terrestrial exoplanet observability is limited by the brightness contrast between the planet and its host star, which can range from 10−610^{-6} for a hot Jupiter to ≤10−9\leq 10^{-9} for an Earth-like exoplanet (Claudi and Mesa, 2024). This ratio can be improved by observing in the infrared (Cagigal and Canales, 2001), which would require a space-based telescope to bypass the thermal background associated with a ground-based telescope. Extremely large ground-based telescopes (ELTs) (Zhang et al., 2024) will also be powerful enough to resolve terrestrial exoplanets; however, they are limited to nearby stars only. In space, existing missions such as Kepler, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) and the James Webb Space Telescope have already laid the groundwork for space-based exoplanet observations through their detections of several thousand planetary candidates. Unfortunately, none of these missions are capable of performing the detailed characterization of temperate exoplanet atmospheres required to meet the science goals outlined in ASTRO2020 and Voyage 2050.

Furthermore, a key bandwidth of interest for exoplanet spectroscopy is the mid-infrared (MIR) regime, since it encompasses known biosignatures that are not detectable or not present in the optical/near-UV wavelength regime (Quanz et al., 2018). In order to observe terrestrial planets in the MIR, contrast ratios on the order of 10−710^{-7} with respect to the host star must be overcome (Zhang et al., 2024). These high spatial resolution and sensitivity requirements can only be met through nulling, an interferometric technique that exploits the path length difference between the host star and planet to nullify the host star.

Proposed by Bracewell in 1978 (Bracewell, 1978), nulling interferometry involves multiple science telescopes at known relative distances observing a singular target. The telescopes are positioned such that when received light is interfered by a recombiner apparatus, an on-axis target is destructively interfered (nulled), while light from an off-axis source is constructively interfered. This allows us to position a target planet within a bright fringe, while light from the corresponding host star is nulled, effectively relaxing the contrast requirement. Additionally, a proposed MIR telescope system must be space-based, in order to bypass the thermal background associated with the Earth’s atmosphere. In order to perform nulling interferometry in space, formation flying, ie. the controlled positioning of multiple satellites operating as a single constellation, is required. Specifically, a potential space-based interferometer would require formation flying technology capable of positioning multiple combiner satellites (science telescopes) to sub-wavelength displacements, relative to a recombiner satellite. No such mission has been launched as of this work. It is because of this, and the recommendations from ASTRO2020 and Voyage 2050, that the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE) initiative was created.

The LIFE Collaboration (Glauser et al., 2024) is a European-led mission aimed at launching the first MIR space-based formation flying nulling interferometer capable of probing thermal emission from terrestrial exoplanet atmospheres. LIFE aims to detect 30 to 50 terrestrial exoplanets, focusing on characteristics that are not possible to determine using transit or reflected light techniques, such as effective temperature and radius. It will also look for important molecular signatures such as water (H2​OH_{2}O), carbon dioxide (C​O2CO_{2}), ozone (O3O_{3}) and methane (C​H4CH_{4}) – the presence of the latter two in exoplanetary atmospheres can currently only be explained by biological activity (Quanz et al., 2021). Technology for multiple subsystems is in development for LIFE, including the Nulling Interferometric Cryogenic Experiment (NICE) (Ranganathan et al., 2022), waveguides and integrated optics (Montesinos-Ballester et al., 2024), detectors (Atkinson et al., 2020), piezo-electric deformable mirrors (Huisman et al., 2021), and a compact delay line for space interferometry (Glauser et al., 2024). Formation flying technology, specifically the metrology required to enable formation flying fringe tracking, has not yet been demonstrated.

papers.title: Improved Approximation for Weighted $k$-Set Packing via a Simple Two-Phase Approach
papers.abstract: Weighted $k$-set packing asks for a maximum-weight collection of pairwise disjoint sets, each of cardinality at most $k$. For every fixed $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm with approximation factor $\left(1- 1/{\sqrt3} \right)k+O(\log k) \approx 0.4226k + O(\log k)$, improving the previous best factor of $0.4621k + O(\sqrt{k})$ through a simple two-phase approach. In a first phase, our algorithm constructs a packing by processing random weight buckets of varying widths with an unweighted packing algorithm. We show that a small expected weight of this packing relative to the optimum forces a large expected total surplus in the optimum. Surplus quantifies the potential for improving a packing through star swaps. In the second phase, we solve and round a configuration LP to turn sufficiently large surplus into an increase in expected weight. Our procedure can easily be derandomized.
papers.intro:
Weighted kk-set packing is a central packing problem in combinatorial optimization. Given a family of sets of cardinality at most kk, the goal is to select pairwise disjoint sets of maximum total weight. The problem generalizes maximum weight matching in graphs to hypergraphs and provides a basic model for optimization under disjointness constraints. Its approximability has been studied extensively for decades, with local search and linear programming playing prominent roles [8, 1, 2, 5]. Determining the best approximation factor achievable as a function of kk remains a fundamental open question.

Each e∈Ee\in E has an element set v⁡(e)⊆Uv(e)\subseteq U of cardinality between one and kk. A packing is a subfamily F⊆EF\subseteq E whose element sets are pairwise disjoint, and its weight is w⁡(F)≔∑e∈Fw⁡(e)w(F)\coloneqq\sum_{e\in F}w(e). We seek a packing of maximum weight and write OPT⊆E\mathrm{OPT}\subseteq E for an optimal packing. Smaller sets can be padded with private dummy elements, so allowing cardinality at most kk is equivalent to requiring cardinality exactly kk. The problem includes kk-dimensional matching, where UU is partitioned into kk parts and every input set contains exactly one element from each part. All approximation guarantees for kk-set packing therefore also apply to this special case.

The natural greedy algorithm repeatedly selects a heaviest remaining set and discards every set that intersects it. This gives a kk-approximation: each selected set can exclude at most kk disjoint optimum sets, each of no greater weight. This guarantee is tight, since greedy may select a single set instead of kk mutually disjoint sets of almost the same weight. Going beyond this basic factor spawned a long line of research on local search algorithms, which iteratively improve a packing by replacing some of its sets with disjoint sets of greater total weight.

papers.title: Improving Radio SLAM via Information Sharing: Collaborative Performance Bounds
papers.abstract: This paper studies the fundamental performance limits of radio-based collaborative simultaneous localization and mapping (C-SLAM) in dense vehicular environments towards the 6G integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) era. We consider a collaborative estimation task consisting of multiple user equipments (UEs) with unknown local state variables together with joint estimation of unknown states of the environment landmarks or targets, using cellular radio measurements. Specifically, a posterior Cram\'er-Rao bound (PCRB) is derived for such centralized multi-UE cellular radio SLAM with information sharing, capturing the effects of the number of involved UEs, their geometric configuration, and their mutually different abilities to measure or observe different landmarks. The analysis reveals how information sharing scales with UE density, identifies regimes of diminishing returns, and provides estimator-independent limits for collaborative radio-based environment mapping and localization. The provided numerical results validate the proposed framework in a vehicular system context, while also demonstrating substantial gains against more ordinary single-UE radio SLAM approach.

papers.intro:
The ISAC is expected to be one of the main new paradigms and key technical enablers in the future 6G networks [1], transforming the conventional connectivity-driven radio interface into a joint communication–sensing platform with situational awareness capabilities. The ability to sense the environment and extract situational awareness is of fundamental importance, for example in various vehicular applications, allowing to enhance the location awareness and localization capabilities [2, 3]. Cellular radio measurements-based SLAM (SLAM) is one of the most challenging and tempting prospects of 6G ISAC [4, 5, 6], and is also the main technical scope of this paper.

In general, SLAM has its original roots in robotics research in the 1980s [7], also sometimes being referred to as concurrent mapping and localization (CML) [8], where the sensing entity is traditionally referred to as a robot or an agent. Fundamentally, SLAM is a probabilistic state-estimation problem in which an agent infers both its own position (localization) and the structure of the surrounding environment (mapping) – via a chosen measurement modality, such as LiDAR or camera. Classical SLAM formulations are typically solved by a single agent without prior knowledge of either its location or the environment [9]. However, the estimation process has also been extended to multi-agent settings, where several agents jointly operate in the same unknown area [8, 10, 11] while sharing information such as measurements or local state estimates [12]. Such collaborative SLAM (C-SLAM) approach is, in general, known to expand the coverage of unexplored regions or areas, accelerate joint map construction, and improve the overall estimation accuracy and consistency [13, 14, 15].

One timely and appealing use case of bistatic cellular radio SLAM relates to future connected vehicles and other vehicular systems where timely and accurate situational awareness is decisive [1, 2, 3]. In general, urban traffic densities span a wide range depending on the city structure and congestion levels. State-of-the-art vehicular use cases consider urban environments with densities reaching up to 12,000 vehicles per square kilometer [17], represented by heterogeneous traffic composed of both unconnected and connected vehicles [18, 19]. Importantly, as the proportion of connected vehicles increases, this density creates a natural advantage and opportunity for collaborative radio SLAM – with more cooperating UE, the jointly explored area expands, shared observations accumulate, and the overall estimation uncertainty decreases [20]. Although the 12,000 vehicles/km2 figure represents the upper extreme of dense metropolitan traffic, the use case specifications in [17] adopt also a reduced density of about 2,000 vehicles/km2 as a downscaled but still representative approximation of heavy urban conditions.

The above provides direct motivation and purpose for this paper and work, in the form of examining and understanding the gains and underlying performance bounds of collaborative radio SLAM. Specifically, in this work, we seek to assess and quantify the benefits of collaboration within dense-traffic vehicular scenarios and derive the corresponding fundamental performance gains and limits using PCRB, capturing the impact of cooperating UE in a cellular SLAM setting independent of any specific parameter estimator scheme. The main scientific novelty and technical contributions of our paper stem from the following three directions or aspects: (i) deriving the PCRB of collaborative bistatic radio SLAM for the first time in the literature, to the best of the authors’ knowledge; (ii) analyzing the impact of the number of collaborative UE on the achievable estimation accuracy in terms of UE position error bounds, UE heading error bounds, UE clock error bounds, as well as landmark position error bounds; and (iii) investigating the collaborative performance bounds for a wide variety of parameter settings including the number of landmarks, magnitudes of process and measurement noise, and different UE trajectories. The provided numerical results in the considered vehicular scenario demonstrate major accuracy gains in both UE state estimation as well as in landmark state estimation, when compared to ordinary single-UE radio SLAM.
