papers.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
papers.abstract: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.

papers.title: Policy Iteration Convergence for Exploratory Two-State Mean-Field Control Problems
papers.abstract: This paper studies the theoretical policy iteration convergence for two-state mean-field control (MFC) problems with Wright--Fisher common noise under entropy regularization. The population dynamics lead to a degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation of Kimura type. After an arcsine transformation, the degeneracy becomes a singular Bessel drift whose coefficients and weights depend on the feedback stochastic policy. This policy dependence prevents a direct application of estimates for a fixed operator. We establish weighted Sobolev estimates and H\"older embeddings uniformly over the admissible policy class. Combining these estimates with logarithmic entropy bounds and boundary estimates that remain valid when the policy changes, we prove the well-posedness, monotone improvement and convergence of policy iteration to the optimal solution. We also establish the convergence to the original MFC problem when the entropy parameter $\lambda$ tends to zero. Both the regularization error and the performance loss of the regularized optimal policy are bounded by $O(\lambda(1+|\ln\lambda|))$ in a weighted H\"older norm. An epidemic containment example of MFC is presented to illustrate the policy iteration convergence and the vanishing entropy convergence.

papers.intro:
Recently, continuous-time reinforcement learning (RL) theories and algorithms have attracted considerable attention in the communities of stochastic control and quantitative finance. The dynamic exploitation in RL to achieve the maximum reward naturally connects the learning problem to continuous-time stochastic control, in which some mathematical tools such as relaxed control, dynamic programming and martingale characterization can be invoked again in the new context to understand the learning mechanism. The pioneer work Wang, Zariphopoulou and Zhou [37] proposed the entropy regularization to the so-called exploratory control formulation to facilitate the characterization of the optimal stochastic policy. Later, Jia and Zhou [24, 25, 26] laid theoretical foundations for policy evaluation, policy gradient and policy iteration RL algorithms in learning the optimal policy in classical diffusion models. The fast growth in continuous-time RL also motivated interesting theoretical studies such as the model-based policy iteration convergence. In the classical stochastic control setting, Kerimkulov, Šiška and Szpruch [27] established exponential convergence and stability of of policy iteration for drift-controlled diffusions on a finite horizon, using BSDE techniques. In the exploratory formulation, Huang, Wang and Zhou [21] proved the policy iteration convergence over an infinite horizon by combining Sobolev and Hölder estimates with a sublinear entropy bound. Tran, Wang and Zhang [36] studied the convergence of policy iteration with controlled diffusion or unbounded coefficients under a large-discount condition. Ma, Wang and Zhang [30] developed a probabilistic approach based on representations of solutions and their derivatives and obtained quantitative convergence under suitable assumptions. Huang, Yu and Zhang [22] employed this probabilistic approach in the exploratory time-inconsistent control problem and proved the convergence of policy iteration towards the equilibrium policy.

Meanwhile, continuous-time RL theories and algorithms have been rapidly generalized in various applications beyond the classical models, among which the extension of continuous-time RL to mean-field control (MFC) has been an appealing research direction with many exclusive new features. MFC concerns the cooperative population where all agents share the same goal to attain the social optimum, which is often interpreted as an optimal control problem by a social planner on behalf of interacting agents. Just to name a few, Wei and Yu [39] firstly extended the q-learning theory to MFC in the McKean-Vlasov diffusion model by developing the integrated q-function and model-free policy iteration algorithm; Ren, Wei, Yu and Zhou [32, 33] further established the integrated q-function, two-layer fixed point characterization of the optimal policy and model-free policy iteration algorithms in MFC with controlled common noise; Frikha, Germain, Laurière, Pham and Song [18] studied the stochastic policy gradient algorithm in MFC problems; Bayraktar, Hennandez, Yan, Zhu [4] investigated the stochastic policy gradient for ergodic MFC problems; Cheng, Guo, Pham and Zhang [9] proposed a deterministic policy gradient algorithm for extended MFC problems. In the continuous-time framework, the mean-field HJB equation involves the derivatives of the value function in Wasserstein space with respect to the population law. Consequently, the standard PDE estimates and probabilistic arguments in the aforementioned studies on the policy iteration convergence in the single agent’s RL problem cannot be applied to the mean-field model, thereby leaving the convergence of policy iteration for MFC in McKean-Vlasov diffusion model still an open problem. This gap between the well-performed mean-field RL algorithms and the under-developed convergence analysis of model-based policy iteration motivates the present study. To circumvent the profound challenge due to the lack of proper estimates for the derivatives of the value function with respect to probability measures, we consider the MFC problem with finite states under entropy regularization. To facilitate the arguments and presentation, we focus on the case of two-state model in this work. The general cases with multiple states will be left for future study.

Increasing research interests have been seen in finite-state MFC and mean-field game (MFG) problems. Cecchin [7] studied finite-horizon finite-state MFC, characterizes the value function as a viscosity solution of an HJB equation on the simplex, and establishes convergence from centralized finite-agent control problems. Bayraktar, Cecchin, Cohen and Delarue [2] introduced Wright–Fisher common noise to establish uniqueness in finite-state MFGs through a nonlinear Kimura master equation. Their subsequent work [3] derived this formulation as a limit of weighted finite-player games. In the potential setting, Cecchin and Delarue [8] examined a stochastic MFC problem with Wright–Fisher common noise, establish classical solvability of its parabolic HJB equation under sufficiently strong boundary repulsion, and use vanishing common noise to select MFG equilibria. These studies demonstrate the role of Kimura operators in mean-field models.

Notably, even in the mean-field model with finite states, the social planner’s state variable is the population distribution, which takes values in a continuous probability simplex. In the presence of common noise, this distribution becomes stochastic, and the associated Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation contains second-order terms. Wright–Fisher common noise has a covariance structure adapted to the simplex and degenerates at its boundary, leading to differential operators of Kimura type. This boundary degeneracy creates substantial difficulties in studying the regularity of value functions and the convergence of the policy iteration. In particular, the previous studies in single agent’s model show the importance of uniform derivative estimates in policy iteration. However, their results do not directly apply to the boundary structure considered in the finite-state MFC problem: the diffusion is degenerate in the original population variable, while the transformed equation has a singular drift that may be merely measurable.

papers.title: Slower but Faster: When Self-Organized Traffic Flows Beat Traffic Signal Control
papers.abstract: Urban traffic flow networks are complex adaptive systems, whose variability challenges centralized, top-down control. We study decentralized alternatives in which order emerges from local interactions, comparing the network-wide performance of roundabouts in SUMO against fixed-time and actuated control as well as self-organizing signals on a 4$\times$4 grid and a rewired, irregular variant of it, across demand levels and periodic surge amplitudes. In our computer simulations of the regular grid, converting the single most central intersection already lowers delays by 2 to 3\% relative to actuated control; each additional conversion lowers them further, and full conversion outperforms every signalized alternative under all conditions studied. In the irregular traffic flow network with full conversion of all intersections into roundabouts, this holds only up to a critical load, where traffic flow breaks down sharply, when the time-averaged demand reaches about 3.1 times the base load. Beyond that point, the self-organizing traffic signals show the lowest delay of any network-wide strategy and is nearly insensitive to surges. Interestingly, roundabouts are favorable solutions even at lower speed limits: in the regular grid, compared to the mean speed under actuated control at a speed limit of 50\,km/h, roundabouts match that speed at a speed limit of about 40\,km/h. Compared to traffic signal control, this establishes a slower-is-faster effect. Furthermore, travel times in self-organized traffic flows are more predictable than in networks with conventional signals.
papers.intro:
Urban traffic flows are a complex adaptive system in which local interactions give rise to traffic jams, stop-and-go waves, and network-wide congestion [33]. This makes it hard to predict and manage traffic flows [59], which is an NP-hard optimization problem. The prevailing solution is centralized traffic signal control, which pre-calculates timings from historical or predicted demand [36, 2]. Yet, the “typical conditions” for which such plans are optimized rarely occur [63]: demand fluctuates from minute to minute, such that deviations from the calculated signal plans cause unnecessary delays and stops [16]. While online adjustment of offsets and splits try to fix the mismatch [1], even adaptive systems have to rely on simplified signal control approaches for large networks [2]. The behavior of such networks under surges and disruptions is a central focus of resilience research [47, 38].

The behavior of such networks under surges and disruptions is a central focus of resilience research [47, 38].

Decentralization and self-organization offer an alternative, in which robust global order emerges from local interactions without a central authority [32, 42, 27]. This has inspired novel kinds of software for signals that switch based on local, real-time information. Examples reach from self-organizing priority rules [42] to max-pressure control [60] and multi-agent reinforcement learning [13, 31]. The underlying decisions of these approaches can be decentralized, and one could even allow road users to vote for one of several signal control policies, each trained for a different goal. Such democratic approaches to governing intersections can achieve high performance with respect to several (“pluralistic”) goals [39]. Focusing now on hardware, roundabouts pursue the same idea of self-organization, but with a single spatial priority rule, yielding circular traffic flows (Fig. 1) [55, 54]. The comparison made here is, therefore, between two forms of decentralization and self-organization: (i) a spatial rule embedded in junction geometry and (ii) a temporal rule implemented in the signal software, such as the Analytic+ implementation [40] of the self-control approach proposed by Lämmer and Helbing [42].

At a single junction, the case for roundabouts is largely settled, with a well-established safety benefit [17, 54] and capacity models supporting routine design [55]. In contrast, their suitability for road networks is still disputed. In Switzerland, many roundabouts introduced since the mid-1980s now saturate at rush-hour peaks, prompting a shift back to signals: Lucerne plans to replace seven roundabouts, Ostermundigen has replaced three with sensor-controlled signals, and the Federal Roads Office reports simulations favoring signals on a dense section of the A13, though opponents argue roundabouts work well off-peak [5]. The literature offers little guidance, because roundabouts have been mostly studied one junction at a time. The few corridor and grid studies [11, 57], however, consider neither self-organizing signals, demand that varies within the operating period, nor partial conversion (Sec. II), which are precisely the conditions of the Swiss case. Gap-acceptance models take the arrival flows at each entry as given and, therefore, cannot represent junctions that spill back into one another [15, 4], while network studies of decentralized signal control treat junction layouts as fixed [51].

papers.title: PointZip: Statistically Lossless Compression for Climate Data with Pointwise Error Bounds
papers.abstract: High-resolution climate simulations generate data volumes that increasingly strain storage, I/O, and data dissemination. Error-bounded lossy compressors can reduce these costs, but their tolerances are usually user-chosen and difficult to standardize across heterogeneous climate datasets. We address this limitation with statistically lossless compression, where the pointwise compression error is bounded by the pointwise data uncertainty. We propose PointZip, a two-stage compressor that combines a rate-distortion-efficient base layer with error-bound-aware residual coding to enforce pointwise guarantees. On outputs from the widely used climate modeling framework ICON, PointZip makes 1km simulations practical by reducing storage bandwidth requirements by 72x. On the ERA5 climate dataset, PointZip reaches 69.3x on the most representative variables, reducing the commonly used subset to 4 TB. In downstream evaluations, PointZip preserves data spectra, extreme events, and air parcel trajectories, while increasing neural weather forecast RMSE by less than 1%, with negligible impact on the Fractions Skill Score (FSS).
papers.intro:
Climate simulations and reanalysis systems are continuously increasing in spatiotemporal resolution, and their storage demands are growing accordingly [1, 2, 3]. This pressure is already evident in extreme-scale simulation workflows. Recently, the ICON model [4, 5, 6] has been awarded the Gordon Bell Prize for Climate for high-resolution simulations at 1km spatial resolution and 10s temporal resolution [7]. With a 3-hourly output frequency, it generates 16 TiB of data per checkpoint and requires 200 GiB/s of storage write bandwidth and 620 GiB/s of read bandwidth, even in a configuration focused on showcasing the compute capability. The Earth Virtualization Engines project [8] has reported up to 1 TB/s storage bandwidth requirements for high-resolution climate simulations.

Recently, the ICON model [4, 5, 6] has been awarded the Gordon Bell Prize for Climate for high-resolution simulations at 1km spatial resolution and 10s temporal resolution [7]. With a 3-hourly output frequency, it generates 16 TiB of data per checkpoint and requires 200 GiB/s of storage write bandwidth and 620 GiB/s of read bandwidth, even in a configuration focused on showcasing the compute capability. The Earth Virtualization Engines project [8] has reported up to 1 TB/s storage bandwidth requirements for high-resolution climate simulations.

These numbers show that storage and I/O are becoming primary bottlenecks in high-resolution climate simulations [8, 7]. Institutions around the world generate enormous volumes of climate data every day. In one of the highest-resolution ICON runs [7], the simulation sustained 145.7 simulated days per day, meaning that a 3-hour simulation can be completed in 74.1s. However, the I/O time needed to output a single time step at full spatial resolution is 82.2s, which is longer than the simulation time itself.

This imbalance is problematic because it limits our ability to analyze the high-spatiotemporal-resolution data generated by these simulations. To better understand the climate system, we need to be able to store and analyze the data produced by these simulations at intervals much shorter than 3 hours. That requires not only simulation models with higher computational performance but also the ability to store and transmit much larger volumes of data. The challenge is not limited to a single model. In particular, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) reported producing 230 TB of data per day in 2021, and next-generation systems are expected to approach the petabyte-per-day scale [1, 2]. However, even for current-generation simulations, the required 1 TB/s of storage bandwidth is available at only a few supercomputers. For example, Alps [9] provides 1.1 TB/s of write bandwidth. Current workloads therefore place severe pressure on storage systems, I/O bandwidth, and data dissemination.

Data compression is a promising solution to reduce storage and I/O costs. Purely lossless compressors [10, 11, 12] provide limited help at this scale. Although prior evaluations [14, 15] suggest that some downstream tasks degrade only modestly at high compression ratios, users must be careful for unknown applications without explicit control of the compression error.

To address this issue, several error-bounded lossy compressors have been developed for scientific datasets [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Recent work has also proposed error-bounded designs tailored to climate data, including EBCC [22]. These methods provide strict guarantees on the maximum compression error. However, in most existing workflows the tolerance remains a user-chosen global parameter, typically expressed as an absolute, relative, or range-relative bound. For a heterogeneous climate dataset such as ERA5 [23], a single global tolerance may be too strict in some regions and too permissive in others, and appropriate values differ across variables and downstream tasks. As a result, users must repeatedly tune and validate bounds for their own applications, which makes it difficult to apply them in practice.

To make climate and weather data compression practical at scale, an ideal compression algorithm should satisfy four properties. (1) The error guarantee should be directly linked to intrinsic properties of the data rather than to application-specific tuning. (2) The algorithm should achieve a high compression ratio to efficiently reduce pressure on the I/O system and make the compressed dataset more portable. (3) The algorithm should have high compression throughput to handle large data volumes with low resource usage. (4) The compressed dataset should not introduce significant degradation in downstream applications.

Definition of statistically lossless compression. In this work, we propose statistically lossless compression that meets the desired properties for climate data compression. In this new paradigm, instead of using artificially defined global error bounds, we define a compressed dataset to be statistically lossless with respect to the original dataset if the pointwise compression error is less than or equal to the pointwise uncertainty at every data point. In other words, statistically lossless compression ensures that the compression error at each point does not exceed the intrinsic data uncertainty at that point. Under this definition, compression does not move a value outside the pointwise uncertainty interval already represented by the dataset.

papers.title: Polynomial bounds for quasiplanar graphs
papers.abstract:
A graph $G$ is $k$-quasiplanar if it can be drawn in the plane without $k$ pairwise crossing edges. It was a longstanding conjecture that $n$-vertex $k$-quasiplanar graphs have $O_k(n)$ edges. This was recently resolved by Sadhu and, independently, by Pach, Tardos, and Zeng, based on a theorem in topology proven by Beeker and Lazarovich. These papers showed that $k$-quasiplanar graphs have at most $k^{O(k)}n$ edges.
  In this note, we greatly improve the dependence on $k$ and show that every $k$-quasiplanar $n$-vertex graph has at most $O(k^2n)$ edges. The proof is based on a geometric charging scheme and Erd\H{o}s-Szekeres type combinatorial arguments.
papers.intro:
A graph GG is planar if it can be drawn in the plane with no two edges crossing. Planar graphs are among the most extensively studied graph families, both from a structural and an algorithmic perspective. A beautiful theorem of Fáry [10] (first proved by Wagner in 1936) is that every planar graph can be drawn in the plane with straight line segments as edges. Moreover, it follows from Euler’s polyhedral formula that the maximum number of edges of an nn-vertex planar graph is at most 3​n−63n-6, which is optimal. This bound puts a heavy restriction on which graphs can be drawn without crossings.

A natural relaxation of planarity was introduced in the early 1990’s. A graph GG is kk-quasiplanar if it can be drawn in the plane such that no kk edges pairwise cross. Compared to planarity, which corresponds to the case k=2k=2, kk-quasiplanarity is much less understood for k≥3k\geq 3. The difficulty of this notion stems from the fact that 3-quasiplanar graphs can already exhibit strange behavior. For example, Brandenburg [6] showed that the complete graph K10K_{10} is 3-quasiplanar, however, it has no 3-quasiplanar drawing with straight line segments. Furthermore, Ackerman and Tardos [2] showed that there exist 33-quasiplanar graphs such that in every 3-quasiplanar drawing, there are pairs of edges that cross more than once.

papers.title: Variational and geometric time-dependent density-functional theory of electronic systems
papers.abstract: A central problem in time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) is to construct a time-dependent many-electron wave function that reproduces a prescribed time-dependent electron density. This problem admits a natural geometric interpretation, which in turn leads to at least two distinct formulations of TDDFT. The first is the usual variational formulation of TDDFT, in which the density constraint is enforced with a real-valued local potential. The second is geometric TDDFT, introduced in recent works, in which the same density constraint is enforced with an imaginary local potential, or equivalently with a Hermitian nonlocal potential. In this work, we develop this unified viewpoint for continuous electronic systems and systematically compare the two formulations. We formulate the corresponding time-dependent Kohn-Sham schemes and derive a number of exact conditions for geometric TDDFT, including conditions associated with causality, time-reversal symmetry, uniform-coordinate scaling, translational invariance, energy and momentum equations of motion, one-electron self-interaction, and the adiabatic limit. The paper also contains a mathematical section where we provide a fully rigorous justification of some parts of the text. We particularly discuss the mathematical properties of two operators underlying the two formulations of TDDFT and establish sufficient conditions for their invertibility. We explain the functional-analytic subtleties underlying the geometric interpretation of TDDFT and the two formulations of TDDFT. This unified perspective clarifies the mathematical and conceptual relation between variational and geometric TDDFT and provides a foundation for the development of approximations within geometric TDDFT.

papers.intro:
Time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) is one of the major computational approaches for describing the quantum electron dynamics of electronic systems subject to a time-dependent external potential (see, e.g., Refs. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7). The usual formulation of TDDFT is based on the idea that a given one-electron density trajectory can be generated from a fictitious Hamiltonian with an effective time-dependent external potential, whose uniqueness (modulo time-dependent constants) for a given initial state is established by the Runge-Gross theorem [8] under certain regularity conditions [9]. In the time-dependent Kohn-Sham (TDKS) scheme [8, 10], this is exploited to obtain, in principle exactly, the physical density trajectory of an interacting electronic system by solving a time-dependent Schrödinger equation (TDSE) with an auxiliary noninteracting Hamiltonian with an effective time-dependent external potential. The main practical difficulty of TDDFT lies in constructing accurate density-functional approximations to this effective time-dependent external potential. In particular, most practical TDDFT calculations rely on the so-called adiabatic approximation which, although remarkably successful in many applications, is known to have important limitations in describing strongly nonadiabatic electron dynamics (see, e.g., Ref. 11).

In particular, most practical TDDFT calculations rely on the so-called adiabatic approximation which, although remarkably successful in many applications, is known to have important limitations in describing strongly nonadiabatic electron dynamics (see, e.g., Ref. 11).

Recently, some of the present authors [12, 13] introduced an abstract formulation of TDDFT in terms of the geometry of the space of many-body states having a given density at a given time. The density constraint fixes the component of the wave-function velocity normal to the set of states with the prescribed instantaneous density, while leaving the tangential component free. This general formulation leads to different ways of constructing fictitious Hamiltonians leading to the same density trajectory. The usual TDDFT formulation in which the density trajectory is imposed using an effective time-dependent real-valued local potential is only one possible construction. This usual TDDFT formulation can be understood as resulting from imposing the time-dependent variational principle (or stationarity of the action), and for this reason we will refer to this usual TDDFT formulation as variational TDDFT. It turns out that the geometric interpretation of the abstract TDDFT problem leads to another very natural construction in which the density trajectory is imposed using an effective time-dependent imaginary local potential, or equivalently a time-dependent Hermitian nonlocal potential, whose uniqueness can be established by an extension of the Runge-Gross theorem referred to as the geometric Runge-Gross theorem [12]. This leads to a new formulation of TDDFT that we refer to as geometric TDDFT.

Of course, the practical utility of this geometric TDDFT approach will depend on whether accurate approximations can be developed for the effective imaginary local potential or Hermitian nonlocal potential. Preliminary studies on toy-model systems [12, 13] suggest that, for strongly nonadiabatic electron dynamics, the effective imaginary potential of geometric TDDFT might be easier to approximate than the effective real-valued potential of usual variational TDDFT.

In Ref. 13, a fully mathematically rigorous account of this abstract geometric formulation of TDDFT was given for the case of finite-lattice systems, and the new geometric TDDFT approach was numerically illustrated on the Hubbard dimer. In Ref. 12, this approach was extended to electronic systems in continuous space, with states in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and numerically illustrated on two-electron systems on the real line. papers.title: Gravitational Waves from Population III Black Hole Mergers in Primordial Gas Disks: Constraining Astrophysical Scenarios with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna and the Einstein Telescope
papers.abstract: The first generation of metal-free Population III (Pop~III) stars provides a possible formation channel for the black hole (BH) seeds in the early Universe. Their remnants may grow through gas accretion and mergers, producing gravitational wave (GW) signals detectable by future observatories. We develop a semi-analytical model of fragmentation in a primordial self-gravitating gas disk within minihaloes at $z > 15$, motivated by high-resolution cosmological simulations. The resulting Pop~III stars form around a central primary, some leaving massive BH remnants that migrate towards the central BH through dynamical friction from gas and dark matter, while the central BH grows through accretion and mergers. For a $10^6~{\rm M_\odot}$ halo at $z=20$, we explore how the initial mass function (IMF) and BH accretion efficiency affect detectability with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Einstein Telescope (ET). We find that both detectors can potentially reveal mergers of Pop III remnant BHs, but favor different astrophysical conditions. LISA pinpoints more massive central BHs ($\sim10^3$-$10^4 {\rm M_\odot}$), grown rapidly through mutual mergers alongside efficient gas accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=1$), and a relatively top-heavy IMF ($\alpha=0.8$). In contrast, detectability with ET favors lower-mass BHs, with less efficient accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=0.01$) and a steeper IMF ($\alpha=1.5$). These results highlight the potential of LISA and ET to probe Pop~III BH formation, growth, and mergers across different regions of parameter spaces, jointly constraining Pop~III star formation and early BH seed evolution.

In this work, we develop a semi-analytical framework connecting primordial disc fragmentation, Pop III star formation, and stellar remnant production to their subsequent orbital decay, accretion, and mergers with a central BH. We investigate whether dynamical friction can bring these remnants towards the central BH within the isolated-halo evolution time-scale and, assuming prompt coalescence, whether the resulting GW signals could be detectable by LISA or ET. By exploring the disc properties, Pop III initial mass function (IMF), and BH accretion efficiency, we identify the astrophysical conditions favouring detection in each frequency band. Rather than predicting cosmological merger rates, our goal is to demonstrate the possibility of detectable events and investigate the complementary potential of LISA and ET to probe early BH formation and growth.

papers.title: Commissioning of GEM Detectors for the Super Bigbite Spectrometer
papers.abstract: We report on the commissioning and cosmic characterization of the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) trackers for the recently completed first round of the Super Bigbite Spectrometer (SBS) experimental program conducted in Hall A of the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility. The SBS GEM trackers rank as one of the largest deployments of triple GEM detectors in operation and were critical to the success of the SBS program. Categorized by their readout strip orientation, the 56 individual SBS GEM modules range in active areas from 60cmx50cm (XY) to 150cmx40cm (UV, XW) and were fabricated at the University of Virginia. Large area layers were assembled from four XY GEM modules or a single UV or XW GEM module. The front-end electronics were based on APV25 chips with output sent to custom developed 40 MHz Multi-purpose Digitizers (MPDs). Prior to the installation of the GEM-based tracking systems for SBS experiments, the GEM modules underwent extensive cosmic-ray testing to characterize the performance of each module, including detector stability, efficiency, uniformity, timing performance, and spatial resolution.

papers.title: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles
papers.abstract: As new models become available, existing ensembles must be updated to be competitive, making them intrinsically dynamic. Deciding whether to add a candidate model can require inference on an entire annotated dataset. Such a screening becomes prohibitive for models with costly inference especially when they ultimately add no value. Even under simple convex aggregation, relying on benchmark scores can be misleading as strong standalone performance does not guarantee ensemble improvement, and fitted ensemble weights can hurt test performance. In this work, we study candidate screening and show how early rejection can be achieved safely, exploiting residual geometry for stratification and rejecting the candidate when the best possible remaining predictions cannot achieve the necessary improvement. The key result that justifies this approach is that, under convex aggregation and squared or Brier loss, the population optimum improves if and only if a candidate induces a prediction change positively aligned with the residuals of the population-optimal existing ensemble. An optimistic quadratic program (QP) provides certified early rejection, while posterior-scenario sampling offers an alternative heuristic. We evaluate the approach by showing the tradeoff between saved calls and screening accuracy, which refers to recovering the same accept/reject result as for the entire annotated dataset. We assess empirically whether full-dataset decisions predict candidate usefulness on a held-out test set. On two LLM panels, stratified screening with certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate calls while keeping 100% screening accuracy. In our experiments, sampling posterior scenarios further increases call savings to approximately 37%, with a loss of less than one percentage point in screening accuracy.

Routing methods such as RouteLLM instead select a model for each input to reduce inference costs while maintaining response quality [39].

papers.title: SURMA: Efficient Fine-Grained Communication Offload for SuperPOD
papers.abstract: GPU SuperPODs underpin large language model (LLM) serving, but growing bandwidth and round-trip times make inter-GPU communication consume increasing compute resources. SM-driven remote memory access occupies shared memory or registers for in-flight data and competes for SM-to-NoC bandwidth. Dedicated engines can free these resources, but must handle fine-grained transfers, down to a 576\,B KV-cache entry. NVIDIA's CopyEngine uses less than 1\% of NVLink bandwidth at 7\,KB granularity. We present SURMA, an on-die Scale-Up Remote Memory Access engine. Adapting RDMA requires overcoming slow doorbell submission, excessive per-application connection state, head-of-line blocking of completion notifications on shared connections, and costly ordering for multipath transfers. SURMA uses a credit-based shared send queue to reduce submission latency from 1.2\,$\mu$s to 400\,ns; fused write-with-atomic semantics to share connections while independently notifying each transaction; and Network Per Path Ordering to ensure data arrives before the completion flag without Sender or Receiver Ordering. We implement SURMA in RTL on a two-FPGA prototype and evaluate it with two 8-GPU NVLink servers. At 512\,B granularity, SURMA saturates attainable bandwidth with a single SM, whereas NVLink needs over 14\% of the SMs. SURMA occupies under 0.5\% of GPU area and accelerates inference on four models by 1.05--1.26$\times$ over NVLink.

papers.intro:
GPU SuperPODs join tens to thousands of accelerators through a scale-up fabric that exposes the HBM of every device in a global address space, as in NVIDIA NVL72 (NVIDIA, 2024b), NVL576 (NVIDIA, 2026b), and Google Ironwood (Google, 2025). They have become the main platform for LLM training (Shoeybi et al., 2019; Lepikhin et al., 2021), LLM inference (DeepSeek-AI, 2025b; DeepSeek-AI, 2025a; Patel et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025), and scientific computing such as molecular dynamics (Doijade et al., 2025). While operator-level optimizations reduce computation (Wang et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b) and local memory traffic (Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026), scaling LLM execution across these systems requires efficient inter-GPU communication. Two trends in SuperPOD evolution make this communication increasingly demanding: (1) Scale grows, and so does the round-trip time (RTT). An NVL72 connects its GPUs through a single tier of switches, but larger SuperPODs such as NVL576 span racks with a second switch tier (NVIDIA, 2026b), which adds switch hops and longer links to every round trip. (2) Bandwidth grows. Per-GPU scale-up bandwidth has risen 12×\times in under a decade, from 150 GB/s per direction with NVLink 2 (NVIDIA, 2025c) to 1.8 TB/s with NVLink 6 (Alvarez et al., 2026).

(2) Bandwidth grows. Per-GPU scale-up bandwidth has risen 12×\times in under a decade, from 150 GB/s per direction with NVLink 2 (NVIDIA, 2025c) to 1.8 TB/s with NVLink 6 (Alvarez et al., 2026).

On current GPUs, both trends land on the SMs. Communication libraries such as NCCL, NVSHMEM, and DeepEP execute remote memory access with the load/store units or the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) of the SMs (NVIDIA, 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025d; DeepSeek-AI, 2025a; NVIDIA, 2025a), so communication takes two SM resources that computation also needs (Figure 2(a)). (1) SMEM or RF. By Little’s law, sustaining a bandwidth BB over a round trip R​T​TRTT keeps B×R​T​TB\times RTT bytes in flight, the bandwidth–delay product (BDP), and the SM must hold them in its shared memory (SMEM) or register file (RF) until each access completes; we call this the outstanding buffer. (2) The SM’s NoC port. Every byte that the SM reads or writes, local or remote, passes through the fixed-bandwidth port that connects it to the network-on-chip (NoC). On an 8-GPU Hopper server, DeepEP needs 12.8% of the SMs to reach its attainable bandwidth (§2.2), and our model shows this share rising with both RTT and bandwidth (Figure 1). SM-mediated communication thus couples fabric throughput to compute-side storage and access bandwidth.

Offloading data movement to a dedicated engine decouples the two: the outstanding buffer moves to HBM, and the payload moves from HBM to HBM without passing through the SMs’ NoC ports (Figure 2(b)). Such offloading is not new: the CopyEngine (CE) underlies zero-SM collectives in NCCL 2.28 (NVIDIA, 2025a; Jeaugey et al., 2025), DMA engines have been proposed to offload ML collectives (Pati et al., 2025), GPU-Initiated Networking (GIN) lets the SMs drive RDMA (Jeaugey et al., 2025), and soNUMA and NIsplit integrate remote memory controllers on CPU dies (Novaković et al., 2014; Daglis et al., 2015). The open question is whether such an engine remains efficient for the transfers of LLM serving, and on a Hopper server existing engines do not: at a 7 KB granularity, the CE uses less than 1% of the NVLink bandwidth, and moving 1 MB takes 1.6×\times as long as on the TMA path. RDMA fares no better: even with its bandwidth scaled to match NVLink, a ConnectX-7 RNIC (NVIDIA, 2023) takes 1.94×\times as long as the TMA path to move the same 1 MB.

These transfers are small and fine-grained. Long contexts limit the batch size, so even with a context of 1M tokens a single transfer moves only a few hundred kilobytes; a token of MoE dispatch carries only 4 or 7 KB, a KV-cache entry only 576 B. At this granularity, moving the payload is no longer the expensive part: a 7 KB token crosses a 450 GB/s link in about 16 ns, whereas an RDMA-style engine takes about 1.2 μ\mus to accept the request through a doorbell and about 2 μ\mus to order its completion flag behind the data. Fine granularity also demands a high request rate: sustaining 450 GB/s with 576 B transfers means admitting about 7.8×1087.8\times 10^{8} requests per second, or about 50 GB/s of 64 B request descriptors. Once a dedicated engine moves the payload, fine-grained efficiency is thus set by how fast the endpoint admits requests, organizes transactions, and publishes completions.

We study this problem in an on-die engine built on RDMA, whose semantics GPUs already use (DeepSeek-AI, 2025a; Jeaugey et al., 2025) and whose architecture, unlike the CE’s, is open to analysis. Our question is how an on-die remote memory access (RMA) endpoint can share bounded state among many SMs and applications while keeping fine-grained transactions progressing and completing independently. Straightforward designs pay latency or on-die state at three points, quantified for a 512-GPU SuperPOD. (1) Request admission. Doorbell submission takes 1.2 μ\mus; direct submission into per-QP on-die queues needs 4.5 GB of SRAM. (2) Connection sharing. Per-context connections need 144 MB of state; sharing them (Tsai and Zhang, 2017; Monga et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025b) bounds the state, but in-order execution and completion let a 1 MB transfer delay the small ones behind it by 2.2 μ\mus. (3) Multipath completion. Keeping the flag behind data sprayed over many paths costs an extra RTT with Sender Ordering or megabytes of per-transaction state with Receiver Ordering, and the GPU’s internal bus, unlike PCIe, may still let the flag overtake the data in device memory.

papers.title: Model-based neural network for global floodplains analysis
papers.abstract: We address the super-resolution of multispectral remote sensing imagery for long-term floodplain monitoring, enhancing Landsat acquisitions towards Sentinel-2 resolution. Exploiting the period during which both missions observed the same areas, we build DLhasa-L2S , to our knowledge the first paired dataset dedicated to multispectral super-resolution for river analysis. It covers the Lhasa River (Tibet), whose strong anthropogenic changes and diverse hydromorphological profiles make it an ideal study area. We developed two model-based neural networks: a forward-backward (FB) plug-and-play scheme and an unfolded FB scheme. We compared them against learned neural networks baselines (SwinIR, RDN) on synthetic data, on real scenes, and through a statistical test over the whole real paired Landsat-Sentinel dataset. The unfolded network achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM on the real RGB components with fast inference, offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost. For NDWI-based water segmentation, its performance shows no statistically significant difference from that of the best methods.

papers.title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First
papers.abstract: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

papers.title: Finite-size scaling of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking decoupled from thermodynamic criticality in a complex-conjugate Ising model
papers.abstract: We study a two-dimensional anisotropic Ising model with complex-conjugate couplings. Analytic continuation of the exact anisotropic Ising critical condition yields a candidate thermodynamic critical line, which is independently supported by finite-size scaling confirming the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Exact diagonalization of the transfer matrix and finite-size extrapolation reveal that the spectrum becomes complex, defining a separate $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry-breaking boundary in the thermodynamic limit. We find $K_{\rm PT}<K_c$ throughout the parameter range studied, leaving an intermediate regime with a complex spectrum while the system remains thermodynamically disordered. The spatial correlations remain short-ranged at $K_{\rm PT}$, in contrast to the critical correlations at $K_c$, directly distinguishing the spectral transition from thermodynamic criticality. The complex-conjugate anisotropy modifies the finite-size free-energy amplitude, and accounting for the corresponding anisotropy factor recovers the Ising central charge $c=1/2$. These results demonstrate that spectral $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking can occur without thermodynamic criticality, establishing a decoupling between spectral and thermodynamic transitions in a two-dimensional non-Hermitian statistical system.

papers.title: Subwavelength resonances and localization in finite resonator chains with a size defect
papers.abstract: We study subwavelength resonances of a finite chain of $N\ge2$ close-to-touching spherical resonators in three dimensions with a single radius defect of relative size $\tau\in(0,1]$ and gap width $\varepsilon$. Taking the high-contrast limit before the narrow-gap limit, we prove that the positive generalized eigenvalues of the weighted chain coupling matrix with respect to the volume matrix determine the leading relative resonant frequencies. After eliminating the finite tails, we obtain an exact characteristic determinant and identify a unique critical ratio $\tau_*\in(0,1)$ at which the largest eigenvalue crosses the upper edge of the homogeneous recurrence band $[0,4]$. For every $0<\tau<\tau_*$, exactly one eigenvalue lies above this band, and its eigenvector decays geometrically along the tails. As $\tau\to\tau_*^-$, its recurrence decay length diverges like $(\tau_*-\tau)^{-1/2}$. As $\tau\to0$, exactly one eigenvalue diverges like $\tau^{-2}$ and its eigenvector concentrates at the defect; if the defect is interior, one additional positive eigenvalue has order $\tau$. For suitably normalized relative resonant modes, the sequential limit of the $\varepsilon$-scaled gradient supremum in each gap equals the absolute difference between adjacent reduced amplitudes. For the largest-eigenvalue mode, this yields defect-adjacent gradient concentration as the defect shrinks.

papers.intro:
Controlling waves with structures much smaller than the operating wavelength is a basic capability in subwavelength physics. The classical example is the Minnaert resonance of an air bubble in water [18, 9], whose resonant wavelength can far exceed the bubble diameter. Coupling NN such resonators hybridizes their individual resonances into NN subwavelength modes. At leading order in the contrast, layer-potential methods reduce a finite system to a generalized eigenvalue problem involving the capacitance matrix and the resonator volumes [13, 5]. Related reductions are discussed in [6]. For periodic crystals, Floquet–Bloch theory gives a family of quasiperiodic problems on a unit cell, leading to subwavelength spectral bands and gaps [11]. For finite arrays, the analysis must connect two levels of description: the discrete spectral data and the continuous resonant field.

A finite homogeneous chain is periodic in its interior but terminated at two ends, and those ends affect the leading spectrum. A radius defect changes both the volume of the affected resonator and its capacitive couplings to its neighbors, so the response cannot be inferred from either change alone. This distinction matters especially for close-to-touching resonators, whose narrow gaps produce strong coupling and large field gradients. Our aim is to determine the radius ratios that produce an above-band mode, to describe the spectrum as the defect shrinks, and to relate the resulting discrete amplitudes to the gradient in each gap.

Geometric defects have been studied extensively in infinite periodic subwavelength media. Ammari, Fitzpatrick, Hiltunen and Yu [10] showed that changing the radius of a single bubble in a two-dimensional periodic bubbly crystal can create a localized mode with frequency inside a subwavelength band gap. Their point-defect analysis covers both dilute and non-dilute regimes. Ammari, Hiltunen and Yu [12] subsequently considered a line of smaller bubbles in a dilute two-dimensional crystal. They proved that the resulting defect band intersects the bulk band gap for arbitrarily small size perturbations and lies entirely within the gap once the perturbation is sufficiently large. The band is not flat, allowing propagation along the defect line while the field remains localized in the transverse direction.

Localization also arises from material perturbations and disorder. Ammari, Davies and Hiltunen [4] related localized modes caused by material-parameter perturbations to the spectrum of a generalized capacitance operator, including a single defect in an infinite periodic structure. For a one-dimensional wave equation with interval resonators, Ammari, Barandun and Uhlmann [3] studied finite chains with spatial disorder and used a discrete Green function to predict localized modes induced by changes in the wave speeds. Related results include topological edge modes in chains of three-dimensional resonators [7], interface modes in finite one-dimensional chains [1], and eigenpair formulas for perturbed block Toeplitz matrices describing non-Hermitian dimer systems [2]. Li and Zhao [17] extended the analysis to pairs of close-to-touching convex resonators. More recently, Li and Zhang [16] determined leading resonant-frequency distributions for several configurations of closely spaced spherical resonators, including homogeneous chains, and obtained asymptotics of the resonant fields in narrow gaps. We ask how a radius defect affects the above-band threshold, the shrinking-defect spectrum, and the associated gap fields.

papers.title: Decorated lattices: hyperuniformity and limit theorems
papers.abstract:
We introduce \emph{decorated lattices}, a point process obtained by placing finite random point configurations in lattice cells. A stationary mark field selects the motif laws and acts as a random environment transmitting dependence between cells, while allowing flexible local arrangements. Using this construction, one can efficiently generate large regions of disordered patterns with desired local behavior while the random environment controls the asymptotic density fluctuations.
  Under moment and summability assumptions, we derive an explicit decomposition of the Bartlett spectral measure into contributions from conditional motif fluctuations and correlations between marks. This yields criteria for hyperuniformity, or generally $p$-uniformity. Independent, nondegenerate count fluctuations destroy hyperuniformity, whereas suitable dependence governed by the random environment can restore it despite random and unequal cell counts. Once count fluctuations are sufficiently suppressed, motif geometry and its spatial correlations govern the finer order of uniformity. Under mixing assumptions, we also establish central limit theorems for linear statistics, with fluctuations governed by cell counts or, at a finer scale, by the first spatial moments of the motifs.

papers.intro:
Point processes provide a natural framework for modelling spatial configurations of particles or the locations of constituents of a heterogeneous material; see [15, 3] for general background. In such applications, both the local geometry and the fluctuations of the number of constituents over large regions can be relevant. Lattice-based constructions offer a convenient way to prescribe local configurations while retaining a tractable description of their spatial dependence. A central question is how much freedom these constructions allow at the local scale without losing control of their large-scale fluctuations.

Point processes provide a natural framework for modelling spatial configurations of particles or the locations of constituents of a heterogeneous material; see [15, 3] for general background. In such applications, both the local geometry and the fluctuations of the number of constituents over large regions can be relevant. Lattice-based constructions offer a convenient way to prescribe local configurations while retaining a tractable description of their spatial dependence. A central question is how much freedom these constructions allow at the local scale without losing control of their large-scale fluctuations.

This question is closely connected to hyperuniformity. A stationary point process Ξ\Xi is called hyperuniform if Var⁡(Ξ⁡(Br))λd​(Br)⟶0as ​r→∞,\frac{\mathrm{Var}(\Xi(B_{r}))}{\lambda_{d}(B_{r})}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{as }r\to\infty, where BrB_{r} is the ball of radius rr centred at the origin. Thus, its number variance grows more slowly than the volume of the observation window, in contrast to the volume-order fluctuations of a homogeneous Poisson point process. The concept was developed in statistical physics in [19] and provides a common description of suppressed density fluctuations in crystals, many quasicrystals, and certain disordered systems. For perspectives from physics and materials science, see [18]; mathematical surveys include [13, 2, 11].

The coexistence of local disorder and suppressed density fluctuations has motivated applications to materials design. For example, [12] constructs disordered dielectric structures with large, complete photonic band gaps from hyperuniform point patterns. A related construction principle appears in [14], where space is partitioned into cells and particles are placed within them so that each cell has the same local packing fraction. This produces hyperuniform two-phase materials and illustrates how local constraints can control fluctuations at much larger scales.

Beyond identifying hyperuniform models, an important practical question is how to generate large realizations efficiently. This challenge is highlighed in [2, Section 3.6], with particular emphasis on amorphous hyperuniform patterns containing millions of points. Perturbed lattices provide a computationally simple starting point, but their spectra generally retain Bragg peaks inherited from the underlying lattice. These peaks can nevertheless be eliminated by a suitable choice of the perturbation law: the cloaking construction of [8] produces large hyperuniform samples without Bragg peaks, although the lattice structure may remain detectable through higher-order correlations. More recently, [9] establishes conditions under which invariant transports preserve hyperuniformity and constructs hyperuniform point processes by sampling within the cells of fair partitions. The work [16] develops these ideas further through spatial moment constraints, including constructions of isotropic processes with arbitrarily high orders of pp-uniformity that admit simulation in linear time.

We investigate a complementary mechanism: controlling density fluctuations through dependence between cells, while allowing their populations and internal arrangements to vary. We introduce a stationary random environment that selects the motif laws and transmits dependence between cells. This makes it possible to prescribe local arrangements while controlling large-scale count fluctuations through the environment. The resulting model also allows for fast generation of large datasets with desired level of pp-uniformity.

papers.title: VoxMel TTS Technical Report
papers.abstract: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

A central design choice in these systems is the acoustic representation to be generated. Most existing approaches autoregress over learned, compressed representations, including discrete codec tokens (Défossez et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023) and continuous latents from trained autoencoders (Peng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). Consequently, synthesis quality depends in part on the learned encoder and the fidelity of its reconstruction.

Consequently, synthesis quality depends in part on the learned encoder and the fidelity of its reconstruction.

Mel spectrograms offer a complementary alternative. As a standard acoustic target in TTS (Shen et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2021), they avoid the need for a learned acoustic tokenizer and remain interpretable and model-independent. Although a vocoder is still required to convert mel spectrograms into waveforms, it can be independently upgraded without retraining the autoregressive generator. Despite these advantages, mel spectrograms have received limited attention as continuous autoregressive targets (Meng et al., 2024). Direct autoregression over full-band mel spectrograms presents two challenges. Strong temporal redundancy may let a model rely on acoustic history under teacher forcing instead of using the text condition. Moreover, each sampled frame, including its fine-grained details, is fed back into the history, where prediction errors may accumulate. Frame patching (Jia et al., 2025) and low-frame-rate learned latents (Peng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026) reduce the number of autoregressive steps, but their generated patches or latents still enter the history. Token-wise coarse-to-fine methods (Wang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025) likewise feed reconstructed full-band frames into later steps.

papers.title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
papers.abstract: Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

papers.intro:
Image-based phenotyping enables close examination of how biological systems react to chemical or genetic perturbations, thereby deepening the understanding of how these systems work [3]. Research areas for which image-based phenotyping is central include developmental biology, drug discovery, and toxicology [5, 9, 38]. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) embryos are a prominent model organism in these contexts [5, 30, 8, 37], as they carry direct relevance for human biology, with 70% of human genes having at least one obvious zebrafish orthologue [22]. The virtually transparent embryos develop externally, reaching phenotypically relevant stages within a day. This, combined with the high fecundity of zebrafish, makes them ideally suited for large-scale imaging. Using zebrafish embryos in drug discovery or toxicity tests is in line with the 3R principles that aim to replace, reduce, and refine animal experiments for more humane research [36].

Today, machine learning (ML) can perform much of the evaluation of generated image data that would otherwise require trained experts [46]. For example, Čapek et al. have shown that ML models can rival experienced researchers in zebrafish embryo phenotyping [5]. Many such models have been proposed for the phenotyping of embryos [5, 40] and already hatched embryos called eleutheroembryos that are not yet freely feeding [24, 39, 15, 45, 43]. All of these rely on supervised training, leading to practical limitations. First, supervised models need extensive amounts of labeled data for training. Especially in large-scale imaging, representative images can be acquired cheaply while expert labels are costly. Second, supervised models generally lose accuracy when imaging conditions change. Changes in microscope, illumination, or treatment protocols can degrade performance. This complicates sharing models between laboratories.

Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both limitations by learning transferable image representations without labels [44]. A model first learns these general representations, compact numerical descriptions of an image, from raw, unlabeled images by solving an auxiliary task, for example, recognizing that two randomly cropped and distorted versions of the same embryo image belong together. The learned representations can then be used for training on downstream tasks such as classification or segmentation with far fewer labels. The practical outcome hinges on several choices, such as SSL algorithm, pretraining strategy, and augmentations, i.e., random image modifications such as flips, rotations, or blur that are applied during training, which remain poorly understood for most biological domains. SSL algorithms vary in their auxiliary task for learning representations, making the choice of algorithm crucial. The pretraining strategy also plays a substantial role, namely whether to pretrain on a large natural-image corpus, e.g., ImageNet-1k (IN1k) [14], or on domain images. Augmentations are critical as well, since the learning signal in most methods is tightly coupled to comparisons between differently augmented views of an image [44]. Which specific augmentations are suited for a given domain is rarely studied.

papers.title: Ramsey sets are canonically Ramsey
papers.abstract: A set $A$ of points is called Ramsey if, for each $r$, every $r$-coloring of a sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space contains a monochromatic congruent copy of $A$. We show that for each Ramsey set $A$, every $r$-coloring of a sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space, regardless of the number of colors used, contains a monochromatic or a rainbow congruent copy of $A$. This answers a question raised in virtually every paper on the topic.

Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer and Straus introduced this notion and, among many other results, proved that every Ramsey set is finite [4, Theorem 19] and spherical [3, Theorem 13], i.e., lie on the surface of a hypersphere. Graham conjectured [9] that these two necessary conditions are also sufficient, while Leader, Russell, and Walters [13] posed a ‘rival conjecture’. Both were were recently refuted. First, Pálvölgyi [18] constructed a 77-point counterexample to the first one, while shortly after, OpenAI [17] found a 44-point counterexample to the ‘rival conjecture’. Moreover, OpenAI [17] announced a complete characterization of Ramsey sets in terms of a tensor condition over their coordinate fields, see Theorem 2 for a precise statement. We refer the reader to the work [1] of Axenovich, Liu and Sagdeev for the background on this subject and its rich bibliography.

papers.title: A widely-tunable printed-circuit-board-based resonant electro-optic modulator
papers.abstract: We present a simple, printed-circuit-board (PCB)-based resonant electro-optic modulator (EOM) featuring a wide operational frequency range. By utilizing a low-loss, high-frequency variable capacitor, the resonant frequency can be continuously tuned by typically 30% within a single band, e.g., from 161.0 MHz to 233.5 MHz. Furthermore, by swapping a radio-frequency transformer, the EOM's resonance is reconfigurable across the 17.7-489.7 MHz range, with quality factors ranging from 46 to 109. Using this design, we demonstrate the EOM's applicability by generating strong 228 MHz sidebands to verify its utility for ^6Li laser cooling and by locking a 780 nm laser to the Rb D2 transition using retroreflected modulation transfer spectroscopy at 20 MHz resonance. The device's reconfigurable wide frequency range and high quality factors make this EOM versatile for laser cooling of multiple atomic species, including ^6Li, ^39K, and ^41K, as well as for laser frequency locking. This design offers a flexible, robust, and practical solution for undergraduate teaching laboratories and quantum optics research groups.

papers.title: Beyond Finite Dimensions: Duflo-Serganova Cohomology, the Formal Superdimension, and a Kac-Wakimoto Theorem for Unitarizable Supermodules
papers.abstract: The main results of this manuscript are fourfold. First, we introduce relative holomorphic discrete series supermodules over basic classical Lie superalgebras $\mathfrak{g}$ and $\mathfrak{sl}(n\vert n)$. These are unitarizable highest weight supermodules whose $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar{0}}$-constituents are Harish-Chandra modules of relative holomorphic discrete series representations. We show that these are exactly the unitarizable highest weight supermodules whose globalizations have supermatrix coefficients square-integrable modulo the center. Second, we define the formal superdimension of a relative holomorphic discrete series supermodule as the parity-weighted sum of the formal dimensions of its $\mathfrak{g}_{\bar{0}}$-constituents. We show that it equals, up to sign, the value at zero of an $L$-packet supercharacter obtained by averaging over the Weyl group. Third, we prove a Kac-Wakimoto theorem for formal superdimension: it is nonzero if and only if the highest weight is maximally atypical. For integral highest weights, it equals the superdimension of a finite-dimensional simple supermodule with the same degree of atypicality. We realize these supermodules through derived Zuckerman functors. For nonintegral highest weights, it is computed by generalized Duflo-Serganova cohomology. Finally, to establish the Kac-Wakimoto conjecture, we develop the theory of generalized Duflo-Serganova cohomology for unitarizable supermodules. We prove that the cohomology of a unitarizable simple supermodule is unitarizable and either zero or simple.

papers.title: A Lifted Hessian-Riemannian Gradient Flow for LQR Synthesis under Passivity Constraints
papers.abstract: The static state-feedback gain that renders a linear system passive at an external port and minimizes a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost cannot be computed by convex optimization, since the passivity certificate and the LQR cost are coupled bilinearly through the common gain. A previous indirect approach restricts the gain to a convex inner approximation of the passivity region, which is conservative and whose construction scales exponentially with the number of gain entries. This paper proposes a direct approach. The set of strictly passivating gains is the image of a convex lifted set of inverse storage matrices and transformed gains. We describe this set by a strict linear matrix inequality and an affine equality for every feedthrough matrix with positive semidefinite symmetric part, including feedthrough matrices with a singular symmetric part, and minimize the LQR cost over it by a gradient flow whose metric is the Hessian of a logarithmic barrier. For multi-input systems, this Hessian is singular along gain changes that preserve the storage function, and we complete the metric along these directions by the metric of the gain space. We prove that the flow exists for all times, that every gain along the flow is strictly passivating with an explicit storage function, and that the cost decreases monotonically while the gains remain in a compact set of stabilizing gains. Numerical examples show that the flow attains a lower cost than the indirect approach, that the completion is required for multi-input systems, and that the flow can converge to a local minimizer on nonconvex passivity regions.

papers.intro:
Passivity describes the input-output behavior of a dynamical system by a dissipation inequality at its port [1, 2]. Feedback interconnections of passive systems inherit stability properties [3, 4, 5], where the precise statements depend on the type of interconnection, on the strictness of the passivity properties, and on detectability conditions. Passivity at an external port therefore permits stable interconnections with passive subsystems that are unknown a priori, but it does not ensure a sufficient transient performance. This motivates a state feedback that renders the closed-loop system passive at an external port and, among all such gains, minimizes a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost of the isolated system [6].

Each of the two requirements alone leads to a convex synthesis problem. For linear systems, the Kalman–Yakubovich–Popov (KYP) lemma characterizes passivity by a linear matrix inequality (LMI) in a storage matrix [7, 8]. For the closed loop, this inequality is bilinear in the storage matrix and the feedback gain, and a change of variables turns the synthesis of a feedback gain with a passivity requirement into an LMI problem [6, Proposition 3]. Likewise, the LQR problem admits convex reformulations through the covariance formulation [9, Section 2] or the Riccati inequality [7, p. 115]. If both requirements, passivity and LQR performance, are imposed jointly, however, they are coupled through the common gain, which results in a bilinear equality. Hence, the resulting formulations admit no convex reformulation [6, Propositions 5 and 6], and the set of passivating gains is nonconvex in general [6, Lemma 10]. The indirect approach of [6] therefore certifies cubes in the gain space by a common storage function, inner-approximates their union by a convex polytope, and minimizes the LQR cost over this polytope by a projected gradient flow. Its gain is suboptimal whenever the constrained minimizer lies outside the polytope, the number of cubes grows exponentially with the number of gain entries, and computing the largest inner polytope is open for more than two gain entries [6, Remark 4].

This paper proposes a direct approach. The set of passivating gains is the image of a convex lifted set under the map from the inverse storage matrix and a transformed gain to the gain. The LQR cost is nonconvex in the lifted variables, but the lifted set admits a logarithmic barrier, which we use as the metric of a Hessian–Riemannian gradient flow [10]. The flow evolves the gain and its storage function jointly and generates passivating gains at all times.

papers.title: LAMOST III Low-resolution Spectroscopic Survey: Overview and Target Selection
papers.abstract: We present an overview of the LAMOST III Low-resolution Spectroscopic Survey (LRS), including its scientific goals, target selection strategy, and current observing status. Targets in the main survey are selected via weighted random sampling, using the inverse local density in the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram and in the G-magnitude distribution, with additional enhancement in selected regions of the HR diagram. The main survey is complemented by 35 dedicated add-on catalogs (including very metal-poor star candidates, halo stars, hot/young stars, wide binaries, extragalactic sources and so on) and a time-domain program providing multi-epoch spectroscopy of binaries and other peculiar systems. LAMOST III LRS is designed to map the structure and evolution of the Galactic disk, reconstruct the assembly and early chemical-enrichment history of the Galactic halo, improve stellar-parameter calibration, and characterize rare and variable objects. By June 2025, the LAMOST III LRS had obtained 1.53 million low-resolution spectra from 658 plates, corresponding to 1,264,052 unique sources. Relative to LAMOST I+II, the current sample is enriched in O/B stars, subgiants, main-sequence turn-off stars, metal-poor stars, and other previously underrepresented populations. In particular, the fractions of metal-poor and very metal-poor stars increase from 3.8% and 0.4% in LAMOST I+II to 9.0% and 1.1% in LAMOST III LRS, respectively, demonstrating the improved efficiency of the revised target-selection strategy for Galactic archaeology and stellar astrophysics.

The Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST; [17, 20, 106, 50]) is a 4 m quasi-meridian reflective Schmidt telescope with 4000 fibers feeding a 5∘ field-of-view focal plane. Since commissioning, LAMOST has operated through the pilot survey (2011.10.24--2012.06.17), LAMOST I (2012.09.28--2017.06.16), and LAMOST II (2017.09.19--2023.06.15), collecting more than 20 million low- and medium-resolution stellar spectra between October 2011 and September 2024. The eleventh data release (DR11)11 1 https://www.lamost.org/dr11/v2.0/ provides 11.93 million low-resolution spectra from 6,283 observing fields and 13.16 million medium-resolution spectra from 2,395 fields. For the low-resolution survey (LRS), DR11 also includes stellar-parameter estimates for approximately 11.57 million sources.

With a dataset now exceeding several tens of millions of spectra, LAMOST is among the most productive spectroscopic survey facilities worldwide. As reviewed by Yan et al. [92], LAMOST observations over the past decade have driven advances across a broad range of astrophysical topics, including the structure, formation, and evolution of the Milky Way (e.g. [27, 84, 45, 36, 83, 12, 105, 29]), stellar astrophysics and chemical evolution (e.g. [90, 86, 91, 87, 15]), exoplanetary systems (e.g. [75, 13, 65]), and the discovery of rare and compact stellar objects (e.g. [49, 60, 38, 96, 47, 56, 79, 31, 37, 98]).

Early LAMOST target selection adopted uniform sampling in the color–magnitude diagram [99], constrained by the photometric surveys available at the time—primarily the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; [97, 95]), the 2MASS All-Sky Point Source Catalog (2MASS; [66]), Pan-STARRS1 (PS1; [74]), and the Xuyi Schmidt Telescope Photometric Survey of the Galactic Anti-center (XSTPS-GAC; [51, 102]). Although effective for constructing large samples with a relatively simple and well-defined selection function [11], this strategy underrepresented several key populations. Metal-poor (MP; [Fe/H] <−1<-1) and very metal-poor (VMP; [Fe/H] <−2<-2) stars constitute only ∼\sim3.8% and 0.4% of the sample, respectively, with the VMP stars corresponding to approximately 2×1042\times 10^{4} in total. Giant stars account for <20<20%, and distant stars are underrepresented: half of the sample lies within 1 kpc, and only 1.5% lies beyond 10 kpc, implying comparatively low fractions of outer-disk and halo stars. In addition, the relatively low signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of many LAMOST spectra limits the precision of derived stellar ages and chemical abundances. Building on these developments, LAMOST III LRS officially commenced in September 2023, with its completion date yet to be determined. Leveraging the new generation of photometric and astrometric catalogs, it expands coverage of metal-poor stars, giants, halo stars, main-sequence turn-off and subgiant stars, young stars, cluster members, wide binaries, high-tangential-velocity stars, and anomalous objects in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. Relative to LAMOST I/II, the corresponding sample sizes increase by factors of several to tens, improving completeness and sampling efficiency and enhancing the survey’s discovery potential in Galactic structure and evolution, stellar astrophysics, and rare-object searches.
