papers.title: The Exact Optimal Delivery Scheme for the Cyclically $L$-Separated Placement in Multi-Access Coded Caching
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the $(K, L, M, N)$ multi-access coded caching (MACC) system introduced by Hachem et al. The system consists of a server storing $N$ equal-sized files, $K$ cache nodes, each with a storage capacity of $M$ files, and $K$ users, each accessing $L$ consecutive cache nodes in a cyclic wrap-around topology. The server transmits coded information to the users via an error-free capacitated broadcast channel, such that each user obtains its own requested file as a combination of the server transmission and the accessible caches' content. Our objective is to minimize the worst-case transmission load over all possible user demands. First, for the cyclically $L$-separated placement, we derive a new converse bound using the acyclic index coding bound. By carefully counting all valid cache supports, the proposed converse improves upon an existing bound for the same placement. We then develop a linear coded caching scheme based on a novel determinant-based interference alignment strategy, which achieves the new converse bound exactly. Exploiting the determinant structure of a random generating matrix (each of whose columns corresponds to one user), this scheme simultaneously aligns interference across all users into low-dimensional subspaces, while preserving the decodability of their desired packets. Furthermore, by averaging acyclic index coding bounds over cyclic user permutations, we derive a general converse bound applicable to arbitrary uncoded cache placements. By combining the proposed scheme with memory sharing, we demonstrate that the achievable transmission load is within a factor of two of the global bound under uncoded placement. Finally, theoretical and numerical comparisons demonstrate that the proposed scheme generally achieves a strictly lower load than existing schemes.

papers.intro:
Coded caching, introduced by Maddah-Ali and Niesen [1], is an effective technique for reducing the transmission load in content delivery networks. By jointly designing data storage during off-peak hours and coded transmissions during peak hours, it enables a single coded multicast transmission to serve multiple users simultaneously, even when they request different files. It has been widely studied in various network settings, including device-to-device (D2D) networks [2], hierarchical networks [3], wireless networks [4], multi-access networks [5], and combination networks [6].

By jointly designing data storage during off-peak hours and coded transmissions during peak hours, it enables a single coded multicast transmission to serve multiple users simultaneously, even when they request different files. It has been widely studied in various network settings, including device-to-device (D2D) networks [2], hierarchical networks [3], wireless networks [4], multi-access networks [5], and combination networks [6].

Among these settings, multi-access coded caching (MACC) was first introduced by Hachem et al. [5] to model edge caching in heterogeneous wireless networks. The motivating architecture combines densely deployed access points, such as small-cell base stations or Wi-Fi access points, that provide high data rates over short distances with sparsely deployed macro base stations that provide wider coverage at lower rates per link. By equipping the access points with caches, users can recover their requested files using both cached content retrieved from multiple nearby access points and broadcast transmissions from a macro base station. To reflect users’ access to nearby caches, Hachem et al. [5] considered a system model in which each user can retrieve cache content from consecutive caches, with cyclic wrap-around for symmetry.

In a (K,L,M,N)(K,L,M,N) cyclical MACC system, a server storing NN equal-sized files serves KK users without local caches over an error-free shared link. There are KK cache nodes, each with capacity equal to the size of MM files. User kk accesses the LL consecutive cache nodes indexed by k,k+1,…,k+L−1k,k+1,\ldots,k+L-1, with indices interpreted cyclically over {1,2,…,K}\{1,2,\ldots,K\}. A MACC scheme consists of two phases: placement during off-peak hours and delivery during peak hours. During the placement phase, the server places data of total size at most MM times the file size in each cache, without knowledge of future user demands. If file bits are stored directly without coding, the placement is called uncoded placement. During the delivery phase, each user randomly requests one file from the library. Given these demands, the server broadcasts coded messages that enable each user to recover its requested file using the received messages and the contents of its accessible caches. The transmission load RR is defined as the maximum total amount of data broadcast by the server over all possible user demands, normalized by the file size. Our objective is to jointly design cache placement and delivery to minimize RR for a given cache size MM.

There are many studies on improving the cut-set lower bound derived in [1], both for general placement [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13] and under the restriction of uncoded placement [14, 15, 16, 17]. Ajaykrishnan et al. [7] obtained tighter bounds by jointly analyzing cache contents and transmissions for different demand vectors. For N=K=3N=K=3 and M=1M=1, their bound is 3/23/2 times the cut-set bound, increasing the lower bound from 2/32/3 to 11 and matching the MN load. Sengupta et al. [8] strengthened the cut-set bound using Han’s inequality [18, Thm. 17.6.1]. Wang et al. [9] derived additional converse bounds by reducing cooperating users to a single user requesting multiple files. Ghasemi and Ramamoorthy [10] developed a labeling algorithm on directed trees, yielding a bound that includes the cut-set bound as a special case and is strictly tighter in certain parameter regimes. Tian [11] exploited problem symmetry in entropy linear programming to characterize the exact trade-off for two-user systems and obtain further bounds for other small systems. Wang et al. [12] derived improved bounds using conditional mutual information inequalities and Han’s inequality. Yu et al. [13] strengthened the cut-set argument by exploiting the individual decoding constraints of users on the same side of a cut. Under uncoded placement, Wan et al. [14, 16] applied the acyclic index coding bound to prove the optimality of the MN scheme for N≥KN\geq K. Yu et al. [15] characterized the optimal memory–load trade-off for arbitrary NN and KK using a delivery scheme that removes redundant transmissions arising from repeated requests and a matching genie-aided converse. Krishnan et al. [17] developed a general data-exchange converse using induction, recovering several known uncoded-placement bounds.

For N=K=3N=K=3 and M=1M=1, their bound is 3/23/2 times the cut-set bound, increasing the lower bound from 2/32/3 to 11 and matching the MN load. Sengupta et al. [8] strengthened the cut-set bound using Han’s inequality [18, Thm. 17.6.1]. Wang et al. [9] derived additional converse bounds by reducing cooperating users to a single user requesting multiple files. Ghasemi and Ramamoorthy [10] developed a labeling algorithm on directed trees, yielding a bound that includes the cut-set bound as a special case and is strictly tighter in certain parameter regimes. Tian [11] exploited problem symmetry in entropy linear programming to characterize the exact trade-off for two-user systems and obtain further bounds for other small systems. Wang et al. [12] derived improved bounds using conditional mutual information inequalities and Han’s inequality. Yu et al. [13] strengthened the cut-set argument by exploiting the individual decoding constraints of users on the same side of a cut. Under uncoded placement, Wan et al. [14, 16] applied the acyclic index coding bound to prove the optimality of the MN scheme for N≥KN\geq K. Yu et al. [15] characterized the optimal memory–load trade-off for arbitrary NN and KK using a delivery scheme that removes redundant transmissions arising from repeated requests and a matching genie-aided converse. Krishnan et al. [17] developed a general data-exchange converse using induction, recovering several known uncoded-placement bounds.

papers.title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
papers.abstract: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly enable generalist agents to control interactive environments from raw pixels [27, 4, 17, 26, 38, 22], with GameWorld [23] standardizing state-verifiable browser-game evaluation. Beyond in-distribution training environments, open-ended deployment on user-generated content (UGC) platforms, indie web portals, and HTML5 mini-games requires cross-game generalization: transferring reusable visual-motor skills to unseen games without target-game parameter updates. Because accessing private simulator state or running per-game RL for every new title is infeasible at deployment, we consolidate source-game teachers into a single pixel-only student operating solely on screenshots and public instructions.

Adapting VLMs for zero-shot cross-game generalization faces challenges in both action grounding and closed-loop training. At the decision interface, autoregressive VLMs exhibit token-to-action misalignment: factorizing commands into variable-length subword sequences over an open vocabulary biases raw likelihoods toward shorter strings rather than optimal actions, distorting action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Furthermore, conventional post-training struggles under closed-loop transfer: offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT) compounds errors once the agent drifts into unfamiliar states [29], whereas traditional on-policy RL [32, 35] either requires costly trial-and-error in the target game or overfits to a single source game. Consolidating diverse source experts via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [21] thus offers a natural paradigm to learn closed-loop recovery without target-game access.

Consolidating diverse source experts via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [21] thus offers a natural paradigm to learn closed-loop recovery without target-game access.

However, scaling MOPD across heterogeneous source games exposes a critical bottleneck: multi-teacher policy conflict. Source games often obey incompatible control rules in visually similar situations—for example, steering toward foreground geometry to land on platforms (e.g., NS-Shaft) versus steering away from foreground blocks to dodge obstacles (e.g., Cubefield). Combining such contradictory teacher corrections indiscriminately—via uniform MOPD [21], gradient projection [43], or weight-space merging [14, 39, 42, 7, 15, 16, 10]—pulls the shared student in opposite directions and causes severe negative transfer. Identifying which teachers conflict without target-game data is also non-trivial: unlike language-domain MOPD where every large language model (LLM) teacher can score any text prompt [33], privileged game teachers read game-specific internal simulator variables (e.g., ball coordinates or tile grids) rather than raw pixels, so a teacher for one game cannot be executed on another game to measure inter-teacher agreement.

To address these challenges, we propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), which resolves multi-teacher conflict within an aligned semantic action space (Fig. 1). Rather than generating raw subwords, Complete-Action Alignment scores full legal commands per token to establish a calibrated student policy and visual specialist proxies for the privileged rule teachers. Selective On-Policy Retention then rolls out the student across source games, querying teachers only on uncertain or erroneous boundary states [45]. Finally, because visual specialists operate on pixels rather than private simulator variables, Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher Consolidation cross-evaluates them across peer source games to estimate teacher reliability and compatibility without target-game data. At deployment, all teachers and probes are discarded, leaving a single pixel-only Qwen3.5-4B policy evaluated zero-shot on GameWorld. We eliminate subword length bias via length-normalized candidate scoring over each game’s legal action set, yielding calibrated decision margins for selective on-policy retention and enabling pixel-only specialist probes across distinct action sets. • Conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation. We formulate a target-free disagreement matrix by cross-evaluating source specialists, coupling in-game visual identifiability with cross-game control compatibility to reweight on-policy recovery gradients before consolidation. • Zero-shot transfer and boundary analysis. papers.title: Reference Forcing: Long Video Generation with Region-Guided Drift Correction
papers.abstract: Long video generation should keep the subject and background consistent while supporting rich, natural motion. However, autoregressive models are often distilled with distribution matching distillation (DMD) over short windows, which does not train them to keep this consistency over long ranges. As a result, the subject and background can drift over time. Methods that manage the key-value (KV) cache retain or retrieve history to reduce drift. Yet this history may itself have drifted. We propose Reference Forcing, which uses the initial frames as an appearance reference. We first build a teacher that uses attention masks to force each region of a new frame to attend to the same region in the initial frames. The teacher finds these regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models. We then distill this behavior into a separate attention path of the student, which needs no external models at inference. We further introduce value correction, which corrects drifted values in the KV cache toward the matching values of drift-free initial frames. Experiments show that Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency among long-video methods on different base models, and its advantage grows with video length. Ablations show both components are needed to gain consistency without losing motion. More visualizations and code are available at https://zhaosheng-thu.github.io/reference-force/

papers.intro:
Recent video diffusion models generate short clips with high visual quality [1, 49, 19, 40]. Autoregressive video diffusion models extend generation to longer videos by generating one chunk at a time, using previously generated frames to guide each new chunk [2, 55, 11, 37, 3]. With few-step distillation and a key-value (KV) cache that stores recent frames, these models can generate videos lasting a minute or longer in real time [48, 25, 4]. However, long videos must preserve the appearance of subjects and backgrounds while maintaining rich and natural motion. In practice, errors accumulate during autoregressive generation, gradually changing the appearance of subjects and backgrounds, e.g., a red jacket slowly turns orange [11, 48, 17].

One reason for this drift lies in how these models are trained. LongLive [48], for example, uses distribution matching distillation (DMD) [54], which matches the distribution of generated video clips within short windows. However, this objective does not explicitly require subjects and backgrounds to retain their earlier appearance. A generated clip can therefore look realistic and receive a low distillation loss even if its appearance has gradually drifted.

papers.title: Interaction between fluids and Helfrich membranes
papers.abstract: We propose a finite-element method to determine the dynamics of a fluid interacting with a membrane---a fluid layer equipped with a Helfrich elastic free energy [W. Helfrich, Z. Naturforschung C, 28, 693, (1973)]. Our analysis is based on a partitioned approach, where the state of the fluid, of the membrane, and of the mesh, are solved for at staggered steps. We show the predicting capabilities of the method by considering a macroscopic example of an elastomer membrane, which bulges as it interacts with air injected through a channel. We demonstrate that our method allows for describing large membrane deformations which are not accessible by perturbative methods. We discuss the limitations of our method, by characterizing its added-mass instability. Finally, we show how our analysis allows for understanding the physical mechanism of bulge formation, which is due to a combination of elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.

papers.title: Multi-Assay Antibody Developability Prediction with Shared Structure-Language Representations
papers.abstract: Early assessment of antibody developability is critical in drug discovery, but computational approaches remain limited by the scarcity of experimental data. We explore two strategies for working within that limit. First, we designed per-residue physicochemical descriptors encoding the local structural environment, including new terms such as directional charge asymmetry and screened electrostatic potential. These feed a convolutional network, combined with protein language model (PLM) embeddings in a two-stream architecture: the two are encoded and predicted independently and merged only at the prediction stage. Second, a shared trunk with per-assay heads passes information between related assays. Both are implemented in the Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) and evaluated on eight assays: HIC, heparin affinity (HAC), AC-SINS, and polyspecificity ELISA against BVP, dsDNA, insulin, ovalbumin and soluble membrane proteins (SMP), with labels from 29 open sources. Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) on several assays; combining the streams gives a small but consistent gain in accuracy and reduces seed-to-seed variance. Multi-assay training raises Spearman rho for ovalbumin and SMP by about 0.1, where assays correlate and share sequence space. Under cluster-split cross-validation the strongest results are for HAC, ovalbumin, insulin, SMP and HIC (rho = 0.70-0.82); AC-SINS, BVP and dsDNA are weaker (0.50-0.55). In these three, sequence clusters largely coincide with data source, so a held-out fold measures transfer to differently calibrated measurements as well as to new sequences. On the 80-antibody GDPa3 hold-out, performance falls by rho around 0.1 for all but SMP (0.22). Transfer to the VHH panel of Ginkgo GDPa5 gives comparable results, and scFv validation against binary SMP labels yields F1 = 0.89, AUC = 0.95.

papers.title: Large language models as oncology world models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize cancer patient cases, but their internal representation of oncology, or world model, has not been explored systematically. By only specifying tumor type, we show that LLMs tend to generate similar patients per cancer, with on average 81.0% to 93.2% of a cancer's patients sharing the most frequent value of each baseline feature. By systematically varying patient features in 12 clinical scenarios, we show that they follow biomarker and treatment logic in 29 of 36 model-scenario assessments, against 1 of 12 when previous treatment or frailty matters. Continuing real patient trajectories, an LLM predicted 89.9% 12-month survival, and 79.2% with similar patients as examples, against 72.2% observed. To represent these trajectories, we developed the Clinical State Space, a dynamic representation framework that we also applied to real patients. Despite the limits we show, improved world models may support digital twins, which our framework can evaluate.

papers.title: Run, Read Back, Refine: Observation Fidelity in Execution-Grounded EDA Agents
papers.abstract: Design engineers lose the most time orchestrating flows and patching the gaps where closed EDA tools refuse to interoperate. We present an execution-grounded LLM agent for PyAether, SKILL, and Tcl that closes a generate-execute-refine loop over unified MCP tools (API retrieval, documentation, sandbox execution) and is already deployed in production EDA flows, with a grounding-gap framework positing that EDA-scripting correctness is bottlenecked by observation fidelity at the L4 (situated) layer, which model scale alone cannot reach. On EDA-Scripting-Bench (449 tasks, three languages, four commercial runtimes), the system reaches 76.5% pooled Pass@1 versus 19.7% (pure LLM): the system-level observation axis spans 56.8 percentage points with the model fixed, exceeding the 23.3-percentage-point backbone range with the harness fixed---two axes answering different questions; observation is an under-invested axis whose returns are measurable and graded.

papers.intro:
Design engineers’ daily work is less about fresh scripts than about orchestrating design flows and patching the gaps between EDA tools that refuse to interoperate—a flow that cannot run end-to-end is the single largest source of lost design time. Commercial EDA tools are closed: where they leave a gap, the only recourse is hand-written glue (a Makefile target, a Tcl driver, a SKILL wrapper), precisely the small intent-to-code synthesis at which LLMs excel. This reframes EDA scripting as the connective tissue letting a general coding agent orchestrate flows and fill the breaks.

papers.title: OGLE-2018-BLG-0829L: A Microlensing System with a Planet Orbiting a Star Possessing a Brown-Dwarf Companion
papers.abstract: We analyze the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0829, whose light curve exhibits a weak short-term anomaly in addition to the prominent caustic-crossing features of a binary lens. The anomaly cannot be explained by a binary-lens single-source (2L1S) model. We therefore investigate both binary-lens binary-source (2L2S) and triple-lens single-source (3L1S) interpretations and find that both models reproduce the additional anomaly, with the 3L1S model being favored by $\Delta\chi^2=15.1$. Under the favored 3L1S interpretation, the anomaly arises from a caustic induced by a planetary-mass companion, whereas the prominent caustic-crossing features are produced by the underlying binary lens. Combining the measured event timescale, $t_{\rm E}=7.55\pm0.30$ days, and angular Einstein radius, $\theta_{\rm E}=0.325 \pm 0.059$ mas, with a Bayesian analysis, we infer a lens system consisting of an M dwarf of mass $0.193^{+0.300}_{-0.098}\,M_\odot$, a possible brown-dwarf companion of mass $0.068^{+0.105}_{-0.034}\,M_\odot$, and a Saturn-mass planet of mass $0.337^{+0.522}_{-0.171}\,M_{\rm J}$. The companions have projected separations of approximately 3.6 au and 1.6 au from the primary, respectively. However, the physical interpretation remains tentative because potentially important higher-order effects have not been considered, and the dynamical stability of the proposed configuration remains uncertain. If confirmed, this would be the third star--brown dwarf--planet system identified through microlensing, highlighting the potential of microlensing to detect planets in complex multiple systems.

papers.intro:
Most stars are thought to form in binary or higher-order multiple systems rather than in isolation [16, 39]. Consequently, understanding planet formation requires investigating not only planets orbiting single stars, but also those residing in dynamically complex multiple systems. The presence of a stellar or substellar companion can substantially modify the structure and evolution of a protoplanetary disk through tidal truncation, enhanced dynamical perturbations, and accelerated disk dispersal, thereby influencing both the formation and long-term survival of planets [5, 33]. Planetary systems in multiple-star environments therefore provide important observational constraints on theories of planet formation under conditions that differ markedly from those around isolated stars.

Brown dwarfs occupy the mass range between stars and planets and are thought to form through a variety of mechanisms, including turbulent fragmentation, disk fragmentation, and dynamical ejection [42, 35]. Their role in planetary systems remains poorly understood. In particular, whether planets can efficiently form and survive around stars possessing brown-dwarf companions remains an open question. Such systems probe a poorly explored regime in which the gravitational influence of the brown dwarf may significantly alter the conditions for planet formation and subsequent planetary evolution.

The first, KMT-2020-BLG-0414Lb [45], consists of an M dwarf hosting an Earth-mass planet together with a brown-dwarf companion. More recently, Han et al. [27] reported KMT-2024-BLG-0404L, in which a Uranus-mass planet orbits a close binary composed of a late M dwarf and a brown dwarf. Interpreting multiple-lens microlensing events, however, is challenging because their anomalies can exhibit a wide variety of morphologies arising from the interplay of multiple caustics [11, 12, 10, 22]. This diversity frequently gives rise to degenerate or non-unique solutions, making detailed light-curve modeling essential for identifying the correct lens configuration. In some cases, the presence of an additional planet is revealed only through a subtle perturbation to the caustic structure generated by the underlying binary lens, making its detection considerably more difficult than in ordinary planetary microlensing events. Expanding the sample of such systems is therefore important not only for understanding planet formation in dynamically perturbed environments but also for exploring the full discovery space of gravitational microlensing.

In this paper, we present an analysis of the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0829, whose light curve exhibits a weak anomaly in addition to the prominent caustic-crossing features of a binary lens. We investigate two possible explanations for the weak anomaly: a binary-source interpretation and a triple-lens interpretation. Our analysis favors the triple-lens model, in which the lens system consists of a stellar primary and two lower-mass companions. According to the favored model, Bayesian analysis suggests that the system comprises an M dwarf, a brown dwarf, and a Saturn-mass planet, although the inferred masses are subject to substantial uncertainties. If confirmed, this would be the third star–brown-dwarf–planet system discovered by microlensing. This event illustrates the potential of microlensing to detect planets through subtle perturbations in binary-lens light curves, while highlighting the challenges of uniquely characterizing such complex lens systems.

papers.title: Intervals in affine Bruhat order
papers.abstract: Let $(W,S)$ be an irreducible affine Coxeter system. We study Bruhat intervals in $W$ via the well-known characterization of Bruhat order in terms of galleries. We start by using folded galleries to formulate an analogous order on the coweight lattice, which we call Iwahori order. This allows us to reduce the description of certain Bruhat intervals to that of the corresponding Iwahori intervals. We next give closed-form descriptions of all Iwahori intervals, using the quantum Bruhat graph (QBG). More precisely, we show that lower Iwahori intervals saturate pseudo-Weyl polytopes (that is, certain intersections of negative cones), and upper Iwahori intervals saturate certain unions of positive cones, with the cone points given by explicit formulae involving paths in the QBG. We then describe arbitrary Bruhat intervals by partitioning them into their core, a large region which is (in most cases) completely determined by an Iwahori interval, and their crust, the complementary boundary region. We conclude by proving that, under a super-regularity assumption, the crust is covered by certain locally-defined tesselating shapes. All statements and proofs are rank- and type-free.

papers.title: Exploring Energy Landscapes for Functional Materials: Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$
papers.abstract: Energy landscape exploration requires extensive energy and force evaluations, making efficient access to interatomic potentials an important practical challenge. We present a persistent socket interface that connects the landscape exploration tools in the GMIN, OPTIM, and PATHSAMPLE programs to potentials available through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The persistent design keeps both the calculator and socket connection active throughout the search, avoiding repeated initialisation. We apply this framework to understand and predict the properties of Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ using two NequIP-based potentials, and construct kinetic transition networks describing complex vacancy configurations and migration pathways. Temperature-dependent analysis of the dominant paths reveals how the most probable migration sequence can change, with the mechanism governed by global properties of the network, rather than simply the highest energy barrier. Visualisation, mean first-passage times, and heat capacities enable us to connect the organisation of the landscape to relaxation time scales and thermodynamic observables. The interface extends energy landscape methods to ASE-compatible atomistic models, providing a general framework for combining global optimisation, transition state searches, kinetic network analysis, and thermodynamic characterisation with recent developments in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

papers.title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
papers.abstract: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

papers.intro:
Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is designed to improve generalization by minimizing an approximate worst-case loss within a local parameter neighborhood, rather than optimizing only the empirical loss at the model’s current parameters (Foret et al., 2021). It was originally motivated by the geometric intuition that flat solutions, whose training loss remains low under small parameter perturbations, tend to generalize (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997).

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) is designed to improve generalization by minimizing an approximate worst-case loss within a local parameter neighborhood, rather than optimizing only the empirical loss at the model’s current parameters (Foret et al., 2021). It was originally motivated by the geometric intuition that flat solutions, whose training loss remains low under small parameter perturbations, tend to generalize (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997).

At each training step, SAM first computes an approximate adversarial parameter perturbation that increases the minibatch loss within a fixed radius neighborhood, and then updates the original parameters using the gradient evaluated at the perturbed point. Although SAM often improves generalization, it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior.

Although SAM often improves generalization, it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior.

Analyses of SAM emphasize loss landscape geometry, relating its behavior to curvature regulation and movement toward flatter regions (Wen et al., 2023b; Bartlett et al., 2023; Agarwala and Dauphin, 2023). However, final solution sharpness does not consistently account for SAM’s generalization behavior (Vani et al., 2024). Motivated by these geometric accounts, we first test simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue. In our preliminary experiments, neither reproduces SAM’s validation behavior, as reported in Appendix D. This motivates us to examine perturbation construction more directly. Minibatch stochastic gradient noise within SAM perturbations can play an important role in generalization (Li et al., 2024b). Random parameter perturbations provide only marginal improvements in some settings (Andriushchenko and Flammarion, 2022), whereas carefully constructed random weight perturbations can achieve strong generalization performance (Li et al., 2024a). The allocation of SAM perturbations across model layers can also affect optimization (Haas et al., 2024). These studies analyze or modify perturbations within the training trajectory being optimized. Our work takes a complementary diagnostic perspective by examining which information remains useful when local statistics of recorded SAM perturbations are transferred to an independent trajectory.

We record perturbations from reference SAM trajectories and summarize them using elementwise means and standard deviations over local training windows. During independent SGD training, we sample new perturbations from these summaries and apply them during gradient evaluation, a procedure we call statistical replay. This discards the exact recorded directions and their coupling to the source trajectory. We examine two variants: pure statistical replay uses only the recorded summaries, whereas mixed statistical replay supplements their elementwise variation with an isotropic Gaussian component. To determine whether the effect of mixed replay requires the recorded statistics, we also compare it with pure isotropic perturbations. We vary the source and temporal assignment of the recorded statistics and the layers receiving the perturbations. Replay examines what remains useful outside SAM, but it does not determine whether an arbitrary direction is sufficient within the original SAM update. We therefore include a complementary control that substitutes an equal radius random direction while leaving the remaining procedure unchanged. These interventions are intended as preliminary diagnostics rather than proposed replacements or a complete explanation of SAM.

papers.title: Reflection Is Not Always Worth It: Budgeted Reflection Allocation for Recommendation Agents
papers.abstract:
This work aims to make recommendation agents more efficient by reducing unnecessary LLM reflection while preserving full-catalog ranking and inference reranking. Since BRAVE changes only how training-time reflection is allocated, it does not introduce new user data requirements or additional LLM exposure beyond the base agent protocol. The main potential risk is that a poorly calibrated allocator may assign less reflection to users whose preferences are sparse, niche, or under-represented, which could weaken personalization for those users or indirectly affect item exposure.
  This risk can be mitigated through deployment-time auditing and conservative allocation design. In practice, reflection budgets should be evaluated not only by aggregate Recall or NDCG, but also across user-history lengths, item popularity groups, and application-relevant cohorts when such analysis is permitted. The allocator should rely on task-side ranking evidence rather than sensitive attributes, and fallback policies can reserve a small portion of the budget for random or fairness-aware coverage when subgroup robustness is important. Privacy risks can be controlled with the same protections required by the base recommendation agent: minimizing user text sent to the LLM controller, anonymizing user identifiers, retaining only necessary interaction evidence, and applying standard access-control and logging policies. Overall, BRAVE is designed as a cost-aware allocation layer, and its ethical deployment depends on validating that the saved computation does not come at the expense of vulnerable users or responsible exposure.

Large language models (LLMs) have become an appealing interface for recommender systems because they can reason over user histories, item text, and intermediate ranking evidence (Bao et al., 2023; Geng et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026a). Yet direct LLM recommendation is still poorly matched to full-ranking scenarios: LLMs may hallucinate non-existent item IDs, struggle with large catalogs, and incur substantial latency when asked to reason over many candidates (Ji et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2025). A recent line of work therefore casts the LLM as an agent that orchestrates conventional recommenders as external modules (Zhao et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026a), echoing the broader shift from passive generation to language agents that call external modules and APIs (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024). In this setting, recommender tools provide valid full-catalog rankings, and the LLM reasons over their exposed evidence.

This architecture raises a question that classical recommendation rarely needs to ask: how should reflection be allocated? Existing recommendation agents mainly study prompts, memories, and recommender-tool interfaces, and typically apply reflection to every sampled user once reflection is deemed useful. The policy is simple, but the value of reflection is not uniform. Recent LLM routing and cascade studies make a similar point at the system level: expensive LLM computation should be invoked selectively when cost and quality must be balanced (Chen et al., 2023; Yue et al., 2024a). In recommendation agents, some users have sharp and mutually consistent recommender-tool rankings, so the mixture over recommenders is nearly determined before LLM feedback. Others have flat score margins or conflicting recommender evidence, where a small change in personalized tool-mixture memory can move relevant items near the top of the list. Treating both groups identically conflates reflection capability with reflection allocation. The distinction matters because LLM judgments are useful but noisy: unnecessary updates can consume calls and perturb reliable mixture memories, especially when LLM evaluators exhibit order or self-evaluation biases (Wang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024).

We instantiate this idea as BRAVE, short for Budgeted Reflection Allocation via Value Estimation. Before invoking the LLM, BRAVE estimates which users are likely to benefit from reflection and allocates the limited budget to those users. The estimator is gated: margin-based ranking fragility is the primary signal, while cross-tool disagreement is admitted only when the current ranking is sufficiently fragile. This requires no additional model training and no extra LLM calls. BRAVE is not a new recommender backbone or reflection prompt; it decides when the existing reflection operation should be spent. The recommender tools still rank the whole catalog, and inference-time reranking remains unchanged, isolating the paper’s central claim that reflection should be allocated rather than automatically spent.

The design also clarifies a common intuition about uncertainty. Cross-tool disagreement sounds like a natural reason to reflect: if recommender tools disagree, the LLM should decide which recommender to trust. This intuition is related to classic query-by-committee active learning, where committee disagreement identifies informative examples (Seung et al., 1992). In recommendation agents, however, disagreement is not always value. It may indicate a recoverable conflict where one recommender exposes the relevant neighborhood, or it may indicate that all recommenders are locally unreliable. In the latter case, reflection spends calls reallocating weight among weak alternatives. We therefore distinguish ranking fragility, which measures whether a memory update can change the decision, from cross-tool disagreement, which measures whether recommender tools produce different evidence. BRAVE operationalizes this distinction with a gate: margin uncertainty first identifies users near a ranking decision boundary (Tong and Koller, 2001), and disagreement is then used only as a conditional secondary signal.

Across datasets and reflection budgets, BRAVE preserves the accuracy benefits of uniform reflection while using fewer LLM calls, and its strongest budget setting improves top-ranked quality over a full-reflection agent baseline. We also find that disagreement is useful only when conditioned on ranking fragility. The broader message is that recommendation agents should optimize not only how they reflect, but also when reflection is warranted and which uncertainty signals should control that decision.

papers.title: Take a Step Back: A Dual-Granularity Raw Feature Empowered Intermediate Fusion Graph Convolutional Network for Multimodal Recommendation
papers.abstract: Although multimodal recommendations have shown the ability to learn user preferences and item properties by leveraging explicit multimodal information, they remain constrained by two critical limitations: low-quality representation learning and modality fusion. For the former, existing solutions primarily focus on multi-granularity representation learning; however, we argue that training such representations is difficult due to the inherent data sparsity problem in recommendation scenarios. For the latter, existing solutions often rely on contrastive learning to align representations of different modalities to facilitate modality fusion, yet alignment-only objectives may over-compress valuable modality-specific information. To this end, we suggest \underline{``Take a Step Back"} and propose a \textbf{D}ual-granularity raw feature empowered \textbf{I}ntermediate fusion \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}onvolutional \textbf{N}etwork (\textbf{DIGCN}) for multimodal recommendation. DIGCN leverages the multimodal understanding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct dual-granularity raw features directly. Furthermore, DIGCN introduces an intermediate fusion graph convolutional network equipped with dynamic cross-modality weight correction, designed to capture cross-modality signals and achieve effective modality fusion. Comprehensive experiments on four real-world datasets validate that DIGCN consistently outperforms a variety of strong baselines. Additional analyses confirm its superiority under varying levels of data sparsity and cold-start scenarios. Notably, DIGCN demonstrates high extensibility, capable of further benefiting from additional contrastive learning-based alignment tasks.

papers.intro:
The proliferation of online information has created an overload of content, making effective recommender systems critical to navigating this complexity (Xu et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025c). Traditional recommender systems predominantly infer user preference through historical interaction data (He et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024b; Xu et al., 2025h). However, their performance is fundamentally limited by the data sparsity problem, as inferring comprehensive user and item profiles from sparse interactions remains a significant challenge. To mitigate this limitation, recent works have increasingly turned to multimodal recommender systems, leveraging rich auxiliary data from explicitly multimodal information to enrich representations and alleviate data sparsity problem (Xu et al., 2025f; Jiang et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2025b).

Building upon multimodal data, existing multimodal recommender systems nevertheless face two persistent bottlenecks (Zhou et al., 2023a): low-quality representation learning and modality fusion. For representation learning, current solutions to multi-granularity representation learning struggle to acquire sufficiently nuanced and discriminative features, primarily due to the intrinsic data sparsity in recommendation scenarios, which provides inadequate supervisory signal for training such complex representations (Chen et al., 2025b; Ren et al., 2025). For modality fusion, current fusion strategies often rely on contrastive learning to align representations across modalities (Xu et al., 2025c; Wei et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025g). While promoting consistency, alignment-only objectives may over-compress modality-specific information by minimizing inter-modal distance, thereby weakening unique, discriminative features that are crucial for recommendation. These two limitations, ineffective representation learning and information loss during fusion, work together to slow down further progress of multimodal recommendations. Let us Take a Step Back! We therefore rethink these two limitations from a foundational perspective. First, if multi-granularity representation learning increases training difficulty, could we take a step back to construct multi-granularity raw features before training phase, thereby obtaining the desired representations directly? The powerful multimodal understanding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a feasible and potent means to realize this goal (Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Second, given that alignment-only multimodal objectives may weaken modality-specific information, could we take a step back to capture cross-modality signals before obtaining final representations via late fusion11 1 According to a recent survey (Xu et al., 2025i), most advanced works adopt late fusion, integrating modalities after GCN.? We use the message-passing stages in Graph Convolution Networks (GCNs) to realize this goal.

papers.title: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging
papers.abstract: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.

papers.title: Klein four slices of the representation suspensions of $H\underline{\mathbb{F}_2}$
papers.abstract: We study the regular slice filtration of representation spheres $S^V\wedge H\underline{M}$. For every finite group $G$, we locate all slices in an explicit interval $[n(V),k(V)]$ and show that both endpoints occur. We introduce a \emph{defect vector} to measure a slice's failure. For the Klein four-group with $\underline{\mathbb F}_2$-coefficients, a balanced defect allows us to move $S^V\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$ by certain $RO(G)$-graded cohomology classes to its $\dim V$-slice, which is again a representation sphere, while an odd defect obstructs any spherical slice. As an application, we obtain closed formulas for the bottom slice of $\Sigma^nH\underline{\mathbb{F}}_2$ for every $n$, recovering the computation of Guillou and Yarnall by a different method. Along the way, we determine the complete slice tower of $S^{\infty\alpha_i}\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$ and consequently, the partial tower for $S^{n\alpha_i}\wedge H\underline{\mathbb F}_2$.

papers.title: Model-Driven Stellar Spectroscopy with the Total Differential Spectral Model (TDSM): Framework and Its Application to 11 Million LAMOST Low-Resolution Spectra
papers.abstract: Deriving stellar astrophysical parameters from large-scale spectroscopic surveys requires accurate modeling of spectra across a wide wavelength coverage and a broad range of stellar parameter space, which remains a great challenge. In this work, we present \texttt{TDSM}, a physically motivated neural network architecture that self-consistently emulates both the flux and its first-order derivative of the ab initio stellar spectra. The method enables accurate and precise emulation of Kurucz synthetic spectra with severely blended features at $R \simeq 2000$ in a high-dimensional parameter space, achieving a typical pixel-wise flux precision of 0.05\% in the wavelength range $3700<\lambda<9000${\AA} over the parameter range of $3000 < T_{\rm eff} < 45,000$~K, $-1 < \log g < 5$, and $-4.0 < \mathrm{[Fe/H]} < 0.5$. The model is applied to LAMOST DR10 to derive stellar parameters for 11 million spectra spanning the full model parameter range. We conduct detailed refinement and calibration efforts to mitigate systematic errors, which are revealed to be significant and complex due to imperfections in the ab initio model atmosphere. The resultant catalog provides eight stellar labels -- $T_{\rm eff}$, $\log g$, $v_{\rm mic}$, [Fe/H], [$\alpha$/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Mg/Fe] -- for 8 million unique stars (11 million spectra including repeat observations) across the full parameter space. This adds a valuable dataset for studies of Galactic structure and archaeology, stellar populations, and related areas of astrophysics.

papers.title: Long-Term Radio Evolution of the Type Ia Supernova SN 2020eyj: Evidence for a Dense Helium-rich Circumstellar Shell
papers.abstract: The nature of progenitor systems of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and their explosion mechanism remain controversial. Radio observations provide a powerful probe of the interaction between SN ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM), offering important constraints on the mass-loss histories of their progenitor systems. We present extensive Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) observations of SN 2020eyj at 1.5-10 GHz, tracing its radio emission to approximately 1300 days after discovery and revealing, for the first time, the long-term radio evolution of an SN Ia. The radio light curves of SN 2020eyj exhibit a relatively flat evolution at early epochs, followed by a gradual long-term decline, while its radio spectra show a power-law behavior with a low-frequency turnover. These characteristics appear to be consistent with synchrotron emission associated with shock interaction. Modeling the radio light curves favors a thick circumstellar shell with an inferred mass of approximately 0.3-0.4 solar masses over the simple wind-like configurations. Combined with the optical spectral signatures of SN 2020eyj, our radio observations provide strong evidence for substantial helium-rich mass loss from the progenitor system prior to explosion. The inferred CSM properties pose significant challenges to existing SN Ia progenitor models, although the ejection of a common envelope shortly before explosion may offer a plausible explanation.

papers.title: Validation of Ariel candidates orbiting K-M stars
papers.abstract: One of the key goals of planetary population studies is to achieve broad coverage of the parameter space, which is not yet fully represented by confirmed planets. This limitation can be mitigated by including planets that have been statistically validated through a vetting procedure, even if they are not fully confirmed. In preparation for the Ariel mission, a Mission Candidate Sample has been assembled, comprising both confirmed planets and several unvalidated candidates. In this context, we apply a vetting analysis to a selected subsample of these candidates. Our methodology is based on the TRICERATOPS tool, aimed at confirming the presence of transiting planets or ruling out false-positive scenarios. We applied TRICERATOPS to a sample of 318 targets drawn from the last three Ariel TESS Planet Candidates catalogues. The analysis includes evaluation of statistical probabilities, as well as checks on stellar binarity indicators such as the Renormalized Unit Weight Error (RUWE) and the IPD_frac_multi_peak values from Gaia Data Release 3. Our analysis validated 56 candidates as planets, identified 29 false positives, and classified 35 as likely planets. These results are intended to support the Ariel mission by providing a probabilistic priority ranking to guide follow-up observations and optimise targets for atmospheric characterisation studies.

papers.title: Orbital decomposition and evolution of LEGA-C-like galaxies in IllustrisTNG from z = 1 to z = 0
papers.abstract: Stellar orbits encode the dynamical history of galaxies and provide a physically motivated link between galaxy structures and assembly processes. Although orbit-based decompositions are well established in the Local Universe, their evolution across cosmic time, especially at higher redshifts, remains poorly explored. We investigate the orbital structure of \texttt{LEGA-C-like} galaxies in the \texttt{TNG100} simulation from $z=1$ to $z=0$ to identify how stellar mass, star formation activity, environment, merger history, gas content, and ex situ stellar mass growth shape their orbital transformation. We decomposed the stellar orbital structure of simulated galaxies into cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating (CR) components using time-averaged orbital circularities. We find a strong mass dependence of orbital structure at $z=0$ as well as at $z=1$. Galaxies below $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)\sim11.2$ have a combined warm and cold orbital fraction of $\sim70\%$, whereas more massive systems have a hot-orbit fraction of $\sim60\%$. These trends are consistent with assembly pathways driven predominantly by wet and dry major mergers, respectively. Tracking the same galaxies to $z=0$ reveals a systematic, but mass-dependent, evolution toward lower rotational support: At both low and high stellar masses, the hot-orbit fraction increases, whereas the relative change is greater in low-mass galaxies. The survival of cold structure depends strongly on the star formation state at $z=1$; star-forming progenitors retain substantially larger cold fractions than the quiescent progenitors. At both redshifts, the orbital fractions show a rise (decline) in hot and CR (cold and warm) orbits with the ex situ stellar mass fraction at a fixed stellar mass. These results provide the first evolutionary framework for interpreting orbit-based decompositions of galaxies at the \texttt{LEGA-C} epoch.

papers.title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

papers.title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
papers.abstract: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

papers.title: A COMPASS to the Galaxy: Joint nucleosynthetic yield set comparison and parameter inference in Galactic chemical evolution
papers.abstract: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $\alpha_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $\alpha_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

papers.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

papers.title: Unexpected Plateau: The Constant $ \rm \log \epsilon (Th/Eu)$ Ratio of Actinide-Boost Stars
papers.abstract: The astrophysical site of the rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) is still one of the major open questions in astronomy. A key mystery is the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio found in the so called actinide-boost stars, with $ \rm \log \epsilon (Th/Eu)>-0.35$. Here we present the largest sample of Th measurements in stars formed in an external galaxy, Gaia Sausage Enceladus. From this sample, we present the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars discovered to date, $\rm -1.6<[Fe/H]<-1.1$. In addition, we measured Th in a comparison sample of Milky Way stars formed in situ, and compiled Th measurements from the literature which do not account for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects. After applying NLTE corrections to the combined sample, a bimodality in the $\rm\log\epsilon (Th/Eu)$ ratio is revealed. Unexpectedly, actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow $(\sigma=0.02)$ plateau of $\rm \log\epsilon(Th/Eu)=-0.2$, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most (if not all) of the actinide-boost stars in our sample originate from outside the Milky Way. Chemical evolution models show that such a plateau can arise, even at [Fe/H] = $-$1, when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system. Combined with other evidence, our results suggest that mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

papers.title: How did data sharing evolve in the decade since the FAIR Principles?
papers.abstract: A decade after the publication of the FAIR Guiding Principles, what have we learned about data sharing, and what do data availability statements (DAS) and other materials accrued over that period tell us about how data-sharing practices, attitudes, and infrastructures evolved? Here, we present a large-scale longitudinal analysis of over 6.8 million biomedical articles from the PMC Open Access Subset, spanning 2011 to 2025. Using an automated pipeline, we extracted and classified DAS, repository links, accession numbers, and supplementary materials, assigning each article a data-sharing score and independently FAIR-assessing a subset of cited dataset URLs. We find that explicit DAS adoption rose from ~2% in 2011 to 68% in 2025, while "available on request" statements grew in parallel from near zero to over 19%. The corpus growth amplifies both patterns: articles with a DAS containing an explicit repository mention rose from 132 in 2011 to 94,697 in 2025, while "available on request" articles rose from 77 to 173,474 over this span. Structural biology and genomics consistently achieved the highest data-sharing scores, while clinical research and public health ranked lowest. Gold Open Access journals showed a small advantage over subscription journals, while Diamond Open Access journals outperformed both. Internationally collaborative articles scored higher than domestic ones. A gender gap emerged: female first-authored articles' scores declined more than male first-authored ones. The analysis further covered additional dimensions, from compliance with funder/journal mandates and JATS XML tagging standards to computational reproducibility signals and the co-occurrence of DAS with ethics statements. A decade on, the gap between declaring data availability and actually sharing machine-readable, reusable data persists across fields, infrastructures and demographics.

papers.title: Overview of the Plagiarism Detection Task at PAN 2026
papers.abstract: The generative plagiarism detection task at PAN 2026 aims at retrieving the original scientific sources for given automatically generated textual plagiarism. We created two novel datasets of synthetically generated plagiarism following the premise of a malicious actor trying to generate papers with minimal effort while evading detection of undisclosed re-use. We utilized four widely available LLMs: GPT-OSS 120B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 3.5 27B FP8, and DeepSeek-R1 Distill Llama 8B. In this task overview paper, we outline the creation of this dataset and summarize and compare the results of all participants with three baselines. For this year's task, we received 26 submissions from six teams that significantly outperformed our baselines.
