papers.title: Global Lanczos with stochastic error correction for trace estimation of matrix functions
papers.abstract: We propose a new method for computing the trace of a matrix function $f(A)$, where $A$ is a large, sparse, symmetric matrix. Our approach combines a deterministic global Lanczos approximation with a stochastic correction of its error. Starting the global Lanczos process with the identity matrix yields a direct approximation of the trace through a small tridiagonal matrix. The resulting basis matrices are polynomials in $A$, allowing the process to be implemented using sparse matrix-matrix multiplications when low-degree polynomials in $A$ have moderate fill-in. However, increased fill-in may limit the number of iterations that can be performed efficiently. To address this limitation, we derive an exact representation of the global Lanczos error as the trace of a matrix function and apply a stochastic estimator to the remainder. Even a moderately accurate estimate can substantially improve the accuracy, combining the deterministic method with the rapid initial convergence of stochastic trace estimators. We discuss error bounds and variance reduction, and present numerical experiments that compare the resulting method with existing ones.

papers.title: Adaptive Precision Cholesky with Error Guarantees
papers.abstract: Modern accelerators increasingly support low-precision formats such as 8-bit floats and integers to speed up machine learning. We show that a Cholesky factorization in which both GEMM and TRSM are implemented using the fixed-point Ozaki 1 scheme satisfies the same backward error bounds as the standard floating-point Cholesky factorization, and that the same holds for a Cholesky factorization computed using a low-precision MicroScaled GEMM. We then use our error analyses to construct an adaptive precision Cholesky factorization that exploits low-precision formats while respecting a prescribed element-wise error bound, as long as the factorization succeeds. We test it in two settings. First, we use it to choose the number of Ozaki 1 slices at each iteration, with SYRK/GEMM and TRSM emulated in INT8 fixed-point arithmetic to attain double-precision accuracy. Second, we use it to build a low-precision Cholesky preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method (PCG), in which SYRK/GEMM take low-precision inputs and accumulate in high precision, with the input format selected adaptively for each panel; if the factorization breaks down, diagonal perturbation still yields a valid preconditioner, at the cost of the error bound guarantees. On an NVIDIA GH200, the adaptive Ozaki 1-based factorization is up to 29% faster than a right-looking Cholesky using a fixed slice count of 7, and up to 69% faster than one using cuBLAS' Automatic Dynamic Precision (ADP), while maintaining the same error guarantees. For PCG, FP8 factorizations with diagonal perturbation form effective preconditioners on the 13 tested SuiteSparse matrices, reducing the number of PCG iterations by up to $12\times$ over CG on the same matrix diagonally scaled by powers of two. For synthetic matrices with arithmetic spectra, and geometric spectra with $\kappa \le 10^4$, FP8 preconditioners also reduce the number of CG iterations.

papers.title: Oxygens breathe, electrons jump
papers.abstract: Electronic transport in polyanionic battery cathodes proceeds through small-polaron hopping between transition-metal sites and is commonly assumed to be tightly coupled to the motion of charge-compensating mobile ions. Using olivine Li$_x$MnPO$_4$ as a prototypical platform, we use first-principles molecular dynamics with extended Hubbard functionals to follow, in real time and at finite temperature, the adiabatic evolution of Mn oxidation states and atomic sublattices. We find that polaron hopping and cation migration are dynamically decoupled: Mn$^{2+}$/Mn$^{3+}$ valence exchanges occur frequently while the intercalated ions remain confined to their sites, and hopping is gated by the local oxygen framework. Freezing the six oxygen atoms of an individual MnO$_6$ octahedron excludes that site from the hopping network, while increasing the fictitious oxygen mass slows down electronic transport. Each valence exchange coincides with a concerted breathing of the donor and acceptor octahedra ($\Delta V \simeq 2$ $\r{A}^3$), with their volume asymmetry crossing zero at the transition, consistent with the Holstein-Marcus coincidence condition. The hopping rate yields an activation energy of $E_a = 0.20 \pm 0.03$ eV, closely matching the elastic energy scale of the two coordination cages ($\lambda_V/4 \approx 0.20$ eV). These results identify the oxygen coordination cage, not the mobile cation sublattice, as the dynamical gate for small-polaron transport: a site can accept the electron only if its cage can breathe, and the barrier is governed by cage elasticity. Selective constraints and mass scaling applied to first-principles dynamics provide a general route to link electronic and lattice degrees of freedom in redox-active materials, opening the door to framework engineering in intercalation and mixed ionic-electronic conductors.

papers.title: A High-Resolution TOA Estimation Algorithm Based on Compressed Sensing for Coherent Multi-Band Signals
papers.abstract: High-resolution time-of-arrival (ToA) estimation is crucial for accurate ranging and localization in future wireless networks. While multi-band operation can synthesize a large virtual bandwidth by probing several separated subbands, the resulting non-contiguous frequency layout induces pronounced sidelobes and dense local maxima in the delay response, making reliable ToA estimation challenging. This paper studies coherent multi-band ToA estimation from a single multi-band channel state information (CSI) snapshot. We derive a multiband least-squares formulation and analyze its point-spread function (PSF) and Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) to characterize the effects of the subband layout on delay accuracy and sidelobe ambiguity. Building on this analysis, we propose a low complexity two-stage particle swarm optimization estimator and incorporate it into orthogonal matching pursuit with a RELAX-type cyclic refinement procedure for multipath delay estimation, mitigating basis mismatch and improving robustness to the dense local maxima induced by non-contiguous multi-band layouts. Numerical results are consistent with the PSF and CRB analyses and show that the proposed framework approaches the CRB in the single-path setting and achieves accurate multipath delay estimation with low computational complexity. Real channel measurements further validate the predicted impact of different subband layouts on delay-estimation performance.

papers.title: Set-based State Estimation for Unknown Dynamical Systems from Noisy Output Data with Probabilistic Guarantees
papers.abstract: We develop a methodology for set-based state estimation from noisy input-output trajectories, without a predefined model structure for the unknown state dynamics or access to training state measurements. We derive a bound on the state set diameter that depends on the sensor map and leverage it as a surrogate to formulate a tractable linear program balancing state set tightness against output trajectory coverage. Combining this certificate with deterministic or probabilistically certified measurement noise sets and leveraging the results from scenario optimization with relaxation, we provide joint a posteriori probabilistic guarantees for state inclusion and state set diameter. Numerical simulations corroborate our developed theoretical guarantees.

papers.title: Geomagnetic Q-Response Inversion as a Calder\'on-Type Inverse Boundary Value Problem
papers.abstract: Whether electrical conductivity can be uniquely determined from magnetic measurements alone is a fundamental question in geomagnetic induction sounding. For a spherical conductor in the magnetoquasistatic model, we establish an equivalence between the complete Q-response and a restricted magnetic boundary operator, connecting geomagnetic induction to Calderon-type inverse boundary value theory. For axisymmetric conductivities, we derive exact representations of the zero-frequency zonal response derivatives as conductivity-weighted spatial moments. These formulas give an explicit interpretation of individual response derivatives, and completeness of the moment family yields conductivity uniqueness. For layered axisymmetric models with known shell interfaces and piecewise-constant radial dependence, we further establish uniqueness at a single nonzero frequency. Finite-dimensional subclasses also admit uniqueness and stability estimates from finitely many response coefficients at sufficiently low nonzero frequencies. These results identify complementary mechanisms for conductivity recovery from magnetic-only observations, while uniqueness for general three-dimensional scalar conductivities from ideal magnetic-only Q-response data remains unresolved.

papers.title: In-context learning predicts clinical endpoints from bulk transcriptomes across diseases and platforms
papers.abstract: Bulk transcriptomes carry information on diagnosis, treatment response and survival, but clinical cohorts are small, and each gets a model of its own that often fails in the next cohort. Here we present PRTS, a 220-million-parameter model that reads a labelled cohort as context and predicts binary, multiclass, continuous or survival endpoints for new samples from whole transcriptomes, without per-cohort training. PRTS was pretrained on 6.0 million tasks generated from public RNA-seq profiles. On 175 held-out tasks and 44 tasks from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), it had the highest mean predictive accuracy, narrowly ahead of TabPFN v3.5, the strongest pre-specified comparator. The lead came from within-cohort prediction and, on TCGA, mainly from survival tasks; across cohorts and at unseen sites, PRTS was level with the strongest tabular models while running more than twice as fast as TabPFN v3.5. The same weights transfer labels to new cohorts from public references, forecast accuracy from pilots, flag suspect labels and attribute predictions to genes. We release the prior, the pretraining code and the model with its weights, together with RealBulk, a collection of 1,160 curated public cohorts, and its benchmark.

papers.title: Cleanly-DINO: Efficiently Learning Visual Task Spaces for Robotics
papers.abstract: Learning manipulation tasks from few demonstrations requires abstractions that capture the changes relevant to task completion, such as object poses in rigid-body manipulation. However, tasks such as cleaning are defined by changes in visual state rather than object pose, making the choice of task representation less clear. In this work, we propose Cleanly-DINO to learn visual task spaces from few demonstrations. Given a mask of a task-relevant region and frozen ViT features, Cleanly-DINO fits a projection to isolate a task space and fit a progression metric to it. We train the model on diverse cleaning examples and evaluate its ability to localize incomplete task regions and transfer across visual domains. We also study its utility for robot learning by using it as an observation encoder and reward signal in a reinforcement learning setting. Finally, we deploy our fitted model within a real-world robotic wiping pipeline to evaluate its use in guiding task execution.

authors.name: Jose Arce y de la Borbolla

papers.title: Radiation Effects on Breakdown Voltage and Quenching Resistance in SiPMs
papers.abstract: This study investigates the suitability of the Hamamatsu S13360 series as replacement photodetectors for the RICH upgrade II detector. I-V curves enabled a statistical analysis of breakdown voltage and quenching resistance before and after irradiation, quantifying the dependance of damage on neutron fluence and the mitigation effect of cooling. The results show that breakdown voltage degradation increases with fluence and becomes statistically significant only at high irradiation levels. Quenching resistance, by contrast, shows only a limited increase except at 6 x 10^13 neq/cm2, where substantial degradation appears. Both parameters exhibit a clear reduction in radiation-damage impact when operated at cryogenic temperatures.

papers.title: Stochastic control representations for extremal solutions of HJB Dirichlet problems with measurable coefficients
papers.abstract: We study stochastic control problems for uniformly elliptic controlled diffusions on bounded domains whose coefficients are merely measurable in the state variable and whose drift is dominated by an $L_d$-function. The associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) Dirichlet problems may have more than one $L_p$-viscosity solution, so that the equation alone does not determine the value function. We show that the control problem selects the minimal solution: for all $p$ in a range $(d_0,d)$ determined by the spatial dimension, the ellipticity constant and the drift bound, the value function is the minimal $L_p$-viscosity supersolution of the HJB Dirichlet problem. In particular, every continuous $L_p$-viscosity supersolution bounds the optimal cost from above, which yields a one-sided verification theorem without regularity assumptions. We further prove the existence of optimal relaxed control rules for running costs dominated by an $L_p$-function, and the lower semicontinuity of the value function under perturbations of the coefficients. An example shows that upper semicontinuity may fail even when the coefficients are Lipschitz continuous in the control variable and the approximating coefficients are smooth, so that regularization may overestimate the optimal cost. The proof approximates arbitrary supersolutions from below by Sobolev supersolutions of HJB equations whose coefficients are modified only on sets of vanishing measure, and passes to the limit by means of Krylov estimates and martingale problem techniques.

papers.title: Log Hodge-de Rham degeneration beyond the toroidal case
papers.abstract:
Let $\phi\colon X \to S$ be a flat and proper one-parameter degeneration of algebraic varieties with a single degenerate fiber $X_0$. If $\phi\colon (X|X_0) \to (S|0)$ is log smooth and saturated, the log Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence is known to degenerate at the page $E_1$. Adding to that some further well-known related properties, we say that the log de Rham complex $\Omega^{\bullet,\mathrm{log}}_{X/S}$ is cohomologically flat as a filtered complex, short cffc. Furthermore, if $\phi\colon (X|X_0) \to (S|0)$ has only toroidal log singularities, it is known that the reflexive log de Rham complex $\mathcal{W}^\bullet_{X/S}$ is cffc. A major motivation to study this property is that in the Calabi-Yau case, $\mathcal{W}^\bullet_{X/S}$ being cffc implies that a certain logarithmic deformation functor for $\phi_0\colon X_0^\partial \to S_0^\dagger$ is unobstructed.
  In this article, we develop a computational criterion to determine, under very mild assumptions on $\phi\colon X \to S$, whether the reflexive log de Rham complex $\mathcal{W}^\bullet_{X/S}$ is cffc. Applying this criterion, we found many explicit examples of degenerations of surfaces where $\mathcal{W}^\bullet_{X/S}$ is cffc, even though the log singularities are worse than toroidal. We did not find any new examples of degenerations of threefolds such that $\mathcal{W}^\bullet_{X/S}$ is cffc.

papers.title: M-CROSS: A Multisensor Simulation Dataset for SLAM across Water--Land Transitions
papers.abstract: Water--land cross-domain robots require continuous localization across land, transition and underwater phases, where sensor characteristics and availability change abruptly. Existing datasets and conventional metrics are not designed to capture transition-induced degradation and failures. We present \textbf{M-CROSS}, to the best of our knowledge, the first multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for SLAM across continuous water--land transitions. It provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth measurements; 6DoF pose ground truth; sensor-wise medium-state annotations; and medium-dependent sensor degradation models. We establish a transition-aware protocol comprising the Trajectory Completion Rate (TCR), Piecewise Absolute Pose Error (PW-APE), Transition End Error (TEE), and Transition Survival Period (TSP), which measure trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and localization survival under prolonged partial immersion, respectively. Experiments with 6 representative SLAM systems show that existing methods fail to maintain both localization accuracy and trajectory continuity across the full set of water--land transitions, exhibiting transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures. M-CROSS is publicly available https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCross-Dataset

authors.name: Shaoqiang Qiu
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Rotation-Invariant Machine Learning for Highly Symmetric Molecular Configurations
papers.abstract: Atomistic machine learning can approximate expensive quantum mechanical calculations at a fraction of their computational cost, but accuracy depends strongly on how the three-dimensional atomic environments are represented. Invariant representations enable fast computation but can fail to distinguish geometrically distinct configurations, especially in highly symmetric environments. We introduce a lightweight benchmark to evaluate expressivity on $n$-fold symmetric configurations, and use it to expose degeneracies in both invariant and equivariant architectures. Guided by these results, we construct a new invariant basis for HIP-HOP which resolves most of the identified failures. On a methane simulation dataset, the extended basis achieves the lowest error among the HIP-HOP variants and has similar accuracy to EquiformerV3 while running $3.2\times$ faster at inference. These results show that carefully constructed invariant representations can mitigate key expressivity limitations while balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

authors.name: Alice Elisabeth Anastasia Allen
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research

papers.title: Continuous superradiant lasing on a narrow optical transition
papers.abstract: Lasers with ultrastable frequency are at the foundation of optical clocks, which enable precision tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale. Such lasers inherit their frequency stability from the length stability of a sophisticated optical resonator, which is hard to maintain outside a well-controlled laboratory environment and limited by thermal and technical noise. Superradiant lasers promise to overcome these limitations by storing their coherence in the atoms making up the laser's gain medium. Superradiant lasing has been demonstrated on narrow optical atomic transitions with pulsed and quasi-continuous operation. However, atom loss has prevented truly continuous operation, which severely limits their suitability for clocks. Here we demonstrate a superradiant laser on a narrow optical transition in $^{88}$Sr that operates truly continuously. We sustain emission for more than eight hours and measure a linewidth of 320(40) Hz, more than 20 times below the natural linewidth. The emission frequency remains anchored to the atomic transition, making the laser itself an atomic frequency reference. Our results provide a route towards a laser that reaches short-term frequency stability comparable to that of the best resonator-stabilized lasers. Furthermore, truly continuous operation gives us access to physics beyond the transient regime, enabling the exploration of robust nonequilibrium steady states and sustained coherent collective dynamics.

authors.name: Ying Cui
authors.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

papers.title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
papers.abstract: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and cutting DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.

papers.title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
papers.abstract: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

papers.title: Reference Replay for Excitation Injection and Subsequent Exponential Convergence under Concurrent Learning Adaptive Control
papers.abstract: Concurrent learning (CL) guarantees precise identification of unknown parameters---if data with finite excitation (FE) happens to be collected online. To improve the reliability of CL, this work establishes a mechanism allowing FE-occurrence to be verified a priori: We propose replaying a given training segment in the reference until data with finite excitation is collected online. Provided the training segment fulfills a certain off-line excitation test, FE then occurs in unknown, but finite time. Moreover, we provide an upper bound on the time-to-FE. Even though this bound involves a dependency on the unknown initial Lyapunov-function value, its structure shows that FE occurs in arbitrarily early replay cycles when increasing the control gain; which may motivate employing a high-gain strategy. The theoretical findings are verified on an academic simulation example.

papers.title: EndoComparer: Comparative Surgical Video Question Answering with Pseudo-Siamese Visual Adaptation and Perceive-then-Compare Reasoning
papers.abstract: Purpose: Surgical training benefits from explicit comparison between cases: in patient condition, in technique and in skill proficiency. Surgical vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising and flexible interface for this purpose. Yet current VLMs typically see one video at a time, and they often fall short when asked to compare videos. Methods: We propose EndoComparer, a VLM for comparative surgical video question answering with two components. (a) A Pseudo-Siamese Visual LoRA (PSVL) gives each video slot its own low-rank adapter over a shared frozen vision encoder, separating the two videos in the visual pathway at the cost of a single encoder pass. (b) A Perceive-then-Compare chain of thought (PtC-CoT) trains the model to first state what each video shows, then derive the answer from these statements. We further curate EndoDiffVQA, a benchmark of nearly 11K multiple-choice questions on video-pair over cholecystectomy and gastric bypass procedures, covering anatomy, tool, action and skill. Results: EndoComparer outperforms strong generalist and surgical VLMs on detecting and specifying difference between videos. Ablations show that two proposed components contribute complimentarily, and the model remains more robust under a video-swap control that exposes confusion between the two videos. Conclusion: Providing a dedicated visual reasoning path through PSVL and PtC-CoT makes cross-case comparison of surgical videos more robust for VLMs. EndoDiffVQA and EndoComparer provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for this task. Project page: https://camma-public.github.io/endocomparer

papers.title: On divisible domains of the flat affine space with parallel volume
papers.abstract: We consider a domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ divisible by a discrete subgroup $\Gamma$ of the unimodular affine group $\operatorname{SL}_d(\mathbb{R})\ltimes\mathbb{R}^d$. We prove that $\Omega=\mathbb{R}^d$ if $\Gamma$ is virtually solvable or if its linear holonomy is virtually contained in a semisimple Lie subgroup of real rank one. In particular, we establish the Kleinian Markus conjecture in both cases.

papers.title: Counterfactual Screening of Rare Secondary Overloads in Power Grids with a Stochastic Surrogate for Electromagnetic Transient Simulations
papers.abstract: Power-system operators continually ask what would happen if a component failed now. Single-phase-to-ground faults cleared by single-pole tripping and automatic reclosure usually have no lasting consequences. In rare cases, however, the transient excited during the open-phase interval drives distant lines or transformers into overload that persists after the faulted line is restored. We develop a counterfactual screening framework for these secondary overloads, combining a linear stochastic swing surrogate with cross-entropy importance sampling. The surrogate represents the open-phase corridor through an effective coupling factor and localized multiplicative noise, with both parameters learned from electromagnetic-transient (EMT) simulations rather than prescribed. Closed-form propagation of the mean and covariance permits deterministic calibration without Monte Carlo sampling. On the reduced WECC 240-bus system, a globally calibrated model substantially improves finite-time agreement with the EMT electromechanical state. The global models are calibrated at reclosure and tested on disjoint faulted lines under a longer open-phase interval. Line- and operating-state-specific models use additional reclosure data from the assessment lines and provide smaller further gains at the cost of more separate fits. The fitted coupling is lower than the phase-counting baseline, consistent with the direction anticipated by sequence-network analysis. Cross-entropy importance sampling directs computational effort toward contingencies associated with persistent overload and yields rare-event probability estimates together with a map linking initiating faults to the elements they endanger. By separating offline EMT calibration from repeated surrogate evaluation, the method supports probabilistic contingency screening and identifies where detailed high-fidelity assessment is most valuable.

papers.title: Directionality of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO experiment
papers.abstract: Electron-recoil directionality can help distinguish solar-neutrino interactions from backgrounds and, together with recoil-energy measurements and three-dimensional tracking, enable neutrino-energy spectroscopy. We study the reconstruction of the initial direction of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO optical time-projection chamber, focusing on the 50 L LIME prototype and its high-granularity scientific CMOS (sCMOS) readout. A dedicated algorithm identifies the interaction point from the asymmetry of the track light distribution and estimates the recoil direction from the early portion of the ionization trail, before multiple scattering erases most of the directional information. The method is characterized with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of electron recoils and detector response. Samples spanning 15 keV to 70 keV are used to optimize the algorithm parameters by minimizing the width of the reconstructed-minus-true projected-angle distribution. The projected angular response is modeled by two Gaussian components that account for its dependence on track inclination. The narrower component, associated with favorable projections approximately parallel to the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) plane, has a width that improves from about $20^\circ$ near 20 keV to about $12^\circ$ at 60 keV. We also quantify the fraction of events in the correctly reconstructed angular core and discuss the dominant limitations of a camera-only two-dimensional measurement.

papers.title: Ocular Recognition: Interoperability, Multi-Resolution, and Spectrum Challenges
papers.abstract:
Ocular recognition is typically developed under controlled acquisition conditions, limiting its use in semi-controlled and on-the-move scenarios. A key obstacle is the lack of representative data spanning real-world capture conditions. At a border checkpoint, for example, images may range from low-resolution visible-light periocular crops (RGB) to high-resolution near-infrared iris images (NIR). Using this heterogeneous evidence raises three questions: whether resolution-specific processing improves recognition, how to compare templates from different processing routes, and how to allocate training data across resolution specialists.
  We investigate resolution-specific processing and parameter sharing using three AdaFace-based architecture families: fixed-resolution specialists; Independent Backbones with Shared Heads (IBSH); and models with resolution-specific front-ends for 40x40, 80x80, and 160x160 inputs, followed by a shared identity trunk and embedding projection. We evaluate each architecture with route-specific training subsets and with a full-pool strategy, in which every specialist uses the complete selected training set.
  Results reveal a trade-off among same-resolution specialization, cross-resolution interoperability, and common-route re-extraction. Route-specific training produces distinct performance profiles across routes, whereas full-pool training makes route performance more uniform and primarily benefits the 160x160 route. Thus, adding training data does not improve all resolution routes equally.

authors.name: Christoph Busch
authors.institution: National Research Center for Applied Cybersecurity ATHENE

papers.title: From Viral Exposure to Engagement: A Causal Mediation Framework for Digital Platforms
papers.abstract: At Roblox, viral hits can change how exposed players engage with the viral game and with the rest of the platform. We develop a causal mediation framework to decompose the effect of viral-game playtime on subsequent player engagement into a direct effect and indirect effects through measured player interaction and discovery behaviors. The framework uses a causal DAG to state the assumed causal structure and a time-ordered design that measures covariates, exposure, mediators, and outcomes in non-overlapping time windows. Under stated identification assumptions and a model linear in the exposure and each mediator at fixed covariates, we estimate every path as a function of player covariates with cross-fitted R-learners, which use only prediction models and therefore scale to platform-size data. Averaging the fitted surfaces inherits their regularization bias, so we add a per-player bias correction before averaging (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). In simulation, the correction restored nominal coverage of 90% to 95%, against at most 39% for intervals built by averaging the surfaces. Counterintuitively, interval coverage worsened with more data on a difficult mediator-outcome path, bias shrank more slowly than the standard error, reducing corrected coverage from 93.6% to 57.3% as n increased from 2k to 200k. We applied the same design to two de-identified viral games with different lifecycle histories, comparing effects across outcome scopes, player subgroups, and a placebo window without a viral event. The results indicate that subsequent engagement is not explained by viral exposure alone, player interaction behaviors mediate 46% engagement within the viral game, whereas new game discovery mediates 52% engagement in other games. Finally, we compare the estimator with its alternatives and generalize the study design into a reusable framework for similar mediation studies across product domains.

papers.title: Few-Shot Visual Concept Extraction for Steering Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Image steering aims to provide fine-grained control over concepts in generated images, enabling targeted and continuous manipulation without broadly altering the generation process. Recent steering methods for diffusion models primarily focus on the text-conditioning space or rely on costly auxiliary training. Deviating from that, we here propose a novel steering approach that extracts visual concept directions directly from the image-side activations of Diffusion Transformers. Specifically, we showcase few-shot concept extraction in the activation space using a simple difference-of-means estimator over intermediate residuals. We observe (a) scene-level concepts such as lighting, weather, and style are distributed across image tokens, as well as (b) local concepts such as object colors, textures, materials, and facial attributes are concentrated in specific regions. Towards controlling both concepts, we introduce a new unified training-free framework that uses global difference-of-means for (a) distributed concepts and masked difference-of-means for (b) local concepts, preventing local signals from being diluted by global averaging. Notably, using only a handful of positive and negative prompt pairs, our method identifies and extracts reusable concept directions that can be injected at inference for continuous steering. Quantitatively, our method outperforms text-encoder steering and training-free activation-editing baselines, as well as is competitive with specialized editing models. Our results suggest that as concept directions can be applied at patch level, our method enables precise targeted and compositional steering, manipulating multiple concepts in the same image.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Complexity of CAQE: A Proof-Theoretic Analysis of its Core Procedure
papers.abstract: CAQE (Clausal Abstraction for Quantifier Elimination) is currently the most successful algorithmic paradigm for solving Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF) in practice, clearly dominating recent QBF competitions. While apparently being a very strong solver, not much is known about CAQE in theory. We propose a framework for formalising runs of the basic CAQE algorithm (where failed assumptions are not considered) as proofs in a proof system CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$, which we use to analyse the algorithm proof-theoretically and which provides methods for future work to separate it from optimised versions of CAQE that are used in practice. We show that one can perform strategy extraction on the CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ proof system in such a way that strategy size serves as a lower bound for basic CAQE runs. Furthermore, we introduce a measure, which we call CAQE width, which not only acts as a lower bound on CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ proofs, but -- with the number of $\exists\forall$ alternations as exponent -- as an upper bound as well. Using this analysis, we prove that Q-resolution with an NP oracle simulates CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ on QCNFs of bounded quantifier alternation. The same holds for QCDCL (Quantified Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, formalised as a proof system) on $\Sigma_3^b$ QCNFs when purely propositional CDCL steps are not counted, after a simple preprocessing step. In this setting, both systems are indeed strictly stronger than CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$, where the separation of QCDCL from CAQE$^{\mathsf{Core}}$ uses cube learning.

papers.title: How Far Is Too Far? Object Recognition Declines Monotonically with Semantic Distance
papers.abstract: Vision models are sensitive to object-background context, yet it remains unclear how recognition changes as the semantic distance between objects and backgrounds increases. We introduce ImageNet-OOC1k, a benchmark enabling graded control of object-background relationships along a continuous consensus visual-semantic dissimilarity axis. This formulation reveals a highly consistent monotonic decline in recognition accuracy across 35 models spanning convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, and vision-language models. Internal analyses of Vision Transformers reveal patterns consistent with aggregation failure, where object evidence is present at the patch level but not consolidated into the final prediction. Using this characterization as a diagnostic probe, a simple spatial re-ranking strategy recovers a subset of these errors and improves in-sample accuracy by up to 5.7 percentage points. These results establish context sensitivity as a continuous and predictable property of modern vision systems, with Vision Transformer analyses suggesting that aggregation limitations may contribute to some failure types even when object evidence remains available.

papers.title: XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute
papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.

papers.title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.

authors.name: Jiaxing Zhao
authors.institution: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research

authors.name: Haoxuan Che
authors.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
papers.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.

papers.title: An Alternative to Crawlers: Scalable P2P Network Monitoring Using the Network Scale-Up Method
papers.abstract: \Ac{p2p} networks have remained an active area of research and development for decades. Originally used for data dissemination, they have later become instrumental to decentralized payment systems, blockchains, and Web3 applications. Since decentralization is a crucial property of these networks, they are continuously monitored to track attributes such as the geographical distribution of nodes, which serve as indicators of infrastructure concentration and resilience. However, monitoring typically relies on network crawls to derive accurate snapshots, which requires substantial computational and network resources. In contrast, \ac{nsum} is a statistical tool that estimates the prevalence of subpopulations based on responses to questions such as \enquote{How many people do you know in a specific group?} This work leverages the information embedded in Kademlia routing tables to develop a lightweight \ac{nsum}-based measurement and estimation framework that infers global network attribute distributions from a small set of nodes, offering an alternative to full-network crawls. As a case study, we evaluate our approach on \ac{ipfs}, a well-researched and widely used Web3 data storage and retrieval network. This is the first application of \ac{nsum} to decentralized network measurement. We evaluate our methodology on two datasets: the first comprises 360 full-network crawls collected over one month to assess our measurement-estimation approach across multiple simulated measurement scenarios, while the second dataset was collected through a deployment of the proposed lightweight measurement framework during May 2026. The results show that local Kademlia routing views, with only 10 nodes, preserve sufficient information to accurately estimate global attribute distributions, achieving normalized biases below \SI{10}{\percent} and closely tracking temporal changes in network composition.

papers.title: Evaluation of Performance of the p-stop fabrication process variations in ATLAS18 strip sensors, Pre- and Post-Irradiation
papers.abstract: The High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) requires the replacement of the ATLAS Inner Detector with a new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk). Radiation-hard n-in-p micro-strip sensors were developed for use in the ITk. During quality control (QC) and quality assurance (QA) procedures performed on ATLAS18 production sensors and test chips, ATLAS ITk strip sensor institutes identified instances of low p-stop density in certain production batches. To investigate the origin of these issues and to try some technological improvements, two dedicated sample batches with four variations of the p-stop fabrication process were produced. These process types (1-4) were systematically evaluated to determine their effectiveness and uniformity. In total, 56 full-size sensors, along with numerous miniature sensors and test chips, were tested. A number of samples were used in the irradiation campaign reaching the maximum expected levels for the HL-LHC operation after 10 years - with neutrons up to 1.6E15 neq/cm2, and with gamma rays from a 60Co source up to 66 Mrad. The goal of this evaluation program is to assess the impact of of p-stop fabrication process variations on interstrip isolation performance and to provide feedback for future sensor development. This paper describes the applied test procedures and presents the corresponding results, which demonstrate good sensor performance for all investigated p-stop types. The findings confirm the reliability of the evaluated designs and identify specific advantages that can inform further optimization of strip sensor fabrication.

papers.title: Zariski Topology of (Krasner) Hypermodules
papers.abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative Krasner hyperring with identity and $M$ an $R$-hypermodule. We consider the prime spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}_R(M)$, consisting of all prime subhypermodules of $M$. In this paper, we introduce a Zariski topology on $\operatorname{Spec}_R(M)$ and investigate its fundamental topological properties, including irreducibility, connectedness, compactness, and separation axioms, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for each. In particular, we prove that $\operatorname{Spec}_R(M)$ is irreducible if and only if the nilradical of $M$ is a prime hyperideal, and that it is connected precisely when the underlying hyperring is not a nontrivial direct product. We further investigate the functoriality of the Zariski topology in the category of Krasner hyperrings and hypermodules. Moreover, using the fundamental relation $\epsilon^{*}$, the smallest regular relation on $M$ for which the quotient $\overline{M}=M/\epsilon^{*}$ becomes an $\overline{R}=R/\Gamma^{*}$-module, we establish a correspondence between the Zariski topologies of $M$ and $\overline{M}$. We show that this correspondence is functorial and thereby relate the hypermodule-theoretic setting to the classical theory of modules over rings.

papers.title: Distance-Certified Safe Control in Unknown Environments via Spatio-Temporal Composition of Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a distance-certified safety control framework for unknown and dynamic environments. The proposed strategy relies on a spatio-temporal composition of Gaussian Process (GP) barriers from environment point clouds. A point-cloud-dependent covariance kernel is constructed to smoothly combine individual GP representations, yielding a continuously differentiable posterior mean and a diagonal observation Gram matrix that avoids dense covariance inversions. We then derive a closed-form calibration of the GP length scale accounting for spatial approximation errors and finite point-cloud coverage, guaranteeing a prescribed minimum distance from the true obstacle boundary. To handle moving obstacles and updated observations, the scan-based barriers are certified over finite validity horizons and smoothly combined into a time-varying Control Barrier Function (CBF). Under problem feasibility conditions, the associated CBF-based safety control guarantees forward invariance of the certified safe set, thereby ensuring the prescribed distance from the obstacles. Unicycle simulations with static and moving obstacles illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

authors.name: Stefano Di Gregorio
authors.institution: Ospedale Regionale di Bellinzona e Valli

papers.title: Automated detection of wild and cultivated plants in citizen science records
papers.abstract: Citizen science plant occurrences may help the early detection of naturalisations of alien species, yet they are affected by misclassifications of cultivated plants as wild occurrences. To differentiate cultivated from wild observations, we proposed a decision framework for the manual annotation of records. We annotated this cultivation status for 1,491 iNaturalist records in Cape Town, comprising 12 invasive alien plant species. To automate the classification, we trained algorithms on annotated records based on 39 predictors from split into 4 sets: (i) basic record and observer features, (ii) visual features extracted from images, (iii) geographic features, and (iv) iNaturalist observer statistics. 11 Classification algorithms were trained on 8 combinations of predictor sets, to assess predictors importance, yielding 88 models evaluated with crossvalidation. 25.2% of all annotated records were cultivated, and 21.2% among Research Grade records, while 24.8% of annotated records were doubtful. Automated classification yielded an accuracy in distinguishing cultivated from wild records reaching 87%, improving over the iNaturalist cultivation tag (74%), and the accuracy was robust when predicting on new species (85%). Model performance was overall highest when combining iNaturalist-specific, geographic and visual predictors, but visual predictors alone performed better for certain species. Our results highlight the potential to automatically distinguish cultivated and wild-growing plant records to support invasion risk assessments and sanitise ecological analyses currently contaminated by cultivated records. Our framework is transferable to other crowdsourcing platforms, even though the manual annotation capacity can limit transferability.

authors.name: Christophe Botella
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.institution: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Botany

papers.title: Flat and very flat pro-quasi-coherent pro-sheaves on ind-schemes
papers.abstract: This is a paper about homological algebra of flat pro-quasi-coherent pro-sheaves. We recall and collect various techniques such as accessibility and deconstructibility, and adopt them to ind-schemes under various assumptions. We also discuss the foundations of the notion of an ind-scheme.

authors.name: Leonid Positselski
authors.institution: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Preserver Problems for Products of Operator Differences
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate surjective maps $\Phi:\mathscr B(H)\to\mathscr B(H)$ preserving various operator quantities associated with products of differences, namely, $$\alpha\big((\Phi(A)-\Phi(B))\Phi(C)\big) =\alpha\big((A-B)C\big) \quad \text{for all}~ A,B,C\in\mathscr B(H),$$ where $\alpha$ denotes one of the following: the numerical radius, maximal numerical range, minimum modulus, surjectivity modulus, reduced minimum modulus, or spectral radius. Under suitable assumptions, we establish structural characterizations of these maps and determine their possible forms.

authors.name: Arup Majumdar
authors.institution: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
papers.abstract: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

authors.name: Ondrej Tichy
authors.institution: Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Information Theory and Automation

papers.title: Two channels of magnetic renormalization in the terahertz lattice response of FePS$_{3}$
papers.abstract: Interlayer vibrations probe how magnetic van der Waals layers are stacked and coupled. In the zigzag antiferromagnet FePS$_3$, ultrafast experiments show that the interlayer shear couples strongly to the magnetic order, but not how magnetism renormalizes the shear stiffness and damping. Here, using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, we measure the anisotropic conductivity of FePS$_3$ from 1.6 to 300 K and in fields up to 7 T normal to the layers. We observe absorption bands at 0.6-0.8 and 1.3-2.4 THz that persist into the paramagnetic phase. The lower one is consistent with an interlayer shear resonance; the magnetic order stiffens one of its in-plane components and softens the other, reversing their splitting at the N\'eel temperature. We identify two channels of magnetic renormalization: frequency shifts are confined to the ordered phase, whereas the linewidths of this resonance and most oscillator strengths follow short-range spin correlations persisting well above the transition. The field acts mainly on the higher resonance in one orientation: near 3.2 T, its softening accelerates and its linewidth has a cusp-like minimum, consistent with critical slowing down of a field-induced order parameter. These results give an equilibrium view of spin-shear coupling, which is anisotropic and persists above the N\'eel temperature through short-range correlations.

authors.name: Zdenek Sofer
authors.institution: University of Chemistry and Technology, Prague

papers.title: Detection of minimum ionising particles with internal gain in the first Silicon Electron Multiplier demonstrators
papers.abstract: The Silicon Electron Multiplier (SiEM) is a novel sensor concept for minimum ionising particle (MIP) detection that uses internal gain achieved through a composite electrode structure embedded within the silicon bulk. Unlike conventional gain sensors (LGADs, APDs), the SiEM achieves amplification through applied electric potentials rather than doped gain layers, potentially offering superior radiation hardness above $10^{16}\,n_{\mathrm{eq}}/\mathrm{cm}^2$. Following initial conceptual studies and simulation work, several fabrication approaches were explored, including Deep Reactive Ion Etching (DRIE) at Centro Nacional de Microelectr\'onica (CNM) and Metal Assisted Chemical Etching (MACEtch) at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI). This paper reports the first experimental results from functional SiEM demonstrators produced by Hamamatsu Photonics K. K. (HPK) using a single-electrode configuration with modified geometry. Electrical characterisation through I-V measurements and test beam studies with minimum ionising particles demonstrate clear evidence of charge multiplication, with gains comparable to simulation predictions.

authors.name: Sara Cesare
authors.institution: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Milano Bicocca

papers.title: A Polynomial Time Approximation for the Minimization of Implication Systems and Horn CNFs
papers.abstract: An implication system is a collection of rules of the form $B \imp H$, where the set $B$ of Boolean variables is the {\em body} of the rule, while $H$ is the set of its {\em heads}. Such a rule is an aggregate representation of individual implications $B\imp h$, for $h\in H$ which correspond to the clauses of an equivalent CNF representation of a Horn Boolean function. An implication system is {\em body-minimum}/{\em clause-minimum} if it has the minimum number of bodies/clauses among all logically equivalent implication systems. The corresponding minimization problems appear not only in the context of implication systems, but also as problems for closure systems, directed hypergraphs, representation of dependencies in relational databases, or in Horn CNF minimization. While body-minimization is known to be solvable in polynomial time (and there are several algorithms in the literature that solve this task), clause-minimization is known to be NP-hard. In fact, body-minimization has a particular canonical solution, called the GD-basis of the underlying Horn function that also can be computed efficiently. In this paper, we utilize a known connection between the two minimization problems stating that for every implication system there always exists a logically equivalent clause-minimum implication system which has the same bodies as its canonical GD-basis, see (B{\'e}rczi and B{\'e}rczi-Kov{\'a}cs, 2017), and (Adaricheva and Nation, 2014). We use this fact to design a polynomial time approximation algorithm which for any $\delta>0$ outputs a $(\frac{1}{4} + \delta)n$-factor approximation of the logically equivalent clause-minimum implication system on $n$ variables. This is an improvement from the best known algorithm so far that provides only an $(n-1)$-factor approximation, see (Hammer and Kogan, 1993).

authors.name: Endre Boros
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: A counterexample to the subgraphings approximate the cost problem
papers.abstract: We prove that for every $k\ge 2$, the free group $\mathbb{F}_k$ on $k$ generators admits a finite generating set $S$ such that the Schreier graphing of the Bernoulli action of $\mathbb{F}_k$ with respect to $S$ does not admit spanning subgraphings that would approximate the cost of the action. In particular, this gives an example of a graphing that spans a treeable countable pmp equivalence relation, but does not admit a spanning subtreeing.

authors.name: Zoltan Vidnyanszky
authors.institution: HUN-REN Research Centre for Natural Sciences

papers.title: The Velocity Curves and Three-Dimensional Kinematics of the Milky Way from Gaia DR3
papers.abstract: We investigate the fundamental kinematic parameters of stellar motions in the Milky Way using a statistical sample of 27,485,720 stars with measured three-dimensional velocities from the Gaia DR3 catalogue. From these data, we determine the local solar velocity $(U_{\odot},V_{\odot},W_{\odot}) = \left(10.5\pm0.7,14.5\pm0.9,7.33\pm0.1\right) ~\mathrm{km/s}$, the average rotation velocity\linebreak $\mathrm{V}_{0} = \left( 228\pm4\right) $ km/s, and the circular velocity $\mathrm{V}_{c} = \left( 234\pm4\right) $ {km/s,} both at the radius $R_{\odot}$. Next, within the range of $3-14$ kpc, we derive the Galactic circular velocity curve $\mathrm{V}_{c}(R)$ and determine the average spherical components of the stellar velocities as functions of both Galactocentric radius $R$ and distance from the Galactic plane $\left\vert Z\right\vert $. Two-dimensional $R-Z$ maps of these components reveal a complex three-dimensional kinematic structure. In particular, the pattern observed at $R\lesssim5$ kpc can be associated with the influence of the Galactic bar. To facilitate the description of the observations, we employ a simplified axisymmetric Monte Carlo model with several free parameters that reproduces the main kinematic trends.

authors.name: Petr Zavada
authors.institution: FZU - Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences

authors.name: Karel Piska
authors.institution: FZU - Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Explicit Tartakowsky theorem and universality criterion sets over totally real number fields
papers.abstract: We prove an explicit version of Tartakowsky's theorem over all totally real number fields. Namely, a positive definite integral lattice of rank at least five represents every totally positive integer that it represents locally, provided that the norm of the integer exceeds an explicit bound, exponential in powers of the volume of the lattice and of the discriminant of the field. As an application, we give explicit criterion sets for universal quadratic forms over all but finitely many real quadratic fields. Finally, we determine the minimal criterion sets for an infinite family of real quadratic fields.

papers.title: On Schroedinger operators with subordinated complex potentials
papers.abstract: We disprove a decade-old conjecture about a spectral stability of Schroedinger operators with potentials which are small in a subordination sense. Our counterexample is based on a complex perturbation of a critical attractive square well.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Decision Support in Gait Analysis: A Proof-of-Concept
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential for clinical decision support but lack specialized biomechanical knowledge required for accurate gait analysis interpretation. We developed and evaluated a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to enhance LLM-generated clinical explanations for ankle fracture rehabilitation using ground reaction force data. Using the GaitRec dataset (503 subjects: 211 healthy, 292 ankle fracture patients), we implemented a five-stage pipeline integrating: (1) machine learning classification (91.3\% accuracy); (2) Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for explainable feature identification; (3) RAG knowledge base from peer-reviewed biomechanics literature; (4) GPT-5 explanation generation with and without retrieval augmentation; and (5) double-blind evaluation by experienced physical therapists across five clinical criteria. RAG augmentation produced statistically significant improvements in Clini-cal Benefit (mean difference=0.60, p=0.047, {\delta}=0.49) and Completeness (mean difference=0.70, p=0.049, {\delta}=0.49), both demonstrating large effect sizes. Baseline GPT-5 achieved strong performance across all criteria (\textgreater4.0/5.0). This proof-of-concept demonstrates that augmenting general-purpose LLMs with domain-specific knowledge meaningfully enhances actionable, evidence-based clinical guidance---dimensions most critical for rehabilitation decision-making. The framework provides a scalable approach for integrating AI into specialized clinical workflows without costly model retraining.

authors.name: Djordje Slijepcevic
authors.institution: University of Applied Sciences St Pölten

papers.title: Adapted Wasserstein Distance for Credit Risk: Rating Information and Model-Transfer Hedging
papers.abstract: Two credit models can quote the same bond prices today and still disagree on how information about the issuer unfolds over time. We quantify this disagreement by means of the adapted Wasserstein distance, an optimal transport distance between laws of processes consistent with the flow of information associated with them. For defaultable bond price processes, the squared distance is the smallest probability by which the two default indicators must disagree. This yields closed-form distances for rating reviews and a dynamic programming principle for multi-period rating migration. For a single review, the distance can be estimated from observed posterior survival probabilities at the parametric rate without losing calibration. For intensity models, we obtain an explicit formula for the adapted distance between bond prices that controls the error of bootstrap hedges along a quoted term structure, determine its sharp range over hazard schedules calibrated to the same prices, and show that it is stable under perturbations of the hazard rates. Finally, we complement the theoretical findings with applications to S&P transition data and Monte Carlo experiments to illustrate the size of these effects.

authors.name: Francesco Mattesini
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences

papers.title: Bright-Dark State Interplay Governs Vibronic Decoherence in Molecular Aggregates
papers.abstract: In this study, we establish a spectroscopy-driven framework that connects optically bright vibronic eigenstates to their subsequent decoherence dynamics in excitonic molecular aggregates. Combining the Multiparticle Holstein Formalism with explicit system--bath interactions, we demonstrate that relaxation-induced purity loss is governed by three interconnected factors: (i) the bath spectral window, which determines the accessibility of intra- and interband relaxation pathways; (ii) the local network of dark vibronic states surrounding the optically prepared bright state; and (iii) the energetic placement of the bright state, which controls downhill relaxation. Remarkably, states with different excitation energies exhibit nearly identical purity dynamics when their local relaxation networks are similar. The resulting H--J asymmetry further reveals the importance of energetic directionality. These findings establish a reliable connection between optical spectroscopy, vibronic band structure, and state-selective loss in purity.

papers.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
papers.abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

papers.title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education
papers.abstract: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

papers.title: Astrophysical Constraints for Bosonic Dark Matter in and Around Quark Stars
papers.abstract: We investigate the structure, stability, and mass-radius relations of compact stars composed of quark matter within the non-ideal MIT Bag Model mixed with self-interacting bosonic dark matter with a $\phi^n$ self-interaction potential. By solving the coupled two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for boson masses between 200 MeV and 1 GeV and self-interaction strengths with $n=4$ and $n=40$, we show that strong self-interactions and higher boson masses enhance the stability of compact star configurations at high central pressures, though they reduce maximum overall masses. Ultra-compact solutions with $C \ge 1/3$ capable of mimicking black holes are significantly restricted compared to hadronic models, emerging only for strong self-interactions and dark matter fractions exceeding 90\%. Depending on the parameters, the compact stars form either extended dark matter halos or compact cores: stronger self-interactions and higher boson masses suppress the radial extension to favor compact cores of dark matter. Matching our models against observational constraints highlights PSR J1614$-$2230 and XTE J1814$-$338 as potential window of opportunity for dark matter detection. Notably, XTE J1814$-$338 could confirm a dark sector, given its requirement for light boson masses ($m_b \approx 200\text{--}300\text{ MeV}$) and strongly DM-dominated configurations.

papers.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
papers.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

authors.name: Sebastian Gombert
authors.institution: DIPF | Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education

papers.title: P = W conjectures for varieties with nilpotent fundamental group
papers.abstract: We prove the cohomological and the geometric $P=W$ conjectures for the moduli spaces of $G$-Higgs bundles and $G$-local systems on any smooth complex projective variety $X$ with nilpotent fundamental group, and any connected complex reductive group $G$. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the first instances of $P=W$ conjectures beyond curves and abelian varieties. Finally, we provide examples of our theorem for classical groups: as a byproduct of this analysis we investigate when symplectic resolutions of the corresponding character varieties exist.

authors.name: Camilla Felisetti
authors.institution: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia

papers.title: Graph Neural Network based non-local models: Toward application to RANS turbulence modeling
papers.abstract: Most machine-learning closures for the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations are local, predicting the closure quantities at each point solely from local flow features, despite the non-local nature of turbulent interactions. We propose a non-local closure framework based on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) that exploits the mesh connectivity. Each finite-volume cell becomes a graph node, and cells sharing a face are connected by an edge. Through message passing, each layer aggregates information from neighboring nodes, so that after $k$ layers the prediction at a cell depends on its $k$-hop neighborhood, which naturally accounts for non-local effects. To make training feasible when each simulation yields a single large graph, we also introduce a breadth-first-search $k$-hop subgraph sampling strategy, which acts as data augmentation and cuts the cost per processed graph during training. We compare GCNs with feed-forward networks (FNNs) of equal size on two periodic-hills benchmarks: a laminar advection-diffusion transport problem that mimics the non-local character of RANS closures, and the turbulent eddy-viscosity prediction of the Closure Challenge dataset at $Re = 5600$. In the laminar case, FNNs are accurate only within the training regime and with sufficiently informative inputs, whereas GCNs generalize better to unseen geometries, including out-of-distribution flows, and partly compensate for missing input features. In the turbulent proof-of-concept case, the graph-based models achieve modest but consistent improvements compared to FNNs, supporting GCNs as a promising route to non-local RANS closures.

authors.name: Davide Oberto
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

papers.title: CISyn: Human Mesh Recovery in Close Interactions with Physics-Simulated Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) in close-interaction scenarios is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately annotated training data: real capture is expensive, and existing synthetic datasets rarely include physical contact. We introduce CISyn, a large-scale synthetic dataset purpose-built for close human-human interactions, generated via physics simulation and Blender-based rendering. By simulating collision dynamics between SMPL-X-rigged humanoids, CISyn naturally produces the contact, mutual occlusion, and pose entanglement that characterize close-interaction scenes, with no manual annotation effort. The released set provides 25,000 sequences with accurate 3D annotations. We further propose an uncertainty-aware loss that allows models to learn more effectively from the heavily occluded examples in our data. Augmenting state-of-the-art HMR training with CISyn and replacing the regression loss with our uncertainty-aware variant yields consistent improvements on close-interaction benchmarks, validating CISyn as a scalable complement to real-world data. The dataset, generation pipeline, and code are available at https://github.com/yfde/CISyn.

authors.name: Yufan Deng
authors.institution: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

papers.title: Stability of the tangent bundle on del Pezzo surfaces
papers.abstract: In this article, we study the Bridgeland stability of the tangent bundle on del Pezzo surfaces. We obtain a complete description of the region where the tangent bundle is (un)stable with respect to the standard Bridgeland stability conditions associated to the anticanonical polarization.

authors.name: Yun Shi
authors.institution: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

authors.name: Shing-Tung Yau
authors.institution: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications

papers.title: Singular limits of the subelliptic Allen-Cahn equation and geometric flows
papers.abstract:
This paper investigates the singular limits of a bistable reaction-diffusion equation in a subelliptic setting, where the standard Euclidean diffusion is replaced by a subelliptic operator defined by a family of vector fields. We introduce a Riemannian approximation of these vector fields to regularize the problem, yielding a uniformly parabolic equation whose ellipticity degenerates as the singular parameter vanishes.
  We prove that the family of solutions converges globally in time to the stable equilibria away from a propagating interface. Our approach uses the definition of generalized geometric flow developed by Barles--Souganidis, uniquely defined through the level-set equation and viscosity solutions. The behavior of the interface depends on the traveling wave speed c: when c is not 0, the front propagates with constant normal velocity governed by a first-order subelliptic eikonal equation.
  When c = 0, the front evolves according to the horizontal mean curvature flow equation defined by the original vector fields. At present, this case comes with limitations: it requires a more restrictive condition on test functions at characteristic points to define generalized flows, where the horizontal gradient vanishes and standard arguments break down. This framework relies on our earlier work, where the equivalence between the generalized flow and the level-set approach was established when the vector fields generate a step-two Carnot group. We also assume that the comparison principle holds for the level-set equation in order for the level-set approach to be well-posed.

papers.title: Disaggregated LLM Inference in Space: A Communication Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Orbital data centers could enable large-scale AI inference, but efficiently serving a frontier language model to many users may require several compute satellites to cooperate over optical links.
