While disaggregated inference, which splits large language model (LLM) serving across machines, is well established in terrestrial data centers, its viability under the unique constraints of orbital deployments remains an open question. This article investigates how link capacity and satellite separation affect two types of disaggregated LLM serving, in both compact satellite formations and distributed constellations. Prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) migrates a large KV cache once per request, while attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) exchanges small activations at every mixture-of-experts layer for every generated token. The two respond to distance in different ways. PDD is limited mainly by link capacity and, with fast enough links, tolerates separations of up to a thousand kilometers. AFD is limited mainly by propagation delay, which accumulates layer by layer and forces attention and expert instances within about a kilometer of each other. Based on these results, we propose a hierarchical orbital inference architecture and provide network design guidelines for future orbital data centers, including the role of ground access latency.

papers.title: A physics-constrained emulator for time-discretised landslide runout modelling
papers.abstract: Numerical simulations of landslides are commonly used to forecast impact areas. Full physics-based models provide accurate predictions, but their computational expense can preclude their use for large parameter sweeps. To achieve efficient modelling for such cases, we developed a physics-constrained neural network to emulate full landslide runout in a time-discretised manner. This emulator is trained on over 200,000 samples, each consisting of a pair of landslide thicknesses and velocities on a given DEM with a fixed time interval. To constrain the model's physical consistency, we define physics-based loss functions based on mass conservation and the system's kinetic energy loss. The model demonstrates high fidelity across the test dataset, achieving root mean square errors of approximately 0.06 m for thickness and 0.11 m/s for velocity in single-step predictions. In autoregressive rollout, these errors evolved modestly to about 0.21 m and 0.09 m/s after 110 iterations, while greatly improving computational efficiency by more than 50 times.

authors.name: Fawu Wang
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

papers.title: Equivariant geometry of quadrics blown-up along a twisted quartic
papers.abstract: We prove that $G$-Fano threefolds which are given by the blow-up of a smooth quadric along a twisted quartic curve are $G$-birationally superrigid if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{A}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_2$. We also prove that the action of $G$ is linearisable if and only if $G$ does not contain a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_2^3$.

papers.title: GNN-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Coastal Emergency Response under Extreme Water Levels
papers.abstract: When a storm surge approaches a coastal town, the emergency plan must be put into action quickly using water-level forecasts, flood extent, road access, vulnerable residents and shelters. Bringing this information together under time pressure is slow and depends on the duty officer's expertise. This paper is one step in a wider research line from data to safe decisions: machine learning to understand the hazard, reinforcement learning and planning to choose actions, large language models (LLMs) to explain and cross-check them, and an assurance layer that keeps people in charge. Here we address the action step on a real place. We ask whether a policy can learn the timing of emergency actions from decades of real events. Lido di Venezia is represented as a heterogeneous graph built from public elevation, road, building and census data and driven by hourly tide-gauge records from 1983 to 2024, with seven actions taken from the municipal emergency plan. A PPO policy is trained on this graph and compared, on storm windows unseen in training, with a rule-based system simulating the officer's discretionary decisions. On 18 historical test scenarios, PPO achieves a similar reduction in population exposure to the rule. With uncertain forecasts and limited protection it again performs similarly but does not outperform the tuned rule, and removing graph message passing does not substantially reduce performance. PPO therefore learns an effective protective response from an outcome-based reward alone: it is given the plan's actions and when each is allowed, but not the thresholds that tell the comparator when to act. Next steps test harder edge cases, move closer to a digital twin of the territory, and replace the simulated officer with assessment by emergency-management stakeholders, supported by LLM-based interpretation of each recommendation.

papers.title: Mining Architectural Models in the Wild: A Curated Dataset of AADL Models
papers.abstract: Empirical research on software architecture maintenance and evolution is hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, validated, and richly annotated model datasets. Existing benchmarks are limited in scale, provide only model-level annotations, or lack alignment with reference architectures, thereby restricting reproducible studies of architectural reuse, conformance, and AI-driven analysis. To address this gap, we present A3D, a curated dataset of 1,115 Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) models mined from public GitHub repositories and validated with the OSATE tool. The dataset spans 7 generic domains and 52 specific-problem clusters, and provides two annotation layers: (i) domain- and problem-level labels, which capture different model aggregation criteria, and (ii) component-level mappings to three reference architectures, which have been externally validated through a user study. Models are released in AADL and JSON formats with full provenance, a reproducible mining pipeline, and the validation protocol.

authors.name: Maria Teresa Rossi
authors.institution: Azienda Socio Sanitaria Territoriale degli Spedali Civili di Brescia

papers.title: The dual of separated metric compact Hausdorff spaces is an infinitary variety of algebras
papers.abstract: A metric compact Hausdorff space is a Lawvere metric space equipped with a compatible compact Hausdorff topology (which does not need to be the induced topology). These spaces maintain many important features of compact metric spaces, but the resulting category is much better behaved. We prove that the category of separated metric compact Hausdorff spaces is dually equivalent to a variety of infinitary algebras.

papers.title: Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical Systems: A Literature Survey
papers.abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) operate in dynamic, dependable environments where sensing, communication, decision-making, control, and assurance are affected by uncertainty. This paper characterizes CPS uncertainty through a literature survey comprising 186 primary studies. We (i) characterize uncertainty types, (ii) identify uncertainty sources, (iii) relate uncertainty to life-cycle phases in which they occur, and (iv) overview the possible uncertain mitigation strategies. The findings show that uncertainty is most often conceptualized as an assurance issue. Safety and specification uncertainty is the most prevalent category, followed by environmental and model/epistemic uncertainty. Domain mapping reveals broad cross-domain engagement, while safety-critical sectors such as autonomous systems, energy systems, and robotics CPSs display domain-specific uncertainty patterns. The life-cycle analysis indicates that uncertainty is not limited to the development or testing phases but also arises during runtime operation, underscoring the need for continuous assurance approaches. Mitigation strategies primarily include runtime monitoring, robust and adaptive control, and probabilistic reasoning. In summary, this survey contributes to a thorough characterization of CPS uncertainty and provides a discussion of articles on this topic.

authors.name: Beena
authors.institution: Pandit Bhagwat Dayal Sharma Post Graduate Institute of Medical Sciences

papers.title: A PTAS for Euclidean Capacitated Vehicle Routing
papers.abstract: In the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), introduced by Dantzig and Ramser in 1959, we are given an $n$-node graph $G=(V,E)$ with metric edges costs $c(e)$, a depot $r\in V$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost collection of tours, each containing the depot and visiting at most other $Q$ nodes, such that the tours cover all the nodes. In this paper we focus on the Euclidean CVRP problem, where the nodes represent points on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the edge costs are the respective Euclidean distances. Euclidean CVRP generalizes the classical NP-hard Euclidean TSP problem (the special case with $Q=n-1$), that admits a PTAS [Arora FOCS'96/Mitchell SODA'96]. A long-standing open problem has been generalizing the latter PTAS to Euclidean CVRP. A polynomial-time $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation for this problem follows from the PTAS for Euclidean TSP and the tour-partitioning technique for CVRP [Haimovich, Kan Math. OR'85]. This was the best known until a recent improvement of the approximation factor to slightly below 2 [Friggstad, Grandoni, Mousavi SODA'26]. There have been a series of papers presenting improved QPTASs by Das and Mathieu [SODA'10] (time $n^{\log^{O(1/\epsilon)}n}$), Jayaprakash and Salavatipour [SODA'22] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log^6 n)}$), and recently Sitters [ArXiV'25] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)}$). In this paper, we solve the mentioned long-standing open problem by presenting a PTAS for Euclidean CVRP.

papers.title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
papers.abstract: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.

authors.name: Loris Roveda
authors.institution: Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research

papers.title: Spectral Steering: Local Inverse Geometry for Frozen Diffusion Generators
papers.abstract: A frozen diffusion generator may need to change several output properties while preserving others. We study when guidance faithfully realizes such a structured request and whether local inverse correction improves its direction. Our account links this benefit to the interaction between the request and the objective-specific remaining-sampler Jacobian: conditioning alone is insufficient. Spectral steering combines a request-specific cosine-gain predictor with damped inverse correction and fixed-time relinearization for finite edits. Scalar nulls and matched-movement controls test the predicted mechanism. Across 8,923 instances in a retrospectively identified local regime, predicted and realized gains correlate at Spearman 0.79, versus -0.11 for condition number. Experiments span images, audio, robotics, and control and planning, including complex character motion generation. On 50 paired inpainting cases, four corrections improve unobserved-pixel PSNR over Adam by 3.25 dB at equal total derivative traversals. Together, the analysis and controls connect request-dependent geometry to directional gains and establish where these gains translate into downstream performance.

authors.name: Alessandro Leanza
authors.institution: Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research

authors.name: Loris Roveda
authors.institution: Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research

papers.title: A Fast Algorithm for the Familywise Loss
papers.abstract: The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in $O(K)$ time, where $K$ is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

papers.title: Interface-Selective Extreme Ultraviolet Second Harmonic Generation Away from Linear Absorption Edges
papers.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (XUV) second harmonic generation (SHG) combines interface selectivity with core-level element specificity but has so far been limited to linear absorption edges. Here, we measure XUVSHG from an indium tin oxide capped MoO$_3$/SiO$_2$/Si photovoltaic heterojunction for fundamental energies of 60--76\,eV, below the Si L$_{2,3}$-edge. Where linear absorption is a featureless valence background, we observe a strong, structured XUVSHG response with maxima near 70 and 76\,eV. Layer-resolved first-principles calculations reproduce both maxima and assign them to the Si/SiO$_2$ interface, the 76\,eV peak to the bridging Si monolayer and the 70\,eV peak to the near-interface substrate. Bethe--Salpeter calculations for bulk Si connect the signal to Si 2$p$ excitons at 140--160\,eV. At the Si L$_{2,3}$-edge, the calculated response is instead governed by MoO$_3$-induced asymmetry at the oxide interface. These findings establish off-edge XUV SHG as a powerful approach for selectively probing distinct buried interfaces within complex material heterostructures.

papers.title: Multi-year forecasting of F10.7 and F30 solar radio flux using an adaptive Kalman filter and hemispheric solar activity
papers.abstract: The F10.7 and F30 radio flux indices drive thermospheric and radiation-environment models, and long-term predictions are needed for satellite mission planning, orbital-lifetime estimates, and re-entry assessments. We develop multi-year predictions of both indices for lead times of 1 to 84 months using three complementary contributions. First, we apply the McNish-Lincoln (M&L) method and demonstrate its predictive skill over multi-year horizons, with RMSE of 11-22 sfu for F10.7 and 7-14 sfu for F30. RMSE largely stabilizes after roughly 36 months, indicating near-constant forecast skill over the seven-year horizon. Accuracy also depends strongly on the solar-cycle phase at which the forecast is issued, with the most favorable starting intervals occurring progressively earlier in the cycle for longer lead times. Second, we update the initial predictions using an adaptive Kalman filter with noise statistics identification, which assimilates the latest monthly observations to reconstruct the current smoothed flux, remove the delay introduced by centered smoothing, and improve solar-cycle state estimation, reducing forecast errors by up to 70%. Third, we introduce synthetic hemispheric components of solar radio flux to account for the separate evolution of the northern and southern hemispheres, and incorporate them into a hemispheric M&L formulation. Compared with the initial M&L predictions, it reduces RMSE by up to 55% for F10.7 and 58% for F30, showing that hemispheric asymmetry contains predictive information lost in the full-disk index. These results extend solar-cycle forecasting to multi-year timescales relevant for long-term space-weather applications and operational planning.

authors.name: Zaina Abu-Shaar
authors.institution: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Tatiana Podladchikova
authors.institution: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Simulating high-speed solar wind streams from coronal holes using an L5-L1 configuration of Lagrangian points
papers.abstract: Coronal holes (CHs) are known to be sources of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), yet the physical mechanisms linking CH position and characteristics to solar wind (SW) behaviour remain unclear. Our results reveal that the latitude of CHs, especially smaller ones, combined with the heliographic latitude of the solar disk's central point (B0 angle), plays a critical role in driving discrepancies in SW velocity across the heliosphere. To investigate this, we use archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A, and Earth to simulate an L5-L1 configuration, where L5 is a vantage point approximately behind Earth in its orbit (as proposed for the Vigil mission), and L1 is between Earth and the Sun where SW measurements are typically taken. We use these insights to develop a predictive algorithm for HSSs, beginning with an analysis of the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1. We then introduce a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties and the B0 angle to adjust for changes in SW velocity at L1. Our results show that the L5 viewpoint demonstrates the capability to significantly improve the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions, enhancing our understanding of the CH-HSS relationship and potentially improving space weather forecasting.

authors.name: Tatiana Podladchikova
authors.institution: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Modeling Risks with Masked Causes and Variable Exposure
papers.abstract:
Cohort studies and surveys often record how much time each subject spent under each of two or several treatment conditions and whether an event occurred, but not the condition under which it occurred. We develop two models for such data, for binary and count outcomes. Both start with events under each treatment condition as independent Poisson counts, and estimate rate ratios between treatment and control conditions. In the binary model, only an indicator of any event is observed, and the event probability under each condition follows a complementary log-log model with a log-exposure offset; development is done for general link functions, including log and logit. The interpretation of the treatment effect changes accordingly. In the count model, the number of events combined over all treatment conditions is observed; overdispersion is handled by Pearson scaling. Parameters are estimated either by the expectation-maximization algorithm or by direct maximization of the observed-data likelihood with Fisher scoring; standard errors are available via observed or expected information. When total exposure is common to all subjects, a relative slope summarizes the treatment effect and, unlike the rate ratio, does not depend on the assumed total exposure. In simulations, interval coverage was near nominal when enough events occurred during each treatment condition. The models are implemented in the R package maskcave.
  The work was motivated by the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study of 10,948 children. Assuming 16 waking hours per day, the adjusted sport-to-non-sport rate ratio for mild traumatic brain injury was 8.78 (95% confidence interval 4.47-17.27). We applied the count model to concussions during sports reported for 6,379 children at the Year 5 visit: the concussion rate per hour of football was 2.46 (1.37-4.43) times that of the other reported sports.

papers.title: Maximum likelihood degrees of 3D polytopes built from polygons of ML degree one
papers.abstract: We construct 3D polytopes that admit a scaling with maximum likelihood (ML) degree one by using codimension zero toric fiber products of lower-dimensional polytopes and classify all the 3D polytopes that can be constructed in this way. We also study a family of 3D polytopes whose faces admit ML degree one scalings. We give a tight lower bound for the ML degree of these polytopes with a square base and we show that every value between this bound and the normalized volume of the polytope can be attained. These values depend on counting common and repeated roots associated to certain univariate polynomials. This is similar in spirit to the description of the possible ML degrees of rational normal scrolls.

papers.title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
papers.abstract: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

papers.title: Self-assembly of dipolar nanoclusters on an attractive substrate: A coarse-grained simulation approach
papers.abstract: Recently, Thomas et al. [Nanoscale 17, 18291 (2025)] showed that bismuth oxido nanoclusters (BiO-NCs) of the type [Bi$_{38}$ O$_{45}$ (Boc-L-Phe-O)$_{24}$] form chains when deposited onto gold or pyrolitic graphite substrates. This chain formation is significantly enhanced when the bismuth in the BiO-NCs is partially replaced by cerium through doping. In this work, we study a simplified, coarse-grained model of this process, namely (magnetic) Stockmayer particles in the presence of an attractive substrate. The model is investigated by means of molecular dynamics simulations. The deposition experiment is mimicked by a rapid quench from high temperature to a low temperature below the bulk coexistence curve. The results are found to be qualitatively similar to the experimental observations reported earlier. In our simulations, we find significant chain formation in the bulk even at rather low concentrations, which is in contrast to the BiO-NCs in ethanol for which dynamic light scattering reveals negligible aggregation in the absence of the substrate. This lends support to a scenario, conjectured in the work of Thomas at al., where the dipole moments are induced by the particle-substrate interaction and hence there is little dipole moment in the bulk. In a second part, we study the system in equilibrium. We consider the scaling of chains, the number of layers populated as a function of two-dimensional density, and we draw analogies to polymers on interfaces, which have been extensively studied over the past decades. Most notably, it is found that the chains behave as self-avoiding walks at low densities, which gives way to rod-like scaling at higher densities.

authors.name: Harshita Chauhan
authors.institution: SRM Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: On the relation of secondary motions to large- and very-large-scale motions
papers.abstract: The coexistence of secondary motions with large-scale and very-large-scale motions (LSMs/VLSMs) is investigated by direct numerical simulations of turbulent open-channel flow over streamwise-aligned Gaussian ridges, varying the ridge spacing $S$ and height $h$. First, the ridge height controls the secondary-motion strength and thereby the coexistence with VLSMs. VLSMs are suppressed for $h \geqslant 0.05\delta$, with $\delta$ the open-channel height, and re-emerge at $h = 0.025\delta$, where the mean secondary motions are comparable in strength to those over strip-type surfaces. Previously reported differences between strip- and ridge-type surfaces thus reflect secondary-motion strength rather than surface type. Second, proper orthogonal decomposition and conditional averaging reveal instantaneous secondary motions that span approximately $2\delta$, fill the channel height irrespective of $S$ and $h$, and are stronger than their mean. These are identified as LSMs spatially locked and amplified by the ridges. Over dense ridges, their alternation between neighbouring ridges yields weak, near-wall confined mean secondary motions, although VLSMs are suppressed over the full channel height. The ridge height thus sets the strength of the locked LSMs, whereas the ridge spacing sets where and for how long they persist. For weak locked LSMs, ridges spaced at their natural spanwise extent increase the VLSM energy, indicating that persistent locked LSMs concatenate into VLSMs. Third, large-scale instantaneous secondary motions persist over dense ridges in the absence of long streaks. This suggests that secondary motions are driven by intermittent cross-sectional motions rather than by long streaks, similar to the streak-less bursts in near-wall turbulence.

papers.title: Symmetric Chemical Reaction Networks: Realizations and Steady States
papers.abstract: We investigate symmetric chemical reaction networks and their steady states. From classical equivariant dynamical systems and network theory it is known that the mass- action ODE of any symmetric chemical reaction network is equivariant. For symmetries that permute the species, we prove that any equivariant mass-action ODE is realized by a symmetric chemical reaction network and construct a sparsest such realization. We apply the half-degree principle to show that a symmetric CRN that has a steady state also has one with few distinct coordinates.

authors.name: Nils Gubela
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics

papers.title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

authors.name: Adam Boncz
authors.institution: Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience and Psychology

papers.title: Feature-Space Latent Forecasting for Endoscopic Surgical Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Surgical workflow assistance is inherently anticipatory: systems must reason about how procedures evolve, not just recognize the current frame. However, many prior approaches perform prediction in pixel space by synthesizing future frames, which primarily focuses on appearance fidelity rather than the semantic representations required for downstream reasoning. To address this limitation, we propose a feature-space semantic forecasting framework that models temporal dynamics directly within the representations of a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM). Specifically, we build a hierarchical target representation from multi-layer VFM features, replace future-frame feature tokens with learnable \texttt{[MASK]} tokens, and train a masked transformer to forecast the corresponding future latent features from observed context, thereby formulating procedural evolution as masked future feature prediction. Experiments on public laparoscopic benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in phase anticipation, multi-label tool presence prediction, and remaining-time estimation over RGB-based forecasting baselines, while enabling a plug-and-play representation interface for lightweight downstream heads.

authors.name: Songtao Hu
authors.institution: National Institute of Clean and Low-Carbon Energy

papers.title: Uniqueness and Nondegeneracy of Positive Bounded Solutions for Semilinear Dirichlet Problems in Exterior-Star Domains
papers.abstract: We prove the uniqueness and nondegeneracy of positive bounded solutions for the Dirichlet problem $$-\Delta u=f(u)\,\ \ \text{in}\ \ \Omega, \ \ u=0\,\ \ \text{on}\ \ \partial\Omega,$$ where $f$ is a positive reaction and $\Omega\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^d$ is a uniformly $C^{2,\gamma}$ domain with a star-shaped complement. Our uniqueness result gives a positive answer to Open Question 1 of [H. Berestycki and C. Graham, ARMA, 2026].

papers.title: The Grid's Own Language: A Common Information Model Layer for LLM Grid Assistants
papers.abstract: Assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are entering power system operation. Current designs delegate computations to validated solvers, but the agent still infers the type, role and state of each element from its name and tool-specific formats, and errors propagate to every study. The Common Information Model (CIM), the IEC standard in which operators already exchange network models, defines unambiguously what each element is and how it connects. We propose a CIM layer for LLM grid assistants and implement it in CONDUCTOR, an open-source assistant. Both the agent and its power-system studies read the layer. It labels the provenance of each fact (stated in the data, suggested only by a name, or inferred from topology), loads operators' CGMES models directly, and builds in $\leq$1\,s on the 9,241-bus PEGASE network. Deterministic checks compare every answer with solver results and the layer. On 37 tasks about the CIGRE medium-voltage and IEEE 30-bus networks, the agent gets right 97\,\% of the graded facts with the layer, such as a unit's energy source or a switch's normal state, against 55\,\% without it. We argue that a CIM layer should be a default component of grid assistants.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
papers.abstract:
SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics.
  We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

papers.title: Optical writing of Dzyaloshinskii N\'eel-type skyrmions
papers.abstract: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a route to write nanoscale topological magnetic textures for information processing. Magnetic skyrmions are prototypical examples, yet optically generating them with controlled position, type, and, in particular, chirality remains challenging. This challenge arises because magnetic dipolar interactions, which often drive skyrmion formation, preserve the degeneracy between opposite chiralities, leaving no uniquely selected spin configuration. Here, we show that in an ultrathin Co/Pt film, sequences of picosecond circularly polarized laser pulses can write N\'eel-type, fixed-chirality skyrmions stabilized solely by the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Combining Lorentz transmission electron microscopy and magneto-optical microscopy, we comprehensively reconstruct their internal spin structure across multiple length scales, ranging from nanometres to micrometers. Using asymmetric skyrmion-expansion measurements, we determined the sign and magnitude of the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and identified the written chirality. Our findings connect deterministic optical writing with the controlled spin structure of skyrmions, advancing optical control of topological textures for opto-spintronic applications.

papers.title: CompCert4Lean: Porting a Verified C Compiler to Lean in Six Weeks with Parallel Coding Agents
papers.abstract:
We present CompCert4Lean, a large-scale port of CompCert 3.17's verified compiler core from Rocq to Lean, completed in approximately six weeks by one expert directing parallel LLM agents. Our migration workflow partitions the development along its dependencies, audits translated definitions and theorem statements before large-scale proof reconstruction, and then reconstructs proofs in parallel against stable interfaces. The resulting compiler covers typed CompCert C through x86-64 assembly, discharges all 4,908 recorded proof obligations without project-specific axioms, and produces executable Linux binaries. The workflow enabled the expert to concentrate on organizing the work rather than supplying technical solutions. Of 1,071 human interactions, 88.8% concerned workflow and coordination, while only three supplied technical direction.
  Optimization campaigns further demonstrate the benefit of the Lean port for agent-driven verified development. Under matched budgets of 24 active hours, GPT-6-astra produced a Lean candidate with 11.7% lower generated-program runtime across 29 small-tests programs, compared with 2.3% lower for its Rocq candidate, both relative to original CompCert 3.17 and while preserving the end-to-end correctness theorem. These results show that parallel LLM agents can support large-scale migration with limited human technical direction and subsequently improve the migrated compiler while retaining its formal guarantees.

authors.name: Martin Rinard
authors.institution: MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory

papers.title: A counterexample to the Jordan tuple conjecture of Ball and Helton
papers.abstract: This article constructs a pair of bounded commuting 3-symmetric operators with no Jordan-family extension. The operators are coordinate multipliers on a Sobolev space of functions with values in three dimensional complex Euclidean space with an equivalent Hilbert norm. Their quadratic symbol has no operator polynomial factorization, even with an auxiliary target Hilbert space. The construction transfers the nonfactorability of the matrix quadratic used by Russo to the symbol of a commuting 3-symmetric tuple. The factorization approach of McCullough--Russo and Russo then supplies the obstruction to a Jordan-family extension.

papers.title: Schatten isometries of Grassmann spaces
papers.abstract:
We characterize all (not necessarily surjective) Schatten $p$-isometries of the Grassmann space of rank $k$ projections on a complex Hilbert space for every $p\in(0,\infty]$. We prove that every such isometry is induced by a linear or conjugate-linear isometry of the underlying Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, with the additional possibility of composition with orthocomplementation when $\dim \mathcal H = 2k > 2$.
  Our result generalizes Wigner's theorem, which plays a central role in the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics. It also extends previous results on Schatten $p$-isometries of Grassmann spaces, including characterizations of surjective isometries by Geh\'er and \v{S}emrl for $p=\infty$ and by Qian et al. for $0<p<\infty$ and that of not necessarily surjective isometries by Geh\'er for $p=2$.

authors.name: Jyoti Rani
authors.institution: Guru Jambheshwar University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Isometries for Hilbert's metric on vector lattices of continuous functions
papers.abstract: In this paper Hilbert's projective metric on the interior of the positive cone of an Archimedean vector lattice with a strong order unit is studied. We show that every surjective isometry between two such projective cones is induced by a lattice isomorphism, possibly composed with the inversion map, and that the inversion occurs precisely when the vector lattice is a bounded inverse closed $f$-algebra. In particular, two such projective cones are isometric if and only if the underlying vector lattices are lattice isomorphic, and we determine the corresponding isometry groups. We apply these results to spaces of H\"older continuous functions, absolutely continuous functions, and continuous functions of bounded variation, for which we describe the surjective isometries explicitly. Finally, we show that the projective cones of these spaces of functions on an interval all have the same metric completion, but that no two of them are isometric.

authors.name: Mark Roelands
authors.institution: Netherlands Organisation for Applied Scientific Research

papers.title: $p$-ellipticity for systems of elliptic equations with complex coefficients
papers.abstract: We extend the concept of $p$-ellipticity for (single) elliptic operators, that we introduced in arxiv:1611.00653, to the case of systems of elliptic equations with complex coefficients. The $p$-ellipticity condition from this paper turns out to be equivalent, up to a factor depending on $p$, to a condition for systems introduced (and equally named) by Dindo\v{s}, Li and Pipher in arXiv:2007.13190. We prove several key properties of $p$-ellipticity akin to those that have been known to hold in the scalar case (arxiv:1611.00653). In some respects, however, the vector case fundamentally differs from the scalar one. As an application we establish the contractivity on $L^p$ of the operator semigroup generated by systems of elliptic equations with complex coefficients and subject to Dirichlet, Neumann or mixed boundary conditions.

papers.title: Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the $S=1/2$ Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States
papers.abstract: Whether the spin-$1/2$ kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts a gapped $\mathbb{Z}_2$ or a gapless $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid remains a central open question in frustrated magnetism. Here, we address this question by directly computing the triplet gap with a neural-network quantum state that does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure. Applying a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based ansatz to clusters of up to $768$ sites, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies on two-dimensional lattices with periodic boundary conditions and estimate an energy per site of $-0.43873(12)$ in the thermodynamic limit. Finite-size scaling of the magnetic order parameter and triplet excitation gap shows that both extrapolate to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Together, these results provide independent and direct evidence of a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with the $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid. More broadly, they demonstrate that neural-network quantum states can resolve ground-state properties of frustrated quantum magnets that remain challenging for conventional numerical methods.

authors.name: Andreas Raikos
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Flexible ground-state search algorithm on hybrid Clifford-tensor network manifolds
papers.abstract: Tensor network algorithms face challenges in highly entangled regimes, such as systems with periodic boundary conditions (PBC), long-range interactions, or higher dimensions, where the required bond dimension quickly renders computations infeasible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that integrates the stabilizer formalism directly into the traditional density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm. While previous methods have used Clifford unitaries to minimize ground-state entanglement, fundamentally limited to distilling that away utilizing local two-qubit operations, our framework optimizes Clifford transformations to minimize the state's energy. We benchmark our method against standard DMRG at fixed bond dimensions for the Ising model on a ring (including long-range interactions) and on a torus. We observe systematic gains in models with local interactions - as drastic as a factor of 40 decrease in bond dimension in two dimensions. Our algorithm is readily implementable in standard DMRG codes and provides a practical way to substantially reduce algorithm costs, paving the way for large-scale simulation at volumes beyond what is presently achievable.

authors.name: Hari Timsina
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

authors.name: Antonio Francesco Mello
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

authors.name: Meghadeepa Adhikary
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

authors.name: Marcello Dalmonte
authors.institution: The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP)

papers.title: Unveiling Hidden X-ray Broad Line Region in Centaurus A: Broadband Analysis with XRISM and NuSTAR
papers.abstract: We present a broadband X-ray spectral analysis of the radio galaxy Centaurus~A, utilizing simultaneous \textit{XRISM} (Resolve and Xtend) and \textit{NuSTAR} observations. Unlike the previous phenomenological analysis of the Fe K$\alpha$ line (Bogensberger et al. 2025), we employ physical reflection models developed with the radiative transfer code SKIRT. They self-consistently predict the continuum and fluorescent lines from a clumpy torus and an X-ray broad line region (xBLR). The Fe K$\alpha$ complex is well reproduced with a three velocity component model. We interpret this as two narrow torus components (FWHM $= 310\pm50$ and $1900\pm400$~km~s$^{-1}$) and an xBLR component (FWHM $= 6000_{-800}^{+1100}$~km~s$^{-1}$). The inner torus radius of 0.13~pc is 10 times the dust sublimation radius (0.013~pc), implying that the torus in a low-luminosity AGN is not determined by dust-related physics. The xBLR has a substantial covering factor of 0.11--0.36, a hydrogen column density ($5 \times 10^{23}$~cm$^{-2}$), a radius of 0.014~pc from the SMBH, and a mass of $>0.9 M_\odot$. Its mass supply rate is comparable to the accretion rate inferred from the bolometric luminosity, implying efficient xBLR formation even at low Eddington ratios. The xBLR line width also provides a novel estimate of the black-hole mass, $\log{(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})} = 7.00\pm0.34$, via the optical BLR mass-scaling relation to the Fe~K$\alpha$. This agrees with dynamical measurements within a factor of $\sim5$, consistent with the scatter of the optical relation. We also infer the abundance ratios of $A_{\rm Ca}/A_{\rm Fe} = 1.1_{-0.1}^{+0.2}$ and $A_{\rm Ni}/A_{\rm Fe} = 1.4_{-0.2}^{+0.1}$ solar.

authors.name: David Bogensberger
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Kotaro Fukushima
authors.institution: Japan Association of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

papers.title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
papers.abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with \texttt{grep}. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over $91$ repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

authors.name: Jin Qin
authors.institution: The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP)

papers.title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

authors.name: Marta Monti
authors.institution: The Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP)

papers.title: Explaining Cross-Label Decision Structure in Multi-Output Tree Ensembles
papers.abstract: A multi-output tree ensemble predicts several binary labels through decision paths that it largely shares across those labels, yet the attribution methods commonly used to explain such models treat each output in isolation. We propose multi-sink Decision Predicate Graphs (ms-DPGs), which extend decision predicate graphs with one sink per label: each leaf contributes to the sink of every label its in-bag positive count for that label. On this representation we define Shared Predicate Flow (SPF), the share of a label's decision mass that passes through conditions active for both labels of a pair, and a contracted view of the graph in which label-specific lifts indicate whether a shared condition raises the probability of both labels or of one at the expense of the other. Controlled experiments show that SPF captures shared decision conditions rather than mere feature overlap. On nine multi-label benchmarks, native multi-output forests share substantially more decision structure than Binary Relevance on eight, including five of the six on which the two are at predictive parity, even at equal hyperparameters, whereas per-label TreeSHAP rankings register the change of architecture without showing whether more is shared. Because a native forest routes every label through the same splits, SPF describes the fitted model rather than the data, and on eight of the nine benchmarks it rises when the feature-label signal is removed; a high SPF is therefore not evidence of shared predictive information. ms-DPG offers a global, predicate-level account of how a multi-output ensemble reuses decision conditions across its labels.

papers.title: Non-thermal emission from molecular clouds illuminated by continuous cosmic-ray accelerators: application to the stellar cluster W43
papers.abstract: Context: Cosmic rays escaping from their accelerators produce gamma-ray emission through interactions with ambient gas. While the scenario of an impulsive injection of cosmic rays has been extensively studied, that of a continuous injection in time has received comparatively less attention. The latter scenario is particularly relevant for stellar clusters, which may contribute to a non-negligible fraction of Galactic cosmic rays. Aims: We intend to characterize the excesses of cosmic rays around their accelerators and to assess the detectability of the gamma-ray emission resulting from the interactions of cosmic rays in nearby molecular clouds. We focus in particular on star clusters and seek to apply these considerations to the case of W43. Methods: We derive analytical estimates for the cosmic ray excess around sources as a function of source properties and transport parameters. We also evaluate under which conditions the predicted gamma-ray emission from illuminated molecular clouds can be detected by current and future instruments. We then apply these results to explain the gamma-ray emission from the the W43 region. Results: We find that producing detectable gamma-ray emission from molecular clouds illuminated by cosmic rays escaping from star clusters generally requires either suppressed diffusion relative to the Galactic value or anisotropic diffusion, with the latter scenario requiring a smaller global energetic. We applied this approach to the case of W43 and by fitting its gamma-ray emission we were able to constrain the underlying CR transport parameters.

papers.title: Analysis and Design of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes for Pulsed-Jamming-Resilient Space Telemetry
papers.abstract: Jamming is a major threat to space telemetry downlinks, which operate under severe power and bandwidth constraints. This paper develops a jamming-aware analysis and design framework for protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. For pulsed jamming with jamming state information (JSI) at the receiver, we derive a two-state protograph-based extrinsic information transfer (PEXIT) recursion that tracks the messages originating from clean and jammed symbols separately and merges them at the check nodes through a mutual-information-matched Gaussian approximation. For non-interleaved pulsed jamming, we map each pulse realization, through the serialization of the lifted codeword, to a profile of jammed fractions over the variable-node types, and we prove that, under random lifting, this profile determines the local channel-state statistics. The resulting position-dependent thresholds are the objective of a constrained differential-evolution search over protographs, coupling memories, and edge spreadings. At different code rates, the designed ensembles are compared with the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) accumulate, repeat-by-4, and jagged accumulate (AR4JA) LDPC codes whose block length matches the SC-LDPC constraint length, with longer AR4JA codes whose block length is comparable with the size of the sliding window decoder, and with non-optimized SC-LDPC codes. Under pulsed jamming with random pulse positions and with JSI, the ensembles designed over random pulse realizations, decoded through sliding window decoding, reach a bit error rate of $10^{-4}$ at lower signal-to-noise ratios than all the benchmarks.

authors.name: Marco Baldi
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

papers.title: Hund physics in the quarter-filled two-band Hubbard-Kanamori model: Crystal-field splitting and non-local Correlations
papers.abstract:
We address the effect of crystal-field splitting and non-local correlations in the quarter-filled two-orbital
  Hubbard-Kanamori model. The role of the Hund's coupling in this configuration is not obvious since the atomic ground state
  has only one electron per site. Yet, previous works identified fingerprints of the Hund's coupling defining a weak Hund's
  metal at least at finite temperature.
  Using single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) and two-site cellular DMFT based on a selected
  configuration-interaction solver we investigate the zero-temperature properties of the weak Hund's metal. Within DMFT we draw
  the boundary for the weak Hund's metal, which is consistent with previous finite-temperature results.
  Interestingly, we find that the fingerprints of the Hund's coupling are quite robust to the lifting of the orbital
  degeneracy and they survive up to splittings of a quarter of the bandwidth, well beyond those at which a two-stage Kondo
  screening disappears.
  Including non-local correlations in cluster DMFT demonstrates the robustness of the single-site DMFT picture, even if Mott
  localization occurs at smaller interactions. In the metal the intersite correlations are weak and insensitive to $J$, while
  in the localized state we find nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic, antiferro-orbital correlations that are manifest also in the
  mutual information between sites.

authors.name: Diego Florez-Ablan
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

authors.name: Carlos Mejuto-Zaera
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Massimo Capone
authors.institution: Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati

papers.title: A new chemical network to explore the disequilibrium chemistry of silicates and iron in hot gas giants
papers.abstract: Chemical equilibrium modeling of gas giant planet atmospheres has shown that the production and condensation of silicates plays an important role in shaping their final composition. However, no chemical kinetics network for these species are available, preventing the opportunity to analyze the impact of chemical disequilibrium processes. In this paper we present \texttt{SILANE}, a new chemical network that include Mg, Si, Fe and 15 carriers of these elements, including MgSiO$_3$ and Mg$_2$SiO$_4$, ready for use in the VULCAN code. We compare the results of our network with a chemical equilibrium model and discuss them in relation to previous results from literature. We then apply our new network to the analysis of a vertically mixed, Solar-composition atmosphere with equilibrium temperatures $T_{eq}$ in the [700, 1600] K range, finding that (i) rock-forming silicates disappears from the upper atmosphere already at 1100 K, (ii) SiH$_4$ reaches concentrations of $10^{-7}$ in the upper ($P\le 1.0$ bar) atmosphere for planets with $T_{eq}\in$ [800, 1100] K and (iii) the amount of oxygen in refractories decrease from 21\% at $T_{eq}$=700 K to essentially zero already at 1000 K, while in the classical equilibrium framework it remains constant up to $T_{eq}$=1300 K. By applying our network to the case of the young hot Jupiter YSES-1 c and comparing both the mixing ratios of volatile species and the enstatite fraction in the silicate mix, we find evidence of a well-mixed atmosphere, possibly with an average $K_{zz} \ge 10^{10}$ cm$^{2}$s$^{-1}$ up to the $10^{-4}$ bar level.

authors.name: Diego Turrini
authors.institution: Fondazione ICSC Centro Nazionale di Ricerca in High Performance Computing, Big Data e Quantum Computing

papers.title: Hybrid quantum learning for imbalanced blood-cell classification: domain adaptation and classifier design
papers.abstract: Limited annotated data, class imbalance, and morphological similarity make white blood cell classification challenging. We benchmark hybrid variational quantum classifier heads against an affine baseline on 821 microscopy images across seven morphological classes. Using ImageNet-initialised ResNet34 backbones and repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation, we first compare direct transfer with intermediate adaptation on MLL23, a larger peripheral blood cell microscopy dataset. To guide the head comparison, we explore different encoding strategies, variational depth, and the number of independent circuit blocks. We then compare the classifier performance using the affine head and two hybrid heads across multiple random seeds, under a shared training and evaluation protocol. For this comparison, all backbones share the same MLL23-adapted initialisation. Intermediate adaptation increases mean macro-F1 across all four affine-head fine-tuning configurations. The largest gain occurs with a frozen backbone, where macro-F1 rises from $0.685$ to $0.786$, a relative improvement of approximately $14.7\%$. The shallow two-block hybrid head achieves a mean pooled out-of-fold macro-F1 of $0.865 \pm 0.010$, compared with $0.879 \pm 0.008$ for the affine head. The corresponding balanced accuracies are $0.886 \pm 0.008$ and $0.889 \pm 0.010$, respectively. In the architectural exploration, the two-block hybrid head achieves the highest macro-F1 and balanced accuracy among the evaluated hybrid configurations, while the effect of encoding varies across the considered metrics. Our results help guide the design and evaluation of hybrid classifier heads for imbalanced microscopy by linking architectural choices to overall performance and class-specific precision-recall trade-offs.

authors.name: Gabriele D'Angeli
authors.institution: HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland

authors.name: Gianluca Nicchiotti
authors.institution: School of Engineering and Architecture of Fribourg

authors.name: Jerome Extermann
authors.institution: HES-SO University of Applied Sciences and Arts Western Switzerland

papers.title: Regular subgroups of wreath products and Cayley Cartesian products
papers.abstract: The Cartesian product of Cayley graphs is again a Cayley graph. For connected graphs, the converse question reduces to Cartesian powers of Cartesian-prime graphs, and consequently to the study of regular subgroups of wreath products in the product action. We prove that, for a transitive permutation group $G$ of degree $2p$ or $4p$, where $p$ is prime, $G\wr S_2$ contains a regular subgroup if and only if $G$ does, and construct counterexamples of degree $8p$ for every prime $p\equiv3\pmod4$. By modifying this construction, we obtain an infinite family of connected non-Cayley graphs whose Cartesian squares are Cayley graphs, giving a negative answer to the converse question. The smallest graph in our family has $120$ vertices and valency $27$. In contrast, we prove that a connected vertex-transitive graph of order $pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are primes, has a Cayley Cartesian power if and only if the graph itself is Cayley.

papers.title: Sumsets modulo ideals: Baire category and descriptive complexity
papers.abstract:
Given an ideal $\mathcal I$ on the nonnegative integers, we study the family $\Sigma(\mathcal I)$ of all sets for which every $\mathcal{I}$-small modification is not a nontrivial sumset $A+B$. We prove that $\Sigma(\mathcal I)$ is comeager whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an Erd\H{o}s--Ulam ideal generated by a nonincreasing sequence of positive weights. This answers an open question for the ideal $\mathcal{Z}$ of asymptotic density zero sets in [Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. \textbf{151} (2023), 3681--3689].
  We also show that $\Sigma(\mathcal I)$ is either empty or a dense $G_\delta$-complete set whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an $F_\sigma$ ideal which is invariant under finite modifications. This implies that the family of nontrivial sumsets $A+B$ is $F_\sigma$-complete (hence, Borel). On the other hand, we construct a meager ideal $\mathcal{I}$ for which $\Sigma(\mathcal I)$ is neither meager nor comeager. Finally, we prove that $\Sigma(\mathcal Z)$ is coanalytic and not $F_{\sigma\delta}$.

papers.title: A generic $p$-Wasserstein space is isometrically rigid
papers.abstract: We prove for any parameter $p \geq 1$ that the $p$-Wasserstein space $\mathcal{W}_p(X,d_X)$ of a generic compact metric space $(X,d_X)$ is isometrically rigid, that is, its isometries are precisely the push-forwards of the isometries of $(X,d_X).$ We also study the question whether the isometry class of a $p$-Wasserstein space completely determines the isometry class of the underlying space. We prove for any $p\geq 1$ that for a generic compact metric space $(X,d_X),$ its $p$-Wasserstein space $\mathcal{W}_p(X,d_X)$ is isometric to another $p$-Wasserstein space $\mathcal{W}_p(Y,d_Y)$ if and only if $(Y,d_Y)$ is isometric to $(X,d_X).$ En route we prove that a stronger property, which we call the Dirac preservation property, is also generic.

authors.name: Tamas Titkos
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

authors.name: Daniel Virosztek
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Continuous Phase-Coherent Readout of a Magneto-Mechanical Resonator Using a Phase-Locked Loop
papers.abstract: Magneto-mechanical resonators are wireless sensors that encode a measurand in their natural frequency. Existing systems estimate this frequency from repeated cycles of excitation and ring-down, which limits the precision and bandwidth range. Here, we introduce a continuous, phase-coherent readout based on a phase-locked loop. In a benchtop setup, one record stayed within 4 % of the precision-bandwidth limit over more than three decades of bandwidth, while conventional readouts remained about a factor of 4 above it.

papers.title: Clustering-Based Artificial Tree Ensembles for Random Forest Approximation
papers.abstract: Random Forests (RFs) offer strong prediction performance but are difficult to interpret. Most representative trees (MRTs) and artificial representative trees (ARTs) provide surrogate explanations, but a single tree may miss patterns within a forest. We investigate benefits and limitations of clustering-based representative tree ensembles for RF surrogate modeling and assess the contribution of similarity-based clustering relative to random tree partitions. Using linear and nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, we evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability against equally sized ensembles of top-ranked MRTs and randomly selected trees. Increasing ensemble size generally improves fidelity, accuracy, and prediction stability. ART ensembles show higher fidelity in simulations and often greater prediction stability for small ensembles. Compared with random tree partitions, similarity-based clustering generally improves ART fidelity in simulations and often on benchmarks. On benchmark datasets, MRT-based ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and prediction accuracy, whereas ART ensembles have fewer terminal nodes. ART ensembles provide compact surrogates when reduced complexity matters and their fidelity and prediction accuracy meet application requirements. These findings clarify both the trade-offs of representative tree ensembles as RF surrogates and the contribution of similarity-based clustering beyond random clustering.

papers.title: Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors for Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights from the CAPSARII project
papers.abstract:
The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback).
  As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: $\mathrm{Accuracy}=0.901\!\pm\!0.023$, $\mathrm{F1}=0.920\!\pm\!0.019$), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ($0.963\!\pm\!0.025$), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains.
  A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.

papers.title: Noise and quasi-periodic oscillations in black hole accretion flows
papers.abstract: Temporal fluctuations of the viscosity parameter at different radii in an accretion flow are known to give rise to variability in the accretion rate onto the black hole. The power spectrum of accretion-rate fluctuations is expected to exhibit a broad-band power-law dependence on frequency (e.g., flicker noise). We show that viscosity fluctuations can also generate quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the power spectrum. In our model, QPOs are caused by reflection of accretion-rate fluctuations at the outer radius of the accretion flow and arise near the low-frequency break of the power spectrum, which corresponds to the inverse viscous timescale at the outer radius. These QPOs occur in geometrically thick advection-dominated accretion flows but are absent in geometrically thin cooling-dominated flows.

papers.title: Measurement of Magnonic Quantum Geometry
papers.abstract: Quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in macroscopic quantum phenomena, including quantum Hall effects and flat-band superconductivity. However, since quantum geometry is encoded in wavefunctions rather than energy spectra, direct experimental characterization remains a formidable challenge. This challenge is particularly acute for quasiparticles in quantum materials, whose wavefunctions are generally inferred from effective low-energy models rather than measured directly. Here, we establish an experimental framework for characterizing the quantum geometry of magnons, a ubiquitous Bosonic quasiparticle of magnetically ordered states. We show that the inelastic neutron scattering (INS) cross-section measures geometric parameters of the spinor wavefunctions of ferromagnets. By tracking the energy- and momentum-dependent INS intensity, we extract the quantum geometric tensor without requiring detailed knowledge of microscopic spin-spin interactions. Our results establish magnons as an ideal arena for experimentally probing quantum geometry and open new avenues for exploring geometry-driven magnon transport and quantum Fisher information in magnetic materials.

papers.title: Blow-up profile decomposition and optimal Harnack inequalities for the $n$-Liouville equation
papers.abstract: We consider the problem $- \Delta_n u = h(x) e^u$ in a bounded domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb R^n$, where $\Delta_n$ stands for the $n$-Laplacian and $h$ is a continuous function satisfying $0 < a \leq h \leq b$. Several new a priori estimates are obtained for the sets of solutions whose boundary oscillation is uniformly bounded by some constant. Those results are exploited to provide a profile decomposition in $L^\infty$-sense for a sequence of blowing-up solutions. We also present an optimal Harnack type inequality, which states that on a compact set $K \subset \Omega$ we have a universal estimate $\displaystyle \sup_K u + (n-1)\displaystyle \inf_{\Omega} u \leq C$.

papers.title: Hydration-induced local diffusivity heterogeneity modulates aqueous $H_2+OH$ reaction kinetics
papers.abstract: At room temperature, a Kramers reaction rate calculated with homogeneous solvent friction exceeds the measured rate of the aqueous reaction $H_2 + OH -> H + H_2O$ by about an order of magnitude. We show that spatially correlated hydration-induced diffusivity fluctuations increase effective friction and suppress the predicted escape rate. Estimates based on hydration-shell properties bring the theoretical rate closer to experiment. The suppression weakens with increasing temperature, linking local solvent heterogeneity to activated aqueous reaction kinetics.

papers.title: Chang's Omitting Types Theorem in Lukasiewicz Logic
papers.abstract: We prove Chang-style omitting types theorems for standard first-order Lukasiewicz logic. Starting from a prescribed model $M$, we obtain an extension that omits higher-complexity types while preserving lower-level types already realized in $M$. If $T$ is a $\Pi_{n+2}$-theory, every model of $T$ has an exact extension that preserves its realized $\Sigma_{n+1}$-types and omits every $\Sigma_{n+2}$-type not generated by a $\Sigma_{n+1}$-type. An iterated construction also omits infinity-universal types, whose unbounded quantifier complexity cannot eventually be generated by the corresponding lower-complexity fragments of a single type. The main tool is a refinement of Robinson's infinite forcing sensitive to the quantifier complexity of formulas.

papers.title: The automorphism group of the super Jordan plane
papers.abstract: We complete the description of the automorphism group of the super Jordan plane $\mathcal B$ over a field of characteristic zero, extending the classification of super-automorphisms obtained by N. Andruskiewitsch and F. Dumas in \cite{AD}. We characterize a subgroup $\mathbb L$ stabilizing two one-dimensional vector spaces and obtain two semidirect product decompositions of it. This subgroup contains all super-automorphisms and its structure motivates our main result. Precisely, we prove that $\operatorname{Aut}\mathcal B=\operatorname{Inn}\mathcal B\rtimes\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{super}}\mathcal B$, where $\operatorname{Inn}\mathcal B$ and $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{super}}\mathcal B$ denote, respectively, the groups of inner automorphisms and super-automorphisms of $\mathcal B$. We also characterize the nilpotent elements of $\mathcal B$ and prove that every nonzero nilpotent has nilpotency index two. Furthermore, we give a geometric interpretation of three distinguished families of nilpotent elements. After degree truncation and projectivization, two of these families yield projective linear subspaces, while the third yields quadratic Veronese varieties of arbitrary dimension.

papers.title: Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay for Continual Cardiac Ultrasound Segmentation
papers.abstract: Conventional experience replay typically applies fixed preservation constraints to historical exemplars, overlooking variations in how learned representations, predictions, and anatomical structures change during sequential training. To address this limitation, we propose Drift-Conditioned Structural Replay Loss (DCSRL), an exemplar-adaptive supervision mechanism that regulates anatomical preservation according to source-referenced knowledge drift. DCSRL operates within a reliability-guided replay framework that selects informative historical exemplars using anatomical content and boundary characteristics while adaptively regulating replay during training. For each retained exemplar, DCSRL constructs a frozen source-task reference signature and subsequently measures changes in feature representations, class probabilities, boundary responses, and predicted anatomical structures. These complementary drift measurements are aggregated and normalized to generate bounded, exemplar-specific coefficients that dynamically adjust boundary and structural replay losses without modifying the underlying memory-selection policy. We evaluate DCSRL under sequential learning across CAMUS, CardiacNet, and EchoNet-Dynamic, comparing its performance with regularization-, distillation-, and replay-based continual-learning approaches. Experimental findings indicate that DCSRL improves overall final segmentation performance and anatomical boundary preservation, particularly under heterogeneous imaging conditions, although trade-offs remain in knowledge transfer across tasks. These findings suggest that source-referenced multidimensional drift conditioning offers a promising direction for adaptive anatomical knowledge preservation in continual cardiac ultrasound segmentation.

papers.title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
papers.abstract: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circ\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.
