papers.title: Functional Information, Optimal Channel Simulation and Lossy Source Coding
papers.abstract:
We characterize, within a constant number of bits, the minimum achievable rate for several one-shot coding problems, such as channel simulation and lossy source coding. The basis of our work is a new information measure between random variables $X, Y$ that we call the functional information $I_F(X \to Y)$. We show that this quantity characterizes the minimum one-shot rate $R^*(X \to Y)$ of channel simulation, in which a sample $Y \sim P_{Y \mid X}$ is communicated in the presence of common randomness: $I_F(X \to Y) \leq R^*(X \to Y) < I_F(X \to Y) + 1.45$. For the achievability result, we construct an explicit code using the Poisson functional representation.
  Using these results, we develop new bounds for one-shot variable-rate lossy source coding: given some distortion measure $\Delta$, we use $I_F(X \to Y)$ to define the functional rate-distortion function $R_F$. Then, letting $R_O$ denote the one-shot operational rate-distortion function with private encoder randomness and distortion measure $\Delta$, we make use of our channel simulation result to show that $R_F(D) \leq R_O(D) < R_F(D) + 2.45$ at every positive distortion level $D$.
  Finally, we generalize our channel simulation result by introducing the R\'enyi $\alpha$-functional information $I_{F, \alpha}(X \to Y)$ and show that it characterizes the minimum Arimoto-R\'enyi conditional entropy for channel simulation, ${R^*_\alpha(X \to Y)}$, associated with the Campbell cost: ${I_{F, \alpha}(X \to Y) \leq R^*_{\alpha}(X \to Y) \leq I_{F, \alpha}(X \to Y) + O(1/\alpha)}$.

papers.title: Solving the Discretised Shallow Water Equations on Distorted Structured Grids with Neural Physics
papers.abstract:
This paper presents a method for solving the shallow water equations on highly distorted structured grids using convolution-based operators following the Neural Physics approach. By mapping distorted physical grids to a uniform computational domain with Jacobian transformations, the governing advection and diffusion operators are reformulated in a structured convolutional form. This enables the use of efficient stencil-based operations and, following the Neural Physics concept, we do this through convolutional layers whose weights are determined by the chosen numerical methods rather than by training.
  The method introduces consistent mass-lumped formulations, conservative and non-conservative advection forms, and a diffusion operator, all expressed as convolutions. A nonlinear Petrov-Galerkin stabilisation is incorporated to control numerical oscillations on distorted meshes. Two approximations for the Laplacian operator are also proposed to accelerate pressure and diffusion solves. The framework is validated using the Carlisle 2005 flood event, demonstrating accurate predictions of water depth and velocity on distorted meshes for both linear and quadratic discretisations.
  The results show that distorted structured grids can retain conservation, stability and accuracy, whilst adapting the mesh statically. The convolutional formulation makes the method well suited to Neural Physics implementations and GPU acceleration, offering a scalable approach for flood modelling and large-scale geophysical simulations.

papers.title: Pair Correlation Conjecture for the Zeros of Artin $L$-functions I: Simple and Critical Zeros
papers.abstract: In 1973, Montgomery posed the pair correlation conjecture (PCC) for the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Motivated by PCC, Montgomery conjectured that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are almost surely simple, and proved that at least $2/3$ are simple assuming the Riemann hypothesis (RH). In 1978, Mueller and Gallagher were able to prove asymptotically $100\%$ are simple assuming PCC and RH. Recently, Goldston et al. noticed that the assumption of RH can be removed in Mueller and Gallagher's method. In fact, assuming PCC by itself without RH is sufficient to prove that asymptotically $100\%$ of the nontrivial zeros are both simple and on the critical line. We adapt the notion of horizontal multiplicity from Goldston et al. to show that the nontrivial zeros of Artin $L$-functions attached to irreducible linear representation of the Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ are almost surely simple and lie on the critical line without assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH). We will assume the appropriate version of PCC along with some other widely believed conjectures.

papers.title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
papers.abstract: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

papers.title: Efficient Multi-View Generation with Iterative Global-Local Proxy Attention
papers.abstract: Generating consistent multi-view RGB images and normal maps from a single input image provides complementary appearance and geometric cues for 3D reconstruction. However, maintaining cross-view consistency requires information exchange across viewpoints, and dense cross-view attention becomes computationally expensive as the number of views and spatial resolution increase. In this paper, we propose Global-Local Proxy Attention (GLPA) to reduce cross-view communication costs while preserving fine-grained within-view processing. Specifically, GLPA retains full-resolution interactions within each view and uses compact global proxies for cross-view communication. To further leverage the exchanged information, GLPA incorporates iterative proxy refinement, which rebuilds the proxies from updated features and reuses the same attention parameters for subsequent interactions within a single denoising step. We evaluate GLPA on two structurally different diffusion backbones, FLUX and Stable Diffusion. Experiments on FLUX show that GLPA achieves a $2.65\times$ speedup in attention computation per denoising step over dense attention, while improving reconstruction IoU from 0.6849 to 0.7019 and reducing NVS LPIPS from 0.086 to 0.076. Results on Stable Diffusion further demonstrate the effectiveness of GLPA, with a $1.80\times$ attention speedup and improvements across all five quality metrics.

authors.name: Kunming Luo
authors.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: MSAR: Next-Scale Autoregressive Forecasting for Time Series via Modular Multi-Scale Decoupling
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting underpins critical applications in finance, energy, healthcare, and transportation. Although deep models have achieved strong results, most adopt single-scale modeling or restrict multiscale processing to the input side, causing a misalignment between multiscale inputs and single-scale outputs and limiting predictive power. We introduce the Modular Scale-wise Autoregressive Framework (MSAR), a model-agnostic design that forecasts progressively across multiple temporal resolutions. MSAR offers three advantages: (1) scale-wise aligned modeling, which disentangles heterogeneous temporal patterns by aligning inputs and outputs at each scale; (2) scale-wise autoregression, where coarse-scale predictions guide finer-scale forecasting through hierarchical information flow; and (3) a modular architecture, enabling seamless integration with diverse backbones such as CNNs, MLPs, and Transformers. Extensive experiments across a broad set of datasets and forecasting models demonstrate that MSAR achieves consistent improvements in both accuracy and inference efficiency, validating the effectiveness of scale-aligned autoregression for multiscale time series forecasting. The code is available at: https://github.com/Oryxo/MSAR.

papers.title: Parametrised-Quadratic Interface Reconstruction and Geometric Velocity Extension in the Volume-of-Fluid Framework
papers.abstract:
A conservative Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) framework using local parametric-curve interface reconstruction (PI-VOF) is developed for geometric interface propagation on fixed Cartesian grids. While VOF methods achieve conservative and second-order accurate interface advection under prescribed velocity fields, normal-velocity-driven interface propagation requires the interfacial velocity to be extended to neighbouring staggered-grid locations.
  Existing studies on interface evolution employ auxiliary distance functions, kernel smoothers, or high-resolution VOF in multiple grids to compute propagation velocities and address first-order-accuracy limitations. In contrast, PI-VOF directly employs higher-order parametric interface geometry for local normal-velocity extension, aiming to achieve second-order accurate interface evolution on fixed Cartesian grids. The resulting velocity field is employed in conservative geometric advection using a directionally split Eulerian-implicit and Lagrangian-explicit (EI-LE) scheme, while the reconstructed interface provides the geometric information required for curvature evaluation and the ghost-fluid finite-difference discretisation of sharp interfacial Dirichlet conditions. Static reconstruction and reversible-vortex advection tests demonstrate higher-order interface geometry and approximately second-order transport convergence, with mass conservation to the chosen tolerance on refined grids. Prescribed normal-velocity and curvature-dependent propagation tests establish near second-order convergence. Coupled Stefan benchmarks involving capillarity and attachment kinetics demonstrate approximately second-order thermal convergence and decreasing interface errors under mesh refinement. The results establish a geometric formulation connecting conservative VOF transport, local normal-velocity extension, and sharp Stefan conditions for evolving interfaces.

papers.title: Galaxy number counts in area distance space
papers.abstract: We investigate how galaxy clustering changes when area distance is used as the radial coordinate. We derive the linear relativistic number counts for a flux-selected population and compare them with redshift and luminosity distance space. Source motion does not change the beam area at a fixed emission event, so area-distance clustering has no Kaiser distortion. Lensing changes both the angular and radial positions of sources, and can enhance area-distance clustering while weakening its correlation with redshift-space clustering. Observer motion shifts area-distance shells in the opposite direction to redshift and luminosity-distance shells, allowing their kinematic dipoles to point in opposite directions. A combination of the three count fields cancels their common intrinsic density and explicit evolution and magnification biases, leaving a signal dominated by velocities nearby and optical effects at larger distances. We relate this signal to galaxy-size magnification, so that its correlations can be inferred statistically without precise distances to individual galaxies.

papers.title: Palmprint Decomposer: Interpretable and Editable Factorization via Synthetic Learning and Instance-Wise Refinement
papers.abstract: Palmprint recognition and synthesis methods focus on extracting discriminative textures or generating images with varied textures and appearances. However, they do not generally provide an explicit image-level representation that separates palmprint texture from its underlying base appearance for independent analysis or controlled editing. We introduce Palmprint Decomposer, an interpretable framework that represents a palmprint through independently editable factors and reconstructs the image through a multiplicative composition model. A color map and a light map characterize the base appearance, while a structure map and a global texture strength parameter describe texture modulation. However, accurate reconstruction alone does not guarantee separation of palmprint texture from base appearance, as fine palmprint textures may leak into the estimated base appearance. To mitigate this ambiguity, we train the decomposer exclusively on synthetic data with direct factor supervision, using asymmetric decoding paths and decomposition constraints to suppress texture leakage. Instance-Wise Refinement further improves real-image reconstruction by directly optimizing the predicted factors for each input without relying on the trained network. Experiments across seven datasets demonstrate high reconstruction fidelity, with the extracted structure maps generally achieving verification performance comparable to the original images. Compared with existing methods, our approach achieves better factor separation while preserving more discriminative palmprint texture information.

papers.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

papers.title: Finite-order exponential mixing does not imply the central limit theorem for unique equilibrium states
papers.abstract: Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold of dimension at least three, $\varphi:M\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and $R\ge2$ be an integer. We construct a $\mathcal C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $T:M\to M$ and an observable $f\in\mathcal C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ such that $(T,\varphi)$ has a unique equilibrium state $\mu$ and $\mu(f)=0$. The system $(T,\mu)$ is exponentially mixing of order $R$ but not of order $R+1$ for H\"older observables, and $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f\circ T^i$ does not satisfy the central limit theorem. The main results have been formalised in Lean 4.

papers.title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
papers.abstract: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

papers.title: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging models are predominantly developed on healthy sleepers and generalize poorly to clinical populations with fragmented sleep. Across three cohorts (patients with stroke, isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder, and other sleep disorders), we observe 2-3x more awakenings per hour, nearly twice as much N1, and less REM sleep than in healthy sleepers. We propose a label-efficient teacher-student framework for wearable-scale sleep staging. SleepGPT (136M parameters), adapted using labels from 25% of training patients, supervises a causal CNN-GRU (31k parameters; 122 KB) that stages EEG, EOG, or both in real time. We introduce Gcv-TAD, a new black-box transition-aware distillation loss. It emphasizes uncommon stage transitions while discounting those that vary across patients, using a prior estimated from labelled patients. In patient-wise 10-fold cross-validation, Gcv-TAD improves per-patient macro F1 over supervised training on the same labels by +3.2 to +7.6 points on average. Gains are largest on N1, and performance approaches full-label training.

papers.title: The $N$-channel white-noise Schr\"odinger operator in all three Dyson classes. I. Explicit stationary admittance distribution, density of states and outgoing Kontsevich matrix Airy integrals
papers.abstract: We obtain an explicit stationary distribution of the matrix Riccati variable---the boundary admittance---for an $N$-channel Schr\"odinger operator with Gaussian white-noise disorder, in all three Dyson symmetry classes $\beta=1,2,4$. Uniform absorption regularizes the Riccati dynamics, and the distribution's normalization factorizes into outgoing Kontsevich matrix Airy integrals. This gives a common route to the density of states and the sum of Lyapunov exponents, extending Halperin's scalar solution to coupled channels. Exact finite-$N$ formulas connect two spectral regimes: the Lifshitz tail, including its symmetry-dependent prefactor, and the collective large-$N$ edge. We reduce the $\beta=4$ and even-$N$ $\beta=1$ problems to unitary orthogonal polynomials and an auxiliary recursion. Their critical double-scaling limit yields edge profiles on the $N^{-4/5}$ energy scale, governed by a complex Painlev\'e-I tritronqu\'ee solution and a linear auxiliary equation. We conjecture that these profiles describe a universal edge regime of random band matrices.

papers.title: Reconstruction and Forecast of Extreme Waves from a Single Observation
papers.abstract: The state space of a dynamical system can, under suitable conditions, be reconstructed from a single observational time-series through delay-coordinate embedding. However, reconstructing the spatiotemporal evolution of nonlinear water waves from highly sparse measurements remains a considerable challenge. Here, by combining deep learning, compressed sensing, and the self-similarity properties of unidirectional nonlinear water wave evolution equation, we show that the evolving surface elevation of a highly nonlinear wave field can be reconstructed from observations collected at a {\it single} measurement location. We subsequently use these reconstructions to forecast rogue waves associated with self-focusing soliton dynamics from point observations obtained in controlled water wave tank experiments, demonstrating excellent agreement with measurements of the fully evolved wave field. Our results show that extreme wave events can be forecast from remarkably sparse observations and provide a framework that may be extended to other nonlinear dispersive systems governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity.

papers.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
papers.abstract: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

papers.title: On the regularity of branching loci for $\mathbb{Z}_2$-harmonic spinors
papers.abstract: We show that the branching locus of a $\mathbb Z_2$-harmonic spinor is smooth (resp. real-analytic) near every point of frequency $\frac{1}{2}$ for smooth (resp. real-analytic) ambient defining data. This partially strengthens the previous regularity results obtained by Clifford Taubes and Boyu Zhang.

papers.title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
papers.abstract:
These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly.
  The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students.
  The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

papers.title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
papers.abstract: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

papers.title: Stability-Compensated Threshold Calibration for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-\delta$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.

authors.name: Zhiyuan Wang
authors.institution: China University of Petroleum, East China

authors.name: Xiaoshuang Shi
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
papers.abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

papers.title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
papers.abstract: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

authors.name: Siyuan Du
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Beijing

authors.name: Yuxin Liu
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making
papers.abstract: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.

papers.title: Quantum Cohomology and irrationality of K\"uchle fourfolds
papers.abstract: We prove that very general K\"uchle fourfolds of types (c1), (c6), (b8), and (b11) are irrational. The key ingredients are a new rationality criterion, based on the theory of Hodge atoms due to Katzarkov--Kontsevich--Pantev--Yu and its integral extension by Gu\'er\'e, and a computation of the action of quantum multiplication on the vanishing cohomology of these fourfolds, which uses a version of the Quantum Lefschetz Hyperplane Principle. Quantum multiplication acts as a scalar on the vanishing cohomology, and we give an enumerative interpretation of this scalar.

papers.title: SPLAT: An Event-Specific System Response Model for Continuous-Domain List-Mode TOF PET
papers.abstract: Modern position-sensitive PET detectors provide continuous estimates of photon interaction position and event-specific timing, energy, and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. We introduce Spatial Probability Localization and Transformation (SPLAT), a continuous-domain, event-specific projection model for time-of-flight (TOF) list-mode PET. Each coincidence is represented by a three-dimensional spatial response kernel incorporated into consistent forward and adjoint operators without detector-coordinate binning. While supporting general response distributions, we develop an anisotropic Gaussian implementation whose center is determined by measured interaction positions and TOF difference, and whose full covariance follows from propagating measurement uncertainties through event geometry. The model accounts for DOI, photon non-collinearity, and energy-dependent, correlated, and depth-dependent detector responses. Using GATE Monte Carlo simulations with known annihilation positions, we compare continuous and virtually segmented representations of identical accepted coincidences. Event-localization diagnostics and point-source and brain-phantom reconstructions assess model accuracy and image formation. The Gaussian formulation also yields information-equivalent count gain, an approximate measure of relative spatial information accounting for localization uncertainty and detection efficiency. Results support the value of event-specific modeling, particularly measured DOI, while an optimized GPU implementation demonstrates computational feasibility. SPLAT provides a flexible framework for incorporating detailed detector measurements directly into PET reconstruction.

papers.title: Renormalization group study of critical behavior of $O(m)$ model with cubic anisotropy and extended defects: two-loop approximation
papers.abstract: We study the impact of quenched extended defects correlated in $\epsilon_d$ dimensions and randomly distributed in the remaining $d - \epsilon_d$ dimensions on the critical properties of a $d$-dimensional $O(m)$-symmetric system with cubic anisotropy. Exploiting the field-theoretic renormalization-group approach within the minimal subtraction scheme, we compute the two-loop renormalization-group functions. Applying resummation techniques to analyze the asymptotic series, we estimate the marginal values of $\epsilon_d$ above which disorder becomes relevant for the physically important cases $m = 2$ and $m = 3$ in $d = 3$. We report numerical values of the critical exponents for the disorder-induced universality classes.

authors.institution: Yukhnovskii Institute for Condensed Matter Physics of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine

papers.title: Where AI Use Is Normalized, Author Seniority but Not AI Disclosure Biases Code Review
papers.abstract: Code-review tools increasingly display whether an author used AI when preparing pull requests. Recent studies report that AI disclosure makes reviewers rate otherwise identical work as less competent, with the penalty falling hardest on already-marginalized authors. In a within-subjects experiment in an AI-normalized organization, 447 software engineers each reviewed the same four code snippets under an AI-use disclosure embedded in the commit message and author-seniority labels. AI disclosure did not bias perceptions of code effectiveness or author competence, whereas a seniority label significantly biased both. Together, these findings show no detected penalty for disclosed AI use in this setting, while confirming that the author information shown in code review can still bias evaluations.

authors.name: Jina Suh
authors.institution: University of the District of Columbia

papers.title: Level Up! AI-Driven Challenges and Adaptations to Code Review Practices
papers.abstract: AI can write code faster than humans can review, causing a bottleneck and necessitating changes to code review practices. This bottleneck is hotly debated, giving rise to two extreme and orthogonal imagined futures: one where humans continue to be firmly entrenched in the review process, and one where AI agents merge pull requests entirely without human involvement. Yet, these futures remain rooted in folk wisdom. Through a mixed-methods study of interviews ($n = 24$) and a survey ($n = 2{,}590$) at a large, multinational software company with widespread access to AI, we identify AI-driven code review challenges and strategies reported as effective to meet them. We found that AI enables, necessitates, and complicates a shift in the human reviewer's role toward high-level concerns (e.g., design and intent). We found that AI-assisted authoring results in increased burden for reviewers due to challenges such as a lack of author stewardship and PR volume and size, potentially leading to downstream debt. Our survey showed AI review usage was not correlated with less difficulty keeping up with PR volume, indicating using AI for review alone is not sufficient for solving AI-driven review challenges. Developers found the most useful strategies to be organizations supporting and resourcing review, pushing review burden upstream, and prioritizing reviewer attention on the concerns that matter most.

papers.title: A Taxonomy and Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark Reduction for Spreadsheet Tasks
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets let millions of end users without programming training do computational work, and teams are increasingly building AI agents to help them. Evaluating each candidate agent configuration across many tasks is costly. Benchmark reduction can lower this cost by selecting a small subset of tasks whose outcomes predict full-benchmark scores, but selecting tasks only for predictive accuracy can leave whole categories of spreadsheet work untested. We contribute a taxonomy of spreadsheet tasks, grounded in a review of benchmarks and refined with the Excel Agent product team at Microsoft, and a benchmark-reduction method that favors taxonomic diversity among similarly predictive choices. On benchmark logs from Microsoft, taxonomy-guided selection broadens coverage at little or no cost in predictive accuracy and often improves prediction on configurations excluded from selection. Broader coverage can therefore support, rather than compromise, predictive accuracy. Generalization remains limited across time: subsets selected using little recent history predict poorly for configurations much later in time. Beyond benchmark reduction, the taxonomy provides a reusable framework for auditing gaps in task coverage, as teams at Microsoft have done.

papers.title: Averaging for multi-scale McKean-Vlasov equation
papers.abstract: We consider a system of Stochastic Differential Equations with two time scales, so called slow-fast system of SDEs. As customary when studying slow-fast dynamics, we seek a coarse grained description of the system, obtained, in the limit of scale separation, by 'averaging out' the fast component of the dynamics (so-called averaging limit). We study slow-fast systems where the fast variable is described by a process which is non-linear in the sense of McKean i.e. by an SDE whose coefficients depend on the law of the process itself, while the slow variable is a linear SDE (linear in the sense of McKean). We show that, when the fast variable is a McKean-Vlasov process and, additionally, the coefficients of the SDE depend on the position of the slow process, the limit of scale separation is not provided by the usual ansatz which one would expect by applying classical averaging paradigms. We identify the limit and provide complete proof.

papers.title: Relaxation of one-dimensional variational problems without growth constraints
papers.abstract: We study the integral representation of the relaxation of integral functionals of the form u-> \int f(x,u(x),u'(x)) dx, for Sobolev functions u\,: (a, b) $\rightarrow$ RN with fixed Dirichlet boundary conditions. Unlike classical works on the subject, we require a very mild growth condition on the Lagrangian f to make our statement as natural and general as possible. We state four different situations in which we manage to obtain an explicit expression for the relaxation on BV , which is usually the natural framework for such weak growth conditions. Our goal is also to express a few unifying assumptions on the Lagrangian to obtain the expected relaxation formula.

papers.title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
papers.abstract: We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design variables.We focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic specification.We instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional routing.This turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

papers.title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

authors.name: Chao Zhang
authors.institution: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs

papers.title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
papers.abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

authors.name: Runze Zhang
authors.institution: Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: Cluster-Robust Inference in Small Samples Using Bias Corrections
papers.abstract: This paper derives an exact expression for the bias of the linearized estimator of the variance for cluster-robust inference, which generalizes an earlier result derived by Bell and McCaffrey (2002). Both cases of continuous and binary treatments are discussed. Under the former it is shown that the bias of the linearized variance estimator and its jackknife variant are of order $G^{-1}$ relative to the true variance, where $G$ denotes the total number of clusters. A bias-corrected variance estimator (BCCV) is then proposed and shown to have a relative bias of order $G^{-2}$. In the case of models with binary treatments the orders of the bias of standard estimators and the proposed bias-corrected one are shown to be $\max (G_{1}^{-1},G_{0}^{-1})$ and $\max (G_{1}^{-2},G_{0}^{-2})$, where $G_{1}$ and $G_{0}=G-G_{1}$ are the numbers of treated and untreated clusters. Scale and degrees of freedom adjustments to the $t$-statistic computed using bias-corrected standard errors are also proposed. Small sample properties of the proposed BCCV test are investigated using Monte Carlo experiments. It is shown that the proposed test generally outperforms tests based on conventional and jackknife cluster standard errors, and performs comparably to wild bootstrap inference and the recent jackknife distribution-adjusted testing procedure by \cite{hansen2026jackknife}. The utility of the proposed test is illustrated\ using three empirical applications from the literature.

papers.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

papers.title: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
papers.abstract: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

papers.title: Clinician Assessment of Laryngeal Disease with Auditory AI before Laryngoscopy: A Paired Reader Study
papers.abstract:
Background: Before laryngoscopy, clinicians assess the likely cause of hoarseness and whether to suspect a precancerous or malignant lesion. Whether voice-based artificial intelligence (AI) supports pre-laryngoscopic categorization is unknown.
  Methods: We developed an auditory large language model that generates a patient-level assessment card (provisional category, voice-quality ratings, and rationale) and a prespecified malignancy alert from voice recordings, patient information, and acoustic measures obtained before laryngoscopy at one center. We evaluated both in a held-out test set and a later cohort. In a sequential reader study, 32 otolaryngology clinicians categorized held-out cases without AI and, 1 to 2 weeks later, reviewed their initial categories with the card (without the alert).
  Results: Across 800 paired assessments, reader accuracy was 49.8% before and 56.8% after review (difference, 7.0 percentage points; 95% CI, 1.7 to 13.5; P < 0.001); 99 categories changed from incorrect to correct and 43 from correct to incorrect (ratio, 2.30; 95% CI, 1.22 to 5.31). Accuracy rose 14.7 points when the model was correct and fell 8.7 when incorrect. Provisional-category accuracy was 72% in held-out testing and 67% in temporal validation. The malignancy alert flagged 85.7% and 86.8% of precancerous or malignant lesions. Sensitivity for precancerous or malignant lesions increased from 53.9% to 75.0% after AI-assisted review (difference, 21.1 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.3 to 42.0).
  Conclusions: In this single-center study, clinicians' pre-laryngoscopic categorization accuracy was higher after reviewing the AI assessment card, although the sequential design cannot fully separate AI assistance from reassessment; gains depended on model correctness without clearly selective adoption. Randomized and external evaluations, including of the malignancy alert, are needed.

authors.institution: Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ, USA (United States)

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

papers.title: Streaming across viewing conditions - The effect of viewing distance and display luminance on video quality
papers.abstract: The visibility of streamed video distortions is affected by the user's display and viewing conditions, such as their display's luminance or the viewing distance. Distortions become less visible at lower luminance levels or farther viewing distances. However, most image and video quality metrics assume fixed optimal display and viewing conditions, making them insensitive to the viewing conditions. In this work, we demonstrate how existing metrics can be adapted to account for both factors and compare such an adaptation with the metrics that natively model viewing conditions. First, we collected a new video quality dataset, HDR-VDC, which contains streaming distortions in 4K HDR videos. The dataset consists of 12 4K and 4 FHD HDR source video content, each distorted with AV1 encoding and Lanczos upscaling from a lower resolution. The quality loss due to the distortions was measured at two viewing distances, corresponding to 60 and 120 pixels per visual degree, and two display mean luminance levels, varying by a factor of 8 in terms of luminance. Next, we developed a pre-processing framework that lets us adapt many quality metrics so that they can evaluate content across the viewing distances and luminance levels. The framework employs a display model and perceptually uniform encoding, PU21, to account for the effect of display luminance, and perspective projection scaling (PPS) to account for the effect of viewing distance. We used the framework to compare the performance of 35 state-of-the-art metrics. This allowed us to identify a selection of existing quality metrics that can be effectively adapted to account for the viewing conditions.

papers.title: Estimating Outpatient Visit Prices from Hospital Price Transparency Data using Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
Objective: Hospital care prices in the United States have increased substantially, yet patients lack effective tools to access and compare costs. We aimed to develop and evaluate an LLM-based approach for improving access to and use of hospital price transparency (PT) data.
  Materials and Methods: To estimate visit prices, we used a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework to analyze PT files from three major hospitals in Maryland and the surrounding region. We compared BM25, OpenAI embedding models, and a GPT-BM25 hybrid against a no-RAG baseline for cost estimation of individual procedures and procedure groups, then evaluated the best approach for symptom-based visit cost estimation using synthetic simulations.
  Results: Across hospitals, the GPT-BM25 retriever achieved the best performance, with average price MAPE of 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for groups, compared with 147.98% and 82.82%, respectively, for the no-RAG baseline. In simulations, our framework correctly identified approximately 50% of reference procedures and reduced MAPE relative to the LLM-only baseline at two of the three hospitals, while achieving comparable performance at the third.
  Discussion: Our framework uses RAG to improve care price estimation in real-world settings. Compared with the no-RAG baseline, it substantially improved cost estimates for both individual procedures and procedure groups. Improvements were smaller in synthetic simulations, likely because inferring procedures from clinical information is more complex. Practical challenges remain, including heterogeneous PT file formats, unexplained duplicate entries, and limited availability of insurer-negotiated rates.
  Conclusion: LLMs that effectively integrate PT data show strong potential to provide patients with more accessible and accurate healthcare cost estimates.

papers.title: QASK-Edit: Adaptive Sparse Attention Across Queries and Key Sources for Efficient Video Editing
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.

papers.title: One Code per Material: Neural Representation and Generation of Measured BTFs
papers.abstract: Measured bidirectional texture functions (BTFs) capture the full appearance of real materials--including parallax, self-shadowing and inter-reflections that analytic SVBRDFs cannot express--but each measurement is billions of values, and every new material requires a new capture. Existing neural BTF representations encode each material as large per-texel latent maps rather than as a point in a shared space from which new materials could be sampled. We present neural representations of measured BTFs at two operating points. A per-material coordinate network outperforms the recent neural BTF of Xia et al. at matched size (+3.2 dB PSNR) and all prior baselines on every metric. A compact model represents each material by a single 256-dimensional code that conditions a shared decoder; it exceeds the PSNR (+1.2 dB) and colour accuracy of the per-texel latent maps of Rainer et al. with 256 numbers per material instead of millions, and one decoder shared by all materials. Because each material is a single point in this code space, measured BTFs can be sampled: a class-conditional flow over the codes, trained on the 84 materials enlarged with colourways and hue rotations, generates materials that render and relight as full BTFs.

papers.title: Body of Evidence: Triangulating 3D Human Pose with Geometry-Conditioned Depth
papers.abstract: Even in multi-camera setups, occlusions can leave individual body joints with only a single usable 2D observation. Such an observation defines a viewing ray but leaves the joint's depth undetermined. We introduce Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D joint locations. To reduce monocular depth ambiguity, we propose geometry-conditioned depth prediction, which combines image features with previously reconstructed 3D body geometry as contextual depth cues. We further introduce learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT), which augments differentiable algebraic triangulation with predicted depth constraints, enabling reconstruction even from a single contributing camera while preserving the benefits of geometric triangulation when multiple views are available. The reconstructed 3D poses subsequently guide depth prediction in the next iteration, allowing depth estimates and 3D geometry to progressively refine each other. Experiments on CMU Panoptic demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average performance across evaluated camera subsets and unseen camera arrangements. BoE is particularly effective under sparse camera coverage, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the challenging three-camera setting.

papers.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models
papers.abstract:
Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing.
  To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.

papers.title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.

papers.title: Even Loose Proximity Constraints Make Makespan-optimal Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding Hard
papers.abstract: We study \textsc{$r$-Connected Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding} ($r$CUMAPF), a variant of MAPF where interchangeable agents have a proximity range $r\in \mathbb{N}$, and agents must form a single group in a given graph $G$ through limited-range communication at all times. The problem arises in fundamental applications such as self-reconfiguration and platooning, while standard MAPF does not capture proximity constraints. For the problem of finding a makespan-optimal solution, prior work shows \NP-hardness for $r=1$ and polynomial-time solvability when $r$ is sufficiently large; the complexity for the intermediate case $2\le r$ is largely unknown. To narrow this gap, we show that finding a solution to $r$CUMAPF with makespan at most $2$ is \NP-hard for $2\le r= O(|V|^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $0<\varepsilon\le 1$ is a fixed constant and $|V|$ is the number of vertices. As a consequence, we show that the labeled analogue of $r$CUMAPF is also \NP-hard under the same condition.

papers.title: The Sample Complexity of Channel Coding
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for the study and evaluation of the fundamental limits of channel coding, emphasizing genuinely nonasymptotic results. The {\em channel coding sample complexity} $n^*({\cal W},\epsilon)$ of a channel ${\cal W}$ is defined as the smallest blocklength at which it is possible to transmit information through that channel with error probability below $\epsilon$ and at a rate at least as high as that given by an appropriate constraint also in terms of $\epsilon$. This formulation follows analogous developments in statistics, computer science and, more recently, in lossless source coding. For any discrete memoryless channel we derive nonasymptotic bounds on the sample complexity, with explicit constants. These bounds show that the sample complexity is characterized not by the usual channel capacity, but by the channel's Augustin--Csisz\'{a}r capacity of order $1/2$, which coincides with the cutoff rate as well as with the channel's Sibson capacity of order $1/2$. The proof is partly based on a new channel-coding one-shot converse in terms of hypothesis testing. We also examine extensions of the sample complexity framework to general target rates. Moreover, we derive corresponding results for the sample complexity of the additive white Gaussian noise channel with a quadratic power constraint. Their proof relies on new, explicit upper bounds on the best achievable error probability, which may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Compositions of Exoplanetary Debris Shaped by Milky Way Stellar Abundance Patterns
papers.abstract: Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) predicts large-scale variations in exoplanet compositions with host star elemental abundances, reflecting the Milky Way's history of star formation and elemental enrichment from stellar feedback. We investigate the impact of GCE on the compositions of exoplanetary bodies using polluted white dwarfs (WDs), which probe the bulk elemental abundances of planetary debris. Using a literature sample of 70 polluted WDs, we calculate iron mass fractions for the accreted bodies and compare these to tracers of the WD progenitor's initial abundances, including age and kinematics. We demonstrate predicted trends using a sample of main sequence stars, and we show that these are generally reflected in the polluted WD sample. In particular, H-dominated WDs show preferentially larger iron mass fractions amongst younger and less dynamically excited systems. This trend is weaker amongst He-dominated WDs, and we show that this may be attributed to uncertainties in their observed phases of accretion. Continuing to combine WD pollution compositions with stellar parameters and kinematics could be a valuable way to constrain large-scale versus local drivers of planetary compositions.

papers.title: Automatic techniques for security bug report identification: A systematic mapping study
papers.abstract:
Several studies have investigated the use of automated techniques to help practitioners identify security bug reports early in the defect management process. However, currently there is no comprehensive overview of this research area. Such an overview will help identify future research directions and consolidate the potentially relevant existing solutions. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of automated techniques for identifying security bug reports. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic mapping study and identified 28 primary studies.
  The study's findings show that the literature has evaluated various automatic techniques for identifying security bug reports, including traditional machine learning, deep learning, and more advanced large language models. The two main challenges identified are the lack of labeled data and data imbalance. Furthermore, we observe that existing studies lack evaluations in real industrial settings and rely mostly on archival data from open-source repositories. The most commonly used data sources in these studies include Wicket, Ambari, Camel, and Derby. Overall, the literature appears fragmented, highlighting the need for future work to focus on comprehensive evaluations of the most promising techniques.

papers.title: AstroSat Observations of Stellar Mass Black Hole X-ray Binaries: Towards a Unified Accretion Disc Configuration
papers.abstract: We present spectro-temporal review of $34$ black hole X-ray binaries (BH-XRBs), classified as persistent-cum-variable, persistent and transient, observed with \textit{AstroSat} during its first decade of operations. Using over $12$ Ms of data, wide-band multi-wavelength coverage in UV/Optical and X-rays, and $\sim10\,\mu\text{s}$ temporal resolution, we probe accretion-ejection dynamics in strong gravity. LFQPOs ($0.1-8.0\text{ Hz}$) are detected across several sources, exceeding $40\text{ keV}$ in MAXI J1535$-$571 and H 1743$-$322, while Swift J1727.8$-$1613 exhibits the first detection of LFQPOs up to $100$ keV, indicating the dominant Comptonized emission. In GRS 1915$+$105, we identify a new variability class ($\tau$), expanding known classes to fifteen, and detect $\sim70\text{ Hz}$ HFQPOs in the $\gamma$, $\kappa$, $\delta$, $\omega$, and $\tau$ classes, implying a `compact' oscillating corona within $\lesssim 10\,r_g$. Among persistent sources, we report the first detections of a type-A LFQPO ($\sim2.7\text{ Hz}$) in 4U 1957$+$11 and type-B LFQPOs ($4-8\text{ Hz}$) in 4U 1630$-$472. Broadband thermal disc along with Comptonization modelling reveals tight correlations among QPO frequency, time-lag, rms variability, photon index ($\Gamma_{\rm th}$), disc-to-Comptonized flux ratio ($F_{\rm ratio}$), and bolometric luminosity ($L_{\rm bol}$), tracing disc-corona-jet coupling and identifying `canonical' spectral states (LHS, HIMS, SIMS, HSS). Type-C QPOs exhibit soft-lags with occasional reversals at high coronal fractions ($>0.8$), whereas type-B QPOs show hard-lags at lower fractions ($<0.5$), linking to disc-jet coupling. Supported by simulations and radiation driven spectral modelling, these results favor a unified accretion framework while outlining limitations, challenges and future prospects.
