This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

papers.title: Self-similarity of axisymmetric Marangoni flows on a deep viscous subphase
papers.abstract: Local gradients of surface tension caused by inhomogeneous distributions of surfactant molecules are known to generate Marangoni flows, the mechanics of which have important consequences in various areas of science and engineering. In this paper, we investigate the deposition of insoluble surfactants on the surface of a deep, viscous subphase, which propagate axisymmetrically without diffusing. We study these flows from the perspective of self-similarity, i.e., seeking solutions which show universal features on appropriate length and time scales. We first present a closed form, self-similar solution of the first kind for the axisymmetric spreading of surfactants, which is globally valid at long times. We then numerically study `filling' flows of surfactant, where the surfactant distribution is locally depleted such that inward flows are generated to `fill' the surfactant-free area. These flows have the special feature of forming cusp-like structure in finite time, which have been studied extensively in the literature of self-similarity of the second kind. We show that these flows admit a countably infinite number of stable similarity solutions based on the local behavior of the initial surfactant concentration profile. We remark on a few unique features of these results in contrast to filling flows in other physical limits.

papers.title: DAPPT: Domain-Aware Policies from Procedural Trajectories for Sim-to-Real Dexterous Tool Use
papers.abstract: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformable and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DAPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain represen-tation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DAPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8x in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.

papers.title: A Proof of Stein's Equidissection Conjecture
papers.abstract: In 1970 Monsky showed that a square cannot be dissected into an odd number of equal-area triangles. His proof used an ingenious colouring of the plane based on a 2-adic valuation on $\mathbb{R}$ together with Sperner's lemma. Subsequent work established similar results for regular polygons, centrally symmetric polygons, and polyominoes. In 2000, Stein proposed a common generalisation of the centrally symmetric and polyomino cases to balanced polygons. In 2014, Rudenko introduced a new perspective on the problem and proved Stein's conjecture for dissections with rational vertex coordinates. Building on and streamlining his approach, we resolve the conjecture in full.

papers.title: Bending Rigidity of Smectic Filaments
papers.abstract: Many biological and engineered filaments exhibit internal structure or fluidity that alters their elastic behavior. We study the elasticity of microscale filamentous smectic condensates, grown during liquid-liquid crystal phase separation. We use a Fourier analysis of their thermal bend fluctuations to measure their persistence length, which follows a non-classic linear scaling with their cross-sectional area, in contrast to the classic quadratic scaling for elastic filaments. We rationalize this scaling using the Helfrich energy to compute the free energy of bending a filament with internal smectic fluid ordering. Our analysis then provides a direct method to measure the bend modulus K, which quantifies the rigidity of smectic layers; providing the first method to directly measure K for dispersed smectic phases. We quantify the softening of filaments in the presence of shorter alkyl-tail mesogen dopants, decreasing K by up to ~35%. Out results suggest how nanoscale smectic organization and molecular composition determine filament-scale elasticity, informing the control of filament mechanics and self-assembly in biomimetic and engineered materials.

papers.title: Finite-time blowup in a one-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics model
papers.abstract: We prove finite-time blowup of both the velocity and magnetic field in a one-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) model starting from smooth odd initial data. The construction combines the dynamical rescaling approach with weighted stability estimates. Both the velocity and magnetic field remain in $L^2$ before the blowup time.

papers.title: Cold stellarator coils that outlast power plant lifetime
papers.abstract: We show that a two order-of-magnitude reduction in stellarator coil peak neutron flux and heating can be achieved by moving coils much farther from the plasma if the plasma shape may change slightly and the vessel shielding is increased. Alternating coil and plasma optimizations move the closest coils of our main design over 25 cm out, without substantial degradation in key engineering and physics requirements. The field error decreases and the plasma boundary moves about 1 cm on average. Such coils would be at 4.2 K, use only one third to half the superconducting tape of the original, and require no replacement during the plant's lifetime. This reduced coil flux and heating could significantly enhance the viability of stellarator power plants.

papers.title: Taking Time Out of TOCTOU: From Race Reproduction to Security Discovery
papers.abstract: Time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races are hard to reproduce and lost races can make vulnerable programs look fixed. We present Chronos, a framework that separates intervention timing from verdict evidence and builds reusable one-trial security regression oracles from declared races for deterministic reproduction, commit bisection and CI. Race Specifications compose reusable hold engines, actions, observers and outcome rules. When the declared hold is reached and the attack completes while held, Chronos orders it before the use under blocking and interference assumptions. Chronos uses seccomp notifications to enforce declared hold-attack-release ordering at syscall boundaries on stock Linux; ptrace and a KVM guest gate provide holds at userspace and kernel instruction sites. One decision procedure labels every mechanism's runs: fixed requires positive, case-specific evidence of preservation, justified refusal, omission under checked coverage, or a declared rule; missing or contradictory required evidence remains indeterminate. On known-vulnerable builds, effect-only checkers made over 800 false-fixed classifications in failed-intervention trials; Chronos made none. All 17 syscall-held cases and four of six instruction-held cases had vulnerable and fixed labels. Two kernel cases remain one-sided. All 27 historical bisections recovered the expected boundaries. For runc's masked-path bisection with one victim per launch, fixed retry and Git Bayesect took medians of 475 and 398 natural launches; Chronos used seven held trials including endpoint checks. Since a label means the same however a fix is written, we also ran the specifications and attack variants on releases, distribution packages and other runtimes. There, Chronos helped us uncover three issues: incomplete fixes in chrony and rpm, and a Debian rpm package its tracker listed as fixed.

papers.title: Generic finiteness of rotating relative equilibria in the planar $N$-vortex problem
papers.abstract: For every $N\ge2$, we prove that Zariski-generic nonzero real circulations, with any prescribed signs, admit at most $N^{2N}$ labeled, collision-free rotating relative equilibria modulo translations, rotations in $SO(2)$, and positive scaling. The excluded parameters lie in an explicit finite union of quadratic hypersurfaces. The proof combines a logarithmic-residue obstruction to positive-dimensional complex solution sets with B\'ezout degree bounds.

papers.title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.

authors.name: Qishi Zhan
authors.institution: Statistical and Applied Mathematical Sciences Institute

authors.name: Ziheng Chen
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Zihan Dong
authors.institution: Institute of Forest Resource Information Techniques

papers.title: Zero-shot diffusion image compression with sectioned codebooks and one channel code
papers.abstract: Zero-shot diffusion codecs such as Turbo-DDCM compress images without any training. In each coded step, the encoder selects noise vectors from one codebook and transmits a single index for the selected set. We propose sectioned codebooks. A coded step is divided into sections, and each section has its own large codebook and transmits its best vector as a short field of bits. A model based on order statistics quantifies how well the bits of a step are used and predicts the gain of sectioned codebooks from measurements of Turbo-DDCM alone. Fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms make sections of $2^{20}$ vectors practical. At equal bits, sectioned codebooks improve the PSNR of Turbo-DDCM by 0.18 to 0.51 dB on three datasets, improve LPIPS and DISTS, and save 16 to 21% of the bits at equal PSNR. Codecs that are robust to channel errors by design are usually compared only with unprotected codecs. We compare them, at equal total bits, with a codec protected by one channel code. With one BCH code, the sectioned codec outperforms all reported results of Robust Turbo-DDCM and BitFlat on two datasets, by up to 7.74 dB at the highest bit error rate. At the lowest bit error rate its margin over BitFlat is only 0.08 to 0.16 dB. When the code fails, the receiver can still decode the fields as received. Additional experiments cover burst errors and packet loss, and all observed gains of robust codecs stay within a limit derived from the channel capacity.

papers.title: Compositional Exploits in Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics and Ephemeral Defense
papers.abstract: Autonomous coding agents (such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenHands) rely on third-party tools to inspect files, run commands, and call external APIs. Today's security auditors evaluate these tools almost entirely in isolation: static linters and AST checkers verify that each individual tool contains no malicious code at installation time. In this paper, we show that isolated tool auditing is fundamentally flawed. We expose compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, an emergent vulnerability class where an agent chains individually harmless tools to execute an unauthorized attack. Much like code-reuse attacks in binary exploitation, this threat requires no malware; instead, the agent stitches together legitimate tool operations across turns over shared workspace files, environment variables, and chat memory. Across a 560-task benchmark suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes and 200 benign developer and cloud workflows), unprotected frontier models (Gemini 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash) execute compositional exploit chains with a 72.9% to 84.5% success rate, while five leading single-tool pre-distribution scanners exhibit a 0% detection rate across all constituent tools. To eliminate compositional exploits, we present CompGuard, an OS-grounded defense uniting two planes: (1) a Cognitive Control Plane that issues single-skill capability leases and tracks dataflow provenance, and (2) an OS Kernel Enforcement Layer using Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, and an ephemeral loopback proxy to close the invocation gap. CompGuard achieves a 100% Defense Block Rate (0.0% to 0.8% pre-teardown Net ASR) at 61.4 microseconds interposition overhead, preserves a 98.0% solve rate on benign developer workflows, and triggers zero false alarms across 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.

papers.title: Reasoning Again with a Quarter of the Experts: Retry First, Then Train
papers.abstract: Removing three quarters of the routed experts from a 122B-parameter reasoning mixture-of-experts model makes it fit in a 12 GiB file, and breaks it in a specific way: on LiveCodeBench it enters verbatim reasoning loops that run to the token limit on 44 of 120 development problems, where the unpruned model at the same 2-bit quantization loops on none. We study how much of that loss can be recovered without changing the kept experts' quantized bytes, in three steps of increasing cost. On development problems, a sampling penalty recovers part of it. Stopping a reply when it starts to loop and drawing again recovers more on top of it, with no weight change. Our method, B, adds rank-8 trained corrections to the kept experts, loaded as an adapter, and restores two experts per layer; it is fitted layer by layer to the unpruned model's expert block on the pruned model's own activations. In a pre-registered comparison on 130 easy and medium LiveCodeBench problems that no part of the study had touched, with both arms given the same sampling penalty and the same stop-and-redraw policy, B solves 116 problems against 104 (+9.2 pp, 95% CI [+3.1, +15.4]; 15 problems gained, 3 lost). A training-free weight edit aimed at the loops, tested the same way earlier, did not help. B removes more wrong answers than loops, and costs 1.7x the wall time. On two older benchmarks used as regression checks, B stays inside a pre-set 2 pp tolerance but shows no gain (HumanEval+ +0.6 pp, MBPP+ -1.9 pp). The evidence is one model, one quantization and one benchmark family; we state what it does and does not show.

authors.name: Anik Jha
authors.institution: Annapurna Neurological Institute and Allied Sciences

papers.title: Normal ordering of Riemann-Liouville operators and a probabilistic formula for generalized Stirling numbers
papers.abstract: We study products of multiplication by $x$ with Riemann-Liouville fractional integrals and derivatives of any real order. For the integral $I^\alpha$ of order $\alpha$, the commutator with $x$ gives the relation $uv-vu=hv^s$ with $s=1+1/\alpha$. The coefficients of the normal ordering for this relation are the generalized Stirling numbers $S_{s;h}(n,k)$. We show that these operators give a faithful representation of the algebra in which the real powers of $v$ are defined. We expand $(XI^\alpha)^n$ and $(I^\alpha X)^n$ on locally integrable functions for every $\alpha>0$, and $(XD^\beta)^n$ and $(D^\beta X)^n$ on the range of $I^{n\beta}$ for every $\beta>0$. The kernel of $(XI^\alpha)^n$ is an expectation over the Dirichlet distribution. This gives a probabilistic formula for $S_{s;1}(n,k)$, $s>1$. By de Finetti's theorem, the formula describes an urn with $n$ colours: fractional integrals correspond to P\'olya urns, and derivatives of integer order correspond to drawing without replacement. The urn probabilities are the terms of a product formula that follows from the recurrence. The cases $s=1,0,2$ give the Stirling numbers of both kinds and the Bessel numbers. The same method gives the kernels of all words in $x$ and fractional integrals.

papers.title: Hilbert-Kunz Multiplicity and Smirnov's conjecture
papers.abstract:
In this paper, we study Smirnov's conjecture: Let $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ be a Noetherian local ring of characteristic $p>0$ and dimension $d$. Let $I$ be an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideal. If $R$ is weakly $F$-regular, analytically unramified and Cohen-Macaulay, then $\displaystyle L_1(I)=e(I)-e_{\mathrm{HK}}(I)$ if and only if $I$ is stable. Here, $e(I)$ and $e_{\mathrm{HK}}(I)$ denote the Hilbert-Samuel multiplicity and the Hilbert-Kunz multiplicity of $R$ with respect to $I$, respectively. Moreover, $\displaystyle L_1(I)=\lim_{q\to\infty}\frac{e_1(I^{[q]})}{q^d},$ where $q=p^e$ and $e_1(I^{[q]})$ denotes the first Hilbert coefficient of $R$ with respect to the $q$th Frobenius power of $I$.
  We prove the conjecture when $R$ is either excellent and strongly $F$-regular, or excellent of dimension $3$.

papers.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
papers.abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

papers.title: Guiding AI Agents to Generate Conjectures by Encoding How Theorems Build on One Another
papers.abstract: Recently, LLMs have been making headlines, and headway, in mathematical research. Much of this work focuses on proving existing open conjectures. Deciding what to prove is harder and less studied, because of the lack of a clear criterion for what makes a conjecture worth pursuing. We present a method for conjecture generation that builds on the observation that mathematical theorems build on one another: new theorems can modify the setting or hypotheses of earlier theorems, strengthen their conclusions, or extend their scope. We encode these relationships in a new kind of graph, the Theorem Evolution Graph (TEG), which we instantiate as an online search method for LLM agents. An agent builds a TEG in two steps: (1) identifying relevant theorems from papers found by following citations backward and forward from a seed paper; and (2) comparing those theorems to record how one builds on another. LLM judges and an expert mathematician preferred TEG-generated conjectures over those from an unconstrained baseline. LLM judges favored TEG conjectures for significance, ambition, and insight, and favored baseline conjectures for plausibility. Ablations suggest a benefit from constructing and using a TEG even when the available papers are fixed.

authors.name: Lyle Ungar
authors.institution: Leonard Davis Institute of Health Economics

papers.title: Scaling of the Radial Motion and Size of Filamentary Structures in the Scrape-Off Layer Inferred from 100 kHz Visible Imaging on 294 MAST Discharges
papers.abstract: Filaments are important carriers of cross-field transport in the scrape-off layer of a tokamak. Analytic models predict that their radial velocity varies with their size. We measured the radial velocity and size of a large population of filaments on MAST, using data recorded from a 100 kHz, 48 x 256 pixel camera in the outboard midplane in the FAIR-MAST archive. Computer vision techniques were used to automate the identification of filaments and tracking of their trajectories, which yielded 86,042 filament tracks over 294 discharges in 4 campaigns. The archive does not contain spatial calibration, so we have obtained a pixel scale by regression of the plasma limb column in the image on the EFIT outboard LCFS radius, with bootstrap intervals. The scale is 2.7-5.2 millimetres per pixel. We find a median velocity of 424 m/s, and median radial width of 3.6 cm. The dependence of velocity on size is mild, with a log-log slope of +0.05 (95% interval +0.03 to +0.07) when the effects of exposure blurring are corrected for. This is because filaments are not in either velocity regime; they span the range $\hat{a}$ = 0.13-1.97 in two-region units, which straddles the maximum velocity predicted by the two-region model, but the normalized velocity $\hat{v}$ is much smaller than the scale of the model, at $\hat{v} \approx 0.06$.

papers.title: Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers from rainbow Tur\'an numbers and beyond
papers.abstract: The Hadwiger-Debrunner number $\operatorname{HD}_d(p,q)$ is defined as the maximum piercing number over all finite families of compact convex sets in $\mathbb R^d$ in which among every $p$ sets, some $q$ have non-empty intersection. We develop three complementary constructions that improve lower bounds for Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers. For any fixed $q>d\ge 2$, a randomly sparsified family of hyperplanes, analyzed using hypergraph containers, yields $\operatorname{HD}_d(p,q)\ge p^{(d+q-2)/(q-1)+o(1)}$ as $p\rightarrow\infty$. To deduce further bounds, we establish a transfer argument from upper bounds on the sizes of sufficiently general-positioned subsets of high-dimensional integer grids to lower bounds for Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers. Two methodologies are adopted to derive the former: one connects rainbow Tur\'an theory and general-positioned grid sets, and the other uses full spark linear reduction of tuples with bounded-size preimages. As a combinatorial ingredient, we describe the rainbow Tur\'an behavior under suspension operations, which may be of independent interest.

authors.name: Wenchong Chen
authors.institution: Zhejiang University of Water Resource and Electric Power

papers.title: Random Cut Forests, Games and Diffusion over Approximately Nested Anisotropic Local Geometry
papers.abstract:
Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming.
  Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements.

papers.title: Arc connected continua and the double commutant property
papers.abstract: Let $K$ be a compact metrizable space. For $f\in C(K)$ let $M_f$ be the largest lower semicontinuous map with $k\in M_f(k)\subseteq f^{-1}(f(k))$. We say that $K$ has the double commutant property if for every $f\in C(K)$ every continuous function that is constant on all sets $M_f(k)$ is constant on the fibres of $f$; this is exactly the condition that the double commutant of every multiplication operator on $C(K)$ is the closed algebra generated by the operator and the identity. We show that an arc connected continuum has this property if the points having an open locally connected neighbourhood are dense, and we extend this to some continua that are not arc connected. We then develop new techniques that work when such points are not dense, or do not exist at all, and prove that several well-known continua have the property: the Cantor comb, the Cantor fan and, more generally, the cone over every compact metrizable space, every smooth fan with a closed set of end points, and the Cantor grid $(C\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times C)$. The property passes to open images. Examples show that the hypotheses cannot be weakened in several directions. For individual functions we show that, on a continuum all of whose arc components are dense, every function that is constant on no arc satisfies the double commutant condition, and that on every smooth dendroid and every fan the functions satisfying it are dense.

papers.title: ARMFUL: Learning Whole-Arm Grasp Configurations for Single-Arm Pickup of Large Objects
papers.abstract: Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG (Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects, with 1.7~million joint configurations across 793 objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object's point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4\% lift success on training and 69.9\% on held-out objects, and it lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.

papers.title: KuroshioVis: Hypothesis-Driven Discovery of Mesoscale Air-Sea Interaction through Coarse-to-Fine Exploration
papers.abstract: Mesoscale air-sea interaction occurs throughout strong sea surface temperature fronts such as the the Kuroshio Extension, but its strength is highly non-uniform and can be resolved only in kilometre-scale coupled simulations. The response of any single eddy is weak relative to synoptic variability, so evidence supporting a hypothesis of systematic air-sea coupling must be accumulated across many eddies rather than inferred from individual cases. We present KuroshioVis, a hypothesis-driven, coarse-to-fine visual analytics workflow. The coarse stage extracts and aligns mesoscale eddies into composite representations of their air-sea responses, and provides a global view for exploration. The fine stage investigates these responses through three coordinated views: the composite in terface view, the cross-interface flow view, and the evidence matrix view. These coordinated views support air-sea coupling analysis from surface patterns to cross-interface dynamics and quantitative statistical evidence. We demonstrate the workflow using the coupled C1440-LLC2160 simulation of the 2026 SciVis Contest.

authors.name: Xi Duan
authors.institution: Affiliated Hospital of North Sichuan Medical College

papers.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
papers.abstract:
Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation.
  In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

papers.title: Neurosymbolic Synthesis of Contraction Metrics with Certified Verification
papers.abstract: We study counterexample-guided synthesis of contraction metrics for continuous-time autonomous systems on compact domains. A learner proposes a metric; a sound verifier certifies its matrix inequality or returns diagnostic points for retraining. The neural extension pairs a learned metric factor with symbolic contraction conditions and rigorous numerical verification; main ablations use polynomial features. We give computable polynomial bounds in arbitrary dimension and outward-rounded verification for polynomial, trigonometric, and neural representations. Loop soundness is separated from conditional finite-grid termination under idealized feasibility assumptions. We analyze why scaling and fixed-margin training can leave valid metrics uncertified. The scaling construction requires a scale-closed family, which the experimental fixed-floor class generally lacks. Verified slack improves the contraction rate and quantifies model-error tolerances using certified residual and Jacobian bounds. Finite-distance conclusions require connecting paths whose flows stay in the verified region. Experiments include controlled ablations, three-dimensional verification, and transfer from a fitted surrogate with known-truth residual certification. A physical swing-model study compares neural learning objectives with shared verification and invariant energy regions. Verified constant metrics certify the polynomial benchmark and smallest swing-model domain; neither result requires neural state dependence. Exploratory refinement certifies additional frozen candidates at a larger verification budget. In matched polynomial operating-grid experiments, trace normalization and margin coupling did not demonstrate a certification-count advantage within the tested budgets. These choices address specific failure mechanisms without guaranteeing optimizer convergence or general empirical superiority.

papers.title: Local topology hallucinations in universal machine-learned interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: Predicting metastable states with universal machine-learned interatomic potentials requires that they preserve the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface. Here we identify local topology hallucination, in which distinct model minima relax into the same reference basin. This failure arises from mode-selective curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet and M3GNet. Curvature signs predicted by two of the three models agreed with density-functional calculations in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases. In LiGe$_2$S, two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle relaxed into one density-functional basin. Reference relaxation likewise returned nine of ten selected model minima to their reference basins. A directional test with two displaced reference calculations rejected 9 of 12 prospectively tested model instabilities. Model agreement alone therefore cannot establish that predicted minima are distinct metastable states.

papers.title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

authors.name: Kai Wang
authors.institution: Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania

papers.title: On the multiplicity of the Laplacian eigenvalue 1 of a graph
papers.abstract: A connected graph $G$ with $n\ge 2$ vertices and $\varepsilon$ edges is called a \emph{$k$-cyclic graph} if $k=\varepsilon-n+1$. The Laplacian matrix is defined as $L(G)=D(G)-A(G)$, where $D(G)$ is the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees and $A(G)$ is the adjacency matrix of $G$. Let $m_{G}(1)$ be the multiplicity of the Laplacian eigenvalue $1$ of $G$. In this paper, we show that for fixed integers $n\ge \big\lceil\frac{3+\sqrt{8k+1}} {2}\big\rceil$ and $k\geq0$, if $G$ is a $k$-cyclic graph of order $n$, then \begin{equation*} \displaystyle m_{G}(1)\leq n-\big\lceil\frac{3+\sqrt{8k+1}} {2}\big\rceil \end{equation*} and moreover, we completely characterize all extremal graphs attained the upper bound.

authors.name: Kai Wang
authors.institution: Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania

authors.name: Tao Wang
authors.institution: Taiyuan University of Science and Technology

papers.title: A Gravitomagnetic Bootstrap: from Newtonian gravity to general relativity via localizing rotational and conformal symmetries
papers.abstract: Newtonian gravity, in the light of the Equivalence Principle, is best understood as a localization of Galilean inertial structure --- or at least, of the part of Galilean inertial structure that defines rectilinear acceleration. I consider what kind of theory can be constructed if we also localize rotational inertia and spatial and temporal scales. The resultant theory, given weak assumptions, is unique up to a constant with the dimensions of velocity and an overall sign. For an appropriate choice of these, it coincides with the first post-Newtonian approximation to general relativity, so that this construction gives a method to bootstrap from Newtonian gravity to general relativity without explicitly presupposing special relativity.

papers.title: High-inclination Centaur or Captured Halley-Type Comet? Observational and Dynamical Characterization of C/2024 L1 (PANSTARRS)
papers.abstract: The high-inclination (`high-i') Centaurs of the middle and outer Solar System are of uncertain origin. While many have been captured directly from the Oort Cloud, making them less-evolved analogues to the Halley-Type Comets, this process alone cannot produce the number of observed objects. The most discussed alternate origin is direct excitation of trans-Neptunian Objects into high-i orbits by the action of some unfound massive planet beyond Neptune. It is thus critical to find ways to discern the origins of these objects to provide new constraints on the various unfound planet hypotheses. This work assesses the only known active high-i Centaur: C/2024 L1 (PANSTARRS). Our dynamical investigations show that L1 has not decreased its semimajor axis in at least the past 1810 years, unlike all known TNO-derived active Centaurs at lower-i whose activity initiates after orbital changes. We also imaged L1 on five nights in the year before its April 2025 perihelion and found its brightness and optical colors to be stable and that its tail grew steadily. While this is like many Halley-type comets, few active low-i Centaurs have such stable activity. We thus propose that L1 is a captured Oort Cloud comet analogous to lower perihelion Halley-types and is thus a highly attractive target for large aperture follow up. The number and active fraction of these high-i objects should help us discern their origins and survey telescopes like Roman and Rubin could help us figure out where in the Outer Solar System the mystery lies.

papers.title: Stabilizing Parabolic Vector Bundles
papers.abstract: For an irreducible parabolic flat vector bundle of rank $r < 2\sqrt{g}$ on a genus $g$ curve, we prove that an analytically general isomonodromic deformation is stable. This refines Landesman-Litt's semistability result for bundles of rank $< 2\sqrt{g+1}$. The proof applies the non-generically globally generated (non-GGG) lemma to establish infinitesimal obstructions to extending destabilizing subbundles of semistable bundles.

papers.title: How Specification Explicitness Shapes Failure in LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: When LLMs turn requirements into code, every underspecified constraint becomes behavior that the model must decide during generation. We test when specifications move beyond structure and begin to control generated behavior. In a controlled experiment, 72 participants implemented and revised Python tasks with an LLM under three levels of specification explicitness. The results show a clear break between lightweight structure and explicit behavioral obligations. Lightweight structure reduced hidden-test failures by only 8.7%. Requiring participants to specify constraints, invariants, negative requirements, edge cases, tie-breaking rules, and exception handling cut failures by 47.2% and reduced the number of distinct failure modes by 20.5%. The largest drops were in failure modes tied to implicit obligations. Invariant violations fell by 66.1%, and unsupported assumptions fell by 59.5%. After a requirement change, specifications with explicit behavioral obligations produced regressions in more submissions, but each affected submission lost less previously correct behavior. Explicit specifications also changed how developers judged generated code. Without explicit obligations, participants overestimated generated-code correctness by about 23 percentage points. With explicit obligations, they produced better code but judged it more cautiously. Thus, the lesson is sharper than "better specifications help." Lightweight structure barely helped, while explicit behavioral obligations nearly halved failures, made regressions shallower, and improved calibration.

papers.title: The M\'ezard-Parisi formula for diluted Potts models
papers.abstract: We obtain the M\'ezard-Parisi formula for the antiferromagnetic Potts model on random uniform hypergraphs, including the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi graph. The upper bound in the graph case was proved by Contucci, Dommers, Giardin\`a, and Starr, whose interpolation extends to uniform hypergraphs. Here we prove the matching lower bound for a general class of diluted models with finite spin alphabets. The proof follows closely the corresponding argument for diluted Ising models, so we outline only the adjustments needed for several colors.

papers.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
papers.abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

papers.title: Oriented Semi-DETR for Semi-Supervised Aerial Object Detection
papers.abstract: Semi-supervised object detection has recently been extended to DETR, where oriented boxes introduce an ambiguity that does not arise for axis-aligned boxes: the map from parameters to rectangles is two-to-one, since $(c_x,c_y,w,h,\theta)$ and $(c_x,c_y,h,w,\theta+\pi/2)$ denote the same rotated rectangle. Losses and matching costs are computed from the parameters, so two boxes that coincide in space can be far apart in the metric that drives training. A correctly localized student box is then penalized by the regression loss, and the inflated matching cost leads the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) filter to discard it. We propose Oriented Semi-DETR, which removes this ambiguity wherever a pseudo box enters training. Swap-aligned Target Selection regresses towards the encoding closer to the student prediction. A Swap-invariant Reliability Cost minimizes over the two encodings inside the matching cost, so the filter decides on geometry alone. Swap-aware Pseudo-label Denoising starts denoising earlier, ramps its loss weight linearly, and weights each query by the teacher score and encoding margin. All three are parameter-free and require no additional forward pass. Across all label ratios of DOTA-v2.0, Oriented Semi-DETR outperforms DETR-based supervised and semi-supervised baselines, with the largest gains at the strict IoU threshold.

papers.title: Knowledge Fermentation: Learning from Shared Variation in Few-Shot Classification
papers.abstract: A classifier built from a handful of labeled examples knows where each class sits in feature space but not how it varies, which is why prototype rules and linear probes overfit in the low-data regime. Knowledge Fermentation (KF) recovers this second-order knowledge by letting classes exchange what they know about variation. Residuals around class prototypes act as carriers; the variance of each direction is measured on classes that took no part in estimating it, and directions above the level of the surrounding medium define a structured noise that acts on a linear classifier as a closed-form change of geometry. A convex objective trains the classifier at a noise strength calibrated on the distances between prototypes, and unlabeled examples, when available, join as carriers in repeated rounds. We prove that the held-out variances are unbiased for the directions on which they are measured, that the fermented map never expands a direction, and that damping caused by wrong assignments limits itself. On 14 datasets from vision and language and 8 frozen encoders, with all constants fixed, KF is on par with the best of six tuned inductive baselines. With unlabeled carriers it raises one-shot accuracy from 52.4% to 65.8% on average and attains the highest average accuracy among nine transductive methods, significantly so on vision encoders, while information maximization stays ahead on sentence encoders. Controlled studies attribute the gain to the task-level geometry and show that it grows with the within-class variation that the classes of a task share.

papers.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
papers.abstract: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

papers.title: RoShift: Lazy Shift and Weight-aware Rotation for Activation Sparsity in LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Activation sparsity accelerates LLM decoding by skipping unnecessary weight reads and computation. However, SiLU-based LLMs exhibit little natural sparsity, and imposing high sparsity can substantially degrade accuracy. We propose RoShift, a training-free method that transforms activations into sparsity-friendly representations. RoShift introduces lazy shift, which recenters SiLU activation distributions around zero and defers correction to the end of the FFN to obtain additional sparsity. It also reduces sparsification-induced output error through rotation that jointly accounts for activation and weight information. By fusing the corrections required for shifting and rotation, RoShift translates these gains into decoding speedup. At 50% and 60% sparsity, RoShift improves average accuracy over TEAL by 1.60 and 3.29 percentage points, respectively, across five models. It achieves up to $1.72\times$ decoding speedup over the dense model on an RTX 5090 at 50% sparsity and yields a better accuracy-speedup Pareto frontier than TEAL. Code is available at https://github.com/hulahula3247/RoShift

papers.title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models
papers.abstract: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, without adding parameters or requiring fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and increases average scaffold-split property-prediction performance, while molecular description and text-to-molecule generation are improved or preserved in single-run ablations. These results show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.

papers.title: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

authors.name: Yuheng Wu
authors.institution: Southwest University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Dongman Lee
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
papers.abstract: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

papers.title: Learning inadequacy of Bayesian neural operators for PDE-constrained inference and design
papers.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin predictive modeling across science, engineering and medicine. Their use in digital twins, parameter inference and optimal design requires repeated solutions across parameters and scenarios. For nonlinear, transient and multiphysics systems, these calculations can make numerical simulation prohibitively expensive. Here we introduce the residual-informed Bayesian neural operator (RI-BNO), which learns operator inadequacy using a posteriori error estimates from the governing PDEs and incorporates its correction and uncertainty into Bayesian training and prediction. We establish local error bounds for the residual-informed estimates under stability and smoothness assumptions. We demonstrate RI-BNO on a non-linear reaction-diffusion benchmark with DeepONet and latent-subspace architectures, Markov chain Monte Carlo inference of glioma parameter fields from magnetic resonance imaging, and Monte Carlo risk-averse optimization of three-dimensional thermal breaks in building envelopes under manufacturing uncertainty. Across the evaluated examples, RI-BNO improves agreement with finite element (FE) reference predictions, parameter posteriors and optimized designs while using half as many full nonlinear or transient training simulations as the vanilla Bayesian neural operator (vBNO). For thermal break design, online optimization time decreases from 178 hours with the FE model to 18 minutes with RI-BNO. These results demonstrate the value of explicit inadequacy modeling in neural operators for reliable PDE-based inference and design.

authors.name: Pratyush Kumar Singh
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

authors.name: E. Bruce Pitman
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

authors.name: Danial Faghihi
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift: process limits, estimated weights and efficiency
papers.abstract: Weighted split conformal prediction handles covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio $v=dQ_X/dP_X$; its training-conditional coverage is a functional of the self-normalized weighted empirical distribution function $\hat F_m$, and we study the process $\sqrt m(\hat F_m-F_Q)$. It converges in $\ell^\infty$ to the Gaussian process $W(G(t))-F_Q(t)W(K^2)$, with $G(t)=\mathbb{E}_Q[v\mathbf{1}\{S\le t\}]$ and $K^2=1+\chi^2(Q\|P)$, if and only if $\chi^2(Q\|P)<\infty$ (for non-degenerate scores); $\sup v$ plays no role. The limit gives the joint law of the coverage across levels, consistent bootstraps, inflations asymptotically exact uniformly in the level, and Berry-Esseen-type rates. With estimated ratios, a uniform expansion remains valid when the estimate uses the calibration covariates; the estimation error enters through a covariance term that can reduce the variance below the oracle's, and a pairs bootstrap reproduces it. When the ratio is known, the weighted conformal threshold is semiparametrically efficient if and only if the ratio and the coverage indicator are uncorrelated under the test distribution, with an explicit efficient correction otherwise. When $\chi^2(Q\|P)=\infty$, the ratio has a regularly varying tail of index $p\in(1,2)$ and the score decouples from it in the far tail, the finite-dimensional limits are $p$-stable at the rate $m^{1-1/p}$ up to a slowly varying factor.

authors.name: Mehrdad Pournaderi
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Impact Angle Control Guidance Law with Field-of-View Constraint
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel impact angle control guidance law to address the challenge of achieving any desired impact angle while satisfying the seeker's Field Of View (FOV) limit and maintaining acceleration continuity. The guidance problem is decomposed into two two-dimensional (2D) engagement planes. In the first plane, a pure proportional navigation guidance (PNG) law is employed toward a virtual target to align the missile velocity vector with the line-of-sight (LOS) to the target. In the second plane, a two-stage time-varying biased PNG (TVBPN) strategy is utilized to accurately shape the trajectory and achieve the desired terminal impact angle while maintaining compliance with FOV limitations. The position of the virtual target point ensures a smooth and continuous lateral acceleration at the transition between the first and second stages. The effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed law were validated through numerical simulations.

authors.name: Sayantan Pal
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Prediction-Driven Contract Matching with Controlled Overbooking for Cloud-Edge DDoS Scrubbing Markets
papers.abstract: Cloud-edge distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) scrubbing requires ex-ante capacity commitments under uncertain traffic, heterogeneous budgets, resource costs, and fulfillment risks. We develop a prediction-driven two-stage contracting mechanism coordinating business entities (BEs), edge scrubbing nodes (ESs), and a cloud scrubbing center (CS) through BE-ES (B&E) main-service and ES-CS (E&C) supplementary contracts. In the first offline phase, Transformer forecasts generate candidate reserved scrubbing rates, generalized Nash bargaining determines candidate prices, and interim many-to-one B&E matching permits controlled overbooking under scenario-based aggregate ES shortfall-risk assessment. In the second offline phase, formal E&C reservations are established subject to capacity and payment constraints; their finalized rates and prices update ES-side proxy scores and guide localized risk-aware B&E contract adjustment. During online fulfillment, an edge-first, cloud-assisted weighted proportional allocation policy allocates scrubbing capacity under finalized contracts without rematching, renegotiation, or additional cloud reservations. Experiments with CICDDoS2019-derived workloads show that the proposed mechanism satisfies the prescribed empirical shortfall-risk criterion across all 100 evaluated horizon-instance pairs, whereas the NoRisk ablation violates it in all 100. Runtime measurements indicate lightweight online fulfillment relative to offline contract formation. The evaluated configurations also exhibit limited overall scrubbing coverage and near-zero realized cloud utilization.

authors.name: Minghui Liwang
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Not All Steps Matter: Temporally Adaptive Spectral Control for Concept Removal in Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: As text-to-image diffusion models see widespread deployment, removing unsafe or undesirable concepts without retraining has become a pressing need. Spectral methods are attractive because they are training-free and reversible, yet current variants apply the same output-value (OV) circuit intervention at every denoising step, assuming concept information is temporally uniform. This wastes intervention where concept energy is low while degrading image quality, an inefficiency that compounds across concept types. Through timestep-resolved spectral analysis, concept-specific energy is found to follow a consistent temporal hierarchy: content concepts decay fastest, object concepts are intermediate, and style concepts persist longest. This paper proposes Timestep-Adaptive Spectral Nullification (TASN), which adapts suppression strength and spectral components to the concept energy profile. Cross-attention at each timestep is decomposed into concept-aligned and concept-orthogonal components, and it is proved that when the orthogonal component is approximately stable, the collateral-minimizing schedule sets suppression proportional to concept energy. TASN implements this with a timestep-adaptive spectral subset tracking only active concept directions, strictly generalizing uniform Spectral Nullification (SN). On five red-teaming benchmarks, TASN lowers attack success rate below uniform SN while recovering the majority of its quality loss; ablations confirm gains arise from temporal targeting rather than reduced suppression, generalizing across concept categories and architectures.

papers.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
papers.abstract: A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight. A law of softmax attention predicts that a growing crowd of bounded scores dilutes the attention on any patch or register whose score stays fixed. The same law gives a remedy that needs no training: multiply every score, the sink's included, by the ratio of the logarithms of the test and training token counts. Given sufficient margins at the training resolution, this keeps the attention on a match when one is present, and on a sink such as a register when none is, though trained models need not meet those margins. We test these predictions in public vision transformers and in controlled models read far above their training token count. Attention spreads as predicted. Registers lose their share, though production models compensate in part, and the rescaling holds the share of DINOv2's registers nearly level. Applied at test time without training, the rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy in nearly every model, with absolute or rotary positions and with registers, and on images with native detail. The calibrated multiplier rises with the logarithmic ratio on average and varies across models. Its rise is steeper than the square-root rule used in image generators; in controlled models the log ratio is also more accurate, while in the public models the two rules' accuracy difference remains unresolved. The rescaling does not restore the attention a model learned, and why it helps, beyond countering the dilution, remains open.

papers.title: Non-Deterministic Finite Automata for Telugu Letters and Visualizations for Metrical Poetry
papers.abstract: Syllabic weight is central to Telugu metrical poetry. Syllabically, every letter (aksharam token) is either light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu). Poets classify it using a set of pre-defined rules. This paper formalizes aksharam token, the atomic unit of syllabic classification, as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with the regular expression$\colon$ $(A_h+A_d+A_p)(\epsilon+V_s)+A_m+H^+G(\epsilon+H+V_s+V_v)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes a null string, $A$ denotes a vowel (achchu), comprising hrasvam ($A_h$), deergham ($A_d$), plutham ($A_p$), and miscellaneous ($A_m$), $H$ a pure consonant (pollu\_hallu), $G$ a vowel diacritic (gunintha\_chihnam), $V_s$ the sunna (anusvara), and $V_v$ the visarga, the latter two being nasal and aspirated sounds respectively. We then present automata diagrams and regular expressions for (i) a necessary condition satisfied by every light letter, and (ii) a sufficient condition for a letter to be heavy. Finally, we propose graphical visualizations for the 9 Telugu poem types.

authors.name: Boddu Sri Pavan
authors.institution: Rajiv Gandhi University of Knowledge Technologies

papers.title: High-dimensional limit theorems for adaptive variants of SGD I: Ballistic limits
papers.abstract: We develop the high-dimensional effective dynamics for adaptive, momentum-based variants of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). These effective dynamics are given by a Markov process. They key observation is that the non-Markovianity in the algorithm due to the exponential moving average and preconditioning can be treated using the method of averaging. Our approach applies to a broad class of algorithms including to Adaptive momentum estimation (ADAM), Momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schultz (MUON), and its variants. It also applies to a broad class of learning tasks, such at tensor PCA, Gaussian projective models, teacher-student networks, and a multi-layer neural network trained on the XOR problem using a hybrid of MUON and ADAM as commonly done in practice. We demonstrate how to this technique can give precise, quantitative comparisons between algorithms. In particular, we find interesting phenomena, such as the cross-over phenomenon where online SGD has better generalization than ADAM early in training until the learning curves cross and ADAM dominates. Furthermore, we prove a version of the Edge of Stability phenomenon. In particular, we introduce an analogue of the infinity Laplacian that sharply characterizes the Edge of Stability.

papers.title: On the false discovery rate of one-sided p-values under Gaussian dependence
papers.abstract: We study the false discovery rate (FDR) of the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure for $K$ hypotheses at nominal level $q$ under Gaussian dependence of one-sided p-values. We ask whether the global null is least favorable after optimizing over correlation matrices. We show that the global null attains the worst-case FDR for $K\le3$ at every level. In dimension eight, an explicit mixed-null construction has FDR $21q/20$ for $0<q<1/2$. It exceeds the global-null maximum for all sufficiently small $q$, by a uniform extension of the known fixed-matrix small-level Simes bound. For $0<q<1/2$, we identify eight as the first inflation dimension in the monotone rank-one class and prove that $21q/20$ is its exact eight-dimensional maximum. In the same level range, the sharp multiplicative bound over all dimensions in this class is twice the omega constant $w = W(1)$, where $W$ is the Lambert $W$ function. This bound is approached as the dimension increases. We also give scale conditions for stability around the independence benchmark $m_0q/K$, where $m_0$ is the number of true nulls, and obtain a dimension-free upper bound of $q+q^2/2+O(q^3)$ at small levels under the global null with nonpositive correlations.

authors.name: Chenxin Lyu
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory Fluid Power and Mechatronic Systems

papers.title: TileCache: Serving Multi-Round Diffusion Image Editing with Compressed Activation Caches
papers.abstract: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.

papers.title: Wake-Powered Spreading of Encapsulated Drops Impacting Under Liquid
papers.abstract: A drop impacting a wall in air spreads by converting its own kinetic energy into surface energy. We show that this picture fails when the wall is submerged in liquid. Millimetric perfluoropolyether drops, bare or encapsulated in an ultrathin silicone-oil shell, impacting a glass wall in water are flattened by the squeeze flow in the draining gap and shed most of their kinetic energy before impact. Nevertheless, they spread to more than twice their diameter on a water lubrication film that never ruptures, creating more surface energy than their entire kinetic and gravitational energy could supply. A two-stage energy scaling resolves this deficit. The liquid set in motion in the drop's wake supplies more than 90\% of the energy for spreading, so that the maximum spreading is governed by the Weber number of the ambient liquid rather than that of the drop. The shell acts mainly through its interfacial tension, while its biaxial-extension dissipation, negligible before impact, becomes appreciable during spreading.

papers.title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
papers.abstract:
Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis.
  To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.

papers.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.

papers.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
papers.abstract: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

authors.name: Jaime C. Acosta
authors.institution: United States Army Combat Capabilities Development Command

authors.name: Anantaa Kotal
authors.institution: The University of Texas at El Paso

authors.name: Aritran Piplai
authors.institution: The University of Texas at El Paso

papers.title: Support recovery of diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis
papers.abstract: We study diffusion models under the manifold hypothesis with possibly large score estimation and discretization errors, and show that while they may not exactly recover the data distribution, they will exactly recover the support (or data manifold). In continuous time, we use a Lyapunov function to show that even if the relative score estimation error is fixed (and not necessarily vanishing), then the rate at which the process approaches the support is $O(\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|})$ as $t \to T$, where $T$ is the final time. In discrete time, we use geometric time steps with a fixed (non-vanishing) ratio and show that with a fixed (also not small) relative score estimation error, the process approaches the data manifold exponentially with the number of iterations. The proof relies on controlling a Gaussian measure of a neighborhood of the cut-locus of the data manifold, using a polynomial approximation argument combined with quantitative semi-algebraic estimates.

papers.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).

authors.name: Sicong Jiang
authors.institution: Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital

papers.title: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models
papers.abstract: We study a random-feature method for pricing and calibrating European options under jump-diffusion (Merton, Kou) and stochastic-volatility (Heston, SABR) models. The network has one hidden layer with a probit activation and fixed random inner weights, so fitting it to the pricing equation, the payoff and the boundary conditions is a single regularised least-squares problem, with no iterative training. For Merton and Kou the jump integral of each feature is explicit, so no quadrature is needed. One factorisation of the least-squares matrix gives the price at every state and time, its Greeks, and the exact derivatives of the prices with respect to the model parameters for gradient-based calibration. For the jump models, subtracting the Black-Scholes price removes the payoff kink and reduces the pricing error by about two orders of magnitude. The method is then about as accurate as a standard Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme at the same run time, although a finite-difference scheme that also subtracts the Black-Scholes price is about two orders of magnitude more accurate still. On the test problems of a recent physics-informed neural network study, the method matches that network's accuracy in seconds instead of about half an hour.
