These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.

papers.title: Interplay of interfacial energetics and selective Ni segregation in the morphology of co-precipitates in low-alloy steels
papers.abstract: Coupled precipitation and interfacial segregation in low-alloy steels change precipitate stability and morphology, which influence strengthening and embrittlement. Cu-rich precipitates (CRPs) and Mn-Ni-Si-rich precipitates (MNSPs) frequently form core-shell or appendage morphologies, but the interfacial energetics controlling this change are not well quantified. We combine a density-functional-theory-trained cluster expansion with lattice Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the Fe/CRP, Fe/MNSP and Cu/MNSP interfaces within one Hamiltonian. The three coefficients based on excess internal energy follow gamma_Cu/MNSP < gamma_Fe/CRP <~ gamma_Fe/MNSP and give a positive work of adhesion and a negative spreading parameter, consistent with favorable Mn-Ni-Si attachment to a CRP and partial coverage. Only Ni segregates to the Fe/CRP boundary. Mn and Si segregate weakly on their own but become more enriched when Ni is present and co-segregate with Ni at the boundary. Ni forms an interfacial layer about one monolayer thick with an excess of 7.4-9.6 atoms/nm^2, develops B2-like local order and shows an energy reduction that increases with Ni coverage. At 1 at.% matrix Ni, a Gibbs adsorption analysis gives a Fe/CRP free-energy reduction of about 0.15 J/m^2. These interface coefficients and segregation trends connect segregation, interface energy and co-precipitation and support compositional optimization in low-alloy steels.

authors.name: Anshul Kamboj
authors.institution: Government of the United States of America

papers.title: Enumerating Solutions to Type (2,3) Composition Identities of Finite Endofunctions
papers.abstract: We enumerate ordered pairs $(f,g)$ of endofunctions on a finite labeled set $X$ satisfying a composition identity of type $(2,3)$, with two factors on one side and three on the other. For all sixteen forms up to exchanging $f$ and $g$, we derive formulas involving finite sums and generating functions. The arguments use images and fibers, homomorphisms between functional digraphs, and isomorphism types of iterates. A common construction decomposes weighted allocations of fibers into trees and cycles, yielding determinant expressions for several generating functions. Colored functional digraphs provide further formulas. As a by-product, for arbitrary prescribed endofunctions $A,B$ on $X$, we derive an inclusion--exclusion formula over subsets of $X$ for the number of endofunctions $g$ on $X$ satisfying $B=gAg$.

papers.title: On Pairwise Independent and Strongly Correlated Random Variables
papers.abstract: Characterizing joint distributions that maximize the centered third-order moment under prescribed marginal distributions and pairwise independence has various statistical applications. This problem can be formulated as a multistochastic optimal transport problem. In this work, we generalize the results on the $(3,2)$-multistochastic Monge-Kantorovich problem to cost functions of the form $c(x,y,z)=f(x)f(y)f(z)$, where $f$ is defined on $[0,1]$ through dyadic expansions: $f(x)=\sum_{i\geq 1} a_i x_i$, with $x_i\in\{0,1\}$. Under summability and domination conditions on the coefficients, we show that an optimal transport plan is concentrated on the Sierpinski tetrahedron. We also characterize mixtures of geometric coefficient sequences through Hausdorff moment sequences and construct a recursive dual solution with its integral representation for costs with geometric coefficients.

authors.name: Alexander Kolesnikov
authors.institution: Government of the United States of America

papers.title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.

authors.name: Xuannan Liu
authors.institution: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

authors.name: Zekun Li
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Xing Cui
authors.institution: Shandong University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: Semantic Validity vs. Graphical Arrangement in Visualization Grammars
papers.abstract: Systems for modular, declarative and compositional specification for data visualizations, otherwise known as visualization grammars, often claim Wilkinson's Grammar of Graphics as motivation, inspiration or foundation. However, despite the shared intellectual lineage, visualization grammars can vary greatly in design scope and focus. In particular, systems that strongly adhere to domain-specific notions of correctness must trade-off expressivity for validity. This trade-off between semantics and graphical flexibility is currently under-articulated, leading to difficulty integrating various GoG-inspired visualization contributions, especially between InfoVis and Statistical Graphics. We propose three new types of visualization contributions to support such integration: Semantic Validity Theories, Semantic Visualization Systems and Graphical Arrangement Systems. The first two prioritize the adherence of data visualizations to correctness conditions, such as statistical or mathematical transformations and data semantics, whilst the third largely leave validity concerns to the user. We illustrate these new contribution types using examples from two recent grammar of graphics inspired papers, and show how they supported more nuanced notions of expressivity and usability in evaluation and design of visualization systems.

papers.title: Team Stability: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: Teams emerge organically when individuals decide on their own their activities and collaborators. I develop and test a theory in which teams form with consent, interactions reflect team composition, and payoffs feature externalities and several forms of congestion. Stability constraints concern group interactions and require each team member to be willing to remain rather than withdraw or pursue a project alone. Empirical analysis of research collaborations among economists at the Federal Reserve Board suggests that: (i.) these constraints help explain observed teams beyond the payoffs to collaboration; (ii.) estimated violations point to large teams of entrants that appear to be assigned; (iii.) a compensatory mechanism mitigates the effects of variation in policy workload, which appears to affect team composition more than total research output; and (iv.) shifting workload toward experienced economists increases entrants' research output and collaboration, at the cost of lower output among experienced economists who compensate for this shift in policy workload with increased interactions with entrants.

papers.title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
papers.abstract: Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

authors.name: Sai Harshitha Aluru
authors.institution: International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad

papers.title: FiReIQ: Field-Level Confidence Estimation with Reasoning and Image Quality in Document Extraction
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in structured document extraction, yet their deployment in high-stakes applications requires reliable confidence estimates for individual fields. Existing uncertainty estimators often aggregate signals across an entire generation, obscuring field-specific reasoning uncertainty while overlooking visual degradations that may lead to confident extraction errors. To address these limitations, we introduce FiReIQ, a field-level confidence estimation framework that combines field-aligned reasoning signals from a single VLM generation with local and global image-quality features through quality-conditioned visual fusion. To facilitate systematic evaluation, we further introduce FiReIQ-Bench, a benchmark spanning financial receipts and legal contracts. Experiments with two reasoning VLMs show that FiReIQ consistently improves confidence discrimination, selective prediction, and probabilistic accuracy over existing estimators. These gains extend to private financial service data, where FiReIQ improves AUROC by 6.8% and coverage at 95% precision by 10.6% over an existing baseline. Together, these results highlight the potential of FiReIQ to reduce manual review while enabling more reliable document automation.

papers.title: LMEG-Doc: Layout-Grounded Multi-View Evidence Graphs for Multimodal Long-Document Retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieving relevant evidence from multimodal long documents remains challenging, as supporting information is often distributed across different pages and modalities. Existing retrieval methods primarily rank document elements by their individual similarity to a question, often overlooking relationships among complementary evidence. Consequently, relevant figures and tables may receive low retrieval scores even when they contain essential information. To address this limitation, we introduce LMEG-Doc, a layout-grounded multi-view evidence graph framework for multimodal long-document retrieval. We first construct an evidence graph that captures structural and contextual relationships among document elements, and introduce Cross-Page Relation Refinement (CRR) to discover additional connections across distant pages through VLM-based verification. Building on this graph, we combine multimodal retrieval signals with graph-guided relevance propagation to recover connected supporting evidence at both layout and page levels. Experiments on MMDocIR, DocScope, and FinRAGBench-V demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements, including outperforming retrievers fine-tuned on MMDocIR without task-specific training. Furthermore, augmenting existing question-answering pipelines with our retrieved evidence improves answer accuracy by 7.6% on DocScope and 15.8% on FinRAGBench-V, demonstrating the effectiveness of relationship-aware multimodal retrieval.

authors.name: Changcheng Fu
authors.institution: Guangxi Key Lab of Manufacturing System and Advanced Manufacturing Technology

papers.title: Spectral Landmarks: Alignment of Landmark Kernel Translates with the Leading Eigenfunctions of a Kernel Operator
papers.abstract: We study the problem of choosing $m$ landmark points so that the span of the kernel translates is as close as possible to the leading $s$-dimensional eigenspace of a positive-definite kernel. The natural measure is the Hilbert-Schmidt operator discrepancy between the reproducing-kernel-Hilbert-space (RKHS) projectors onto the two subspaces. We give a closed form spectral alignment function in terms of the truncated Mercer kernel and relate it to the classical integrated power function (Nystr\"om trace error) through a two-sided sandwich bound. Minimizing the function by gradient descent on the landmark coordinates produces landmark sets that are evenly spaced. Theoretical results show that optimal configurations are those whose eigenfunction sampling matrix is a scaled isometry. On homogeneous spaces these are exactly the minimal equal-weight cubature rules for products of leading eigenfunctions, and for every $m\ge s$ they are the configurations whose sampled eigenfunctions form a unit-norm tight frame. Experiments on $\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\mathbb{S}^2$ agree with the theory. On the circle, with $s\le2m$ and a moderate bandwidth, every random start converges to equispaced landmarks, and on the sphere the optimizer recovers the regular tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron from random starts. Finally, we analyze the numerical conditioning of the problem.

papers.title: Free energy profile computations for force-induced melting of a short B-DNA using Jarzynski equality
papers.abstract: We initially equilibrate a system of solvated 12-base pair canonical B-DNA of a specified sequence in a state of no external force acting on it (state $A: f=0$). A switching experiment is then performed by pulling one end of the DNA while restraining its other end. The pulling force is taken up to a maximum of 400 pN (state $B$), at a specified constant rate. The non-equilibrium work done W associated with this finite-time process is determined by integrating the extension of the DNA molecule with respect to the applied force. The distribution of the work values $P(W)$ is obtained by repeating the pulling process several times, wherein each time, the process is started with macroscopic state $A$. The free energy profile $\Phi(f)$ is obtained by a suitably devised method from the Jarzynski equality. The conformational space of the DNA is also sampled in an equilibrium method of umbrella sampling by considering the end-to-end length $\xi$ as the reaction coordinate. The associated potential of mean force (PMF) $\Phi(\xi)$ is then computed by invoking the weighted histogram analysis method (WHAM). From the results, we observe that the equilibrium free energy difference between two states, $A$ and $B$, $\Delta F_{AB} ~(=F_B -F_A)$ obtained through both methods, is in close agreement with each other, despite the differences along the profiles $\Phi(f)$ and $\Phi(\xi)$, attributed to their distinct pathways of unzipping.

papers.title: A Matter of Stages: Energy-Latency Trade-offs in Multimodal LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Online serving of multimodal large language models requires deciding whether to separate visual encoding (E), prefill (P), and decode (D) across GPUs and how to configure their frequencies. EPD disaggregation enables independent stage control, but it also changes communication and queueing behavior. Lowering one stage's frequency can increase queueing and prolong execution across the EPD pipeline. Consequently, reducing power at one stage does not necessarily reduce total GPU energy per request. In this paper, we systematically characterize fused and EPD-disaggregated serving across four multimodal models under a fixed three-GPU budget, followed by single-stage and uniform downclocking experiments across 18 workload combinations. We find that disaggregation reduces GPU energy per successful request by 13.3-37.0% at nearly identical output-token throughput, but increases mean TTFT. Downclocking exhibits distinct stage sensitivities, and aggressive frequency reductions can offset power savings through queueing and longer execution. Across the evaluated workloads, uniform downclocking to 80% reduces GPU energy by 11.7-18.6% with modest mean-latency changes. Guided by these findings, we develop a budgeted frequency exploration strategy to select energy-efficient configurations under latency constraints. Evaluation shows that four probes can identify the lowest-energy feasible configuration among 25 measured candidates across all 288 evaluated positive-margin SLO scenarios. These results provide practical guidance for energy-efficient multimodal serving.

authors.name: Yifan Sun
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Beyond Raw Similarity: Prior-Aware Fusion for Out-of-Distribution Detection
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in vision-language models presents unique challenges due to the reliance on cross-modal similarity. Even when embeddings are well separated for in-distribution (ID) data, similarity scores can remain overconfident for OOD inputs. A common remedy is to adapt the model on ID data, but adaptation discards the pretrained geometry that made the similarity meaningful. We propose multi-modal logit fusion (MM-Log), which keeps both by pairing a gradient-free zero-shot prior with a task-adapted branch in each modality and fuses their four cross-modal similarity channels into a single OOD score. Because the zero-shot priors are never adapted, the cross-channels act as a consistency check between the pretrained and adapted geometries: an OOD input that fools the adapted branch through a shortcut must additionally agree with frozen CLIP to retain a high score. We formalize this as a margin bound showing that the fused score is provably penalized by disagreement between the zero-shot and adapted branches, a signal to which adapted-only scores are structurally blind. MM-Log requires no auxiliary OOD data, negative prompts, or test-time adaptation, and trains on few-shot ID data alone. Across Far-OOD, Near-OOD, and Hard-OOD benchmarks, MM-Log consistently outperforms strong CLIP-based baselines.

papers.title: From Twelve Leads to Single: Cross-Lead Knowledge Distillation for Domain-Generalized Atrial Fibrillation Detection
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) detection from long-term ambulatory electrocardiography (ECG) is critical because AF is a leading cause of stroke yet is frequently missed by conventional diagnostics, particularly in wearable settings that demand strong cross-domain generalization. Deep learning has improved AF identification by exploiting rhythm patterns, but methods such as BMIRC and SJTU-ECGNet still struggle to generalize across heterogeneous single-lead wearable datasets. To address this issue, we propose X-LeadGen, a two-stage cross-lead distillation framework for single-lead ECG AF detection that explicitly targets domain generalization. First, a 12-lead teacher network distills rich multi-lead information into a single-lead student through cross-lead knowledge transfer and a simulated self-distillation branch within the teacher, improving cross-lead representation alignment and AF discrimination. Second, we introduce a domain-generalization strategy that applies domain-adversarial training in both teacher and student stages, complemented by GANs-based augmentation in the student phase to learn domain-invariant features and enhance robustness to distribution shifts. Across seven public ECG datasets under real and simulated Lead-I settings, X-LeadGen consistently outperforms existing approaches in accuracy and F1-score, demonstrating strong generalization for real-world wearable AF monitoring. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Aveiro-Lin/X-LeadGen, enabling further research and validation in the ECG community.

authors.name: Yaomin Shen
authors.institution: Jiangxi University of Water Resources and Electric Power

papers.title: Mutual Colormap Dependence: How Recoloring Biomedical Images Changes Vision-Language Model Answers
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are being built to answer questions about biomedical images, yet they never see the measured intensities, only the colors that a colormap has assigned to them. For questions about image content, the colormap should not change the answer. We call the extent to which it does Mutual Colormap Dependence (MCD), the mutual information between the colormap and a model's answer, which is zero exactly when every colormap yields the same answer distribution. Because VLMs sample their answers, we compare recoloring with a control that uses the same number of calls to ask again about the unchanged gray image, so that ordinary resampling is not mistaken for an effect of the colormap. We test GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Qwen3-VL-235B under six luminance-monotonic colormaps (gray, viridis, plasma, inferno, magma, and cividis) on 50 medical visual-question-answering items from 16 SLAKE images, 64 ChestX-ray14 chest radiographs, and 200 BBBC039 fluorescence-microscopy images for exact nucleus counting. Every prompt tells the model to ignore the colormap. Even so, with three answers per colormap on the chest radiographs, the answers of all four models depend on the colormap (all Holm-adjusted $p \leq 0.002$). For Claude, some colored map overturns the majority answer on 29 of the 64 radiographs, where resampling gray alone overturns about 4, and Qwen's accuracy falls from 0.54 under gray to between 0.32 and 0.41 under the colored maps, mostly because it abstains. With one answer per colormap, recoloring adds disagreement beyond repeated sampling in 5 of 12 model-panel cells under per-cell 95% intervals, and repeating the instruction to ignore color does not reliably reduce it. The colormap is therefore part of what a VLM sees, and it can change the answer.

papers.title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.

authors.name: Tianhang Zhang
authors.institution: Ministry of Emergency Management of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: Flat-band driven bipolar anomalous Nernst effect towards volt-scale transverse thermoelectric conversion
papers.abstract: Unipolar anomalous Nernst thermopiles are critically plagued by metallic interconnects, which induce heavy Joule dissipation and compromise the module's packing density, ultimately capping voltage generation. Here, we circumvent these limitations by establishing an intrinsic bipolar anomalous Nernst effect (BANE) paradigm, enabling seamless series integration analogous to Seebeck n-p pairs without passive metallic bridges. Focusing on flat-band topological systems, through machine learning assisted screening across multiple target properties, we identified 249 BANE materials, exhibiting near-room-temperature polarity switching. Guided by this predictive framework, we experimentally realized this phenomenon in single crystals of the Weyl ferromagnet, Co$_2$TiGe. Strikingly, while its intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) remains rigorously temperature-invariant up to the Curie temperature, the anomalous Nernst signal undergoes a sharp polarity inversion across $T \approx 225$ K. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to the interplay between flat bands and Weyl nodes, where thermal depopulation shifts the chemical potential across the band edge, inverting the sign of $\partial \sigma_{xy} / \partial \epsilon$ via the Mott relation. This work opens an avenue toward compact, monolithic transverse thermopiles capable of volt-scale generation free from interfacial parasitic dissipation.

authors.name: Peng Di
authors.institution: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs

authors.name: Jinlan Wang
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: Log-optimal two-sample testing by betting
papers.abstract: For each standard Borel observation space, we construct a single anytime-valid two-sample procedure that is asymptotically log-optimal for every pair of unknown probability laws and every limiting ratio of diverging sample sizes, including zero and infinity. For independent balanced pairs, the optimal log-wealth rate is $2\JS(P,Q)$, where $\JS$ is the Jensen--Shannon divergence. Unequal sizes yield weighted Jensen--Shannon information and the one-sample limit $\log W(n_1,n_2)/n_2\to\KL(Q\|P)$ when $n_1/n_2\to\infty$. Refining finite partitions and logarithmic-loss learning with measurable characteristic kernels provide universal constructions. Our main contribution is the generality of our construction, and its connections to classical batch efficiency notions. Practical implementations allow continuous classifier fine-tuning, as demonstrated on finite alphabets, Gaussian data, and handwritten digits.

papers.title: DyTransRM: A Unified Simulation-to-Real Framework for Dynamic Radio Map Prediction
papers.abstract: Dynamic radio map (RM) prediction enables proactive wireless network control by forecasting future propagation conditions from historical observations. However, collecting temporally continuous and spatially dense real-world RMs is prohibitively expensive, while models trained on large-scale simulated data often suffer from limited transferability to real environments. To address this issue, we propose DyTransRM, a unified simulation-to-real framework for dynamic RM prediction under sparse real-world measurements. DyTransRM first introduces RadioCLIP to learn physics-semantic representations by aligning environmental evolution with the corresponding propagation evolution, thereby improving both prediction accuracy and cross-domain transferability. To further bridge the simulation-to-real gap, SparseUOT employs sparse-mask simulation refinement to mimic realistic measurement patterns and unbalanced optimal transport to selectively align compatible propagation representations across domains. Experiments on RadioMapMotion and real-world datasets demonstrate that RadioCLIP achieves an NMSE of 0.0018 and an RMSE of 0.012 in simulation-domain prediction. After sparse real-domain adaptation, DyTransRM achieves an NMSE of 0.023, RMSE of 0.079, and MAE of 0.064, outperforming representative adaptation baselines without requiring spatially complete real RMs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DyTransRM for transferring simulation-learned dynamic propagation knowledge to practical sparse-measurement scenarios.

authors.name: Simin Wang
authors.institution: State Grid Shandong Electric Power Company (China)

papers.title: The stable false discovery rate
papers.abstract: When a discovery depends on analysis choices, a list of selected hypotheses that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) gives little indication of how easily the finding could change: the selected set may be very sensitive to a variety of analyst choices, like the target FDR level, which machine learning algorithms are used in the pipeline, the choice of test statistics, and so on. We propose that scientists should measure and control a new metric called the \emph{stable FDR} (sFDR), and give methods to control it, including simple wrappers around existing FDR analysis pipelines. sFDR is a natural continuous extension of the FDR: we assign each hypothesis an allocation between zero and one, and the sFDR equals the expected fraction of null allocation to total allocation. If one runs multiple analyses of the same data by varying different reasonable choices, allocations can be determined by simply dividing each run's selection indicators by its discovery count, then averaging across analyses and rescaling. The resulting sFDR equals the average of the ordinary FDRs of the runs, even though the runs are dependent: thus sFDR control holds under the same assumptions that the original FDR control held. (In contrast, naively reporting just fractions of times each variable was selected need not control the sFDR.) It is interpretable: hypotheses that were always selected are allocated 1 and those never selected are allocated 0. In leukemia expression and neuroimaging analyses, findings with larger allocations were more often supported in separate samples. We also develop procedures that can assign stable allocations directly from p-values, e-values, or knockoff statistics, resulting in stable-BH, stable e-BH and stable knockoff procedures. A representation by e-values describes which allocation rules control the error rate and gives ways to optimize allocations for different follow-up goals.

papers.title: Charge-Transfer Energy Governed by $f$-$d$ Coulomb Interaction in Rare-Earth Systems
papers.abstract: The $f$-$d$ Coulomb interaction ($U_{\rm fd}$) plays a central role in low-energy theories describing valence fluctuations and quantum valence criticality in rare-earth systems. In contrast, core-level spectroscopies have conventionally been analyzed using the phenomenological charge-transfer energy ($\Delta$), and the relationship between these two descriptions has remained unclear. Here, we develop a spectroscopic framework demonstrating that the charge-transfer energy contains an $f$-$d$ Coulomb contribution $U_{\rm fd}n_d$ arising from the $d$-electron occupation ($n_d$), leading to the charge-transfer energy $\Delta'$. We apply this framework to the prototypical valence-transition compound YbInCu$_4$ and demonstrate, from combined analyses of core-level photoemission and $L$-edge x-ray absorption spectroscopy, that the observed spectroscopic evolution across the first-order valence transition is consistently interpreted in terms of the variation of $\Delta'$.

papers.title: Turning Errors into Successes: Designing LLM Tutoring Around Scaffolded Error Correction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could make personalized tutoring available at scale, but it remains unclear how they can best support the instructional processes that make one-on-one instruction effective. We compared two ways of using LLMs after students make errors: providing personalized explanations of those errors, or engaging students in additional cycles of scaffolded practice and feedback, with a Socratic tutor guiding students toward the correct answer. In a preregistered online experiment, 400 adults practiced setting up constraint equations and, after each attempt, received the correct answer, a generic explanation, a personalized LLM explanation of their error, or Socratic tutoring. Socratic tutoring helped: participants resolved 64% of their errors through the dialogue and scored 0.24 SD higher on practice-aligned posttest questions than those who received generic or personalized explanations. Socratic participants also found the session more interesting, less frustrating, and less costly, even though it took nearly twice as long. In contrast, we found no evidence of a benefit of personalized explanations over generic ones, and neither type of explanation reliably outperformed simply seeing the correct answer. These findings suggest that LLM tutors may add the most value not by explaining errors more precisely but by helping students correct those errors themselves through scaffolded practice. This pattern fits a mastery-experience account of tutoring, in which an effective tutor notices when a student is struggling, steps in with guidance, and works with the student until the struggle resolves into success. AI tutors may be most effective when designed around this principle.

authors.name: Paulo F. Carvalho
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: A formally verified convergence theorem for the tug-of-war scheme of the normalized $p$-Laplacian
papers.abstract: We present a complete formalization, using Lean 4, of the convergence of $p$-harmonious functions to the viscosity solution of the Dirichlet problem for the normalized $p$-Laplacian, $2 \le p < \infty$, as the step size goes to zero. By $p$-harmonious functions we mean solutions of the dynamic programming principle of tug-of-war with noise. Our proof follows the argument of Barles and Souganidis and is formalized in full, depending only on Mathlib and the standard axioms of Lean. In particular, we include the asymptotic expansion of the scheme, the viscosity properties of the half-relaxed limits, existence and uniqueness for the discrete problem, the comparison principle and uniqueness for the homogeneous equation, Aleksandrov's theorem, and Jensen's lemma.

papers.title: Supporting Community Members Navigating Reentry with Revisable Future Envisioning
papers.abstract: Future-planning tools often treat agency as individual and leave out the institutional conditions that shape how aspirations become action. We examine this tension in the context of reentry from incarceration and recovery from substance use disorder, through a partnership with a nonprofit organization. Building on participants' physical vision-board practices, we designed a digital future-envisioning tool that helps users represent current circumstances, desired futures, and pathways that connect goals to concrete resources. We draw on data from three workshops involving 18 participants and follow-up interviews with 10 participants to examine how they used future envisioning within a fragmented support system. Participants described reentry and recovery as ongoing processes in which the everyday work of staying stable was central to progress. Envisioning futures supported this work by surfacing constraints and interdependencies, by reframing personal strengths and institutional supports as assets, and by helping participants move from abstract hopes toward articulated goals and contingent plans. We theorize revision as maintenance work and conclude with design implications for community-embedded interactive systems that support revisable, dependency-aware planning.

papers.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
papers.abstract: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.

papers.title: PerturbJEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning of Cellular Perturbation Responses
papers.abstract: Identifying the drug and dose that produced a cellular response requires preserving treatment effects within each cellular background. A joint-embedding predictor can match its targets while ignoring the intervention if its encoder preserves differences across backgrounds but erases differences between treated and control populations within each one. We call this failure interventional contrast collapse. PerturbJEPA encodes the difference in mean gene expression between treated and control populations as an effect vector. It aligns the displacement between their latent centroids with this vector and regularizes the vectors to preserve variation across population pairs. We show that the measured displacements cannot all coincide within a batch when effect-vector variation exceeds the root-mean-square alignment error. Trained with separate drug and dose ranking objectives, the model predicts candidate responses from a common control population and matches them to the observed response without cell pairing or expression reconstruction. We evaluate 3,592 Tahoe-100M queries on held-out combinations of known interventions and cellular backgrounds, each with over 700 drug-dose candidates in a fixed, background-specific catalog. PerturbJEPA achieves 91.46% macro joint drug-dose Recall@1, exceeding STATE by 3.40 percentage points (95% drug-cluster bootstrap interval of 1.72 to 5.07 points). Controlled diagnostics show that treatment-control differences can shrink even when representations remain globally dispersed. With the drug ranking objective fixed, adding effect-vector regularization to alignment raises joint Recall@1 from 18.57% to 87.47%.

authors.name: Huinan Xu
authors.institution: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

papers.title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
papers.abstract: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.

authors.name: Zhen Tao
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
papers.abstract: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

papers.title: Optimal Ordering-Free Two-Dimensional Insdel Reed-Solomon Codes via Cross-Ratios
papers.abstract: Insertion-deletion (insdel) codes correct synchronization errors. By the half-Singleton bound, an ${[n,2]}_q$ code has minimum insdel distance at most $2n-4$. The smallest field size of two-dimensional Reed--Solomon (RS) codes attaining this bound is $\Theta(n^3)$. Unlike the minimum Hamming distance, the minimum insdel distance of an RS code depends on the ordering of its evaluation points. An evaluation set is called ordering-free if every ordering of its points gives an RS code attaining the half-Singleton bound. In this paper, we first show that for $n\ge6$ every ${[n,2]}_q$ code attaining the half-Singleton bound is an RS code, and hence $q\ge\binom{n}{3}+2$. Secondly, we show that an ordering-free evaluation set with $n\ge6$ points in $\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfies $n<q^{1/3}+2$, and that it has at most $r+1$ points if $q=r^3$ for a prime power $r\ge3$. Finally, by using cross-ratios, we construct an ordering-free evaluation set with $r+1$ points in $\mathbb{F}_{r^3}$ for every prime power $r$. Hence, the bound $r+1$ is attained for $r\ge3$. Moreover, the constructed set is even robust against permutations combined with insdel errors.

papers.title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
papers.abstract: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

papers.title: The Maximum Number of Sets for 16 Cards is 26
papers.abstract: In SET, each card has four properties with three values each, and three cards form a \emph{set} when every property is all the same or all different. We prove that the maximum number of sets among $13$, $14$, $15$, and $16$ cards is $16$, $19$, $23$, and $26$, respectively. Viewing cards as points of $\mathbb{F}_3^4$ and sets as lines, we show that a configuration that leaves one of the $40$ line directions of $\mathbb{F}_3^4$ unused projects into $\mathbb{F}_3^3$ without losing a set, which reduces the problem to three properties, where exhaustive search is feasible. We force an unused direction by counting repeated directions in the planes through a card on many sets, and treat configurations containing a magic square separately.

papers.title: KVMARK: Fragile Watermarking for KV-Cache Integrity in Latent Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Latent multi-agent communication directly transfers Key-Value (KV) cache tensors between transformer-based agents, bypassing text serialization entirely. While computationally efficient and reasoning accurate, this communication channel is opaque and vulnerable to man-in-the-middle tampering, a threat vector unaddressed by existing text-based or behavioral watermarks, which cannot operate on continuous internal representations. To address this vulnerability, we propose KVMark, a training-free, zero-bit KV-cache watermarking framework to verify inter-agent handoff integrity. Our framework introduces four core technical components: (1) position-dependent sign patterns that guarantee first-order statistical invisibility while preserving downstream attention survival; (2) per-head sign patterns with aligned detection to defeat head-averaging attacks; (3) a three-tier depth-aware strength schedule that equalizes detection sensitivity across transformer layers while maintaining invisibility against nine statistical profiling strategies; and (4) content-bound key derivation that cryptographically binds watermarks to input contexts, preventing replay attacks under Kerckhoffs's principle. Empirical evaluation on a four-agent latent pipeline demonstrates $100\%$ detection across $1{,}500$ handoffs with a $0.0\%$ false positive rate ($\text{AUROC}=1.0$), $100\%$ layer-level tamper localization ($17/17$ attacked layers identified with $0/19$ false positives), and no statistically significant reasoning accuracy degradation across four benchmarks ($N{=}300$--$500$). Furthermore, the framework enables multi-hop cascade verification to isolate compromised agents (500/500 detection at three hops), withstands adaptive white-box adversaries and the Out-of-Sight DiffMean attack (up to $\alpha=8.0$), and generalizes seamlessly to Qwen3-8B without re-tuning (1,500/1,500 TPR).

authors.name: Ronghua Xu
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix
papers.abstract: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.

papers.title: Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attacker's Auxiliary Information
papers.abstract: Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual's data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher's dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Clustering Algorithm and Parameter Selection for Collaborative Population Stratification Using Distributed PCA
papers.abstract:
We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top-$r$ principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing.
  Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility--scalability trade-off in our setting.

papers.title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
papers.abstract: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.

papers.title: Non-tempered GGP conjecture for classical groups: the Bessel case
papers.abstract: In their recent paper, Gan, Gross and Prasad proposed a precise conjecture to describe the restrictions of representations of classical groups that lie in an L-packet of Arthur type. On top of local root numbers, the main notion considered is the relevance of two A-parameters. In this paper, we establish that the relevance of two A-parameters is sufficient for the existence of a Bessel period for a pair of representations in the associated L-packets. Moreover, such a pair is unique. We also prove the necessity of relevance for co-tempered A-parameters, and give several counterexamples in the general case.

authors.name: Jing Quan Chong
authors.institution: NUS High School of Mathematics and Science

papers.title: Effective and Efficient Rumor Assertion Over Large-Scale Social Networks (Technical Report)
papers.abstract: Nowadays, social networks, like Facebook, X, Reddit, YouTube, and so on, have become essential online platforms for users to connect with friends daily, post/share news, and express their opinions/comments. Meanwhile, however, the rapid and widespread dissemination of rumors and misinformation across social networks has become a serious concern. Such misleading information can distort public opinion and potentially cause significant social and economic consequences in real-world scenarios, including product promotion, elections and voting, and even cyberbullying. Therefore, accurately and efficiently verifying whether news spread on social networks is rumor or truth has become an increasingly important yet challenging problem. While previous works usually identified rumors by their contents, in this paper, we propose a novel \textit{user behavior model} to capture the users' judgment/discriminative abilities, which is learned via our well-designed evidence-aware probability reconstructor. We develop a general framework for tackling \textit{rumor assertion over large-scale social networks} (RA-SN), which can efficiently and effectively determine whether a given news item is a rumor with high confidence, based on users' behaviors, in a scalable manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed RA-SN approach on both real-world and synthetic graphs.

papers.title: Altermagnetism in moir\'e quasicrystals
papers.abstract: Altermagnetism is a collinear compensated magnetic phase with zero net magnetization and momentum-dependent spin polarization. Quasicrystalline altermagnetism extends altermagnetism beyond periodic crystals, with noncrystallographic symmetries allowing high-order spin polarization patterns. Here, we propose a symmetry-based approach to realizing quasicrystalline altermagnetism by twisting collinear magnetic layers. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $30^{\circ}$-twisted honeycomb lattice bilayers form the dodecagonal quasicrystals supporting an $i$-wave altermagnetic phase. We further find that $45^{\circ}$-twisted bilayers preserving fourfold rotational symmetry support a mirror-driven $l$-wave phase with eight nodal lines. We characterize these altermagnetic patterns through plane-wave-projected spin-resolved spectral functions and spin-resolved conductances. Our work provides a systematic route to high-angular-order quasicrystalline altermagnetism through twist engineering.

papers.title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

papers.title: Borrowed Strength, Imported Risk: Capability Gaps and Reception Govern Heterogeneous LLM Debate
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous LLM debate is often attributed to collective reasoning that creates capability beyond any member. In the matched panels we study, the aggregate gain is dominated by capability transfer: a peer supplies task competence and receivers absorb a measurable fraction. Across nine matched directions, honest benefit and first-exchange adversarial exposure open when the peer has a positive same-task advantage, and honest gain is closely described by the empirical decomposition $\Delta A_d^{\mathrm{hon}}\approx\kappa\Gamma_d^+\rho_d$, the product of that advantage and the receiver's reception. Two fixed-receiver directions provide held-out validation without refitting: reception remains stable within uncertainty as a larger peer advantage produces a larger gain. A matched, single-direction open-answer MuSiQue scope probe reaches the negative-gap side of the same gate. Qwen-7B trails the Gemma-3-12B receivers by 10.78 points; despite 62.50% reception, it produces only +1.17 points of controlled first-exchange gain. Reception cannot substitute for positive aggregate peer advantage. When an influential peer is assigned an adversarial role, the same influential peer slot removes the borrowed gain and can push the panel below homogeneous debate. Across all five full-reference settings, the best observed majority correctness does not exceed the influential member's best observed accuracy, despite unused complementary answers. Heterogeneous debate is therefore a measurable transfer decision with a measurable failure mode, not a benefit conferred by diversity alone.

authors.name: Nagaraj N Bhat
authors.institution: Shri Madhwa Vadiraja Institute of Technology and Management

papers.title: The unitary group $U_3(4)$ as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$
papers.abstract: We prove that the simple unitary group $U_3(4)=\operatorname{PSU}_3(\mathbb{F}_4)$, of order $62400$, is the Galois group of a regular extension of $\mathbb{Q}(t)$, and hence of infinitely many extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. The extension has four branch points, with inertia groups of orders $2$, $2$, $3$, $3$, and it is the only extension with these properties up to a rational change of the coordinate $t$. We give an explicit polynomial of degree $65$ for it.

papers.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.

papers.title: LLM Facilitation of Group Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Human groups often fail to integrate information distributed across their members, converging on incorrect decisions. We ask whether large language models (LLMs) can help groups reach the correct decision in such settings. In an online, chat-based experiment, 138 three-person groups (N = 414) completed a hidden-profile hiring task that required selecting the best candidate using public information available to all group members and private information available only to individual members. The randomized human-subject experiment included three conditions: no facilitation, an individual-level LLM that messaged each member privately, and a group-level LLM that messaged the whole group. The LLM facilitation consisted of adaptive interventions that summarized the discussion, nudged quiet members, and played devil's advocate. The LLM did not know which candidate was correct. Both LLM conditions significantly increased the rate at which groups reached consensus on the correct candidate, from 32.6% without facilitation to 56.5% with LLM facilitation. LLM-facilitated groups exchanged more consensus messages signaling agreement on the group's choice. Participants in the group-level condition also disclosed significantly more information about the correct candidate, whereas those receiving individual-level facilitation repeated public information less often. Finally, group-level facilitation received more favorable usability ratings than individual-level facilitation. These results show that LLMs can deliver adaptive, theory-informed interventions that improve group decision-making, and that the design of these interventions may shape how people respond to them.

papers.title: Mining Unity VR Repositories for Refactoring Patterns and Technical Debt
papers.abstract:
Maintaining virtual reality (VR) applications poses challenges tied to real-time performance, hardware dependencies, and complex interactions. Yet little is known about how developers refactor these applications, which kinds of technical debt they address, or how well automated tools capture VR-specific changes. We mined 1,755 candidate refactoring commits from 176 open-source Unity VR repositories and manually examined a sample of 303 commits, of which 270 contained at least one refactoring. We also extended RefactoringMiner to create VRRefMiner, a tool that detects conventional refactorings in C# scripts used by Unity applications.
  Our analysis found both conventional and VR-specific refactorings. VR-specific changes addressed concerns such as interaction logic, performance, and Unity-specific artifacts. Code debt was the most prevalent category overall, while interaction debt and UI/UX debt were the main categories addressed by VR-specific refactorings. Across the repositories, VRRefMiner detected 15,549 operations spanning 68 refactoring types, with structural moves and extractions accounting for 31.0% of detections. It detected conventional refactorings in 216 of 246 commits labeled as general refactoring. In the 24 commits labeled as VR-specific, the tool could detect conventional changes but identified no VR-specific refactoring categories. These results point to a need for detection techniques that account for both source code and the Unity artifacts involved in VR maintenance.

papers.title: From Cloud to Edge: A Fully Local Pipeline for Pothole Risk Assessment and Driver Warning Generation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models can turn road images into clear, geometry-aware pothole warnings, but current systems depend on commercial cloud services. Our earlier five-stage pipeline needed two cloud calls per scene, taking about 20 s and USD 0.105, and could not run offline. We rebuild every stage to run on a single local GPU and evaluate it with the same data, prompts, and protocol. Segmentation keeps the original Segment Anything weights but runs them in half precision with graph compilation, which makes it 2.7x faster without changing any downstream risk class; five lightweight variants could not match its masks on small road defects. Severity is graded by six ConvNeXt students distilled from 3092 cloud labels. They reach Cohen's kappa = 0.268 against human consensus at 28 ms per pothole, close to the cloud model's 0.321, within the camera setup they were trained for. A local 8-billion-parameter vision-language model writes the warnings under a grammar that admits only in-lane maneuvers. Three blind, independent raters scored these warnings safer than the cloud warnings (4.18 vs. 3.65 of 5; p = 0.001; 50 scenes) and equally clear, whereas an automated LLM judge ranked them the other way. The complete pipeline runs at 1.27 s per scene, 16x faster than the cloud system, offline and at no per-scene cost.

papers.title: Matching two-dimensional statistics does not certify three-dimensional transport in battery electrodes
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional battery electrode structures reconstructed from two-dimensional micrographs are routinely used to predict transport, assuming that matching the measured 2D statistics reproduces the relevant 3D properties. We test this premise on X-ray tomograms of three all-solid-state cathodes. With a differentiable conductivity solver, we optimise voxel structures that match the real electrode in phase fractions, boundary density, two- and three-point correlations and lineal-path functions, on all section planes, slab by slab and layer by layer, within measurement noise. Every sample has statistical twins conducting 10-88-fold less than the real electrode, robust to 5^3 majority filtering, whereas the most conductive are at most 3.3-fold above it. The twins rearrange rather than remove material, severing or funnelling through-plane paths. A classifier on 2D sections detects them, as it does current 2D-to-3D generators: the information is in the images but not in the statistics. Matching standard 2D statistics therefore does not certify 3D transport.

papers.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.

papers.title: Identification and external validation of the sets of 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hour CGM motifs
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in using CGM for purposes other than those initially intended. Recent work of Lobo et al. identified $\Omega$: a set of motifs such that almost any daily CGM profile (the 24-hour CGM time series starting at midnight) can be classified - matched to a motif in $\Omega$. This work generalizes the prior work by identifying sets of motifs for 4-, 6-, 8-, 12-, and 24-hr CGM profiles where an $x$-hr CGM profile does not have to be 24 hours in length, and does not have to start at midnight. The prior work methods are modified to identify the five new sets of motifs using data from the same 6 studies in the original work. The newly identified sets were subjected to rigorous external validation using a data set comprised of data from 21 studies (3,455 subjects, 289,592 days of CGM data). The external validation data set has both temporal and geographic transportability and addresses limitations of the data set used to define the five new sets of motifs. The results of the external validation indicate that the prior work generalizes well: the performance of each $x$-hr set of motifs on the external validation set is almost identical to that obtained for $\Omega$. The generalization of the original work broadens the potential use cases of the framework to include short term predictions (e.g., impending hypoglycemia) and diagnostics which rely on detecting changes in CGM time series which are less than 24 hours in length.

papers.title: Bilateral Log-Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

papers.title: SWAN-Rx: Efficient and Bandwidth-Scalable Neural Reception for MIMO-OFDM
papers.abstract: We present a Scalable Windowed Axial-attention Neural Receiver (SWAN-Rx) for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. The receiver improves reception accuracy and reduces forward-pass computation while supporting frozen-weight reuse across bandwidth allocations and channel conditions. It combines a common resource-element representation of received observations and pilot context with alternating time-axis and local frequency-axis attention. Shared parameters and relative positional information permit soft detection across allocation lengths without inference-time parameter updates. At fixed subcarrier spacing, model configuration, and symbol count, bounded frequency neighborhoods give linear growth of forward-pass computation with bandwidth. Evaluations compatible with the 5G New Radio physical layer reuse weights trained on four physical resource blocks (PRBs) at up to 273 PRBs and on unseen channels. At the training bandwidth, SWAN-Rx achieves lower pre- and post-decoding bit error rates than the implemented three-step neural receiver (NRX) and DeepRx-MIMO baselines, with 16.9% and 39.7% fewer parameters and 56.3% and 35.7% fewer forward-pass operations, respectively. The same weights achieve lower pre-decoding error rates than these baselines throughout the evaluated bandwidth-extrapolation and 16-PRB channel-transfer tests, with an estimated 0.4-0.9 dB signal-to-noise ratio reduction relative to NRX at a pre-decoding error rate of $10^{-2}$ in the 16-PRB tests.

papers.title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
papers.abstract: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

authors.name: Weile Luo
authors.institution: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

authors.name: Jia Li
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: A Bias-Variance Framework for Estimating Stochastic Speed-Density Relationship Considering Constrained Sample Size
papers.abstract: Accurate calibration of traffic speed-density fundamental diagram models is essential for freeway traffic flow analysis, yet existing approaches estimate parameters from fixed datasets without examining how estimates evolve as data availability increases.
