Without a CQ that is uniform in the band width, however, a shrinking band loses the $K$-independent exponent: with width $\epsilon$ and fixed $K\geq2$, deterministic zero-respecting methods need $\Omega(\epsilon^{-(K+3)/4})$ calls on a hard instance whose control dimension grows with $1/\epsilon$. We prove our assumptions for smoothed kinematic and dynamic multi-robot navigation among segment obstacles. In navigation experiments, PSK, tuned per case, reaches every goal with sixteen levels and, at equal time, reaches a lower loss than tuned unrolling in 17 of 18 cases, while implicit differentiation is lower in 10.

papers.title: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
papers.abstract: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

papers.title: Exstill: The Most Efficient Single-Chip Processor for the Next Token
papers.abstract: Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

papers.title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

papers.title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

papers.title: How Much Do Foundation Models Add to Gradient Boosting on Financial Event Sequences?
papers.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

papers.title: Eclipse-minimising sun-synchronous orbits in a mean-Sun rotating frame
papers.abstract: A satellite in low Earth orbit normally passes through Earth's shadow on every revolution. A dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit largely avoids it: J2 precession keeps the orbit plane facing the Sun all year, but it follows only the Sun's average position, the mean Sun. In reality the Sun wanders up to 23 degrees around this average, enough to push the plane into shadow for part of the year. We introduce MSSI, a coordinate frame that rotates with the mean Sun. In it, a sun-synchronous orbit is a fixed ring and the real Sun traces the analemma, so the yearly eclipse question becomes static geometry. From that picture we derive how much of each orbit is in shadow, the yearly eclipse for every plane orientation, maps of which directions are never, sometimes or always eclipsed, and the margin a mission has. Fixed planes become eclipse-free above about 1400 km, within a window of node offsets that widens with altitude, and the 06:00 and 18:00 lines turn out to be equivalent. The closed form is checked against a full-force-model numerical propagation and against the published eclipse seasons of three flying missions; the model, its code and an interactive 3-D visualizer are published as open source.

papers.title: Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context?
papers.abstract: Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning method, but selecting an appropriate algorithm and set of hyperparameters for a specific dataset can require many possible configurations and evaluations. In this work, we investigate whether a Vision-Language Model can instead visually evaluate clustering results and use those decisions to then tune an explicit clustering algorithm. We study this through three progressive experiments using Qwen3.5-27B and five controlled synthetic clustering scenarios. First, we test whether the VLM can distinguish the best clustering result from a pair of plots. Second, we test whether it can assign numerical scores to those plots where a higher score represents a better result. Finally, we use these judgments within an agentic loop in which the VLM scores a k-means clustering and proposes updated hyperparameters that may result in better clustering. Our exploratory results show that the VLM performs well when clear cluster structure is present, while struggling on more ambiguous and noisy settings. In the full agentic experiment, the VLM produces clustering configurations with silhouette scores relatively close to those of grid search and Bayesian optimization, while terminating in much fewer iterations. Overall, these results provide an initial proof of concept that VLM-based visual feedback can be used to autonomously tune an explicit clustering algorithm.

papers.title: Psyquandle Fares
papers.abstract: We introduce a new infinite family of invariants of singular knot and links and of pseudoknots by extending the biquandle fares construction to the case of psyquandles. We give the axioms explicitly for four cases of fare-based invariants: 1-fares, signed crooked 2-fares, signed through 2-fares and signed complete 2-fares. We provide examples of each type, illustrating the method of computation and collecting some results for toy examples using small-cardinality psyquandles and abelian coefficient groups.

papers.title: The PHAROS Spectral Library: Data Processing, Spectral Reconstruction, and Uncertainty Propagation
papers.abstract: We document the data reduction, reconstruction choices, and available uncertainty propagation underlying fifteen PHAROS stellar spectral energy distributions from 0.5 to 5000 nm. A catalogue timeline and a practical FITS guide introduce the available products, their column and extension conventions, and examples of reading, integration, and uncertainty display. Shared methods are presented once, including flux geometry, support-aware integration, X-ray likelihoods, the 2025 X/EUV luminosity relation, intrinsic Ly$\alpha$ inference, airglow treatment, spectral junctions, and covariance-aware resampling. Target sections record the adopted observations and alternatives, including spatially separated binary components, unresolved system-level EUV measurements, direct EUVE constraints, optical stellar-twin transfer, and literature-anchored cases where new spectral inference is unsupported. The distinction between native measurement errors, conditional model intervals, empirical predictive scatter, and physical-method sensitivity is maintained. Signed measurements and nonnegative irradiation products are distinguished. Each target section concludes with the final nominal spectrum and its available uncertainty bounds on common axes. This library provides the detailed provenance and interpretation needed to accompany the catalogue paper and its machine-readable products.

papers.title: Hochschild Cocycle and Universality of Merge
papers.abstract: The Hopf algebra Markov chain dynamical system, on the Hopf algebra of non-planar binary forests, that models the action of Merge on workspaces in Chomsky's Minimalist Model of syntax, satisfies a universal property, determined by the fact that the Merge operation is a Hochschild 1-cocycle. This universal property has an interpretation in terms of models of the syntax-semantics interface, as it shows that, if the side of semantics possesses a sufficiently rich compositional structure, then that structure is uniquely induced by the syntactic Merge, once the semantic values of lexical items and syntactic features are assigned. We illustrate how this universality works by showing, in particular, full compatibility of this Hopf algebraic formulation with Heim-Kratzer semantics.

papers.title: Generalized particle systems: a locality-factorized metamodel for self-propelled particles and agent-based models
papers.abstract: We propose a single formal object, the generalized particle system (GPS), under which self-propelled particle systems (SPPS) and agent-based models (ABMs) are instances of one construction. A GPS is a typed finite population, a per-particle state space with arbitrary internal structure, a global environment, a neighbourhood map that may depend on the configuration, and type-indexed local rules; these assemble into a generator whose iteration is a monoid action, i.e. an autonomous dynamical system. Update schedules and stochastic rules are added at the same generality, so sequential and noisy models (the original Primordial Particle System, Vicsek) are covered, not approximated. The construction isolates the one ingredient separating the two communities: in the classical ABM reading the dependency graph is fixed; in an SPPS it is a function of the state. Under an exchangeability axiom (rules see neighbours only through the multiset of their types and states) the generator is equivariant for type-preserving permutations and descends to a dynamical system on counting measures, the setting of kinetic limits of swarming models. We read the tuple as a metamodel: its structural components coordinatize a space of models inside which numerical parameters live. Six pre-registered experiments on one engine implementing the generator test the claims: freezing the neighbourhood map destroys alignment ($\varphi = 0.91 \to 0.04$) while yielding a different, non-aligned aggregation; the realized neighbourhood graph rewires up to 64% of its edges per step, its rewiring rate anti-correlated with order ($-0.99$); a topological instead of metric neighbourhood reshapes a flocking phase diagram; the same rule with cohesion and separation off shows a Vicsek-type transition whose susceptibility peak grows with system size. One prediction failed and one subsumption claim is unconfirmed; both are reported.

authors.name: Igor Strozzi
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro

papers.title: Equivariant homomorphisms and Mordell--Weil groups of twists of Albanese varieties of cyclic multiple planes
papers.abstract: Let $X'\to X$ be a Galois cover of smooth projective varieties over a field $k$ with group $G$, and let $G$ act on an abelian variety $A$ over $k$. We prove an exact sequence relating the Mordell--Weil group of the twist of $A$ by $k(X')/k(X)$ to the group of $G$-equivariant homomorphisms from the Albanese variety of $X'$ to $A$; the remaining obstruction is killed by $|G|$. This corrects structure theorems in two earlier papers of the author and in a corrigendum to the first, where the equivariance condition was omitted. For the twists of Albanese varieties of cyclic multiple planes considered in those papers, we determine the rank and the torsion subgroup. Over number fields we describe the rank through the Galois action on endomorphisms and prove a specialization result. When $F(x,y)=0$ is the dual of the Fermat cubic, the Mordell curves $y^2=x^3+16F(a,b)$ have rank at least $3$ over $\mathbb Q$ for all $(a,b)\in {\mathbb Q}^2$ outside a thin set.

authors.name: Sajad Salami
authors.institution: Universidade do Estado do Rio de Janeiro

papers.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

papers.title: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
papers.abstract: Local feature attributions are computed over a feature representation chosen by an upstream data-engineering step, yet they are read as statements about the underlying quantity. We ask how discretizing one continuous feature changes local KernelSHAP and LIME explanations when the classifier is held fixed, and whether the two explainers respond differently. A random forest is trained on UCI Adult and frozen; age is collapsed onto equi-width or quantile bin representatives (k in {3,5,10}) before the model receives it, and the same 120 held-out instances are explained in every condition across multiple seeds. We show analytically and numerically that for KernelSHAP this is exactly equivalent to explaining the unchanged model at the quantized instance against a quantized background, so the comparison is between two effective inputs rather than a pure explainer effect; for LIME no such equivalence holds. Each attribution change is compared with a seed-noise floor from re-running the explainer on the unchanged condition. KernelSHAP's age attribution exceeds its noise floor in all 6 pre-specified conditions (median ratios 2.4-59, all significant after Holm correction); on the raw scale LIME's exceeds its floor in only 2 of 6 and in the rest is no larger than its own run-to-run variation. SHAP's normalized change exceeds LIME's in every condition (rank-biserial 0.81-1.00), while LIME is 2.5-4.6x less consistent across repeats. Predicted classes change for only 0.8-5.8% of instances and held-out ROC-AUC never falls below 0.9097, yet 45-94% of instances show a large SHAP attribution change with no class flip. Feature-importance rankings barely move (median Spearman >= 0.979, top-3 overlap 1.00). The representation change and the change in effective input cannot be separated within a frozen-model design.

papers.title: From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
papers.abstract: Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

papers.title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmea- sured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses.

papers.title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
papers.abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

papers.title: Quaternionic Wave Numbers and the Dirac Equation: Resolving the Nielsen--Ninomiya Barrier and Infinities
papers.abstract: We exemplify the applicability of the rational wave numbers by formulating the relativistic Dirac equation on the discrete sequence space $\mathbb{H}^\mathbb{Z}$ over the quaternions $\mathbb{H}$ and demonstrating how this resolves fundamental issues relating to Dirac's equation. Generating $\mathbb{H}^\mathbb{Z}$ from the primitive basis $\mathcal{P}_0 = \{E_Z, E_{\bar{1}}\}$ as both a static closure and a dynamic enumeration, we show that coupling local quantum kinematics with global cosmological expansion leads to the following results: (1) Dirac 4-spinors and the Clifford algebra $\mathrm{C}\ell_{1,3}(\mathbb{R})$ emerge from the second Cayley--Dickson doubling (biquaternions $\mathbb{H} \otimes \mathbb{C}$); (2) under dynamic generation on an integer clock lattice with causal horizon $\Lambda_m$, relativistic difference operators require temporal depth, establishing clock beat $m = 2$ as the universal Matter Genesis Threshold; (3) the Nielsen--Ninomiya fermion doubling barrier is circumvented on modular sequences $\mathbb{Z}/Q\mathbb{Z}$ because candidate zone-edge doubler modes ($p = Q/2$) are actively pruned at the generational boundary by the coprime sieve projector $\mathcal{S}_Q$ ($\gcd(Q/2, Q) > 1$), preserving exact chiral symmetry without Wilson terms; (4) the discrete fermionic Green's function $S_Q(n, m)$ possesses no coincident-point singularity ($n = m$), converting ultraviolet loop integrals into finite Dedekind and Kloosterman character sums, realizing Dirac's demand for an infinity-free theory; and (5) Zitterbewegung is resolved as an observable stroboscopic beat against vacuum reference $E_Z$, identifying rest mass $m_0$ as a vacuum coupling beat frequency for stationary periodic cycles on the saturated quotient graph.

papers.title: A Multigrid Finite State Projection Algorithm For The Solution Of The Reaction-Diffusion Master Equation
papers.abstract: We develop a multigrid method for the direct solution of the reaction-diffusion master equation (RDME). The RDME describes stochastic chemical dynamics through reactions in well-mixed spatial cells, called voxels, and diffusion between them. Its unknowns are probabilities of molecular count configurations, and the growth of this state space is the main computational challenge. Grouping neighboring voxels and summing their counts gives smaller equations down to a chemical master equation on one voxel. Restriction sums residual entries with the same coarse counts, and prolongation distributes corrections by multinomial weights. We derive coarse reaction and diffusion rates and, for reversible diffusion, bound the error omitted by coarsening through graph energy, with a constant independent of population for fixed aggregates and rates. Tests with standard multigrid cycles and Gauss-Seidel smoothing examine spatial and population refinement, reaching 7.16 million states and resolving probabilities of order 1e-7.

papers.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
papers.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

papers.title: Comets in Kepler background photometry: the ion tail and tail disconnection of C/2009 K5 (McNaught) and an analysis of comets crossing the Kepler field
papers.abstract: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 to 2013, an archive that we use to study comets. During 2010 April 14-21 a narrow band of excess light swept across the field at 1.46 deg/day. This feature is the ion tail of comet C/2009 K5 (McNaught), whose head passed just beyond the edge of the detector array. We trace the tail from 0.9 deg to ~13 deg from the nucleus at surface brightnesses of 26.7-30 mag/arcsec^2; its aberration implies a solar-wind speed of ~500-750 km/s. At 30-min cadence we follow a tail-disconnection event on 2010 April 17-19 whose timing and geometry are consistent with a flank encounter with a coronal mass ejection, although other triggers cannot be excluded. We then analyze all 21 known comets with perihelion distance q < 15 AU whose heads crossed the detectors, using photometry at the predicted head positions calibrated against displaced control tracks. Eight comets are detected, including C/2010 J4 (WISE) a few days before its discovery and two comets at 6.3-7.4 AU with one-sided streaks that we interpret as dust tails. The undetected comets give 3-sigma limits of typically Kp > 16.6-18.1 within 5 arcmin of the head. A blind shift-and-stack search for moving diffuse sources, roughly 50% complete at Kp ~ 15.5-16 for rates of 0.3-1 deg/day, recovers four known comets and finds no unknown ones. Animations show the K5 tail and comets C/2011 L3 and C/2010 J4 crossing the field.

papers.title: Kepler as an accidental heliospheric imager: Thomson-scattered solar-wind structure in four years of background photometry
papers.abstract: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 May to 2013 May while staring at a fixed 12-degree field at ecliptic latitude +65 degrees. From this archive we isolate a large-scale layer that measures brightness variations relative to an 8-day running median. This layer contains fluctuations of 0.02-0.1 electrons per second per pixel (about 1e-17 of the mean solar surface brightness) that sweep across the field in a day or less. Four lines of evidence show that these are sunlight Thomson-scattered by solar-wind electrons. (1) The sweeps propagate away from the Sun (84 percent within 45 degrees of the anti-solar direction; 25 percent expected by chance), and their direction follows the Sun through each quarter and across all 16 spacecraft rolls. (2) The field brightness correlates with the near-Earth (OMNI) proton density within a day of zero lag (r = 0.19, p < 1/150), but not with the energetic-proton flux. (3) Time-elongation maps show fronts moving outward at a median 15 degrees per day, as forward models of radially moving density structures predict. (4) The amplitude is about one third of a parameter-free Thomson-scattering prediction and varies by a factor of about 3 over the year, as predicted. Half of the scattered light comes from within 0.4-0.7 AU of the spacecraft. Fronts are strongest in slow wind. Kepler's background pixels thus provide a four-year, high-cadence, out-of-ecliptic record of solar-wind structure near 1 AU. Standard Kepler processing removes these signals, changing stellar light curves by less than about 1 ppm.

papers.title: Cross-species digital xenocortication model delineates molecular correlates of human brain connectome
papers.abstract: Cross-species digital xenocortication (CSDX) model based on pairing of a human brain structure with one or more mouse brain structures was constructed and implemented to dissect the molecular correlates of the human brain connectome. Design of the CSDX model is based on the assumption that a human brain region and its named mouse counterpart occupy corresponding positions in an evolutionary conserved mammalian brain connectome plan, so that a projection strength measured between two mouse structures is informative about the relation between the two human structures paired with them. In the CSDX model, gene expression for the node was measured in the human brain, while connection strength between two nodes was measured in the mouse brain. CSDX models of different parcellations were employed to explore the potential regulatory associations of brain connectome patterns and constituents of protein-protein interaction (PPI) cascades of hybrid assembly pathways of endogenous multiprotein complexes. Metrics of continuous engagement of the PPI cascade nucleated protein dimers of CORUM multiprotein complexes have been identified as statistical components of the multivariate transcriptome-connectome associations. It accounts for additional connectome associated variations beyond the five measured axes in the 82 nodes CSDX model. Comparisons of the seven arm models of transcriptome-connectome associations demonstrate that the mouse derived model generally fits the mouse brain connectome better, while the human derived model assigns a significantly larger fraction of its transcriptome-connectome association to unique rather than net shared contributions. This study nominates elite panels of top scoring candidate protein dimers and CORUM multiprotein complexes for follow up mechanistic studies of their potential roles in structural functional features governing mammalian brain connectome.

papers.title: Uniform compactness in a family of $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problems
papers.abstract: In their paper on non-coercive boundary value problems, Kohn and Nirenberg show that a priori estimates for all forms satisfying $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann boundary conditions follow from a compactness estimate. Inspired by Hamilton, we show that these a priori estimates are stable under deformations of the complex structure, the hermitian metric and the volume form of the underlying manifold. We use a parameter $m$ to encode a deformation of this data. We show that if a family of $\bar{\partial}$-Neumann problems depends smoothly on $m$ and the compactness estimate(s) hold (with constants uniform in $m$), then the family of solution operators also depends smoothly $m$. As a consequence we obtain sufficient conditions for the Bergman kernel to vary smoothly in a family of domains. We also provide a sufficient condition for the uniform compactness estimate(s) to hold in a family of domains.

papers.title: How Much Determinism Can Fine-Tuning Buy? Margin Regularisation Against Batch-Induced Token Flips
papers.abstract: Greedy decoding at zero temperature is widely assumed to be deterministic, although the exact same prompt may yield different tokens depending on the number of other prompts sharing the batch for inference. The currently available solutions operate during inference, trading determinism for throughput. Can we train a model in such a way that fewer decoding steps would be susceptible? We characterize the perturbation empirically across six model families and three numerical precisions and observe two empirical facts about the measurement: the perturbation depends exactly on the representable precision (8.00x for bfloat16 vs float16, 8192.0x for float16 vs float32, in line with predictions based on mantissa bits) and the batch invariance happens accidentally at certain tensor shapes, allowing a practitioner to achieve zero nondeterminism merely by setting the sequence length. Then we apply hinge penalization of the model's top-1 / top-2 logit gap, scaled to twice the measured noise quantile. On GSM8K dataset it leads to a 35% reduction in token flips and divergence from 53.8% to 38.1%, at the cost of 1.3 - 2.9 accuracy points, increasing monotonically with the margin size. It does not affect the gap threshold sufficient for determinism: the logit gaps of surviving flips are unchanged (median 0.125 for all arms), as the hinge is a soft penalty and the largest hardware perturbation remains the same. We reject seven hypotheses, including a per-model viability diagnosis, holding on six models and falsified on the seventh.

papers.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
papers.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

papers.title: Stability conditions on Lazarsfeld-Mukai bundles over abelian surfaces
papers.abstract: We study the stability of Lazarsfeld-Mukai bundles associated with smooth curves over abelian surfaces. When the general curve in $|L|$ have Clifford dimension one and maximal gonality, for $\rho \gg 0$ we show that every component of the relative Brill-Noether loci \(W^1_d(|L|)\) dominating the linear system parametrizes generically \(\mu_L\)-stable rank-two Lazarsfeld-Mukai bundles. We also apply Bayer-Li wall-crossing to higher-rank bundles: if \(\operatorname{NS}(S)=\mathbb Z\cdot L\), \(A\) is a globally generated complete linear series of degree \(d\) on a smooth curve \(C\in|L|\), \(h^0(C,A)=r+1\) with \(r>2\), and \(d\ne g-1\), then the associated bundle \(E_{C,A}\) is \(\mu_L\)-stable and \(L\)-Gieseker-stable. The corresponding object \(E_{C,A}^{\vee}[1]\) for \(d<g-1\), or \(E_{C,A}\) for \(d>g-1\), is stable in the adjacent chamber, as its reduction. These results connect dimension estimates for Brill-Noether loci with stability and wall-crossing on abelian surfaces.

authors.name: Graciela Reyes-Ahumada
authors.institution: Universidad Autónoma de Zacatecas "Francisco García Salinas"

papers.title: On the volume of amoebas of complete intersections
papers.abstract: We study the $2k$-dimensional volume of the amoeba of a smooth complete intersection $V$ of dimension $k$ in $(\C^*)^n$, $n\ge2k$, with Newton polytopes $\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_{n-k}$. For $n=2k$ we prove $\Vol(\A(V))\ge\mathcal M(V)/\MV(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_k,-\Delta_1,\dots,-\Delta_k)$, where $\mathcal M(V)$ is the coamoeba volume counted with multiplicity, and we show $\mathcal M(V)\ge\pi^{2k}$ for plane curves ($k=1$, $n=2$) whose Newton polygon is not centrally symmetric, for nondegenerate varieties with odd $\MV(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_k,\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_k)$, and for smooth towers of curve fibrations. We determine the equality case for curves and towers, and prove that $k$-planes in general position never attain the bound. For $n>2k$ we prove two-sided bounds for $\Hm^{2k}(\A(V))$ through coordinate projections, and show that for generic coefficients almost every fibre of the amoeba map is an orbit of a finite group. For lines we prove that in several random models the area of the amoeba of a line in $(\C^*)^n$ is asymptotic to $\frac\pi2n\log n$, and we compute its limit under degenerations of the configuration. Finally we characterise the varieties attaining the extremal volumes. For $n=2k$ every regular fibre of the amoeba map has an even number of points, divisible by $4$ for real varieties with $k\ge2$; the volume-maximal varieties are those with two-to-one amoeba maps and maximal rolled coamoebas, and they are never real when $k\ge2$; a volume-minimal plane curve is characterised by a group of symmetries of maximal order, and its amoeba has no holes. For $n>2k$ the extremal varieties lie in translates of $2k$-dimensional subtori.

papers.title: Context Matters: Improving LLM-Based Code Summarization with Hierarchical Information
papers.abstract: Source code documentation plays an important role in software quality activities, such as code review, program comprehension, maintenance, and bug fixing. However, it is often fragmented across individual code elements and focuses on local implementation details, providing little information about their surrounding context. This limits both developers' understanding of software systems and the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs), whose reasoning is constrained by finite context windows. Enriching documentation with hierarchical context has the potential to improve software comprehension and support downstream, quality-related tasks for both developers and LLM-based tools. In this paper, we present an in silico study that showcases the impact of augmenting context on the generation of code-level documentation, using a variety of LLMs. By varying the function, class, and module hierarchy visible to the LLMs, we assess whether this variation produces a significant difference in the resulting code documentation compared with the existing documentation, which serves as a proxy for developer intent. Our results show that Documentation-Aware prompts with class or module-level context consistently yield summaries that are closest to the original documentation. Adding surrounding documentation yields statistically significant improvements over the baseline across models, with effect sizes ranging from negligible (DeepSeek) through weak (GPT-4o-mini) to medium (Gemini). We restrict the study to this immediate hierarchical context; call-graph traversal and cross-module dependency context fall outside our scope and are left to future work. These findings provide a clear path to improve automated documentation tools and enhance LLMs' ability to reason about codebases for downstream tasks, such as code retrieval.

papers.title: The Dedekind-MacNeille Completion as a Functor
papers.abstract: We study the Dedekind-MacNeille completion through representable functors on the wide subcategory $\mathbf{Pos}_{\mathrm{cl}}$ of posets and lower cut-continuous (closed) maps. On this category the completion is contravariantly functorial and naturally isomorphic to $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Pos}_{\mathrm{cl}}}(-,[1])^{\mathrm{op}}$, via $A\mapsto\chi_A$ and its inverse $f\mapsto f^{-1}(\{0\})$. The naturality of this identification makes the Yoneda lemma applicable: uniqueness of the representing object and the endomorphism monoid of the completion follow formally. We also show that $\mathbf{CLat}_\vee$ is full in $\mathbf{Pos}_{\mathrm{cl}}$, that $\mathbf{CLat}_\wedge$ is equivalent to a full subcategory of $\mathbf{Pos}_{\mathrm{cl}}^{\mathrm{op}}$, and that the covariant adjunction refines to a $2$-adjunction whose idempotent monad has Eilenberg--Moore algebras equivalent to $\mathbf{CLat}_\vee$.

papers.title: Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities
papers.abstract: Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.

papers.title: Denoising-Induced Recovery of Effective Dynamics
papers.abstract: Recovering dynamical equations from data is a central problem in nonlinear science. In practice, measurements are corrupted by noise and often contain fast oscillations that are not part of the slow dynamics of interest. For this reason, data are typically pre-processed before model recovery or classsification. Here, we reveal the effects of filtering, a specific denoising technique, on recovery. Our analysis show that equation discovery performed on filtered data recovers, up to a fixed precision, the normal-form (effective) equations rather than the original system.

papers.title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
papers.abstract: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

authors.name: Supriadi
authors.institution: Universitas Islam Negeri Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi

papers.title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
papers.abstract: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.

papers.title: Integrated Co-design Framework for High-Efficiency Assembly and Integration of Small Satellites
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of small-satellite constellations has increased the need for higher manufacturing throughput, lower production costs, and shorter turnaround times. This makes efficient assembly, integration, and testing (AIT) increasingly important. Building on our prior work, this paper presents an integrated design-for-AIT approach for the 65 kg Lumelite-5 satellite. The integrated approach incorporates co-designing the satellite configuration, structural interfaces, subsystem placement, harness routing, and ground support equipment to facilitate efficient AIT. Service interfaces are centralized on one satellite side to simplify electrical ground support equipment access and routing. Skeletal support interfaces are developed to retain mounted components and service interfaces when removable enclosures are opened to expose internal harness-routing paths for inspection, troubleshooting, and rework. Defined mechanical references further support controlled removal and reinstallation of sensors and components. A removable double hinge ground-support mechanism allows the top deck to open up to 180 degrees relative to the bottom deck while accommodating interconnecting-harness articulation, without introducing permanent hinge mass and complexity to the satellite. Finally, dedicated harness-routing and tie-down provisions provide predefined yet adjustable restraint locations to accommodate as built routing variations and maintain controlled harness articulation during top-deck rotation. Through this work, we demonstrate how co-designing satellite architecture and AIT processes from the early development stages can support more scalable, repeatable, and efficient constellation production.

papers.title: HongguoTrending: A Longitudinal, Multimodal Archive of Trending Videos and Topics on a Leading Micro-Drama Platform
papers.abstract: Micro-dramas (duanju) are reshaping digital production and consumption, yet a lack of longitudinal data connecting series to their platform visibility persists, limiting our understanding of the emerging medium. We introduce HongguoTrending, a longitudinal, multimodal dataset of hourly snapshots from seven trending lists of Hongguo, China's largest micro-drama platform. Collected through a two-stage asynchronous pipeline, the archive links 63,200 ranking entries across 632 web list-hours and 157 client hours (889 distinct series) to metadata, cover images, sampled episode videos, and audience engagement metrics. Exploratory analyses show distinct turnover rates between web and mobile trending lists, production-driven mainstream values alongside kinship-centered synopses, genre-specific cover palettes, and strong associations between user sharing and next-day rank gains. Accessible via a RESTful API, this dataset supports empirical research on algorithmic gatekeeping, popularity dynamics, and multimodal digital culture.

papers.title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
papers.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.

papers.title: Sim-to-Real Room-Mediated Object-Goal Navigation with ROS 2 and Nav2
papers.abstract: Although object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) approaches are usually evaluated in simulation, which offers scale and repeatable environments, real-world deployments are rarely examined beyond feasibility demonstrations. This paper presents the deployment of Room-Mediated Co-occurrence, an ObjectNav policy that reasons over Room Probability Vectors (RPVs), on two robotic platforms (Boston Dynamics Spot and Clearpath Robotics TurtleBot 4) through a robot-agnostic ROS 2 bridge. We study how these semantic priors generalise to physical environments and describe the adaptations required to transfer RPV from simulation to hardware, covering sensing, localisation, and the action interface. Across 66 trials on Spot, searching for 11 object categories from two starting positions in a university postgraduate research facility, RPV achieves a raw Success Rate (SR) of 0.455. Our analysis identifies undetected glass walls, entry into off-limits areas, limited usable depth range, target size, and mismatch between the room lexicon and physical layout as plausible contributors to the 8.4 percentage-point gap between the real-world SR and the reported simulated SR of 0.539. Code is available at https://github.com/Matthew-K-Chua/rpv-ros2-bridge.

papers.title: Frac-BKT Under Mechanism Scrutiny: Response Assimilation and a Failed Fractional-Memory Test
papers.abstract: Long-horizon knowledge tracing requires more than an evocative memory mechanism: the implementation must assimilate observed responses non-anticipatorily, and the mechanism must survive matched controls. We subject Frac-BKT, a BKT-style model with an elapsed-time-scaled truncated fractional history, to both tests. The repaired model predicts response $n$ from a prior mastery state and uses response $n$ only to update the posterior state for later events. A five-seed evaluation uses 676,848 ASSISTments 2017 interactions from 1,694 learners and 19,249 learner--skill trajectories, with chronological 80/10/10 suffix splits. The response-aware model reaches AUC .5860 overall, .5638 after gaps of at least 30 minutes, and .5668 after at least 14 days. Relative to the earlier non-response implementation, the gains are .0473, .0316, and .0277 AUC, respectively. However, the fractional mechanism gate fails: the full model is not better than the matched $\alpha=1$ control and is worse than the matched $\tau=0$ control by .0090 AUC on both long-gap slices. Student-cluster wild-bootstrap intervals exclude zero, both Holm-adjusted $p$-values are .00006, and all five per-seed differences favor $\tau=0$. Compact AKT-, SAKT-, and DAS3H-style references also remain stronger on long gaps. The contribution is therefore a response-assimilation repair and a falsifiable audit showing that response assimilation helps while the evaluated fractional-history term does not---not a state-of-the-art or causal-retention claim.

authors.name: Nizam Kadir
authors.institution: Singapore University of Technology and Design

papers.title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
papers.abstract: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

papers.title: Partial Borrows in Rust
papers.abstract: Rust ensures memory safety by requiring exclusive access to mutably borrowed data. However, a borrow can prevent access to more data than necessary. For example, a method with an &mut self parameter borrows the entire struct, even when the method uses only some of its fields. Calling the method can therefore conflict with an existing borrow of a field the method never uses, causing Rust to reject the program. Resolving such conflicts can require programmers to compromise useful abstractions, make non-local changes to their programs, or worse, resort to unsafe code. We introduce view types, a backward-compatible refinement of reference types that specifies which fields a reference may access. This allows methods to partially borrow a struct, accessing only the fields they need without blocking access to the rest. We establish the first fully mechanized foundation for Aeneas in Rocq. Along the way, we uncover and fix gaps in the original semantics and proofs. Building on this foundation, we formalize partial borrows and prove the extended borrow checking sound. We implement view types in rustc and extend the Aeneas interpreter to support partial borrows. Our evaluation shows how view types systematically resolve borrowing conflicts across method boundaries at no runtime cost.

papers.title: Convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity via gluing and projection
papers.abstract: This paper studies convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity. Following the method proposed in~\cite{tran}, we bound the Hausdorff distance between the set of sparse truncated moment sequences and sparse truncated pseudo-moment sequences. The central step is a quantitative gluing lemma on a clique tree: local moment errors and separator discrepancies in total variation control the error of a joint approximating measure. Over hypercube, polynomial kernels give the convergence rates $O((\log_2r)^3/r^2)$ for the correlative sparse quadratic module and $O(r^{-2})$ for the correlative sparse preordering, where the certificate degree is $2r$. On compact basic semialgebraic sets, slack variable lifting and global atom projection yield $O((\log_2r)^{3\Lo/2}/r^{\Lo})$ and $O(r^{-\Lo})$ with a {\L}ojasiewicz exponent $0<\Lo \le1$. These bounds hold for fixed-degree Hausdorff distances and polynomial objective gaps. We also extend to result to the correlative sparse quadratic-module rate for scalar objectives with clique-local polynomial matrix constraints.

papers.title: Explicit cohomological transfer for Morita equivalent Lie groupoids
papers.abstract:
It is well known that Morita equivalent Lie groupoids have isomorphic differentiable cohomology. At the cochain level, however, explicitly transporting a cocycle from one groupoid to a Morita equivalent one is less straightforward.
  We provide explicit formulas for such cohomological transfers in arbitrary degree. More precisely, for the pullback of a Lie groupoid along a surjective submersion, we construct an explicit cochain-level homotopy inverse to the natural pullback map. We first treat \v{C}ech groupoids, where the construction only involves a partition of unity, and then extend it to arbitrary surjective submersions, for which the extra choice of local sections is needed.
  We also show that the resulting operators preserve the complexes associated with $\mathcal{VB}$-groupoids, including homogeneous and $\mathcal{VB}$-cochains. As an application, we obtain explicit transfer maps for deformation cocycles of Morita equivalent Lie groupoids and recover the Morita invariance of deformation cohomology.

papers.title: Twister After Dark: Diagnosing a Damaging Nocturnal Tornado in Iloilo, Philippines (08 August 2026)
papers.abstract: (Abridge) At ~1430 UTC (2230 LST) on 08 August 2026, a significant tornado struck the Mandurriao and Jaro districts of Iloilo City, Philippines. Its parent supercell developed within the southwest monsoon enhanced by Typhoon Dolphin, under weak synoptic forcing, as a nocturnal low-level jet of ~40 kt near 1.5-3 km advected warm, moist marine air onshore. ERA5 depicted MUCAPE of ~2000 J/kg, negligible inhibition, an LCL below 300 m, and nearly purely streamwise low-level vorticity, but deep-layer shear (DLS, 0-6 km bulk wind difference) below 3 m/s. Hodographs from the newly operational Iloilo S-band dual-polarization radar (S-ILO), ~5-7 km from the storm, revealed low-level shear (LLS, 0-1 km bulk wind difference) of ~16 m/s and 0-1 km storm-relative helicity of 124-211 m^2/s^2. The storm exhibited a hook echo with a weak echo hole, a $Z_{DR}$ arc and ring, an elevated 55-60 dBZ rear-flank core consistent with a descending reflectivity core, and a ~50 dBZ ring interpreted as a debris ball. A survey of 31 damage indicators documented a ~2.9 km long and up to ~340 m wide path rated IF2 on the International Fujita Scale. Processor smoothing of the radial velocity and a $\rho_{HV}$ threshold for rainfall estimation masked any tornadic vortex or debris signature, although a radial velocity simulation shows that a narrow vortex (core radius ~50-100 m) with a rotational velocity of ~35-45 m/s could have been concealed. This case shows that significant tornadoes can develop at night during the Philippine monsoon season and that operational radar quality control should be revised to retain severe-storm signatures.

authors.name: Generich H. Capuli
authors.institution: Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration

papers.title: Bi-Lipschitz right-left equivalence of finite plane-to-plane germs
papers.abstract: We show that the bi-Lipschitz right-left equivalence of finite holomorphic map germs $(\mathbb{C}^2,0)\to(\mathbb{C}^2,0)$ admits continuous moduli, already among finitely determined polynomial germs of corank one and degree five. The moduli come from a new invariant of finite germs: for two tangent branches of the critical set whose images are tangent, the limit of the ratio of the norms of the images of nearby points is preserved by bi-Lipschitz right-left equivalence. For germs $(F,H)$ with quasihomogeneous components the invariant is computed from the height functions of $F$ and $H$: it is given by the moduli of the values of the height function of the component of lower weighted degree at the roots of a weighted Wronskian. As a first application we obtain a continuous invariant for the germs $(Y^3+3tYX^4+X^6,\,X^N)$, $N\ge7$, built from the Henry--Parusi\'nski family.

papers.title: Spectral Moments of the Projected Hubbard Configuration Graph: Connectivity, Exchange, and Virtual Doublons
papers.abstract: At strong on-site repulsion, the lowest band of $n$ lattice fermions is the spectrum of the hopping projected onto configurations without double occupancy, $H_\infty=P_0H_tP_0$. We study its moments, for few fermions in the square-lattice Hubbard model and, where the arguments allow, on any finite graph. (1) For spin-independent Hermitian hopping (no on-site terms) on any $N\geq2$-site graph, $\mu_2=\frac{n(N-n)}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}|t_{ij}|^2$, for any spin composition. (2) On any finite graph, $\mu_4$ is exactly linear in the same-spin pair count, as four hops permute particles by at most a transposition or 3-cycle; for uniform hopping on a simple graph with $N\geq4$ the slope is $\alpha(N,n)=-8C_4(N-n)(8N-11n-2)/[N(N-1)(N-2)(N-3)]$, fixed by the number $C_4$ of 4-cycles. (3) At large finite $U$, the second-order Schrieffer-Wolff correction is Hilbert-Schmidt orthogonal to $H_\infty$ on every triangle-free graph, so the band variance has no $1/U$ term; its $U^{-2}$ coefficient, an exact trace checked by exact diagonalization, is negative at the low fillings computed. (4) Under a Peierls flux, the exchange slope $\alpha(N,2,\Phi)=-\frac{64}{N-1}\cos\Phi_\square$ ($L\times L$ tori, $L=3$ or $L\geq5$) carries the ordinary charge-$e$ harmonic, while the doublon (bound-pair) hopping acquires a doubled phase, $t_de^{2iA_{ij}}$: the second-order single-doublon Hamiltonian is exactly $\pi$-periodic ($h/2e$) under a boundary twist, and the exact two-electron U-band follows numerically, up to $O((2\lambda)^L/U^{L-1})$. Result (1), the permutation bound, the orthogonality in (3) and the doubled phase are machine-checked in Lean 4. Repulsive binding and the pair charge $2e$ are known; new are the exact moment structure and the derivation of the doubled phase. We make no claim about many-pair phase stiffness, off-diagonal long-range order or superconductivity.

authors.name: D. Souza
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: Learning and Verifying Stabilizing Controllers with Structured Neural Control Lyapunov Functions
papers.abstract: This work investigates the joint learning of neural controllers and control Lyapunov functions (CLFs) for nonlinear discrete-time systems. We exploit the structural properties of Input Convex Neural Networks and Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz Networks to guarantee positive definiteness of CLF candidates by construction, reducing the conditions requiring formal verification. We develop a mixed-integer programming framework to formally verify the remaining stability conditions and introduce an iterative region of attraction (ROA) expansion procedure to enlarge the certified ROA without retraining. Experiments on an inverted pendulum and a path-tracking system demonstrate the advantages of structured neural CLFs, particularly PLNets, and illustrate how their structural bounds influence the geometry of the certified regions. Our code is available at: https://github.com/JLedesMart/Structured-Neural-Control-Lyapunov-Functions.

authors.name: Patricia Pauli
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: The Akhmediev breather for the Dysthe equation and the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave
papers.abstract: In this article we define and compute the breather of the Dysthe equation for deep water waves, the analogue of the Akhmediev breather of the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation (NLS). When a single pair of modes is unstable, the unstable manifold of the Stokes wave consists of the Stokes wave and the translates and time shifts of a single solution, the breather. The construction uses only gauge and translation invariance, not integrability or a Hamiltonian structure. We use the parameterisation method to find the breather as a power series whose coefficients follow recursively from linear equations. This is not an asymptotic expansion: the series is the Taylor series of the breather itself. For deep water waves we map the envelope amplification over steepness and group length and give a simple formula, based on the linear stability analysis, that summarises it to within a few per cent. Our results agree well with Euler simulations: the edge of the instability band of the Dysthe equation lies much closer to the onset of growth than that of the NLS, and, away from the onset and below breaking, the crest and height amplifications lie less than 5% below the Euler ones.

papers.title: PREFACE: Separating Shared Corrections from Prefix Conditioning in PEFT
papers.abstract: Does input-conditioned parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) improve because it uses the current input, or because it adds a useful learned correction? We investigate this distinction with PREFACE, a bounded channel controller for PEFT-adapted projections that requires no test-time gradients. The controller reads observed context; in multiple-choice likelihood scoring, its state is independent of the candidate continuation. Our central study freezes IA3, tuned LoRA, and DoRA adapters and matches controller architecture, initialization, batches, and updates across current-prefix and learned-global controls. Across ARC-Challenge and SciQ, current-prefix control improves all six mean accuracies over frozen adapters, but none of its paired contrasts with learned-global control excludes zero. Replacing its corrections with their training-prefix mean changes accuracy by at most 0.34 percentage points; input-varying corrections contribute only 1.8-2.8% of correction RMS. On ARC test, frozen-adapter current/global controls score 25.68%/25.77%, distinct from the earlier jointly trained 23.1% to 26.4% gain over IA3. We derive and evaluate static compilation of fixed corrections, separating deployment simplification from statistical equivalence. Broader GPT-2, Pythia, and Qwen experiments show family-, task-, and scoring-dependent gains, with modest recent-model effects. The study provides an intervention-based evaluation of conditional PEFT: improvements over a static adapter do not by themselves demonstrate a benefit from input matching.

papers.title: Weighted $H^p$--$L^q$ estimates for fractional operators with multiple kernels under a strengthened H\"ormander condition
papers.abstract: We study a scale of strengthened fractional H\"ormander conditions, indexed by $\delta\ge0$ and adapted to the Hardy spaces $H^p$, $0<p<1$, which was recently considered by Han and Wu [Y.~Han, H.~Wu, \emph{The weighted $H^p$ estimates for commutators of fractional integrals}, Potential Anal. \textbf{59} (2023), 1827--1850] for fractional integrals with a single kernel. We show that these conditions form a strictly decreasing scale in $\delta$, and we compute the exact range of $\delta$ for a natural family of homogeneous kernels. We then apply them to the integral operators \[ T_\alpha f(x)=\int_{\RR^{n}}k_1(x-A_1y)\cdots k_m(x-A_my)\, f(y)\,dy, \] where $A_1,\dots,A_m$ are invertible matrices and $\frac n{q_1}+\dots+\frac n{q_m}=n-\alpha$, $0<\alpha<n$. Assuming that each kernel $k_i$ satisfies an $L^{p_i}$ size condition of order $n-n/q_i$ and the H\"ormander condition of order $\delta=n(\frac1p-1)$, we obtain, for $\max\{\frac n{n+1},\frac n{n+\alpha}\}<p<1$ and $1/q=1/p-\alpha/n$, the $H^{p}_{w^p}(\RR^{n})-L^{q}_{w^q}(\RR^{n})$ boundedness of $T_\alpha$ for weights $w$ such that $w^{a}\in\mathcal A_1$, where $\frac1a=\frac1q-\sum_i\frac1{p_i}$, and $w(A_ix)\le c\,w(x)$ a.e. For a single kernel, this relaxes the smoothness and weight conditions of a recent result of Han and Wu. No homogeneity is assumed on the kernels; the case $k_i(x)=\Omega_i(x)|x|^{-n/q_i}$ with $\Omega_i$ homogeneous of degree zero is included. Finally, we show that the strengthened condition cannot be replaced by the classical fractional H\"ormander condition.

papers.title: FiuMD: Heterogeneous Batching for Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics with Neural Network Potentials
papers.abstract: FiuMD is a GPU molecular dynamics engine that advances many independent biomolecular simulations as a single batch, even when the systems differ in size, topology, force-field parameters, periodic box, timestep, or thermostat parameters. All systems are concatenated into global tensors, so the classical interaction terms and a shared TorchMD-Net neural network potential are evaluated for the whole batch at once, while each system keeps its own integration and thermostat. FiuMD started as a fork of TorchMD and reworks its system representation, force evaluation, and integration to handle such heterogeneous batches. We test it with coarse-grained C$\alpha$ models of chignolin, Trp-cage, BBL, and $\lambda$-repressor. In double precision, forces within a heterogeneous batch agree with isolated FiuMD and TorchMD evaluations to within the precision of repeated evaluations, with a maximum relative difference of $7\times10^{-16}$ across 60 systems. Over 1000 steps without a thermostat, batched trajectories deviate by at most $2.5\times10^{-11}$ Angstrom from isolated ones, even when periodic images lie within the neural network cutoff. With a different target temperature for each system of the ensemble, the mean and width of each system's kinetic temperature match the values expected from its own thermostat. We show that when individual simulations are too small to fill the GPU, batching can improve throughput several-fold over TorchMD. On a single GPU, batching four different protein systems achieves a 4.6-7.8-fold speedup per step compared with sequential TorchMD simulations. Compared with sequential homogeneous FiuMD batches, heterogeneous batching provides up to a 4-fold speedup for smaller batches while maintaining comparable performance for larger ones.
