papers.title: Delaunay Combinatorics of the Moduli and Teichm\"uller Space of Closed Genus-Two Riemann Surfaces
papers.abstract: Every closed Riemann surface of genus two is hyperelliptic, so it is determined by six branch points on the sphere, which become cone points of angle pi in the quotient orbifold metric. The Delaunay decomposition of these cone points, dual to the Voronoi diagram of the Weierstrass points, gives a trivalent graph with eight vertices, twelve edges and six faces. We classify these graphs. When the dual triangulation is simple there are exactly two types, dual to the octahedron and to a stacked triangulation, with orientation-preserving automorphism groups of orders 24 and 2, and we determine the Whitehead-move (diagonal-flip) orbit connecting them. Allowing bigons, the orbit closes at exactly twenty types. Iterated edge contraction from the two simple types gives a seven-level hierarchy of 2, 6, 22, 32, 22, 5 and 1 types, ending at two vertices joined by six parallel edges; closing under both contraction and expansion gives all 280 maps on the sphere with six vertices and no vertex of degree one. The rank of the linear cone-angle system of each type equals the real dimension 6 of the Teichm\"uller space. We realize both simple types by explicit hyperbolic cone spheres, in closed form for the octahedral type, build the corresponding genus-two surfaces by cutting and doubling, and show that the boundary x_e = 0 of the angle system is exactly the concyclicity of four branch points. The classification, the automorphism groups and the flip orbit are formally verified in Lean 4, and every enumeration is reproduced by an independent program, which also determines which types are realized by Delaunay decompositions.

papers.title: Self-adjoint boundary conditions for equation-free multiscale modelling
papers.abstract: Equation-free modelling is a computation multiscale modelling scheme for the simulation of complex dynamical systems. Efficient computations are achieved by solving the given microscale model in small, well-separated `patches' spread across the space-time domain, with each patch providing a data point for the macroscale simulation. Patch coupling bridges the unsimulated space between patches and supports the macroscale dynamics. Accurate simulations require coupling conditions that preserve underlying symmetries of the microscale equation. Failing to preserve such symmetries may result in an unphysical macroscale simulation that does not satisfy required conservation laws. Here we develop equation-free modelling that preserves self-adjoint symmetry for microscale models defined by a compact self-adjoint operator on a bounded domain with fixed boundary conditions. This new design for equation-free modelling greatly increases the range of systems for which equation-free modelling is applicable.

papers.title: Exists, Valid: Calibrated Validity of Stored 3D Geometry Across Long Observation Gaps
papers.abstract: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at https://github.com/anwaarua/life4d.

papers.title: How to Agree Without Agreeing
papers.abstract: Consensus lets institutions decide without a central authority, but a record of agreement reveals neither its basis nor its credibility. We model support, standing aside and veto as responses to a proposal. A proposal can pass without active support, and the member least willing to allow passage limits what can be adopted, however many members oppose the proposal. Letting proposers moderate their demands can ease agreement while undermining the prescribed punishment. Proposal restrictions or deviation costs can preserve that threat. Across the initialisations tested, learning agents agree frequently even though many reconstructed rules allow profitable departures. In our sample of Antarctic Treaty working papers, 80% of proposals revising existing arrangements were adopted at submission, against 38% of new proposals. Consensus can keep producing agreement on what already exists while new protection waits.

papers.title: Exciton-polarons in monolayer semiconductors with drifting electrons
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the optical absorption of moderately doped two-dimensional semiconductors can be described in terms of exciton-polarons. In this picture, interactions between a photoexcited exciton and a Fermi sea of excess charge carriers split the exciton spectrum into a lower-energy attractive polaron branch and a higher-energy repulsive polaron branch. Due to the negligible in-plane momentum of photons, however, optical measurements probe only exciton-polarons near zero momentum, leaving their finite-momentum physics largely unexplored. Here we propose accessing this regime by measuring the absorption in the presence of an electric bias current. In effect, this displaces the electronic Fermi sea in momentum space, such that an optically active exciton-polaron at rest acquires finite momentum relative to the charge carriers. Using a diagrammatic formulation of the exciton-polaron problem, we derive exact relations between the spectral and quasiparticle properties of current-biased exciton-polarons and their finite-momentum counterparts in an equilibrium Fermi sea. These relations show that absorption measurements with drifting electrons can reconstruct the momentum dependence of the quasiparticle properties for both branches. We estimate that experimentally accessible currents can probe a broad momentum range while remaining within the linear-response regime.

papers.title: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
papers.abstract: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

papers.intro:
A classifier that runs on a microcontroller is usually trained on a small set of labelled photographs from its target setting, starting from weights pre-trained on ImageNet [1, 2]. Rendered images are a tempting second source: a game engine can produce labelled scenes in any quantity at almost no labelling cost, and computer-game imagery has been used as training data since at least 2016 [3]. Whether a synthetic pre-training stage still helps once the model has been shrunk, quantised to 8-bit integers and put on the chip is a separate question, and building a synthetic corpus is only worth the time if the answer is yes.

The study this paper re-examines is Bird et al. [4]. They trained a model on rendered images of six scene classes, carried all its weights over to real photographs, and compared the result with the same model trained on the photographs alone. Their model was an ImageNet VGG16 convolutional base (14.7M parameters [5]) with one dense layer, trained on a desktop GPU with no quantisation. The ImageNet base is in both arms, so what they compared is ImageNet initialisation with and without a synthetic stage. Their headline gain is +7.15 pp+7.15\text{\,}\mathrm{pp}; over the working range their table gives about +1.6 pp+1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{pp}, which I use as the planning value (Section 2.1).

There are two reasons to expect a gain of that size to disappear at microcontroller scale. One is capacity: for very small CNNs, Muralidharan et al. [6] find the difference between pre-trained and from-scratch training usually falls inside run-to-run variance. The other is precision: full-integer post-training quantisation [7, 8] costs accuracy, and nothing guarantees that it costs two differently initialised models the same; here the cost was of the same order as the gain in question. Neither says what the model costs to run, which has to be measured on the device, or whether the device computes what the host scored.

Two labels run through the paper. An arm is how a model is initialised before it trains on the real photographs. Arm A starts from random weights and arm B from ImageNet weights. Arms C and D start as A and B do but train on the rendered images first. B against D therefore isolates the synthetic stage on a pre-trained start, and it is the comparison every registered test is built on. A row is one model on a five-step size ladder (Table 1). Row 0 is a full-width MobileNetV2 [9] at 224 px224\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}, the anchor. Rows 1 to 3 keep a 96 px96\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} input and narrow MobileNetV2 from width 1.0 to 0.35. Row 4 is a 61K-parameter CNN at 48 px48\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x}. No ImageNet weights exist for the CNN, so at row 4 arms B and D start from Imagenette weights and are written B′ and D′. Row 3 is the main deployable model and carries the primary test, and row 4 carries the secondary. Section 3.3 gives the full definitions.

The paper makes four. 1. The paired four-arm comparison in float32 and INT8. Four initialisation arms, including from-scratch and ImageNet controls, are carried through post-training quantisation, paired by fold and replicated over seeds at the rows that carry the confirmatory tests. A difference-in-differences puts the quantisation-interaction question into a single number with a confidence interval. 2. The sub-1M-parameter question, set against run-to-run variance. Latency, memory and energy per inference are measured across the ladder on two MCUs, including the ESP32-S3 arena’s placement in internal SRAM or external PSRAM, measured both ways on the same model, and the RP2040’s flash-capacity limit. 4. papers.title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
papers.abstract: Linear probing is a common technique in mechanistic interpretability despite the fact that the decodability of a given feature does not necessarily imply the network uses that feature. Intervention faithfulness, not merely decodability, is the appropriate criterion for whether a feature serves a defined active role in the model. Meanwhile, probe regularization has been used for feature discovery, but the impact of regularization on feature causality remains unclear. We study probe regularization systematically, starting with unregularized ordinary least squares (OLS) regression and considering increasing amounts of regularization via ridge regression. We show theoretically that OLS probes amplify low-variance directions in activation space that have spurious correlations with the target feature, whereas regularization reduces influence from these directions. Empirically, we find in a toy transformer and Llama-2-7B that intervention faithfulness increases up to a point, and then decreases again, and that the optimal regularization strength leads to features bearing striking similarity (in both direction and variance) to those learned by optimizing for intervention outcomes directly. Together, these results provide mechanistic justification for regularizing regression probes.

papers.title: Target Detection with Tightly-coupled Wideband Antenna Arrays
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on tightly coupled antenna (TCA) array systems with high mutual coupling, resulting in wideband signals. We analyze the target detection capability of such systems with joint time and frequency approaches. We assume a target whose echo signals are unknown wideband signals and show the opportunity that TCAs create in target detection. We consider temporal and spectral dynamics of the signal as either constant, slowly or rapidly varying in frequency and time, giving nine possible cases in total. For each case we derive a detector and present thorough analysis for the distribution of the detector test statistic, considering frequency-dependent noise correlation due to mutual coupling. For the cases with a signal changing slowly in at least one domain we propose a novel detection approach based on estimation of the signal via local averaging of the samples. We also derive a detector that results in an upper bound on detection performance for comparison. We compare our analytical results with simulations, showing perfect accuracy of our derived distributions. In addition, we assess the performance of the detectors under various time/frequency variation rates. We show the superior performance of our proposed detection approach in comparison to other detectors including an extended energy detector we derive for correlated noise as well as both frequency and time samples.

papers.title: Ternary-Valued FDTD Method for Nonlinear Optics: Third-Harmonic Generation on a Multiplier-Free Solver
papers.abstract: I show that a finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solver with field variables restricted to the ternary alphabet $\{-1,0,+1\}$ can reproduce nonlinear optical physics quantitatively on both CPUs and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Building on the general ternary-valued FDTD algorithm, in which each Yee cell stores an integer state that accumulates the discrete curl of neighbouring symbols without being drained, I extend the scheme to inhomogeneous and Kerr media and to Mur absorbing boundaries, without performing any multiplication operations. Dielectric contrast is implemented as a multiplexer, since the difference between ternary symbols takes only a few values, the instantaneous Kerr nonlinearity as a coefficient look-up table and the Mur boundary coefficients as canonical signed-digit shift--add chains. The scheme reproduces the third-harmonic conversion efficiency of a floating-point reference to within $1.4\%$. A symmetry of the governing physics, expressed through the even harmonics forbidden by centrosymmetric $\chi^{(3)}$, provides a reference-free self-check for both ternary and floating-point models. The complete solver fits on a small, low-cost FPGA and contains no multiplier anywhere in its datapath, placing nonlinear optical modelling within reach of embedded and autonomous platforms rather than of high-performance computers.

papers.title: An Implementation of the 3-Dimensional Extended Persistent Homology Transform
papers.abstract: The Extended Persistent Homology Transform (XPHT) describes a shape through the extended persistence diagrams of its directional height functions. We present an algorithm for computing a finite directional sample of the three-dimensional XPHT from a triangulated boundary. Our main construction determines essential first-homology pairings by combining an ordered tree-cotree decomposition with evaluation-dual cocycles. The decomposition supplies a homology basis compatible with the height filtration, while the cocycles are used to determine the essential birth-death pairs. Degree-zero persistence and duality determine the remaining boundary diagrams. Under the boundary-reduction hypotheses and with critical-point sign labels, these diagrams yield the extended persistence of the solid. The resulting procedure uses graph constructions and linear algebra over F2 on boundary meshes extracted from three-dimensional binary images.

papers.title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Computational modelling has become a cornerstone of materials science, with advances in atomistic simulations, high-throughput computation, and artificial intelligence transforming how materials are understood, discovered, and designed. These developments build upon generations of theoretical innovations that have translated complex mathematical and physical principles into practical predictive tools. However, the growing diversity of computational methods presents challenges for practitioners seeking a coherent understanding of their theoretical foundations. Drawing upon the author's research experience, this monograph provides a practitioner-oriented, pedagogical overview of computational materials science, unified through the concepts of potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling. It explores how these concepts underpin structural stability, phase behaviour, and electronic and magnetic properties, through a systematic treatment of empirical force fields, density-functional theory, many-body electronic-structure methods, statistical sampling, and property prediction. It further examines high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and the probabilistic foundations of artificial intelligence. Particular emphasis is placed on atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models, highlighting the roles of symmetry, group theory, differential geometry, and stochastic processes in modern materials modelling. By connecting established physical theories with emerging data-driven approaches, this monograph offers a unified perspective on computational materials science and identifies opportunities and challenges toward physics-informed, efficient, and reliable materials discovery.

papers.title: Electronic bridge for the $J=0$ state and effects of electrons on frequency and lifetime of the nuclear clock transition in $^{229}$Th$^{2+}$ ion
papers.abstract:
We investigate the electronic bridge (EB) process for excitation of the $^{229}$Th nuclear isomer in Th III ions initially prepared in the metastable electronic state with $J=0$. This state is of particular interest for developing a nuclear clock with suppressed electronic hyperfine interactions. Using a combination of configuration interaction and coupled-cluster methods, we calculate EB transition rates for several excitation schemes involving one or two laser fields. We express the rates in terms of the enhancement factor $R$, defined as the ratio of the EB transition rate to the direct nuclear M1 transition rate. Schemes that return the ion to its initial $J=0$ state have relatively small enhancement factors, $R \sim 1$. However, allowing the final electronic state to differ from the initial state produces a strong resonant enhancement: $R$ reaches $5\times10^3$.
  In addition, we calculate the shift in the nuclear transition frequency caused by changing the electronic state from the ground state to two excited metastable states. We also examine how the electronic state affects the nuclear transition lifetime and calculate the probabilities of electron transitions induced by nuclear decay. The EB mechanism shortens the nuclear decay lifetime by a factor of 2.6 when the electrons are initially in the ground state and by a factor of 6.85 when they are in the metastable $J=0$ state.

papers.title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
papers.abstract: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

papers.title: Using machine learning approaches to classify false-positives generated by static analysis tools - An empirical study using small datasets
papers.abstract: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools are vital for software development to reduce the cost and time required for manual code reviews. It was established in our previous study that the best tools reported in the software engineering community return high false-positive and false-negative rates when used for code analysis. Several approaches have been taken in existing studies to identify false-positive alarms generated by SCA tools, in helping to enhance the utility of these tools. However, existing studies reveal several limitations, chiefly among which is the tendency to focus on a limited number of alarm types or failing to evaluate a large breadth of Machine-Learning (ML) techniques comprehensively. This study has addressed this opportunity. We identified the best Code Representation Learning (CRL) techniques and ML algorithms for identifying false-positives, where results show that performance outcomes vary based on the characteristics of the training datasets and the goal of the model building. Given the evidence established in this study, we recommend further investigations targeting specific configurations of advanced CRLs and ML Algorithms, including simple ML models.

papers.title: Beyond Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models and Agentic Patterns for Static Code Analysis Warning Classification
papers.abstract: Context: Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools support software verification and validation, reducing the time and cost of code reviews. However, the best SCA tools in the practitioner community generate a high volume of false positives, which developers tend to ignore, leading to genuine warnings being overlooked. Accordingly, studies increasingly adopt Large Language Models (LLMs) to identify and reduce false positives. Existing studies have produced promising results on public datasets, but underperformed on unseen datasets. Moreover, researchers do not leverage the full potential of Agentic patterns in LLMs or incorporate established code quality standards for warning classification. Objectives: This study utilises four manually annotated datasets to evaluate the performance of three contemporary LLMs for SCA warning classification in real-world applications, and incorporates Agentic patterns and established coding standards to enhance models' performance, addressing gaps identified in existing studies. Method: Three LLMs were selected using the LiveCodeBench benchmark, and the Structured Chain-of-Thought (SCoT) prompting technique was used to evaluate these LLMs. Furthermore, we incorporated Agentic patterns, such as Debating and Self-Consistency, to potentially improve performance in SCA warning classification. Results: Our results show that the performance of different LLMs varies with the characteristics of the dataset, ranging from 0.52 to 0.96 F1-Score for the best models. Additionally, the use of Agentic patterns does not improve LLMs' performance in most scenarios. Conclusions: SCA warning classification using LLMs works best only with certain warning types. We recommend evaluating LLMs in real-world applications rather than using publicly available datasets/benchmarks to understand their full utility.

papers.title: A simplified temporal logic completeness proof
papers.abstract: A temporal logic discussed in the author's book "Logics of Time and Computation" is given a simpler proof of semantic completeness, eliminating some flaws in the original.

papers.title: Where Does an On-Device Prescription Reader Lose Medications? A Frozen-Replay Study, from a 270M Language Model to a 2B Vision-Language Model
papers.abstract: On-device models let a phone read a prescription without sending the photograph anywhere, but small models fail in ways that are hard to attribute: to the camera, the OCR, the model, or the rules around it. We study a phone-based pipeline that reads a prescription photograph with PaddleOCR, extracts medications with a 270M-parameter language model, and filters the result with a deterministic backstop before showing suggestions. Replaying identical frozen inputs through each configuration, with deterministic generation verified, we compare configurations with paired document-level intervals on 49 captures of 15 synthetic prescriptions (6 typed, 9 handwritten by one writer). Production recall is 8%, and 0 of 45 on handwriting. The backstop removes no correct medication and cuts unsafe outputs from 45 to 1. On handwriting nearly all medications never reach the model in readable form; on typed sheets the model mostly picks the wrong text. We trace much of the handwriting floor to a defect in our own crop step, then replace the pipeline: rotated-box crops, a 2B-parameter vision-language model that re-reads prescription lines and extracts the medications, and per-line numeric grounding. On the same captures recall rises from 8% to 67% (paired +59 points, 95% CI +40 to +78): typed 19% to 100%, handwritten 0 to 20 of 45, with no unsafe output. Rotated crops account for most of the reading gain and the model for most of the recall gain, and the OCR confidence gate is now the main limit. The cost is 61 s per photograph against about 12 s, and about 1.9 GB of memory. An earlier claim that better OCR lowered recall does not survive the controlled comparison, and we withdraw it. All results are in-sample, from one writer and one device.
papers.intro:
Handwritten and printed prescriptions are a daily source of structured information that people must read correctly: which drug, how often, for how long. Reading them by machine is attractive for the person holding the paper, who may want a reminder, and sensitive for the same reason: the photograph names a patient, a diagnosis and a medication. Running the whole pipeline on the phone avoids sending that photograph to a server. It also restricts the model. A language model that fits a phone has a few hundred million parameters, runs at a few tokens per second, and is easy to distract with text on the page that is not a medication.

Whether such a pipeline works is usually answered with an end-to-end accuracy figure. That figure hides where the pipeline fails. A prescription passes through a camera, an OCR engine, a quality check, a language model and a set of rules, and a missed medication could have been lost at any of them. Studies that vary one component on separate captures also confound the comparison with the capture itself: a different photograph, a different operator, a different lighting. We encountered this directly: an early result suggested that a better OCR engine lowered recall, and it did not survive a controlled comparison.

We hold the input fixed by replaying frozen captures through each configuration on the phone itself, verify that this is faithful, and compare configurations with paired document-level intervals. We then report the pipeline that replaced it on 3 November, built around a 2B-parameter vision-language model, and measure how much of the change comes from which part.

papers.title: Latent Fusion: Channel Stacking for Structure-Preserving Image Editing
papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editing models must condition on the source image, either by sequence concatenation, which appends source tokens to the target sequence (FLUX.1 Kontext), or by channel-wise concatenation, which stacks the source latent onto the noisy latent and widens the input projection (InstructPix2Pix, FLUX.1 Fill). The FLUX.1 Kontext report found channel-wise concatenation worse in initial experiments at 1K resolution with a 12B model and a large corpus. We explore channel-wise concatenation as the lower-cost option for a common production regime: structure-preserving edits that change appearance (sky, exposure, foliage, cleanup) but not layout, about 1,400 training pairs, a 4B non-distilled backbone, and 2K frames. It keeps the sequence at its original length, where sequence concatenation doubles it and roughly quadruples attention cost, and needs only single-scale classifier-free guidance (two forward passes per step instead of three). Starting from FLUX.2 Klein 4B base, we widen only the input projection and train both schemes with the same trainer, data, and hyperparameters. Channel-wise concatenation keeps the output pixel-aligned with the source; in our runs sequence concatenation, which must learn the correspondence between 10,880 target and 10,880 source tokens from fewer than 1,500 pairs, displaced structure, an observation we report without claiming a general ranking. On 29 held-out images the editor reaches 20.3 dB PSNR and 0.198 LPIPS against the human edit (unedited source: 15.0 dB), and counterfactual conditioning tests show it largely learned a global grade of the source rather than a selective edit, which we report as the open problem of this recipe. We also compare against an SD3.5-Medium editor trained with the same surgery and report the full training recipe, including failure modes. Code: https://github.com/complete-dope/LatentFusion
papers.intro:
Instruction-based image editing [1] has become a standard application of generative models: given a source image and an instruction, a conditional diffusion model produces the edited image with no per-image optimisation. Most benchmarks in this area reward content-changing edits, where the instruction asks for new objects or a rearranged scene and some deviation from the source is acceptable. In many production settings, however, the edit is conservative. A photograph is submitted, and the expected output is the same photograph with a replaced sky, a corrected exposure, healthier foliage, or a distraction removed. The buildings, streets, furniture, and people must remain pixel-aligned with the source, because the result is inspected side by side with the original and any drift is a defect. The two settings place different demands on how the source image is fed to the network.

Most benchmarks in this area reward content-changing edits, where the instruction asks for new objects or a rearranged scene and some deviation from the source is acceptable. In many production settings, however, the edit is conservative. A photograph is submitted, and the expected output is the same photograph with a replaced sky, a corrected exposure, healthier foliage, or a distraction removed. The buildings, streets, furniture, and people must remain pixel-aligned with the source, because the result is inspected side by side with the original and any drift is a defect. The two settings place different demands on how the source image is fed to the network.

Transformer-based editors condition on the source image in one of two ways. FLUX.1 Kontext [2] and most recent editors use sequence concatenation: the source-image tokens are appended to the target sequence and distinguished by a positional offset. This design lets the network read the source from any position, which suits content generation, but the correspondence between source and target tokens must be learned through attention, and the sequence length doubles. InstructPix2Pix [1] and FLUX.1 Fill [3] instead use channel-wise concatenation: the source latent is stacked onto the noisy latent along the channel dimension and the first layer of the network is widened. Each token then carries its own source content, the sequence length is unchanged, and the source-target correspondence is fixed by construction. The Kontext report notes that channel-wise concatenation performed worse in their initial experiments, conducted at 1K resolution with a 12B model and a large editing corpus.

In this work we explore channel-wise concatenation on a Flux backbone as the lower-cost conditioning for the structure-preserving regime, and we call the resulting channel-stacked editor Latent Fusion. The motivation is cost, not a rejection of sequence concatenation: channel-wise concatenation keeps the sequence at LL tokens where sequence concatenation needs 2​L2L, so attention cost stays that of the base model, and at inference it needs only standard classifier-free guidance, two forward passes per step, where the InstructPix2Pix two-scale guidance needs three (Section 3.3). Our setting differs from the Kontext comparison on every axis: the edit must leave structure and identity intact, the training set consists of 1,398 pairs from a single professional workflow, the backbone is the 4B non-distilled FLUX.2 Klein base model [4], and the frames are 2048×13602048\times 1360, i.e. 10,88010{,}880 image tokens. We implement both conditioning schemes in the same trainer and train both on identical data with identical hyperparameters. We observe that channel-wise concatenation preserves object placement and scene structure and changes appearance without moving anything. In our run of sequence concatenation, with the same backbone and data, the source content itself moved: objects shifted and structure was regenerated rather than preserved, so the output was no longer registered to the source (Section 5). We report this as what we saw on this data with a single run of each scheme, not as evidence that sequence concatenation is the weaker design on Flux.

Our contributions are as follows: • A recipe for adapting the FLUX.2 Klein 4B base model into a paired editor with channel-wise concatenation conditioning: only the input projection is widened, its new half is zero-initialised and the layer is trained with its own learning rate, and training mixes native-resolution crops with downscaled whole frames under conditioning dropout. All hyperparameters are reported (Section 3). • A matched comparison of channel-wise concatenation against sequence concatenation on the same backbone, data, and hyperparameters in the structure-preserving regime, by inspection of held-out outputs, with full-frame metrics against human reference edits for the channel-wise editor, together with the compute and guidance cost of the two schemes (Sections 3.3 and 5). • A comparison against an SD3.5-Medium editor trained with the same surgery at the same resolution, and an analysis of what the widened input layer learned, counterfactual conditioning tests that expose copying rather than editing, and a cross-architecture control on SD3-Medium (Section 6). • A record of the training failures we encountered and how each was diagnosed (Appendix A). Code for the trainer, both conditioning paths, the sampler and the evaluation scripts is released in the Latent Fusion repository.

papers.title: Field algebras associated with non-symmetric lattices
papers.abstract: Field algebras, introduced by Bakalov and Kac, generalize vertex algebras by replacing locality with a weaker associativity-type axiom. We develop the structure theory of field algebras with a view toward geometric examples in which a natural bilinear form fails to be symmetric. We prove a reconstruction theorem for field algebras, producing a field algebra structure from a generating family of fields. We associate to every finite-rank lattice $L$ equipped with an arbitrary bilinear form a canonical field algebra $V_L$, generalizing the Heisenberg and lattice vertex algebras. We then study potential definitions of commutants in this setting and analyze when they are realized as subfield algebras. Finally, we realize these constructions geometrically by looking at the homology of the moduli stack of complexes of quiver representations, extending previous results from Dominic Joyce.

papers.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
papers.abstract: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.
papers.intro:
China’s local-government debt raises a question that cannot be answered by the size of a balance sheet alone: who absorbs the adjustment, and through which decisions does it reach international competition and financial markets? A refinancing operation, a bank recapitalization, a reduction in public services, and a household portfolio response have different resource and valuation consequences. Treating them as interchangeable steps obscures the conditions that determine the final outcome.

A refinancing operation, a bank recapitalization, a reduction in public services, and a household portfolio response have different resource and valuation consequences. Treating them as interchangeable steps obscures the conditions that determine the final outcome.

RAND’s recent study connects local-debt measurement, institutional responses, contrasting city cases, and adjustment scenarios to U.S.-China competition. It does not equate local fiscal strain with an immediate reduction in national strategic effort [1]. The present paper extends that motivating inquiry to a conditional Bitcoin mechanism; the report does not identify this transmission.

RAND’s recent study connects local-debt measurement, institutional responses, contrasting city cases, and adjustment scenarios to U.S.-China competition. It does not equate local fiscal strain with an immediate reduction in national strategic effort [1]. The present paper extends that motivating inquiry to a conditional Bitcoin mechanism; the report does not identify this transmission.

Three distinctions organize the argument. First, the recognition of a liability differs from the creation of a new liability. An exchange of local-government financing vehicle (LGFV) obligations for government bonds can change the recorded stock and creditors’ risk weights without canceling aggregate principal. Second, current strategic spending differs from the economic base that sustains future competition. An allocation rule can protect a spending priority while imposing costs on public services and private production. Third, demand for assets outside a domestic currency differs from effective Bitcoin demand. Investors can choose dollar claims, lose access to trading services, or liquidate risky positions at the same time that their concern about domestic fiscal conditions increases.

The financial literature provides reasons to keep these distinctions explicit. Huang, Pagano, and Panizza find historical crowding out of private investment through local funding constraints [6]. Li and coauthors, studying the 2015 debt-to-bond swap, identify a countervailing risk-weighting channel that supports private credit and productivity [7]. These studies concern different interventions and samples; they should not be turned into an invariant coefficient on all public debt. On the asset side, Che and coauthors document the importance of U.S. monetary policy and institutional risk taking for crypto markets [8]. Recent work by Drexler, Guettler, and Sun also finds increasing broad-equity exposure for Bitcoin [9]. Neither result identifies the effect of Chinese local debt.

On the asset side, Che and coauthors document the importance of U.S. monetary policy and institutional risk taking for crypto markets [8]. Recent work by Drexler, Guettler, and Sun also finds increasing broad-equity exposure for Bitcoin [9]. Neither result identifies the effect of Chinese local debt.

Existing research already examines Chinese policy uncertainty and Bitcoin. Cai and coauthors report time- and frequency-dependent relationships rather than a universal hedge property [10]. The present contribution is consequently narrower than a discovery that Chinese uncertainty matters for cryptoassets. It joins liability recognition and loss allocation to protected spending and a constrained BTC–stablecoin allocation block. The resulting propositions state what follows from the assumptions and what remains unidentified. The elementary accounting and optimization results are not presented as new general theorems.

The paper has two completed analytical components. The first shows how a debt resolution can preserve principal yet change bank credit headroom and the composition of public spending. The second derives effective-demand and price-pressure sign conditions with separate access, preference, and global-funding channels. The components share a stress variable, but the policy responses are conditional primitives: the framework is not a jointly estimated fiscal-monetary equilibrium. Numerical exercises illustrate its restrictions and counterexamples. No probability is attached to a scenario, and no realized Bitcoin return is attributed to a local-debt announcement.

papers.title: Determinants of amphichiral knots of braid index at most three
papers.abstract: We show that an odd number n is the determinant of an amphichiral knot of braid index at most three if and only if both n and n + 4 are sums of two squares. The proof rests on the known description of amphichiral knots of braid index three as closures of alternating 3-braid words with a rotation or reflection symmetry (Birman--Menasco, Stoimenov, Jung). Determinant formulas for closed 3-braids are also known (e.g. through the reduced Burau representation at t = -1); what is added here is their evaluation on the two symmetric families, which gives the condition on n + 4, and an explicit construction for the converse. For amphichiral knots of braid index three this describes which determinants occur, which bears on the determinant part of a question of Jung. We did not find the statement in the literature we searched. As a consequence, for an odd n with n + 4 not a sum of two squares, every amphichiral knot with determinant n has braid index at least five; we test this on 4,999 amphichiral knots of Burton's census with up to 19 crossings whose determinant satisfies this hypothesis.

papers.title: Magnon binding in a quantum Hall ferromagnet with a periodic electric field
papers.abstract: A spin wave in a filling-one quantum Hall ferromagnet is neutral but carries an electric dipole perpendicular to its momentum. A spatially periodic electrostatic potential therefore creates parallel channels for spin waves. We use this established mechanism to calculate how confinement changes the exchange binding of magnons travelling in the same direction. Narrower channels increase the overlap of their transverse wavefunctions and strengthen the effective attraction. In an isolated harmonic channel, the energy required to remove one magnon from a cluster of $N$ is $\pi(k_*\ell)^4N(N-1)/4$ times the transverse level spacing to leading order, where $k_*$ is the mean wave number along the channel and $\ell$ is the magnetic length. We predict the frequency and momentum dependence of the spectral line for adding a second magnon to one already present, both in an isolated channel and in a coupled array. Tunnelling in a wide array can make the binding energy exponentially small, while a strip narrower than the transverse pair size recovers one-dimensional binding at sufficiently weak attraction. We also find that a moving potential can carry a single wave packet with less spreading than free propagation when its initial group velocity matches the potential's speed.

papers.intro:
How does confining a spin wave change its interaction with another spin wave? We study a two-dimensional electron gas in a strong perpendicular magnetic field. At filling one (ν=1\nu=1), one electron occupies each orbital of the lowest Landau level, with all spins aligned. Metal electrodes above and below the electron layer screen the Coulomb interaction. We separately impose a smooth electrostatic potential that varies periodically along xx and is uniform along yy. In a device, patterned electrodes (gates) could produce such a modulation. Within the lowest Landau level the uniformly filled spin branch is stationary under this potential. Its excitations respond to the field even though the reference state stays fixed.

A spin flip replaces an up-spin electron by a down-spin electron, leaving a positively charged hole in the up-spin branch. In a magnon, the quantum of a spin wave, the centres of the electron and hole cyclotron orbits are displaced perpendicular to the wave momentum [10, 6]. A magnon travelling along yy thus carries a dipole along xx. Its energy is lowest where the electric field is strongest along the dipole. These minima confine the magnon across xx, leaving it free to propagate along yy. Reversing the momentum reverses the dipole and shifts the preferred channel by half a period. Experiments in graphene have generated and detected Hall magnons [20] and sensed their dipoles through their coupling to an interferometer [1].

Bychkov and collaborators derived the equation for a single spin exciton (the electron–hole description of a magnon) in a periodic potential and found its confinement levels [2, 3]. Separate microscopic work established attraction and binding between distinct Hall magnons [22, 7]. We connect these two results. Magnons sharing a spatial rotation of the spin direction lower their exchange energy, and a narrower channel increases the probability that they are close enough to interact. The electrostatic potential can thus tune their effective attraction at fixed electron interaction and filling.

We derive the effective interaction for magnons in the transverse ground state and check its coefficient against microscopic electronic states. The resulting one-dimensional Bose gas has a known exact solution [13, 16]. It gives a breakup energy in terms of the measured spacing of the transverse levels and the magnon momentum. For two magnons we calculate how the energy and strength of the line for adding a second spin flip reveal the pair’s binding and size. We then follow the same line as tunnelling opens up relative motion across neighbouring channels. The number of channels determines whether that additional motion can be treated as continuous at the binding energy.

papers.title: Discrete Hyperbolic Cosecant Distributions
papers.abstract: We introduce three families of discrete hyperbolic cosecant probability distributions, supported either bilaterally on $\mathbb{Z}$ or unilaterally on $\mathbb{N}_0$, inspired by series evaluations of Srinivasa Ramanujan. We determine their exact normalization constants in terms of singular values of complete elliptic integrals and the Gau\ss ian constant $G=\varpi/\pi$ with the lemniscate constant $\Gamma^2(1/4)/(2\sqrt{2\pi})$ by explicitly calculating some series, e.\,g. $$ \sum_{\kappa \in \mathbb{Z}} 2\kappa \operatorname{cosech}(\kappa \pi) = G^2 + \frac{1}{\pi}. $$ Furthermore, by connecting these distributions to Fourier transforms of powers of the hyperbolic secant and applying the Poisson summation formula, we obtain closed-form evaluations for even moments and hyperbolic secant lattice sums, e.\,g. $$ \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathrm{sech}^4(k \pi) = \frac{2}{3} \left(G^4 + G^2 + \frac{1}{\pi}\right). $$ This machinery proves conjectures on lattice sums arising in electrostatics proposed by Vigren and Dieckmann (Symmetry, 2020).

papers.title: Odd-degree cycles and rationality of Peskine sixfolds of discriminant 24
papers.abstract: Benedetti and Faenzi conjectured that, for a general trivector $\sigma\in\mathcal D^{1,6,10}$, the Peskine sixfold $X_1^\sigma$ is rational if the Brauer class $\beta$ on the associated K3 surface vanishes. We prove this implication for every $\sigma$ in a nonempty Zariski open subset $U\subset\mathcal D^{1,6,10}$. When $\beta=0$, we construct a line on the generic fiber of the Peskine fibration after a cubic field extension and use odd-degree descent to obtain a line over the original function field. We extend criteria for rationality to smooth complete intersections of an arbitrary number of quadrics under suitable hypotheses. Finally, we describe the derived category of the generic fiber of the Peskine fibration in terms of a twisted nodal curve of arithmetic genus two.

The rationality problem for algebraic varieties is a classical problem that remains central to algebraic geometry. Clemens–Griffiths and Artin–Mumford gave distinct obstructions to rationality for unirational threefolds [15, 3].

We also formulate relative odd-degree cycle criteria for intersections of quadrics and study the bounded derived categories of coherent sheaves on the related varieties.

papers.title: Rigidity for Families of Abelian Varieties over $\mathcal{M}_{g,n}$
papers.abstract: We provide a new proof of Farb's theorem on the global rigidity of the period map $\mathcal{M}_{g,n} \to \mathcal{A}_g$. We extend this classification to essentially include the period map for $\mathcal{M}_{2,n}$. We also provide a classification of holomorphic maps $\mathcal{M}_g \to \mathcal{A}_{h}$ for $h \leq 2g-1$. The only nonconstant maps in this range are given by taking the Jacobian of a curve and attaching a fixed Abelian variety. In addition to the group theory of the mapping class group, we make extensive use of the theory of variations of Hodge structures and the birational geometry on $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_2$.

papers.title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
papers.abstract: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

At deployment, a frozen chunked policy has two coupled compute decisions: how much work each policy call spends generating an action chunk, and how often to call the policy again from a fresh observation. We call the first decision refinement and the second replanning frequency. Each policy call predicts KK actions. The environment executes the first hh, then the policy receives a new observation and runs again. Thus, hh sets the policy-call frequency: one call every hh executed actions. For SmolVLA, dd sets the number of denoising steps within each call.

papers.title: DynaDFlash: Dynamic Feature Projection for Block Diffusion Speculators
papers.abstract: DFlash trains a parallel draft model on hidden features from its target model. Inspired by the previous work of DFlare that introduced per layer combinations of target hidden states, we test whether context dependent weighting of these states helps improve acceptance length of block diffusion speculators. We trained both a DFlash baseline for the Qwen 3 of block size 16, and a dynamic model that computes gates for each layer to affect the magnitude of hidden features before projection. While mean acceptance length between the dynamic model and the DFlash baseline didn't significantly differ, we notice that the dynamic model excels for drafting in the context of math. In an evaluation of 700 prompts from the MetaMathQA and Orca-Math datasets, the mean accepted length improves by 5%. We also found this lead to a 4.1% higher throughput for a subset of the same dataset in the context of speculative decoding.
papers.intro:
Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to predict tokens that are then verified by a larger target model [1, 2]. DFlash does this by training a block diffusion model to draft multiple tokens in parallel, using hidden states from the target model as additional context that is injected at each layer [5].

Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to predict tokens that are then verified by a larger target model [1, 2]. DFlash does this by training a block diffusion model to draft multiple tokens in parallel, using hidden states from the target model as additional context that is injected at each layer [5].

DFlare builds on this idea by learning different combinations of target hidden states for different draft layers [6]. However, these combinations remain fixed for each layer after training. We wanted to test whether allowing the weights to change depending on the input context could further improve drafting.

papers.title: Bayesian Inference for Multivariate Stable Distributions via LePage Representation with von Mises -- Fisher Spectral Measure
papers.abstract: We develop Bayesian inference for multivariate $\alpha$-stable distributions with von Mises--Fisher spectral measure, motivated by the hitting distribution of Brownian motion on the unit sphere. Inference proceeds via a LePage-type series representation with latent radial, spectral, and Poisson components; truncation bias is absorbed through a Gaussian error term, yielding a likelihood that is smooth in $\alpha\in(0,2)$ with no special treatment at the Cauchy boundary $\alpha=1$. The stability index $\alpha$, spectral concentration $\kappa$, mean direction $\eta$, and spectral mass $\Gamma_\infty$ are estimated jointly by Markov chain Monte Carlo. At the Gaussian boundary $\alpha\to 2$, the limiting covariance matrix equals twice the second moment matrix of the spectral measure, with explicit parametric form determined by $\eta$ and $\kappa$; in particular, the anisotropy of the limiting Gaussian distribution is controlled solely by the spectral concentration $\kappa$. Simulation across $\alpha\in[0.25, 1.99]$ confirms reliable recovery of all parameters.
papers.intro:
Stable distributions are increasingly being used in both theoretical and empirical investigations in applied literature. Starting with a well cited article by Mandelbrot (1963), there has been empirical support for thick tail laws in general and stable laws in particular. McFarland and Sung (1982) used symmetric stable laws to study returns from foreign exchange market; as a continuation of this paper, So (1987) observed that return distribution follow negatively skewed stable laws. Buckle (1995) in his analysis of return of a share price observed negatively skewed stable laws. Tsionas (1999) used sub-Gaussian univariate stable laws in a stable regression setup. Carr and Wu (2003) used negatively skewed stable laws in analyzing persistence of volatility smirk across maturity spectrum in the context of S&P 500 Index options; they observed that a skewed univariate stable law does a better job of fitting option prices as compared to stochastic volatility models. Rachev and Mittnik (2000) has extensively used thick tails distributions. Thus, skewed univariate stable law has been receiving the attention of researchers in empirical finance.

There has been increased attention towards multivariate stable distributions in the last two decades. Here again, majority of the applications that we are aware of are from applied finance, mainly with the objective of modeling financial returns from a portfolio. Commonly studied examples are from foreign exchange markets and stock markets, such as, joint movement of a basket of currencies or a set of stock indices. Also, there are occasions where distribution of the basket as a whole is necessary; computation of Value at Risk (VaR) of a portfolio is one such example. Most computations of VaR are currently based on multivariate Gaussian laws, which is known to underestimate losses. Limitations of multivariate Gaussian laws led researchers to practical alternatives, such as historical simulation methods (Jorion, 2007; Bradely and Taqqu, 2003), and copula functions (Bradely and Taqqu, 2003; Cherubini et al., 2004).

Basic properties and tail dependence structures of multivariate stable laws are expressed in terms of the spectral measure.

papers.title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study of LLM Agents Against Credential Deception and Alert-Driven Revocation
papers.abstract: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.

Defenders have long relied on deception to detect such activity early: honeypots [8, 11], honeytokens and honeywords [5], and planned adversary engagement [6]. Recent work argues that LLM agents may be especially susceptible to deception because they read and act on whatever text the environment returns [1, 2, 3].

This paper tests that intuition in a controlled lab and asks what deception contributes when it is measured against an equivalent defense without it. Given ordinary hardening, does adding deception further reduce an LLM agent’s success at exfiltration? • RQ3 (response). Can a real honeypot alert be turned into fast, attributable and narrowly scoped enforcement without harming legitimate clients?

papers.title: A Backdoor Trigger Is Legible in Fine-Tune Weights
papers.abstract: A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.
papers.intro:
The short version. Somebody hands you a fine-tuned model and you suspect it has a hidden trigger phrase—type the phrase and the model misbehaves, leave it out and the model is fine. You want to know what the phrase is. Today the only way to find out is to run the model many times and search for an input that makes it misbehave, which means executing software you do not trust, on inputs you have to guess. This paper shows you can often read the trigger directly out of the weights instead, without running the model at all, and get one of the trigger’s own tokens as the single top candidate out of a vocabulary of tens of thousands—49,152 for the model most of our experiments use, 151,665 for the largest. It also shows, by building the attacks ourselves, exactly where that reading breaks: an attacker who knows the statistic can suppress it during training at no cost to their backdoor.

An auditor receives a fine-tuned checkpoint. It may contain a backdoor: a phrase that, when it appears in the input, switches the model into behaviour its owner did not ask for. The auditor wants to know what that phrase is. Every published method for answering this question executes the model—optimising inputs against a loss, searching decoding configurations, or attributing activations—which means running an artefact that is under suspicion precisely because it may do something unwanted on an input nobody has guessed yet.

This paper asks whether the question can be answered from the weights. It can. We define a statistic over the difference between a suspect checkpoint and a trusted reference, standardise it per token against a population of clean fine-tunes, and read off the top-ranked token. The statistic never runs the suspect. It runs the base model—the artefact the auditor already trusts—once, to build a basis that is cached and reused for every suspect thereafter.

The result we want to be judged on is a held-out one. The pipeline was fixed in writing, including its site-selection rule, its null, its basis and its output criterion, and then applied to trigger designs built afterwards and to two architectures it had never been run on. No threshold was retuned. Section VI reports what came out.

Contributions. 1. Weights-only trigger recovery. A statistic that names an exact trigger token as the single top-ranked alphabetic candidate, with no forward pass of the suspect and no poisoned examples, at rank 1 in 14 of 14 ordinary backdoors on two architecture families, with a third agreeing (Sec. VI). 2. Robustness to parameter-restriction attackers, and the two that defeat it. The same rule recovers the trigger from attackers who freeze the scanned layers, camouflage that freeze at five strengths, inject a real clean fine-tune’s weights into it, or train at a quarter or twice our learning rate. Two attackers defeat it: one that freezes past the scan window and fills the frozen block, on all 16 such models but at the price of destroying the backdoor in 4 of 8; and one that adds the statistic itself to the poisoning loss, which costs nothing at all (Sec. VII). 3. A design principle for site selection, obtained by breaking our own rules. Every selection rule we built that reads the suspect’s weight magnitudes was defeated by a cheap attack: an exact-zero test by camouflage, a cross-model norm threshold three separate ways, and a within-model threshold on the trend of its own cost curve. The rule left standing reads the suspect only where the statistic is undefined, and Sec. VIII shows it is not safe either. 4. Scale-normalised detection. Rescaling each model’s delta to the clean median norm before differencing removes the false positives that a recipe mismatch otherwise produces, at no cost in sensitivity: 0 of 6 clean models flagged against 2 of 6 for the unnormalised statistic, with every backdoor still detected (Sec. X). 5. Two measurement results the statistic depends on. Per-token standardisation against a clean–clean null, and probing each layer in the basis of that layer’s own input rather than the embedding, are each the difference between recovering a trigger and missing it (Sec. IX).

papers.title: Lower bounds for the Kolmogorov widths of global attractors of dissipative systems
papers.abstract: We introduce the notion of a strengthening set in a Hilbert space and prove an exponential lower bound for its Kolmogorov widths. For compact sets containing the origin, the strengthening property is equivalent to the existence of such a bound. As an application, we obtain an exact formula for the widths of the global attractor of a diagonal dissipative system.
papers.intro:
The notion of Kolmogorov width was introduced by A. N. Kolmogorov [1]. Width theory in function spaces is surveyed by V. M. Tikhomirov [2], and a general treatment is given in [3]. The Kolmogorov width of order nn of a set MM in a normed space XX is the quantity dn​(M,X)=infL⊂Xsupx∈Minfy∈L‖x−y‖X,d_{n}(M,X)=\inf_{L\subset X}\sup_{x\in M}\inf_{y\in L}\|x-y\|_{X}, where the infimum is taken over all linear subspaces LL of XX with dimension at most nn. The width gives the best uniform error of approximation of MM by such subspaces. For a totally bounded set MM, its ε\varepsilon-entropy with respect to XX is the base-two logarithm of the smallest number of closed balls of radius ε\varepsilon in XX covering MM [4].

papers.title: An $(\infty,1)$-category of conically smooth stratified bordisms
papers.abstract:
To study derived defect topological quantum field theories, we construct an $(\infty,1)$-category of stratified bordisms and sketch its $(\infty,d)$-dimensional analogue.
  In the first chapters we develop a method for constructing symmetric monoidal $(\infty,1)$-categories, inspired by Segal spaces but better suited to geometric inputs, which we call interval Segal spaces. Using this framework, we construct the $(\infty,1)$-category of $d$-dimensional smooth manifolds via smooth $\infty$-sheaves thereof, in an attempt to address fibrancy issues present in prior work on this subject. We further equip this category with a symmetric monoidal structure, compute its homotopy 1-category, and extend the construction to manifolds endowed with tangential structures, obtaining the interval Segal space of $d$-dimensional bordisms with tangential structure.
  To model the stratifications supporting topological defects, we work with conically smooth stratified spaces, a suitably smooth framework for conical stratifications.
  We define stratified topological manifolds as stratified $\mathcal{B}$-manifolds for a suitable $(\infty,1)$-category of basics $\mathcal{B}$. Using these, we construct an interval Segal space whose objects are compact closed stratified topological $(d-1)$-manifolds and whose 1-morphisms are stratified $d$-dimensional bordisms, and we endow it with a symmetric monoidal structure. We also use tangential structures on conically smooth stratified spaces to formulate a notion of defect labels, aiming toward bordisms with labeled defects in the style of Carqueville et al.
  Finally, we sketch a higher-dimensional generalization of the interval category to a category of $d$-cubes for $d>1$, conjecturally presenting $(\infty,d)$-categories, and outline how stratified factorization homology may be used to produce derived stratified defect TQFTs.

papers.title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
papers.abstract: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $\Delta h$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|\Delta h\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

papers.title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.

Software agents built on large language models have moved from suggesting code to acting on it. A coding agent today may read a repository, run tests, push a branch, open a pull request, comment on an issue tracker through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, publish a package, or provision cloud resources. Each of these actions requires authenticating to a service that was designed for human users or for traditional workloads.

In practice, agents inherit whatever credentials sit in the developer’s environment: an SSH key, a GitHub personal access token, a cloud CLI profile, an npm token in a configuration file. These are bearer secrets. Whoever holds them can use them, from any machine, for anything they permit. Three properties of agents make this arrangement worse than it is for human developers. papers.title: Func-JEPA: Learning a Sobolev Space of Functions as Latent Vectors
papers.abstract: Pretraining an encoder once and reusing it across tasks is a widespread approach in vision and language. However, neural symbolic mathematics still trains a dedicated sequence-to-sequence model for each task, so that no representation of a function is shared. In this work, we propose the Function Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Func-JEPA, abbreviated f-JEPA): an encoder of mathematical functions, pretrained on their symbolic form, whose latent space imitates the Sobolev space H^1 and in which differentiation is a learned latent operator. The norm of a latent is computed exactly from the function, whereas its direction is learned to match Sobolev angles. The frozen encoder is then reused by lightweight modules for decoding, composition, integration, and regression from samples. The representation and four downstream tasks are evaluated within and outside the pretraining distribution. f-JEPA recovers exact formulas from noisy samples more often than the compared symbolic-regression methods, whereas computer algebra and task-specific models remain stronger on standard integration and differential-equation benchmarks.
papers.intro:
Nowadays, encoders pretrained once on large corpora and reused for many downstream tasks are the standard approach in language and vision [18, 2]. Neural symbolic mathematics has not followed this path: integration, the solution of ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and symbolic regression are posed as translation problems, each solved by a dedicated sequence-to-sequence transformer trained on its own synthetic corpus [28, 12, 7, 23, 16]. Whilst these models achieve remarkable accuracy, the representation of a function learned for one task is not reused by the others.

A reusable encoder of functions should reflect what a function is in analysis: an element of a vector space with an inner product, on which differentiation, integration, and composition act as operators. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) [29, 2, 6, 13] are well-suited to this purpose, since they predict the representation of a target from that of a context: the context is a function ff, the target is its derivative f′f^{\prime}, and the predictor is the derivative operator. However, a predictive loss alone is minimised by collapsed representations, which current methods avoid with architectural asymmetries [20, 2] or with regularisers on the distribution of the embeddings [5, 4]. For functions, a stronger anchor is available: the inner product of two functions can be computed exactly from their values, so the target geometry of the latent space is defined by the data, a property that existing embeddings of mathematical expressions do not exploit [1, 34].
