papers.title: A New Record for the Katz-Tao Sum-Difference Exponent
papers.abstract: We prove the record bound $C_{3b}\le 209357544569848128/114631769327023765=1.8263483657186\ldots$ for the Katz-Tao sum-difference exponent, valid in every abelian group without $2$-torsion. Using only Shannon inequalities, conditional copies and Katz-Tao's original directions, whose classical single-grid argument gives $11/6$, we break $11/6$, obtaining $2762/1509$ and $152/83$. For every abelian group we prove the universal bound $C_{\mathrm{all}}=10304335425987192362/5641833174538280329=1.8264161855212\ldots$, which is below the previous record for the real Katz-Tao constant. In the AlphaEvolve study (arXiv:2511.02864v3), the search for extremal distributions improved this constant's lower bound in the eighth decimal place and left its upper bound at $11/6$. Our upper bounds are proofs discovered by CASPAC, the computational mathematics engine of the CASP research system, and certified by independent exact checkers. The proofs use stacked entropy certificates; we supply the complete rational identities, proofs of every auxiliary inequality, and exact verification over the stated group classes.

papers.title: Before the Word: Name Information in Description-Derived States of Small Language Models, With and Without Naming Failure
papers.abstract: The tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state, knowing an object but not its name, motivates this study as an analogy only. We ask whether small language models form a name-predictive state from a name-free description, and whether it differs when naming fails but description selection succeeds. In an internally pre-registered study (a frozen document, no external registry) of Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-3-mini with 200 items, we combine a similarity read-out, a Patchscopes-style read-out and activation patching with matched controls. H1 (name information in the state) was supported in all nine model-by-description-type combinations; the agreement rule was met by the similarity measure together with patching, while Patchscopes stayed near chance. Post-hoc robustness checks after internal review (logit lens, single-position patch, manipulation check) temper this reading: name information in middle layers is clearest under the multi-position patch and the similarity measure, and weak under single-position patching at 50% depth. H2' (description-paraphrase consistency of name-free states not lower in failure items) is mixed: the SmolLM2 deficit test is significant under the pre-registered specification but not robust; Phi-3 non-inferiority holds across margins and a word-overlap covariate, although its bootstrap interval includes zero; Qwen2-0.5B is inconclusive. A capacity explanation remains untested. We report vehicle-level signals only, not meaning.
papers.intro:
A speaker can know exactly what an object is for and still fail to produce its name. In the classic tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) paradigm, participants are given a definition and asked for the word; in a subset of trials the word is not retrieved although the participant feels it is known and can often report partial properties of it (Brown and McNeill, 1966; Brown, 1991). In staged theories of lexical access, this pattern is explained by a separation between preparing a concept, selecting a lexical entry, and encoding its form (Levelt et al., 1999). The motivation for the present study was a similar experience of the author: knowing what a technical object does without knowing a word for it. We use the human phenomenon only as motivation and as a declared analogy; we make no claim that the models share the experience or the underlying mechanism, and our measures do not operationalise the TOT state.

The question is the following. When a language model reads a functional description of an object, does it form an internal state that (i) is related to the object’s name beyond what surface form and domain would predict, (ii) contributes causally to producing that name, and (iii) differs when the model fails to produce the name? We deliberately speak of name information and of a vehicle-level signal above control: we measure an activation state and compare it with matched controls. Following the vehicle/content distinction of an earlier study of activation states by the author (Cárdenas Piepereit, 2026), we report vehicle-level signals only and make no claim about meaning, content, or knowledge.

Related work probes parts of this question but, to our knowledge, not the combination. Reverse-dictionary prompts, which map a description to a word, have been used to analyse conceptual information in language models (Xu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). Names of entities can be read from intermediate states when the name itself is the input (Morand et al., 2025). Intermediate entities that are never written out can be resolved internally (Yang et al., 2024b; Biran et al., 2024), and a model may hold more factual information internally than it produces (Gekhman et al., 2025). To our knowledge, none of these works compares a description-derived state with the name’s own state layer by layer, tests it causally in a naming context, and splits items by whether naming succeeds (Section 2).

papers.title: Spectral coincidence and generalized Hua inversion in rings and Banach algebras
papers.abstract: For additively coupled elements with invertible sum and selected commuting outer inverses, we study coincidence of the core idempotents and inversion of the Hua element. Intertwining forces coincidence for finite-Drazin data in unital rings and for generalized-Drazin data in complex unital Banach algebras. Under coincidence, the output splits into an invertible core and a complementary parallel sum, called the residue, yielding exact criteria for inverse existence and success of the prescribed candidate. Explicit ring examples show that strict generalized-Drazin input inverses need not force coincidence under intertwining, and that a common core with a Harte-quasinilpotent residue need not give a strict output inverse. For rings finite as modules over a commutative central subring with the same identity, we prove intertwining transfer and automatic bicommutation for commuting outer inverses with Harte-quasinilpotent remainders, without Noetherianity. This gives input-core coincidence under intertwining. If the central subring is Noetherian, every Harte-quasinilpotent element also has separated left and right powers. For common-core data in the finite-central class, the candidate is a strict output inverse exactly when the residual parallel sum is Harte-quasinilpotent. In the Banach setting, uniform input spectral gaps characterize continuity of the core and candidate along convergent input pairs, with intertwining and quasinilpotent input remainders at every term and at the limit. The output gap is equivalent when the residues of the sequence and limit are also quasinilpotent. Exact defect identities give local estimates on augmented inverse data. At an exactly intertwined base with invertible coefficient operators, we determine the feasible first-order defect space and its sharp norm constant, with a norm-specific matrix calibration.
papers.intro:
Hua’s identity has the algebraic form a−a​b​a=a​(a+c)−1​c=(a−1+c−1)−1,a+c=b−1,a-aba=a(a+c)^{-1}c=(a^{-1}+c^{-1})^{-1},\qquad a+c=b^{-1}, when the displayed inverses exist. Replacing the input inverses by generalized inverses presents two different difficulties. The inputs may carry incompatible core idempotents. Even if these idempotents coincide, the complementary part of the output need not satisfy the condition required for the proposed inverse. In the present paper, we treat these two issues separately. papers.title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.
papers.intro:
Red teaming probes how generative AI systems fail in use. Lessons from red teaming more than 100 products emphasize human judgment as an essential part of this work [2]. PyRIT is used for recurring tasks [3], and the “break-fix” cycle connects red teaming to safety post-training [4]. Training a model to generate attacks extends beyond hand-written test cases [5, 6], and reinforcement learning lets that model adapt to the defender it faces.

Bullwinkel et al. AdvGRPO study [1] reports diversity reduction during attacker–defender co-training with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) [7]. This experiment aims to reproduce the attack diversity reduction with specific models, stabilized updates and pre-specified diversity reduction criterion. An attacker that repeatedly applies similar attacks gives the defender a narrower range of failures to learn from and successfully defend. In order to make AI models that defend against diverse attack vectors, attack diversity needs to be maintained throughout a red teaming exercise. In this experiment the attack narrowing phenomonena is tracked with open-weight models and public benchmarks.

Uniform-reward groups have zero advantage, leaving a sparse set of rows to drive an update [9]. The design of the experiment addresses these artifacts with four stabilization techniques and a pre-specified rule for stopping a degenerate run.

papers.title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
papers.abstract:
Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16).
  A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

A popular explanation: human writing passes through a subvocal/inner-speech layer, so human text naturally carries prosody; LLMs trained purely on text lack this layer, producing AI flavor. Injecting speech, phoneme, or prosody signals into training should help. This paper tests the hypothesis with controlled interventions—the answer is no at the 0.6B text-only scale, across three routes (§4). The negative results are not empty: they move the question from “should we add speech signals” to “can evaluation perceive the difference,” which motivates the methodological core of this paper.

Evaluating AI-flavor interventions faces a dilemma: automatic features can detach from perception, and human blind evaluation is power-limited (§3) and fatiguing. We propose a three-layer framework, RA-Eval: an objective feature library, a human blind-eval protocol, and a calibrated LLM-judge pipeline—the judge must prove its sensitivity on known-answer calibration sets before annotating, under a fixed protocol (pairwise blind judgment, A/B swap double-pass, two independent judges, disagreement counted as a tie). The same framework uses judges both as evaluators and as preference annotators, making the evaluation signal and the training signal commensurate.

papers.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
papers.abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.
papers.intro:
Agent decisions can remain in memory after the facts supporting them change. A supplier selected under an earlier delivery estimate may become ineligible; downstream spend, approval, and reminder decisions can then become stale. Revising a fact alone is insufficient, while recomputing every output may incur unnecessary work. Explicit dependencies offer a way to select candidate decisions for review, but their usefulness depends on the completeness of the extracted support structure and the evidence available during repair.

Revising a fact alone is insufficient, while recomputing every output may incur unnecessary work. We investigate this trade-off with a prototype context graph and a controlled executable workflow benchmark. The central question is not whether reverse reachability identifies graph descendants, but whether a graph extracted from an agent’s actual observations supplies enough information to maintain a correct plan across successive updates. An initially sufficient read trace need not describe every alternative that can become relevant later. This creates a mismatch between initial planning and future repair.

Our contribution is an empirical evaluation rather than a claim that dependency tracking or cascading invalidation is new. We provide: (i) sequential workflows with executable reference decisions, (ii) comparisons that include initial planning, memory construction, maintenance, and repair cost, (iii) paired dependency and context ablations, and (iv) fresh-workflow evaluation of a simple observable-directory enhancement. We report failures and limitations alongside successes. The results do not support an unconditional replacement of full-context recomputation with extracted graph repair.

papers.title: CHERI under Fault Injection: An Emulation-Based Security Evaluation of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions
papers.abstract:
Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to dominate real-world exploit chains despite decades of research into software mitigations. CHERI is a hardware architecture that enforces spatial and temporal memory safety by augmenting pointers with hardware-checked metadata, thus preventing software-based exploitation, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection. This thesis investigates whether targeted fault injection can undermine CHERI's memory-safety guarantees in a pure-capability CHERI-RISC-V environment. Two fault classes are considered: bit flips corrupting capability metadata, and fault-induced check skipping on capability store instructions.
  We implement fault injection primitives in a QEMU-based emulation environment, which enables deterministic, repeatable experiments without specialised hardware. With them, we demonstrate four attack scenarios: buffer overflows, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, and use-after-free. Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). Check skipping offers an alternative route to control-flow hijacking and data-only attacks, with a minimum of one fault.
  These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.

papers.title: Count Constraints and Conditional Benchmarks for Roster-Based Network Reconstruction
papers.abstract: When everyone reports contact counts for known groups, roster-based aggregated relational data (ARD) can determine individual links. In our sparse circular design with 40 nodes and eight groups, the complete counts fix 35.6% of realized edges on average. Zero counts alone exclude 91.1% of nonedges on average, and the full set of counts raises that share to 91.7%. We assess ranking on the unresolved pairs by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Uniform weighting of compatible graphs yields higher mean AUC than the direct scores from either a circular latent-position fit or a nuclear-norm fit. In a follow-up analysis, using the same fitted probabilities to weight compatible graphs reverses the comparison for the circular fit. With the generating circular form and interaction strength supplied, its mean AUC exceeds uniform by 0.016-0.019 across three paired density settings. The gain is 0.007 under a stochastic blockmodel, where the circular form is misspecified. Nuclear-norm plug-in scores remain below uniform in mean AUC. For independent Bernoulli edges with fixed probabilities strictly between zero and one, we characterize when an oracle using the true probabilities gives the same edge marginals as uniform weighting for every feasible count array. This occurs exactly when the conditional graph law is uniform on every such array, or equivalently when log odds are additive in node-by-group effects. We recommend reporting fixed edge states, ranking on unresolved pairs, and generating-probability error separately.

Complete roster-based aggregated relational data (ARD) can reveal who is connected to whom. Each respondent reports how many contacts they have in each known group. A zero count rules out every link from that respondent to that group. Even when all counts are positive, the reports together can force particular links to be present or absent (Figure 1). We call the pairs for which either state is still possible the unresolved set 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Ranking these pairs measures what a score adds beyond the states the counts already fix.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Agent Harness: Decisions, Invariants and Corner Cases
papers.abstract: An agent harness is the program around a language model that turns its replies into actions: it builds each request, runs the tools the model asks for, decides what the model may do without asking, stores the conversation, recovers from failures, and shows a person what happened. Most of these decisions are made in code and rarely written down, so each harness meets the same corner cases again. This paper writes them down as invariants to test. It gives a system model with trust boundaries; 30 decision cards in six groups, each with options and costs, an invariant, the corner cases that break it, a test and an evidence tag; six cause classes for failures; a test method built on scripted providers, recorded behaviour and planted changes; and a checklist. The cards come from building one desktop harness, Crewroom, the author's own, and from manually testing ten other harnesses and studying open-source harnesses as reference; some patterns in the cards were adopted from those, so the catalogue is not independent of them. Of the 83 invariant clauses, 56 are tagged Tested, 12 Believed and 15 Open. The checklist is applied to the author's harness as one worked example, by its builder with no second rater: of its 30 items, 11 hold, 14 do not and 5 were not tested. It is not a ranking. The paper makes no claims about answer quality or cost or other platforms, and does not evaluate or rank other harnesses.

papers.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
papers.abstract: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

papers.intro:
Neural networks trained on a sequence of tasks lose performance on earlier ones, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). It matters most for models that keep learning after deployment, such as a crop-disease classifier that is taught a new disease or a clinical model updated with data from a new region. In those settings the old data is often no longer available, for reasons of privacy, data agreements or storage, so the damage cannot simply be measured by re-testing.

It matters most for models that keep learning after deployment, such as a crop-disease classifier that is taught a new disease or a clinical model updated with data from a new region. In those settings the old data is often no longer available, for reasons of privacy, data agreements or storage, so the damage cannot simply be measured by re-testing.

Forgetting comes in two practical forms. In some settings it is fast: accuracy on the old task collapses within a few update steps, and any monitor that looks at the old task catches it. In others it is slow: each update removes a little, the loss is easy to miss, and it accumulates. The slow case is where an early, data-free warning would be most useful, and it is where existing signals are weakest.

This paper studies one candidate signal. Gradient descent on two losses does not commute: training on AA then BB and training on BB then AA end at different weights. For small steps the difference is governed by the Lie bracket of the two gradient fields. I test it, and I ask a practical question the conjecture does not address: can the bracket be estimated without the old task’s data, and is it then a better predictor of forgetting than the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), the standard data-free method?

papers.title: Relative involutions and inverses in monoidal dualities and slice constructions
papers.abstract: Our goal in this paper is to work towards developing a framework for characterizing dualities of weak categorical structures. It is often the case that duality involutions are characterized by relations which are more general than $f^2=1$. Moreover, it is also true that many dualities cannot be expressed using involutions alone. We develop a framework of relative involutions and relative inverses to express these dualities at least within categorical and bicategorical structures. In particular, we utilize this framework to express the dualities of virtual double categories and some important constructions on them. In the second part, we explore the problem of slicing and consider how dualities of monoidal structures interact with slice constructions. We end by providing a construction for both enriched slice model categories and enriched coslice model categories.
papers.intro:
Our primary motivation to write this paper comes from two questions, which are broadly related under the microcosm principle. The first one concerns the dualities of categorical structures. Consider the op1\mathrm{op}_{1} duality on 𝟏​𝐂​𝐚​𝐭\mathbf{1\mathbf{Cat}}, expressed as a 22-functor op1:op2​(𝟏​𝐂​𝐚​𝐭)→𝟏​𝐂​𝐚​𝐭\mathrm{op}_{1}\colon\mathrm{op}_{2}(\mathbf{1\mathbf{Cat}})\rightarrow\mathbf{1\mathbf{Cat}}, which satisfy the relation op1∘op2​(op1)=1\mathrm{op}_{1}\circ\mathrm{op}_{2}(\mathrm{op}_{1})=1. Clearly, this is not an involution in the traditional sense of satisfying op1∘op1=1\mathrm{op}_{1}\circ\mathrm{op}_{1}=1, since this composition is simply not defined. Rather, it is an involution relative to a higher involution op2\mathrm{op}_{2}. This motivates the definition of a relative involution.

papers.title: EWMA Principal Eigenportfolios of Equity Returns: Market Representation and Beta-Hedging Performance
papers.abstract: This study examines whether an adaptively estimated principal eigenportfolio improves equity beta hedging relative to capitalisation-weighted and equal-weighted market benchmarks. Using stock returns from a historically changing S&P 500 universe, it constructs a portfolio from the leading principal component of an exponentially weighted second-moment matrix of volatility-standardised returns. The resulting portfolio, EWMA-PC1, is compared with SPY and RSP under a common beta-hedging procedure across randomly generated portfolios of varying sizes and weighting schemes. Evaluation considers variance reduction and average pairwise residual correlation, with paired blockbootstrap inference. EWMA-PC1 exhibits broad market participation and achieves greater mean variance reduction and lower average residual correlation than SPY across all tested configurations. Its incremental advantage over RSP is smaller and mixed. For 50-stock Dirichlet portfolios, mean variance reduction is 92.17% under PC1, compared with 79.03% under SPY and 91.93% under RSP; RSP instead achieves greater mean variance reduction for multistock liquidity-tilted portfolios. Statistical evidence of improvement is more consistent against SPY than against RSP. These findings distinguish the extraction of a market-like component from incremental hedge effectiveness and highlight the importance of benchmark weighting and targetportfolio composition. The results concern gross statistical risk reduction and exclude additional trading, financing, and borrowing costs.
papers.intro:
Stock returns reflect both company-specific developments and influences shared across the market. This shared variation, or market comovement, means that holding more stocks can reduce idiosyncratic risk while leaving substantial exposure to broad market fluctuations. Investors seeking to retain selected stock positions while reducing this exposure therefore need an instrument whose returns capture the movement they wish to hedge. Broad equity index funds provide natural candidates, but their weighting rules determine which exposures they represent. Capitalisation weighting gives larger companies greater influence, whereas equal weighting distributes allocations evenly across constituents. Neither rule explicitly selects weights from the dependence observed among stock returns. This motivates a data-driven alternative: estimate a common return direction from those relationships, construct a corresponding portfolio, and test whether it provides a more effective market hedge.

Principal component analysis (PCA) offers an established foundation for this approach. Research on equity correlation matrices associates the leading component with broad market movement [12], while eigenportfolio research translates statistical components into portfolio allocations and examines their interpretation as market proxies [2]. PCA-derived factors have also been compared with ETF-based factors in statistical-arbitrage strategies [3]. Exponential weighting provides a way to update the estimated return relationships as new observations arrive [8]. These foundations motivate an adaptive principal eigenportfolio, but its market resemblance does not by itself establish its usefulness as a hedge. Nor does the performance of a residual-based trading strategy directly establish how much risk a single market instrument removes. The question addressed here is whether an adaptively estimated principal eigenportfolio offers incremental beta-hedging effectiveness over both capitalisation-weighted and equal-weighted benchmarks, and how that comparison varies with the portfolio being hedged.

papers.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
papers.abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.
papers.intro:
A retail forecast is used for more than its number. When a merchant plans a promotion, the question is not only how much will sell but how much of it the promotion will add, and whether a deeper price cut would add more. Forecasting models that see the plan can answer that directly: they forecast the item with the plan as made, and again with nothing planned, and the difference is the lift the plan adds. The world model and the lift model of our companion paper [35] are built this way: each forecast is a baseline under the nothing-planned plan plus a lift, and the lift is exactly zero when nothing is planned. The split is what a merchant reads ("the promotion added 40 units"), plans on, and is judged by.

The explanation literature separates two properties [1, 37]: an explanation is faithful if it reflects what the model does, and correct if it reflects what happens in the world. Retail has a property chemistry lacks. papers.title: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization
papers.abstract: We transpose the Surprise-Gated Memory recipe, a frozen encoder plus a calibrated novelty signal that gates a one-shot episodic store consolidated by periodic replay, from continual visual learning to live speaker diarization. The moment-to-moment question a streaming diarizer must answer, whether an arriving voice belongs to an already-heard speaker or a new one, is a known-versus-novel decision, exactly the decision the surprise gate is built for. On a frozen fine-tuned DiariZen backbone, our online system SGM-Diar recovers 4.8 of the 9.2 diarization-error points separating a naive online baseline from the offline oracle on AMI-SDM (52%) and 1.9 of 2.3 points on VoxConverse (82%), in the end-of-meeting revisable mode, with calibration frozen on development data and transferred cross-domain without adjustment. These are single-seed runs on three AMI meetings and five VoxConverse sessions, so the ordering of conditions rather than the absolute rates is the result. Beyond error rate, we measure the gate's behaviour directly and find a coherent memory-like profile: one-shot speaker recall at 0.857, a novelty response that habituates as speakers become familiar, re-identification that is invariant to the length of intervening silence, and a false-novelty rate of 0.001. Two ablations reproduce, now on audio, the central prediction of the visual SGM work: a sliding replay window is worse than no replay at all. The memory is strictly intra-meeting and is wiped at the end, and no gradient touches the run-time system. We report SGM-Diar as a proof-of-concept and state its limitations explicitly.

papers.title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.
papers.intro:
AI tools are increasingly used within organizations and are involved in high-stakes decisions such as investment decisions, recruiting or even employee evaluation. From an ethical perspective, this calls for regulatory evidence that the decisions supported or made by such tools are robust to potential biases inherent in the underlying Large Language Models. While one could assume that this regulatory requirement of bias testing is still a rather hypothetical one, first examples from practice exist: Since July 2023, New York City’s Local Law 144 has required employers to commission an independent bias audit of AI tools they use as part of their hiring process (nycdcwp2023), and the EU AI Act requires conformity assessment and post-market monitoring for high-risk AI systems (aiact2024). Such regulatory requirements of AI-based recruiting systems provide snapshots in time of the tested system, and in New York City the test result serves as regulatory evidence for up to a year. This comes with the implicit assumption that such systems behave rather stably over the duration of a year and as such the snapshot provides a reliable representation of the system’s behavior. In this paper, we aim to understand whether this assumption holds for language models that organizations buy from providers and draw implications for AI governance.

In this context, we built an AI-based venture capital investment system: a language model receives a startup pitch and a founder profile and then decides whether to invest and how much. We audited the language models of five providers at three points in time: in September 2025 (t0), in September 2026 (t1) and five weeks later in October 2026 (t2), 248,400 API calls in total. At each point, each model had to decide whether and how much to invest in a startup pitch that was held fixed within each study, while the founder differed only by name and university. Study 1 compares t0 and t1 for the one model that was still served under its 2025 identifier. Study 2 compares the four t0 models with the successors their providers offered at t1. Study 3 then asks whether such disparities depend on the business being pitched by varying the industry sector while keeping the rest of the pitch constant.

Nevertheless, providers change, replace or retire the underlying Large Language Models under their own terms. Out of the four models audited in September 2025 for this paper, two were retired, one was withdrawn from the access path used for auditing and the fourth, still called by its name, did not act as recorded one year later. This results in a regulatory challenge: The regulated systems become a moving target while audit carries no or delayed expiry. Managing AI has accordingly been described as managing ever-changing technology, a task that “can never be finished” (berente2021, p. 1437).

In this context, ligoel2025 demonstrate what makes an AI system auditable and argue for AI audit becoming a professional accounting task.

This leads to three research questions: RQ1: Does a fairness audit of a provider-served language model still describe the model one year later? RQ2: Which provider practices govern when a served model changes, and do they give advance notice of it? RQ3: What does this mean for the fairness audit as an instrument of regulation? In this context, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring in Section 2.4. RQ1 is answered by studies 1 to 3 in form of an empirical analysis. The document analysis in Section 7 answers RQ2 and shows which provider practices lie behind the model changes we observed. Finally, in Section 8 we answer RQ3 by discussing what misanchored evidence means for regulators and deployers and by deriving instruments for them.

In short, an audit result is a dated claim about a provider-controlled object. In this context, we are not able to make reliable claims about the duration of validity of an audit result. Furthermore, we know that there are two mechanisms with the potential to erode an audit result sampled at a specific point in time. One mechanism is version drift meaning that the provider changes how a model is served while the ID still denotes the same model. The other mechanism is product drift referring to a change in what the ID denotes, such as the replacement or retirement of a model for a newer version. Until the impact of these mechanisms on what was measured by an audit is understood, the corresponding results cannot be treated as evidence with a duration of validity beyond the day of collection.

papers.title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
papers.abstract: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

Agents that act for a user are being tried on tasks where the rules are written down and the consequences are real: a UPI payment that was debited but not credited, a GST invoice that must be computed exactly, a KYC form, a trip plan under rail quota and waitlist rules, a refund request written in Hinglish. These tasks have checkable answers. They also differ from the usual English-language tool-use tests in the details: Indian number formats, PAN and IFSC patterns, place-of-supply rules, code-mixed text.

We built Navital Gym to measure whether an agent gets such tasks right, with results that anyone can reproduce. Three design choices shape it. 1. Written rules, no judge model. A task is solved only if every applicable named rule passes. Each grader recomputes the result from the sandbox world and does not read what the agent claims about its own cost, score or success. Garbage input scores 0 and the grader does not crash. 2. Honest refusals. Many tasks have no valid answer. The agent must say so and give the right reason. A refusal with a wrong reason is marked wrong. 3. Hidden fields stay hidden. The agent sees the prompt, the tools and the policy text. Expected answers, feasibility labels and designer notes never reach it, and a test checks this for every task in every environment.

papers.title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
papers.abstract: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

papers.title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
papers.abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

papers.title: N\'eron Functions on Jacobians of Odd-Degree Hyperelliptic Curves
papers.abstract: We express N\'eron functions on Jacobians of odd-degree hyperelliptic curves of arbitrary genus in terms of admissible pairings, using the pullback of the theta divisor via a generalized Abel--Jacobi morphism. Over non-archimedean local fields, we relate N\'eron functions to local N\'eron pairings on the curve and, moreover, deduce a comparison between unramified $p$-adic N\'eron functions and unramified local Coleman--Gross height functions. Furthermore, we decompose the N\'eron function into an intersection term $I$ and a Green function term $T$, and compute $T$ for specific semistable reduction types. We compare our decomposition with other decompositions in the literature.

Néron [31] and Tate constructed the canonical height function on an abelian variety AA over a number field FF associated to a symmetric line bundle LL. It can be expressed as a sum of local components, called Néron functions, defined over the completions of FF. Algorithms for computing canonical heights have numerous applications, for instance, in computing generators of A⁡(F)A(F) and the regulator of A/FA/F, which appears in the Birch–Swinnerton–Dyer conjecture.

However, the dimension of the embedding projective space is 2g−12^{g}-1, which makes such explicit embeddings difficult to control as gg increases.

papers.title: Generalized Limits of Finitely Additive Measures on Locally Compact Groups
papers.abstract: Let $\mathscr{E}=\{E_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I}$ be an increasing family of Borel subsets of a locally compact topological group $G$, indexed by a linearly ordered set $I$ with no greatest element. We call a nonnegative finitely additive $\sigma$-finite measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $G$ admissible if it takes finite values on the sets in $\mathscr{E}$ and these values are not bounded above. Every admissible measure $\mu$ can be normalized to have total mass one by applying a generalized limit pointwise to the net of measures $\left\{B\mapsto\frac{\mu(B\cap E_\alpha)}{\mu(E_\alpha)}\right\}_{\alpha\in I}$, defined for all sufficiently large $\alpha$. We study invariant finitely additive measures obtained by normalizing admissible measures. We show that every invariant measure constructed in this way can be obtained by normalizing a measure of a special form. An example is given showing that not every measure of the type under consideration can be obtained by normalizing a countably additive measure. We obtain a generalization of the Yosida-Hewitt decomposition to finitely additive $\sigma$-finite measures.

papers.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
papers.abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.
papers.intro:
The uneven distribution of healthcare resources continues to limit access to high-quality care [1]. Developments in medical AI and generalist foundation models [2, 3] offer new ways to support personal health management [4], clinical practice [5], and the organization of care [6]. Evaluating these applications requires benchmarks that reflect diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings [7]. Existing benchmarks span examination questions in MedQA and MedMCQA [8, 9, 10], open-ended health conversations in HealthBench [11], and simulated healthcare workflows in MedAgentBench and CHI-Bench [12, 13]. HELM and MedHELM support comparisons across tasks and datasets [14, 15], while the Artificial Analysis Healthcare & Medical Index aggregates selected benchmark results into an overall score [16]. However, the meaning of an overall score depends on what the included benchmarks assess and whose needs they represent [17]. For inclusive healthcare, this raises the question of how benchmarks can be selected and organized so that an index reflects diverse needs and supports comparisons relevant to different uses of medical AI [18].

We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks along two axes: healthcare role and AI capability. The role axis identifies whose needs or work a task represents, distinguishing patients and the public, healthcare professionals, and healthcare administration professionals. The capability axis identifies the principal AI capability assessed, distinguishing knowledge, reasoning, and agency. We map each benchmark or healthcare-relevant subset to an Atlas cell based on the predominant role–capability combination among its tasks. Benchmark inclusion is guided by six audit criteria: healthcare relevance, trustworthiness, availability and permitted use, complementary coverage, timeliness and data independence, and discriminative capacity (Figure 2b). The Atlas design makes clear which healthcare needs are represented by the included benchmarks and where coverage remains limited.

For the first release, we collected 388 candidate benchmarks from the published literature, public platforms and repositories, and community contributions. With large language model (LLM) assistance, we compiled benchmark cards linked to their source materials (Figure 2a). Applying the audit criteria yielded a shortlist of eight candidates. Independent reproduction revealed score saturation in three medical knowledge benchmarks and limited discrimination among models on HealthBench. We therefore retained four public benchmarks or subsets: HealthBench Professional [19], PhysicianBench [20], the Health and Medicine subset of ALE-CLI v1.0 [21]11 1 Hereafter referred to as ALE-CLI v1.0: Health and Medicine., and CHI-Bench [13]. We also included InclusionMed-DxFiles, a private benchmark we developed to assess diagnostic reasoning. These five benchmarks cover three of the nine Atlas cells, reflecting gaps in suitable public benchmarks for evaluating AI across diverse healthcare roles and needs.

We evaluated 22 models on the benchmarks included in the current Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, giving each benchmark equal weight. Overall Index scores ranged from 17.5 to 49.1 on a 0–100 scale. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, revealing differences in both model rankings and score levels. For example, role-specific Index scores were consistently lower for healthcare administration professionals than for healthcare professionals, while GPT-6 Luna ranked eighth in reasoning but twentieth in agency. For finer-grained analysis, we used task-level tags to compare the ten highest-ranked models in the Index within individual benchmarks across three attributes: clinical specialty, medical expertise, and healthcare workflow. On HealthBench Professional, all ten models scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. On both HealthBench Professional and PhysicianBench, treatment planning and implementation had lower median scores than clinical assessment and diagnosis. Estimated inference costs also varied widely among models with similar Index scores, with an approximately 24-fold difference in mean cost per task run in one comparison. These findings highlight the importance of context-specific model selection that considers performance on relevant healthcare tasks alongside the associated inference cost.

InclusionMed welcomes contributions that help medical AI evaluation reflect diverse healthcare needs. Contributors can share benchmarks, datasets, or tools; propose benchmark ideas; submit evidence-based corrections; and offer expert guidance or partnerships. These contributions can broaden benchmark coverage and make model comparisons more relevant to healthcare practice. Through successive releases of the Atlas and Index, this open collaboration aims to ensure that the diverse healthcare needs of people worldwide guide how progress in medical AI is defined and measured.

papers.title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity
papers.abstract: A network in which every bank pays in full can nevertheless admit a self-fulfilling settlement freeze under the same balance-sheet fundamentals. Thus, observing full repayment does not establish the uniqueness or robustness of the payment equilibrium. We derive this result from a precautionary-liquidity choice: banks may delay otherwise feasible payments to insure an interim funding need, trading a positive settlement-discipline cost against the marginal value of retained cash. The optimal reserve is a critical quantile of future liquidity requirements, and the repayment rule nests Eisenberg-Noe maximal feasible clearing exactly. Counterparty underpayment both reduces current cash and raises desired reserves. We characterise network amplification and the conditions for coexistence, including a homogeneous two-bank GPD frontier in which interbank exposure and maximum funding pass-through enter through one dimensionless index. A two-date settlement accounting rule distinguishes payment timing from ultimate default. The main result concerns equilibrium coexistence; the conditional best-response adjustment diagnostic does not assign selection probabilities.
papers.intro:
Full repayment does not imply a financially robust payment network. A system in which every institution currently honours its obligations may have the same observables as one in which a low-payment equilibrium also exists. Our question is when an institution that can pay its creditors rationally delays a portion of its obligations, and when that individual decision makes the network vulnerable to a self-fulfilling settlement freeze. The standard proportional-clearing rule of Eisenberg and Noe (2001) requires a bank to remit as much as contemporaneous resources permit. It is an economic benchmark for capacity, not a theory of why a bank with payable cash might temporarily withhold it.

The standard proportional-clearing rule of Eisenberg and Noe (2001) requires a bank to remit as much as contemporaneous resources permit. It is an economic benchmark for capacity, not a theory of why a bank with payable cash might temporarily withhold it.

We introduce an interval between the initial settlement window and the final contractual cut-off. A bank choosing early payment obtains a benefit from timely discharge of obligations, but forfeits liquidity insurance against an intervening funding requirement. The withheld contractual amount remains due: it is settled at the final cut-off where resources permit and otherwise defaults. The marginal liquidity benefit is a critical fractile of the funding-need distribution; proportional delay discipline preserves a positive incentive to pay at the full-payment boundary. This yields a continuous strategic repayment rule that nests maximal feasible clearing without a limiting approximation. Counterparty underpayment acts twice: it removes immediate resources and, through confidence-dependent funding needs, increases desired liquidity retention.

Our main implication is an observational-equivalence problem for settlement-based monitoring. Confidence sensitivity can make an all-zero settlement equilibrium available without changing the full-payment equilibrium. This occurs even when the mechanical network is uniquely clearing because it has outside creditors. We derive bank-level coexistence conditions, a necessary strongly connected feedback component, and a joint viability frontier in the shortage-to-discipline cost ratio and liquidity-risk shape. For the homogeneous two-bank GPD configuration, the viability frontier depends on interbank exposure and the pass-through bound through a dimensionless ratio. The frontier is the main quantitative illustration; a deliberately borderline two-bank calibration demonstrates one possible realisation. A terminal accounting completion distinguishes prompt settlement, delayed principal and eventual default.

The distinction from the literature is specific. Jackson and Pernoud (2024) already derive self-fulfilling insolvencies, multiplicity, dependency cycles, and optimal bailout policies in financial networks. We neither replicate their bailout analysis nor claim that multiplicity or spectral methods are new. Our contributions relative to that work are the funding-risk microfoundation for a continuous settlement wedge, the exact nesting of the Eisenberg–Noe rule when delay discipline is sufficiently strong, and the separation of an early-payment freeze from ultimate principal default under a specified terminal settlement rule. Bertschinger et al. (2020); Allouch et al. (2023) study strategic payments and default; Bech and Garratt (2003); Bech (2008) study payment-timing incentives. The critical-fractile reserve argument connects to Edgeworth (1888) and the precautionary-liquidity literature (Acharya and Skeie, 2011; Heider et al., 2015; Su, 2018; Denbee et al., 2021). Spectral interaction and crisis amplification are also studied by Ballester et al. (2006); Bramoullé et al. (2014); Gai et al. (2011); Brunnermeier and Reis (2023).

Payment-system evidence supports the economic ingredients. Using Fedwire balances and transactions, Ashcraft et al. (2011) document precautionary reserve holding and reluctance to lend during the 2007–08 turmoil. Armantier et al. (2008) document a shift and concentration of Fedwire payments later in the day, linked in part to liquidity-related operating incentives. These findings establish that liquidity management and payment timing respond to financial conditions; they do not directly estimate our counterparty-to-funding pass-through or prove that the particular strategic withholding mechanism studied here occurred. Section VI.D collects the modelling boundaries in one place. The paper proceeds from the financial environment to strategic repayment, network equilibria, terminal implications, and quantitative illustrations before concluding.

papers.title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.
